title: kube-proxy doesn't recover from outdated events

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
After running a 0.7.2 cluster in GCE over the weekend, service connections seemed flaky. 

The following lines are recurring in the kube-proxy log on all minions in my cluster. 

```
W0105 17:28:25.587865    5051 api.go:188] Got error status on WatchEndpoints channel: &{TypeMeta:{Kind: APIVersion:} ListMeta:{SelfLink:/api/v1beta1/endpoints ResourceVersion:} Status:Failure Message:401: The event in requested index is outdated and cleared (the requested history has been cleared [578/235]) [1577] Reason: Details:<nil> Code:0}

W0105 00:17:07.886554    5042 api.go:124] Got error status on WatchServices channel: &{TypeMeta:{Kind: APIVersion:} ListMeta:{SelfLink:/api/v1beta1/services ResourceVersion:} Status:Failure Message:401: The event in requested index is outdated and cleared (the requested history has been cleared [348/234]) [1347] Reason: Details:<nil> Code:0}
```

The indices in the error message do not change over time.

kube-proxy seems to be stuck in an endless loop on this condition and seems to fail to get service and endpoint updates.

title: Umbrella: Allow a 3rd party plugin to run on top of a Kubernetes cluster

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
This is a tracking issue to cover the open issues and features necessary for running a significant 3rd party extension on top of a Kubernetes cluster.  Depending on the complexity of an extension, some or all of these may be needed.  At this time, the most complex extension is [OpenShift](https://github.com/openshift/origin) and the items below these derive from those use cases, but I expect as other components that wish to extend or integrate with the cluster (logs, heapster, auditors, cluster integrations) are developed these will be useful.

The end result of this issue, as required features are implemented, should be a document describing how to build new cluster components that expose new capabilities on top of the core cluster services, what best practices should be followed, what design patterns to avoid, and to encode useful patterns into libraries and examples when someone wishes to "extend Kubernetes to do X".  Some of the items discussed below may not fit into that document - they will be moved into other umbrella issues or their own as time goes on.  Note, some of these overlap with regular application features, but are specifically listed here because in an ideal cluster components become aware of their environment and can use its APIs to leverage the flexibility the cluster manager provides.
### Use cases (still WIP)
- Allow components running on the infrastructure...
  - To be highly available
  - To have persistent storage that can survive the death of individual nodes for data persistence
    - In small clusters, it is sufficient to allow some components access to the core etcd (suitably protected)
    - In larger clusters, it is preferable to allow components to run their own available data stores (overlaps with database use case)
  - To have new versions deployed predictably
  - To securely connect to the API server with high level authority (delegate cluster admin control to a component) and be configured with that authority automatically
  - To perform pass through or delegated authentication for an API consumer that has a token for accessing the core services
  - To set and configure security policy via API (or allow an admin to easily define additional policy)
- Allow core client tools to...
  - Discover REST resources provided by a plugin and operate on them in a generic fashion (simple CRUD operations) - [discussed](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/pull/1355)
  - Apply standard patterns of templatization, creation, and behavior to any resource that follows the core patterns [discussed](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/1702)
  - Be easily reused by 3rd party client creators (kubectl, pkg/client, future UI) to build extensions of the core behavior - [implemented](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/pull/2682)
    - Design the kubectl commands so they can easily be tweaked to add new resources, or change the display and help text
    - Ensure reviewers are aware of the additional reqts on the kubectl code
    - Add unit tests to `pkg/kubectl` that verify generic kubectl commands do not depend on Kube specific globals
- Allow a cluster to be configured...
  - To use a different scheduler - [implemented](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/357) / [example](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/cmd/kube-scheduler/scheduler.go)
  - To use a different authentication / identity provider - [designed](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/design/access.md#authentication)
  - To use a different policy engine for authorization - [discussed](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/design/access.md#authorization)
    - An endpoint that could be configured via cluster config to make authorization decisions, provided by OpenShift or other service
  - To use a different admission controller on pod (or service, or RC, etc) so that different decision processes may be possible - [designed](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/design/admission_control.md)
  - So that an external plugin can contribute environment variables, volume configuration, or potentially security information into running pods without having to replace the scheduler or alter the code of the apiserver

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
In #687, we explicitly set cpu shares to 0 for containers with 0 cpu specified. However, @yujuhong and @gmarek say that Docker gives such containers 1024 shares. If true, we should give such containers minimal shares (10? 50?) instead. Otherwise, containers that specify no cpu would get a lot more shares than those that explicitly specify a small amount of cpu, including due to the default in LimitRange.

cc @rjnagal @vmarmol @vishh @dchen1107

labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.0-candidate
milestone.description: These are candidates for inclusion to v1.0 but will be pushed to v1.0-bubble if they're triaged as not meeting the v1.0 bar as a required launch blocker.

body:

title: Simplified resource generation (was kubectl command to create a namespace)

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

body:
A variety of issues have raised the specter of the need to make it easier to create a new `Namespace` from `kubectl` rather than handcrafting YAML.

I want to use this issue to drive resolution on the desired UX prior to submitting a PR.

**Option 1** 

Add a command `kubectl new-namespace`

Pros:
1. Clear what it does

Cons:
1. new-\* syntax is a little different than other command options today

**Option 2**

Modify `kubectl namespace` command to create the named namespace if it does not exist.

Pros:
1. Avoids a new-\* pattern in case folks don't like it.

Cons:
1. Changes the meaning of a command that existed previously, but we did deprecate it previously, so maybe this is not an issue.

**Option 3**

Add a `kubectl new <resource> <name> --flag1 --flag2` command syntax to support the following:

`kubectl new namespace myname | kubectl create -`

Pros:
1. The new pattern works nicely with subcommands that need specific flags

Cons:

**Configuration of Namespace**
There has been some side discussion on pre-configuring a newly created `Namespace` with some additional default resources.  For example, create a namespace could also create a `LimitRange` that set default cpu limits to make scheduler better behaved.

In OpenShift, we have a `new-project` command that creates a namespace, assigns the user as the admin of that namespace via our policy stuff, and let's the user set a display name and description that get stored as annotations on the namespace.  The namespace can also have some pre-defined content in it based on the new-project-template that is configured.  We do not have a template notion yet in Kubernetes, but in theory, we can use that to set the default `LimitRange` stuff.  

https://docs.openshift.com/enterprise/3.0/admin_guide/selfprovisioned_projects.html

Absent a template concept, we would need to add some additional flags to either command in Option 1 or 2 above if we want to populate with some additional content.  

If we want to pursue that, we could do the following arguments that provisioned a `LimitRange`.

Arguments that 

```
--default-cpu=the default cpu assigned to a container if not specified
--default-memory=the default memory assigned to a container if not specified
```

Feedback requested: @bgrant0607 @deads2k @smarterclayton 
@ghodss

body:
Implementing should give us significant performance improvements, because:
- we avoid sending multiple watch requests to etcd that send as huge amount of unnecessary data
  (e.g. currently all Kubelets are watching for pods, but since filtering is done at the apiserver level, there are O(#nodes) watches to etcd open all the time , each of them sending all pods)
- on top of that we can build some Indexer - see  https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/4817#issuecomment-89437368 for more details

cc @lavalamp @davidopp @bprashanth @timothysc

title: Possible data corruption on rbd storage

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
etcd cluster backing apiserver died spontaneously, after restart apiserver pulled up the pods on different machines. Node storage was backed by ext4 over rbd, which became mounted on several nodes at once. That could have possibly led to data corruption.

I guess that the proper way to mount rbd volume is to take a lock on it first, which will at least fail if it's locked somewhere else, requiring manual intervention, but not destroying data. The lock should be optional, in case a proper cluster fs is mounted over the rbd.

In this case there was clearly no need for accessing the data from several pods so ext4 is deemed a proper fs.

title: Harden master API against web attacks

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
In #8871 we hardened the usage of "kubectl proxy" but the same issues apply if you use the master API directly from a Browser. Also currently the XSRF protection in the proxy works by blocking POST requests completely which prevents valid use cases so it would be good to have a better approach to XSRF protection.

The attack scenario would look like this:
- a cluster admin uses the master API in Chrome and is authenticated with http basic auth
- in the same browser, the admin surfs to evil.com
- evil.com can now execute arbitrary code in the cluster _if he knows the IP of the master API_ by doing cross-origin requests to the API to start a new container or use the kubelet's /exec endpoint.

I'd suggest:
- all POST requests should have a form of XSRF protection, maybe requiring a custom header might be easy to implement and sufficient for this use case. Though whatever protection is used, it should be disabled for anything under /proxy since those services should come with their own XSRF protection.
- /exec and /run of the kubelet API should require a POST method since they are state changing requests (and then XSRF protected)
- I'm still concerned about the /proxy endpoints. Any XSS in one of the proxied services could be used to read secrets from the API or to bypass any XSRF protection that is in place. The best mitigation would be if every proxied service would be served from a different origin. For example every proxied service could be served from a different port using the same basic auth credentials as the master API and the proxy endpoints could simply redirect to the right port.

- look at the node "e2e-scalability-minion-k2n5"

title: kube2sky can not resolve kubernetes service DNS name

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
There seem to be a chicken and egg problem with the current _kube-dns_ replication controller (v3).

As I mentioned [there](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/commit/2feb658ed7a6a9f9726b04ac4c890b5dee14c0a8#commitcomment-11696141) removing the `-kube_master_url` flag forces kube2sky to use the _kubeconfig_ file to find the address of the master, but this file contains the DNS name of the service, which can not be resolved:

```
clusters:
- name: local
  cluster:
     server: https://kubernetes
     insecure-skip-tls-verify: true
```

As a result _kube2sky_ fails with the error:

```
I0623 22:22:32.315145       1 kube2sky.go:451] Using https://kubernetes for kubernetes master
I0623 22:22:32.315168       1 kube2sky.go:452] Using kubernetes API 
E0623 22:22:32.322136       1 reflector.go:136] Failed to list *api.Endpoints: Get https://kubernetes/api/v1beta3/endpoints: dial tcp: lookup kubernetes: no such host
```

This happens in a k8s 0.19.3 cluster powered by CoreOS, on AWS.
Surprisingly, running the exact **same** replication controller with the **same** secret in a cluster started via kube-up.sh, also on AWS, works perfectly fine:

```
I0623 22:38:36.231746       1 kube2sky.go:451] Using https://10.0.0.1:443 for kubernetes master
I0623 22:38:36.231760       1 kube2sky.go:452] Using kubernetes API v1beta3
```

This behaviour feels pretty random and I can't figure out the reason why in the second scenario `https://kubernetes` is converted to `https://10.0.0.1:443`, where is the magic?

body:
Setup a 3 node cluster, it'll look like:

```
NAME                                               READY     REASON    RESTARTS   AGE
elasticsearch-logging-v1-trk5e                     1/1       Running   0          2m
elasticsearch-logging-v1-u0pcb                     1/1       Running   0          2m
fluentd-elasticsearch-e2e-test-beeps-minion-12g9   1/1       Running   0          1m
fluentd-elasticsearch-e2e-test-beeps-minion-5bqu   1/1       Running   0          1m
fluentd-elasticsearch-e2e-test-beeps-minion-jir8   1/1       Running   0          1m
kibana-logging-v1-fgfdf                            1/1       Running   0          2m
kube-dns-v3-n17tg                                  3/3       Running   0          2m
monitoring-heapster-v4-plzg4                       1/1       Running   0          2m
monitoring-influx-grafana-v1-hpic0                 2/2       Running   0          2m
```

3 nodes, 9 containers, in theory we should end up with 3 per node but we rarely do because the node scores are affected by the rate of creation of the fluentd pods. 

Create an rc with 100 pods in a custom namespace and you'll end up with all 100 on the same node. This is because the occupancy score of the one node never catches up to the other 2, because the cluster addons have container cpu and memory populated via the default limit range while the 100 pod rc does not.

body:
PR #9975 added hardcoded protection of the default namespace to the Lifecycle admission controller. This mechanism at least needs to be configurable, since Openshift and Kubernetes have additional infrastructure namespaces they'd like to protect. However, it also needs to be possible to remove the protection to shut down a cluster #4630, without making it susceptible to accidents. One solution would be to add a `protected` field to metadata of any object. `protected: true` would prevent deletion until the object was updated to set `protected: false`. This would also make it straightforward to protect the special Kubernetes services, addons, and other self-hosted components, while still making it possible to update them and to delete all resources during shutdown. 

cc @derekwaynecarr @lavalamp

body:
We realized just recently that HostNetwork pods aren't given a pod IP.  I wanted to get agreement on how we can make that pod visible. 
1. The effective ip of the pod is the host ip (which we also set).  
   1. We could set podIP to hostIP when in host networking and all higher level components would work
   2. We could change higher level components like the endpoints controller to look at hostIP instead of podIP in this case
2. The pod should get an ip assigned by the network plugin, but the network plugin makes the decision

We could do both of the above.  i don't know that we've formally stated hostIP is the internal cluster IP - because podIP is guaranteed to work in the cluster I think we would have to formalize that.

I'm looking for a quick decision (if possible) on whether 1.1 or 1.2 are acceptable - if they are, we are considering carrying a patch.

milestone.title: v1.1
milestone.description:
Release 1.1.

P1 features:
* 250+ nodes, at our published SLO
* kube-proxy perf. improvements (via IPTables)
* Docker 1.8.x
* Horizontal pod auto-scaling
* Job
* Ingress
* Schema validation in kubectl
* Experimental API and API groups
* Graceful pod termination

body:
## Introduction

Continued from #7111 and #2306 (also relevant: #3806, #6363).

There is a strong desire for kubernetes to support multiple API prefixes. This would allow us to split to the API into a more logical structure and introduce support for an experimental API prefix. Additionally, we would like to separately version different parts of the API and provide sensible scoping rules for API objects.

OpenShift serves its own objects separately from kubernetes objects using the /osapi endpoint. However, it registers its objects under the kubernetes api.Scheme (instead of a separate runtime.Scheme) and is forced to follow the kubernetes version numbers. Moreover, OpenShift's "kinds" must be unique to avoid clashing with those in kubernetes. We would like a more general approach to avoid these limitations.
## Proposed Hierarchy

To achieve this, the api could have the following hierarchy: provider/apigroup/version/kind with the following properties:
- Any version/kind should be convertible to the corresponding version/kind within the same API group
- API groups within the same provider should be able to refer to objects within other groups. This is needed for things like namespaces and lists, as well as experimental API groups.

In the existing API server, a runtime.Scheme somewhat approximates a provider/apigroup, while an apiserver.APIGroupVersion corresponds to a version.
## Challenges
- Much of the code assumes that only one prefix, runtime.Scheme, and related structures exist. This is especially problematic for things like namespaces.
- Referring to types in other runtime.Schemes requires that they (along with conversion and defaulting functions) be registered with the current runtime.Scheme and version.
- The master does core API-specific work ([link](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/15596ede41adf72ba5eac66404732be0c7f3c3b0/pkg/master/master.go#L458))
- Registering new prefixes/versions/objects requires dealing with too many things (see #2306 and #7111)

Tried to deploy new GCE instance using latest container-vm image (container-vm-v20150611) and found few issues then setting up manifest file. According to article https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/containers/container_vms the container volumes should be mounted in manifest like:

```
volumes:
    - name: string
      source:
        hostDir:
          path: string

If I checked api spec from http://kubernetes.io/third_party/swagger-ui/#!/v1beta3/ or http://kubernetes.io/third_party/swagger-ui/#!/v1 then I found that working manifest is

```
  volumes:
    - name: string
      hostPath:

title: Cap docker resource cgroup's limit

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
Forked from https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/9788#issuecomment-112512299:

The only unrecovered node is caused by docker memory leakage. It is a known issue since docker 1.3.0, might even earlier version (docker/docker#9139). Docker 1.7.0-rcX (the one I am currently validating) should have a fix for it. Once you restart docker, the problem should be gone, and the node should be recovered. I saw a similar problem before. On each node, there is a monit healthchecking docker daemon process periodically, in most cases, the docker in such bad state will be restarted by monit.

Before we have such fix from docker 1.7, we can set docker's hard memory limit to 70% of node capacity since we already put docker into a cgroup with unlimited limit today. This could be a temporary workaround recovering node from bad state. 

Related docker issue: https://github.com/docker/docker/issues/9139

cc/ @lavalamp @bprashanth

body: Kubernetes v0.19.0 breaks kube-addons.sh on CoreOS because it includes some Python code. I am running a setup where Fleet installs Kubernetes on CoreOS from the official tar-ball, basically extracting and installing Kubernetes similar to how Salt does it. This works fine in Kubernetes v0.18.2, but kube-addons.sh now fails on CoreOS because of the use of Python. It would be good if system services avoid Python and other heavy interpreted languages that require big installs that might not be available on all platforms.

title: After replication controller is deleted, some nodes do not kill running containers

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
Discovered this while debugging with @ArtfulCoder 

Some nodes do not kill containers after associated replication controller is deleted.

**Repro steps:**
- You may use a standard GCE 4 node cluster `n1-standard-1 (1 vCPU, 3.8 GB memory)`
- Download [sleepypod.yaml](https://gist.github.com/saad-ali/7d04ff21534729c6c42a)
  - It defines a replication controller with 300 replicas with 10 containers per pod using a _tiny_ container which contains a statically compiled C program that just starts up and goes to sleep for a very long time.
- Execute `./cluster/kubectl.sh create -f sleepypod.yaml` to create the replica controller
- Execute `./cluster/kubectl.sh describe rc sleepypod` repeatedly to check how many pods are scheduled.
  - Monitor `Pods Status`
  - Wait until the number of scheduled pods stops increasing (depending on the size of your cluster, you will not be able to schedule all 300 replicas, that's ok).
- Call `./cluster/kubectl.sh delete -f sleepypod.yaml` to delete the replica controller
- Call `./cluster/kubectl.sh get pods` verify there are no `sleepypod-...` in the response
- SSH into each node machine and execute `sudo ps | grep sleepy`

**Expected result:**
- All nodes should have no running `sleepypod-...` containers

**Actual result:**
- One or more nodes will not terminate the `sleepypod:` and associated `pause` containers running on it:

```

title: VPC name is hardcoded (AWS cloud provider)

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
The name of the VPC used to create ELB instances is [hardcoded inside the AWS cloud provider](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/release-0.19/pkg/cloudprovider/aws/aws.go#L1372). This prevents the creation of services with type `LoadBalancer` inside a VPC with a different name from what is expected ("kubernetes-vpc" for instance).

A solution could be to query the metadata service in order to get the current VPC id, like:

``` bash
MAC_ETH0=`curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/mac`
VPC_ID=`curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/network/interfaces/macs/$MAC_ETH0/vpc-id`

echo $VPC_ID
```

title: Readiness probe tears down container if initial delay is not passed

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
We have a scenario with no liveness probe defined, and a readiness probe defined with an initial delay.  It appears that this logic:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L146

results in tearing down the container immediately because the initial delay has not passed so the probe returns failure.

My understanding is that readiness probe failures are not supposed to result in a container teardown unless the readiness probe has previously succeeded, but I don't see any indication of such logic here:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/dockertools/manager.go#L1351-L1365

@smarterclayton @rcernich

body:
This seems like a bug to me

```
$ kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"0", Minor:"19+", GitVersion:"v0.19.0-222-g3ce7fe8310ff08-dirty", GitCommit:"3ce7fe8310ff081dbbd3d95490193e1d5250d2c9", GitTreeState:"dirty"}

$ echo $?
```

No output, and command exits success... wat. Have to explicitly pass `--api-version=v1beta3` to see expected output.

```
$ kubectl get nodes --api-version=v1beta3
NAME                                 LABELS                                                      STATUS
k8s-mycluster-a5ea41fb-node-vm2i   kubernetes.io/hostname=k8s-mycluster-a5ea41fb-node-vm2i   Ready

If the `kubectl` client version is greater the server version, it should be making requests based on the server's newest accepted apiversion.

body:
1. I have a RC with one pod whose container has readinessProbe.sh
2. The service run in container can not be 'ready' until about 2 min, so readinessProbe.sh exit with 1.
3. kubelet execute readinessProbe.sh every 10s by default, so it always get a status of 'False'
4. kubelet will kill and restart the container
5. goto 2, so it run into a loop of failure 

I remembered that readinessProbe fail does not cause container restart in v0.15.0, however livenessProbe will. And I checked the design in pod-states.md which keeps same behavior as before. So I am sure it is a bug in v0.18.1.

body: During a rolling update we default an rc with no spec.Replicas to the replicas of the old rc (https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubectl/cmd/rollingupdate.go#L232). with the v1 api we default an rc with no spec.replicas to have 1 replica. This effectively means rolling-update behaves differently in the 2 versions.

title: Prometheus stats holding onto a fair amount of memory (potential unbounded rest stats)

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Right now the faceted search stats from cadvisor, the rest client, and the apiserver are holding on to a fair amount of memory:

https://github.com/openshift/origin/issues/3053#issue-87005876

Prometheus is holding about 225mb, 35 from the rest client, probably 40-50 from the apiserver (we log more summary data there), and then the bulk is probably from cadvisor.

The growth is proportional to the number of containers running (cadvisor) but should be capped out for apiserver (because we only expose a limited number of endpoints). 

However REST is capturing the URL, which means that every URL endpoint that the API server uses to talk to itself (including every unique named resource fetched by a controller) creates one new summary.  I think we either need to:

a. limit the cardinality of the rest call
b. age out the stat points (does prometheus support this?)
c. garbage collect the stats on REST

This applies to both the kubelet and controller manager, since both hold a long running rest client that is used to fetch individual resources.

body: Setup http://kubernetes.io (gh-pages branch) for publishing transformed copies of the user documentation (source .md files remain in the master branch). **Details**: - _(updated)_ All non-kubernetes-contributor documentation will be transformed to .html and published on http://kubernetes.io/ (this site will be the main source for all user facing documentation) (#7034) - Including the content in these folders: docs, examples, getting-started-guides Excluding: designs, proposals, devel, man - A site navigation tree will be added: - Structured to separately display multiple release versions (#8969) - Organized by user role "Cluster Administrator" and "Application Developer" (#7299) - Google Custom Search Engine will be integrated - Stable versions and an "in-development" version of the documentation will be published: - Stable versions of the documentation represent released versions: - _(update)_ Once a version is 'released' to gh-pages, all maintenance is done there in gh-pages (.html files). In other words, the .html files in gh-pages become the source files for a released version. - Only one version behind HEAD is in-scope for maintenance - Maintenance changes can include Bugs and new or changed content but nothing that is not supported in that release - Fixes or changes implemented to a stable version should also get pushed into the "in-development" version (if applicable) - The unstable (in-development) version reflects development's HEAD: - Contributor can deliver changes, updates, and fixes to this "in-development" version - This version should be/remain in-sync with development _(update)_ The following are no longer issues because the source files for examples, api, and cli docs will remain in the master branch ~~**Other dependencies that need ATTENTION**:~~ - ~~Examples folder is also included in product image. _We need to resolve how this will work._~~ - ~~Swagger API gets automatically generated (master branch: hack/update-swagger-spec.sh). _We need to ensure docs at HEAD remain current._~~ - ~~kubectl CLI gets automatically generated (master branch: hack/run-gendocs.sh). _We need to ensure docs at HEAD remain current._~~ - ~~Other scripts? .md file analytics?~~ **New file handling process**: - "stable" versions of the files will live in a folder (folder name = version #) in gh-pages - "unstable" (HEAD/in-development) versions of the files will live in a folder (folder name = HEAD) in gh-pages - _(update)_ The copy of HEAD will be transformed and copied to gh-pages to maintain currency. - _(update)_ To update a released version, you update the previously transformed .html files in the corresponding folder in the gh-pages branch **TODO**: - DONE: ~~Create new site navigation tree and map all existing documents (and issues)~~ - Fix all linking (apply linking changes that reflect necessary file directory changes in gh-pages (for handling multiple "versions" of the docs)) (#1571) - Create corresponding Jekyll and Liquid site files (.yml, _layout/.html, and _scss/.html files) for: - Create site navigation tree - Individual help topics - A topic specific header (to include search box) - Landing pages (ie set of getting started guides, examples, tutorials, troubleshooting) - Add support for Google Custom Search Engine - Test, review, get approval in Fork before publishing **For Development Team:** (Chao Xu owns this) - Add the following steps to the release process: - Script in the "[front matter](http://jekyllrb.com/docs/frontmatter/)" to the top of each each file: `---` `layout: docwithnav` `---` - Process all [link text](../linktofile.md) links so that they point to .html files -> link text - For the release process, copy "user-facing" docs from master to corresponding folder in gh-pages - DONE: ~~Change hard coded links/URLs from "http:docs.k8s.io/_filename.md_" to relative URL "../../docs/_filename.md_" (#3059, #1571)~~ **Known issues:** - On page refresh (or when navigating directly to a page) the site navigation tree does not open nor select the corresponding topic - DONE: ~~Images need to be manually resized (or need to create some targeted scripting to resize)~~

title: monit is too aggressive in killing docker

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
When we get into a low-memory situation, docker is slow to respond and monit kills it:

```
[UTC Jun  8 18:19:46] error    : 'docker' failed protocol test [HTTP] at UNIX[/var/run/docker.sock] -- HTTP: Error receiving data -- Resource temporarily unavailable

[UTC Jun  8 18:19:47] info     : 'docker' trying to restart
[UTC Jun  8 18:19:47] info     : 'docker' stop: /etc/init.d/docker
[UTC Jun  8 18:19:48] info     : 'docker' start: /etc/init.d/docker
```

However, if you have a lot of containers, it can take a long time for Docker to restart and get healthy again.  If you're under a lot of pressure, it will still be recovering at the next check-time (5 minutes later).  (At least I think that is what is happening.)

I don't know what we should do here.  We could make kubelet responsible for health-checking & restarting Docker, because it is talking to Docker all the time so it has a much better idea than monit when Docker is healthy or not.  We could turn down the interval with which monit checks (or allow more time after a restart).

I suppose the right answer is that I should stop over-committing machines!

title: Service IP mapping issue

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
On several occasions now, kube-proxy has ended up in a weird state where it is trying to open up connections to the wrong IP.

I have a service "turnstile":

```
$ kubectl get endpoints turnstile
NAME        ENDPOINTS
turnstile   10.244.20.49:8080,10.244.20.49:10000
```

And the service definition:

```
$ kubectl get service turnstile
NAME        LABELS                         SELECTOR         IP               PORT(S)
turnstile   name=turnstile,role=frontend   name=turnstile   10.100.213.187   8080/TCP
                                                            172.31.13.122    443/TCP
```

The following rules are in iptables:

```
REDIRECT   tcp  --  0.0.0.0/0            10.100.242.60        /* production/turnstile:http */ tcp dpt:8080 redir ports 56310
REDIRECT   tcp  --  0.0.0.0/0            172.31.13.122        /* production/turnstile:http */ tcp dpt:8080 redir ports 56310
REDIRECT   tcp  --  0.0.0.0/0            10.100.242.60        /* production/turnstile:https */ tcp dpt:443 redir ports 35366
REDIRECT   tcp  --  0.0.0.0/0            172.31.13.122        /* production/turnstile:https */ tcp dpt:443 redir ports 35366

DNAT       tcp  --  0.0.0.0/0            10.100.242.60        /* production/turnstile:http */ tcp dpt:8080 to:172.31.13.122:56310
DNAT       tcp  --  0.0.0.0/0            172.31.13.122        /* production/turnstile:http */ tcp dpt:8080 to:172.31.13.122:56310
DNAT       tcp  --  0.0.0.0/0            10.100.242.60        /* production/turnstile:https */ tcp dpt:443 to:172.31.13.122:35366
DNAT       tcp  --  0.0.0.0/0            172.31.13.122        /* production/turnstile:https */ tcp dpt:443 to:172.31.13.122:35366
```

Performing a `curl http://10.100.213.187:8080` simply hangs (as the iptables mapping seems to be wrong). 

Performing `curl http://172.31.13.122:56310` gives the following in the kube-proxy log:

```
                856 proxier.go:116] Accepted TCP connection from 172.31.13.122:38499 to 172.31.13.122:44595
1:57.381394     856 proxier.go:116] Accepted TCP connection from 172.31.13.122:58990 to   172.31.13.122:56310
1:58.381677     856 proxier.go:85] Dial failed: dial tcp 10.244.20.45:8080: i/o timeout
2:00.381935     856 proxier.go:85] Dial failed: dial tcp 10.244.20.45:8080: i/o timeout
2:00.385905     856 proxier.go:85] Dial failed: dial tcp 10.244.20.45:8080: no route to host
```

As you can see, something seems screwed up with the service IP mappings. The iptables rules seem out-of-date and kube-proxy is trying to connect to some IP (10.244.20.45) that doesn't match the endpoint (10.244.20.49).

This just happened suddenly after the service had been running fine for many days.

title: Indefinite retries of failing objects

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
From: _Uday Kumar Raju ruddarraju rudaykumarraju@gmail.com_

I have run into a wierd situation using the FIFO queue in the ServiceController. We (at ebay) have modified the openstack cloud provider to suit our installation of openstack, where all the Pod IPs are reachable outside the cluster. So we have changed out cloudprovider to read the pods belonging to a service and create a tcp load balancer with pod IPs as the members. We saw a wierd case recently with the way ListWatcher is enabled.

Here is the pseudo code of our CreateTCPLoadbalacer:

``` go
func CreateTCPLoadbalancer(lbName) {
  GetAllPodsUnderService() // A call to API server to get all the pods with the same selector as the service
  CallOpenstackToCreateLBPool(PodIPs, method)
}
```

You can see this is a little different from all the public providers where, none of the other providers have a dependency back to the apiserver during this operation.

I have run into a situation where servicecontroller indefinitely tries to call the CreateTCPLoadbalancer even when it fails everytime. My failure case happened to be this:
- Called Create Service for a set of Pods. Created a delta on the fifo queue
- The CreateTCPLoadbalancer call failed due to a connection reset on the Openstack endpoint due to a network issue, so the event has been put back on the FIFO queue as the CreateTCPLoadbalancer failure is always considered to be a retriable failure. 
- I deleted the service to try again. This has been pushed in as a delta again (while the api server has already deleted the service from etcd and hence querying the apiserver after this would always return service not found)
- Now my FIFO queue looks like this  (Add Service) <- (Delete Service)
- Since my Add Service (CreateTCPLoadbalancer) always relies on the service object (in my cloud provider) in the apiserver, this call would fail every single time hence forth. And is pushed back to the queue everytime (retriable is True) and the delete event does not get processed at all. 

I was able to reproduce this by inducing an error in the createTCPLB call everytime. I know there can be several ways to handle this but wanted to check with you guys first if my analysis on this problem makes any sense.

title: Make DNS required (update docs, add conformance test)

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
This issue is a follow on from the discussion in PR #5284 by @piosz where folks like @pires and @eparis @nzwulfin  and maybe @derekwaynecarr complain about changing the key guestbook example to use DNS which makes it a nicer example for Kubernetes deployments that have a DNS add-on but breaks it for other clusters that don't. A very good point was made: the key example that most people try out should work on bare Kubernetes without the need to assume any add-ons services.

Although we can imagine some post 1.0 fixes (e.g. absorb DNS functionality into core Kubernetes @thockin ) I think it is very important to get our examples and documentation in very good shape for the 1.0 release so that everyone has a very good out of the box experience with the key guestbook example for any Kubernetes deployment that we explicitly support.

I propose the following approach for 1.0:
- Produce a variety of guestbook examples which make different assumptions about the type of the Kubernetes deployment.
- Have a `guestbook-bare` example that works without DNS.
- Have a `guestbook-dns` example that works with DNS.
- Have other `guestbook-XXX` examples that work with other Kubernetes deployments that can provide an alternative to our DNS add-on to achieve the same effect.
- Produce a clear matrix in our documentation that explains which example should be run depending on your deployment.
- Make clear at the beginning of the `README.md` for each of the examples the deployment that is expected.
- Perhaps modify the examples to make sure the pre-requisites are available before running e.g. in a Makefile as a pre-check?

@RichieEscarez @bgrant0607

title: Harden kubectl proxy

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
The current default behavior of kubectl proxy is to listen on all addresses on port 8001. Thus anyone on the same network gets full access to the apiserver of my cluster.
It would be good to default to listen on localhost and maybe add a flag to override this behavior.

The second issue is that the proxy is vulnerable to dns rebinding. I.e. if I'm running a kubectl proxy and browse the web at the same time, a malicious website can interact with the local apiserver. The recommended way to protect against dns rebinding is to check the Host header for expected values if present.

title: kubelet should rectify corrupt pod status

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
Forked from #8335

Currently, kubelet sends pod status update whenever it discovers that the newly-generated status differs from the copy in its internal cache. However, it does not check the pod status received from the apiserver at all. What this implies is that if a user or another component changes the pod status via apiserver, kubelet will not correct the status until there is an actual update. We should make kubelet detect corrupt pod status and rectify it.

There are a couple of things that need to be ironed out for this:
1. Kubelet, as of now, filters out pod status update by default, i.e., it will trigger an update only if the pod spec is changed. Kubelet will not be able to view the status it updates in a short-period of time.
2. When kubelet generates the pod status, it sets `StartTimestamp` for the pod before storing it into status manager (the internal cache). The timestamp needs to be at the second-level precision to match with the status received from the apiserver (after json marshalling).

title: Measure our 1.0 scaling goals under different cluster configurations

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
Our 1.0 scaling goals as described in #3952, #4521, and #3954 are for 100 nodes with 30 pods/node.

It would be interesting to see what happens when we use more nodes and fewer pods/node, since I suspect few people will need 30 pods/node while some may want more than 100 nodes. For example, I would suggest trying
- 200 nodes and 10 pods/node
- 200 nodes and 15 pods/node
- 250 nodes and 10 pods/node
- 300 nodes and 10 pods/node

BTW we should make it clear when we talk about N pods/node whether we are or are not including cluster add-on pods (like the ones used for logging and monitoring).  

We aren't changing the 1.0 performance goal, but it would be good to understand the space of configuations a little better, if we have time.

@wojtek-t @fgrzadkowski (feel free to reassign, and this is not critical for 1.0, just a "nice to have" so we can possibly give more than one data point in our announcement for 1.0)

I realize this example is probably deeply unhelpful unless you have a zookeeper image lying around, but here's what I observed...

justinsb@kubernetes-minion-nyy1:~$ echo ruok | nc 10.244.1.5 2181
imok
justinsb@kubernetes-minion-nyy1:~$

 kubectl port-forward -p zookeeper-rplo3 2181

and then

imok
<hangs>
```

I hope to publish this zookeeper image early this week, if you can't find another test-image where the server closes the connection.

title: e2e test for tmpfs must specify RestartPolicy: RestartPolicyNever

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
In test/e2e/empty_dir.go, we run a pod that basically runs once and logs status about the mounts, which we then validate.

In the test, we start the pod, wait for it to exit, and then get the logs.

But, we don't specify a restart policy.  The default is restart always.  So it will keep restarting.  So testContainerOutputInNamespace, which calls waitForPodSuccessInNamespace, will never exit: `ci.State.Termination` will be nil, though `ci.LastTerminationState.Termination` is getting set.

I will propose a PR that sets RestartPolicy to never for the empty_dir test.  But there is a deeper issue - how did this test _ever_ pass?  How would it ever happen that State.Termination would be set, with RestartPolicy: Always?

(I am hoping it is the other bug I found with kubelet restart, but I don't know that I entirely believe that)

body:
We have a mix of styles in our current cluster creation pushing code. We should fix this soon after 1.0.
## Current state
- apiserver - put into container, tar’d, uploaded to gcs, and curl’d into to cluster at kube-up time.
- scheduler - put into container, tar’d, uploaded to gcs, and curl’d into to cluster at kube-up time.
- controller-manager - put into container, tar’d, uploaded to gcs, and curl’d into to cluster at kube-up time.
- kubelet, kube-proxy - n/a (run as binaries)
- Addons: kube2sky (dns), heapster, network-tester, etc - occasionally built, and pushed to gcr.io, with an ad-hoc version that doesn’t reliably correlate with any revision in git.
## Problems
1. Difficult or impossible to get a consistent cluster (including addons) from source.
2. Addons leave lingering dependencies (accidental push could break all cluster turnups).
3. Also not possible to start a cluster using config + a set of containers already in gcr.io
## Desired state

Build and version a complete set of containers, including addons.
1. For official releases, push to official registry and throw away the keys (or do the closest moral equivalent). This lets you start most of a cluster just with config files referencing the official containers for that version.
2. For unofficial releases, a choice:
   1. Push to cluster via gsutil/curl, like now.
      1. cons: doesn’t work well for addons, which might need to run on any node.
   2. Push to a (potentially private) registry, under the user’s name, so that my dev containers can’t collide in name with yours (filed #8517).
      1. pros: code reuse with the official release method.
   3. Run a private registry in the cluster by default, and push to that. (bootstrapping problem to solve!)
      1. additional pro: no need for user to set up a private repo before using.
3. The build process then makes a set of config that references these containers.

body:
I'm trying to launch a kubernetes Cluster with ubuntu. I saw the docs must be updated [#8373](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/8373). During the process the verify-ssh-prereqs in utils.sh in ubuntu folder failed :

```
    Could not find or add an SSH identity.
    Please start ssh-agent, add your identity, and retry.
```

I changed the function by :

```
 local rc

  rc=0
  ssh-add -L 1> /dev/null 2> /dev/null || rc="$?"
  # "Could not open a connection to your authentication agent."
  if [[ "${rc}" -eq 2 ]]; then
    eval "$(ssh-agent)" > /dev/null
  fi

  rc=0
  ssh-add -L 1> /dev/null 2> /dev/null || rc="$?"
  # "The agent has no identities."
  if [[ "${rc}" -eq 1 ]]; then
    # Try adding one of the default identities, with or without passphrase.
    ssh-add || true
  fi

  # Expect at least one identity to be available.
  if ! ssh-add -L 1> /dev/null 2> /dev/null; then
    echo "Could not find or add an SSH identity."
    echo "Please start ssh-agent, add your identity, and retry."
    exit 1
  fi
```

a lot inspired by the vsphere utils.sh and now it works.

I think `eval "$(ssh-agent)" > /dev/null` must be added somewhere before ssh-add

A number of tools rely on the metadata name resolving to access service accounts, etc.

The name resolves fine on the GCE host.

title: panic in servicecontroller.go

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
In https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/cloudprovider/servicecontroller/servicecontroller.go, I found a logic error (when I had a broken cloud implementation):

If createLoadBalancerIfNeeded returns err, then cachedService will have service = nil.  This causes updateLoadBalancerHosts to panic.

It would be easy to skip cacheService if service=nil, but I wasn't sure whether this should then be included in servicesToRetry or not. 

Another problem (by inspection) is that I think there's a race condition where updateLoadBalancerHosts can run immediately after getOrCreate, before the service field has been set.

apiVersion: v1beta3
kind: Pod

    - name: foo
      image: foo/bar
      ports:
        - name: foo-tcp
          containerPort: 2049
          protocol: tcp
          hostPort: 2049
        - name: foo-udp
          containerPort: 2049
          protocol: udp
          hostPort: 2049
```

title: kubectl command aliases/renames

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
We've discussed these a few times. Recording in an issue for discussion/triage.

The proposals are to use more conventional terminology in kubectl for "porcelain" commands:
1. "run" rather than (or in addition to) "run-container". (ok, my bad)
2. "scale" rather than (or in addition to) "resize". https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/1629#issuecomment-93776977

These would match the terminology used by Docker, [Heroku](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/one-off-dynos#formation-dynos-vs-one-off-dynos), [CloudFoundry](http://docs.cloudfoundry.org/devguide/deploy-apps/cf-scale.html), and others.

We've also had feedback that it's unintuitive that run-container pods run forever by default. That's not the case in these other systems. Run once should probably be the default #4366.

And it should be possible to specify the command on the run command line #5581.

cc @smarterclayton @ghodss @jlowdermilk @brendandburns

title: How to cleanup unused containers and images?

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/support
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as a support question.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
I've seen many issuses about that, but none solve it.  like https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/1148

Maybe it is a problem docker should solve. Here is my solution:

```
# cat docker.cleanup.sh 
#!/bin/sh

docker ps -a -q | while read cid
do
    fini=$(docker inspect $cid | grep FinishedAt | awk -F\" '{printf("%.19s", $4)}')
    diff=$(expr $(date +"%s") - $(date --date="$fini" +"%s"))    
    echo $diff
    if [ $diff -gt 86400 ]
    then
        docker rm $cid
    fi 
done

docker rmi $(docker images -a)
```

It deletes containers that stopped before 1 day, and all unused images. 

Hope it helps

title: kubectl e2e tests broken

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.description: These are candidates for inclusion to v1.0 but will be pushed to v1.0-bubble if they're triaged as not meeting the v1.0 bar as a required launch blocker.

body:
Several of the kubectl e2e tests were broken today by #8249, which added a missing check of an err return value, all of which now fail when doing cleanup and calling `kubectl stop`.

Example:

```
kubectl guestbook should create and stop a working application

/go/src/github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/_output/dockerized/go/src/github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/test/e2e/kubectl.go:125
Error running &{/jenkins-master-data/jobs/kubernetes-e2e-gce/workspace/kubernetes/hack/../cluster/../platforms/linux/amd64/kubectl [kubectl --server=https://104.197.99.179 --kubeconfig=/var/lib/jenkins/jobs/kubernetes-e2e-gce/workspace/.kube/config stop -f examples/guestbook] []  <nil>  Error: [Resizing the controller failed with: replicationControllers "frontend" not found; Current resource version Unknown, Resizing the controller failed with: replicationControllers "redis-master" not found; Current resource version Unknown, Resizing the controller failed with: replicationControllers "redis-slave" not found; Current resource version Unknown]
[] <nil> 0xc2083e6860 exit status 1 <nil> true [0xc20803a3f8 0xc20803a438 0xc20803a470] [0xc20803a3f8 0xc20803a438 0xc20803a470] [0xc20803a430 0xc20803a468] [0x657730 0x657730] 0xc20841cc60}:
Command stdout:

stderr:
Error: [Resizing the controller failed with: replicationControllers "frontend" not found; Current resource version Unknown, Resizing the controller failed with: replicationControllers "redis-master" not found; Current resource version Unknown, Resizing the controller failed with: replicationControllers "redis-slave" not found; Current resource version Unknown]
```

I think this may have been originally broken in #6194. That change refactored the implementation of Stop, which started masking the error, but it also changed the order of code a bit.

Previously, the Stop implementation in `pkg/kubectl/stop.go` first queried for ReplicationControllers before creating the ResizeCondition; the first thing in the method was

``` go
  rc := reaper.ReplicationControllers(namespace)
  controller, err := rc.Get(name)
```

After the change, this is done following the ResizeCondition in `pkg/kubectl/resize.go`:

``` go
rc := &api.ReplicationController{ObjectMeta: api.ObjectMeta{Namespace: namespace, Name: name}}
```

Is it possible that we're trying to query for something that's already been deleted, and thus it will always fail?

cc @quinton-hoole @roberthbailey

title: Large throughput performance regression

labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

body:
**Test:**
Running a very simple wide guestbook (1000 pods) on a 23 node bare metal cluster, with a side script continually calling 'kubectl get pods' once a second to parse the state. 

Note: This is similar to many other tests we've ran in the past, and the model we would like to add to the e2e data dumping. 

---

**Environment:** 
Atomic 7.1.1 bare metal cluster with 23-nodes. 
GitVersion:"v0.16.2-649-g738f403eea96d4", 

---

**Expected Results:**
Linear damped impulse response curve with consistent slope (throughput).  We previously had seen consistent numbers. 

Before regression 4/22/2015:
![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/169553/7593162/9ca84724-f89d-11e4-81ae-7373ce064b69.png)

---

**Actual Results: 5/12/2015**

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/169553/7592559/9a35bfa2-f899-11e4-9fc9-a804befbce46.png)

histogram - bad distribution: 
![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/169553/7592822/59519900-f89b-11e4-86ec-b92df3751bbd.png)

---

**Other Notes:**
Anecdotal: 
- It now appears that garbage collection is batched, when it does run it seems to grind the apiserver to a halt as seen in the graphs.  Previous version would show spikes but they were not as high and did not affect overall performance.  

My initial suspicions are the apiserver changes, but I need more proof.

For testing master upgrades, we will need a test harness that:
1. Launches a cluster at some known version (e.g. latest release)
2. Runs some amount of work on the cluster
   - Running e2es would be ok, but e2e tests tend to try and clean up after themselves and therefore a test that is better suited would be one that keeps running during the upgrade
3. Upgrade the master to a new version (e.g. latest release running in jenkins)
   - For GCE, we should use [cluster/gce/upgrade.sh](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/cluster/gce/upgrade.sh) for this part (and fix it as necessary)

5. Runs e2e tests against the upgraded cluster.

body:
This makes cluster startup pretty painful and have wide variance, causing problems for monitoring and testing cluster turnup. After the kubelet can first talk to the apiserver, in can be from ~0 seconds to ~2 minutes until the kubelet can "get" its own node. Only then can it start pulling images to get pods running.

E0505 02:03:19.746214    4659 kubelet.go:1534] error getting node: node <node name> not found
E0505 02:03:26.003989    4659 kubelet.go:1710] error updating node status, will retry: error getting node "<node name>": minion "<node name>" not found
```

this has, I believe, been plaguing us for quite a while. It would be really great if we could figure out why. The master logs, if I recall correctly, don't have anything interesting in them (similar errors). (The most recent cluster I had that had these problems is gone, but I'll check further in the next.)

title: Eliminate Phase and simplify Conditions

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: sig/architecture
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Architecture.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
Forked from #6951.

This is also discussed https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/1899#issuecomment-93900072 and elsewhere. 

Users and developers apparently think of phases as states in a state machine, regardless of how much we try to dissuade them:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/api-conventions.md#spec-and-status

This interpretation conflicts with [the declarative, level-based, observation-driven design](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/design/principles.md), as well as limiting evolution. In particular, the phase should be derivable by observing other state and shouldn't require durable persistence for correctness. 

In my experience, the danger to system extensibility is significant, and results from assumptions baked into clients.

Phases aren't themselves properties or conditions of their objects, but clients inevitably infer properties from them. 

For example, a client might try to determine whether a pod is active, or whether it has reached a permanent, terminal state, such as with a switch statement, as follows:

```
switch pod.Status.Phase {
case api.PodPending:
    // not active yet
    ...
case api.PodRunning:
    // pod active
    ...
case api.PodSucceeded:
    fallthrough
case api.PodFailed:
    // terminated and won't re-activate
    ...
case api.PodUnknown:
    // WTF!
    ...
default:
    glog.Fatalf("unexpected phase: %s", pod.Status.Phase)
}
```

However, let's say someone wanted to add a new Phase where the pod would also be active (containers running/restarting, etc.), as in #6951. That would mean that every client/component that made decisions based on the phase would need to also then consider the new phase.

Enums aren't extensible. Every addition is a breaking, non-backward-compatible API change. We could create a new major API version for every such addition, but that would be very expensive and disruptive. At some point, it will just become too painful to add new phases, and then we'll be left with an unprincipled distinction between phases and non-phases. Creating all imaginable phases up front would not only create a lot of complexity prematurely, but would also almost certainly not be correct.

Conditions are more extensible since the addition of new conditions doesn't (shouldn't) invalidate decisions based on existing conditions, and are also better suited to reflect conditions/properties that may toggle back and forth and/or that may not be mutually exclusive.

Rather than distributing logic that combines multiple conditions or other properties for common inferences, such as whether the scheduler may schedule new pods to a node, we should expose those properties/conditions explicitly, for similar reasons as why we explicitly return fields containing default values.

Proposal:
1. Add LastTransitionTime, Reason, and Message to PodCondition (similar to NodeCondition)
2. Add new Condition types (e.g., PodCondition and NodeCondition), as needed. At minimum, we need to be able to identify whether the pod has reached a terminal condition or not. We could add a Terminated condition for that. The Reason could distinguish Succeeded from failed -- any reason other than Succeeded would be considered a failure. We have at least a couple dozen such failure reasons internally.
3. Add Conditions to whatever other objects currently have Phase but not Conditions
4. Eliminate *.Phase and PodStatus.Message from the v1 API

cc @smarterclayton @derekwaynecarr @thockin @timothysc @davidopp @markturansky

title: Consider publicly exposing some or all RollingUpdater annotations

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
The RollingUpdater makes use of some annotations to drive behavior:

```
kubectl.kubernetes.io/desired-replicas
kubectl.kubernetes.io/update-source-id
kubectl.kubernetes.io/next-controller-id
```

In OpenShift deployments, we found it useful to [reuse one of these annotations](https://github.com/openshift/origin/pull/2097) for scale factor preservation between deployments. We chose the private upstream annotation because it not only provided the right semantics, but as a bonus also lets our deployments (ReplicationControllers) be more compatible with RollingUpdater.

Does it make any sense to expose `desired-replicas` (and/or others) publicly for these reasons? If the intent is to try and converge the deployment systems (#1743) it might not make sense in the absence of other external demand.

/cc @bgrant0607 @brendanburns @smarterclayton @abhgupta

Display one or many resources.

> ```

> ```
> 
> Here are my nodes:
> 
> ```

>    NAME            LABELS              STATUS
>    45.55.192.230   <none>              Ready

title: Preserve container's working directory on kubectl exec

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Hi there! I'm not familiar with Kubernetes' code base.
I traced the inner workings of `kubectl exec` to an [`ExecAction`](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/api/types.go#L552-L553), which is documented to be executed inside the container, and the working directory for the command  to be root ('/') in the container's filesystem.

This is, however, dissonant with how `docker exec` works:

``` bash
$ docker ps | head -n 2
CONTAINER ID        IMAGE                                                                                                        COMMAND                CREATED             STATUS              PORTS               NAMES
555a2fd94619        172.30.17.221:5000/default/django-example:e0566c8be42b1611b11f47ed0c30706e4d3a72df79acd5e333e9976ed59795f3   "/usr/local/sti/run"   25 hours ago        Up 25 hours                             k8s_django-demo.597a8f9e_frontend-1-m7674_default_2eb052bb-f258-11e4-a47d-080027c5bfa9_765aba96      

$ openshift kubectl exec -p frontend-1-m7674 pwd                                             
/

$ docker exec 555a2fd94619 pwd                                                               
/opt/openshift/src
```

This behavior prevents us from running commands that use paths relative to the container's `WORKDIR`.

For instance, if we have a Django project inside a container, we'd like to use `kubectl exec` to run `python manage.py check` inside the container, but that's not possible unless we pass the full path to `manage.py`.

body:
Repro:
- Create a persistent volume in GCE:
  `gcloud compute disks create --size=200GB --zone=us-central1-a my-disk`
- Create a persistentVolume against the persistent disk:

``` yml
kind: PersistentVolume
apiVersion: v1beta3
metadata:
  name: mypv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 200Gi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  gcePersistentDisk:
    pdName: "my-disk"
    fsType: "ext4"
```
- create persistentVolume:
  `gcloud alpha container kubectl create -f persistentVolume.yml`
- get persistent volume status:

```
$ gcloud alpha container kubectl get pv
NAME      LABELS    CAPACITY       ACCESSMODES   STATUS    CLAIM
mypv       map[]     214748364800   RWX
```
- get yml output:

``` yaml
$ gcloud alpha container kubectl get pv -o yaml

title: kubectl --validate flag doesn't complain about unknown fields

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
My understanding of kubectl's --validate flag is that it's supposed to error out if it can't parse its input as a valid API object. Maybe my understanding is wrong, but if it isn't, then the --validate flag is currently broken.

This came up when a user's service was coming up without a load balancer when they used the following yaml:

```
kind: Service
apiVersion: v1beta3
metadata:
  name: locust-master
  labels:
    name: locust
    role: master
spec:
  ports:
    - port: 8089
      targetPort: 8089
      protocol: TCP
      name: locust-master-web
  selector:
    name: locust
    role: master
createExternalLoadBalancer: true
```

The createExternalLoadBalancer parameter is incorrectly at the top level, when it's supposed to be inside the spec. Running `kubectl create -f locust-master-service.yaml --validate` happily succeeds, with the server never seeing the createExternalLoadBalancer parameter.

You can make this even more extreme by throwing in arbitrarily named fields that don't exist anywhere in the API:

```
kind: Service
apiVersion: v1beta3
metadata:
  xxxxxxxxx: yyyyyyyy
  name: locust-master
  labels:
    name: locust
    role: master
spec:
  aaaaaaaa: bbbbbbbbb
  ports:
    - port: 8089
      targetPort: 8089
      protocol: TCP
      name: locust-master-web
  selector:
    name: locust
    role: master
```

Running `kubectl create -f locust-master-service.yaml --validate` with this input file also happily succeeds.

@brendandburns @jlowdermilk

title: Versioned API objects should be in a self-contained package

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
TL;DR: The versioned API types should be self-contained package. For example, the file "pkg/api/v1beta3/types.go" is not self contained and contains tendrils to other internal types (see below). This is somewhat cruddy for other clients wanting to import minimal source from k8s just to call its APIs. It'd be nice to have a single package to import to get the API object definitions (i.e. for json unmarshalling, etc).

Observed outside of package depencies in "pkg/api/v1beta3/types.go":

"pkg/runtime" - The "List" type contains a field "Items []runtime.RawExtension". "RawExtension" is a trivial struct containing only a "[]byte".

"pkg/types" - Various places uses the "types.UID" struct, which is an alias to "string".

"pkg/util" - Two types from this package are used: "util.Time" and "util.IntOrString". The former is a wrapper on Go's Time object, with extra functions for custom JSON serialization (RFC3339 compliant) in "pkg/util/time.go". "IntOrString" is the dual-mode struct holding an int value or a string ("pkg/util/util.go").

"pkg/api/resource" - The "ResourceList" object is a map whose keys are "resource.Quantity" objects. The "Quantity" object contains a field to "inf.Dec", which is an infinite precision decimal package imported from "speter.net/go/exp/math/dec/inf". This is the only package which is external to k8s.

I know that some of the json annotations added are to support swagger, but the go->swagger->go thing seems like an unnecessary complexity.

title: apiserver incorrectly returns 405 when 404 expected during a HEAD request

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
I think this is the root of the reason why the new Kibana to Elasticsearch setup failed to work (even with basic auth). I think a 404 response is incorrectly being turned into a 405 response.

In these example I am running a Kibana service which maps to a pod running a Kibana server.

```
POD                    IP           CONTAINER(S)     IMAGE(S)                              HOST                                    LABELS                                                   STATUS    CREATED
kibana-logging-88fi0   10.244.0.6   kibana-logging   gcr.io/google_containers/kibana:1.3   kubernetes-minion-02dr/104.197.15.218   kubernetes.io/cluster-service=true,name=kibana-logging   Running   44 minutes
CONTROLLER       CONTAINER(S)     IMAGE(S)                              SELECTOR              REPLICAS
kibana-logging   kibana-logging   gcr.io/google_containers/kibana:1.3   name=kibana-logging   1
NAME             LABELS                                                   SELECTOR              IP            PORT(S)
kibana-logging   kubernetes.io/cluster-service=true,name=kibana-logging   name=kibana-logging   10.0.32.105   5601/TCP
```

Note that the Kibana service has the IP 10.0.32.105. If we ssh into a minion and curl against this we get the expected response i.e. "a .kibana index does not exist". This is the correct expected behavior.

```
$ curl -X HEAD -i  10.0.32.105:5601/elasticsearch/.kibana
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
X-App-Name: kibana
content-type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8
content-length: 0
Date: Wed, 29 Apr 2015 18:57:21 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
```

However, the Kibana dashboard reports an error when it tries to connect to Elasticsearch (which it does by going through its own URL with the subpath `elasticsearch`) saying the method is not allowed:

```
https://104.197.26.147/api/v1beta3/proxy/namespaces/default/services/kibana-logging/elasticsearch/.kibana Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 405 (Method Not Allowed)
```

If we ssh to the master and perform the same HEAD request against the apiserver we get a 404 Forbidden:

```
$ curl -X HEAD -i  http://localhost:7080/api/v1beta3/proxy/namespaces/default/services/kibana-logging/.kibana
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Date: Wed, 29 Apr 2015 19:07:37 GMT
Content-Length: 29
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
```

Adding the basic auth we get a 405 Method Not Allowed:

```
$ curl -X HEAD -i -k -u admin:REDACTED  https://localhost/api/v1beta3/proxy/namespaces/default/services/kibana-logging/.kibana
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Wed, 29 Apr 2015 19:08:36 GMT
Content-Length: 234
```

However, we should have got the same answer as doing a HEAD request on `10.0.32.105:5601/elasticsearch/.kibana` i.e. a 404 Not Found.

I think this is a bug and this is what is preventing Kibana from speaking to Elasticsearch.

@thockin @roberthbailey @lavalamp 
Thanks to who @ArtfulCoder who helped diagnose what was going on.

title: Demo service account to replace kubernetes-ro use cases in demos

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
# Problem
- Several of our examples use kubernetes-ro.  
  - cassandra, hazelcast, and rethinkdb examples use it for getting endpoints
  - phabricator examples uses it for getting pods
  - other examples may use it, pending further testing
  - probably other config not in our repo probably uses it.
- We have use cases where nodes/pods need to reach the master over the internet, rather than over a private network.  In those cases, we want to disable the kubernetes-ro service.  Otherwise, it leaves cluster information exposed to the world.
# Options
1. disable kubernetes-ro and let examples be broken on those types of clusters described above.
   - problem: breaks examples, and provides inconsistent cluster semantics for config authors to deal with. 
2. something on the node proxies the kubernetes-ro service from the pod over ssl-with-auth to the master.
   - problem: introduces a mechanism with apparently limited general utility
3. change all the examples on the site to use the http://kubernetes service, using an credential which allows readonly access.  
   - problem: We could change the ones on this site, but there may be others
   - problem: It is a non-trivial amount of work to get all the examples working, as they use a variety of languages and libraries, which may not support https with token-based auth as well as our pkg/client.

Recommendation: Last option.  It is a uses an existing, general mechanism (secrets) and keeps all clusters working the same.
# Proposal
- Add a "readonly-user" 
  - adds a service account token/name at cluster startup, in the same way other service accounts have been added.
  - adds a secret containing this token.
- Set policy for this service account to allow reading (events, endpoints, pods, services, rcs)
- Merge https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/pull/7101 by @liggitt 
- For each example currently using kubernetes-ro:
  1. update each pod to set "pod.spec.serviceAccount" to "readonly-user".
     - with #7101, causes pod to automatically be filled in with a secret volume containing a token for the readonly-user account.
  2. update places that use http and kubernetes-ro service to use https and kubernetes service.
  3. in those same places, add a token to header of the request.
  4. in those same places, set https options to use insecure connection.  (Or find a way to inject the master certs into the pod)

There are a number of details to sort out once there is general agreement on the general approach.
