title: Persist CI e2e test cluster logs for debugging purposes

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
We need to be able to diagnose e2e test failures after the relevant test cluster has been shut down.

Right now this almost works, but not quite.

Fluentd can currently only be configured to send log files to one place, for example:
1. Google Cloud Logging, or
2. ElasticSearch (running as a pod in the e2e test cluster, and saved to local disk on the node).

With the current configuration in hack/e2e.go, logs typically go to ElasticSearch (and there is an e2e test to check that that works correctly), and tears down the e2e test cluster after each test run, so the logs are deleted.

The proposed solution is to have fluentd configurable to send to multiple log collector backends, and configure it as such to both Google Cloud Logging and ElasticSearch for CI e2e test runs to facilitate easier debugging.  Satnam6502@ has offered to sort this out.

title: Kube-addons should be upgradeable

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
If config in cluster/addons changes, then I'd like to be able to upgrade my cluster to pick it up.

The folks designing upgrades should decide how this is accomplished.  Probably one of:
1. Do a kube-push, salt runs, kube-addons runs again, and it patches the existing configs.
2. A specific upgrade script runs.

If 1 is the plan, then several things are broken at the moment.
- When you try to run `salt-call state.highstate` on the master after modifying an addon, you get an error like: `:Failed when setting service kube-addons to start at boot, but the service is running`
- Kube-addons forks children that run forever, and stopping the init script doesn't top the children
- Kube-addons uses kubectl in a way that creates objects but won't update them.  It needs to either patch the objects or create-and-destroy them.

Setting up for KUBERNETES_PROVIDER="gce".
Project: [project]

Running Suite: Kubernetes e2e Suite run 1 of 1
==============================================
Random Seed: 1429310022 - Will randomize all specs
Will run 34 of 39 specs
...
```

I checked, and this is also true for our Jenkins runs.

Currently it looks like test/e2e/shell.go and test/e2e/kubectl.go have this bug, though only the former actually skips the test, I think.

The issue appears to be that the code inside the top-level `Describe()` in these files is being run before the testContext struct is filled out (and before `ginkgo.RunSpecsWithDefaultAndCustomReporters` is even called), and so testContext.Provider is empty.

I'm not immediately sure what the proper fix is; I'm also worried that there might be other things broken by the fact that these blocks are called before initialization is complete.

We also probably investigate if there is a better way to mark these tests as skipped; right now, there's no indication in the test report (JUnit.xml, Jenkins test report, etc) that these tests were skipped.

title: Proposal: Add "Termination Notice"

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Pods running on Kubernetes cluster may be stopped for a various reasons (e.g. resizing Replication Controller, rolling update, autoscaling number of nodes). The goal is to let them shut down gracefully by providing preemption notice a while before being stopped.

Possible errors caused by pods being killed instantly:
- not freed resource,
- broken TCP sessions,
- inconsistent state of PD.
### Draft solution

Once Kubelet observes request to delete a pod it manages from master’s state (etcd), each container running in the pod will receive SIGTERM signal. If a container has any cleanup stuff to do it must handle the signal. After defined time period Kubelet will actually delete the pod.

We need an additional support from cloud provider to handle preemption notice. We assume that cloud provider will notify the intention to remove a node from the cluster before actually removing it (ie. [STOPPING](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances#checkmachinestatus) state in GCE). After receiving the notification, node controller will delete pods on the node to allow Kubelet to send preemption notices to containers and then remove pods. Also Node Controller will mark the node as Unschedulable.

title: "kubectl delete namespace" has odd stateful behaviour.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
There is a funny subtle behvaiour in get namespaces, in  which if i call `kubectl delete ns...` more than one time, it seems that the removal from **Terminating** state is accelarated.  

It seems this might indicate a bug, or **maybe its not a bug and the eventual semantics** of `kubectl get ****` is a little funny sometimes.

in any case, **here's what we are seeing** : 

1) when i **delete a namespace the first time** usning kubectl, we get a state change  to `(Terminating)`.  that is correct, of course.

2) but ... if make the call a **second time**,  then the same status line `(Terminating)` is immediately **removed** from `kubectl get namespaces`.

Expected behaviour : **A second call to "kubectl delete ..." shouldn't have any effect on the timing of removal  of a namespace from 'Terminating' state**... So i guess there is some "eventual consistency" subtle bug that is resolved by repeated calls to `kubectl delete ...`

body:
Currently RC has the following logic:

MainLoop():
1. Watch for new RC and sync them immediately
2. Every 5 sec list all RC and sync them

SyncRC():
1. List all pods matching selector for RC
2. Add/Remove pods

This is suboptimal on both layers. We should use watch for both RC and pods. Current implementation generates very high load in apiserver.

body:
Currently Watch is broken every 5 minutes. It is then "recreated", which sometimes requires listing all elements under watch (if there were more than 1000 "uninteresting" etcd writes since then).

I digged deeper into it and it seems this is not related to etcd itself. What happens is:
1. a component (e.g. scheduler) starts watch sending http request to apiserver
2. apiserver initiates a watch on etcd
3. after 5 minutes, the request to apiserver finished (this is something I don't fully understand - is this a timeout?)
4. this triggers "canceling" the request to etcd

cc @fgrzadkowski

title: Decide master VM size for our 1.0 performance goals

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
Several people have brought this up (including @fgrzadkowski and @yujuhong). We have various performance/scalability goals (e.g. #4521, #3954, #3952) but we haven't stated what VM size we will use for the master when making these measurements. (I'm assuming we can just decide a GCE VM size, rather than a node configuration for every cloud provider we support.) 

We've been setting GOMAXPROCS in various places (#4605, #4675). I'm not sure we've been very systematic about it, but either way, or performance presumably depends on # cores of the master. I believe people have mostly been using 4-core masters for the performance measurements? (I can't remember if we've been measuring memory consumption vs. cluster size, but if not, we should to ensure the VM has enough memory for a 100 node cluster).

Unless someone objects, I'm going to assume we are going to use 4-core VM.

@filipg @wojtek-t @satnam6502 @roberthbailey @lavalamp @bgrant0607 @brendandburns

title: kube-proxy keeps adding duplicate iptables rules

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
I noticed that while connections between pods were usually nearly instant, sometimes they took a few seconds and they sometimes hung altogether, so I started poking around. I quickly found that `kube-proxy` is taking up between 80% - 100% of a CPU on each system that it's running on. The logs weren't very interesting, but then I checked the iptables rules:

```
# sudo iptables -L -t nat | wc -l
164757
```

The rules themselves:

```
# sudo iptables -L -t nat
Chain PREROUTING (policy ACCEPT 0 packets, 0 bytes)
 pkts bytes target     prot opt in     out     source               destination         
    0     0 KUBE-PORTALS-CONTAINER  all  --  any    any     anywhere             anywhere            /* handle ClusterIPs; NOTE: this must be before the NodePort rules */ 
    1    60 KUBE-PORTALS-CONTAINER  all  --  any    any     anywhere             anywhere            /* handle ClusterIPs; NOTE: this must be before the NodePort rules */ 
    4   258 KUBE-PORTALS-CONTAINER  all  --  any    any     anywhere             anywhere            /* handle ClusterIPs; NOTE: this must be before the NodePort rules */ 
    6   547 KUBE-PORTALS-CONTAINER  all  --  any    any     anywhere             anywhere            /* handle ClusterIPs; NOTE: this must be before the NodePort rules */ 
   12  1632 KUBE-PORTALS-CONTAINER  all  --  any    any     anywhere             anywhere            /* handle ClusterIPs; NOTE: this must be before the NodePort rules */ 
...
```

The `OUTPUT` chain is just as bad as the `PREROUTING` chain. The `KUBE-*` chains are all sane, having one rule per service port.

For now, I've set up a cron job to periodically flush `PREROUTING` and `OUTPUT` (and recreate the proper 4 rules to hopefully avoid any downtime), but this is obviously a poor workaround.

I'm running release 1.0.6 on CentOS 6.

* Ingress

body:
We've been discussing how to make experimental features available to users. The experimental APIs are currently disabled by default, but are enabled in increasingly many situations: e2e, vagrant (#14507), GKE, ...

RFC: Enable experimental by default. 

We'll need to figure out how to deal with potential future incompatible changes. If we need to make breaking changes to experimental APIs (which is part of the point of experimental), we'll need to delete affected experimental resources before upgrade. That mostly affects 1.2 rather than 1.1.

At minimum, there will be an API version treadmill of configs and storage version to get to stable APIs: experimental -> alpha -> beta -> v1. In order to advance in this progression, we need user feedback on the APIs, ideally more frequently than one step every 3 months.

In the pull request Jenkins, we're running up to 8 instances of verification checks, build, unit tests, integration tests, and e2e tests.

Unfortunately, it seems like several of these components were not designed to run simultaneous to other tests on the same machine.

In particular, several unit tests seem to write to static file names in /tmp (or equivalent), which is a fairly easy fix. labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.1
milestone.description:
Release 1.1.

P1 features:
* 250+ nodes, at our published SLO
* kube-proxy perf. improvements (via IPTables)
* Docker 1.8.x
* Horizontal pod auto-scaling
* Job
* Ingress
* Schema validation in kubectl

body:
Scaling down doesn't work for Deployments in the following scenario:
1. create a simple deployment with 5 replicas
2. wait for rc/pods to be created and running
3. update deployment, change the number of replicas to 1
   result: the rc is never scaled down to 1, its size is 5 all the time.

The problems seems to be in scaleUp method:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/deployment/deployment_controller.go#L234
This method should actually **scale down** the new rc, but it seems it doesn't due to condition in:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/deployment/deployment_controller.go#L254
(Please not that scaleDown method works only on old rcs, but there are no old rcs in our scenario).

title: Wrong Codec type when updating job

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Symptoms:

``` console
$ kubectl create -f docs/user-guide/job.yaml
job "pi" created
# Wait for it to start running (not sure if this is strictly necessary)
$ kubectl delete -f docs/user-guide/job.yaml
```

The latter step hangs forever.
So far, in debugging, I have found that:
- kubectl is waiting in the reaper loop
- it is trying to scale down the Job resource.
- it has successfully GETted it, and is trying to PUT (Update) it.
- it gets this error: `Scaling the controller failed with: no kind "Job" is registered for version "v1"; Current resource version 728999`
- this error is coming from the client, not the server
- the client is doing conversion in preparation for sending the Update, and it gets this error.
- when I print out the RESTClient.Codec, it has version "v1".  This is not right for an experimental Kind like Job.

@caesarxuchao @lavalamp helped me get this far.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.description:

* Docker 1.8.x
* Horizontal pod auto-scaling
* Job
* Ingress
* Schema validation in kubectl
* Experimental API and API groups
* Graceful pod termination

body:
From https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/11942#issuecomment-136467907
Assymetric update ex: Replace an rc A with 5 replicas with an rc B with 7 replicas (old and new RCs have different replica sizes).
RollingUpdate rollback rolls back to old RC, but scales it up to the number of replicas, the new RC had (for ex it will rollback to rc A but with 7 replicas).

We need to fix that.
With https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/11942, we now add an "original-replicas" annotation to oldRC, which we should use.

cc @ironcladlou @ghodss

What's surprising is that for 100 node cluster I'm observing way lower e2e startup latency (around 3-4 seconds on 99th percentile). I've seen this on my clusters multiple times, I also checked different project with the same effect.

I was wandering if it's not disk IOPS throttling, but issue persisted after increasing disk size (and thus guaranteed IOPS). Another idea I had was contention on Pod Workers in Kubelet, so I instrumented the code, and I didn't found anything keeping lock for long, and there was a lot of time when lock was open.

I'm not sure if it's the case only for GCE, or other providers show the same behavior, can someone run density test on other provider/bare metal? @timothysc @spiffxp

Until we know if it's not K8s code that's causing this I don't think we should cut 1.1 release. @wojtek-t @quinton-hoole @brendandburns @lavalamp @thockin @fgrzadkowski

title: Better memory manager at node to guarantee QoS

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Forked from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/14452...

We introduced QoS concept and API to Kubernetes 1.1 release, but lack of the support on node side to ensure QoS. Filed this umbrella issue for memory management for current known issues:
1. At node level, the only improvement was introduced is OOM score based on the resource class. This means we fully rely on Kernel sys OOM to react. This is dangerous, which could put the node to totally unstable mode. Based on my experience dealing with internal system, when sys OOM is triggered, before kernel kills some processes, process kswapd might use 100% CPU on a node to reclaim some pages, which could include disk io too, thus. All user processes are significantly slow down. **You can overcommit on request or limit, but Kernel sys OOM should be prevented**
2. This also means we should introduce a userspace memory manager to detect system overcommit on memory at run time. When memory pressure on the node is pretty high, and kubelet should proactively kill some lower priority containers / pods. We don't have this for today. 
3. Docker doesn't do process tracking at all except root pid. This means if sys OOM kills a non-root process in a container, container itself would be still running. 
4. Without userspace OOM handling support, even kernel kills container's root process, Kubelet might restart one to maintain sys OOM situation. 
5. Today all containers are at root level, instead of using cgroup_parent based on QoS. This means, the root cgroup is easily get oom-ed, instead, only some subcgroup. We plan to use cgroup_parent to improve QoS for 1.1 release, but don't have time to really get on it. 
6. Docker daemon uses tons of memory, even with 1.8.2 release. There is no good way to limit / reduce docker's resource footprint today. Currently it runs in a resource-only cgroup called /docker-daemon, and I limited it to 60% of node memory capacity. 
7. Other infrastructure daemons (kubelet, kube-proxy)' memory usage is scaled by workload. More work, more management overhead. We don't limit / budget them today. For 1.0 release, I put each one of them into a subgroup under root without limitation for monitoring / measurement only. We should have budget for them. 
8. We don't control all nodes. This means there are tons of processes / daemons running as native processes on a given node, including sshd. For measnurement / monitoring purpose, I put them in a resource-only cgroup called /system without any limit. We should have budget for them too. 
9. ...

title: RFC: Inert deployments

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
The deployment design (#1743) implicitly supports a deployment triggering use case known as "config change triggering" in OpenShift: when a new deployment state is observed, the cluster works to realize the new state as soon as possible. There is one functional gap in this design: users sometimes need to temporarily disable a deployment. This could be accomplished by allowing deployments to be "inert". Some uses for inert deployments:
- Provides a way for the deployment to exist in the system awaiting external human processes/validations
- Provides a safe way to prepare a deployment resource without iterative changes being rolled out
- A safety switch to prevent a deployment which you don't want to happen

Technically these use cases are satisfied by simply deleting the deployment resource and recreating it when ready, but that places a burden on the user to preserve the old state until it's ready to be recreated.

body:
If you create a pod with a restart policy of never, and you have a container that fails to start (e.g. you set its command to a nonexistent file), the Kubelet currently tries to restart it infinitely because the container never started successfully, and therefore never received an exit code. You end up with something like this from Docker:

```
Cannot start container ebd101cfcd0b1aab572a184ece01a17ce081658114977bd6490cd6c78aff06e3: [8] System error: exec: "start": executable file not found in $PATH
```

Is it worth modifying the code to consider a container that failed to start as actually failed, so the pod's restart policy can govern it?

Originally reported at https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1262753

body:
Today, many cloud provider provide some kind of services, such as RDS in AWS, and they also provide API to create service instances on demand. Also, these services may be more robust (high availability), have  better performance or even have special features than that deployed in some pods.
According to [this document](http://kubernetes.io/v1.0/docs/user-guide/services.html#services-without-selectors), we create a service linking to an external endpoint by ignoring the selector property and creating an endpoint manually. But, the whole process is totally MANUALLY.

The service types vary between different cloud providers, but from the view of k8s, it only need an interface to provision a service instance and get its endpoint, so it is possible to define an consistent API for all kinds of services, such as [The broker api in CloudFoundry](http://docs.cloudfoundry.org/services/api.html).

I want to know if it is possible for k8s to integrate with the cloud provider to create a service instance and configure an endpoint for the service. Are there any BP for similar features?

title: test-cmd.sh is racy

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/flake
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a flaky test.

body:
@smarterclayton @deads2k @kubernetes/kubectl 

```
Successful get nodes 127.0.0.1 {{.spec.unschedulable}}: 
Error from server: node "127.0.0.1" cannot be updated: the object has been modified; please apply your changes to the latest version and try again
!!! Error in ./hack/test-cmd.sh:783
  'kubectl patch "${kube_flags[@]}" nodes "127.0.0.1" -p='{"spec":{"unschedulable":true}}'' exited with status 1
Call stack:
  1: ./hack/test-cmd.sh:783 runTests(...)
  2: ./hack/test-cmd.sh:832 main(...)
```

My guess as to what is happening:
- we do a GET for the node status
- separately, the node status is updated, resource version changes
- we compute the new node state with unschedulable = true using what we got from the GET
- we try to POST with the old resource version and it fails.

The simplest solution is just to wrap the update call in some retry logic.

Longer term, kubectl should probably support the retry itself.

body:
I have a cluster based on "docker-multinode" getting started guide with some changes that adapts it to systemd OS (i.e. Ubuntu 15.04). I have a problem with flannel-based overlay network:

I have a pod with IP `10.1.75.2` (our porter image). I can ping/curl it from a node it runs it:

```
filipg@docker-node1:~$ curl 10.1.75.2:160
foo
```

The same thing does not work on other nodes (master and other nodes):

```
$ curl 10.1.75.2:160
curl: (7) Failed to connect to 10.1.75.2 port 160: No route to host
```

I checked entries in etcd and they look correct:

```
filipg@docker-master:~$ docker -H unix:///var/run/docker-bootstrap.sock exec -t elated_einstein etcdctl ls /coreos.com/network/subnets
/coreos.com/network/subnets/10.1.20.0-24
/coreos.com/network/subnets/10.1.75.0-24
/coreos.com/network/subnets/10.1.61.0-24
/coreos.com/network/subnets/10.1.90.0-24
/coreos.com/network/subnets/10.1.103.0-24
filipg@docker-master:~$ docker -H unix:///var/run/docker-bootstrap.sock exec -t elated_einstein etcdctl get /coreos.com/network/subnets/10.1.75.0-24
{"PublicIP":"10.240.0.2","BackendType":"vxlan","BackendData":{"VtepMAC":"ee:84:9f:f3:57:3e"}}
```

All the nodes seem to be routable:

```
filipg@docker-master:~$ ping 10.240.0.2
PING 10.240.0.2 (10.240.0.2) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 10.240.0.2: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.938 ms
```

title: Containerized kubelet cannot manage image garbage collection properly

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
Part of #13627

```
$ log for kubelet
E0906 09:56:50.896731       1 kubelet.go:737] Image garbage collection failed: non-existent label "docker-images"
```

The gc problem of cadvisor is because it cannot check the mount point of /var/lib/docker.

```
$ mount info for kubelet
Filesystem partitions: map[/dev/mapper/ubuntu--vg-root:{mountpoint:/rootfs major:252 minor:0} /dev/sda1:{mountpoint:/rootfs/boot major:8 minor:1}]\n","stream":"stderr","time":"2015-09-06T09:11:50.726997545Z"}
```

Hence it wont add the required label.

Yet we do have this in the containerized kubelet 

```
# cat /proc/self/mountinfo | grep '/var/lib/docker '
275 181 252:0 /var/lib/docker /var/lib/docker ro,relatime - ext4 /dev/mapper/ubuntu--vg-root rw,errors=remount-ro,data=ordered
```

It's deprecated by https://github.com/google/cadvisor/blob/master/fs/fs.go#L88
'cause we have following already

```
# mount -l | grep '/dev/mapper/ubuntu--vg-root' 
/dev/mapper/ubuntu--vg-root on /rootfs type ext4 (ro,relatime,errors=remount-ro,data=ordered)
```

Related to #4869
/cc @fgrzadkowski

title: Flocker volume plugin

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
[Flocker](https://clusterhq.com/flocker/introduction/) is an open-source container data volume manager for Dockerized applications.

This [PR adds a volume plugin for Flocker](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/14328).
The plugin interfaces the [Flocker Control Service REST API](https://docs.clusterhq.com/en/1.3.1/reference/api.html) to request volume creation and attachment.

Each kubelet host should run Flocker agents (Container Agent and Dataset Agent).

The kubelet will also require environment variables that contain the host and port of the Flocker Control Service. (see [Flocker architecture](https://docs.clusterhq.com/en/1.3.1/concepts/architecture.html) for more).
- FLOCKER_CONTROL_SERVICE_HOST
- FLOCKER_CONTROL_SERVICE_PORT

The contribution introduces a new 'flocker' volume type to the API with fields:
- datasetName: which indicates the name of the dataset in Flocker added
  to metadata;
- size: a human-readable number that indicates the maximum size of the
  requested dataset.

Full documentation (including getting started guides) and e2e tests to follow.

As the plugin is near code complete, we're hoping to make version 1.1.

body:
Given a namespace has several pods, and the pods have `spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds` greater than 0, when the namespace is deleted, the pods are terminated with 0 second grace period, the namespace status is always `Terminating`.

body:
I'm getting the following error on GKE:

```
Failed to inspect image "my-image": <nil>
```

I traced it back to [this code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6f01200188ab0aa6ceef29ab70741a7b6db82b35/pkg/kubelet/container/image_puller.go#L83-L88). The problem seems to be that `IsImagePresent` returns a nil-interface not a nil-pointer. nil-interfaces have a nil-value but a non-nil type. nil-pointers are just what you would expect (not an interface can be can alos be a nil-pointer).

title: Stair-stepping in pods going from Pending to Running

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
We'd like to get this to a more reproducable state with e2e-generated load and some consensus on what a "correct" cluster looks like.  In the meantime, here's what we've been seeing so far.

Provision a cluster in AWS using terraform + ansible
- used https://github.com/Samsung-AG/kraken with terraform.tfvars

```
node_count = 100
aws_apiserver_type = "m4.2xlarge"
aws_master_type = "m4.2xlarge"
aws_etcd_type = "m4.2xlarge"
aws_special_node_type = "m3.xlarge"
aws_node_type = "m3.medium"
kubernetes_binaries_uri = "https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/sundry-automata/hyperkube/v1.1.0-alpha.1.1007%2Bcad5f03311afff-dirty"
```
- master is nginx + controller-manager + scheduler
- apiserver talks directly to etcd node, no local etcd proxy used
- special node is reserved for expensive services via label selectors

Setup a "pause" replication controller that creates gcr.io/google_containers/pause:go pods
- used https://github.com/Samsung-AG/kraken-services/blob/master/pause/controller.yaml

Manually scale the number of pause pods to 2000.  
`kubectl scale --replicas=10 rc pause`

Replication controller creates all pod resources in Pending by the time the `kubectl` call has returned

Total time for all pods to go to Running is ~6m.  Initial burst of >1000 pods goes from Pending to Running within the first ~2m.

Then periodic stairsteps of total number of pods in Running as the scheduler binds pods in chunks
- using prometheus to gather metrics from all kubernetes components, and etcd
- using promdash dashboard: https://github.com/Samsung-AG/kraken-services/blob/master/prometheus/build/promdash/pod-scaling.json
- no observable exhaustion of resources, just period peaks which correspond to pods moving from Pending to Running

There appears to be a ~30s interval during which the scheduler goes quiet and then kicks back to life

The thinking is... there may be some rate limiters and magic constants tuned to hold back a thundering herd.  We'd like to remove those and see if we can find where that moves the raw resource bottleneck (eg: compute, network, memory, etc).

Verified with no other services running via kubectl polling

```
$ k get pods | grep -v pause
NAME          READY     STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
$ k get services
NAME         LABELS                                    SELECTOR   IP(S)        PORT(S)
kubernetes   component=apiserver,provider=kubernetes   <none>     10.100.0.1   443/TCP
```

Scale up to 2000 pods then poll every 10s

```
#!/bin/bash

date -u; 
time kubectl scale --replicas=2000 rc pause; 
date -u;
while true; do 
  echo $(date -u) : $(kubectl get pods --selector=k8s-app=pause | grep -ic running); 
  sleep 10;
done
date -u
```

title: Controller never healed from data loss, exceeded AWS API rate limit

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Admittedly this one is an edge case, but we had an issue that nearly locked us out of our AWS account following data loss on the kubernetes master. Specifically:
1. We turned up a k8s cluster integrated with AWS
2. An issue in our infrastructure caused us to lose the master's etcd storage (since resolved)
3. The new master came up, we recreated some of the lost state (i.e. kubectl create -f service.yml) and the master tried to resync that partial state with AWS, failing on duplicate resources
4. Until those resources were manually removed, the controller retried each operation often enough that our account become API rate limited, degrading access to our infrastructure

The obvious solution is to not lose the master's data, and we have fixed our mistake there. That said, as the flow above nearly locked us out of our AWS account, it would be nice if the controller had responded a little better to the partial data scenario. Two changes that would have helped us:
1. Increasing backoffs (random, exponential, fibonacci, etc.) around AWS API retries especially when the previous call failed due to a "RequestLimitExceeded" – though this does have the downside of pushing out time to convergence when the underlying issue is fixed
2. A way for the AWS integration to self-heal: when it fails to create e.g. a route because that route already exists in the table, a nicer error handling strategy might simply say "Creation successful!" – the situation is more difficult with security groups that have some state that potentially requires diffing, but in our case the issue occurred in the degenerate case where the controller was trying to recreate the exact resource that already existed

For context, the log messages we saw from the controller (there was some variation depending on which exact request was throttled):

```
E0916 23:21:30.178529       1 servicecontroller.go:171] Failed to process service delta. Retrying: failed to create external load balancer for service default/hello-world: error listing AWS subnets: RequestLimitExceeded: Request limit exceeded.
    status code: 503, request id: []
```

```
E0916 22:53:56.348372       1 routecontroller.go:91] Could not create route ROUTE_ID 10.244.0.0/24: error creating AWS route (10.244.0.0/24): RequestLimitExceeded: Request limit exceeded.
```

The underlying issues seemed to stem from:

```
E0916 23:35:37.607891       1 servicecontroller.go:171] Failed to process service delta. Retrying: failed to create external load balancer for service default/hello-world: InvalidGroup.Duplicate: The security group 'SECURITY_GROUP_ID' already exists for VPC 'VPC_ID'
```

```
E0916 22:52:56.239869       1 routecontroller.go:91] Could not create route ROUTE_ID 10.244.3.0/24: error creating AWS route (10.244.3.0/24): RouteAlreadyExists: The route identified by 10.244.3.0/24 already exists.
```

Deleting both of those resources did appear to resolve the problem. Thanks for reading my book!

title: pkg/client: api version to be set at high level, not low level.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Currently pkg/client has logically distinct low level RESTClient (Get, Put, Post...) and high level typed client (PodsNamespacer etc).

The API version (and implictly, group) is currently baked into the low level RESTClient, but this is wrong. We want to use the same low-level code for all API versions and groups, and supply a different high level client for each version.

The action item here is to remove references to "version" from the RESTClient, and put them in the high level client, adding Group(), Version(), and GroupVersion() calls to the client.Request object.

title: kubectl create/replace should support templates

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
When running `kubectl create`, I often find myself making a few trivial substitutions to the input manifest.  For an rc, I will normally add a label with the git sha, and change the docker image label.  Right now this is awkward; I typically do it through messy bash/sed.  I think it would be very helpful if `kubectl create` was able to perform this substitution.

(This is perhaps part feature-request, part "what is the right way to do this?"  I am not sure whether this belongs in kubectl.)

One way this could work would be to use our existing template syntax, with the input source being a set of variables that are specified on the command line.  I suggest it would be an error if the value was not provided (although it would also be nice to allow `{{gitsha | 'latest' }}`).

e.g.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  labels:
    app: myapp
    gitsha: {{gitsha}}
  name: sentry
spec:
  ...
        image: myregistry/mycoolapp:{{gitsha}}
```

then used with something like `kubectl create -vgitsha=12345 -f template.yaml`

One option might be to prototype this in contrib, as a totally separate command e.g.
 `kube-expand -vgitsha=12345 -f template.yaml | kubectl create -f -`

title: Introduce Allocable to API Node.Status

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
Currently Node.Status has Capacity, but no concept of Machine Allocable to serve several purposes:
- For Kubernetes 1.0 release, we introduced "/docker-daemon", "/kubelet", "/kube-proxy", "/system" etc. raw containers, so that we could monitor their resource usage pattern, and detects regression easily. In a long run, we want cap their usage uncertain limit / request. We don't do it know because 1) docker is still using tons of computing resource, and consequence of constraint docker's resource consumption is pretty high. 2) There is no NodeSpec yet, and we cannot control Kubenetes nodes, and OSS users might introduce arbitrary daemons to a given node which makes /system unmanageable. Even with above resources, we cannot do a full resource management / control on the node, but introducing Allocable concept to node could prevent real bad resource overcommit.
- For mesos, hadoop, etc. integration, they might want to partition compute resource on a given node, and limit how much Kubelet use; meanwhile they can query kubelet, and reserve some portion of the rest for their own purpose. 

I proposed 
1) Introduce a flag called --allocable-resources to Kubelet for now, and reports Allocable to upstream layers. In a long run, we could replace such flag with more sophisticated configuration through some machine / node3 management components.
2) All upstream control components including scheduler, kubelet should do feasibility checking against Node.Status.Allocable, instead of Capacity. 

cc/ @bgrant0607 @davidopp @sttts @karlkfi @vishh

title: Update annotations in kubelet broke source annotations

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
PR #13334 allows kubelet to update annotations.

This broke mirror pods because they contain the original source annotations.
- Mirror pod contains all annotations from the original static pod, including `config.source: file`
- When the config watcher first sees the mirror pod from the apiserver, it sets the `config.source: api` to the annotations in the mirror pod and caches it.
- The next time, the config watcher would compare the mirror pod with the copy in the cache, and sees the difference:

```
existing: map[string]string{"kubernetes.io/config.mirror":"mirror", "kubernetes.io/config.seen":"2015-09-11T19:10:12.335167065Z", "kubernetes.io/config.source":"api"}
new: map[string]string{"kubernetes.io/config.mirror":"mirror", "kubernetes.io/config.seen":"2015-09-11T19:09:21.926288705Z", "kubernetes.io/config.source":"file"}
```

The config watcher would then think this is an update and trigger a kubelet pod sync. The mirror pod would also be mistaken as regular pod later on in kubelet, causing more attempts to create a mirror pod. These extra syncs and operations may have caused the cpu spikes observed in #12429

Kubelet should always overwrites the source annotation before comparing existing and the new pods at the config watcher.

body:
Whenever a client is requested from the client cache, it negotiates a version with the API server (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubectl/cmd/util/clientcache.go#L63).  For longer latency connections, this adds noticeable delays to every `kubectl` command to gather information that doesn't change very often.  If we don't change our approach, this problem will be exacerbated by API groups and discovery.

Instead of requesting the information every call, we could cache the api-version information locally.  Based on that cache, the client could choose a preferred version and simply force the `RESTClient` to that particular version.  If we update the API server to add additional headers to the 404 returned when an invalid version is specified, the client could unambiguously know that the api-version is no longer valid.  At that point we could clear the cache, give a good error message, and re-populate it on next `kubectl` command.

I like the idea of a separate cache instead of re-using something like a kubeconfig file, because there's no real reason for user intervention.  I'd like to allow our tooling to mutate the local cache at will and kubeconfig files aren't the right place to make those kinds of modifications.

title: Impossible to completely eliminate insecure access to apiserver

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
The apiserver listens, by default, on 127.0.01:8080 in a completely insecure manor. Even if the scheduler, controller-manager, proxies, kubelets, etc are all configured to use the secure port the apiserver still talks to itself on the insecure port.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go#L340

This is how things like the admission controllers (part of the apiserver) talk to other parts of the apiserver. The problem with having the apiserver talk to itself over the insecure port is that means we cannot block the insecure port from everything else on the host. Any user able to log into the machine running the api-server can connect to the insecure port and do anything they want. Blocking all access to 8080 with iptables means admission controllers and such stop working.

There may be many solutions, but the basic problem is I want to turn off all insecure access to the apiserver.

@liggitt suggested some form of privileged kubeconfig the apiserver would use to talk to itself

It might also be possible to create a unix domain socket pair which only the apiserver could use to talk to itself in an 'insecure' manor similar to how it is currently using the insecure socket, but which everyone else on the host couldn't use.

title: Fix writing secrets in containerized kubelet

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Currently when kubelet is running in a container writing secretes doesn't work. The problematic workflow is:
1. Kubelet mounts `tmpfs` as a secret volume using `nsenter_mounter` in host's namespace
2. Kubelet reads secretes from API server
3. Kubelet tries to write secretes to the newly created volume, but as it resides in host's namespace it fails.

This will be solved with https://github.com/docker/docker/pull/15648, but before it happens we will need some temporary solution. One workaround is to use `nsenter` to write data similarly to how we have mounted it.

This is a blocker to run kubelet and other k8s components as docker containers, which should greatly simplify UX for new setups.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

body:
The rate limiter parameters are DeletingPodsQps and DeletingPodsBurst in
cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/controllermanager.go. The defaults should allow 10 NotReady nodes to have their pods evicted right away, and 1 NotReady node every 10 seconds thereafter.

It's very possible these values are too aggressive. For one thing, they really should be expressed as a percentage of cluster size, not in absolute numbers--since our max supported cluster size is currently 100, we will remove all the Pods in the largest cluster in 900 seconds, and even sooner in smaller clusters. The rate should probably be something like 10% of the cluster every 5 minutes. And the number of nodes per time interval should possibly be exponential rather than constant, so that we can start off very slowly.

ref/ #13412

title: We should handle flaky cloud provider APIs more gracefully

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
From: jonathanbweeks@gmail.com
... we experienced a catastrophic failure this morning when our in-house OpenStack cloud team went to upgrade from Juno to Kilo, and the OpenStack API went away for a period. (We are running Kubernetes on top of Openstack for our internal private cloud.)

We are still trying to completely grok the sequence of events, but from logs and source code inspection (we are on K8s 1.0.1):
1. The kubelets on each node periodically poll the cloud provider API to get network/IP interface information. When the API went away, this update starting failing, causing them to be marked as "Not Ready" by the controller-manager. This would be bad, as it would lead to the scheduler obviously not being able to schedule pods on the affected nodes (eventually all nodes)

However, it is exacerbated by:
1. The controller-manager eventually then ends up evicting (AKA killing) all pods on every "NotReady" node after a timeout (which is quickly all nodes in the K8s cluster)

This means that the entire cluster basically offs itself in a misguided violent purge. (But no one ever expects the Spanish Inquisition).

This issue was at least partially captured today in the IRC, and a related issue logged here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/13398

Now clearly, Openstack should have an HA API and allow seamless rolling upgrades, but cloud providers will likely have occasional unplanned API downtime, and kubernetes needs to be more tolerant and robust in the face of that (at the very least, not kill all running pods :)

We looked at various timeout config settings, but there seemed to be non-trivial side-effects to setting them to "high" values (we continue to investigate this). As a workaround, we are patching our kubelet to keep posting status even if the cloud provider is unavailable and will submit a pull request.

body:
During my work around to fix #12526, it comes to me that postStart life-cycle handler does not work as I expect. Here's the case:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: resouer/myapp:v6
    lifecycle:
      postStart:
        exec:
          command:
            - "cp"
            - "/app/myapp.war /work"
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /work
      name: test-volume
  - name: web
    image: nginx
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /work
      name: test-volume
  volumes:
  - name: test-volume
```

I mean to start two containers in a Pod, and then copy a file from 'nginx' container to Empty_dir volume.

But this handler will lead the container to Terminated status:

```
Containers:
  nginx:
    Image:                      resouer/myapp:v5
    State:                      Waiting
      Reason:                   CrashLoopBackOff
    Last Termination State:     Terminated
      Exit Code:                137
      Started:                  Mon, 31 Aug 2015 22:17:27 +0800
      Finished:                 Mon, 31 Aug 2015 22:17:58 +0800
    Ready:                      False
    Restart Count:              1
    Variables:
  web:
    Image:              nginx
    State:              Running
      Started:          Mon, 31 Aug 2015 22:11:48 +0800
    Ready:              True
    Restart Count:      0
    Variables:
```

It seems postStart command is a exec that will replace the original CMD (`nc -l -p 60001` in this case) , and Pod will then think the container is killed (137).

But as we defined the handler as a postStart, there seems no intention that we want to terminate the original process. So, is it designed to be like this, or I misuse the postStart here, or a bug?

title: Experimental API client should be part of the client.Interface

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Currently the experimental API client is a separate entity from the stable client interface.  This causes problems if anything in the experimental API needs to be accessed by any component of kubernetes.  The only way a kubernetes process can access anything in the experimental API is to change the function signatures for anything that needs access to the experimental API.  This has large consequences for anything using/launching that component as well as any test case that uses that component.

An easy example here is anything that is namespaced.  If you add a new entity that is namespaced, you need to modify the namespace controller to accept an experimental client which impacts all sorts of other bits that invoke a namespace controller, like the mesos integration and tests.

title: URLs that only point to a GitHub directory do not show in the navigation menu on kubernetes.io

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

body:
**Problem**

URLs that do not specify the full URL (URLs that point to a directory and exclude the filename README.html), do not display in the navigation menu. 

In the GitHub repo, the corresponding REAME.md file automatically opens. On GitHub Pages where Kubernetes.io is hosted, corresponding index.html files get displayed (someone has added in renamed copies of the README files (index.html) to avoid 404 errors) but those URLs are not listed/found in the navigation menu. We can only define a single URL in the navigation menu, either */README.html or *index.html. 

**Example**

Example of incomplete URL:  
"http://localhost:4000/v1.0/examples/guestbook-go/", which is found in the "go implementation" link at the top of http://localhost:4000/v1.0/examples/k8petstore/README.html

**Solutions**

In order to get the navigation menu to recognize the incomplete URLs, we need to either:

(1) Fix each URL (although we might continue to see these errors since this is a GitHub repo convention):
- Since the GitHub repo contains the README.md files, we can update each URL in all of the source .md files to include the missing README.md filenames.  

(2) Programmatically detect the URL and find the topic in the nav menu (possibly more effort but will resolve the commonly used GitHub convention if used in the future):
- Add in some javascript to detect these types of URLs, assume the URL is missing "README.html", and then automatically append "README.html" the URL so it maps to an entry in the nav menu.  
  - This should happen in the [findcurnavitem()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/gh-pages/_layouts/docwithnav.html#L18) function so that each time it is called the URL will match entries in the navigation menu (so it gets highlighted and automatically scrolled to).

title: storage.Interface leaks error abstractions

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
`genericetcd` abstracts a key value store, but it does not transform the errors returned (which are needed by callers):

```
    if err := e.Storage.Create(key, obj, out, ttl); err != nil {
        err = etcderr.InterpretCreateError(err, e.EndpointName, name)
        err = rest.CheckGeneratedNameError(e.CreateStrategy, err, obj)
        return nil, err
    }
```

and 

```
    if err := e.Storage.Get(key, obj, false); err != nil {
        return nil, etcderr.InterpretDeleteError(err, e.EndpointName, name)
    }
```

are examples where lower level errors are converted to higher level conditions (because we Get before Deleting to check certain conditions).

Callers still have to handle etcd errors today.
### In general:

Our higher level kv abstraction is really `genericetcd`, so `storage.Interface` is only useful in the context that it provides the primitives `genericetcd` needs.  Having `storage.Interface` support base KV primitives is great, but the granularity of the `storage.Interface` should be matched to `genericetcd` (Or generickv).  An example is guaranteed update - a store that has a built in patch primitive like mongodb or can do JS on the server side would be _better_ at implementing the genericetcd.Update logic than `storage.Interface#GuaranteedUpdate` - so there is no point in having a lowest common denominator storage interface that makes a hypothetical generic KV impl slower than our generic etcd.

/rant

  "kube-up" with AWS ought to build out a highly available and multi-AZ kubernetes cluster following AWS EC2 best practices. There are two large steps to this:

I am only focusing on goal #1 here. These changes center entirely in cluster/aws/util.sh. However, I will need to modify the actual provider code in Go because, while AWS ELBs are brought up with the proper subnets, it appears they do not have multi-availability zone routing enabled.

Thanks!

title: Add more probe control parameters

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.2-candidate
milestone.description: Things to consider for next minor release.

body:
Resurrected from #66 and #761.

Probe currently supports the following control parameters:

```
    // Length of time before health checking is activated.  In seconds.
    InitialDelaySeconds int64 `json:"initialDelaySeconds,omitempty" description:"number of seconds after the container has started before liveness probes are initiated; see http://releases.k8s.io/HEAD/docs/user-guide/pod-states.md#container-probes"`
    // Length of time before health checking times out.  In seconds.
    TimeoutSeconds int64 `json:"timeoutSeconds,omitempty" description:"number of seconds after which liveness probes timeout; defaults to 1 second; see http://releases.k8s.io/HEAD/docs/user-guide/pod-states.md#container-probes"`
```

We should add the following common control parameters (matching, for instance, [AppEngine's parameters](https://cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/managed-vms/config#health_checking) and [GCE's parameters](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/reference/latest/httpHealthChecks)):

```
// How often to probe
PeriodSeconds *int64
// Minimum consecutive successes for the probe to be considered successful after having reached the FailureThreshold; defaults to 1; must be 1 for liveness 
SuccessThreshold *int
// Minimum consecutive failures for the probe to be considered failed; defaults to 1
FailureThreshold *int
```

At some point we'll probably want to add an enable/disable boolean, since it's convenient to be able to disable liveness probes without losing the parameter settings, but that's less critical than the above.

title: kubelet should only trigger relevant pod workers for pod spec changes

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Currently, kubelet receive a set of desired pods through the update channel, and blindly triggers all pod workers to sync as well as performing global cleanup. This is inefficient because a single pod change would engage N workers (goroutines), assuming there are N desired pods. Each worker performs a series inspection which swamps Docker, slowing down the reaction to the actual pod change. I did a simple experiment which showed that there was at least ~30% less SyncPod calls when only the relevant pod workers were called.

Kubelet should react to different type of pod changes according and dispatch the work to relevant pod worker:

```
ADD -->  pod admission -->  pod worker dispatcher
UPDATE --> update validation  -->  pod worker dispatcher
REMOVE --> kill pod worker/cleanup
```

The cleanup work includes removing orphaned pod directories/volumes etc.

In today's kubelet, all the work is done in SyncPods (pod admission/validation/dispatcher and global cleanup). I recently broke down the code in `SyncPods` into functions to isolate the different utilities (#12560) as the precursor for eliminating `SyncPods`. If we separate the each component, there is no need for the `SyncPods` function to exist.

In addition, kubelet needs to know what kind of spec change it receives (ADD/UPDATE/REMOVE). In fact, the [kubelet/config] module (which watches various sources) supports all different update types, however, for reason unknown to me, kubelet is restricted to only receive the SET operation with all pods included in one update. Due to the lost of information, kubelet is forced to [derive the sync type](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/pod_manager.go#L125) later in the code (reverse-engineering!). One way to solve this is to restore the operation types and use them properly.

Known caveats: 
- Handle kubelet restarts
- Handle mirror pods

Marking this p1 because this is a relative low-hanging fruit with potential to improve kubelet's performance significantly.

milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
As the title suggest, if for some reason docker ran into trouble pulling the image (could happen on private registries where all nodes are trying to pull a big  image at once), resulting in `docker images` showing the size of the image as `0 bytes` causes kubelet to be stuck in an infinite loop of trying to start the pod and failing with the following **docker** generated error:

```
Aug 13 17:18:54 minion1 kubelet[26303]: E0813 17:18:54.728489   26303 manager.go:1579] Error running pod "frontend-ba0f5_default" container "frontend": no such image
```

And this repeats endlessly.

To FIX: The administrator of the cluster can go into that particular node and `docker rmi` that image that shows `0 bytes`.  Ideally kubelet would do the same and carry on with life.

Doing the above manually fixes the issue and brings the pod up.

body:
Forked from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/12236.
@davidopp suggested introducing a DisruptionBudget object in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/12236#discussion_r36825964:

> will it be possible to construct enforceable SLOs if each controller that can cause disruptions has 
> a separate disruption budget spec? (An example of another such controller is rescheduler, but I'm sure there will be others, e.g. maybe one that takes machines offline for kernel upgrades.)
> 
> It seems that we may want a new object that lets you define arbitrary collections of Pods (using label
> selectors) and specifies a correspond disruption budget (maxUnavailable like you have here, max rate of churn, etc.). The Spec for this object would be the budget, and the Status would be the
> number currently down or current churn rate or whatever. This object could be owned by a service that controllers ask permission before they initiate a disruption, or the logic for checking if it is OK to disrupt and updating the status could be implemented in a library that is used by all the controllers that
> cause disruptions.
> 
> How will DisruptionBudget in Deployment work? What if a DisruptionBudget (or whatever) object already exists that covers 
> (some of) these Pods? Does it override the one specified in Deployment? (i.e. you only 
> create DisruptionBudget if it doesn't exist?) Is it an error to specify a disruption budget in Deployment if there is a DisruptionBudget object for (some of) the Pods covered by the Deployment object?

In Deployment, we are currently using a maxUnavailable field. We can eventually switch to using a DisruptionBudget.

cc @bgrant0607

https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/pull/9594/files#diff-e77d382a51b51741c1c2b9803fb68fa2R159 introduced the ability to let a single field contain multiple names separated by a literal " or ".

Any client or UI that uses the name of a field in a returned error to correlate errors with inputs will be unable to parse that.

title: Proposal: Make pod log endpoint more useful

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.1
milestone.description:
Release 1.1.

P1 features:
* 250+ nodes, at our published SLO
* kube-proxy perf. improvements (via IPTables)
* Docker 1.8.x
* Horizontal pod auto-scaling
* Job
* Ingress
* Schema validation in kubectl
* Experimental API and API groups
* Graceful pod termination

body:
The Pod log endpoint on the apiserver and Kubelet was implemented as a simple wrapper around Docker logs.  It's intended to provide easy access for users and administrators to the logs of the currently running execution of a container in a pod.  If there is no running execution, it will show the last execution.  There are two flags supported:
- `?follow=true/false` instructs docker to leave the connection open and stream new changes until the container exits or the log connection is closed by the consumer
- `?previous=true/false` uses the previous execution of the container to display logs

When not following logs, the default Docker behavior of returning the entire log file is preserved (Docker `tail=all`).  We currently suppress the timestamp shown by Docker (because the logs may already contain timestamps).
## Problems today:
- A container may generate many megabytes of logs which must be transferred to the client every time the user runs 'logs'
- A container running for several days may generate periodic logs, but a user is only interested in the last few hours
- A user may wish to see when a log statement was generated, but not have added timestamps to their logs themselves

Types of containers and typical uses:
1. Run-once containers are typically used to run jobs - for most users, seeing the entire log of a completed job is useful, or watching the logs until their fail
2. Run-forever containers are usually used to run services - users typically:
   1. want to debug something that has happened recently, or watch for something that has already happened
   2. want to analyze their logs across a larger band of time by searching / scanning for particular behaviors

Finally, for existing systems there may be log aggregators that provide access to historical logs for a pod/container across multiple attempts or deep history.  It would be desirable in the future to be able to abstract access to deep logging in a way that clients can remain oblivious.
## Consuming use cases
- OpenShift is looking to expose log retrieval / scanning via its web console
- OpenShift is looking to integrate ElasticSearch so that it can be used for multi-tenant historical log retrieval, with a simple integration (via the existing log APIs) and then for all other queries via a secured proxy that imposes query restrictions to the elastic search api.
## Suggested changes

To better support clients that want to handle limiting the amount of bulk data they receive, target logging to specific areas of user interest, or more accurately represent the time a log line happened, we should expose a limited subset of the features Docker already supports for log retrieval to allow windowing of requests, without limiting the future ability of the system to be backed by an external log solution.

Minimize the impact to existing runtimes by choosing simple operations that can translate to systemd, Docker, or other local container log systems.

Non goals: 
- Do not build a full log query system
- Do not return structured logs

Consider exposing the following from the Kubelet and the pod logs api:
- `since=<relative or absolute timestamp>` - allow a client to indicate the range of time within which to retrieve logs.  Serves as a useful bound when retrieving historical logs (or, in combination with another flag, to retrieve ranges of logs)
- `tail=<limit>` - starting from the end of the log, return only the X most recent entries. Is valuable for reducing the impact of trying to fetch the logs. Leave default "all" as per Docker
- `timestampn=true/false` - whether to prepend each log entry (line?) with a timestamp
- (potential) `limit=<bytes or lines>` - only return log entries (lines?) until this many bytes or lines have been received, then terminate the connection

title: Pod Cleanup Can Sometimes Delete Content from Persistnet Volumes

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
While trying to reproduce #11231 I ran into a similar issue where content from the mounted volume was getting deleted. It turns out that the rapid creation/deletion of the pod exposes a race condition when results in the volume content getting deleted here https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1315

To fix this we should of course fix the race condition but I also thing it is worthwhile creating a special Remove/RemoveAll which checks to see if the file is under a mount point and/or check for a special lock file which protects content form kube cleanup and prints a warning to the logs. The reason is that while the bug rare and easy to fix the loss of user data is a high cost.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
Update and query semantics have far too many magic numbers which are fairly arbitrary.
e.g. rate limits such as qps and max-requests-inflight, as well as update intervals 

Ideally clients should be able to use back-pressure to determine their update rate within some bounds and back-off where necessary.

Use case in point, when we load balance API-servers we eliminate many of the performance bottlenecks and it clearly shows that the api-server, not etcd, is the gating component.

apiVersion: v1

title: 6 minute TTL for proxy tunnels is bad experience for long-lived connections

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body: We close tunnels 6 minutes after they are opened (1 minute after the 5 minute refresh). A long-lived connection (e.g. `kubectl exec ... -i -t -- bash`) will be forcibly closed anywhere from 1 to 6 minutes after it is started. The new support for attach in kubectl will also run into this.

title: PD tests flaky on `release-1.0` branch

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

title: Rename GCE target pools and forwarding rules to match $CLUSTERNAME prefix convention

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Most GCE resources that k8s creates have a prefix of $CLUSTERNAME, which allows people to get a basic understanding of why a resource exists and what it's used for.  Target pools and forwarding rules do not, which is an ongoing tax with running jenkins tests along with a poor UX.

We should rename them to match convention.

And we should be backwards-compatible so that existing clusters can be upgraded.

title: kubernetes deletes info from all NFS shares when one of the mounts becames stalled (google container engine)

body:
When mounting several shares over NFS to container and when one of the directories is deleted from NFS server, something in the node is deleting content from other shares. I suspect that something goes wrong with "cleanupOrphanedVolumes"? not sure tough.

Use case: php-app is running in container, uses php-sessions for remembering login. php sessions are stored in file and shared through nfs-share between containers. also app code is shared and several other directories to store different data (data dirs are mapped under code, code is in separate share so generated document files don't get to git tree), all is managed by separate integration server (in container), that uses same shares to prepare the code.

This happened first time in GCE with Cluster API version 0.17.something, now it acts same on 1.0.1 and 0.18.2. Problem is repeatable:
First of all you need to install package "nfs-common" to **all cluster nodes**, otherwise you can't map NFS shares at all:

```
apt-get update && apt-get install nfs-common
```

now you need nfs server. I created small instance for that with /etc/export stating:

```
/export     10.240.0.0/16(rw,sync,crossmnt,no_subtree_check)
```

also I made directories under /export/test/:

```
#ls -la ubuntutest ubuntutest2 ubuntutest3
ubuntutest:
total 12
drwxrwxrwx  2 root root 4096 Aug  3 15:07 .
drwxr-xr-x 12 root root 4096 Aug  3 15:06 ..
-rw-r--r--  1 root root 1580 Aug  3 15:06 testifail
ubuntutest2:
total 12
drwxrwxrwx  2 root root 4096 Aug  3 15:06 .
drwxr-xr-x 12 root root 4096 Aug  3 15:06 ..
-rw-r--r--  1 root root 1580 Aug  3 15:06 testifail2
ubuntutest3:
total 12
drwxr-xr-x  2 root root 4096 Aug  3 15:07 .
drwxr-xr-x 12 root root 4096 Aug  3 15:06 ..
-rw-r--r--  1 root root 1580 Aug  3 15:07 testifail3
```

next you need ubuntutest.yaml to start it up (replace nfs server ip with your own):

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  labels:
    name: zubuntu
  name: zubuntu
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    name: zubuntu-rc
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        name: zubuntu-rc
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Always
      containers:
        - image: tutum/apache-php
          name: ubuntu-cont
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
              name: web-port
          volumeMounts:
            - name: test-nfs-1
              mountPath: /app
            - name: test-nfs-2
              mountPath: /app2
            - name: test-nfs-3
              mountPath: /app3
      volumes:
        - name: test-nfs-1
          nfs:
            server: 10.240.175.237
            path: /export/test/ubuntutest
        - name: test-nfs-2
          nfs:
            server: 10.240.175.237
            path: /export/test/ubuntutest2
        - name: test-nfs-3
          nfs:
            server: 10.240.175.237
            path: /export/test/ubuntutest3
```

now start up the pod:

```
kubectl create -f ubuntutest.yaml 
kubectl get pods
```

verify, that the directories are mapped:

```
kubectl exec -ti zubuntu-8y55c bash
# ls -la /app*
/app:
total 12
drwxrwxrwx  2 root root 4096 Aug  3 18:07 .
drwxr-xr-x 69 root root 4096 Aug  3 18:09 ..
-rw-r--r--  1 root root 1580 Aug  3 18:06 testifail

/app2:
total 12
drwxrwxrwx  2 root root 4096 Aug  3 18:06 .
drwxr-xr-x 69 root root 4096 Aug  3 18:09 ..
-rw-r--r--  1 root root 1580 Aug  3 18:06 testifail2

/app3:
total 12
drwxr-xr-x  2 root root 4096 Aug  3 18:07 .
drwxr-xr-x 69 root root 4096 Aug  3 18:09 ..
-rw-r--r--  1 root root 1580 Aug  3 18:07 testifail3
```

now the funny part:
remove directory from nfs server

```
 # rm -rf ubuntutest
```

the zubuntu pod shows:

```
# ls -la /app*
/app:
ls: reading directory /app: Stale file handle
total 0

/app2:
total 12
drwxrwxrwx  2 root root 4096 Aug  3 18:06 .
drwxr-xr-x 69 root root 4096 Aug  3 18:09 ..
-rw-r--r--  1 root root 1580 Aug  3 18:06 testifail2

/app3:
total 12
drwxr-xr-x  2 root root 4096 Aug  3 18:07 .
drwxr-xr-x 69 root root 4096 Aug  3 18:09 ..
-rw-r--r--  1 root root 1580 Aug  3 18:07 testifail3
```

nothing happens on nfs server yet, but just launch the stop command:

```
kubectl stop -f ubuntutest.yaml 
```

and now nfs server shows:

```
# ls -la ubuntutest ubuntutest2 ubuntutest3
ls: cannot access ubuntutest: No such file or directory
ubuntutest2:
total 8
drwxrwxrwx  2 root root 4096 Aug  3 15:18 .

you see, that one file was left, but not for long. this is because root in client does not have root access in nfs-file system, but just after giving rights, the file is gone:

body:
Doing things like `kubectl replace` requires a lot of logic in `kubectl`, such as waiting for RC to scale pods down by polling before deleting the RC itself.

Putting this in `kubectl` makes it hard to replicate in clients written in other languages to get consistent behaviour. Moving this to the api server would mean consistency across languages. 

For background, we created the Java Kubernetes client in fabric8 (https://github.com/fabric8io/kubernetes-client) & I've also contributed to the Ruby client at https://github.com/abonas/kubeclient). Having consistent behaviour means replicating undocumented functionality across clients which seems a bit dirty.

milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
We had a few bugs where we would get into loops which would cause us to get into fast-retries loop, and often we would exhaust AWS API quota.  Sometimes this would even cause AWS to send a warning email.  e.g. #11979 

@brendandburns suggested in https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/11979#issuecomment-126502901 that:

> We should probably add a rate limiter into the AWS client, like we did for GCE:
> https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/util/throttle.go

That seems like something we should have; we should obviously fix any bugs which cause fast-retry loops, but we should have a second layer-of-defense as well.  Also if someone launches a thousand services which require an ELB each, we want to respect the AWS API rate limits, even if we don't have a bug per-se.

title: Horizontal pod autoscaler basing on scale subresource

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/autoscaling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Autoscaling.

milestone.title: v1.1
milestone.description:
Release 1.1.

P1 features:
* 250+ nodes, at our published SLO
* kube-proxy perf. improvements (via IPTables)
* Docker 1.8.x
* Horizontal pod auto-scaling
* Job
* Ingress
* Schema validation in kubectl
* Experimental API and API groups
* Graceful pod termination

body:
We are going to introduce Scale subresource and implement horizontal autoscaling of pods on a base of it. Scale subresource will be supported for RCs and Deployments. HorizontalPodAutoscaler object will be bound with exactly one Scale subresource and will be autoscaling associated RC/deployment through it.
### Scale subresource

Scale subresource will be present for RC or deployment under the following paths:
`api/vX/replicationcontrollers/myrc/scale`
`api/vX/deployments/mydeployment/scale`

It will will contain the following fields: 
`Spec(Count)`, `Status(Count, PodSelector)`

Writing `Spec(Count)` will resize RC/deployment associated with the given Scale subresource.

`Status(Count)` will report how many pods are currently running in RC/deployment, and `Status(PodSelector)` will return selector for the pods.
### HorizontalPodAutoscaler object

We will introduce HorizontalPodAutoscaler object, it will contain the following fields:
`Scale`, `MinCount`, `MaxCount`, `TargetCPUConsumption`.

The autoscaler will be implemented as a control loop. It will query pods described by PodSelector from Status of Scale subresource, and check their average CPU usage from the last 1 minute on heapster (there will be API on master for this purpose). Then, it will compare the current CPU consumption with the TargetCPUConsumption, and adjust the count of the Scale if needed to match the target (preserving condition MinCount <= Count <= MaxCount).
