title: kubelet should be able to hit GCE's v1 metadata server instead of v1beta1

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
GCE's v1beta1 metadata API is no longer documented and probably doesn't have a whole lot of life left. However, GCE's container VM image relies on the kubelet to be able to talk to the metadata server when using it as a manifest URL, and is going to need it to continue working. The [v1 metadata API](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/metadata?hl=en#querying) requires the caller to specify the HTTP header "Metadata-Flavor: Google".

We need to make the kubelet able to attach this header when talking to the GCE metadata server.

title: The waitForOp() function in gce.go should be more robust against transient failures

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
Right now, a single 500 trying to get an operation treats the entire operation as a failure. Granted, downstream clients should be reconciler-ish enough to handle these types of errors, but the gce package could be nicer.

This, plus #9382 was causing us to leak resources. After #11891, we aren't leaking resources, but we still can expose some weird behavior because of the retry logic in the service controller.

I'd propose that we only actually fail operation polling when we get 5 consecutive errors (polling once per second).

title: Document how Secrets are stored and how to secure them

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

body:
For purposes of security and compliance, it's important to my organization to understand how sensitive information is stored, and what the attack vectors are for someone to compromise the secrets.

In the current documentation, it doesn't make any mention of where Secrets are stored at rest. Are they in etcd? Are they stored in plaintext, or are they encrypted?  If they're encrypted, where does the key live?

In other words, if I was an attacker trying to gain access to the Secrets stored in kubernetes, how could I read them and/or change them?  Also, what best practices should an admin put in place to block an attacker?

title: kubernetes-ui: Dashboard gauges don't display if cluster contains nodes without persistent filesystems

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
In my test cluster with 2 minions where one does not have any permanent storage (running CoreOS with a RAM only file system) the UI gauges for all nodes fail to render leaving a Kubernetes Dashboard with an empty white 'content' pane.  The The exception I received in chrome was:

```
TypeError: Cannot read property 'length' of undefined
    at maxMemCpuInfo (app.js:919)
    at app.js:840
    at Qn (base.js:22)
    at Function.ke (base.js:22)
    at $scope.getData.k8sApi.getMinions.success.angular.bind.$q.all.then.$scope.loading (app.js:837)
    at u (base.js:6)
    at base.js:6
    at $.$eval (base.js:7)
    at $.$digest (base.js:7)
    at $.$apply (base.js:7)
```

The line throwing the exception is:

```
      for (var i = 0; i < fsDataArray.length; i++) {
```

This appears to be caused by the 'filesystemData' attribute returned by cadvisor being null.  I was able to resolve the issue by creating a disk backed root overlay on my RAM only node.

body: Rogue kubelets can make N failure events (e.g., out of disk, can't mount secret, can't garbage collect) every poll loop, which can completely overload a kube-apiserver. We should rate limit these.

title: Support rollover

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
Forked from #1353. Needed for Deployment #1743.

Rollover is a generalization of rolling update, where one replaces N replication controllers with one new one.

Scenarios:
- rolling update, pause in middle, create a patched image, perform a rolling update to replace the original image and the botched image
- Deployment: change desired state and kick off rolling update, then change desired state again before it finishes

title: Discuss: Decide the future of "service" spreading.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
Various people risen similar concerns about current spreading semantics:
Currently we do spreading only on Services (and on resources, but that's orthogonal thing), i.e. if scheduling is trying to schedule a pod from some Service (which is defined as existence of a Service that has a selector matching given pod), we'll try to schedule it on a different machine from other pods of this Service (again - meaning pods that has label set matching Service selector). We don't handle the case of multiple services matching the same Pod very well (i.e. we deterministically pick effectively random one - first Service from the list). In principle this is a correct behavior which, I believe, all of us want to preserve. The problem is that it requires users to create services before creating underlying Pods/RCs, which turns out to be not natural (e.g. pretty much all examples create Pods before Services).

This situation was noticed as a problem by multiple people already:
#11144, #10667, #4971

Current logic was introduced by:
#1965

"Short" summary:
#1965 was about spreading by Services as currently implemented instead of identical label sets as it was before. Argument (@bgrant0607) for doing it was:

> This (i.e. full label-set spreading) works well with a single replication controller, but breaks down when one runs canaries, multiple release tracks, rolling updates, etc.

This may indeed be a problem, to : having canary Pods with additional `type: canary` label will make canaries completely independent from production Pods, thus allowing coscheduling of them on the same Node. Not everyone was convinced that this would be a bad thing.

 #4971 was a discussion about why spreading by RC might be more desired than spreading by Service:
@abhgupta

> I had raised the question of why we used services instead of replication controllers for identifying peer pods for spreading by the scheduler. The argument is that services might not be needed and could be avoided in some cases, whereas replication controller will most likely always be there.
> While I agree that there can be multiple replication controllers per service, I still believe that spreading of pods should still happen independently for the replication controllers. Also, we have customer use cases where the services are not created at all and routing/load balancing to a group of pods is being handled by custom middleware.

@bgrant0607 

> Falling back to spreading using the full set of labels on a pod (which would also likely be the labels specified by a replication controller's selector) is a reasonable thing to do in absence of a service.

@danmcp 

> I would certainly want a rolling deployment to schedule independent of any existing replication controllers. Because what matters to me there is that the deployment when it's done is scheduled to the best fit location. I don't care much about the deployment overlapping with the existing deployment for some period of time.
> All else being equal, spreading based on service is reasonable. But it seems like a tertiary concern with the order being:
> 1) spread by replication controller (and whatever other labels you choose to require spreading on)
> 2) provide a reasonably good fit
> 3) spread by service

@bgrant0607 

> Of course, in the case that there is just 1 replication controller, spreading by controller labels is reasonable. However, the controller/service decoupling enables multiple replication controllers to exist indefinitely, which is typical for applications with multiple release tracks (e.g., daily and weekly), which is common for "high-functioning" DevOps teams.

This ended up with creation of headless services, which allow user to create a "Service" that do not proxy anything, but act as a definition of Pod peering. This provides a workaround for the spreading problem, assuming that users will know/remember to create Service before RCs. There's also an important question what's the 'good' level of spreading, i.e. do we want to allow canaries to run on the same machines as production jobs, or do we want to try to schedule them somewhere else. I believe that most people think that the latter is a better option.
#10667 was originally written as a quick fix for 0-limit pod scheduling, which was problematic before @davidopp changed the resource usage computation slightly. What it does is effectively implement @bgrant0607 idea of spreading using 'full set of labels' in the absence of a Service (even though I didn't knew about it when I wrote it).
#11144 was opened by @marekbiskup after speaking with some users and was documentation/example driven. It made @bgrant0607 to update some docs, but examples are still left with wrong order.

@brendandburns suggested going back to the spreading from before #1965:

> We should really spread by label sets, and not just services. That will ensure that we do spreading for both cases and things won't be order dependent.

@davidopp noted:

>  Do you mean any time two Pods have the same value of the same label, we should try to put them in different machines? (...) This is an interesting idea. I think we need to revamp the whole spreading approach post-1.0 so we can take into account multiple levels of the hierarchy (spread across nodes, across various kinds of failure domains, etc.). So we'd have to think about how this could generalize.

I created this issue to have a discussion here, instead of splitting it between multiple other Issues/PRs.

cc @thockin

title: Implement the steps necessary for publishing docs to gh-pages (out of master)

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
As part of the release process, we need to process our .md files, specifically our user-facing documentation under the "docs" and "examples" folders in the master branch, and then copy them over to a release specific folder in the gh-pages (for example, the v1.0 folder is "v1_0" and the corresponding HEAD folder is "vHEAD".

The gh-pages directory structure will be match master with the exception that there will be a version specific container folder at gh-pages root. For v1.0, we need to copy all files into the 'v1_0' and 'vHEAD' folders.

View my fork(WIP) for the current test build: [http://richieescarez.github.io/kubernetes/v1_0/index.html](http://richieescarez.github.io/kubernetes/v1_0/index.html) _(note that ive manually fixed the .md files to get this staging site to work so it contains many broken links and missing files (ie. files in subdirectories of "docs" and all of vHEAD is missing))_

For V1.0, we will utilize the GitHub Pages build (which is a Jekyll build) and to do so, we need the following in order to deliver for v1.0 GA:

(1)
Every file file requires front matter (in every .md file - _for GitHub Pages/Jekyll build to recognize and process the file_). The layout we will use will be located here: gh-pages root > _layouts > [docwithnav.html](https://github.com/RichieEscarez/kubernetes/blob/gh-pages/_layouts/docwithnav.html).

To use that layout for each of our .md files, we need to run a script to insert the "docwithnav" attribute to the top (line1) of each file:

```
 ---
 layout: docwithnav
 ---
```

(_[view example here](https://github.com/RichieEscarez/kubernetes/tree/gh-pages/v1_0)_)

(2)
All the links in each of the .md files, must be process to replace pointers to *.md with *.html. (issue: https://github.com/github/pages-gem/issues/69)

This should cover all types of relative, anchor, and markdown style links (and not affect any external URLs). In order to keep links between files working, we should continue to use relative links so that files only link to those that correspond to that release version (within the same folder in gh-pages root).

Alternatively, we can hard code in the absolute urls and version's folder using `{{ site.url }}`/_vFolderVersion_/*relative_link_here.html.

Examples:  
Links like (but not limited to):

```
`[link text](../filename.md)`
```
- [example](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RichieEscarez/kubernetes/gh-pages/vHEAD/index.md)
  
  `[Getting Started Guides](docs/getting-started-guides)`
- [example](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RichieEscarez/kubernetes/gh-pages/v1_0/README.md)

Must be changed to:

   `[link text](../filename.html)`

   `[Getting Started Guides](docs/getting-started-guides/README.html)`

(3)
Once the .md files are processed (front matter added and links fixed), then in order for us to be able to publish on kubernetes.io, we must copy those processed .md files into the corresponding folders in gh-pages (for v1.0, thats the 'v1_0' folder).

title: Tests to verify that existing pods/services continue to function across cluster resize and/or upgrade

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
We have tests that verify that things work before and after resize, but AFAIK don't sufficiently ensure that everything in the cluster continues working properly in the steady state after an upgrade. #11327 is an instance of a bug where within the first 30-60 seconds after a resize or upgrade, external load balancers on GCE will continue working, but after target pool changes have had time to propagate, they'll stop working.

This issue could just encompass keeping a cluster up for a few more minutes after upgrade/resize to verify the steady state of everything that existed before the upgrade, or it could be something like @mbforbes keeps pushing for -- a soak cluster that doesn't just create and delete resources, but with a bunch of long lived resources.

```
INFO: Wanted all 0 pods to be running and ready. Result: true. Pods: []
```

I'm guessing this was related to the big namespace change? When moving all of the pods out of the default namespace we must have forgotten to update all of the tests that check the infrastructure pods.

title: AWS EBS volume data is deleted in certain cases

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
Hello!

  Kubernetes sometimes deletes all data from my EBS backed volume. Given a controller like so:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  labels:
    name: nginx
  name: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    name: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        name: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: nginx
        name: nginx
        volumeMounts:
        - name: nginx-store
          mountPath: "/var/nginx"
      volumes:
      - name: nginx-store
        awsElasticBlockStore:
          volumeID: aws://REGION/VOLUME_ID
          fsType: ext4
```

One would expect data in "/var/nginx" to persist, however, it doesn't appear to persist when the pod moves between hosts.

Running `kubectl stop pod nginx-ID` works _most_ of the time, but when the pod moves between hosts I see an event like so:

```
Thu, 09 Jul 2015 20:02:57 +0000   Thu, 09 Jul 2015 20:02:57 +0000   1         nginx-f26t2   Pod                                                         failedSync         {kubelet REDACTED}   Error syncing pod, skipping: Error attaching EBS volume: VolumeInUse: VOLUME_ID is already attached to an instance
                                  status code: 400, request id: []
Thu, 09 Jul 2015 20:02:57 +0000   Thu, 09 Jul 2015 20:02:57 +0000   1         nginx-f26t2   Pod                 failedMount   {kubelet REDACTED}   Unable to mount volumes for pod "nginx-f26t2_default": Error attaching EBS volume: VolumeInUse: VOLUME_ID is already attached to an instance
```

The interesting part is that the EBS volume _does_ re-attach to the system the pod is moving to and it _does_ mount properly - it just has no data in it when it is mounted (as if its been `rm -rf`ed)

I am learning Go and eager to grok the Kubernetes codebase a bit, so I wanted to take a stab (more of a wild guess). My suspicion is this code: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/530bff315ff034d0c9098004f35f01d26ab40aaa/pkg/cloudprovider/aws/aws.go#L1316-L1322

It seems to me that if we receive an error message we `return`, which prevents us from reaching `waitForAttachmentStatus`. I get the feeling this causes a race wherein the new pod boots up _while_ the volume is being attached. This would account for my seeing this fairly rarely. It seems to me Kubernetes should block the entire pod creation process while it waits for the disk to be mounted to the correct Node. Instead, it sees the AWS failure and continues on its way.

Any thoughts? Thanks for your time!

body:
First of all, Reason (everywhere in the API) is intended to be a concise, single-world, CamelCase categorization of the status. However, Kubelet is producing phrases, which more properly belong in a Message field. For example:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/7bb9cdf660a00e231d9dcd1a7c9c5985399fb977/pkg/kubelet/dockertools/manager.go#L458

```
                Reason: fmt.Sprintf("Image: %s is ready, container is creating", image),
```

Secondly, important cases are somehow being dropped. Here's an example of a single-container pod, where the container must be Waiting, probably during image pull:

``` bash
$ kubectl get pods
NAME          READY     STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
hello-world   0/1       Running   0          7s
```

kubectl get pods shouldn't say "Running" for pods whose images aren't pulled.

Not sure if the reason is being clobbered or something else is happening:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/7bb9cdf660a00e231d9dcd1a7c9c5985399fb977/pkg/kubelet/dockertools/manager.go#L469

body:
This is a follow up from https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/10265#issuecomment-118595068

There I was asking about documentation on serviceaccounts and certificates. I have already read http://docs.k8s.io/design/service_accounts.md (and a few others), but still there are lots of questions:
- Is the CA certificate in `--root-ca-file=` authenticated by the key in `--service-account-key-file=`?
- If so, I cannot create the `--service-account-key-file=` on the host automatically via a systemd.service unit, unless I also automatically create the `--root-ca-file=` via a systemd.service, correct?
- Is the missing `ca.crt` secret in my default serviceaccount the same as the one I would hand to the kube-controller-manager via `--root-ca-file=`?
- Will I have to distribute these files to the client I run kubectl on?
- Will the kube-controller-manager and/or the kubelets automatically create certificates for themselves signed by `--root-ca-file=`?
- If so, how do I control which host is allowed to get such a certificate, and which will not be allowed to join the cluster?
- How is the certificate for connection with a client kubectl created? Do I need to also automatically create a client certificate using a systemd.service and then fetch the file using e.g. ssh?
- If so, I assume the automatic generation of the key as laid out in the examples is not actually recommended, as it is utterly cumbersome?
- I read that on GCE you use Salt to distribute the (manually created) root certificates. Is there any convenient way to do this on a bare-metal CoreOS cluster? Writing a properly indented `write_files` directive for `cloud-config` appears unflexible and cumbersome on its own.
- Is all authentication between the Kubernetes master (kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler) and the kubelets and kubectls handled via HTTPS and client certificates?

The following question was already answered by @satnam6502 in https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/10265#issuecomment-118595167, but I mention it here for completeness (in case someone wants to write down docs or a FAQ):
- What is the `token` of the serviceaccount being used for?

> One of the uses of the token is to make it more convenient to issue things like curl commands to the API server or application endpoints (e.g. Elasticsearch and KIbana logging endpoints). See https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/getting-started-guides/logging-elasticsearch.md

body:
#10659 for further details.

Copy of comment there:

"Totally agree - soak tests are good place to do this sort of thing, and relatively straightforward. In fact, irrespective of soak tests, an e2e test that checks resource usage and/or response latency of system components (see discussion at end of #10471), and fails if these are out of specification would be both simple to write and generally very useful. It could/would:
1. run concurrently with other e2e tests during pre-merge checks to catch egregious performance regressions before merging,
2. run repeatedly against soak test clusters and detect slow resource leaks like those detailed in #10659 
3. run in our normal serial and parallel e2e tests to detect inconsistent performance/resource usage characteristics of the system, which are typically also an indicator of non-good stuff.

title: --ignore-not-found should not be needed for `kubectl delete all`

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/pull/8628 introduced breaking behavior to `kubectl delete all --all`

It isn't good to require users to specify `--ignore-not-found` in the normal case of deleting all replication controllers (which cascade to pods), then getting NotFound errors on previously resolved pods. Anyone who had previously scripted `kubectl delete all --all` will now get a failure.

I think `--ignore-not-found` should default to true when used with `--all`. Since the user is not specifying a particular resource name, they just want everything found removed, I think ignoring NotFound errors captures the intent.

title: Remove non-mergeable fields from .kubeconfig (such as preferences)

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
As per #9298, there are two fields (Preferences and CurrentContext) in kubeconfig which are destructive when kubeconfigs are merged and prevent clean and transparent merging of kubeconfig files. We should pull out these fields to support the use case of more merging of kubeconfig files (#9298).

.kubeconfig currently holds two kinds of data:
- Maps of data that are _fully mergable_ (save for conflicts across files, which can be considered an error):
  - Clusters - a map of referencable names to cluster configs
  - AuthInfos - a map of referencable names to user configs
  - Contexts - a map of referencable names to context configs
- Unmergeble data that would overwrite each other if merged:
  - Preferences - holds general information to be use for cli interactions
  - CurrentContext - the name of the context that you would like to use by default

By pulling out Preferences and CurrentContext, we can arbitrarily merge in .kubeconfigs in any order without worrying about overwriting or confusion/anger (like that described in #4428).

The proposed design:
- For all non-kubectl programs (kubelet, controller manager, etc.), CurrentContext is either inferred when there is only one context, or something passed in as a command line parameter. It is treated just like any other config param for the program. 
- For kubectl, CurrentContext can be merged into the Preferences struct (since it's really just another kubectl preference), and the Preferences struct can be moved to a new file, ~/.kubectl. It can also be set at the command line or as an env var, given how important a Preference it is.
- For backwards compatibility, if the CurrentContext field is specified in kubeconfig it can continue to be respected (I don't think Preferences is even used anywhere yet), but all our examples/docs/auto-generated kubeconfig files would be updated to not contain it.

I believe this should be in 1.0, if we can resource it.

title: Release validation (running Jenkins on release branches)

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
I spent a little while thinking about this this morning, while working on finally writing up #1883. I would really like us to get in a state where we have a job hitting the N-1 release branch (where "N" is head). So today, it would be helpful if something were actually running against `release-0.20`. 

In particular, I think this requirement isn't just "run against the release". I'd like the cherry-pick procedure to become "cherry pick into release branch, wait for Jenkins to chew on it a while", rather than the existing "run e2es manually", because then the procedure for cherry picks and normal releases is pretty similar (you cut from the branch, always - it's just a matter of which branch you're cutting from).

One of the complications here is that the hack I introduced for "latest" continuous integration was `latest.txt`. If we were just to run `./build/push-ci-build.sh` on a release branch, you'd end up disturbing a bunch of Jenkins jobs.

I propose that `latest.txt` stays as head, but that for branch builds we could do `latest-<branch>.txt` in the CI bucket with a pretty fast modification to the script. (The actual bucket would then be unordered madness, but I'm not actually worried about that part.)

Then we could setup `kubernetes-build-release` Jenkins job, and a `kubernetes-e2e-gce-release` Jenkins job fairly quickly.

This issue is going to get larger as our releases are longer. It would be really nice if cherry picks were just gradual, i.e. people could just propose pull requests to the branch, we could dribble them in and gradually validate, then pull a new patch release.

cc @ixdy @quinton-hoole and cc @mikedanese because of recent involvement in latest.txt fun.

Note: This job is basically the analog of the `gke-test` job, but instead of happening _after_ the release is cut, it happens _before_. _shocking_

title: Idle cluster, CPU usage increasing

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Over the course of ~ 18 hours, my idle cluster's CPU usage went from ~5% -> ~20%. I repeated it with another cluster, which seems to have a single node with increasing CPU usage. 

Surprisingly, kubelet seems to be the hog. I used pprof to figure it out. It turns out to be the **exec based liveness probe** that the kube-dns pod uses. Turning that off makes kubelet stop using so much CPU. The before & after pprof chart was very clear.

I don't have an answer for why the usage grows over time; maybe docker keeps some history such that every exec returns a bit more data than the previous one?

title: Images from a private repository on GKE are not visible to pods within the same project

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
Hi guys, I'm trying to pull an image to a container cluster on GKE from private repository hosted on GKE under the same project, but getting errors that the image is not found. More specifically, I've created a cluster using Deployment Manager and verified that it works:

```
gcloud container clusters describe dev-cluster | grep '<project_id>\|endpoint\|zone'
endpoint: 104.196.xx.xxx
- https://www.googleapis.com/replicapool/v1beta2/projects/<project_id>/zones/us-east1-b/instanceGroupManagers/gke-dev-cluster-08e6bd03-group
selfLink: https://container.googleapis.com/v1/projects/<project_id>/zones/us-east1-b/clusters/dev-cluster
zone: us-east1-b
```

I also made sure that the correct cluster credentials are received:

```
gcloud config set container/cluster dev-cluster
gcloud container clusters get-credentials dev-cluster
kubectl cluster-info
Kubernetes master is running at https://104.196.xx.xxx
...
```

The IP addresses above are the same. After that, I build a docker image locally using the name us.gcr.io/<project_id>/<image_name> and push it to GKE under the same project using

```
gcloud docker push us.gcr.io/<project_id>/<image_name>
```

then verify it on a different system by authenticating on gcloud using the same <project_id> and pulling, which completes successfully and displays the same digest id.
However, when I try to create a pod within the cluster using

```
kubectl create -f pod.yaml
cat pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: <pod_name>
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: <container_name>
    image: us.gcr.io/<project_id>/<image_name>
```

it doesn't create the pod, displaying

```
Failed to pull image "us.gcr.io/<project_id>/<image_name>": image pull failed for us.gcr.io/<project_id>/<image_name>, this may be because there are no credentials on this request.  details: (Error: image <project_id>/<image_name>:latest not found)
```

The same error is displayed when I ssh to these nodes and try to `sudo docker pull`.
What gives? Perhaps there's something I'm missing, but the documents specify that the credentials should be automatically configured for the nodes in a project on GCE/GKE: https://cloud.google.com/container-engine/docs/clusters/operations#passing_cluster_credentials_to_kubectl

Thanks a lot

title: Upgrade the kube bot to identify flakes and open issues automatically

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
Most of the triage of flakes looks like:
1. Have a PR, observe various failures in tests
2. Open an issue (or link to an existing issue), extract relevant snippets, back reference it to the current issue, give it the right labels, 
3. Rerun the tests

It would be nice to automate / unify this process with a command to the k8s-bot... instead of saying:

```
k8s-bot unit test this
```

say

```
k8s-bot unit test flake

> copy and pasted excerpt of the failing test
```

and the bot would spawn the issue, link to the previous PR log run and the current issue, add the snippet to the issue description, and kick off a new test because of the flake.

Some other things we could do are track flakes more formally (maybe have the submit-queue display the list of known flakes?) and track metrics on specific ones reported.  And have a searchable list of builds that are displayed as flakes?

Ultimately, we need to make flakes the responsibility of everyone to squash dead as soon as they're found, and we should have tools to find and identify the flakes as much as possible.

title: Kubectl GET HPA CPU Current isn't refreshed properly under Non Successfully POD creation scenario

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/autoscaling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Autoscaling.

body:
Testing Kubernetes in GKE, I think I encountered an issue related with the behaviour of the HPA in Kubectl, and particularly with the data reported by Kubectl GET HPA CPU Current that isn't refreshed properly under Non Successfully POD creation scenario. 

I was doing some load testing against one of my GKE Instances (1 simple, n1-standard-1 (1 vCPU, 3.75 GB memory)), GKE Kubectl version 1.1.2.

Under this environment, Kube-system namespace consumed about 770m during the Resource allocation (CPU Requests/Limits) running fluentd / heapster / dns / kube-ui / kubedash / l7-lb, being the rest available for the default namespace (that contains my own pods). 

I had 4 pods with some DefaultRequest limits of 50m, and initially I had configured a HPA to scale one of my pods up to 3, when the CPU Utilization reaches the target of 60%. 

Then, I launched the load testing against the system. The result was that after a couple of minutes, the system triggered new replicas but none of them was successfully created. 

Under this scenario, not only the new two replicas were not successfully created but also the `kubectl get hpa` was reporting wrong information (after the load testing was finished and the load reduced, the CPU didn't update to its actual value and the new replicas were not terminated). 

I verified that heapster was indeed reporting the right data (/api/v1/model/metrics/cpu-usage and so). I would have been expecting the pods to be cleared, and the HPA Current being refreshed according to the new data.

title: Cloud provider API downtime still leads to NodeNotReady

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
I'm experiencing the same issue as #16593 but with OpenStack, using Kubernetes 1.1.3. Since that issue is closed and was filed as AWS-specific, I'm opening a new one. #13417 was supposed to fix it and is included in release 1.1.3 (despite having been reverted in master), but it doesn't seem to work properly (as @antoineco also reported in #16593). Also related to issues #13398 and #13412.

In short, cloud provider API downtime leads (seemingly) to minions failing to update their status, being marked as NodeNotReady, and evicting all pods from them. This can happen to all minions in the cluster at about the same time, and can lead to semi-disastrous situations (such as a pod being unable to start on a new node after recovery, because its persistent volume couldn't be detached from the previous node due to the API being down).

Relevant logs:

```
Dec 27 16:28:26 cluster03.s.xxxxxxxxx.com kubelet[929]: E1227 16:28:26.189013     929 kubelet.go:2340] Failed to get addresses from cloud provider, so node addresses will be stale: Expected HTTP response code [200 204] when accessing [GET https://compute.gra1.cloud.ovh.net/v2/xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx/servers/detail?name=%5Ecluster03%5C.s%5C.xxxxxxxxx%5C.com%24&status=ACTIVE], but got 500 instead
Dec 27 16:28:26 cluster03.s.xxxxxxxxx.com kubelet[929]: {"computeFault": {"message": "The server has either erred or is incapable of performing the requested operation.", "code": 500}}
Dec 27 16:28:26 cluster03.s.xxxxxxxxx.com kubelet[929]: E1227 16:28:26.230604     929 kubelet.go:2291] Error updating node status, will retry: node "cluster03.s.xxxxxxxxx.com" cannot be updated: the object has been modified; please apply your changes to the latest version and try again
```

```
Dec 27 16:28:07 master.xxxxxxxxx.com kube-controller-manager[513]: I1227 16:28:07.320025     513 event.go:206] Event(api.ObjectReference{Kind:"Node", Namespace:"", Name:"cluster03.s.xxxxxxxxx.com", UID:"cluster03.s.xxxxxxxxx.com", APIVersion:"", ResourceVersion:"", FieldPath:""}): reason: 'NodeNotReady' Node cluster03.s.xxxxxxxxx.com status is now: NodeNotReady
```

(I'm not sure why the controller-manager changes the node status 19 seconds before the kubelet itself logs an error, but the two always happen at about the same time. The machines' clocks are properly synchronized and the controller-manager has no cloud-provider config specified)

title: Optimization in copy: structs with only primitives (no pointers) can be bulk assigned

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
DeepCopy is used in our etcd caching path, watch paths, and cache store paths.  Some of my upcoming changes (#17922) remove it from the decode critical path except in certain cases.  

Right now it's roughly ~3us and ~25 allocations to perform a copy:

```
BenchmarkPodCopy-8                            300000          4308 ns/op        3280 B/op         25 allocs/op
BenchmarkNodeCopy-8                           300000          3706 ns/op        2464 B/op         18 allocs/op
BenchmarkReplicationControllerCopy-8          300000          3908 ns/op        2960 B/op         22 allocs/op
```

That's not terrible, except this is the most expensive operation in those paths today in terms of master CPU.  A few optimizations to deep copy are worth experimenting with:
- Replace individual primitive assignment of structs with bulk assignment (not sure how well this is optimized)
  
  ```
  func deepCopy_v1_AWSElasticBlockStoreVolumeSource(in AWSElasticBlockStoreVolumeSource, out *AWSElasticBlockStoreVolumeSource, c *conversion.Cloner) error {
      out.VolumeID = in.VolumeID
      out.FSType = in.FSType
      out.Partition = in.Partition
      out.ReadOnly = in.ReadOnly
      return nil
  }
  ```
  
  with copy assignment 
  
  ```
  func deepCopy_v1_AWSElasticBlockStoreVolumeSource(in AWSElasticBlockStoreVolumeSource, out *AWSElasticBlockStoreVolumeSource, c *conversion.Cloner) error {
      *out = in
      return nil
  }
  ```
- Inline public methods for deep copy instead of reflection (nested s.DeepCopy() calls)
- Have all objects expose DeepCopy() method instead of reflection, generate them into individual packages
- Use copy() on arrays of primitives
- Inline common copies? (compiler should do that)

title: Defaulting is 35% of total conversion time and ~10% of total decode time

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Running a before (on top of #19047) and after with defaulting removed from our generated code (not generated), total conversion time drops significantly, and number of allocations is halved.

```
benchmark                                      old ns/op     new ns/op     delta
BenchmarkPodConversion-8                       14676         9143          -37.70%
BenchmarkNodeConversion-8                      12712         7005          -44.89%
BenchmarkReplicationControllerConversion-8     15129         10460         -30.86%

benchmark                                      old allocs     new allocs     delta
BenchmarkPodConversion-8                       81             49             -39.51%
BenchmarkNodeConversion-8                      74             38             -48.65%
BenchmarkReplicationControllerConversion-8     79             53             -32.91%

benchmark                                      old bytes     new bytes     delta
BenchmarkPodConversion-8                       9011          5170          -42.63%
BenchmarkNodeConversion-8                      7267          3425          -52.87%
BenchmarkReplicationControllerConversion-8     9236          5906          -36.05%
```

We should only generate defaulting for objects that have them, and we should inline to public methods (like #19047) rather than going through reflection.  It's likely we can realize most of the before / after improvements with no reflection.  With protobuf in place (#17922), conversion is going to be the slowest part of decode/encode (~9us for pod conversion, 6us for proto deserialize, 5us for defaulting, and 1-2us overhead).

body:
If a container is waiting for an image to be pulled before it can start, it would be nice to see the progress of that pull in kubectl, so that the user can know if they have time for another cup of coffee.

An api endpoint to give a progress update, possibly with a watch option, would be ideal.
It would also be helpful to include this in the container information in each pod.

For example, running `kubectl desribe pod/<pod>` should return, in addition to all info currently returned, a field containing the % pulled (or number of bytes) of the image that each container uses.

Additionally, running `kubectl pull-progress pod/<pod>` should return a json encoded summary of each image being pulled in order to start a pod. This should also support a watch option, to notify the client of changes in the progress. There should be an equivalent HTTP API endpoint for this.

I'm interested in using this capability to provide loading bars on a UI.

# 
# Requirements:

GPU is important to lots of workloads, such as machine learning, video stream decoding/coding, etc... But Kubernetes doesn't support schedule/tracking it which need to be.

```
    1). Kubelet need to provide the GPU hardware information along with the CPU, memory information to the Master. 
    2). Each GPU only have 2 status, in using or not in using. This is because so far GPU only exist in /sys/fs/cgroups/devices, 
        so 1 GPU is the smallest unit we can assign to container.

2. Scheduler support.
    1). To schedule Pods based on GPU, scheduler need to know the below information:
        a. How many GPUs and what types are they on each Node.
        b. What the status (in/not in using) of the GPUs on each Node.
    2). Device mapping. Once know which Node have GPUs could be used, need to map the right GPUs to container, like the "--device" in Docker. To mapping the GPU to
        container, we may need to know below things.
        a. the phsical devices, like /dev/nv0, /dev/nv1 ... This information should be provided by kubelet, kubelet on each Node provides GPU information. And I think 
           we also need to provide more information to ensure the app in container could works fine with the assgined GPU, information like "Vendor ID/Device ID, 
           subsystem_device/sybsystem_vendor".
```

  - containerPort: 80
    devices:
      name: gpu
      type: nvidia
      number: 1

When I rebooted the master instance through the AWS API it did come back online (the instance took 30 minutes to reboot, but I don't think that's a k8s issue).

title: AWS - EC2 API DescribeInstances outage brought down clusters in region

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
On `2012.12.18` the AWS region us-east-1 experienced an outage affecting service of the DescribeInstances and DescribeTags APIs. This is turn brought our two independent clusters operating in the region, as [the Kubelet AWS clustering mechanisms](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7069a811164f68473dd1b94ee2b2abc169e35d81/pkg/cloudprovider/providers/aws/aws.go#L2100-L2119) rely on the DescribeInstances API. Networking was unaffected - master and nodes could still communicate without problem.

I propose that this AWS failure should not bring down a cluster.

The relevant Kubelet log message:

> Error updating node status, will retry: failed to get node address from cloud provider: no instances found for name: ip-_-_-_-_.ec2.internal

There are several issues that relate to this functionality. I am filing this issue to ensure that Kubernetes is not needlessly vulnerable to this type of outage.

_Possibly Related_
#17643 use private ip instead of local hostname for AWS
#18525 We shouldn't use node names as addresses

Incident details from http://status.aws.amazon.com/

> 1:02 PM PST We are investigating elevated latencies and error rates for the DescribeInstances and DescribeTags APIs in the us-east-1 region. Customers may observe elevated error rates or missing tags for instances in the AWS Management Console.
> 1:44 PM PST We have identified the root cause of elevated latencies and error rates for the DescribeInstances and DescribeTags APIs and are currently working to resolve. Customers may observe elevated error rates or missing tags for instances in the AWS Management Console.
> 3:03 PM PST Between 12:30 PM and 2:44 PM PST, we experienced elevated latencies and error rates for the DescribeInstances and DescribeTags APIs. During this period, customers may have observed elevated error rates and missing tags for instances in the AWS Management Console. During this event, instances continued running normally. Tags requested during this period are now visible. This issue has been resolved and the service is operating normally.

title: Scheduler should use node `Allocatable` instead of `Capacity`

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.2-candidate
milestone.description: Things to consider for next minor release.

body:
We added a new field to `NodeStatus`: `Allocatable`. Allocatable represents the _schedulable_ resources on a node, while capacity is the total resources on a node (including resources claimed by non-k8s workloads, such as kernel usage, container runtime, and other native processes). More details here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/proposals/node-allocatable.md

`Allocatable` [defaults](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/api/v1/defaults.go#L202) to `Capacity` when not set, so this change will be backwards compatible with Kubelets that don't set `Allocatable`.

/cc @dchen1107 @davidopp

title: Change scheduling complexity from O(containers) to O(nodes)

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
So far the scheduling algorithm complexity is O(containers) -- not O(pods) nor O(nodes). The scheduling latency becomes higher as more containers/pods get scheduled -- last time we observed 20 ms on 0 pods and it increased to 200ms on 30k pods.

After fixing #18255, #18452, #18466, #18413, #18170, and making use of scheduler test suite #18458, we found that majority of time was spent on `PodFitsResources` and `PodFitsHostPorts` as well as the GC burden they brought.

The root problem of both is that they list all containers for every schedule decision -- O(containers). With caching the entire nodes to pods map and aggregated requested resource of a node and incremental updating, they could be optimized to O(nodes) logically the same.

After optimizing only `PodFitsResources`, we are able to reduce the scheduling latency to 20ms. The scheduling rate doesn’t decrease much as more and more pods get scheduled. The benchmark results:

```
BenchmarkScheduling100Nodes0Pods-4           200           5530781 ns/op
BenchmarkScheduling100Nodes1000Pods-4        200           7058672 ns/op
BenchmarkScheduling1000Nodes0Pods-4          100          15344940 ns/op
BenchmarkScheduling1000Nodes10kPods-4        100          20022489 ns/op
BenchmarkScheduling1000Nodes20kPods-4        100          19291019 ns/op
BenchmarkScheduling1000Nodes29kPods-4        100          24107608 ns/op
```

Before optimized, `PodFitsResources` computes pod request for every node, lists all containers for every node, and calculate aggregated requested resource to compare it with pod request. We added a cache for aggregated requested resource of every node. When a pod is assumed, scheduled, or deleted, a watch based update is made upon the cache. Finally we just consume from the cache along with iterating the nodes. We also reused the cache for `MapPodsToMachines` in `findNodesThatFit` -- optimized from listing all pods to watch based incremental updates.

There are still places for improvement: latest profile output showed that `PodFitsHostPorts` is still a large consumer of cpu cycles; @wojtek-t mentioned in scheduler test suite that listing tens of thousands of pods can potentially affect scheduller performance; priorityFuncs are still O(containers); etc.

Latest benchmark result on master (0f22ba4be3ed9077de3662ab1086a97695ad3a4c):

```
BenchmarkScheduling100Nodes0Pods-4           200           6049842 ns/op
BenchmarkScheduling100Nodes1000Pods-4        200          10174731 ns/op
BenchmarkScheduling1000Nodes0Pods-4           50          22099051 ns/op
BenchmarkScheduling1000Nodes10kPods-4         20          85206355 ns/op
BenchmarkScheduling1000Nodes20kPods-4         5          220729042 ns/op
BenchmarkScheduling1000Nodes29kPods-4         5          211274674 ns/op

```

[benchcmp](https://godoc.org/golang.org/x/tools/cmd/benchcmp) shows our improvement:

```
benchmark                                 old ns/op     new ns/op     delta
BenchmarkScheduling100Nodes0Pods-4        6049842       5530781       -8.58%
BenchmarkScheduling100Nodes1000Pods-4     10174731      7058672       -30.63%
BenchmarkScheduling1000Nodes0Pods-4       22099051      15344940      -30.56%
BenchmarkScheduling1000Nodes10kPods-4     85206355      20022489      -76.50%
BenchmarkScheduling1000Nodes20kPods-4     220729042     19291019      -91.26%
BenchmarkScheduling1000Nodes29kPods-4     211274674     24107608      -88.59%
```

``` go
    // Work out the location of the Docker runtime, defaulting to /var/lib/docker
```

title: Creating a new API group is really hard

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Creating a new API group is really hard.  I'll keep this description up to date as I go through the pain.
1. You have to know to add yourself to the `import_known_versions.go` files in multiple packages to get included.
2. You have to manually update these files to get the generated output:
   1. `hack/after-build/update-generated-conversions.sh`
   2. `hack/after-build/update-generated-deep-copies.sh`
   3. `hack/after-build/verify-generated-conversions.sh`
   4. `hack/after-build/verify-generated-deep-copies.sh`
   5. `hack/update-generated-swagger-docs.sh`
3. You have to manually create `types.generated.go` in every internal and external package to get codec-gen to work.
4.  You have to update `pkg/api/registered/registered.go` to be allowed to install your group.

That's just to get your types registered.  Right now, there's no pluggable way to include custom `RESTStorage` into the API server for my new types.

title: kubernetes service endpoint not in sync with master ip

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
Our apps running on kubernetes is not working after we restart one of the app's service.  After some debugging, we found that the root cause is due to wrong service endpoint of 'kubernetes' service, which is not the master's internal IP address.  This causes trouble for skyDNS to update records for the app service.

We have to manually update etcd to correct the 'kubernetes' endpoints.  During the process, we also found that API server keeps updating etcd to the wrong IP address, so we have to restart API server in order to make the correction.  (we initially thought it is controller manager that does the update, but it turns out to be apiserver).

I'm not entirely sure why master internal IP changed, it could be DHCP.  But it doesn't make sense for kubernetes to forcibly change to wrong IP, did we cache the information aggresively in api server?

title: Ability for the scheduler to place BestEffort pods on nodes with lower utilization

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
I would like the scheduler to make better decisions on what nodes get `BestEffort` pods by taking into account a the node utilization and not just `node.status.allocable` or `node.status.capacity` to further reduce the risk of starving incompressible resources on my node (memory or disk).

If a node has been scheduled to use all of its `node.status.allocable` value, but actual utilization on the node is nowhere near what was allocated, then the scheduler will prioritize placing `BestEffort` pods on that node versus another node that is actually having greater utilization relative to its allocable limit.

Right now, the scheduler is blind as to what node is best capable of supporting a `BestEffort` pod because their utilization impact on the node is not accounted for when making a scheduling decision.

If the node could publish the following values:
- `node.status.capacity` - the total capacity of the node
- `node.status.allocable` - the amount reserved for scheduling pods

To support this solution, we would need a final design solution for reporting node utilization per the PR proposal here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/18634

Then we can make better choices, and further reduce risk of OOM on the node.

**UPDATED** - clarified this has a dependency on Metrics API

title: Timeouts for e2e tests running in a parallel environment

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Many e2e tests running in parallel environments have been experiencing timeouts recently (e.g, #17656). I am not sure if there has been any change in the jenkins settings that have increased the parallelism, @kubernetes/goog-testing would know more. I did notice that image pulling has become the bottleneck quite often since we started serializing the pulling to work around docker bugs (#10959). Instead of bumping the timeouts aggressively, could we do something else instead? For example,
- Upgrade to docker 1.9 (https://github.com/docker/docker/issues/9718)
- Pre-pull images before the tests start
- Disable serialized image puller (this would result in occasional flaky test as discussed in #10959)
- Lower the number of concurrent tests for the test suites

/cc @kubernetes/goog-node

title: `kubectl patch` does not work with admission controller LimitRanger and ResourceQuota

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
REPRODUCE 

latest release v1.1.2
1. Start apiserver with command line `--admission-control=NamespaceLifecycle,LimitRanger,SecurityContextDeny,ServiceAccount,ResourceQuota`
2. Create a pod with

```
kubectl --namespace=rds create -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx
  namespace: rds
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
```

Then try to change Pod `nginx`'s image with

```
kubectl --namespace=rds patch pod nginx -p '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"nginx","image":"nginx:1.9.7"}]}}'
```

Output is

```
Error from server: Pod "Unknown" is forbidden: [Minimum cpu usage per Pod is 1.  No request is specified., Minimum memory usage per Pod is 2Gi.  No request is specified., Maximum cpu usage per Pod is 8.  No limit is specified., Maximum memory usage per Pod is 16Gi.  No limit is specified.]
```

After remove `LimitRanger` from apiserver's command line, repeat `kubectl patch`, the output is

```
Error from server: Pod "Unknown" is forbidden: resource name may not be empty
```

Again, remove `ResourceQuota` from apiserver's command line, repeat `kubectl patch`, the output is `"nginx" patched`

Related resourcequota and limits for this namespace is 

```
$ kubectl --namespace=rds describe limits
Name:           rds
Namespace:      rds
Type            Resource        Min     Max     Request Limit   Limit/Request
----            --------        ---     ---     ------- -----   -------------
Container       memory          2Gi     16Gi    2Gi     2Gi     -
Container       cpu             1       8       1       1       -
Pod             cpu             1       8       -       -       -
Pod             memory          2Gi     16Gi    -       -       -

$ kubectl --namespace=rds describe quota
Name:                   rds
Namespace:              rds
Resource                Used            Hard
--------                ----            ----
cpu                     2               2400
memory                  4294967296      4800Gi
persistentvolumeclaims  0               0
pods                    2               1k
replicationcontrollers  0               0
resourcequotas          1               1
secrets                 1               1
services                0               0
```

I take a look at 

In `pkg/apiserver/resthandler.go#PatchResource`, the admission control kicks in with an _empty_ object, before the `patchedObjJS` is decoded into this object. So `LimitRanger` and `ResourceQuota` admission controllers actually operate on this _empty_ object, which failed the validation.

``` go
        obj := r.New()
        ctx := scope.ContextFunc(req)
        ctx = api.WithNamespace(ctx, namespace)

        // PATCH requires same permission as UPDATE
        if admit.Handles(admission.Update) {
            userInfo, _ := api.UserFrom(ctx)

            err = admit.Admit(admission.NewAttributesRecord(obj, scope.Kind, namespace, name, scope.Resource, scope.Subresource, admission.Update, userInfo))
            if err != nil {
                errorJSON(err, scope.Codec, w)
                return
            }
        }
```

Could this admission control in `PatchResource` be put after the patched object is constructed?

title: Modify conformance test policy to use tests from release branches

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

body:
Currently conformance testing uses the 'conformance-test-v1' branch.  We've run into issues where this branch doesn't get as actively maintained as the release branches.  This is an umbrella issue to cover migrating to a new conformance test policy.  See discussion in #17536 for more details

New conformance tests policy: tests should be run off of the release branch that corresponds to the level of conformance being tested, eg:
- the release-1.0 branch should be used to test that a given cluster conforms up to v1.0
- the release-1.1 branch should be used to test that a given cluster conforms up to v1.1
- conformance tests are not guaranteed to be stable on the master branch, but stabilized once a release-X.Y branch is created

Proposed steps
- [x] update documentation for conformance testing (#14913)
- [x] update conformance test scripts to work according to the new policy
- [ ] ensure conformance tests pass according to the new policy, bug fix / cherry-pick as appropriate
  - [x] release-1.2 branch passes against a v1.2 cluster on AWS
  - [x] release-1.2 branch passes against a v1.2 cluster on GCE
  - [x] release-1.1 branch passes against a v1.1 cluster on AWS
  - [x] release-1.1 branch passes against a v1.1 cluster on GCE
  - [ ] release-1.1 branch passes against a v1.2 cluster on AWS
  - [ ] release-1.1 branch passes against a v1.2 cluster on GCE
- [x] update CI scripts as appropriate
- [ ] cleanup
  - [x] remove hack/conformance-test.sh, cluster/test-conformance.sh

title: Scheduler Performance Testing Proposal

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
We have found that on 1k nodes cluster scheduling takes 60-200 ms and becomes the bottleneck. We want to have a standard way to reproduce scheduling latency metrics result and benchmark scheduler as simple and fast as possible. Only with that can we: 1. figure out underlying behaviors and potential bottlenecks quickly; 2. publish results in a standard way and prevent future performance degradation.

We have the following goals:
- Goal 1: Save time on testing. More accurate scheduling latency.
  - We mock up kubelets and only measure scheduling latency and do not care about the latency to start the pod. This is different from Kubemark -- scheduled pods won’t be run by mocked kubelets. We only need to set up the master components.
- Goal 2: Profiling runtime metrics and find out performance bottleneck.
  - Write scheduler integration test. Take advantage of go test and profiling tools, like cpu-profiling, memory-profiling and block-profiling. This is very fine-grained metrics.
- Goal 3: Reproduce test result easily.
  - We want to have a known place to do the performance related test for scheduler. Developers should just run one script to collect all the information they need. 

We have the following plans for writing scheduler tests:
- density test (by adding a new Go test)
  - schedule 30k pods on 1000 (fake) nodes and 3k pods on 100 (fake) nodes
  - print out scheduling rate every second
  - let you learn the rate changes vs number of scheduled pods
- benchmark (by modifying the existing benchmark in integration or simply add a new one)
  - make use of `go test -bench` and report nanosecond/op.
  - schedule b.N pods when the cluster has N nodes and P scheduled pods. Since it takes relatively long time to finish one round, b.N is small -- level of 10.

We are new to k8s codebase. We also want to know where is the best place (directory) to commit in these tests? 

Any suggestions are welcomed!

title: Handle persistent create route failures and/or route quotas without spamming cloud provider API

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
The kubernetes method that creates routes doesn't handle persistent failures gracefully.  It's in effect a loop that runs once per N seconds, where each loop is: for every route that should exist that doesn't: (gce.create_route etc &):
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ae9f7c8ff895726f5e483449caa55e2e8a4b294e/pkg/controller/route/routecontroller.go#L71

If, e.g. a user has 100 routes quota, but creates a 200 node cluster (or resizes an existing cluster to that size), then the above loop will (a) continuously spam the underlying cloud provider API with create route requests, (b) k8s will happily schedule pods onto nodes without routes, and (c) users have no/little visibility into why nodes/pods aren't working.

P1 would be to stop spamming API calls when route creation persistently failure, because for many providers that's a finite QPS limit and exceeding it can cause other provider requests to fail for that project.  Presumably dropping to ~1 qps or lower would be okay?

@thockin Tim, you understand this space better than I -- can you please triage and file other issues at whatever priority you think appropriate if a single issue is too broad?  (And we'll add better route quota checks to GKE on cluster create, but that's not a perfect fix.)

title: Hung docker daemon yet kubelet remains in 'Ready' status

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
While running density tests against a kubernetes cluster, we will occasionally run into nodes where the docker daemon becomes unresponsive.  Symptoms include:
- `docker ps` hangs
- `kernel: unregister_netdevice: waiting for veth0123456 to become free. Usage count = 1` appears in journal output

Probably an upstream issue.  But I would expect kubelet to notice that its docker deamon is unhealthy and send a 'NotReady' status back up to the controller manager.  Instead, it stays at 'Ready' and the scheduler assigns pods to it, which will stay stuck in Pending.

This is not quite the same as #16601 but our mitigation is the same, we're forced to reboot the node.

title: v2 API proposal "desired vs actual"

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: sig/architecture
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Architecture.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

labels.name: wg/api-expression
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to WG API Expression.

body:
This has come up a bunch in a lot of small ways, and my mind keeps coming back to this idea, so I want to write it down.

In early early kube API we had `desired` and `actual` (or something like that) structs.  Since they were the same struct there were a bunch of things in the struct that were things we didn't want users to set (which eventually became status) and other problems.  As we changed to `spec`+`status`, we lost the concept of "actual" and just folded it into `spec`.

This conflates a couple of ideas and makes it hard to distinguish what the user actually asked for from what was assigned to them.  I am proposing we reinstate that distinction.

I propose that every top-level object (all of them, not just the ones that make sense RIGHT NOW) holds 4 fields (plus ObjectMeta):
- `metadata` - same meaning as today
- `spec` - what the user asked for, with API-defined defaults applied AND NOTHING ELSE.  Every field is available to users.
- `actual` - the exact same structure as `spec`, but with other fields populated  by the system (e.g. nodeName when scheduled, clusterIP when auto-assigned, and so on)
- `status` - same meaning as today

If a user wants to save a pod and move it to another cluster, `spec` is what they want.  If a piece of software wants to know how a pod is operating, `actual` and `status` are what they want.

I chose this layout (which changes the meaning of `spec` because I figured it makes it easier on users to change over, while making it harder for system components (change to `actual`).  This may be wrong, but it's not obvious.  An alternative would be that `spec` means "actual" and `request` means "what the user asked for"; users write `request` and the system writes `spec`.  This has the advantage of software that observes state being easier to change over, but means that users have more pain.  But it is perhaps better to break users, who actually SEE error messages.  Sometimes bigger changes are better because the need to something is obvious (see the bugs people hit with some really subtle v1beta1 -> v1 changes).

It would be nice to make one field writable ONLY by users (create/update) and one field writable only by the system.  We've used binding for scheduling, but there are other things (like clusterIP) that are written directly in-process.  

We could make this round-trippable by embedding `request` under `status` in v1 or even as a new top-level object + sub-resources.

Lastly, there's some question about preserving exactly what the user asked for WITHOUT defaults applied, but I am less sure that is needed or particularly useful.

@bgrant0607 @smarterclayton @lavalamp

body:
Based on #16889 

This issue tracks support for basic disk accounting in kubernetes. Specific work-items are as follows:
## Core Features
- [x] du works today. Use du for all the categories and ensure that it works on both on aufs and overlayfs - [cAdvisor [#962](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/pull/962)]
- [ ] Add device mapper support - [cAdvisor [#959](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/issues/959)]
- [x] Track disk usage of localhost volumes in kubelet. [kubernetes [19741](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/19741)]
- [x] Define a disk manager module in kubelet that will serve as a source of disk usage information for the rest of the kubelet. [kubernetes [19741](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/19741)]
- [x] Ensure that the kubelet metrics APIs (`/stats/summary`) exposes the disk usage information. Add an integration test. [kubernetes [19932](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/19932)]
- [x] Maintain references to originally created Volumes instead of generating from scratch #19741
- [x] Support caching fs metrics in the MetricsProvider #19741
- [x] Expose disk usage information through heapster  
## Clean up items
- [x] Eagerly cache the fs disk results in the resource analyzer.  [kubernetes [19741](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/19741)]
- [ ] Permanently cache ReadOnly fs metrics in the Volume object. Volume objects are re-created on updates
- [x] Add Fs metric support for Secrets [kubernetes [19741](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/19741)]
- [ ] Performance test metrics api 
- [ ] Disambiguate metrics error from "not supported" #20676
- [ ] Prevent expensive metrics collection for a pod from impacting other pods collection and kubelet performance #20675
- [ ] Disambiguate pod volume stats are "empty" from "not yet available" #20679
## Nice to haves
- [ ] volumes that wrap other volumes should delegate
- [ ] Expose disk usage via kubedash (stretch).

title: RegistryPullQPS should have a sane default

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
We've seen several instances now where folks in a crash loop run afoul of GCR's Denial of Service limits (HTTP status: 429), due to a mix of pull policy (e.g. PullAlways) and no configured registry QPS throttle:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bfc60709b1fe69d1d4509f5ba1c83156b84d5c33/cmd/kubelet/app/server.go#L225

There is the customer issue: The kubelet shouldn't eat through a user's QPS quota quite so readily.
There is the registry provider issue: The kubelet shouldn't (D)DoS registry hosts.

This is less of an issue for say GCR than it is for a user's `docker-registry` or DTR instance, which is significantly less HA.

A corollary to this: Does the kubelet do any backoff currently?

body:
Two other notes - Brian and I and a few others discussed defaulting and how that's technically the role of LimitRanger in general (to apply a default to a pod resource).  We discussed having LimitRange evolve into PodPolicy which is the more generic complement to PodSecurityPolicy - to apply simple defaults to pods that are created.  Things that could be defaulted / ranged per namespace:
- node selector
- pod labels
- pod annotations
- environment variables onto pods
- specific secrets
- generic security defaults (vs the more sophisticated defaulting in PSP)

Not a truly generic solution _except_ it allows simple proscriptive control like node selector to be applied by a resource a regular user may not have access to change

title: RollingUpdate fails when no pods are scheduled with percentage based limits

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
See https://github.com/openshift/origin/issues/5787

This is due to rollingUpdate requiring maxSurge or maxUnavailable as seen here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubectl/rolling_updater.go#L213

Despite my dc having this:

``` yaml
strategy:
  resources: {}
  rollingParams:
    intervalSeconds: 1
    maxSurge: 25%
    maxUnavailable: 25%
    timeoutSeconds: 600
    updatePeriodSeconds: 1
  type: Rolling
```

I think the solution is to just set one of the two to 1 if 25% \* pod count = 0. It's a bit difficult to code though, as you would have to track if it was a percentage based input and, if so, minimize it at 1 if the other is not in place. Or create a special case if the pod count is zero, return 1.

One option is to leave the error in place and not allow rollingupdates with percentage based limits when the pod count is zero. If you decide to not change the behavior, I'd recommend adding a more descriptive error message (mention scheduled pods = zero).

title: Nodes test needs to wait for kube-system pods to be running and ready, not just test pods

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
The Nodes test adds and deletes nodes.  This obviously causes re-scheduling events to occur across the cluster.

The nodes test verifies that the pods that it created are successfully ready and running, but it does not attempt to validate that pods in the `kube-system` namespace are ready and running.  In general, it should take a census of all pods running prior to resize, and validate that the same set are ready and running after resize, across all namespaces.

The net result of this means that the test exits with "success" believing that the cluster has been restored.

However, many tests (Reboot tests, I'm looking at you) expect that the cluster is in a sane condition at the start of the test, and they have some low timeouts and other assumptions baked in that get violated if the `kube-system` pods are not running yet.  In particular, reboot only waits `20s` for all of the existing kube-system pods to be running and ready.

This is causing flakes in our reboot e2e tests.

title: Unable to schedule pods in mixed version cluster (scheduler=1.0.7, kubelet=1.1.1-beta.1)

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
When testing a mixed-version cluster it seems that pods will not be scheduled due to an issue with how multiple node conditions are evaluated.

In this case kubelet=v1.1.1-beta.1 and scheduler (and all other components) are v1.0.7.

It seems the issue is surfaced by adding a second node condition (and was also resolved) here:  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/a2570926da1b87856351c783c908c255042a9193#diff-53f28720440ab4b589ef2273346cecfcL139

The v1.0.7 code will always evaluate the status of the last condition in the list (now "OutOfDisk=False"), when it should be checking the "Ready" condition. So now, "Ready" always evaluates to "False".

Then pods fail to schedule with "no nodes available to schedule pods", although `kubectl get nodes` reports nodes as ready.

Not sure if this type of mixed-version use is within the bounds of reasonable, but I'll submit a simple (backported) fix from the above commit in case.
