body:
The umbrella issue for kubelet's scalability: #12540

Kubelet manages and monitors all user pods on a node to ensure their container states meet the desired pod specifications. Every pod and/or container Kubelet manages incurs a certain resource overhead even in the absence of active events (i.e., no spec change or container lifecycle events). The exact per-pod overhead varies based on the detailed pod specification, but in general, such steady-state management overhead of is proportional to the number of active pods/containers. When there no active pods, the resource overhead should be negligible.

Below are some resource usage numbers for the v1.1 kubelet.
## v1.1 Resource Usage*\* (commit: dd1187c3ff9a5)

Cluster setup/workload:
- Three n1-standard-2 nodes on GCE (i.e., 2-core)
- Running all default cluster add-on pods
- 0 and 40 single-container pause pods per node
- 30-minutes measurement period
- The cpu usage numbers are aggregated by ~~10s~~ **_1s**_ intervals
- The working set memory size was hard to measured correctly (see #12422 for details). In the experiments, I set logging level to 0 and lowered the cgroup memory limit of kubelet and docker to create a constant memory pressure, then let them bounce back until the usage was stable. The numbers are approximates and should only be considered as ballparks.
### 0 pause pods per node

|  | median cpu | 95th% cpu | memory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| kubelet | 0.02 | 0.05 | 35MB |
| docker | 0.01 | 0.03 | 35MB |
| kube-proxy | <0.001 | 0.01 | <5MB* |
### 40 pause pods per node

|  | median cpu | 95th% cpu | memory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| kubelet | 0.18 | 0.64 | 55MB |
| docker | 0.01 | 0.62 | 70MB |
| kube-proxy | <0.001 | 0.03 | <5MB* |

_kube-proxy’s memory usage depends on the number of services in the cluster. In this test case, the number of services is 7._

Note that, kubelet syncs all pods periodically, hence even though the median cpu usage tends to be lower, the cpu spikes are significant.
### 90 pause pods per node?

v1.1 does not support 90 pods per node, but I did some rough measurement and the median cpu usage of kubelet and docker combined varies from 0.35 to 1.2 cores -- it was right on the edge of a steep curve. Beyond 70th%, it was consistently > 1.4 core.
### Reaction latency

The latency Kubelet takes to notice a container event (e.g. died) varies and could be up to **10+** seconds, since the sync period is 10s.
## v1.2 Resource Usage Target

For v1.2  we want to set a goal so that we can work towards to it. The goal would affect what approach we pick to tackle the issues.

Below are some tentative targets. Suggestions/comments are welcome.
- Number of pods: 90 pause pods + all add-on pods
- Reaction latency (for majority of the container evens): within 3s
  - This is somewhat arbitrary. We have a pretty long reaction latency today, and we can certainly lower this more _if_ we adopt the docker event stream (#16831). What's an acceptable value?
- cpu usage for kubelet and docker combined:
  - median: 0.2 core (10% of the 2-core machine)
  - 95th%: 0.6 core
  - 99th%: TBD
## Caveats
- The detailed pod spec may affect the resource usage. For example, if every container defines a health check, the overhead of periodic probing may significantly increase the cpu usage. We should also publish the usage numbers of the worst-case scenario.
- We focus on the steady-state resource usage. When there are non-monitoring work involved (e.g. container creation/deletion), the cpu usage would of course increase. We can further restrict the usage by either rate-limiting operations, or set a reasonable cpu share for kubelet and docker. Again, this is not the focus of the issue.
- The built-in cadvisor constantly monitors all containers stats. The cpu usage of cadvisor for 100 pods is not ideal (see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/16296#issuecomment-152365160), but seems tolerable at the moment. We will optimize that if it becomes the bottleneck.
- We will want to optimize the 99th% cpu usage later as well. The current measurements are not very meaningful because kubelet and docker each consumes ~1 core at 99th% cpu usage.
- If we use a smaller cpu measurement interval, we might be able to capture the fine-grained, more dynamic behavior. On the other hand, the measurement overhead would increase.
- The goal will be specifically for docker, but the most of the improvement will apply to rkt as well.

title: How to _not_ create a service account?

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

body:
Is it possible to launch a pod without a service account, or with a null service account?

I've tried creating a serviceAccount and deleting the secret (it is recreated).  I've tried creating a secret without the token line (it is recreated).  Not specifying a serviceAccount means the 'default' serviceAccount is used.

As far as I can tell, every pod created gets full access to the k8s API.  While I know that RBAC are the correct long-term solution here, I think denying a pod all access to the k8s API is a common enough use case that we should be able to support it without telling people to wait for RBAC.

The best I have found is to create the serviceaccount, figure out the randomly named secret, download the secret, modify the token to be 123 (base 64 encoded), and then replace the secret.  But that is very hacky indeed.

body:
Now that #16102 is in, I'm consolidating #15483 and #13339 here, since they're mostly the same work at this point.  There's a lot of stuff, but it's mostly one-liners, wording changes, etc.

Remaining work:
- [x] `build-official-release.sh` doesn’t work for prereleases (#16865)
- [x] Add note to output of `release/cut-official-release.sh` to do stuff in a separate window or tab, like we have in `release/build-official-release.sh`
- [x] `release/cut-official-release.sh` and `release/build-official-release.sh` should use `mktemp`. (#16865)
- [x] clarify when GitHub releases should be marked as latest release versus pre-release (#16930)
- [x] Docs in release language need to point to branch, not tag, per @bgrant0607 (#16930)
- [x] we should probably just never call a release “Candidate"; it's confusing what's a candidate and what's not (#16930)
- [x] use ./ notation for ./release/build-release.sh (#16930)
- [x] `push-official-release.sh` doesn’t work for prereleases (#16919)
  - Note that `kube::release::gcs::verify_release_gt` doesn't know how to compare with pre-releases, so it needs to look a lot more like `kube::release::gcs::verify_ci_ge`, (and we should consider collapsing them somehow).

Lower priority or bigger issues:
- [x] Not doing any release notes for beta, since it’s not clear from where we’d start them.
  - Yup, I don't think this is a problem.
- [x] `release/latest-1` and `release/latest-1.0` didn’t get updated to 1.0.7; we should investigate why and fix it.
  - I believe this was just an artifact of our tooling not being used.  As long as we follow instructions in the future, we should be good.
- [x] “Copying release artifacts to gs://kubernetes-release/ci/v1.2.0-alpha.3/“ sometimes hangs, maybe when `gcloud` isn't up-to-date?  This needs further investigation.
  - Filed #16936.
- [x] There should be a review process built into releasing beyond just the dry-run.
  - Filed #16934.
- [x] `push-official-release.sh` doesn’t check for a valid CI version until after publication, when trying to do version comparison; it should fail fast if it's trying to push a version that's not valid, instead of uploading and then complaining.
  - Filed #16937.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
A number of things we need to do in the near-ish future will involve making sure that discrete chunks of the codebase are independently importable.

Basically, we want to tightly control the dependencies of the client, and of apiserver infrastructure, to start out with. As we clean up the dependencies, we want to keep them cleaned up. This means we need something to test the import paths, to ensure that parts of the codebase that _should_ be logically distinct _are_ logically distinct.

Even if we manage to split parts of our codebase off, this test will be useful in the interim while we prepare for the move.

We can potentially use go2idl for part of this, but how to represent allowed/disallowed packages? Whitelist or blacklist?

title: No easy universal shared storage example

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
We do not have a easy universal shared file storage example.   

This makes it hard to build realistic examples with kubernetes.  For example, any type of batch job typically reads and writes to and from shared storage. 

By universal I mean it should work on most or all cloud providers.  This rules out `GCEPersistentDisk` and  `AWSElasticBlockStore`.

By "shared" I mean multiple pods on multiple machines are able to read and write the same files.  This rules out `GCEPersistentDisk` (again), `EmptyDir`, `GitRepo`, `Secret`,

By "easy" I mean that it does not require configuring additional node software to setup.
That rules out `NFSVolumeSource` (xref #12650 #15668). 

I don't know if any of the remaining Volume sources can work without extra node software (`ISCSIVolumeSource`, `GlusterfsVolumeSource`, `RBDVolumeSource`, `CinderVolumeSource`, and `CephFSVolumeSource`.)

At any rate, I don't care which technology we use.  I just care that I can take a "Conforming" kubernetes cluster, and then do `kubectl create -f some-file-server-rc.yaml -f some-file-server-service.yaml` and have a file server running, and then do  `kubectl create -f some-file-using-pod.yaml` and have it use files served by that server.

It don't care if it works with PVs/PVCs; I think it is somewhat better for expository purposes if it works without them.

I don't care if the storage itself is high-availability, "production-ready", or even persistent.  I just want it to work long enough to be able to build demos and examples that use shared storage, have the user understand the pattern, and then be convinced to go to the extra work to setup a "real" shared storage system. 

@thockin @markturansky

title: Event recorder is too strict in counting cached events, can OOM a server

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Example scenario:
1. Create a replication controller A
2. Set A.Replicas to N+diff
3. A attempts to create diff pods, and is failed for each
4. For each failure in diff, A records an event with the failure

Problem:
If the error message across each failure is unique, the number of events produced can unexpectedly induce an OOM on the master by overloading etcd.  Common reasons for error messages varying slightly would include the following:

a) the error message including the name of the pod
b) the error message including a timestamp
c) etc.

In our particular instance, we encountered (a) and it resulted in 175488 events being spawned on a rather small deployment that induced OOM scenarios for etcd and killed the node.

**Proposal**
Event.Message should not be used in the event_cache algorithm.

It's too easy for any controller to go rogue, and it can confuse the heck out of users why seemingly common errors repeat in event output.  In my case, when looking at 77000 of those events in one namespace, it stumped me to figure out the difference ;-)

Instead, I think event keys should be the following:

```
func getEventKey(event *api.Event) string {
    return event.Source.Component +
        event.Source.Host +
        event.InvolvedObject.Kind +
        event.InvolvedObject.Namespace +
        event.InvolvedObject.Name +
        string(event.InvolvedObject.UID) +
        event.InvolvedObject.APIVersion +
        event.Reason
}
```

And event.Message should just update to the latest observed message.

Thoughts?

@lavalamp @erictune @wojtek-t @bgrant0607 @smarterclayton

title: Clarify Garbage Collection semantics in Kubelet

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Kubelet can manage only one storage partition as of today. 
Kubelet uses cadvisor to identify and track the overall usage of the partition where docker's storage directory is located. 
If the docker daemon's storage directory is different from that of the root filesystem, kubelet will not realize this.
Depending on how the node is setup, kubelet's garbage collection behavior will change.

Single partition scenario:
1. If the storage backend is either `Aufs` or `Btrfs`, kubelet will track the entire root partition usage and perform image & container GC whenever the usage cross a user configurable [high watermark](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b9cfab87e33ea649bdd13a1bd243c502d76e5d22/docs/admin/garbage-collection.md#L83). This includes logs, local disk based volumes, etc.
2. If the storage backend is `DeviceMapper`, kubelet is expected to track the usage of the `pool` device which includes the image layers and the container root filesystems. GC is expected to be triggered whenever the underlying storage availability for the pool device falls below the high watermark.
3. Support for Overlayfs does not exist. Kubelet will not perform any GC on nodes running OverlayFs. Relevant cAdvisor issue [here](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/issues/932).

Multiple partition scenario:
1.  If the storage backend is either `Aufs` or `Btrfs`, kubelet will use the partition where docker's storage directory is located and use it for GC purposes. If `--kubelet-root-dir` (default is `/var/lib/kubelet`) is on a different partition when compared to that of docker daemon, then GC will only happen when the usage on the docker partition crosses the high watermark. 
2. In the case of `DeviceMapper`, kubelet will use the storage device allocated for docker images and container root fs. Excessive logging usage by docker container's will not trigger GC, since log files are stored on a different partition.

From a user's perspective, the system should do everything possible to free up storage on local disk, possibly without any impact to running pods. If that assumption is valid, performing GC even on storage usage by local disk volumes is desirable. 
We want to support scheduling local disk as a schedulable resource in the near future. AFAIK supporting multiple partitions hasn't been considered as a requirement.
Once disk limits can be set on pod (for volumes) and containers (root filesystem and logs), GC might not matter as much as it does today.
The system might evict pods in the future to free up space on the local disk. This might not work as intended with multiple partitions unless kubelet is updated.

The existing GC behavior can be confusing to users. 

I'd like to get a consensus on the desired kubelet behavior when it comes to garbage collection. 

cc @kubernetes/goog-node @bgrant0607 @thockin @smarterclayton

title: Separate out release infra from build infra

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: area/release-eng
labels.description: Issues or PRs related to the Release Engineering subproject

body:
To avoid this kind of thing: #16521.  This was an issue in which our test/release infra needed to change, and we had to cherrypick a bunch of stuff back into the `release-1.0` branch, because we rely on release infra inside that branch.

Instead, we should have separate release infra (probably in contrib) that drives the release process, and relies on a clearly-defined interface with the build infra, (e.g. run `make release`, and expect all artifacts to exist in `_output`).

Specific action items:
- [x] Define a clear contract between build and release
  - Straw man proposal: build logic is invoked with a single command, (i.e. `make release` or something similar,) and promises to put all artifacts for release into a specific local directory that the releasing logic can then push
- [x] Factor out all `kube::release::...` logic from `build/common.sh`, and move all `push-...` scripts to `release/`
  - We might want to move all of the releasing infrastructure to kubernetes/contrib, but that opens up issues of how to deploy to a cluster (see next item)
- [x] Figure out how to handle pushing to GCS from the build logic (for deployment) and how that can play nice with our releasing logic (cc @mikedanese regarding your work on deployment)
- [x] Figure out what to do with `build/release.sh`
- [x] Factor out versioning logic from `push-...` scripts, `cut-official-release.sh`, and `build-official-release.sh`

title: Focus on Spark

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: ug/big-data
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to ug-big-data.

body:
I have #16320/#16498 out to bring Spark up to existing standards for our examples. This bug is both a friction log of things I ran into while working on that PR, and a set of anticipated issues with Spark.

I organized this into two sections, Spark-specific-ish and Kubernetes-general. Some of these bullets have open issues and I'm documenting them as part of the vertical slice involved.

**Please** feel free to correct me if I messed something up obvious about Spark or Kubernetes. I was a former Spark user in a bygone era, but it's moved quite quickly since then so any expertise has rusted.
## Spark specific
- [x] **Where?**: #17027 talks about whether this even belongs in `examples/`, since it works over multiple versions, and isn't a _teaching_ example.
- [ ] **Config**: #16320 puts up a static configuration of Spark. [The Spark configuration alone](http://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/configuration.html) is pretty large, and that's not including [the Hadoop configuration](https://hadoop.apache.org/docs/current/hadoop-project-dist/hadoop-common/ClusterSetup.html) that also influences it. It's difficult to say what a customer would actually want to tune in production, but it's clear that treating Spark as a fully black-box is probably wrong (but has legs for a while). Don't get me wrong, it's not unreasonable to offer an out-of-the-box configuration that just works, but we're going to need a way to inload configuration. In this case, the container is also going to need to compose configuration with the configuration that "just works" (i.e. as a simple example, if we took in a secret for additional `spark-defaults.conf`, we should probably just splat the existing configuration together, or compose them to allow the additional config to override KVs in the base image). See #6477, #4822.
- [ ] **Jar Files**: We're going to need a way to quickly compose base images and other modules. See #831.
- [ ] **Parameterized Resources**: It's not clear how to merge [spark](../tree/master/examples/spark) and [spark-gluster](../tree/master/examples/spark/spark-gluster). The long term answer is probably things like #10527, #11492, etc. Short term, one option might be to assume that you have _some_ storage available that can be mounted as `ReadWriteMany` and instead of assuming gluster, we rewrite the example as either gluster or NFS and use a PV claim. But that's not the only example of a resource that needs to be parameterized / templatized in some fashion.
- [ ] **Pod Local Storage**: The existing example doesn't override `SPARK_LOCAL_DIRS`, so it's only useful for certain workloads, namely in-memory only workloads. This used to be the bread-and-butter of Spark because it was all it could do, but it proved rather limiting not to spill. However, using network or distributed storage for Spark intermediate storage is somewhat naive, but is the most convenient way on our system to configure a ReplicationController for storage. But, for the short term, given that the replication controller itself is `<N>` wide, for anyone in GCE we could add a script to this directory to provision a set of `<N>` volumes and use a claim to resolve it.
- [ ] **Storage Testing**: Spark doesn't necessarily need storage that will outlive the life of the pod (if you blow away a worker on a running job it will recompute the RDD around it, as you'd expect, since storage within Spark is largely annotated caching with `.persist()` and shuffle-spill, both of which are losable). The pod case is different than e.g. [Netflix's Chaos Monkey with Spark](http://techblog.netflix.com/2015/03/can-spark-streaming-survive-chaos-monkey.html) tests, though, because the pod comes back with a different name.
- [ ] **Scheduling**: I kept Spark configured in Standalone mode with a fixed width ReplicationController for the worker pool. There's a lot of really long, interesting conversations to have how to handle this correctly. Mesos does a lot here with fine-grained scheduling to pick up slack capacity on the cluster, YARN integrates slightly differently, we could still take yet another. (Obviously a large TBD bullet.)
- [ ] **Resiliency**: I put some basic liveness probes on the master/workers, but there's some obvious stuff missing: (a) The master either needs to be running in `FILESYSTEM` mode (easiest) or (b) in multi-master backed by ZooKeeper (hardest) in order to withstand a restart with a running application. Similarly, the driver pod itself isn't protect at all right now, but before we protect that, we just want to look at the driver mode, how we want to support Spark app submission in the cluster, and the Zeppelin bullet below.
- [ ] **Test**: If we actually want to productionize an app, we really should have tests of some sort.
- [x] **Zeppelin**: We should definitely get [Zeppelin](https://zeppelin.incubator.apache.org/) working. I morphed the current example into an example familiar to Googlers, a Shakespeare word count example, but it's using the pyspark driver and lacks "pop".
- [ ] **Spark UI**: The Spark WebUI worker links won't work because they're cluster IPs. Spark presents it's worker IPs as if they're globally accessible, not anticipating that we're proxying the connection to the master's WebUI (which seems like an utterly sane). We could obviously proxy all of the worker webuis as well, but Spark doesn't seem to support a URL-rewrite scheme for the master WebUI page, so we'd probably have to slap an nginx proxy in front of it. (See #16949 for one way to maybe solve it.)
## Kubernetes general
- [ ] **Pod Hostname/Service Mismatch**: During the conversion from a `spark-master` pod to a `spark-master` single-pod-replication-controller, the Spark master objected to the slaves because the master started with a hostname that didn't match the service name the slaves were contacting it on. In this case, the slaves connected to the DNS `spark-master`, and `spark-master` saw messages for `spark-master` and said "nope, that ain't me, I'm `spark-master-a1b2d3`, you must have me confused for someone else". (c.f. #386)
- [ ] **Environment Variable Injection Issues**: If you're not actually using the service environment variables, injection can actually throw you off when an environment variable from Docker or Kubernetes overrides something that a vendor script was expecting. For example, I had a service named `spark-master`, which resulted in `SPARK_MASTER_PORT`, which is an environment variable that the Spark `start-master.sh` script will happily pick up. Unfortunately, the script was expecting a single integer, not `tcp://<ip>:7070`. It would be nice if there was a way to disable service env variable injection. See #1768 (which seems to cover that possibility, maybe).
- [ ] **Best Practices Friction**: [Config best practices](../tree/fe6b15ba/docs/user-guide/config-best-practices.md) is at odds with [how we test examples currently](../tree/fe6b15ba/examples/examples_test.go): The resources probably belong in the same file, but I didn't do it that way because of the example schema test. See #16444, just filed.
- [ ] **Slow Dev Iteration**: This was probably the longest I've spent iterating on an ensemble of Docker containers, and I found it somewhat painful (until I automated it slightly) to bump the tag in the Makefile, bumping it in the `.yamls`, etc. Our best practices seem to suggest using image hardcoded tags (which make sense), and I probably would've scripted it further if I had to go much longer. The process itself before presenting a PR is interesting because prior to a PR you basically end up "hiding" the entire thing on a private project, then you end up displaying one "bump" to the world. Do we have any issues discussing how to iterate on "the package" (the set of `.yaml`, Dockerfiles, etc.)? As we get anyhere near packaging, that's going to be one killer feature - the ability to rapidly iterate on actually developing package blobs for k8s (the resources and images both).

cc @davidopp @timstclair @timothysc @wattsteve

title: HPA controller needs more flexibility from APIInstaller

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: sig/autoscaling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Autoscaling.

body:
Spawned from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/16177

 Our `APIInstaller` infrastructure forces all requests for a particular version of a REST endpoint to use an exactly matching version (POSTs to api/v1/namespace/foo/resource must send a v1 object). This breaks the `HPAController` client because it cannot generically include every codec for every (group, kind) that it might want to scale.

// pulling a few comments from the original issue
1. HPA is a central component that should be able to reach out to generic endpoints
2. HPA can only know about a limited number of versions and conversions internally (anything compiled with kube)
3. We want HPA to be able to scale anything that results in pods generically, by virtue of invoking a generic Scale sub resource on endpoints
4. HPA will therefore have to be able to submit things it knows about to endpoints it does not know about.
5. Therefore an API server has to be able to accept the things HPA knows about (Scale, Kube group, v1) and convert it internally to its own recognized format (Scale, OpenShift/3rd party group, v2).
6. Therefore we need to relax the APIInstaller limitation and allow clients to convert.
   @bgrant0607 @lavalamp i think this walks back the previous decision we had to not accept multiple types of input - there is no way for HPA to scale things it doesn't know about unless it can send things to a remote server that it knows about. The remote server is responsibility for taking the Kube type submitted by HPA and converting it to its own internal format.

The contract between HPA controller client and remote API groups that implement Scale is "I will send you one of a set of API versions that I recognize".

title: VersionedParams & API Groups

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Right now, we have the concept packing api query parameters into a struct, converting that to the versioned (serialized wire) format struct, then packing that into URL query parameters. This needs some slight adjustment for API groups.

Options:
1. Change nothing; every group needs its own e.g. ListOptions struct in the internal and external versions.
2. Move common options (e.g. ListOptions) to unversioned.

If we do 2, then we need to modify the code here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/client/unversioned/request.go#L414

Options for modifying this code:
1. RESTClient takes a second "options" codec, which takes a struct, returns JSON, which can be converted to query parameters. (must be a second codec because the codec for the body of the request may be binary.)
2. RESTClient takes a second "options" codec, which takes a struct and returns URL query parameters directly.
3. Develop the concept of internal unversioned vs. external unversioned (UGH).

2.1 & 2.2 both have the advantage that RESTClient doesn't need to know about "convertor" at all any more.

2.1 can be done just by reusing our existing codec, which is nice, but 2.2 is probably clearer? 2.3 is confusing. Option 1 is verbose and error prone.

@smarterclayton @krousey @wojtek-t @caesarxuchao please all of you argue about this :)

title: Exec/attach should create all streams before copying data

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
We create the stdin stream and immediately start copying local stdin to the container. We do the same for stdout and stderr (create stream, start copying immediately). In the kubelet, we wait to receive all the streams before we start the exec and copy between the streams and the container.

The spdy connection frame handling code has 5 frame workers, each with a queue of up to 50 frames. In the event that we try to push more than 50 frames to a single queue before all streams are ready, the 51st attempt to push a frame blocks until there is space available in the queue. But there won't be any space until the server starts reading from the streams, which won't happen until all the streams have been received, so we're stuck at this point.

The fix is to create all the streams first, and only start copying after all the streams have been created and the server is ready to copy between the streams and the container.

Originally reported here: https://github.com/openshift/origin/issues/5377

title: Adding TypeMeta to top-level unversioned types

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.1
milestone.description:
Release 1.1.

P1 features:
* 250+ nodes, at our published SLO
* kube-proxy perf. improvements (via IPTables)
* Docker 1.8.x
* Horizontal pod auto-scaling
* Job
* Ingress
* Schema validation in kubectl
* Experimental API and API groups
* Graceful pod termination

body:
Forked from the discussion in #16082.

Currently most top-level types in pkg/api/unversioned/ do not have TypeMeta, we made them so because we don't want the unversioned types to have an `APIVersion` field. However, it would be beneficial to let these types have the `Kind` field, (quoting @liggitt's https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/16082#issuecomment-151233217), because the `Kind` field
1. Identifies the target struct so a codec can deserialize correctly
2. Prevents decoding garbage JSON as an empty struct of a different kind (for example, we wouldn't want `{"foo":"bar"}` to successfully deserialize to a `Status` object)
3. Allows the codec to implement `Decode` (which your `JSONDecoder` cannot, because it has nothing to use to recognize the target kind)

So the proposal is adding a TypeMeta to the top-level unversioned types, and we should populate the `Kind` field but leave the `APIVersion` field empty.

Comments are welcomed.

title: godep restore failing due to Godep issue

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
The aws-sdk-go library just renamed a package from internal -> private to work around Go's vendoring experiment changes:
https://github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go/commit/c09f1bb2f2270137bd1708d4668dc6beb2fb52f2

But we have a Godep dependency on some of these internal packages (we don't use them directly, but Godeps saves them anyway)

The problem is that godep ignores the branch when first pulling the code because it shells out to `go get`, so it tries to do a fetch on a package that doesn't exist on master: https://github.com/tools/godep/issues/186

I think this combines to mean that `godep restore` is broken right now (or at least returning an exit code; I'm not sure if it actually is OK).  If you have a dirty Godeps tree, `hack/verify-godeps.sh` will also fail (but there is a short-circuit in there when the tree is clean which means that Shippable is still passing).

I don't know really how we should fix this (properly).  A workaround is to manually:

```
rm -rf ${GOPATH}/src/github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go/
go get github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go
pushd ${GOPATH}/src/github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go/
git checkout v0.9.9
popd
godep restore
```

title: HPA needs to handle discovery, controller credentials, privilege escalation protection

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: sig/autoscaling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Autoscaling.

body:
When integrating the HPA controller, we've hit a couple issues.
1. The HPA controller takes an APIGroup, APIVersion, Kind (this should probably have been resource) and attempts to call a `scale` operation on it.  Right now, that's based on a client building a URL.  That client needs to be able to perform API discovery operations in order to locate where the particular (group, version, resource) tuple lives.  Right now it doesn't.
2.  This intersects with authorization because the HPA controller needs to have valid credentials for every (group, version, resource) tuple that it can manipulate.  Given that the end goal is to have some APIGroups hosted in different locations (consider kube and openshift not living in the same API server), we need to have a way to initialize the HPA controller with correct credentials.
3.  Because the HPA controller may escalate the user's authority to actually perform the scale operation, the HPA REST endpoint should perform some authorization of the HPA resource when it is created.  One option is to do this via the `SubjectAccessReview` mechanism described here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/12209.  The remote API is probably needed because you'd want to authorize based on the authorization engine of the API server hosting the (grouip, version, resource).  In the short term, even accepting an `Authorizer` would get you part way.
4. Our APIInstaller infrastructure forces all requests for a particular version of a REST endpoint to use an exactly matching version (POSTs to api/v1/namespace/foo/resource must send a v1 object). This breaks the HPAController client because it cannot generically include every codec for every (group, kind) that it might want to scale.  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/16177#issuecomment-151831609 Spawned https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/16500

@DirectXMan12 @ncdc @smarterclayton @kubernetes/kube-iam @kubernetes/rh-cluster-infra

title: APIGroups are hard to deal with in the code

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
APIGroups are a really useful features, but there are several areas of the code that need improvement to make their usage easier to understand.  These are few things I found while trying to reliably activate and configure the `extensions` group downstream
1. We need a `GroupVersion` object to make it very obvious in the code when a bit of code relies on that.  Right now, sometimes its two strings, sometimes its one string to split, sometimes objects hold both.
2. Validation is needed when starting a master to make sure that combination of `StorageDestinations`, `apiGroupVersionOverrides`, `storageVersions`, and the available `Groups` makes sense.  I suspect that there's a cleaner factorization.
3. DONE Functions like `InterfacesFor` need to decide if they take `GroupVersion` or just an API version.  I'm ok with either one, but right now you get things like an error message saying `unsupported storage version: v1beta1 (valid: v1beta1)` because part of the code thinks its a version and part of it thinks its a `GroupVersion`.
4. REST APIVersions are unrelated to storage APIVersions.  Right now, the REST preferred version is tied to the storage version.
5. Reporting throughout the stack should understand that `Kind` strings are no longer unambiguous.  Types like `StatusDetails` should accept an `APIGroup` as well.
6. Registrations of `GroupMeta` shouldn't be mutable.  I don't see why we'd ever want it mutable and its kind of crazy to change it part way through.
7. DONE (well, differently in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/16062) Type registration and lookups seems to be split across three packages (`install`, `registered`, `latest`), all of which try to take APIGroups into account.  This needs reorganization.  Perhaps we could try a layered approach where `latest` is scoped to versions of a single APIGroup, `install` is responsible for handling registration with a `registered` package which is the source of truth for all metadata.  No other package should expose cross group metadata.
8. Having combined clients makes it harder to trace the effects of disabling an APIGroup and risks potential name collisions going forward.  Splitting Clients on APIGroups seems reasonable.

One of the things that may help with factorization is trying to describe the existing `v1` API as an GroupVersion("", "v1") throughout all of the code.  If its hard to read like that, then there's probably a factorization problem.

title: kube-apiserver HTTP proxy removes Content-Length header

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Kubernetes' HTTP proxy removes the headers Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding from proxied requests. This breaks PUT and POST requests that require the Content-Length header and use chunked transfer encoding. I've created a producer for the problem with k8s configuration, Dockerfile and outputs at https://github.com/tiran/k8n-contentlength

In the reproducer example I'm making a curl POST request to a service via the proxy APO endpoint http://localhost:8080/api/v1/proxy/namespaces/default/services/contentlength/. Both curl -v and tcpdump show that curl is sending a Content-Length header. The simple socket server inside the pod gets all data except for the Content-Length header.

title: Testing doesn't sufficiently cover client/cluster version skew

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
As we're moving forward with the `v1.1` release, we're realizing we don't have sufficient test coverage for version-skew between clients and clusters.  Recently, we put in place upgrade tests:

```
  # kubernetes-upgrade-gke-1.0-1.1
  #
  # This suite:
  #
  #1. launches a cluster at release/latest-1.0,
  #2. upgrades the master to ci/latest-1.1
  #3. runs release/latest-1.0 e2es,
  #4. upgrades the rest of the cluster,
  #5. runs release/latest-1.0 e2es again, then
  #6. runs ci/latest-1.1 e2es and tears down the cluster.
```

When these tests run, the client version always matches the e2e version, so in `3.` and `5.` the client is a `1.0` client, in `6.` it's a `1.1` client.

Problems:
- [ ] We don't cover the reverse case, where we have a `1.1` client working a `1.0` cluster.
  - This is tough because we don't expect `1.1` tests to pass against a `1.0` cluster, so we'd, in theory, have to run `1.0` tests through a `1.1` client, which is tough.

Possible solutions:
- [x] Run `1.1` tests against a `1.0` cluster, and see what breaks (#16041);
- [ ] Figure out a way to link different versions of the tests and client library together;
- [ ] Figure out a way to run the test-command suite against a live, version-skewed cluster.

This is _not_ a `v1.1` blocker.

Please add other cases we don't catch, so we have a sense of where we need to go.

title: Speed-up LIST operations by serving them from memory

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
### Background

Currently, to serve LIST operation in apiserver we do the following:
- read all objects of a given resource from etcd
- filter out objects that user is not interested in
- return the result

This means, that complexity of LIST operation is proportional to the number of all objects of a given type, not to the number of objects returned to the user.

As an example, consider 1000-node cluster with 30.000 pods running in it. If a user has a ReplicationController with, say 10 replicas, then listing them requires requires reading all 30.000 from etcd, filtering them and returning just 10 which are interesting for the user.
### Proposal

We would like to make the LIST operation proportional to the number of elements it returns as a result.

With the "Cacher" layer (used by watch in apiserver: #10475), we already store a copies of objects with a given type in apiserver so if we add an Indexer to it (which should be simple), we would be able to effectively serve list operations from it.

The problem is that a cache in apiserver is delayed (usually by tens to hundreds milliseconds). So if we just start to serve list operations from there we will change the semantics - e.g. it can happen that if you POST an object to apiserver and call LIST immediately after, the returned list may not contain already POSTed object.

In many cases, this doesn't really matter, for example if LIST is only done to start watching from that point, we will get eventual consistency anyway (just the starting point changes). However, it can possibly break some other clients.

I can see 3 main options:
- just change the semantics
- add an option (parameter) to LIST operation to force listing from database; however, in this case we should probably make listing from database by switched off by default to take advantage from it wherever it's possible
- change the LIST operation to take ResourceVersion paramater and ensure that what we return in a result is no older than the given ResourceVersion (however, to make it efficient, we don't give any guarantees on how fresh the result is - we only promise to return the result not older than the given ResourceVersion).

[The third option is the best in my opinion].

What do you think about it?

@kubernetes/goog-control-plane @kubernetes/goog-csi 
@lavalamp @brendandburns @quinton-hoole @bgrant0607 
@smarterclayton @derekwaynecarr

title: kubectl apply umbrella issue

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

labels.name: sig/service-catalog
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Service Catalog.

body:
See #35234 for work items

---
# Apply Details

---

To capture discussion on #1178, #1702, #13007, #17333, and other issues/PRs.
cc @jackgr @ghodss 

Summary (to be transcribed into a doc):

Apply conceptually is intended to enable users to just specify a configuration and "make it so". But it's not that easy.

We represent default values explicitly in the API so that system components, ecosystem components, tools, and users don't need to reason about implicit behaviors, especially since such behaviors can change across API versions.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/devel/api-conventions.md#defaulting

We also want apply to work with automation, such as auto-scaling, and asynchronously filled-in values, such as node or IP assignments.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/devel/api-conventions.md#late-initialization

Therefore, unspecified values are (supposed to be) interpreted by apply as not managed by the user. 

To do this, apply is implemented as a kind of 3-way merge, of their previous configuration, their new configuration, and the live state in apiserver/etcd. Obviously, this means that the previous configuration needs to be stored somewhere. It is currently stored in an annotation on each resource (#16543).

The diff-and-patch process has a few tricky issues. One is that we often don't want to overwrite arrays, which is standard json patch behavior, and we don't want to merge elements positionally, either. Many arrays have primary keys, similar to maps. We created a custom patch strategy to implement this behavior:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/devel/api-conventions.md#strategic-merge-patch

One problem we haven't solved yet is that OneOf / union cases also need to be recognized, so that the previous value can be automatically nulled when a selection is changed (example of a OneOf issue: #24198).

We need to find a way to represent the merge strategy, merge keys, and OneOf relationships in Swagger (probably Swagger 2.0), as well. Otherwise, kubectl apply won't work properly with a cluster of a different release.

We need to clean up all cases in the API types.go files that don't properly allow us to distinguish unspecified values from default values (e.g., using pointers for optional fields).

We should ensure imperative mutations like scale, label, and annotate don't update the last-applied-configuration annotation by default, since that would cause those changes to get removed on the next apply if not added to the user's configuration file.

The user needs to be able to explicitly nil values when performing apply (so that needs to be fixed if it doesn't work).

We should detect conflicts between the live state and the applied state (#13576).

We should fix the handling of secret data (#23564, #20508).

We need a pattern to recommend for rolling out ConfigMaps (#22368). (I _think_ changing the name of the ConfigMap should just work, once we have server-side cascading deletion.)

We should figure out how to automatically test apply #26234.

Search issues for "kubectl apply" to find other misc. bugs and features.

cc @AdoHe @ghodss @kubernetes/kubectl

title: Evaluate overlayfs with docker

labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Docker now supports Overlayfs as a storage backend. Since Aufs doesn't work on all distributions and has caused kernel issues in the past (#10959), we should evaluate `Overlayfs` and see if it can become the default/recommended storage driver for kubernetes deployments.

Kubernetes is already being used with multiple storage backends, but our existing test infrastructure does not test against all the possible docker storage backends. Until we can enhance the existing kubernetes e2e infrastructure, we will continue to recommend users to use the default storage backend, which is `Aufs` as of now.

title: Design Proposal: Handling Volumes Attached to Inaccessible Nodes

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

body:
_Update: detailed design doc in #20262_
# Problem

Volumes remain attached to a node when kubelet on the node is unexpectedly terminated (because, for example, the node was restarted). When a node becomes inaccessible, the scheduler, schedules the pods from the downed node to another node. However, certain volumes can only be attached to one node at a time (for example GCE PDs may only be attached to one instance in RW mode). Pods that require a volume that can only be attached to a single node will be unable to start once rescheduled to a new node, because their volume can not be attached to the new node since it was never detached from the old node.

See issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/14642
# Potential Solutions
1. Node detaches from other node
   - If a node detects that it is unable to attach a device because it is attached to another node, the node should detach it from the other node, and retry attaching it.
   - Cons: Could lead to two nodes fighting each other for a volume.
2. Garbage collection on node
   - Cons: Can’t rely on the node to to do cleanup: for example garbage collection can’t happen if the plug is pulled on a node.
3. Node Fencing
   - The logic on the scheduler that currently determines if a node is up or down and reschedules pods, should also trigger resource reclamation from downed nodes (detaching disks as well as potentially other clean up).
   - Cons: Decoupling attachment and detachment leads to inherent race conditions, as long as the node itself can decide to attach a volume to itself.
4. Volume Attachment/Detachment Controller
   - Move the volume attachment/detachment logic from kubelet to a separate off-node controller (maybe running on master or as a pod).
# Proposal

I think the “Volume Attachment/Detachment Controller” would be the most robust design.

A node should not be responsible for determining whether to attach or detach a volume to itself. Instead the responsibility should be moved (out of kubelet) to a separate off-node “Volume Attachment/Detachment Controller”.

This controller would keep track of:
- Which pods require which volumes.
- Which nodes these pods have been scheduled to.
- Which volumes have been successfully attached to which nodes.

The controller would be responsible for attaching a volume to a node if:
- A pod with a volume is scheduled to a node and the volume is not already attached to the node (no existing pod on the node requires the volume).
- The volumes policy permits attachment to multiple nodes, or the volumes policy permits attachment only to a single node and there are no other nodes that the volume is already attached to.

The controller would be responsible for detaching a volume from a node if:
- There are no pods running on the node using that volume.

Some volume types may not have a concept of attaching to a node (e.g. NFS volume), and for these volume types the attach and detach methods should be no-ops.

Another benefit of this approach is that it allows the controller to ensure that attach and detach do not occur simultaneously for a particular volume (avoiding lots of horrible race conditions).
## Open questions:
- Mount/unmount code must still exist on the node. How does the controller signal to the node that a volume is attached along with sufficient information (mount dir, etc.) for the node to mount it?
  - Could the mounting logic be dumb and just constantly poll a location on a disk? Would it work for all existing and future volumes?
  - Could the attach/detach logic update the PVC/PV object with some state indicating the nodes it is attached to?
- How do you make this controller plugable?
  - As we proposed for the dynamic volume provisioning controller.
    - For v1 all plugins are compiled in (as is the case for existing volume “plugins”).
    - For v2 anyone can implement their own attachment/detachment controller by creating a binary/pod/script/etc. that:
      - Monitoring API server for pod, node, and PVC/PV objects.
      - Writing updates to these objects

CC @thockin @markturansky

title: [RFC] improve `kubectl annotate` and `kubectl label` to increase success rate

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/flake
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a flaky test.

milestone.title: v1.1
milestone.description:
Release 1.1.

P1 features:
* 250+ nodes, at our published SLO
* kube-proxy perf. improvements (via IPTables)
* Docker 1.8.x
* Horizontal pod auto-scaling
* Job
* Ingress
* Schema validation in kubectl
* Experimental API and API groups
* Graceful pod termination

body:
`kubectl label` and `kubectl annotate` work in this pattern: first issuing a "GET" to the API server to retrieve the latest object, then adding the label/annotation to the object, and finally issuing an "PUT" with the modified object. The request will fail if the object stored in the server has been updated between the "GET" and "PUT", even if the update has no conflict with the label/annotate request. In such cases, instead of returning an error, `kubectl` should retry without disturbing the end user.

There are two ways to implement this:
1. retry in kubectl: simply retry the label/annotate process several times if the server rejected the request because the object has been updated. The only exception is when the `--resource-version` [precondition](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubectl/cmd/annotate.go#L52) is set, then kubectl shouldn't retry.
2. use the strategicMergePatch instead of calling Update at client-side. PATCH is more robust because PATCH does the "get, modify, update" in the server-side, so there is less chance to have a conflict, and PATCH will retry at the server-side (see #14758). We need to make some adaptions though:
- kubectl annotate/label has the `--overwrite` [flag](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubectl/cmd/annotate.go#L51), when it's false, kubectl should retrieve the latest object to confirm there is no existing annotation/label of the same key, and then proceed with issuing the patch.
- if the `--resource-version` [flag](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubectl/cmd/annotate.go#L52) is set, ~~we should fall back to the current behavior, because PATCH doesn't support the resource-version precondition.~~ [UPDATE:] we just need to specify the resourVersion in the patch, then it will be treated as a precondition by the UpdateResource() handler in the API server.

I plan to take the first approach as an immediate fix.

@JanetKuo @bgrant0607 @lavalamp

title: Handle deleting external load balancers across kube-controller-manager restarts

labels.name: priority/important-soon

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Right now, the service controller has no sense of responsibility for the load balancer resources that exist in a cloud user's project. It only deletes things that it knows it owns, meaning that if it gets restarted while deleting a load balancer, it won't finish deleting the load balancer when it restarts (or if it's simply not running when a load balancer gets deleted, it won't even start deleting the load balancer).

This should reduce resource leaks, especially in any e2e tests that involve restarting (including upgrading) the master.
Cross-referencing various leak-related issues: #13515, #14597, #15083, #15084

title: Document how examples should be written and convert existing examples to the desired format

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
Forked from #2841, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/4926#issuecomment-78006098, #9399, #11361, #5465, and other issues.

We need to decide how we want examples to be written, document that, and make existing examples conform.

Issues:
- Decide objectives: teaching system concepts, demonstrating system features, getting started quickly with a particular application, providing sample configurations that can be extended by the user for real use cases, ...
- If teaching concepts or demonstrating features, which ones? How many examples need to illustrate the same concepts/features?
- What techniques do we want to use to make the examples engaging: interactivity, rewards, etc.?
- Does it need to be a realistic application configuration (e.g., HA)?
- Should the example demonstrate the application being used?
- System best practices
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/user-guide/config-best-practices.md
    - Show individual files and then combined files?
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/user-guide/pods.md#durability-of-pods-or-lack-thereof
    - Show singleton pods and then demonstrate why controllers are needed for self-healing?
  - Secret
- Cross references to other documentation (e.g., concept and feature documentation)
- Consistent organization (e.g., should the summary appear at the beginning or the end?)
- Keeping examples up to date with new features and evolving conventions
- Repo locations for text vs. config and code
- Whether/how to show multiple solutions (e.g., kubectl run and yaml)
- Shell command format (e.g., prompt or no prompt)
- kubectl output or not
- Screenshots
- How to make it possible to run examples without cloning the whole repo
- System addons that can be assumed (e.g., DNS)
- Examples that show the cluster being created and destroyed in addition to deploying the application
- Cloud-provider-specific examples vs. portable examples
- Unit and end-to-end testing of the examples

cc @aronchick

title: Kubelet should ensure that node does not panic on OOM

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Linux can be configured to panic on OOM. This will impact QoS policy on kubelet since users can explicitly overcommit the node and kernel OOM killer is used to evict lower priority containers when the node is under memory pressure.

Specifically, kubelet needs to check the value of `/proc/sys/vm/panic_on_oom` and if it not equal to `0`, either 
1. Warn the user (event & logs) and mark the node `NotReady` (or)
2. disable `panic_on_oom` - `echo 0 > /proc/sys/vm/panic_on_oom`

https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/sysctl/vm.txt

cc @derekwaynecarr @kubernetes/goog-node

Using Kubernetes on GKE, both `kubectl log --follow` and `kubectl exec` seem to be highly unstable in their connection.

That is to say, both commands, when running a long-running command, eventually simply "stop", and you are returned to your own shell.

It's not even some sort of "no response" timeout, as it happens regularly during typing in a bash shell opened with `kubectl exec <> -it -- bash`.

This highly unstable nature causes the commands to be unfit for use in long-running automated commands (for example, running an automated test-suite on a Kubernetes cluster using `kubectl exec`).

labels.name: kind/bug

body:
I'm seeing a bug where the network plugin fails to configure networking, and yet the containers for this pod are still deployed (without networking configured).

It looks like the following is occurring:
1) Kubelet attempts to create infra container in `SyncPod`
2) Network plugin fails, returns error code.
3) Kubelet detects error and skips pod creation but does not tear down the infra container
4) On the next `SyncPod` call, the kubelet detects that the infra container is running and deploys the other containers in the pod.

The fix here is for the kubelet to clean up the infra container in `SyncPod` when it receives the error from the network plugin and before it returns.

title: Adjust memory overcommit on node for QoS

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
With the current QoS policy, kubernetes guarantees that memory allocations will not fail up until the memory `request` specified by the user. But the nodes are usually set up to fail memory allocations based on [kernel heuristics](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/vm/overcommit-accounting), if there isn't enough memory available to satisfy the request. A _Best-Effort_ container can cause malloc to fail for a _Guaranteed_ container. 
To avoid this, we can change the memory overcommit policy to never fail and let the OOM killer handle real memory allocations.
Kubelet on startup will have to run `echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memory`.

body:
We're seeing some failures for customers that upgrade to k8s 1.2 because the various addons now require more cluster node resources to run (i.e. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/23556). Customers with high cluster utilization or small machine/node configuration may have situations where their v1.1 cluster no longer works properly after an upgrade to 1.2 because of this.

At the least, we need to track the resource utilization/reservation of addons, with a test that also fails if this increases (i.e. a test that schedules an "almost all free resource" pod that fails if kube-system pods resource use increases). Any increase needs to be investigated and justified (it is a "breaking change" of sorts, since it may result in a non-working clusters for some customers).

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/13695
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/13048

title: Proposal: change default behavior of deployment.spec.revisionHistoryLimit to a limit

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

body:
Currently, the default behavior of revisionHistoryLimit of deployments (in other words, if spec.revisionHistoryLimit is not specified) is to keep around all replica sets. This strikes me as unexpected and unreasonable behavior - in normal usage of the deployment object, you will quickly end up with dozens of replica sets with no obvious button or mechanism to clean them up. I think that using deployments in the typical recommended way should not result in unbounded creation of replica sets.

I personally vote for 1 as the default - it gives you basic rollback functionality but doesn't confuse the user by keeping around lots of replica sets and feels the most intuitive to me - but I think any number up to 5 is reasonable.

title: Termination file contents are not truncated in Kubelet

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
A malicious user can create a termination path that exceeds the API size allowed for a pod update, causing the Kubelet to fail to be able to update the pod status via the API (or by creating very large pod objects in etcd, affecting the performance of the cluster).

The length of the contents of the termination file need to be bounded before it is added to the status response from the server.

title: Kubelet: Switch to Docker engine-api and add timeout for all docker calls

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.3
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/master/release-1.3/release-1.3.md

body:
From the first release of Kubernetes, we have been using [go-dockerclient](https://github.com/fsouza/go-dockerclient). It is reliable and updated frequently. However, we still met some problems when using it:
- **No operation timeout.** Functions in go-dockerclient don’t have timeout. Once the Docker daemon hangs, these caller will also hang forever. (Related issues: #9896, #13934, #21029, #21821, #22259 etc.)
- **No compatibility guarantee.** It's not official Docker client. After each Docker release, community people gradually find and fix compatible issues. (Related issue: #19720 etc.).
- **Missing features.** Some wanted features are not supported by go-dockerclient yet. (Related issue: image pull progress #19077 etc.)

Docker [engine-api](https://github.com/docker/engine-api) is the official Golang client for the Docker remote api. It has **cancellable operations**(All the functions use [Context](https://golang.org/x/net/context)), **official support**(The Docker CLI itself is relying on it) and **the same feature set with Docker CLI**. So, we decided to switch to docker engine-api.

[`DockerInterface`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/dockertools/docker.go#L58) is an abstract interface containing a subset functions of go-dockerclient. Kubelet uses it whenever talking to docker. To switch to engine-api, we must refactor all the functions in `DockerInterface` which will touch a lot of code.
To avoid a huge refactoring in one PR, we'll split the refactoring into several steps:
- [x] Implement the original `DockerInterface` with the engine-api. [#23506]
- [x] Refactor the functions in the DockerInterface one by one, and add unit test for complex functions [#24748]:
  - [x] ListContainers [#23699]
  - [x] InspectContainer [#23699]
  - [x] CreateContainer [#23699]
  - [x] StartContainer [#23699]
  - [x] StopContainer [#23699]
  - [x] RemoveContainer [#23699]
  - [x] InspectImage [#23800]
  - [x] ListImages [#23800]
  - [x] PullImage [#23800]
  - [x] RemoveImage [#23800]
  - [x] Logs [#23907]
  - [x] Version [#23907]
  - [x] Info [#23907]
  - [x] CreateExec [#23907]
  - [x] StartExec [#23907]
  - [x] InspectExec [#23907]
  - [x] AttachToContainer [#23907]
- [x] Add timeout and timeout handling in all docker calls. [#24918]
  - [ ] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/25356#issuecomment-217974344 Add kubelet flag making the image pulling timeout configurable.
- [x] Optional: Leverage the image pull progress information and other new features of engine-api if any. [#26145]

/cc @kubernetes/sig-node

title: Reuse nodePort on kubectl apply service

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.3
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/master/release-1.3/release-1.3.md

body:
In release 1.2 the NodePort of a service changes every time the service get's applied:

Example service svc-test.yaml:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  type: NodePort
  ports:
  - port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    name: http
```

First apply, service doesn't exist:

```
lodur:config yves$ kubectl apply -f svc-test.yaml
service "test" created

lodur:config yves$ kubectl get svc test -o yaml
kubectl apply -f svc-test.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration: '{"kind":"Service","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{"name":"test","creationTimestamp":null},"spec":{"ports":[{"name":"http","protocol":"TCP","port":80,"targetPort":0}],"type":"NodePort"},"status":{"loadBalancer":{}}}'
  creationTimestamp: 2016-03-28T19:55:39Z
  name: test
  namespace: default
  resourceVersion: "1603"
  selfLink: /api/v1/namespaces/default/services/test
  uid: 0bd80681-f51f-11e5-8961-080027242396
spec:
  clusterIP: 10.247.144.40
  ports:
  - name: http
    nodePort: 31585
    port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 80
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: NodePort
status:
  loadBalancer: {}
```

Second apply:

```
lodur:config yves$ kubectl apply -f svc-test.yaml
service "test" configured

lodur:config yves$ kubectl get svc test -o yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration: '{"kind":"Service","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{"name":"test","creationTimestamp":null},"spec":{"ports":[{"name":"http","protocol":"TCP","port":80,"targetPort":0}],"type":"NodePort"},"status":{"loadBalancer":{}}}'
  creationTimestamp: 2016-03-28T19:55:39Z
  name: test
  namespace: default
  resourceVersion: "1618"
  selfLink: /api/v1/namespaces/default/services/test
  uid: 0bd80681-f51f-11e5-8961-080027242396
spec:
  clusterIP: 10.247.144.40
  ports:
  - name: http
    nodePort: 32124
    port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 80
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: NodePort
status:
  loadBalancer: {}
```

The nodePort changed form 31585 to 32124.

It would be nice if the port stayed the same:
- External Loadbalancer that use the nodePort don't have to be updated. -> We currently have a half automated LB that can't deal with changing nodePorts after the services have been created.
- Handy for testing your kube config, you don't have to lookup the new port every time you apply the config.

We need a new munger/bot to do the following:

title: ARP cache stops nodes from reaching master

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
Observed this on AWS, but I am unsure why it would not happen on GCE also.  If GCE has a workaround/fix, I would like to use the same one on AWS.

Here's what happened:  I was upgrading from 1.1 to 1.2, which requires launching new nodes.  One of my nodes did not come up, I think (but am not sure) that it had the same address as one of the old nodes.  That node could not ping the master.   The master had an incorrect ARP entry in the arp table for the node in question (compared vs the node's ifconfig).  I flushed the node's ARP entry from the master and immediately ping resumed and the node came up soon thereafter.

I believe this is the problem, it might only affect newer kernels: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=8732151

title: Split the "resync interval" on reflectors into "relist interval" and "resync interval"

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.3
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/master/release-1.3/release-1.3.md

body:
Today the resync interval on a controller forces a LIST, and then as a consequence sends all objects down the reflector.  However, for most controllers LIST is necessary because 
1. Watch is reliable
2. They do not mutate the store themselves and thus might have data out of sync with etcd
3. They do not "drop" events when failures happen (instead they requeue)
4. Their source of data is relatively up to date, or isn't vulnerable to event reordering (B happens before A and is therefore ignored).

We should split "sync" into "sync" (send all events to listeners) and "list" (clear the cache and fetch from etcd).

All reflectors against etcd should have long "list" intervals (12-24h).  Controllers that don't mutate the store or drop events should have long relist intervals AND resync intervals.  For controllers that drop events or mutate the store in a potentially inconsistent way, we should relist infrequently and resync frequently.

The following reflectors are "fast" - every 30s

```
*api.Service from controller/endpoint/endpoints_controller.go:129
*extensions.Job from controller/job/controller.go:140
*api.ReplicationController from controller/replication/replication_controller.go:209
*extensions.DaemonSet from controller/daemon/controller.go:210
*extensions.HorizontalPodAutoscaler from controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go:121
```

These reflectors should have a 24h relist.  We should separate resync, then tune each appropriately.

body:
Hey guys,

I'm currently experiencing an issue regarding LoadBalancers and adding / removing nodes from the cluster. Since I applied EC2 autoscaling to my minion nodes its regularly the case that new nodes join and other nodes leave the cluster. I witnessed that kubernetes automatically removed them after a certain grace period.

However if I'm deploying something while a node is marked as `NotReady` when issuing `kubectl get nodes` my servic fails to update the ELB it is exposing with the error message below. This leads to my application being completely offline until the node was automatically removed by kubernetes and the service re-tries updating the ELB.
Shouldn't the desired behaviour in this case be to "skip" nodes that are `NotReady`? This would simply lead to the ELB having `x out of y` nodes available which is fine from my point of view.

body:
@einyx reported hitting this error:

`aws.go:2076] Error opening ingress rules for the load balancer to the instances: Multiple security groups found for instance (i-XXXX); ensure the k8s security group is tagged`

The instance had 4 security groups, and only one of them was tagged.  However, the logic around picking the security group is incorrect.. if we get two non-tagged SGs before we see the first tagged SG, it throws an error.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8c02a46c4d8a1983df59a0329b491ce74303eee8/pkg/cloudprovider/providers/aws/aws.go#L1508-L1528

We'll want to cherry-pick this to 1.2

title: API: use cases for kubectl attach?

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
In the rkt container engine integration we are trying to get full feature parity with the existing k8s API. We are very close.

The most recent snag we hit though is that rkt does not support the concept of "attach". For those who aren't familiar see the help output of `kubectl attach`:

```
$ kubectl attach --help
Attach to a process that is already running inside an existing container.

Usage:
  kubectl attach POD -c CONTAINER [flags]

Examples:
# Get output from running pod 123456-7890, using the first container by default
$ kubectl attach 123456-7890

# Get output from ruby-container from pod 123456-7890
$ kubectl attach 123456-7890 -c ruby-container

# Switch to raw terminal mode, sends stdin to 'bash' in ruby-container from pod 123456-7890
# and sends stdout/stderr from 'bash' back to the client
$ kubectl attach 123456-7890 -c ruby-container -i -t
```

The reason rkt doesn't support this is quite practical: for applications that are long running we attach the applications stdout/stdin to a logging daemon without a man-in-the-middle. And the stdin is attached to stdin because this is sort of the accepted default for most long-running processes.

Now, rkt does support interactive applications with `kubectl exec`. But, you chose to do interactive ahead of time which means we skip attaching stdout/stdin/stderr to the log daemon and attach it to the calling process instead.

So, attach is this weird middle ground between `kubectl logs` and `kubectl exec` which is rather odd. I really don't understand the use case and the k8s issue introducing attach isn't super helpful either: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/1521

I want to understand what are the use cases for attach and if we can do one of the following things:

1) Simply not support it in the rkt integration because the use cases are so narrow and the complexity is high to implement it

2) Remove attach from the next revision of the API, I feel like nearly all use cases of debugging can be handled with exec or even a proper session inside of the container created with sshd, etc.

3) Enumerate the compelling use cases for attach so we have some concrete use cases to justify the complexity of figuring this out inside of rkt

rkt upstream issue: https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/1799

body:
Observed in v1.2 release. Node is Ready even if route controller fails to create a route for a Node, which allows scheduler to schedule new Pods on it. Those Pods will be running, but the networking for them won't work, which makes it a bad experience for users. Node should be NotReady before route is created for it.
