title: Introducing protobuf tags changes behavior api.ObjectMetaFor

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.3
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/master/release-1.3/release-1.3.md

body:
After running protobuf generator some unit tests are not passing, e.g.: TestAnnotateObjectFromFile

I did some debugging and the issue is basically, that (at least in this particula case):
  api.ObjectMetaFor(&v1.Pod{})
returns:
  unexpected error: couldn't assign/convert *v1.ObjectMeta to *api.ObjectMeta

The reason for that is that:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/runtime/helper.go#L52

underlying is calling:
ConvertibleTo:
https://github.com/golang/go/blob/f2772a49353e09e4e00121ca4e538a3b3302a1de/src/reflect/type.go#L97

And the issue is that ConvertibleTo requires tags for all fields to be exactly the same:
https://github.com/golang/go/blob/f2772a49353e09e4e00121ca4e538a3b3302a1de/src/reflect/type.go#L1410

So we:
- either need to generate tags also for internal types
- review all usecases of ConvertibleTo in our code and change it to our custom code

I think the first one is much better.

@smarterclayton - thoughs?

title: Discussion for Ubernetes scheduler flow

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.3
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/master/release-1.3/release-1.3.md

body:
I am working with Huawei PaaS team on Ubernetes Phase I implementation, and focus on Uberenetes scheduler. I created a sequence diagram to illustrate the process of ubernetes scheduler and want to start some discussions.

**A general principle design spec**
Currently clusterSelector (implemented as a LabelSelector) only supports a simple list of acceptable clusters. Workloads will be evenly distributed on these acceptable clusters in phase one. 
- [ ] Need to make agreement that "evenly distributed" simply means cloning Federation-RC as sub-RC, and assign target clusters, replicas will not be cared in Federation level, that is sub-RC will keep the same value for replicas of Federation RC. 

**Supported cases in phase I**
#1. User specifies clusterSelector in RC Spec, e.g. The following RC is created in Federation-1 with 3 running clusters a, b and c.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  name: nginx-controller
spec:
  replicas: 5
  ...
  clusterSelector:   
  name in (a, b) 
```

The result will be, if scheduling succeeds, the two sub-RC are created, each RC has 5 replicas, one RC is assigned to cluster a, the other RC is assigned to cluster b.
#2. User does not specify clusterSelector in RC Spec, e.g. The following RC is created in Federation-1 with 3 running clusters a, b and c.
- [ ] need to discuss should we support this case?

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  name: nginx-controller
spec:
  replicas: 5
  ...
```

As a result, the RC will be cloned to 3 sub-RC and assigned to all running clusters a, b, and c in Federation-1.

**Code logics, details in the diagram**
- [ ] most of code of package plugin/cmd/kube-scheduler could be reused, minor changes include package import to ube-scheduler, and remove some unnecessary logics.
- [ ] The design of ube-scheduler will be created based on k8s scheduler code, but with some logical changes, highlighted in RED in the sequence diagram.
1. There is no need for binding pod, so Ubernetes scheduler will not check scheduled Federation RC, no code like scheduledPodPopulator
2. Only default predicate and priority plugins are supported in P1
3. No need to watch Federation Services, as there is no need for spreading sub-RC of same Federation Service
4. About scheduler plugins
   a). There will be two predicates plugins, MatchClusterSelector and RCFitsResources
   b).
   From above cases description, I did not see requirement to do prioritize, so only a dummy priority plugin will be created.
5. The plugin will return a list of clusters, the Federation RC will be cloned as sub-RC and each element of the cluster list will be assigned as target.
6. As #1 described, no need for cluster binding, scheduling done after step 5.

**Dependencies**

Need definition of cluster, federation RC and sub RC
- Cluster entity is already in WIP
- [ ] Federation RC and sub RC definition need to be settled ASAP.
- [ ] Need api of accessing new defined entities in pkg/client/cache/listers.go

title: Multiple restarts of Docker based quick start guide kube cluster leads to serviceAccount tokens not functioning

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
Quick context: I like to use the docker image based hyperkube kubelet to allow developers internally to quickly spin up and tear down a local instance of kubernetes to test code and configuration changes.  I use he manifests-multi set of json files (though I noticed it with the normal manifests as well) so that I can quickly reset kube's etcd back to a clean state.  I'm using docker-machine (1.10.3, which is working better than 1.9.1).
The quickstart guide is here: http://kubernetes.io/docs/getting-started-guides/docker/
The related images: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/cluster/images/hyperkube

With the 1.2 hyperkube images I've noticed that if I restart the cluster a couple of times that the service account tokens that we mount work on the first run of the cluster, but on the second or third restart they stop functioning.  This most noticeably causes skydns to stop functioning because kube2sky is unable to connect to the api with the mounted token (and also the cert is out of date so you have to pass --insecure to curl).  

The easiest way to see this is to stop and start the cluster a few times then start a debian image with curl

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: debian
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
  - image: tutum/curl:trusty
    command:
      - sleep
      - "3600"
    name: debian
  restartPolicy: Always
```

Then run:

```
curl --cacert /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" https://10.0.0.1
```

But you'll actually have to do  (because the cert is out of date)

```
curl --insecure -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" https://10.0.0.1
```

If I then shut down the cluster and laboriously clear out /var/lib/kubelet the serviceAccount tokens begin working there.  I'm not 100% sure which state being squirreled away in /var/lib/kubelet which is causing the problem but I hypothesize that it's a race between setupfiles and the api server.  As in the apiserver starts up with the previous certs in /var/lib/kubelet and then setup files comes along and overrites them which the podmaster picks up and uses to create the serviceaccount token.  But I really don't have an idea.

I believe this is the cause of a bunch of issues people are having with skydns that I'm seeing in slack.

title: implement v2 of kubernetes deployments

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

milestone.title: v1.4
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/master/release-1.4/Release-1.4.md

body:
### Edit: a lot has change since this original issue description, read the later comments

It's time to declare bankruptcy on `cluster/salt/`. It served us dutifully but has grown to be unmaintainable. Let's learn form our experience and start building v2.

Some possible improvements I would like to see:
- use ansible, the technology the community settled on
  - or, ideally, eliminate all of Chef/Puppet/Ansible/Salt
  - concrete problems include:
    - Salt and/or python can't be installed on some distros and consumes a lot of space: # 27547
    - People already using one of C/P/A/S don't want to use 2 different systems on the same nodes
    - Even people using Salt want a single set of configuration files; ours are not written in such a way to make that easy
- installation artifact of kubernetes should be packaged in docker. installation step should be `docker run install-k8s [node|master]`. (Some distros can only run Docker containers.)
- installation should be able to run over ssh or a chroot. ansible supports this.
- as little as possible should be installed on hosts
- (eventually) reduce configuration bits by implementing kubelet bootstrap #23172
- kubelet (and maybe the underlying container runtime) should be the only init unit that we install
- use systemd in place of supervisord
- fewer configuration options, fewer differences for different environments
- kubelet is the only thing on the host but will eventually run in a container as well.
  - deploy kube-proxy and fluentd in daemonsets as addons
- installation artifact, which is separate from release artifact, should only package kubelet (until kubelet is run in a container) and various ansible config files. everything else should be pulled from an external docker registry.
- less shell to format yaml and less shell in general
  - shell is prone to subtle failure modes (#7778)
  - hard to make idempotent
  - hard to test
- environment variables not used for configuration
  - parameters are not discoverable
  - it's hard to determine when a change breaks some configuration
- less jinja (especially to format json)
  - the current scripts + salt + jinja approach is nigh incomprehensible
- factor out portable bits from non-portable bits and improve composability
- network plugins that require node agents should also run as daemonsets (depends on #20355)
- failures provide clear information
- cleans up after itself

Please let me know if you think I missed something or if you don't think we should do something on this list.

Open questions:
- do we need a migration plan for current salt or wheter we should start fresh with a new kube-up, bring it up to speed, then deprecate the old?
- do we require python on the host? do we require anything else?
- how do we best reconcile v2 with the [cluster deployment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/proposals/cluster-deployment.md) proposal?

I will try to better formulate a plan of action with explicit steps and goals in the next couple of days.

ref #5472

title: Cgroup 'cpu.cfs_quota_us' error on container creation when CPU limit is low

labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
After upgrading my environment from Kubernetes 1.1.8 to Kubernetes 1.2.0, I see pods creation failing with the following resource limits set:

```
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: 5m
            memory: 25Mi
```

Translated to Docker container info:

| 1.1.8 | 1.2.0 |
| --- | --- |
| "Memory": 26214400, | "Memory": 26214400, |
| "MemoryReservation": 0, | "MemoryReservation": 0, |
| "CpuShares": 5, | "CpuShares": 5, |
| "CpuPeriod": 0, | "CpuPeriod": 100000, |
| "CpuQuota": 0, | "CpuQuota": 500, |

The error message is:

```
Cannot start container <sha>: [9] System error: write /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu,cpuacct/system.slice/docker-<sha>.scope/cpu.cfs_quota_us: invalid argument
```

I can reproduce this by creating containers manually:

```
$ docker run --rm --cpu-shares=5 --cpu-quota=0 --cpu-period=0 tianon/true
[exit code 0]
$ docker run --rm --cpu-shares=5 --cpu-quota=500 --cpu-period=100000 tianon/true
docker: Error response from daemon: Cannot start container <sha>: [9] System error: write /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu,cpuacct/docker/<sha>/cpu.cfs_quota_us: invalid argument.
[exit code 125]
```

Kubernetes should check that the defined CPU restrictions are valid before attempting to create containers.

title: Incorrect annotation copied from deployment to RS after rolling back

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
Scenario:
1) Create a deployment d and record it. Change cause: d = "create", rs1 (v1) = "create" (copied from d). 

``` console
$ kubectl create -f docs/user-guide/nginx-deployment.yaml --record
deployment "nginx-deployment" created
$ kubectl rollout history deployment
deployments "nginx-deployment":
REVISION    CHANGE-CAUSE
1           kubectl create -f docs/user-guide/nginx-deployment.yaml --record
```

2) Update d with apply. Change cause: d = "apply", rs2 (v2) = "apply" (copied from d)

``` console
$ kubectl apply -f docs/user-guide/new-nginx-deployment.yaml
deployment "nginx-deployment" configured
$ kubectl rollout history deployment 
deployments "nginx-deployment":
REVISION    CHANGE-CAUSE
1           kubectl create -f docs/user-guide/nginx-deployment.yaml --record
2           kubectl apply -f docs/user-guide/new-nginx-deployment.yaml
```

3) Rollback d. Change cause: d = "apply" (unchanged since we don't record command in `kubectl rollout undo`), rs1 (v3) = "apply" (copied from d). However, **it should be either "create" or "rollout undo"** (depending on how we want to implement it). This confuses users. 

``` console
$ kubectl rollout undo deployment 
deployment "nginx-deployment" rolled back
$ kubectl rollout history deployment 
deployments "nginx-deployment":
REVISION    CHANGE-CAUSE
2           kubectl apply -f docs/user-guide/new-nginx-deployment.yaml
3           kubectl apply -f docs/user-guide/new-nginx-deployment.yaml
```

labels.name: priority/important-soon

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
Common questions about people wanted to adopt K8s/Docker/Rkt that we should document as FAQs:
1. What graph driver / filesystem do we recommend for distro Foo X.Y? Or how should we choose?
2. What networking solution would you recommend for cloudprovider Bar? Or how should we choose?
3. What network-attached storage system would you recommend? Or how should we choose?
4. We need to do X (e.g., mount over /etc/hosts) before running our app. That gets blown away upon every container restart. Is there a recommended init/setup solution? Or how should we choose?
5. What's the recommended solution for the "pid 1" problem? Or how should we choose?

title: Revisit Container Runtime interface

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
In many threads / meetings I mentioned that we are not satisfied with today's container runtime interface due to many reasons. Here are the top reasons off my head:
- Duplicated code for supporting SyncPod for all container runtime implementations, especially with Kubernetes defined policy: StartPolicy, PullPolicy, etc. We talked about changing today's declarative API to imperative API at this lowest extensible point. 
- Tight coupled with image format: docker runtime supports docker image, while rkt support appc image by converting docker image to its own format. In a long run, we want to add support for other image format without changing each runtime. There is no easy way to achieve that goal with today's API.
- Logging management is very different on different os distro and with different runtime implementation. We should make this pluggable with runtime.
- Part of resource isolation is handled by runtime today, while another part is handled by Kubelet. The decision is ad-hoc without much thinking. We need to decide if we want runtime interface to handle resource management or completely hand over to ResourceManager module in Kubelet since qos policy is defined by Kubernetes, and it might be redefined over releases. 
- ...

In my mind, we should separate image management, resource / cgroup management, logging management from today's runtime interface. After this effort, we effectively make today's runtime interface as pod / container lifecycle management interface.

cc/ @kubernetes/sig-node, @bgrant0607 
cc/ @philips and @jonboulle @yifan-gu from coreos
cc/ @smarterclayton @derekwaynecarr from redhat

body:
The kubectl update mechanism (e.g. for replication controllers) can create orphans. A more consistent approach to this verb (consistent wrt delete for example) would be:

(Proposal is a summary of conversation with Brendan Burns)
update that would create orphans fails with a warning

body:
Just upgraded to hyperkube 1.2.0-beta.0. On creating the 'kube-system' namespace against the apiserver...

`curl -XPOST -d '{"apiVersion":"v1","kind":"Namespace","metadata":{"name":"kube-system"}}' "http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/namespaces"`

I get the following error back.

```
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "the body of the request was in an unknown format - accepted media types include: application/json, application/yaml",

  "code": 415
}
```

Should this default to `application/json` to stop a breaking change?

The following works successfully

v1/namespaces"`

The Content-Type was not required in 1.1.

title: Deleting ReplicationController does not delete pods in API

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Deleting a ReplicationController behaves differently between the command line and the API. From the command line, it will also delete the pods it has created, while in the API the pods are orphaned.

The difference in behavior between command line and API is jarring. Additionally, integrating directly with the API becomes extremely difficult when trying to manage replicationcontrollers directly. We are offering up a set of replicas as a powerful abstraction, but requiring that our customers break the abstraction and clean up after them.

It seems that, since the command line is the primary user interface, its behavior is the preferred one, so is there any plan to unify the two such that deleting a ReplicationController in the API also deletes the resources it has created and is managing?

Is it possible to at least give a choice, through some sort of flag or policy on the ReplicationController object?

title: default `kubectl run` with kubectl 1.2 is not backwards compatible with 1.1 master

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
Tested with:

```
cluster/kubectl.sh version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"2+", GitVersion:"v1.2.0-alpha.8.1354+144e818ae09b33", GitCommit:"144e818ae09b3339e2b54f3d8c1ae615024d6e51", GitTreeState:"clean"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"1", GitVersion:"v1.1.8", GitCommit:"a8af33dc07ee08defa2d503f81e7deea32dd1d3b", GitTreeState:"clean"}
```

Most of the simple basic starting guides direct users to create a cluster with `kubectl run`. If I run kubectl 1.2 against a 1.1 cluster, I'll get the following behavior

```
cluster/kubectl.sh run nginx --image=nginx                   
Error from server: the server could not find the requested resource
```

now I happen to know I can get the old behavior by doing

```
cluster/kubectl.sh run nginx --image=nginx --generator=run/v1
replicationcontroller "nginx" created
```

but I don't expect an average user to know that or be able to find it easily. I'm mainly concerned that we will be breaking recommended flow for GKE users if they happen to use a new kubectl before their cluster's master is upgraded. We _can_ just update our docs, but breaking a "porcelain" command seems like poor form. Other options include defaulting to the `run/v1` generator for a few patch releases, and/or making `kubectl run` do some kind of version check so it can fallback to the `run/v1` generator if deployments/jobs are not available.

@lavalamp @bgrant0607 thoughts?

title: Unable to restrict pod access to Kubernetes API

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/support
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as a support question.

body:
Hi,

I'm using GKE, and trying to set it up so that individual pods can't issue commands to the Kubernetes API.  (I'm planning to run arbitrary code in these pods, so it would be really bad if a single pod getting pwned gave someone access to all the other pods.)

Is there a standard way of doing this?  GKE is automatically mounting a token at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token`, and as far as I can tell:
- There's no way to tell Kubernetes not to mount that secret.
- There's no way to tell Kubernetes to restrict a pod's ability to access the master over the network.
- It _is_ possible to tell Kubernetes to use a specific serviceaccount for a pod, but:
  - It isn't possible to set up a serviceaccount that doesn't automount a token.
  - It isn't possible to set up a serviceaccount with no privileges.
  - It isn't possible to tell the pod to not use a serviceaccount.

---

My current workaround is to do `chmod o-rx /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io` as root on startup and then run the arbitrary code as an unprivileged user, but that seems like a pretty scary solution.  So, three questions:
- Is there any way to not let individual pods access the Kubernetes API?
- Is there any way in general to prevent pods from accessing certain things over the network?
- Is the workaround I'm using at the moment actually safe?

Thanks!

title: Controller manager restart/fail-over causes massive spike in etcd traffic @ scale.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
We are currently running scale experiments and have uncovered a situation which causes a flood of traffic to etcd, to the point of saturating the link and causing a series of other knock-on issues.  

**Precondition:** A fully loaded system , e.g. 1000 nodes with multiple controllers actively running. 
**Event:** Controller manager failure or restart 
**Observation:** On restart the controller manager will aggressively try to refill it's state to the point it will watch-list everything it can.  This causes a saturation of the network link to etcd causing a series of secondary effects, grinds the system to become unresponsive. 
**Reproducability:** 100% 

/cc @kubernetes/sig-scalability @rrati @smarterclayton @ncdc @jeremyeder

title: Controllers can scale expectations ttl

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Currently the ttl is set to: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L44

In theory it can be infinite, but if by some chance (user error/bug) a pod gets orphaned the controller will wait 5m before giving up. It can give up much sooner in most situations. One way aroud this would be to set the timeout to something like: `numPods/(watches per second) + padding`. 

Since we currently don't have an accurate way to track watch latency we need to calculate these value empirically. The comment indicates that watches per second is 10 but it should be set based on the theoretical limit of pods in the cluster, which depends on the number of nodes and allowed pods per node. 

This probably involves opening up a watch on all nodes in the rc manager and only paying attention to adds/deletes (since node udpates are really frequent). It also involves determining watches per second for buckets like 100 nodes, 500 nodes, 1000 nodes etc. 

If we did this, we'd notice a wedged RC in under 10s in the simple case of 3 nodes and a few orphaned pods. 

This would be nice to have for 1.2, I'll try to get to it but anyone with cycles should jump in.

title: etcd server appears twice in componentstatuses

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Moved this from #22231 since it's no longer related.

I noticed that on `v1.1.8`, I had only a single etcd instance listed in componentstatuses, but on `master` had two (despite that I'm only running a single instance). I've added code to `pkg/master/master.go` to print the list of endpoints that it is going to health check during a call to componentstatuses. 

My etcd is configured:

```
advertise-client-urls: "http://127.0.0.1:2379,http://10.0.1.4:2379"
listen-client-urls: "http://0.0.0.0:2379,http://0.0.0.0:4001"
```

In `v1.1.8`:

```
"etcd-0" = { "127.0.0.1" .... }
"controller-manager" = { "127.0.0.1" .... }
"scheduler" = { "127.0.0.1" .... }
```

In `master`:

```
"etcd-0" = { "10.0.1.4" .... }
"etcd-1" = { "127.0.0.1" .... }
"controller-manager" = { "127.0.0.1" .... }
"scheduler" = { "127.0.0.1" .... }
```

Even though "10.0.1.4" _is_ "127.0.0.1".

Is this expected?

(This came to my attention because I originally was advertising a third etcd endpoint that was unreachable and was causing componenstatuses check to timeout. I just ran it again with `master` to confirm and I get a third etcd: `"etcd-2" = { "kube-20160304-112303.westus.cloudapp.azure.com" ... }"`)

cc: @lavalamp @davidopp

body:
Two nodes went away as I updated the instances, but they still appear and, more importantly/confusingly, their daemonset pods are still in Running state. 

```
$ fleetctl list-machines
MACHINE         IP              METADATA
729947b9...     10.0.12.180     role=node
a0883347...     10.0.8.4        instance=m0,role=master
$ kubectl get nodes
NAME                          STATUS                     AGE
ip-10-0-10-222.ec2.internal   NotReady                   2d
ip-10-0-12-147.ec2.internal   NotReady                   1d
ip-10-0-12-180.ec2.internal   Ready                      17m
ip-10-0-8-4.ec2.internal      Ready,SchedulingDisabled   2d
$ kubectl get pods --all-namespaces
NAMESPACE     NAME                    READY     STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
kube-system   fluentd-logging-2gxb1   1/1       Running       0          1d
kube-system   fluentd-logging-33y2f   1/1       Running       0          1d
kube-system   fluentd-logging-b1yuv   1/1       Running       0          17m
kube-system   fluentd-logging-o9hvp   1/1       Running       0          1d
```

There are only two instances and thus two daemons up, not four.
I understand the rationale for not killing the pods outright, but is there a timeout after which they change state or perhaps the nodes do?

My concern is twofold:
1. `Running` is a lie. Things will be confusing for monitoring/accounting/troubleshooting purposes.
2. State about pods and nodes is kept around for a long time. Imagine someone using DaemonSets on a pool of EC2 spot instances...

Problem: We have kubectl flags (--api-version and --output-version) that take an API version. These were designed when we had just one group and it was expected that just specifying the version will be enough.

title: Upgrade to etcd v3 plan

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
The etcd team has do a lot work to make etcd v3 works efficiently in large scale. Recently we have done a prototype that successfully ran k8s with etcd v3 :) Now I think it’s time for us to start initial discussion and work on the upgrade of etcd in Kubernetes.
## What’s new in etcd v3

First, I want to point out the major benefits of etcd v3:
- We would get rid of relist problem in most cases. etcd3 is able to keep millions of keys. So we can easily keep keys of last 1 hour. Now etcd3 can send progress notifications to watchers. If a client disconnects for an hour, we probably should let it die and doing a full recovery instead of a relist.
- One lease per component. We would use only one lease client to keep alive all TTL keys. The lease has its own ID and is not tied to any client session so that we can migrate it easily. The cost of lease is also much lower than previous TTL keys.
- Efficient watch: Use gRPC insead of HTTP + JSON. Multiple watchers per one TCP connection and very efficient encoding.
- Mini-transaction (Txn): simplify multiple key creation logic.
- Reliability: it has much lower memory footprint, nonetheless it's able to run smoothly with GBs of keys in mem.
- Other improvements like consistent range (pagination) over large number of keys, being able to watch all deletions when delete a prefix, etc.
## Attack Plan

@wojtek-t pointed out that “pkg/storage/etcd” package encapsulates all etcd related code. We appreciate the community work on this! I’m thinking about two ways to accomplish v3 upgrade:

The first way is that we can reuse the interface and rewrite the implementation in etcd3. This is the easy way. We can get the work done easily and quickly. The disadvantage is that the interface resembles that of etcd2. We might need to do some workaround for incompatible changes (ttl to lease). In the long term, we also need to add methods to take advantage of new features like Txn. 

The other way is that we can design a new interface for etcd3. We can keep v3 API in mind and make it efficiently use etcd in first place. However, this requires more work and slows things down initially.

Either way we can have it done in parallel with existing storage layer and add a flag to switch to etcd3.

TBH, I’m not leaning to either way. I saw a lot of interest from the community and it’s important for us to coordinate and move as fast as we can. Any thoughts are welcome!

labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Here are some suggestions for improving our API documentation.

By API documentation, I mean:
- _Operations_: http://kubernetes.io/v1.1/docs/api-reference/v1/operations.html
- _Definitions_: http://kubernetes.io/v1.1/docs/api-reference/v1/definitions.html
- and so on for [other api groups](http://kubernetes.io/v1.1/docs/api-reference/extensions/v1beta1/operations.html) and newer versions (like 1.2)
#### CSS Changes
1.  Don't have the k8s.io nav sidebar when viewing docs.  The docs need their own nav sidebar, since docs are so long.  
2. Don't have the k8s.io top nav bar when viewing docs.  If the person has found the API docs, they probably already are comfortable navigating other K8s.io documentation and don't need the top nav bar.
3. Reduce padding in tables, and reduce font sizes so more text fits on the screen.
4. In the parameters table, give the "Description" column more width. 
#### Generated Formatting Changes
1. Remove the Tags field, as it does not have any meaning to users.
2. Remove the "Type" Column and instead have separate headings for "Query Parameters", "Body" and "Path Parameters"
3. Omit "Consumes: /" sections.  This is implied by there being no BodyParameter.
4. Group together all methods that have the same group/version/kind.  Currently, proxy Node and watch Node and create node and get node are scattered throughout a file.
5.  There is only ever one BodyParameter, AFAICS.  So, instead of having the BodyParameter link to "Descriptions", consider inlining the description at the start of the section for that Kind.
#### Client Library Changes
1. Have client libraries for multiple languages.  Swagger can generate these.
2. Have examples for each method for multiple languages, and show next to the method documentation.  For example, look at https://stripe.com/docs/api/python#retrieve_balance.  I'm not sure how to autogenerate these, but it seems possible.

labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

body:
I'm running into an oddity where, as the title says, an update to a Deployment is not fully applying the new PodTemplateSpec onto the previous version, as components of the previous version remain around after the update.

I'm running v1.2.0-alpha8 on CoreOS 835.9.0 

Here's an example of creating a Deployment (v1), and applying an update (v2) which simply removes certain parts of the original spec (the `args` key in this case), to showcase that the new spec isn't fully being applied, even though the Deployment's `last-applied-configuration` says it should have.

`git-deployment-v1.yaml:`

```
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: git-deployment
  labels:
    name: git-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        name: git-deployment
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: git-sync
          image: gcr.io/google_containers/git-sync
          imagePullPolicy: Always
          args:
            - -rev=origin/gh-pages
          volumeMounts:
            - name: markdown
              mountPath: /git
              readOnly: false
          env:
            - name: GIT_SYNC_REPO
              value: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes
            - name: GIT_SYNC_DEST
              value: /git
            - name: GIT_SYNC_WAIT
              value: "120"
      volumes:
        - name: markdown
          emptyDir: {}
```

We create the Deployment:

```
kubectl create -f git-deployment-v1.yaml
```

When the Pod is running, it should not have any annotations regarding the Deployment as it was the initial deployment, and there are no history of updates. We can verify that it is not set by seeing that this cmd returns: `<no value>`

```
kubectl get deployment git-deployment -o go-template='{{index .metadata.annotations "kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration"}}'
```

...and we can check that the `args` key was set, in this case, to pass an arg of `-rev=origin/gh-pages` to the container's entry cmd, by checking:

```
kubectl get po git-deployment-<ID> -o yaml | grep -A 1 "args"
```

it returns:

```
 - args:
  - -rev=origin/gh-pages
```

...which is what we expect as we set it as such in the v1 Deployment

---

After making a change in the PodTemplateSpec, specifically, removing the `args` key all-together (this is the only change made in the spec), we have a v2 Deployment to apply as an update to v1:

`git-deployment-v2.yaml:`

```
 apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
 kind: Deployment
 metadata:
   name: git-deployment
   labels:
     name: git-deployment
 spec:
   replicas: 1
   template:
     metadata:
       labels:
         name: git-deployment
     spec:
       containers:
         - name: git-sync
           image: gcr.io/google_containers/git-sync
           imagePullPolicy: Always
           volumeMounts:
             - name: markdown
               mountPath: /git
               readOnly: false
           env:
             - name: GIT_SYNC_REPO
               value: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes
             - name: GIT_SYNC_DEST
               value: /git
             - name: GIT_SYNC_WAIT
               value: "60"
       volumes:
         - name: markdown
           emptyDir: {}
```

We apply the update:

```
kubectl apply -f git-deployment-v2.yaml
```

...and we can verify that the new PodSpecTemplate for the v2 Deployment is what we wanted it to be by examining the output of the `last-applied-configuration` key for the newly updated Pod:

```
kubectl get deployment git-deployment -o go-template='{{index .metadata.annotations "kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration"}}' | python -m json.tool
```

(this output and the `git-deployment-v2.yaml` manifest should match, and neither should have the `args` key as we specified)

---

However, if you examine the new Pod's `args` again using

```
kubectl get po git-deployment-<NEW_ID> -o yaml | grep -A 1 "args"
```

...it still returns:

```
 - args:
  - -rev=origin/gh-pages
```

...which should not be the case :-1: 

So in my case, its still passing a flag via the `args` key, which in v2 I determined I did not want by removing it, and the existing flag is messing with the updated Pod's execution.

Any ideas what could be taking place? Thanks!

title: Summary API should report network stats from `eth0`

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
Currently the summary API reports network stats summed over all interfaces ([code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bef2b8f1edd509c7bb209a5df8fae53ad0d7ea56/pkg/kubelet/server/stats/summary.go#L299-L304)), but this is not correct.

We should search for the [`DefaultInterface`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bef2b8f1edd509c7bb209a5df8fae53ad0d7ea56/pkg/kubelet/network/kubenet/kubenet_linux.go#L41) and only report the stats for that interface.

/cc @kubernetes/goog-node

title: Container grafana dashboard busted 117, 118, 120a8...

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
Hi,

   Seems one of the most useful dashboard to monitor our pods is seemingly non operational ie the "Containers" dash. I've seen issues posted but does not seem to be a good resolve. As best I can tell there are some issues with expecting a container name and it seems that some of the containers in kube-system ns are unamed. Also on 120a8 looks like the data source is pointing to influx 0.8 and not 0.9. 
   Would really love to be able to monitor our instances but seems this feature as been a bust for a while... Any work around or recommendations?

  Also is there a plan to update the grafana revision? We use prometheus for monitoring and this data source is offered only in later grafana revs. Anyhow could spin our own grafana instance but would be ideal for ops to shop all in one place.

Thank you for your feedback!

title: Long scheduling latency in large clusters

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
After recent changes in scheduler done mainly by @hongchaodeng scheduling latency is much better, but we are still not where we would like to be.

Currently the problem is: SelectorSpread::CalculateSpreadPriority function
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/scheduler/algorithm/priorities/selector_spreading.go#L81

What is happening:
1. We first iterate over all services, replication controllers and replica sets in the system to check if they are matching labels of the pod we are trying to schedule.
2. Then we list all pods in the namespace (which can potentially be all the pods in the system)
3. Then for each service, rc and rs selected in first point 1 we iterate over all pods from point 2 and create a mapping from node to number of pods

So basically scheduling of a single pod is: O(#pods x #matching (RS, RC, services))

title: Master pods in a permanent "Terminating" status after restarting multiple times in a row

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
We've got our master pods in a state where they appear to be functional, however they are all stuck in "Terminating" state, and appear to be not receiving DELETE calls anymore when the master node is deleted.

This is how they've been for about 19 hours now:

```
$ kubectl --server=... get pods
NAME                                     READY     STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
kube-apiserver-sea5m1kmaster1            1/1       Terminating   1          18h
kube-apiserver-sea5m1kmaster2            1/1       Terminating   1          18h
kube-controller-manager-sea5m1kmaster1   1/1       Terminating   2          6d
kube-podmaster-sea5m1kmaster1            2/2       Terminating   0          18h
kube-podmaster-sea5m1kmaster2            2/2       Terminating   0          18h
kube-scheduler-sea5m1kmaster1            1/1       Terminating   2          6d
```

Mining the logs, I see that it started during a stress test I ran, where I performed our restart scenario 10 times in a row, while debugging a different issue. Here's our restart scenario:

```
kubectl --server=https://10.1.4.41:6443 --kubeconfig=... delete node sea5m1kmaster1
node "sea5m1kmaster1" deleted

kubectl --server=https://10.1.4.41:6443 --kubeconfig=... delete node sea5m1kmaster2
node "sea5m1kmaster2" deleted

# generate fresh yamls for apiserver / podmaster / scheduler / controller manager
# restart hyperkube

kubectl --server=https://10.1.4.41:6443 --kubeconfig=... patch node sea5m1kmaster1 -p {\"spec\":{\"unschedulable\":true}}
"sea5m1kmaster1" patched

kubectl --server=https://10.1.4.41:6443 --kubeconfig=... patch node sea5m1kmaster2 -p {\"spec\":{\"unschedulable\":true}}
"sea5m1kmaster2" patched
```

For the first 5 restarts, I see that every time we delete the master nodes, the master pods are deleted as well:

```
I0225 04:44:55.836146 DELETE /api/v1/nodes/sea5m1kmaster2 -> 200
I0225 04:44:56.412127 DELETE /api/v1/nodes/sea5m1kmaster1 -> 200
I0225 04:44:56.501860 DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/kube-apiserver-sea5m1kmaster2 -> 200
I0225 04:44:56.550051 DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/kube-podmaster-sea5m1kmaster2 -> 200
I0225 04:44:56.593235 DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/kube-apiserver-sea5m1kmaster2 -> 200
I0225 04:44:56.624981 DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/kube-apiserver-sea5m1kmaster2 -> 404
I0225 04:44:56.680119 DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/kube-podmaster-sea5m1kmaster2 -> 200
I0225 04:44:56.708637 DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/kube-apiserver-sea5m1kmaster2 -> 404
I0225 04:44:56.711982 DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/kube-podmaster-sea5m1kmaster2 -> 404
I0225 04:45:03.939329 DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/kube-apiserver-sea5m1kmaster1 -> 200
I0225 04:45:04.372131 DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/kube-podmaster-sea5m1kmaster1 -> 200
```

However, on the 6th restart, we only see this:

```
I0225 04:45:17.914927 DELETE /api/v1/nodes/sea5m1kmaster2 -> 200
I0225 04:45:18.213183 DELETE /api/v1/nodes/sea5m1kmaster1 -> 200
I0225 04:45:23.709177 DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/kube-apiserver-sea5m1kmaster2 -> 200
I0225 04:45:24.766486 DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/kube-podmaster-sea5m1kmaster2 -> 200
```

...and on every subsequent restart now, all we see is this:

```
I0225 04:45:35.430470 DELETE /api/v1/nodes/sea5m1kmaster2 -> 200
I0225 04:45:36.834926 DELETE /api/v1/nodes/sea5m1kmaster1 -> 200
```

Are there any additional steps we should take upon restart / upgrade in order to ensure clean behavior?

title: Jessie pod running on GCE cluster can't resolve metadata

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
Repro (offshot of #21819):
- Create cluster at head
- Create rc with spec:

```
kind: ReplicationController
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: jessie
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    component: jessie
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        component: jessie
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: jessie
          image: debian:jessie
          command:
            - sleep
            - "3600"
```

(I created an RC to see if colocality with the SkyDNS pod made any difference.)

Now I've got one pod in the RC that can't resolve naked `metadata`, but _can_ resolve `metadata.google.com`:

```
$ kubectl exec jessie-fzd2c getent hosts metadata.google.internal
169.254.169.254 metadata.google.internal
$ kubectl exec jessie-fzd2c getent hosts metadata
error: error executing remote command: Error executing command in container: Error executing in Docker Container: 2
```

One that originally could resolve neither, but is flaking:

```
$ kubectl exec jessie-1nhmb getent hosts metadata.google.internal
error: error executing remote command: Error executing command in container: Error executing in Docker Container: 2
$ kubectl exec jessie-1nhmb getent hosts metadata.google.internal
169.254.169.254 metadata.google.internal
$ kubectl exec jessie-1nhmb getent hosts metadata
error: error executing remote command: Error executing command in container: Error executing in Docker Container: 2
```

And one that rock solidly replies:

```
$ kubectl exec jessie-xp1ba getent hosts metadata.google.internal
169.254.169.254 metadata.google.internal
$ kubectl exec jessie-xp1ba getent hosts metadata.google.internal
169.254.169.254 metadata.google.internal
$ kubectl exec jessie-xp1ba getent hosts metadata.google.internal
169.254.169.254 metadata.google.internal
$ kubectl exec jessie-xp1ba getent hosts metadata
169.254.169.254 metadata.google.internal
$ kubectl exec jessie-xp1ba getent hosts metadata
169.254.169.254 metadata.google.internal
$ kubectl exec jessie-xp1ba getent hosts metadata
169.254.169.254 metadata.google.internal
```

Pod `jessie-xp1ba` is colocated with the SkyDNS add-on.

body:
Deployment test failed:
https://pantheon.corp.google.com/storage/browser/kubernetes-jenkins/pr-logs/pull/21399/kubernetes-pull-build-test-e2e-gce/30050/?debugUI=CLOUD
http://kubekins.dls.corp.google.com:8081/job/kubernetes-pull-build-test-e2e-gce/30050/consoleFull

```
• Failure [94.575 seconds]
Deployment
/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/dockerized/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/test/e2e/deployment.go:72
  RollingUpdateDeployment should scale up and down in the right order [It]
  /go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/dockerized/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/test/e2e/deployment.go:50

  Feb 23 13:35:27.835: Failed to remove deployment redis-deployment-2 pods!

  /go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/dockerized/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/test/e2e/deployment.go:196
```

There's a lot going on here, but looking closer at the logs

In the test:

```
Feb 23 13:34:57.311: INFO: ensuring deployment redis-deployment-2 rcs were deleted
Feb 23 13:34:57.518: INFO: ensuring deployment redis-deployment-2 pods were deleted
Feb 23 13:35:27.835: FAIL: Failed to remove deployment redis-deployment-2 pods!
```

So the pod was still around from 21:34 -> 21:35 (time skew with the node) and that's why we failed. This is the node: https://pantheon.corp.google.com/m/cloudstorage/b/kubernetes-jenkins/o/pr-logs/pull/21399/kubernetes-pull-build-test-e2e-gce/30050/artifacts/104.197.246.52%3A22-kubelet.log?debugUI=CLOUD

And looking up the container f14f53b81beea84ca81b6ab3f9c01011b62738f57a735f1edb4d44c915fef864

```
I0223 21:34:48.067817    3376 manager.go:1519] DNS ResolvConfPath exists: /var/lib/docker/containers/f14f53b81beea84ca81b6ab3f9c01011b62738f57a735f1edb4d44c915fef864/resolv.conf. Will attempt to add ndots option: options ndots:5

I0223 21:34:48.085143    3376 manager.go:799] Added container: "/f14f53b81beea84ca81b6ab3f9c01011b62738f57a735f1edb4d44c915fef864" (aliases: [k8s_POD.6059dfa2_redis-deployment-2-tztd7-obyq6_e2e-tests-deployment-fkfv5_40f88db0-da75-11e5-b5ae-42010af00002_807d5331 f14f53b81beea84ca81b6ab3f9c01011b62738f57a735f1edb4d44c915fef864], namespace: "docker")
I0223 21:34:48.085983    3376 handler.go:320] Added event &{/f14f53b81beea84ca81b6ab3f9c01011b62738f57a735f1edb4d44c915fef864 2016-02-23 21:34:47.137133486 +0000 UTC containerCreation {<nil>}}
I0223 21:34:48.086109    3376 container.go:386] Start housekeeping for container "/f14f53b81beea84ca81b6ab3f9c01011b62738f57a735f1edb4d44c915fef864"

tl;dr without getting into a more intense debug session:
1. the kubelet got confused. Perhaps: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/21605
2. The deployment test probably shoud wait to confirm that the pod was ready (because from the kubelet logs it doesn't look like redis-deployment-2-tztd7-obyq6 was ever ready)

title: ReplicationControllerManager is too slow to support 1000-node clusters

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
I've finally debugged the main problem that is causing load.go test failures in 1000-node clusters.

The problem is basically getPodController() method:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/replication/replication_controller.go#L202

Here is exactly what is happening:
- in load test in 1000-node cluster, we create ~3500 replication controllers, which altogether have 30.000 pods
- then for each pod ReplicationControllerManager is creating a batch of pods:
  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/replication/replication_controller.go#L344
- and then is waiting for them to be observed via watch
- however, on top of watch, we have an Informer framework in ReplicationControllerManager:
  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/replication/replication_controller.go#L152
- and the problem is that a single addPod/updatePod/deletePod call (which are called sequentially for every single add/update/delete pod action) is calling: getPodController:
  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/replication/replication_controller.go#L202
- and getPodController has complexity O(#replicationControllers)

Which means that for any pod add/update/delete done in the system, ReplicationControllerManager is doing O(#replicationControllers) computations (which are btw non-trivial ones).

This is basically, why density.go (where we have a single RC) works pretty good, but load.go test basically doesn't work at all.

In my opinion this is a blocker for 1.2.

@fgrzadkowski @gmarek @davidopp @lavalamp @kubernetes/goog-control-plane @kubernetes/sig-scalability

body:
In my cluster, I meet a race condition issue which I think happened in kube-scheduler. Here is my phenomena:
- My minion node has CIDR for docker at /27 which allows 32 docker IPs.
- The Pod has been scheduled to one minion node but could not start as expected with the following docker error message:

```
  13m   13m     1       {kubelet kubernetes-minion-100-5034}               FailedSync      Error syncing pod, skipping: API error (500): Cannot start container 26a68f65a401512f52c75cec3d61ec3a51693dd1774c0ffeb0bc0dc99d09b44f: no available ip addresses on network

  12m   12m     1       {kubelet kubernetes-minion-100-5034}       implicitly required container POD       Failed  Failed to start with docker id c6d5e43d1e59 with error: API error (500): Cannot start container c6d5e43d1e59f399c80e45b4fc74acb7f1031e936f1e233a13b9009bebc7772a: no available ip addresses on network
```
- I logon to my minion and find that there are already 30 containers running. So the new scheduled Pod could not get available IP address.

I checked `kube-scheduler` source code and find that it does the following things:
1. Get node information
2. Find nodes that fit the Pod requirements
3. Select one node from prioritized node list
I would assume there is race condition in these steps, that the problem node was not report its status at the right time. And scheduler schedule the new Pod to it.

Would it be make sense to have a double check before `return g.selectHost(priorityList)`?

milestone.title: UX Backlog - Stack Ranked
milestone.description: Closed by @calebamiles after talking with @pwittrock please contact calebamiles (on Slack) with complaints

body:
For 1.3 we'll be considering adding a number of commands developed upstream in OpenShift into kubectl - specifically, commands that assist the user in performing very common mutations to our core objects.

Current implementations are:
- Adding or removing volumes from an object with a pod template
- Adding or removing environment variables from an object with a pod template
- Adding or removing liveness and readiness probes from objects with a pod template.

As proposed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/proposals/deploy.md#kubectl-set, these commands would live under `kubectl set` and operate generically on classes of objects (for the commands above, they would operate on objects with mutable pod templates, for other commands, more generic structure should be possible).

The commands would take as input a JSON/YAML file, a real object on the server, or a synthetic resource generated by looking at multiple server resources, transform the object, and create a patch on the original object that results in the desired mutation.  The patch would be applied to the object and then the object mutated on the server.

It should be possible to specify `-o yaml` and generate a file that can be chained to later commands, for instance:

```
kubectl set volume -f deployment.yaml --add --claim-name=foo -o yaml | kubectl set probe --liveness --get-url=https://foo.bar -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
```

We need to ensure the usability of chaining (both apply, patch, replace, and create are all viable terminations) as part of this work.

In practice, we have found it valuable to have the default mode for the set commands to "list" the current state in a pattern that enables users to guess at what they need to do to change the field.  Mutation via CLI flags is hard - each flag must be carefully chosen to balance ease of comprehension with ability to express most of the API.  It is acceptable to punt some use cases in mutation to the `edit` command.  Most commands should focus on having a "clear" or "remove" flag that can remove a targeted entry, a simple set of flags that set the default values, and where possible try to support the minimum amount of simultaneous change.

Set commands should have a consistent code pattern to make implementing new setters easy.  As much as possible, it should be able to take an existing set command, define a business transformation (adding X to Y) and map that to existing code that is tested in a standard way, following https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/devel/kubectl-conventions.md#command-implementation-conventions.

OpenShift implementations of the various commands need varying levels of cleanup:
- `oc set env` is the oldest of the downstream implementations and does not support downward API flags at the current time.  However, it is tuned very well to make adding and removing structured variables easy.  https://github.com/openshift/origin/blob/master/pkg/cmd/cli/cmd/set/env.go
- `oc set volumes` is the most complex of the commands today - given the number of volumes we have a choice was made to focus on the most common (claims, empty dir, secrets) and force users to patch other commands.  Helpers were added to make creating a claim and adding it to a template very easy.  https://github.com/openshift/origin/blob/master/pkg/cmd/cli/cmd/set/volume.go
- `oc set probe` is brand new and formalizes some of the more recent kubectl behaviors into a set of core library methods (specifically, iteratively patching a set of objects) as well as handling the transformation pattern cleanly.  https://github.com/openshift/origin/pull/7331
- `oc set triggers` represents a command that exposes a generic interface across two similar, but not identical concepts (build and deployment triggers, which result in a mutation of the object based on external stimulus).  It is the most complex because the underlying API is dissimilar, but tries to present a common and simple pattern to users.  It explicitly does not handle setting multiple triggers of certain types at a time as an 80% use case solution.  https://github.com/openshift/origin/pull/7423

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
I set up a 1000 node cluster on GKE using standard GCE advanced route networking.  It wasn't possible for @dchen1107 to ssh to a node because gcloud was unable to add her ssh key to the project -- rate limit exceeded.  Note that some other calls like list instances and resizing the MIG were not impacted, so it might be a particular category of API call that's getting rate limited?

We need to make sure 1000 node k8s clusters don't trigger GCE's rate limiter and make the user unable to use parts of the GCE api for their project.

Is there a vaguely-sane way to understand how much GCE api traffic each of our N controller objects is sending?  Do we e.g. have prometheus metrics of sent calls (and perhaps result code for success/error?)

Note this may share an underlying cause with #21561 where large numbers of GCE calls result in api errors.

body:
Forked from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/21261 since they are totally different issues. 

Reported from @gmarek and @wojtek-t when bringing up a large cluster with 1000 nodes, there were 210 Nodes cannot be Ready state during validation phase (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/21261#issuecomment-185628072)

After some debugging, it turns out that the node cannot join the cluster because it cannot get subnet file /var/run/flannel/subnet.env from flannel_server for about two and half hours, so  that it cannot config the node properly and docker cannot start properly too:

```
I0218 04:22:33.680863    3803 kubelet.go:2671] Flannel server handshake failed Waiting for subnet file /var/run/flannel/subnet.env
...
I0218 06:51:10.022449    3911 kubelet.go:2671] Flannel server handshake failed Waiting for subnet file /var/run/flannel/subnet.env
```

I checked the flannel-server pods, and found the etcd-container within that pod is in crashloop all the time. It turns out the etcd-container is oom-killed on master node.

We need to figure out how much resource required by flannel-server pods, especially the etcd-container one. 

cc/ @bprashanth @thockin @kubernetes/goog-cluster

  if ! curl --insecure -m ${max_seconds} -f -s https://127.0.0.1:{{kubelet_port}}/healthz > /dev/null; then

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

body:
I'm not sure if this is desired behaviour or not but currently if the following scenario happens
1. iscsid.conf has node.startup set to automatic (default value)
2. kubelet is running a pod with a mapped iscsi volume
3. The node reboots/crashes etc
4. Kubescheduler reschedules the pod to another node
5. The node comes up again and will try to re open the session to the target that the pod was using. This can either cause annoyance or worst case data corruption unless the iscsi target is set to reject more than one session per target

If we instead set the following when login into the target the session won't be reopened
iscsiadm -m node --targetname proper_target_name -p target_IP:port -o update -n node.startup -v manual

title: Zone-spread HA master for Ubernetes Lite

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/multicluster
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Multicluster.

body:
The current incarnation of Ubernetes Lite makes the application tolerant to zone outages but does not make the Kubernetes control plane tolerant to zone outages since it doesn't use (zone-distributed) HA master. For a short or medium duration zone outage this is totally fine because the containers will continue running even if the master goes away, but if the zone where the master was running goes out for a long time, eventually there will be problems (since pods from failed nodes won't reschedule, users can't update the containers, etc.). 

It would be good to do a zone distributed HA master for Ubernetes Lite, with at least one etcd replica per zone, at least one API server per zone, and the master-elected components like scheduler and controller-manager distributed across the zones.

cc/ @quinton-hoole @justinsb 

ref/ #17059

title: In-container client config doesn't work for many common use cases because no namespace available

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
This is kind of last minute, but I'd like to consider this for 1.2 because we've had a recent rash of users who want to script this and are effectively blocked.

Today, by default service accounts inject one of their secrets into `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/default`.  That secret enables API access.  We have support in the client config to read that value and provide a default client connection using that service account, which means `kubectl` inside of the container can effectively perform operations as the service account and is easily scriptable.  The one gap today is that `kubectl` does not have access to a default namespace.  Since the point of this injection is to enable easy use of the API by a pod, and most of our APIs that a pod would mutate are namespace scoped, and the service account is scoped to a namespace (although it may have other privileges), the fact that the secret comes with no identifying information as to the namespace means that in order to do "easy" integration with the API, the caller also has to inject the pod namespace via the downward API. 

I would like to add a `namespace` key to each service account token secret, and change in-cluster-config to check for that file and use its value as a default namespace for kubectl and other kubectl like tools.  The secret is a "default injected convention" and the convention is meant to enable easy API integration.  Auto-injecting a downward API volume / env is more complex.  

This enables scenarios like:
- Create a pod that has the command `/bin/sh -c "kubectl rolling-upgrade $SOURCE $DESTINATION && curl -X POST https://myserver/deployment/successful`
- Fetch endpoints for the current service from any pod that has kubectl `kubectl get endpoints db -o jsonpath={.endpoints.subset.addresses}`

body:
Spinning up a new GCE cluster, I get 9 nodes in 3 instance groups, but the validate-cluster call is only checking for 4 nodes (presumably one instance group's 3 nodes plus the master):

`Detected 5 ready nodes, found 5 nodes out of expected 4. Found more nodes than expected, your cluster may not behave correctly.`

Once 4+ nodes are found it happily continues and says that the cluster is running. But if you immediately run `kubectl get nodes` there are multiple nodes in the `NotReady` state, which should block validate-cluster from completing successfully.

title: gce route creation for 1000 node clusters takes too long

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
I created a 5 node cluster on GCE, then cloned the MIGs to have more of them with faster-than-usual VM creation.

It took 7 minutes to create all the VMs, but it took an additional 19 minutes for the route controller to create all of the routes.  It should be a lot faster.

In particular, I think we're throttling calls to the GCE api due to rate limits?

Ideally, the controller would look something like:
- have a max number of outstanding operations on GCE at a time.
- if an API rate-limit token is available AND there's a queued create-operation request AND the number of outstanding operations is less than the max, create a new operation.
- otherwise, if an API rate-limit token is available, poll the most-long-ago-checked pending operation for doneness.
- otherwise, wait until an API rate-limit token is available.

@cjcullen

title: Don't use ":latest" or non-tagged images in e2e tests

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/flake
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a flaky test.

labels.name: area/release-eng
labels.description: Issues or PRs related to the Release Engineering subproject

body:
If a image is not tagged or is tagged with :latest, the image pull policy is defaulted to PullAlways. This causes unnecessary image pulling in e2e tests, leading to various timeout flakes (e.g. #20418). 
Unless a test is meant to test image pulling, we should not allow using of such images.

The alternative is to explicitly set PullIfNotPresent in such cases, which seem harder to enforce.

body:
As we introduce more complex scheduling constraints and preferences (node affinity is in 1.2, pod affinity and taints/tolerations will be in 1.3), we should also start using pods that use these features.

It may be reasonable to have a looser scheduling SLO for workloads that involve a lot of complex constraints, but let's wait and see what effect these more complex scheduling rules have on performance.

title: Ensure Deployment labels adopted ReplicaSets and pods

milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
Basically, we need to do the equivalent of AddDeploymentKeyToReplicationController:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubectl/rolling_updater.go#L641

Otherwise, new RCs produced by Deployment will overlap we pre-existing ones that aren't constrained by the pod-template-hash.

If we can't do this for 1.2, we should document this pitfall.

cc @kargakis @janetkuo @mqliang @ironcladlou

title: Client: Never throttle watch

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.2-candidate
milestone.description: Things to consider for next minor release.

body:
As @wojtek-t notes in #20638, it's possible for our client throttling to allow a list and then block the corresponding watch. This is really bad, because if those two calls aren't close enough together, the window could expire and then we'd have to start all over with another list. Lists are expensive and we want to minimize them.

The first thing that comes to mind is to just not throttle watches. I don't know if it's necessary to be more complicated than that.

title: e2es (especially Conformance) should not rely on Events

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
Per https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/19724#issuecomment-180488608 and further discussion, e2es, especially conformances tests, should:
1. not rely on a pod getting scheduled by a specific scheduler;
2. not rely on that scheduler sending specific events at specific checkpoints.

Perhaps we're okay with tightly coupling some e2es to the default scheduler, but probably not conformance tests, (unless we want to force conformant clusters to have a default scheduler).

title: Rewrite scheduler-centric e2e tests to avoid use of events for validation

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
We should have enough info available in other parts of the API to be able to test:
- whether a pod was scheduled
- scheduling latency per-pod
- reasons a pod failed to schedule

Events are deemed unstable / non-API, so at least the `[Conformance]` subset of tests should not rely on them

ref #19724

title: Hot loop in reflector logging

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body: See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/20652#issuecomment-180112628 -- it logs a message every 10-20 microseconds when etcd goes down. Once a second would be a better retry frequency, and once every 30 seconds would be a better logging frequency. P1 since this could exacerbate an outage by filling logs in the time it takes to get etcd back up.

title: Fluentd pod on master has broken resolv.conf

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
Causing fluentd to fail to export logs from the master, because it can't resolve logging.googleapis.com (or anything else, for that matter). It only seems to affect the fluentd pod, not the other kube-\* pods.

In an affected fluentd pod on the master at HEAD:

```
/etc/hosts:
# Kubernetes-managed hosts file.
127.0.0.1       localhost
::1     localhost ip6-localhost ip6-loopback
fe00::0 ip6-localnet
fe00::0 ip6-mcastprefix
fe00::1 ip6-allnodes
fe00::2 ip6-allrouters
172.17.0.3      fluentd-cloud-logging-gke-249458424157-f624d740e956aedbf6f2

/etc/resolv.conf:
nameserver 10.247.240.10
search kube-system.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local c.projectid.internal. google.internal.
options ndots:5

/etc/resolvconf/interface-order:
# interface-order(5)
lo.inet*
lo.dnsmasq
lo.pdnsd
lo.!(pdns|pdns-recursor)
lo
tun*
tap*
hso*
em+([0-9])?(_+([0-9]))*
p+([0-9])p+([0-9])?(_+([0-9]))*
eth*
ath*
wlan*
ppp*
*
```

In an unaffected kube-apiserver pod on the same master VM:

```
/etc/hosts:
127.0.0.1       localhost
::1             localhost ip6-localhost ip6-loopback
fe00::0         ip6-localnet
ff00::0         ip6-mcastprefix
ff02::1         ip6-allnodes
ff02::2         ip6-allrouters
10.240.0.15 gke-249458424157-f624d740e956aedbf6f2.c.gke-test-us-central1-f-0.internal gke-249458424157-f624d740e956aedbf6f2  # Added by Google

/etc/resolve.conf:
domain c.projectid.internal.
search c.projectid.internal. 365122390874.google.internal. google.internal.
nameserver 169.254.169.254
nameserver 10.240.0.1

/etc/resolveconf/interface-order: doesn't exist
```

In a functioning fluentd pod on the master at 1.1.7

```
/etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 10.159.240.10
nameserver 169.254.169.254
nameserver 10.240.0.1
search kube-system.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local c.projectid.internal. google.internal.
options ndots:5
```

title: Increase the logging level for a GKE test cluster

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: area/provider/gcp
labels.description: Issues or PRs related to gcp provider

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
The logging level of a GCE e2e cluster is set at V4, while a GKE e2e cluster maintains the regular V2. This makes debugging GKE build failures more difficult than necessary. 

For GCE, the logging level is set in [configure-vm.sh](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d8be60ee57fc442ed19acc65060f615bf4accf48/cluster/gce/configure-vm.sh#L313). I am not sure what's the best way to do the equivalent for GKE.

body:

cc @kubernetes/sig-testing  @kubernetes/sig-scalability

milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
The AWS kube-up and the GCE kube-up diverged over time as GCE added functionality.  We should try to get them working similarly - I am going to try to get this into 1.2.

In particular, I want to make sure that:
1. Node and master reboot work properly on AWS (some reports that they sometimes don't)
2. In place upgrade works properly on AWS
3. We build secrets & certs as part of kube-up, paving the way for HA master
4. We run salt on each of the nodes, ending the dependency on salt-master and making for a faster boot
5. kube-push works properly on AWS (less important?)

The completed PoC is in #19799.

Steps:
- [x] Start extracting shared functionality out of cluster/gce/util.sh -> cluster/common.sh (done #19776)
- [x] Extract out certificate builder function into common.sh (#20642)
- [x] Change AWS instance-boot script to share script with GCE, likely by using override-method hack for the moment (in progress; cleaning up #19799)

title: Problem using Auth0 in Kubernetes OIDC Authentication

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
Kubernetes v1.1.2 and v1.1.4

I'm trying to use Auth0 in K8s Authentication.
And have come across this issue. 

apiserver.yaml

```
    - --oidc-issuer-url=https://sample.auth0.com
    - --oidc-client-id=CLIENT_SECRET_HERE
```

apiserver logs 

```
E0202 02:54:58.223319       1 oidc.go:99] Failed to fetch provider config, trying again in 3s: "issuer" in config (https://sample.auth0.com/) does not match provided issuer URL (https://sample.auth0.com)
```

it was able to check the openid configuration using the above url + /.well-known/openid-configuration in the k8s oidc codes

```
https://sample.auth0.com/.well-known/openid-configuration

and fails after comparing the retrieved  issuer from auth0 = "https://sample.auth0.com/"  and the defined issuer in the apiserver
```

Auth0 known configuration 

```
https://sample.auth0.com/.well-known/openid-configuration

{"issuer":"https://sample.auth0.com/","authorization_endpoint":"https://sample.auth0.com/authorize","token_endpoint":"https://sample.auth0.com/oauth/token","userinfo_endpoint":"https://sample.auth0.com/userinfo","jwks_uri":"https://sample.auth0.com/.well-known/jwks.json","scopes_supported":["openid","profile","offline_access","name","given_name","family_name","nickname","email","email_verified","picture","created_at","identities","phone","address"],"response_types_supported":["code","token","code token"],"response_modes_supported":["query","fragment","form_post"],"subject_types_supported":["public"],"id_token_signing_alg_values_supported":["HS256","RS256"],"token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported":["client_secret_basic","client_secret_post"],"claims_supported":["aud","auth_time","created_at","email","email_verified","exp","family_name","given_name","iat","identities","iss","name","nickname","phone_number","picture","sub"]}

```

Changing oidc-issuer-url to `https://sample.auth0.com/`will result to 

```
E0202 05:59:21.796520       1 oidc.go:99] Failed to fetch provider config, trying again in 3s: invalid character 'C' looking for beginning of value
```

Apparently, k8s is calling this link

```
https://sample.auth0.com//.well-known/openid-configuration

Cannot GET //.well-known/openid-configuration
```

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
Forked from issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/18969#issuecomment-177010714

Today kube-up asks to bring N nodes, and wait for timeout check the number (M) of Ready nodes. If M is not equal to N, kube-up just simply quit. The user has to restart the entire kube-up process from the beginning. This is really a bad user experience. We should add self-healing so that nodes that fail to come up are replaced / repaired. There are many ways to achieve self-handling, and at GCE, managed instance group can easily delete nodes or recreate nodes with id:

https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/#delete_from_group 
https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/#recreate_instances

cc/ @bgrant0607 @davidopp @quinton-hoole @roberthbailey @gmarek
