title: Can't generate client and protobuf code simultaneously for API groups with dots in their name

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
In #25634 I'm trying to add an API group called "rbac.authorization.k8s.io" which currently lives in the directory "pkg/apis/rbac"

Unfortunately, client generation with go2idl creates the file pkg/client/clientset_generated/internalclientset/typed/rbac/unversioned/rbac_client.go which has a snippet that looks like this:

```
func setConfigDefaults(config *restclient.Config) error {
    // if rbac group is not registered, return an error
    g, err := registered.Group("rbac")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    ...
}
```

The string "rbac" is wrong since the group's name is "rbac.authorization.k8s.io". However changing it manually causes "hack/verify-codegen.sh" to fail.

```
errors in package "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/client/clientset_generated/internalclientset/typed/rbac/unversioned":
output for "unversioned/rbac_client.go" differs; first existing/expected diff: 
  ".authorization.k8s.io\")\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\tconfig.APIPath = \"/apis\"\n\tif config.UserAg"
  "\")\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\tconfig.APIPath = \"/apis\"\n\tif config.UserAgent == \"\" {\n\t\tconfig."
```

To deal with this I moved the directory from "pkg/apis/rbac" to "pkg/apis/rbac.authorization.k8s.io" so go2idl generates the correct string.

Now protobuf generation fails with a lot of error messages that look like this:

```
k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/apis/rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1alpha1/generated.proto:110:12: "k8s.io.kubernetes.pkg.api.v1.ObjectMeta" is resolved to "k8s.io.kubernetes.pkg.apis.rbac.authorization.k8s.io.kubernetes.pkg.api.v1.ObjectMeta", which is not defined. The innermost scope is searched first in name resolution. Consider using a leading '.'(i.e., ".k8s.io.kubernetes.pkg.api.v1.ObjectMeta") to start from the outermost scope.
```

From what I can tell, it's currently impossible to correctly generate assets for API groups which require client generation, if that group name has a dot in it.

Is there anything I can do to fix the protobuf or go2idl generation?

cc @erictune @sym3tri @gtank

title: [GKE] Pod Can't Mount Volumes (Fails to Create Paths) Won't Leave ContainerCreating State

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
We have a disk "databases-us-central1-b-kube" that contains some protein databases (blast non-redundant, pdb, hhsearch, etc.) It's supposed to be mounted read-only.

We had a replication controller/replica in our "development" namespace (which was created long ago) that was accidentally set to mount this drive as read-write. It was previously the only thing using the drive, so we had no issues then and didn't notice. However, we recently tried to add a second controller/replica that tries to mount the same drive as read-only. When we noticed our mistake in the first controller, we changed it's configuration to expose the drive as read-only, deleted the replication controller with `kubectl delete rc/theservice` and re-created it with `kubectl create -f theservice-controller.yml`.

Now we're having this awesome problem where _almost_ nothing can mount disks. I had the bright idea to restart each node in the cluster via the google cloud console in an attempt to fix things, and now things that mount a disks are failing to start.

title: [AWS] Repeated DescribeInstances calls when KCM restarts

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.3
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/master/release-1.3/release-1.3.md

body:
On AWS, whenever the set of nodes changes, or when controller-manager is restarted, controller-manager calls DescribeInstances once for _every_ service to get detailed information about the nodes. This, together with other AWS API calls, causes the AWS API request limit to be hit when you have enough services.

The call chain is

nodeSyncLoop --->
updateLoadBalancerHosts --->
(for each service) lockedUpdateLoadBalancerHosts --->
s.balancer.UpdateLoadBalancer --->
s.getInstancesByNodeNames

title: Work around KubeProxy panic that makes Node's network not working

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.description: Issues or PRs related to gcp provider

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.3
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/master/release-1.3/release-1.3.md

body:
Currently a Docker bug may cause KubeProxy to crashloop thus making the Node unable to use cluster network, which in turn makes Pods scheduled on this Node unreachable.

To mitigate this issue we need to surface the information about problems with KubeProxy, that will allow scheduler to ignore given node when scheduling new Pods. ProblemAPI is going to address this kind of problems in the future, but we need a fix for the 1.3.

Either Kubelet or KubeProxy needs to update a NodeStatus with the information that Node networking is down. I suggests that we reuse NodeReady Condition for this, as this would make the rest of ControlPlane work out of the box. We will replace this fix with the ProblemAPI use in the future. @thockin @dchen1107 

Another option, which requires more work, is creating a completely new NodeCondition type to handle this case. This would require making Scheduler aware of this new Condition. @davidopp @bgrant0607 

@alex-mohr @wojtek-t @fgrzadkowski @zmerlynn

title: Unable to cleanly stop controllers that use delta fifo in integration tests

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten

body:
I was debugging an integration test flake, and encountered a deadlock that prevents stopping controllers that use a delta fifo.  This prevents cleanly closing a server that a controller is operating against in an integration test.

The root cause is there is no way to tell a `DeltaFifo` to stop waiting:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/client/cache/delta_fifo.go#L370

title: Update documentation examples incorrectly referring to replication controllers with replica sets

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

body:
A number of examples spread across various documentation pages still speak of replication controllers where they should instead say replica sets. Many of these are of an introductory nature and thus tend to confuse Kubernetes newcomers in particular (as determined anecdotally by the number of Slack questions I personally see getting posted in this regard). One particular use case is the application of the `kubectl run` command which is often accompanied by telling the reader to run `kubectl get rc` to see the created replication controllers afterwards where instead it should be `kubectl get rs` these days to list replica sets.

All such occurrences should be updated accordingly. Specifically, I came across
- http://kubernetes.io/docs/user-guide/simple-nginx/
- http://kubernetes.io/docs/user-guide/pods/multi-container/
- http://kubernetes.io/docs/user-guide/walkthrough/k8s201/

There may be additional pages though that I'm not aware of.

I'd be happy to provide a PR to update the pages above and any others people point out.

Thanks.

title: Disk based evictions

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Local disk is shared amongst pods and system daemons on a best effort today. Since we do not support disk as a first class resource, there is no means to restrict disk usage of pods.
Often times, nodes run out of local disk, and kubelet needs to free up disk space. Kubelet can perform several actions to free up disk space - delete old containers, delete unused images, evict pods that use a lot of disk. 
This issue tracks the overall effort of freeing up disk space on demand by the Kubelet.
- [x] Proposal for disk eviction PR - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/25237
- [x] Introduce disk eviction thresholds
- [x] Add support for pod evictions
- [x] Generate disk pressure condition in Kubelet
- [x] Update Scheduler to not schedule pods whenever disk pressure condition is set on a node
- [ ] Refactor image GC such that they it can be run on demand based on eviction thresholds
- [ ] Update Container GC to keep the minimum number of containers that kubelet needs (2 for now) and delete the rest of them by default immediately.
- [ ] e2e tests

---

**Stretch**
- [ ] Extract logs outside of containers and delete containers immediately - depends on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/24702
- [ ] Delete logs and images based on thresholds

title: Limit the number of images exposed as part of NodeStatus

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
`NodeStatus` currently includes a list of all images along with its size. This list can grow arbitrarily large on some clusters and it is bounded only by the disk capacity on each node. 
The main purpose for exposing images in NodeStatus is to aid scheduling, by placing pods on nodes that already contain most of the required images. 
If we can safely assume that the image pull latency for small images is negligible, then we can choose to expose only the largest `N` images on a node. This `N` can either be a fixed number for each node, or can be derived based on some threshold. For example, "expose the largest 20 images" or "expose all images that are larger than 50MB"

title: Watch cache regression: changes behavior of "resource version too old" error

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
When attempting to fetch a resource version that is too old, the behavior of watch (for both HTTP and web sockets) changed when watch cache was enabled.  The watch cache returns a 410 - without the watch cache, we return 200 and then write an "error" entry to the watch stream.  This broke a client that dependent on the watch behavior, and moreover is inconsistent with other errors we set in the registry.  Also, for watch over web sockets, most javascript clients will be unable to get at a 410 error from the connection, because browsers don't get access to the data.

We should restore the watch cache behavior to be consistent with the previous behavior as this is a regression in API semantics.

Resource without watch cache, watching too old:

```

title: resource.Quantity allocates too many objects in conversion and decoding

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Calling the .Round() operation to maintain compat with millisecond values is ~90% of the optimized node conversion/decode path in terms of allocations, and the more resources we have, the more expensive it gets.  In addition, quantities are rarely compared, but we do the decode of the value eagerly, which is expensive.  Quantity needs to get much more efficient.

Some areas to investigate:
1. Can we reduce the number of allocations in normal use of Quantity and inf.Dec without more drastic changes?
2. Can we make .String() on a Quantity much more efficient, and then potentially defer decoding it unless we need to change it?  Right now it's a large part of Node and Pod output, and is likely going to impact the scheduler more than other components.  (a naive implementation of this was tried, but String() is far too expensive to be a speed up).
3. Can we do a "fast path" for Quantities that have less precision than int64 (99.99% of them) that is efficient?
4. We should create benchmarks for the following quantity operations - serialization to JSON, string(), copy, round, and validation

Quantity is now the primary source of allocations during encode/decode/conversion after protobuf and the other conversion improvements are taken into account.  If we can tackle this for 1.3 we can potentially get another 10-25% improvement in master CPU for anything with quantity (pods, nodes, quota, limit ranges, scheduling).

title: Test Flakes: Automatic flake assignment

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/contributor-experience
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Contributor Experience.

body:
Prereq: #24754 (individual test owners)

When a test job (running against head) finishes, something needs to assign any failed tests to their respective owners. If an issue already exists, the new failure should be added as a comment.

However, if many tests fail together, this indicates an infrastructure problem, and the issue should be filed against the test-infra team, not against all of the owners of the broken tests. This is to avoid burning out test owners with a bunch of items that it's difficult for them to do anything about.

One can imagine an algorithm where first you count all the failures of tests which previously had a flake rate of 0; if it's more than e.g. 3 then it's probably an infrastructure problem, and you can just file a single issue for all the failures. Otherwise, file an individual issue for each failure and assign to the test's owner.

Part of #24753

title: Test Flakes: Individual test owners

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/contributor-experience
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Contributor Experience.

body:
Implement a system of ownership for tests.

A test owner should:
- Fix the test in a reasonable amount of time if it is broken.
- Fix the system in a reasonable amount of time if the system is causing the test to fail.
- Drive the test into a non-flaky state, if the test is broken for reasons beyond the owner's control.
- Rewrite poorly designed tests.
- Move tests into the smallest framework possible.

A test owner should NOT:
- Fix parts of the system they have little experience with-- file a bug against the relevant people.
- Fix test infrastructure which is breaking multiple tests. We will do our best to avoid incorrectly filing such issues against individual test owners, but should one slip through, the test owner should contact the test-infra team. We don't want 10 individual test owners all working on the same thing at the same time!
- Paper over system issues by e.g. extending timeouts.

Test ownership can be accomplished in multiple ways. It needs to be machine readable, so that we can use it for assignment and in the OWNERs system. Worst case, we can split out the tests into separate files and do per-file owners.

Part of: #24753

title: Declarative update of configmaps and secrets from the contents of files

body:
Currently AFAIK you can only create a secret from a file using:

```
kubectl create secret generic <name> --from-file=<key>=<file>
```

The drawback is this, If a change is made to the file you need to delete and then recreate the secret:

```
kubectl delete secret <name>
kubectl create secret generic <name> --from-file=<key>=<file>
```

This is awkward because to update the other items (service, deployment, pv) in the same app you just run:

```
kubectl apply -f <filename>
```

I realize that I can create a script to base64 encode the contents of the file and inject it into a secret spec file and then use create/apply/delete as with other API objects but this just feels awkward because the create/apply/delete workflow is so clean.

For context this is a redis config file that contains a password and I'm mounting it with a volumeMount in a deployment:

```
- name: redis-conf-secret
  readOnly: true
  mountPath: /etc/redis
```

title: Total priority can overflow

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
Weight is an int (see [PriorityConfigFactory definition](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dae5ac482861382e18b1e7b2943b1b7f333c6a2a/plugin/pkg/scheduler/factory/plugins.go#L53)). Priority can take the range 1-10. Total priority for a node is sum of weight \* priority for each priority function, and the sum is accumulated into an int (see [PrioritizeNodes](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dae5ac482861382e18b1e7b2943b1b7f333c6a2a/plugin/pkg/scheduler/generic_scheduler.go#L227)). So obviously the total priority can overflow if someone sets the weight(s) too high.

The weights of all priority functions are compiled in (or specified in config file), so we can check to make sure maximum total priority can't overflow an int (take sum over all priority functions of 10 \* weight of that priority function, and make sure that's smaller than int(MaxUint >> 1) which according to StackOverflow is the way to find out what is max int (math package has max Int32, Int64, etc. but not max Int).

Note that scheduler extender is OK because although the policy runs in a separate process, the weight is specified in scheduler config file (ExtenderConfig struct) and the priority is bounded 1-10 as usual.

title: Serialize and write api.Pod/Container spec/status as container annotations

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
Forked from the discussion in #23725.

In short, we've been writing information as docker labels and rkt annotations to container/pods due to the lack of kubelet checkpointing. As the results, we have to handle label/annotation backward compatibility issues. Instead of doing that, we can just serialize the kubernetes pod/container objects and write it as annotations.

After discussing with @vishh and @dchen1107, we may also checkpoint the pod "status" (instead of just the spec), so that we can delete an container as soon as the new one starts.

There are two options:
1. Write the entire pod object (spec/status) to every container in the pod. This is easy to implement, and the last created container has the complete spec and status. 
2. Write pod spec/status to the pod sandbox (i.e., infra container for docker), and container spec/status to individual containers. This is cleaner in general.

@Random-Liu, feel free to grab this one since you were working on docker labels. 
@dchen1107, I marked this v1.3 tentatively.

title: Simplifying specification of multiple files/URLs in kubectl

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
Would make it easier to stand up examples and apps without multiple flags, multiple commands, or a separate tool.

Ideas, some of which have been proposed before:
- Recursive directory traversal: #19767
- Manifest that can specify multiple files/URLs
  - ideally the same file of relative paths could work for both locals files and fetched via http
- Default file/URL manifest (ala Dockerfile or Makefile or maybe git): #3268
- Unpack archive (tgz, zip, OCI image) specified via `-f` and then invoke `-f` on that directory
- URL shortening via default URL prefix (need to fix preferences: #10693)
- kubectl could expand globs: #12123
- kubectl could support a more distinctive well known extension: #15387
- kubectl could support git sources

Ideally they'd be compatible with current `-f` usage.

cc @kubernetes/sig-cli-feature-requests

title: Automate and/or create an interface for spinning up jenkins jobs for a new branch

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/testing
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Testing.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
At the time a new branch is created, [new jenkins jobs need to be spun up](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/devel/releasing.md#manual-tasks-for-new-release-series).  See also #20946.

This is currently a labor-intensive process that requires much specialized knowledge of the current state of jenkins and jenkins in general.   Ideally this can be distilled to a simple interface (config/button/whatever) that can be updated at some point so that the release tooling can easily trigger it when a new branch is created.  Like adding the new branch to a config file.

@ihmccreery had a good idea in a meeting recently that the current master "set" is simply copied to create the new branch (in the same way the code is branched from master), rather than trying to set something up new. 

cc @spxtr @ixdy @fejta

title: Automatic issue triage

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/contributor-experience
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Contributor Experience.

body:
Our build cop looks at issues, attempts to categorize them, and labels them accordingly:
- support, bug, feature, etc.
- team/component

Labels don't appear as notifications, however, so people interested in a particular type of issue need to poll issues with that label.

Also, issues are often miscategorized.

This seems like a job for a machine.

We could have manually written pattern-matching or use machine learning (using old issues for training), but I'd like some means of automatic triage.

I suggest we start with kubectl, as a test case. If an issue mentions kubectl, we could:
- label the issue with component/kubectl and team/ux
- cc "@kubernetes/kubectl"

Lots of misc. bug reports contain kubectl commands, so it would be useful to think about how to filter those out.

Somewhat related: We should create an issue template #21437, which would facilitate some amount of user-supplied categorization.

cc @fejta

title: Endpoints performance is O(n) in the number of IP:port pairs

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
When stress-testing an unrelated component, I scaled up 5000 pods covered by the same service. The latency of the verb=PUT,resource=endpoint requests, as reported by kube-apiserver, went through the roof with a peculiar curve:

![grafana_-_k8s___overview](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/131590/14688384/dd29c61c-0731-11e6-96be-efb09d5bc015.png)

I think the problem is that Endpoint is one object containing a list of IP:port pairs. This list gets larger and larger, thus updating it takes much longer. This should also affect GET but at a much lower level.

The levelling off is the rate of additions going down because each endpoint addition takes longer. I think the behaviour here can be improved; I will file a separate issue for this.

As far as I can tell, this is inherent in the endpoint data structure.

Here is the etcd latency (again, as reported by kube-apiserver) for the same timeframe:

![grafana_-_k8s___overview](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/131590/14688497/61f20fc6-0732-11e6-96ee-9b5204b054f6.png)

relates to #10436

The "DynamicProvisioner should create and delete persistent volumes" test is failing because the volume is being provisioned in a different zone than the node that the pod is being placed onto. Attempting to mount the disk on the pod's node fails with:

```
gce_util.go:187] Error attaching PD "gke-jenkins-e2e-a4fe3d21-dynamic-pv-gce-0xcbx": GCE persistent disk not found: diskName="gke-jenkins-e2e-a4fe3d21-dynamic-pv-gce-0xcbx" zone="us-central1-a"

It's a known issue that dynamically provisioned PVs are created in the master's zone (#23330), but unexpected that the pod created with the claim is being placed in a different zone.

title: Understand periods of scheduler doing nothing

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
I'm running some experiments on scheduler code.
In particular what I'm running is:
- I'm starting 1000-node Kubemark cluster
- Killing scheduler job
- starting density test and wait until enough pods are created (and waiting for scheduling)
- I'm restarting scheduler (with increased qps limit)

I added some logs to understand what is expensive in scheduler and should be optimized - see:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...wojtek-t:test?expand=1

What I'm seeing are some period where scheduler seem to be doing nothing. For example see logs:

```
E0418 15:46:51.086081    4064 generic_scheduler.go:86] AAA -> compute predicates
E0418 15:46:51.092237    4064 generic_scheduler.go:100] AAA -> prioritize
E0418 15:46:51.097980    4064 generic_scheduler.go:237]   -> 4
E0418 15:46:51.098422    4064 node_affinity.go:96]   -> node affinity
E0418 15:46:51.100128    4064 priorities.go:92]   -> least requested
E0418 15:46:51.100347    4064 priorities.go:229]   -> balanced resource
E0418 15:46:51.104830    4064 selector_spreading.go:236]   -> spreading
E0418 15:46:51.105064    4064 generic_scheduler.go:269] AAA -> finished prioritization
```

^^ there are 5ms between "prioritize" and "4", and from the code it seems that there isn't anything happening then:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/scheduler/generic_scheduler.go#L98

This seems to be a very common patter in logs:

```
E0418 15:46:51.229580    4064 generic_scheduler.go:86] AAA -> compute predicates
E0418 15:46:51.235562    4064 generic_scheduler.go:100] AAA -> prioritize
E0418 15:46:51.242312    4064 generic_scheduler.go:237]   -> 4
E0418 15:46:51.242748    4064 node_affinity.go:96]   -> node affinity
E0418 15:46:51.244354    4064 priorities.go:92]   -> least requested
E0418 15:46:51.244551    4064 priorities.go:229]   -> balanced resource
E0418 15:46:51.249022    4064 selector_spreading.go:236]   -> spreading
```

Another similar "pause period" happens frequently after all priority function are already finished:

```
E0418 15:46:48.522108    4064 generic_scheduler.go:237]   -> 4
E0418 15:46:48.522667    4064 node_affinity.go:96]   -> node affinity
E0418 15:46:48.524575    4064 priorities.go:92]   -> least requested
E0418 15:46:48.524576    4064 priorities.go:229]   -> balanced resource
E0418 15:46:48.531036    4064 selector_spreading.go:236]   -> spreading
E0418 15:46:48.538735    4064 generic_scheduler.go:269] AAA -> finished prioritization
```

^^ all priority functions finished and still it took 7ms to "finish prioritization"
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/scheduler/generic_scheduler.go#L262
[Theoretically this 7ms includes time to update combinedScore slice, but in many cases it takes <0.5ms, so it's most probably not that.]

For completeness - we are using Go 1.6., so IIUC this shouldn't be garbage collector.

title: Improve cluster autoscaling

body:
Current hacky version has number of drawbacks:
- works only on GCE
- doesn't support number of cases and we may still have pending pods
- very cloud provider specific
- very hard to update configuration
- UX is very poor

We'd like to improve it to:
- support all cases for pending pods
- provide a reference implementation that could be ported to other cloud providers.

It should support both scaling up (P1) and scaling down (P2).

This an umbrella bug used for referencing PRs etc.

title: Figure out how to handle code in multiple repos

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/contributor-experience
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Contributor Experience.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/testing
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Testing.

labels.name: sig/architecture
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Architecture.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

labels.name: area/code-organization
labels.description: Issues or PRs related to kubernetes code organization

body:
A large monorepo works for Google, but not on github.

We hit the ceiling of achievable velocity of a single github repo in early 2015:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/graphs/contributors

There are many reasons: ACLs, notification management, issue triage, PR reviews, sequentialized submit testing, merge conflicts, etc.

We're chipping away at these issues, but we need more than incremental improvement.

We've discussed moving a number of things to other repos:
- Kubelet: #444
- Generic API infrastructure: #2742
- Client libraries: #5660
- Misc. utilities: #24156
- kubectl
- scheduler
- examples
- cloud providers + cluster code + "getting-started guides"
- auth plugins
- network and storage plugins?
- e2e tests
- contributor documentation

We need to seriously think about how to do this.

Known issues that need to be addressed:
- We need to get sprawl and package dependencies under control: #4851
- We need to make most components ordinary clients of the API: #20193
- We need to figure out dependency management and integration testing

An example of a Go project on github with good repo hygiene:
https://github.com/deis

I have no illusions that breaking the project into separate repos will be a silver bullet: it's necessary, but not sufficient. I also know that it will cause some pain. But that pain already exists: cadvisor, heapster, dashboard, contrib, docs, ....

Speaking of contrib, it needs to be broken up, too: https://github.com/kubernetes/contrib/issues/762

@thockin @smarterclayton @lavalamp @mikedanese @dchen1107 @davidopp @ixdy

title: Support both "type":"any" and "type":"object" in kubectl validation

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
We used to generate our swagger spec with "type":"any" for any type that wasnt supported in swagger (for ex: maps).

It was later pointed out that "type":"object" is the correct representation: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/4700#issuecomment-194719759.

We have now moved to using "type":"object" in our swagger spec (which will be part of release 1.3), but for kubectl to work with old apiservers, we allow both "type":"object" and "type":"any" in kubectl validation code (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/24054).
We cherrypicked that in release 1.2 (so that 1.2 kubectl can work with 1.3 apiserver).

We can stop supporting "type":"any" in release 1.4 (1.4 kubectl will not be able to work with 1.2 apiserver, which is fine since we support version skew of only 1).

Filing this issue to keep track.

cc @bgrant0607 @kubernetes/sig-api-machinery

title: Change interface of priority functions for easier "framework-based" parallelization

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
I'm currently trying to improve the overall scheduling throughput. It seems we can achieve significant gains from different kind of parallelization.
However, I would like to avoid parallizing individual predicate/priority function and support parallelization at the framework level.

For predicate function, it is easy to parallelize computations of them between nodes, since they are independent.
However, it's not the case for priorities - the interface of priority function is that it computes priorities for all nodes at the same time.

It would be much easier to parallelize everything, when priority function would also take a node as an argument and would compute priority wrt to current priority function just for this particular node.
However, there are two problematic functions for now (maybe more in the future):
- SelectorSpreading
- NodeAffinity

Both of them have the same main problem - they are computing some partial scores for nodes independently, but then to compute the final score for the node, they rely on the maximum of those partial scores from all nodes.
### Proposal
1. I'm proposing to change the interface of priority functions to take a node for which they are supposed to compute priority.
2. We also extend the HostPriority type to include "priorityFunctionName" string
3. We will split priority functions into two phases:
4. per-node computations (which are generally cpu-intensive and would benefit from parallelization)
5. aggregation (which is generally much cheaper) and we can afford not parallelizing it

Thoughts?

@davidopp @kubernetes/sig-scheduling @kubernetes/sig-scalability

title: API server recovery actions are destructive

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.4
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/master/release-1.4/Release-1.4.md

body:
Hello! On GCE, we ran into [this incident](https://status.cloud.google.com/incident/compute/16007). The observed symptom was that our API servers were unreachable for a time. During that period, all pods kept running on nodes and we were able to serve production traffic no problem. As soon as the API servers returned, that event caused something to decide to kill every pod in our infrastructure. I think this is not an acceptable failure mode. Is this well understood / as designed right now or is there something that can be done?

For example, I would have been satisfied if it had done rolling restarts of every pod, and probably would not have even noticed the issue. But because it restarted every pod all at the same time, we lost some replication guarantees and lost a fair amount of data, the effects of which we're still recovering from right now.

title: Scheduler infrastructure is too slow

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
I did a simple experiment around scheduling throughput today.
Basically:
- I removed all priorities and predicates functions
- I replaced the whole scheduling algorithm with "choose random node from the existing ones".

This gives us an estimation on the maximum scheduling throughput we can get (assuming that scheduling algorithm is infinitely fast).

The bad news is that I get throughput of ~45pods/second, which is pretty sad.

So, if we want to go higher than that (and I believe we really want and need), we need some deeper changes in the scheduler infrastructure itself (instead of optimizing priority/predicates function for now).

title: kubectl validation fails when creating a non-v1 object in a v1 list

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
In other words, you can't create/replace/delete/apply deployments with kubectl if they're in a list.

Works as expected:

``` console
$ cat nginx-rc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: List
items:
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: ReplicationController
    metadata:
      name: nginx
    spec:
      replicas: 1
      template:
        metadata:
          labels:
            name: nginx
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: nginx
              image: nginx
$ kubectl create -f nginx-rc.yaml
replicationcontroller "nginx" created
```

Does not work as expected:

```
$ cat nginx-dpl.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: List
items:
  - apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
    kind: Deployment
    metadata:
      name: nginx
    spec:
      replicas: 1
      template:
        metadata:
          labels:
            name: nginx
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: nginx
              image: nginx
$ kubectl create -f nginx-dpl.yaml
error validating "nginx-dpl.yaml": error validating data: couldn't find type: v1beta1.Deployment; if you choose to ignore these errors, turn validation off with --validate=false
$ kubectl create -f nginx-dpl.yaml --validate=false
deployment "nginx" created
```

This is a high priority issue for us, since it means we can't (easily) use apply (or any kubectl command) with lists of JSON objects since we've moved all our replication controllers over to deployment objects, which is hampering the UX of our config efforts.

title: Support Cassandra in PetSet

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
**I haven't deployed Cassandra to production, I'll incorporate comments from anyone who has into this missive.**

A cassandra cluster is a ring of nodes. 
- Clients send request to any node (coordinator) which forwards requests to the node with the data.
- Each node is assigned a token. Each row is hashed based on a partition function applied on its primary key. A node stores hashes between its token and the next node's token. 
- A replication strategy picks how data is replicated, eg: 'SimpleStrategy' picks the next N nodes in the ring. The coordinator is also responsible for proxying writes to these nodes based on the consistency level of the request.
## Initial Deployment

To deploy a cassandra cluster you need to pick some "seed" nodes. These are nodes that come up first, and that all other nodes contact to get information about the cluster. They're only used in bootstrapping, after which all nodes cache their peers. All nodes in a cluster must have the same seed. Without at least one seed node, no nodes can join the cluster.

There appear to be many common ways to pick a seed:
See http://docs.datastax.com/en/archived/cassandra/1.0/docs/cluster_architecture/gossip.html.
- Priam uses Amazon's simpleDB to store each node's id as it comes up, and allocates the first in each DC as a seed (https://github.com/Netflix/Priam/wiki/Setup#s3-bucket-and-simpledb-domains). This requires centralized storage that isn't attached to any pet.
- Our [example](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/examples/cassandra) uses Service resolution thorugh a custom entrypoint. If a node finds no endpoints in the Service, it inserts it's own IP into the seed list (TODO: follow up, this feels racy).

Perils:
- Setting all nodes as seeds
- Setting different seeds for different nodes in a single DC 
- Bringing up non-seeds before seeds

Kube implementation notes:    
- Calculate tokens for all nodes (eg: http://docs.datastax.com/en/cassandra/2.1/cassandra/configuration/configGenTokens_c.html)
- First node that comes up is seed, using hostnames is OK (risky to set 2 nodes as seeds that end up waiting on each other, TODO: there are probably better ways)
- Every subsequent node is allocated a segment of the token ring, and told about the seed.
## Scaling

Scaling seems straightforward, there are 3 common ways:
- Double size: Existing nodes can keep their assigned tokens, the new nodes just bisect or trisect the ring.
- Add one node: Leave its inital_token field empty, Cassandra will figure out the heaviest node token and split it.
- Add a random number of nodes: This involves recalculating tokens for the entire cluster and should probably be avoided.

Prefer GossipingSnitch to PropertyFileSnitch, the former requires updating each node with updated DC/rack information with new nodes.
### Adding a DC

The seed list of all nodes should include one node from each DC, or they will be unaware of the entire topology. This might require a total babysitter, and some way to update existing DCs with new seeds. A LOCAL_QUORUM setting is also recommended so we don't round trip to all DCs for every write.
## Failure

Cassandra seems to take a while to detect node failure because it uses gossip. Each node contacts some others periodically, to exchange timestamped heartbeats. These gossip heartbeats could take a while to propogate (or a lack thereof, a while to get detected). The removal of dead nodes is slightly tricky, because of the segmented keyspace and the gossip protocol:
- Confirm node is dead by running nodetool ring
- Set inital_token to dead nodes token (visible in `nodetool ring` output)
- Run nodetool repair on each keyspace of the new node
- Remove the dead node
### Replacing a dead seed
- Promote an existing node to seed
- Remove the dead seed from cassandra.yaml for each node in cluster
- Confirm that all nodes list new node as seed, old node as dead
- Perform steps above to replace a failed node

If a new node is integrated into the cluster before all nodes realize the old node is dead, or see the new seed if the dead node was a seed, the new node might start streaming data from the dead node. The good news is Cassandra will only fail a write if there are too few replicas alive, i.e if it sends a write to a dead node that just hasn't been observed by the cluster, the write will timeout and Cassandra will send the write elsewhere.
## Maintenance and Upgrade

One needs to run nodetool repair periodically on all nodes, within `gc_grace_seconds`. This will cause a spike in cpu. Running on multiple nodes simultaneously might affect throughput. It's also wise to backup SSTables snapshots to cloud storage, since they're immutable.

Upgrade is more tricky. Backup cluster scheme and ring tokens, then on each node:
- Create snapshot (nodetool snapshot)
- Drain node (nodetool drain)
- Stop cassandra
- Purge cassandra/saved_caches. TODO: Is is safer to wait for all nodes to realize this node is down?
- Start new cassandra
## Thoughts

Easier:
- Doubling size of cluster
- Bootstrapping, once you have the seeds up

Harder:
- Deleting nodes, scaling down
- Scaling up to some number of nodes that requires token recomputation
- Upgrading

Periodic backup of sstable snapshots is also recommended by many.
xref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/20961#issuecomment-204485326

title: Kubelet's logic of checking docker running in host does not work in systemd distro

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
I notice that kubelet does not create "/docker-daemon" cgroup if docker is managed by systemd, because the function isProcessRunningInHost call (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go#L448) returns false. As a result, test cases in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/kubelet_perf.go will all fail. This isProcessRunningInHost function (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go#L408) compares /proc/1/ns/mnt with /proc/<docker pid>/ns/mnt to determine if docker is running in host. But this is not true if docker is managed by systemd (such as in CoreOS). You can see that docker has different mount namespace from pid 1, if docker is managed by systemd. But docker and pid 1 process have the same pid namespace.

Why would kubelet check the mount namespace, instead of pid namespace? Could you fix this issue in kubelet container manager?

@dchen1107 @vishh 

cc/ @roberthbailey @fabioy @zmerlynn @wonderfly FYI.

title: SSH Dialer can hang forever.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body: The ssh default timeout is "0" (no timeout). This appears to cause problem for ssh tunnels. A tunnel open attempt can hang indefinitely, and we don't try to kill in-progress open attempts. Most of the time, a failed open attempt will time out after the standard 127 second TCP timeout, but it appears that sometimes it hangs after the TCP connection is established, in the TLS handshake.

title: Support mysql galera in PetSet

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

milestone.title: v1.4
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/master/release-1.4/Release-1.4.md

body:
Synchronous replication for mysql. Each write is replicated across all nodes in the cluster and every server is an effective "master". New nodes added to the cluster download state based on a setting in my.cnf. There are 3 flavors of galera: corership, percona, mariadb, all support the wsrep (write set replication) api ( https://github.com/codership/mysql-wsrep) but are different in other ways. There are 2 ways to transfer state between members:
- SST(Single State Transfer): purge data, copy from a peer. 
- IST(Incremental State Transfer): Normal case only the diff of the binlog index is sent over the network. Some conditions need to be met to trigger this:http://galeracluster.com/documentation-webpages/statetransfer.html.
## Initial deploy

To bootstrap the cluster start a single node up as a reference point for all other nodes, join everyone to this node, restart the reference point. More explicitly:
- Each node needs an initialized database with the correct permissions so peers can download state. This can happen through an entrypoint script.
- Set "gcomm://" and deploy 1 node. It forms a quorum with itself.
- Deploy all other nodes with "gcomm://list-of-nodes", they will join the one node quorum.
- Restart initial node with full list.
  All 3 vendors have a (different) "bootstrap" command that wraps the first step, but one still needs to start mysqld on all the other nodes manually.

Perils:
- Always bootstrap only a single node and restart the others when no node has any state.
- If you have eg: 3 nodes that are all initialized and have varying levels of state, run "bootstrap" on the most advanced node. You can find the most advanced node by comparing `wsrep_last_committed` value from `show status like 'wsrep_%';`.
- If the cluster _already_ has a primary component, don't bootstrap, simply restart the non-primary nodes to force state download.

Kube implementation notes:
- Using predictable hostnames<->volume mappings will result in IST when a container restarts.
- It's easier to deploy all mysql instances standalone, run entrypoint to init tables/add users/grant permissions etc, then pick one and do the dance above.
## Scaling

Adding nodes appears to be easy. Add a new node and specify IPs/hostnames of existing nodes, it downloads state. In practice it's more tricky, a single node is chosen as a "donor" and all state is rsynced. That donor will take a performance hit, the doner is chosen by the clustering algorithm. 

The new node will need permissions to copy data from all nodes in the cluster. Instead of re-granting permissions it might be easier to just do so for eg: 10-dot/16?

TODO: There might be a way to copy the db offline and use IST to get the last few commits.
## Failures

Galera uses quorum for failure handling, there's no failover, minority partition keeps trying to contact others but cannot commit data. Ideally a loadbalancer in front would only send writes to the PC. If nodes diverge in a way that no quorum is possible, one needs to pick and promote a master using the wsrep_last_committed value. Rehabilitation of failed nodes is tricky because SST mode will wipe the data dir (rm -rf essentially) and redownload.
## Upgrade

Known incompatibility issues between some mysql versions, otherwise it doesn't matter which member is chosen for an update unless the cluster is currently bootstrapping.
## Thoughts

Easier
- Adding a member when cluster under low load

Harder
- Bootstrapping cluster
- Rehabilitating members after a net split (this is the same as adding a new member because of SST, but we expect high load at this point).

Galera is simpler to reason about than other clustered solutions in some ways (including mysql cluster), the key differences from some curory research:
- Replication: Galera replicates the entire DB, NDB partitions the dataset and applies a replication factor.
- Loadbalancing: Galera doesn't loadbalance, you need to connect to a specific host, and all hosts have the same data. NDB appears to manage read throughput by being smarter about sending requests to backends where the right stripe of data resides.
- Scaling: Adding more nodes will probably increase latency for Galera (even though writes are in parallel), probably won't for NDB (in fact it will probably increase read throughput).
- Failure: both solutions rely on timeouts and heartbeats, but a single failing node impacts ALL writes in Galera, i.e a node could go down in NDB and not affect an ongoing commit because the cluster is "up" as long as a single node is up and running in each node group.

title: kubelet will never terminate a pod if image registry is unavailable for a pod container

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
After an unbelievable amount of time debugging the following this past week:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/22045
https://github.com/openshift/origin/issues/8176

I discovered that I could reliably cause the `kubelet` to never delete a pod that was `Terminating` if the pod had never been started correctly because the docker image pull returned a `RegistryUnavailable` error.

I verified this by modifying the kubelet to always return `RegistryUnavailable` for a particular image name.  I then created a namespace, added a replication controller that referenced the image, and then watched as the pods got stuck in "Waiting" state but never actually reported a reason.  I then deleted the namespace, and was able to see that in-fact the `kubelet` never properly handled the `terminated` response.

I was able to fix this issue by modifying:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/serialized_image_puller.go#L124

to return `ErrImagePull` when the repository was not available.  This change resulted in letting my `kubelet` properly terminate the pod.  I think this is the correct behavior to not special case `RegistryUnavailable` since in many cases the registry may never become available (its most definitely not a temporary situation).

I suspect this is the potential source of a number of instances of the namespace failed to delete flake because pods remained.

/cc @kubernetes/sig-node @vishh @dchen1107 @yujuhong @kubernetes/rh-cluster-infra

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
In 1.4.x

Create a deployment and wait for an RS to be created.  Check the yaml/json output of the RS

Expected: there should be _something_ on the RS that says what Deployment created it.  The proposal is related to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/proposals/garbage-collection.md

Actual: nothing points back to the deployment.

This is a big problem for clients that want to make associations back to the Deployment that created an RS.  Currently we have to get the entire list of deployments and compare the label selectors.  Generally you need to know what deployment created an RS so that you can point the user to editing the Deployment and not the RS directly.

This issue is filed as a result of investigation done on [29838](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/29838) and the subsequent PR [33010](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/33010)

The main summary of this issue is that the function `printEventList` defined in  `k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubectl/resource_printer.go` is not being used in any path except in one path for the watching for events. I think similar behavior is there for all printXXXList functions. This issue is an attempt to figure out if this was the intended behavior and if not cleanup the code. Its more of an design review bug.

Here is some notes and observation from that investigation:-

1: sorting of events across different resources can be achieved using the command `kubectl get events --sort-by='{.lastTimestamp}'` otherwise they are all mixed up

2: doing `kubectl get events` would show up events in mixed order across all resources(tested with pods). This should show events in sorted order by default, since when events from different resources are shown, the user is only interested in the latest events or events in chronological order. Per resource events are anyways shown in `kubectl describe`

6: Someone more familiar with the framework can confirm how these printXXXList functions are supposed to be used. But for sure in the kubectl get events path, the printEventList is not being called.

7: k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubectl/cmd/get.go as logic which figures if the object is ListType only for watches, but for regular flow, it breaks down the response into individual objs and then calls PrintObj on each obj(rather than calling it on the uber EventList obj), which ensures that the corresponding handlers for api.EventList will never be called even though the response was api.EventList.

8: Further investigation i found `kubectl get events --watch` is the only place printEventList is called. So indeed its  being used, but my feeling is that printEventList should be always used anytime the response is of type *api.EventList which is not the current behavior. We should unify this behavior if we can find why printEventList is not called even if the response is of type *api.EventList in the get events case but only called for watches.

title: Migrating addons from RCs to Deployments.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
Recently we were thinking about running all addons in deployments instead of replication controllers. The main motivation is to support rolling update. A few previous discussion in #32018. As mentioned before, migrating addons from RC to Deployment would affect multiple pieces of work and it is no well explicated yet. So I think it is worth to have a discussion here.

Assumptions:
- All addons will run in deployments in 1.5 release.

Things need to be satisfied: (updated)
- Support rolling update for addons in addon-manager.
- Support upgrade from addons run in RCs to addons run in Deployments. (1.4 -> 1.5 upgrade).
- Support downgrade from addons run in Deployments to addons run in RCs. (1.5 -> 1.4 downgrade).
- Maintain the replicas number of addons while upgrading / rebooting / downgrading.
- Do not affect the behavior of auto-scaling and manually-scaling.
- Well announce the change of update behavior for addon manager.

---

Plan we have currently:
- Finish the WIP #33075 for `kubectl apply --prune` (more detail about this command in proposal #29551). 
- Replace the main logic of addon-manager with a while loop of `kubectl apply --prune`.
- Change addons from RC to Deployment without explicitly describing this transition.

New addon-manager logic:
- `kubectl apply` intuitively supports deployment's rolling update.
- `kubectl apply --prune -f` supports creating / updating / purging resource from configuration file.
- Use label `kubernetes.io/cluster-service` to distinguish resources under addon-manager's control.
- Periodically apply the configuration files.

Old addon-manager logic:
- Periodically poll resources from apiserver and get to know all the resources with label `kubernetes.io/cluster-service`.
- Periodically scan through all configuration files and get to know all the addon resources we should have.
- Comparing resources from apiserver and resources from configuration and figure out resources needed create/delete/update based on the basename, suffix and kind(example: `kube-dns`, `-v19` and `ReplicationController`).

Upgrade process in plan (1.4 -> 1.5):
- After the master is upgraded to 1.5, all the addon objects created by the 1.4 cluster should still work as expected.
- New version addon-manager is started and picks up the new configuration files of addons with Deployments instead of RCs.
- `kubectl apply --prune -l kubernetes.io/cluster-service -f /etc/kubernetes/addons` would properly purge the old RCs and create new Deployments.

Downgrade process in plan (1.5 -> 1.4):
- After the master is downgraded to 1.4, all the addon objects created by the 1.5 cluster should still work as expected.
- Old version addon-manager is started. It begins to poll from apiserver and scans though the configuration files of addons with RCs instead of Deployments.
- Because resource kinds changed, old addon-manager will classify this as RC resources added and Deployment resources deleted. It will first delete the Deployments and the underlying pods, and create the RCs and pods again after.

---

Above is the preliminary thoughts for this work. Please comment if there is any mistake or oversight. Thanks!

@mikedanese @thockin @bprashanth @roberthbailey

title: Force pods to re-pull an image without changing the image tag

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

body:
### Problem

A frequent question that comes up on Slack and Stack Overflow is how to trigger an update to a Deployment/RS/RC when the image tag hasn't changed but the underlying image has.

Consider:
1. There is an existing Deployment with image `foo:latest`
2. User builds a new image `foo:latest` 
3. User pushes `foo:latest` to their registry
4. User wants to do something here to tell the Deployment to pull the new image and do a rolling-update of existing pods

The problem is that there is no existing Kubernetes mechanism which properly covers this.
### Current Workarounds
- Always change the image tag when deploying a new version
- Refer to the image hash instead of tag, e.g. `localhost:5000/andy/busybox@sha256:2aac5e7514fbc77125bd315abe9e7b0257db05fe498af01a58e239ebaccf82a8`
- Use `latest` tag or `imagePullPolicy: Always` and delete the pods. New pods will pull the new image. This approach doesn't do a rolling update and will result in downtime.
- Fake a change to the Deployment by changing something other than the image
### Possible Solutions
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/13488 If rolling restart were implemented, users could do a rolling-restart to pull the new image.
- Have a controller that watches the image registry and automatically updates the Deployment to use the latest image hash for a given tag. See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/1697#issuecomment-202631815

cc @justinsb

title: federation: Support cascading deletion

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/multicluster
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Multicluster.

body:
Problem: There are 2 related problems:
- When user deletes a federated object, corresponding objects created in underlying objects are not deleted. For ex: if user creates a federated service, we create a corresponding service in each cluster. When the federated service is deleted, these services in underlying clusters does not get deleted automatically.
- When a cluster is removed from federation, objects that the federation control plane created in that cluster are not deleted. For ex: if user creates a federated service, we create a corresponding service in each cluster. When a cluster is removed from federation, the service corresponding to the federated service in that cluster does not get deleted automatically.

Now that we have cascading deletion in kubernetes, we should support cascading deletion in federation as well. As in kubernetes, we will give users the option to disable it.

cc @kubernetes/sig-cluster-federation

title: Kubectl 1.4 does not trim --- seperator

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
**Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`):

```
Client: 1.4.0
Server: 1.4.0
```

**Environment**:
- **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**: Any
- **OS** (e.g. from /etc/os-release): Any
- **Kernel** (e.g. `uname -a`): Any
- **Install tools**: Any

**What happened**:
 If I use a template with the `---` seperator, and if the line with the separator has trailing whitespace characters, then kubectl considers that to be the EOF instead of reading further. 

e.g. template 

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  name: testnginx
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    name: testnginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        name: testnginx
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: testnginx
          image: nginx
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80

---    

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: testnginx
  labels:
    name: testnginx
    type: ui
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 8000
    targetPort: 80
  selector:
    name: testnginx
```

**What you expected to happen**:

It should not stop reading if there are trailing whitespace characters, it should just trim the separator line and ignore the whitespaces after the `---`.

This is how it worked until v1.3.0 kubectl version.

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):

Just use the template from above and you'll notice that it won't create the Service, but it'll create the Replication controller.

**Anything else do we need to know**:
This is on kubectl version 1.4.0

title: Disk layout on GCI is incompatible with Kubelet

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
On GCI, the (stateful) partition that kubelet has to monitor is mounted under `/var`. 
Kubelet considers `/` as the primary disk partition and tracks it as `nodefs`. 
It also tracks the partition under which docker is running which is `/var` in GCI and is referred to as `imagefs`.
In the case of GCI `/` seems to be a special partition (`/dev/root`) with limited storage. 

Why is this a problem?

Kubelet's summary API output needs to be carefully examined on GCI since it is different from that of the debian based containerVM. This issue can exist across distros, it is just that it is a behavioral difference in GCE and GKE.

Kubelet is configured to evict pods whenever nodefs availability drops to below 10%. Since on GCI, imagefs is the nodefs that we are going after, disk based evictions will not work with the current config. A simple work around is to update kubelet eviction config to evict based on `imagefs` availability too.

To fix this issue, kubelet should be reporting the stats of the stateful partition under `/var` as the `nodefs` and `imagefs` can be equal to `nodefs`. When this change is made, evictions based on `imagefs` must be removed.  

cc @dchen1107 @kubernetes/goog-image

title: Exersize more of the client cache ( List, Remove ) in scheduler_perf

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
_Problem_

In #31795 
- we found that the List operation in CheckServiceAffinity may be a  dominating factor in scheduler cpu usage,  in the schduler @ scale.  
- _since its using so much CPU_ ideally we would have something simulating this problem in the scheduler_perf tests, so they are more realistic / testing scheduler performance under heterogenous node / affinity conditions. However --  from what i can tell, the cache's `List` is not exersized in the scheduler_perf at all.
- roughly, if we look at the amount of calls during one of the test runs... addpod is really 80% or so of the calls that are happening, i.e. annotating the calls in schedulercache/cache.go. i see the following: 

```
forgetpod:209 
addnode:1100 
addpod:17400 
updatepod:3881
```
- listpod, removepod arent being exersized at all.  (NOTE 3/30): Ravi gudimeta has noted that possibly list/remove are being called elsewhere, i.e. in a shared cache).

_Solution_

We should add a more complex scheduler job / soaking into the scheduler_perf tests, so that we can measure real world scheduling bottlenecks (i.e. 1000s of nodes which need to be filtered and matched to pods). 
- More real world changes (updates and predicate scheduling events)
- More pod data churning (deletions/updates)

This would probably lead to a broader and more real-worldish performance profile, most importantly, it would gaurantee that the demanding aspects of scheduling functionality are exersized. 

cc @kubernetes/sig-scheduling

title: Document API object deletion semantics

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
We have a general deletion mechanism that leaves objects in the system while cleanup is being performed. We need to document this clearly and set expectations.
- What do we call this phase of an object's lifecycle? (Terminating)
- Does this imply a global state machine for all objects? (angry philosophical ranting)
- How do you tell when an object is in this cleanup phase? (deletiontimestamp != nil)
- When is the object really deleted? (when the last finalizer is removed. also something about grace period.)
- Can you add more finalizers to terminating objects? (no)
- Can you make unrelated updates to terminating objects? (yes, currently)
- When is an object's name released for reuse? (after it exits the Terminating phase)

body:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/31640 added events to federation namespace controller, but creating namespace events is failing on our e2e tests:

```
Server rejected event '&api.Event{TypeMeta:unversioned.TypeMeta{Kind:"", APIVersion:""}, ObjectMeta:api.ObjectMeta{Name:"e2e-tests-federation-replicaset-s7xan.147625127063baf8", GenerateName:"", Namespace:"default", SelfLink:"", UID:"", ResourceVersion:"", Generation:0, CreationTimestamp:unversioned.Time{Time:time.Time{sec:0, nsec:0, loc:(*time.Location)(nil)}}, DeletionTimestamp:(*unversioned.Time)(nil), DeletionGracePeriodSeconds:(*int64)(nil), Labels:map[string]string(nil), Annotations:map[string]string(nil), OwnerReferences:[]api.OwnerReference(nil), Finalizers:[]string(nil), ClusterName:""}, InvolvedObject:api.ObjectReference{Kind:"Namespace", Namespace:"", Name:"e2e-tests-federation-replicaset-s7xan", UID:"80f0b389-7f78-11e6-898f-0a580ab50304", APIVersion:"v1", ResourceVersion:"4", FieldPath:""}, Reason:"CreateInCluster", Message:"Creating namespace in cluster federation-e2e-gce-us-central1-f", Source:api.EventSource{Component:"federated-namespace-controller", Host:""}, FirstTimestamp:unversioned.Time{Time:time.Time{sec:63610003489, nsec:135639288, loc:(*time.Location)(0x84ad960)}}, LastTimestamp:unversioned.Time{Time:time.Time{sec:63610003489, nsec:135639288, loc:(*time.Location)(0x84ad960)}}, Count:1, Type:"Normal"}': 'namespaces "default" not found' (will not retry!)
```

It is because, namespaces do not have ObjectMeta.Namespace set and the event recorder library uses that to figure out the namespace in which the event should be generated: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a8053c7c59024a40bac5debe31857084d79729c2/pkg/client/record/event.go#L299.

We have 2 options to fix this:
- Update the library to use the namespace name if the ObjectReference is for a namespace object.
- Ensure that api.NamespaceDefault namespace exists in federation

cc @kubernetes/sig-cluster-federation

title: Rescheduler e2e should not scale kube-dns pods.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
In [rescheduler e2e test](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/rescheduler.go), for It("should ensure that critical pod is scheduled in case there is no resources available"), kube-dns is used as the critical pod target and being scaled out and in.

However, we plan to enable the dns horizontal autoscaling feature in the near future, such as this [WIP](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/33239). If this feature is turned on, the corresponding autoscaler will fight with this rescheduler e2e and maintain the desired number of replicas. Hence this test will be very likely to fail.

So probably we should use another critical pod here, or either create a new critical pod that does not exist before in order to protect the ongoing functionalities.
