title: Shouldn't count the time in pause phase for perma-failed deployment

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
**What keywords did you search in Kubernetes issues before filing this one?** (If you have found any duplicates, you should instead reply there.): 
perma-failed deployment

**Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`):
v1.6.0-alpha.0.191+a132e5c5800108

**What happened**:
Shouldn't count the time in pause phase for perma-failed deployment.

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):
1. Create deployment by deployment-perme-failed-1.yaml and pause the deployment immediately.
```
$ kubectl create -f deployment-perme-failed-1.yaml; kubectl rollout pause deployment/hello-openshift
```
```
# cat deployment-perme-failed-1.yaml
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-openshift
spec:
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 30
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello-openshift
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: hello-openshift
        image: openshift/hello-openshift:123
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```

2. After 30 seconds, check deployment status. 
```
$ kubectl describe deployment/hello-openshift
Conditions:
  Type        Status    Reason
  ----        ------    ------
  Available     False    MinimumReplicasUnavailable
  Progressing     Unknown    DeploymentPaused
```

```
$ kubectl get deployment/hello-openshift -o yaml
  status:
    conditions:
    - lastTransitionTime: 2016-11-08T08:20:41Z
      lastUpdateTime: 2016-11-08T08:20:41Z
      message: Deployment does not have minimum availability.
      reason: MinimumReplicasUnavailable
      status: "False"
      type: Available
    - lastTransitionTime: 2016-11-08T08:20:41Z
      lastUpdateTime: 2016-11-08T08:20:41Z
      message: Deployment is paused
      reason: DeploymentPaused
      status: Unknown
      type: Progressing
    observedGeneration: 2
    replicas: 3
    unavailableReplicas: 3
    updatedReplicas: 3
```

3. Resuming the deployment
```
$ kubectl rollout resume deployment/hello-openshift
```

**Actual results**:
3. The type of `Progressing` change to `false` and `ProgressDeadlineExceeded` immediately after resume deployment.
In describtion of deployment:
```
Conditions:
  Type		Status	Reason
  ----		------	------
  Available 	False	MinimumReplicasUnavailable
  Progressing 	False	ProgressDeadlineExceeded
```

**Expected results**: 
3.1 Conditions should be as below after resume deployment. 
```
Conditions:
  Type        Status    Reason
  ----        ------    ------
  Available     False    MinimumReplicasUnavailable
  Progressing     True    ReplicaSetUpdated
```

3.2 After 30 seconds, the type of `Progressing` change to `false` and `ProgressDeadlineExceeded`.
```
Conditions:
  Type		Status	Reason
  ----		------	------
  Available 	False	MinimumReplicasUnavailable
  Progressing 	False	ProgressDeadlineExceeded
```

**Anything else do we need to know**:
We should concern how to count times for below three scenarios:
1. `progressDeadlineSeconds: 30`, deploy a deployment(with not exist pod image), pause deployment after 10 seconds, hold on 1mins in pause phase, what status after resume deployment?
2. `progressDeadlineSeconds: 30`, deploy a deployment(with not exist pod image), pause deployment after 10 seconds, hold on 5 seconds in pause phase, what status after resume deployment?
3. `progressDeadlineSeconds: 30`, deploy a deployment(with not exist pod image) and pause deployment immediately, hold on 1mins in pause phase, what status after resume deployment?

title: Stop using taint with key=dedicated to mark master node

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
@justinsb brought to my attention that folks have started using a taint with key "dedicated" for marking the master node. While I heartily endorse moving from "unschedulable" to using taints, please do not use key "dedicated" for this taint as we want to use it for the [dedicated nodes](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/design/taint-toleration-dedicated.md]) feature. Also, please make all taints namespaced. The discussion of the justification is here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/31647#issuecomment-257972345

So for tainting the master node, I think we should use the same key as kops is using to label the master node, namely "role" (value is master). And we should use the `node.alpha.kubernetes.io` namespace. So the taint key for the master node should be `node.alpha.kubernetes.io/role` and the value can be `master` as before. (It's debatable whether the namespace should be scheduler.* or node.* but since some taints can trigger eviction, not just block scheduling, I think node.* is slightly better).

Places where it seems people are using taint key "dedicated" -- please change them as described above (since taints are alpha, backward compatibility is not guaranteed, so I don't feel too guilty about this):
* kubeadm (seems to be introduced here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/33262)
* kops: [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kops/blob/d3f69496e410630c219fa8ea35032e5a22eb6991/protokube/pkg/protokube/tainter.go) and elsewhere

Places where it seems people are about to do this (please change the PR to use the taint key I mentioned above): #31647 #35901 #36236

If anyone knows of any other code that is doing this, please add to this issue.

Thanks and sorry for the inconvenience. But I think this will make the system more understandable in the long-run.

cc/ @lukemarsden @errordeveloper @mikedanese

title: kube-dns --federations flag needs to be user modifiable (integration between federation and the new addon manager)

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
## Overview

kube-dns currently receives a list of federation names from a command line flag `--federations`. Setup of a federated set of clusters requires the user to be able to modify the flag (see http://kubernetes.io/docs/admin/federation/#updating-kubedns).

In v1.5, the addon manager was changed (see 0e4e54a6b658fef90194ebc9e910083eccf8f29b) to periodically reconcile the configuration of the addon with a template yaml. The old behavior was to not modify the configuration if the service was present.

The --federation flag will be overwritten by the addon manager unless the template in the add-on manager itself is modified. Users of GKE cannot modify the addon manager configuration and hence will not be able to fix this behavior. User modifications in the past were preserved so this was not surfaced as an issue.

## Impact

Customers using GKE and federation will not be able to see DNS entries for the federated service instances.

## Proposed fix

- Add flag `--config-map` to kube-dns.
- Have kube-dns receive the value of --federations flag from a config map if the config map is present. The config map will have a name `kube-dns` and be in namespace `kube-system`. If the config map is not present, we default to the existing behavior which is to take the value from the command line flag.
- Have kube-dns poll for the config map change.
- Federation will either update the documentation regarding the manual updates (i.e. creation of the config map) or through the new `kubefed` CLI tool (see 2f84a7c8d2f46d52780c585024ff1038bac0a246).

title: Old kubectl tries to register new API version as third party resource and fail

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
Follow up #35791

When older kubectl sees a new API version it doesn't recognize (such as apps.v1beta1), it'll think it's a third party source (TPR) and tries to register it, and then will fail. 

It happens in TPR discovery code. It's trying to identify TPR versions and hacks them into the list of registered APIs:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.5.0-alpha.2/pkg/kubectl/cmd/util/factory.go#L341

-->

**Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`):

```
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"4", GitVersion:"v1.4.0", GitCommit:"a16c0a7f71a6f93c7e0f222d961f4675cd97a46b", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2016-09-26T18:16:57Z", GoVersion:"go1.6.3", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"4", GitVersion:"v1.4.0", GitCommit:"a16c0a7f71a6f93c7e0f222d961f4675cd97a46b", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2016-09-26T18:10:32Z", GoVersion:"go1.6.3", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"} 
```

**Environment**:
- **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**: AWS
- **OS** (e.g. from /etc/os-release): jessie (Debian 8)
- **Kernel** (e.g. `uname -a`): Linux ip-172-20-110-96 4.4.23-k8s #1 SMP Fri Sep 30 13:51:02 UTC 2016 x86_64 GNU/Linux
- **Install tools**: kops
- **Others**: 

**What happened**:
We are applying label selectors to a service that is federated. e.g., 

``` yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: date-time-federated
spec:
  selector:
    name: update-demo
    version: black
  ports:
    -
      protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
      targetPort: 8080
  type: LoadBalancer
```

**What you expected to happen**:
We expect the federated service to be updated on all clusters. Instead, the controller manager reports no changes to the service.

When we print the service YAML from the federation, it contains the new label selectors. When we print the service YAML directly from the clusters' APIs (who are members of the federation) there are no updates to the service whatsoever.

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):
Set `--v=5` on the federation controller manager. Create a federated service. Add some label selectors to the service and apply it through the federation. Watch the federation controller manager logs while applying the new label selectors and observe the logs that indicate there is no update because there are no perceived changes to the service.

**Anything else do we need to know**:
We see that the controller manager is only evaluating the ports for changes to the service. See the  [1.4.0 reference](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.4.0/federation/pkg/federation-controller/service/servicecontroller.go#L397-L411) and the [master reference](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/federation/pkg/federation-controller/service/servicecontroller.go#L419-L433). 

Do we have the correct expectation that update criteria should be broader than just changes to ports? 

Our use case is for deployment update strategies like sticking a canary under the service.

Thanks a bunch!

title: Federated service IP out of sync between AWS LB and CloudDNS records

body:
**Is this a request for help?** No

**What keywords did you search in Kubernetes issues before filing this one?** 
federation dns
federation aws
federation aws cname

---

**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?** (choose one):
BUG REPORT

**Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`): 
v1.4.4

**Environment**:
- **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**:
  GCE for federation control plane
  AWS for cluster1 (federated)
  GCE for cluster2 (federated)
- **OS** (e.g. from /etc/os-release):
  NAME="Debian GNU/Linux"
  VERSION_ID="7"
  VERSION="7 (wheezy)"
- **Kernel** (e.g. `uname -a`):
  3.16.0-4-amd64 #1 SMP Debian 3.16.7-ckt25-2 (2016-04-08) x86_64 GNU/Linux
- **Install tools**:
- **Others**:

**What happened**:
Federation controller creates the appropriate A entries for all federated services on Google CloudDNS, including resolving AWS load balancer DNS name to IPs. But as IP changes for AWS LBs, the A records get outdated, causing service disruption as they become out of sync.

**What you expected to happen**:
I expected the federation controller to either add a CNAME pointing to AWS LB, or to keep the IPs for AWS in sync overtime.

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):
- Deploy a federation control plane at GCE
- Create cluster at AWS
- Add AWS cluster to federation
- create a federated service
- wait 24h (or until AWS Load Balancer IPs change)
- Cloud DNS will be pointing to different IPs than AWS LB.  

**Anything else do we need to know**:
AWS recommends:
- Because the set of IP addresses associated with a LoadBalancer can change over time, you should never create an "A" record with any specific IP address.

title: Make scheduler less dependent on events for metadata and reasons

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
Problem

As of now, the scheduler is slated to make lots of events (per pod) especially on failures.  #20064 attempts to improve the quality of data for scheduling, and may or may not reuse the existing hacky events based data channel .... Specifically, in the scheduler, we need to SPAM less events...

Solution
- _Event is a report of an event somewhere in the cluster._ Is the current definition of an event,  we need to make it more precise to discourage SPAM :) 
- This means, _put a `SchedulingInfo` or similar struct onto Pod objects, that supports meta-scheduling info, that graduates to a first class API call_, so that we dont need to spam the event channel w/ bulk decision info for pods.
- This `SchedulingInfo` data structure  would generate a small amount of data attached to each pod.  Rather than a large amount of global events data. 

(re: `SchedulingInfo` possibly there is stuff we can reuse in scheduling types.go, will look into it more)

**What happened**:
Using `kubeadm init --config /path/to/config.yml` appears to block default values from being set. I first noticed it where a pre-flight check of the Servicer CIDR was presenting itself as an empty string although I had not set it through the command line flag nor in the config file. I also noticed that kubelet requests to the API server were being sent to port 0 as the API server default port had not been set.

A config file should only override defaults, not make it so that no defaults are set.

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):

title: Add discriminators to all unions/oneof in the API

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: sig/architecture
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Architecture.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
Forked from #6979.

We have a number of cases in the API where only one of a set of fields is allowed to be specified -- an undiscriminated union / oneof. `VolumeSource` is the canonical example: `emptyDir` or `gcePersistentDisk` or `awsElasticBlockStore` or ...

Currently we require that exactly one be set, but don't explicitly represent which one we expect to be set.

Adding discriminators to all unions/oneof cases would have multiple advantages:
1. clients could effectively implement a switch instead of if-else trees to inspect the resource -- look at discriminator and lookup the corresponding field in a map (though differences in capitalization of the first letter in the API convention currently prevents the discriminator value from exactly matching the field name).
2. The apiserver could automatically clear non-selected fields, which would be convenient for kubectl apply #15894 and other cases.

For backward compatibility, any request that succeeds today needs to work even after we implemented (2). That would mean that newly added discriminators would have to be optional. 

If the discriminator were set, we'd require that the field corresponding to its value were set and the apiserver (registry) could automatically unset the other fields. 

If the discriminator were unset, behavior would be as before -- exactly one of the fields in the union/oneof would be required to be set and the operation would otherwise fail validation.

The main question: should the discriminator be set by default?

If it weren't set by default, then it couldn't be relied upon for purpose (1), and if-else trees would still be required forever (for the current apiversions). OTOH, if it were set by default, we'd need to change it accordingly when the corresponding union/oneof fields were set and unset. This would be different than all other defaulting in the API and contradicts the letter of an existing convention, though not the spirit. We don't change populated fields in the apiserver, because we don't want to change the user's expressed intent. However, in this case the intent would be inferred from the union/oneof fields instead of the discriminator field. 

The client would otherwise receive an error. We could potentially do stronger consistency validation in some cases. For instance, during creation, we could require the discriminator matched the union/oneof fields if specified. On updates, we potentially could check whether the discriminator changed from its prior value and require consistency if it did, since inconsistency would suggest a mistake or a conflict, though it would force the client's retry logic to reason about whether a validation error could be due to a conflict.

cc @pwittrock

labels.name: kind/design

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Multicluster.

body:
Filing this issue to discuss the design for "per-user cluster authentication, authorization and audit logging" in federation. Ref https://github.com/kubernetes/features/issues/73

Problems that we want to solve:
- Audit: In federation audit logs, we know which user sent a particular request to federation control plane. But in kubernetes audit logs, we do not get to know that a particular kubernetes request was in response to what federation request and by which federation user.
- Authorization: When federation control plane receives a request, we authorize the request in federation control plane, but we do not validate that the user has authority in underlying clusters.
- Authentication: Similar to above. When federation control plane receives a request, we authenticate the request in federation control plane, but we do not know the corresponding authn credentials for that user in each of the underlying clusters. Federation controllers use common credentials for all operations in each underlying cluster.

cc @kubernetes/sig-federation-feature-requests  @kubernetes/sig-auth-feature-requests 
@quinton-hoole Let me know if I missed anything.

title: Proposal: Establish guidelines for where commands should go

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: sig/architecture
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Architecture.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

labels.name: area/code-organization
labels.description: Issues or PRs related to kubernetes code organization

body:
There's been some recent discussion prompted by the addition of `kubeadm` and how `kubectl` will evolve w.r.t. which commands belong where.  
### Questions to answer:
1. What commands and features should we put under `kubectl`?  Under `kubeadm`?
2. Federation wants to add commands to register a new cluster and create a new cluster on top of an existing cluster - should they do that in `kubectl`, `kubeadm`, or separate?
3. For components that are not part of the core project, should they be added directly into the existing commands or be expected to use an extension mechanism (as proposed elsewhere)?
4. Is `kubeadm` part of cluster lifecycle, or is it a general "Kubernetes administration command"?
5. When should we add new CLI commands (should we add `kubefed`)?
### Background

Today, many users of `kubectl` are single cluster admins (one or more devops people who use the whole cluster themselves). However, an increasingly large (and in the future, likely dominant) portion of users will be app-admins using a cluster hosted by someone else.  eBay, Samsung, OpenShift customers, etc are all likely examples where a central ops team owns the cluster and then gives access to namespaces and subsets of the cluster for individual teams.  The user spectrum of kubectl will range from very sophisticated cluster administrators all the way to individual developers making changes on their cluster who need to see the status of some resources.

Points on the user spectrum:
- Cluster administrators and users with control over an entire cluster - admin and deploy apps
- Sophisticated users with delegated access to portions of the cluster who may have access to many clusters
- Unsophisticated cluster-consumers with limited access to non-namespaced resources

Over time, we will continue to add administrative level functionality to Kube.  Some of that functionality has overlap with actions users take (for instance, kubectl get and kubectl apply are used by all classes of user), but some of that is not relevant for unprivileged users, such as `drain`, `taint`, `cordon`, etc.  
### Deciding which commands go where

Some goals we have had for kubectl:
- Keep the list of commands small and focused on core use cases
  - Keeping the command list small helps ease new unsophisticated users into the tool
  - We can also hide / nest / deemphasize certain commands
- Help new users find the important commands first
  - Commands that are not commonly used should not be given equal visual priority and weight as uncommon commands - it's ok if an admin has to type out a few more letters
- Help users understand where to find common function (group like function with like).

We have not yet clarified our goals for kubeadm, but today it is focused on people deploying clusters and adding and removing new components.  This heavily overlaps with the cluster-admin / single-cluster owner user, but does not overlap with the tenant-user case much.  

Some useful experience from OpenShift (which has `oc` which wraps kubectl and `oadm` which contains admin stuff, and `oc adm` which embeds `oadm` under `oc`)
1. In OpenShift, we have 20-30 additional administrative level commands that are part of our `oadm` command that handles: config generation, certificate signing, policy (specifically cluster level policy), installation, management level tasks like resource migration, and other actions that only cluster admins will have.  I believe over time Kube will have all of these, so it's important to clarify that.
2. Once we turn on policy for clusters, typically the actions you can perform are broken down by role - those roles in turn form natural groupings of what you can do (things cluster admins can do, things namespace owners can do, things regular users can do) that can benefit from a cluster setup
3. We will want to create other commands around kubectl that perform more specific workflows - things like the Deis command line and elsewhere.
### Design

We should clarify where we add commands and what belongs where.  Some possible options and rules:
1. `kubectl` contains everything `kubeadm` is only for installation
2. `kubectl` is for generic cluster interaction (app admin level) and for tenant style applications, `kubeadm` is for administrative actions on a cluster (install + configuration)
3. `kubeadm` is for installation and management of clusters, `kubectl adm` is for administrative actions, and `kubectl` is for tenant style applications

Further clarification for federation:
1. Should federation be able to claim the top level `kubectl register` action, or should it be `kubectl federation register` or `kubeadm join-federation`?
2. Should federation should be treated as an extension (because you can add it on top and it doesn't _need_ to be compiled into Kube) and thus we should implement the extension proposal (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/30086)?

title: cAdvisor leaking journalctl processes

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Extracted from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/23491#issuecomment-251777767

```
This appears to be leaking journalctl processes originating here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/vendor/github.com/google/cadvisor/utils/oomparser/oomparser.go#L169
```

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/23491 set kubelet unit files to restart just the kubelet process and this ends up orphaning and leaking `journalctl` processes launched by cAdvisor.
AFAIK, this behavior can leak many other processes like `du`, `ls`, `mount`, etc. 

@kubernetes/sig-node we need to fix this. 

I recommend reverting https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/23491 to begin with as suggested by @wwwtyro

body:
This is for all pods, not just petset pods.

When a pod is deleted by kubectl drain, it goes into DELETING.  Kubectl drain should not return success to the user until the pod is completely deleted.  That way, if the user is scripting automation, and they say something like `kubectl drain $MACHINE && ssh root@$MACHINE shutdown -r now`, that it does not shutdown before the pods are expecting it.  Right now I think it does not wait.

Waiting could mean:

1) remember the uid of the thing you are going to delete,
2) DELETE it
3) poll it until either: you get 404 (it is finally deleted) or you get 200 but the new pod has a different uid (a replacement came quickly).

title: Scheduling errors and OutOfCpu during cluster autoscaling

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
**Is this a request for help?**: No

**What keywords did you search in Kubernetes issues before filing this one?** OutOfCpu
Issue #29846 may be related; however, #29846 is not related to cluster autoscaling and is limited to an OutOfCpu condition.

---

**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?** (choose one): BUG REPORT

**Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`): 1.4.0

**Environment**: Google GKE
- **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**: Google
- **OS** (e.g. from /etc/os-release): Google Container-VM Image V55
- **Kernel** (e.g. `uname -a`): Linux gke-omega-cluster-default-pool-d07fc610-clps 4.4.14+ #1 SMP Tue Sep 20 10:32:07 PDT 2016 x86_64 Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU @ 2.30GHz GenuineIntel GNU/Linux
- **Install tools**:
- **Others**:

**What happened**:
Using cluster of n1-standard-1 nodes, 1 initial node and enabled cluster autoscaling, I started 34 pods requesting 100m CPU each. Since each node has only 1 CPU and 200m CPU is required for Kubernetes services on each node (300m CPU on the first node), each node can run 8 pods (7 for the first node). All 34 pods would, therefore, required 5 nodes. The sequence of events:

Around 15:06:30: All pods are created. As expected, most pods remain in Pending state.
15:06:42: Kubernetes correctly triggers scale-up; however, the scheduler only requests a single node.
15:07:34: Two pods ("out-of-cpurf679" and "out-of-cpuwi5ge") are killed with "Deleted by rescheduler in order to schedule critical pod kube-system_heapster-v1.2.0-3455740371-j973x".
15:09:33: Scale-up is triggered again, scaling from 2 to 3 nodes.
15:11:48: Two other pods ("out-of-cpu3gsro" and "out-of-cpun30p1") fail with OutOfCpu when 10 pods are assigned to the newly added 3rd node.
15:12:31: Next scale-up, going from 3 to 4 nodes.
Eventually, 30 pods are running, 2 pods are in OutOfCpu state, and 2 pods have disappeared.
15:15:16: Another scale-up is triggered from 4 to 5 nodes. The 5th node remains idle as there are no more pods to schedule.

Please refer to this zip file for details:
[out-of-cpu-bug.zip](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/528186/out-of-cpu-bug.zip)

"out-of-cpu-bug.yaml" is the YAML that was used to run the experiment through the following commands:

1> gcloud container clusters create omega-cluster --machine-type=n1-standard-1 --zone us-central1-c --num-nodes 1 --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes=1 --max-nodes=8
2> bash -c 'for i in {1..34}; do kubectl create -f out-of-cpu-bug.yaml; done'

"out-of-cpu-bug-events.txt" is the capture of events from 'kubectl get events -w' up to the final scale-up. "out-of-cpu-bug-pods1.txt" shows the output of 'kubectl get nodes,pods -a' after the OutOfCpu condition of two pods. Note that only 32 pods show up, because 2 pods have been killed earlier and have "disappeared". "out-of-cpu-bug.pods2.txt" shows the nodes and pods after the final scale-up. The new node "gke-omega-cluster-default-pool-d07fc610-w79v" is unused.

**What you expected to happen**:
1. Scale-up should have been triggered to bring the cluster from 1 to 5 nodes in a single step.
2. Pods "out-of-cpurf679" and "out-of-cpuwi5ge" should not have been killed and disappeared.
3.  Pods "out-of-cpu3gsro" and "out-of-cpun30p1" should not have been scheduled onto a full node and should not have received an OutOfCpu condition.
4. Scale-up should not have produced an idle node.

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):

See above. Create a cluster on Google with
gcloud container clusters create omega-cluster --machine-type=n1-standard-1 --zone us-central1-c --num-nodes 1 --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes=1 --max-nodes=8

Schedule pods with the supplied YAML:
bash -c 'for i in {1..34}; do kubectl create -f out-of-cpu-bug.yaml; done'

The exact numbers don't matter.

**Anything else do we need to know**:

The bug(s) appear to include some race condition as the error does not always (although frequently) happen. The more pods that are being created, the more likely the situation is observed. The YAML has a commented-out section to request pod affinity. This seems to increase the likelyhood of OutOfCpu failures. Nonetheless, the above commands will show the failure with a 1 in 2 chance. Increase the number of pods to 60 or more and the problem occurs almost every time. I consider this problem a showstopper for any serious cluster autoscaling application.

title: Field-level versioning

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/architecture
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Architecture.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
We have difficulties around moving fields through alpha, beta, GA. #30819 is one idea. I was talking with Brian earlier today and here is a sketch of something that we could do to solve the general problem.

We begin following semver for our api versions, adding a "patch" version. We define a new tag which can be added in a comment before a field, like this:

`// +version:alpha=v1.5.3`

When the field goes to beta (assuming it doesn't change):

`// +version:alpha=v1.5.3,beta=v1.5.89`

And at GA the field goes like this:

`// +version:alpha=v1.5.3,beta=v1.5.89,stable=v1.5.183`

If at any point in time the field is deleted (or moved and we don't want to autoconvert), and clients referencing the field might still exist, we can say:

`// +version:alpha=v1.5.3,deleted=v1.5.8`

The conversion machinery would enforce that any given version number is only used once (we can store the next version in a file somewhere for human convenience). This complete version should be tracked per-apiserver. (So federation-apiserver would likely have a different patch version.) 

We'd use the same idea behind @smarterclayton's #33900 to allow clients to specify which minor version of the api they're intending to use, via `Accept:` headers.

Conversion routines, validators, swagger generation etc all need to be made to accept a full api version from clients and they can use the hints on the fields to tell whether the client knows about the field or not. Swagger can report whether fields are alpha or beta.

Likewise we can use the alpha/beta distinction to give admins the ability to disallow alpha or only allow stable fields to be used. (We can construct versions like v1.5.35-stable for this purpose)

body:
We are having trouble understanding Kubernetes resource requests.

We run a cluster of 3x 1CPU / 3.75Gb

Our issue is this: We are allocating really small CPU requests to each container in our pods so the pod will be scheduled onto a node. Our containers are basically all web containers running NodeJS or PHP so their CPU is pretty low and occasionally bursts.

I personally just don't see the point in having to declaratively allocate stupidly low CPU requests to each container in our deployments when we know in advanced they will use much more CPU then this request but never exhaust the node as a whole. Its just not a concern although Kubernetes seems to force us into this thinking.

In the beginning we were not allocating any requests at all, although we ran into problems as Kubernetes allocated defaults. These defaults were exceeded when updating our deployments and a rolling update tried to allocate pods to a node with insufficient resources...

**Why does Kubernetes not have default resource allocation of 0 so users can simply ignore these scheduling rules?**

title: Server side defaulting of values prevents diff patches from working

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

labels.name: wg/api-expression
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to WG API Expression.

body:
Server side defaults are easily differentiated from other values set within the kubernetes system (e.g. DeploymentStatus).  `kubectl apply` records the applied config as an annotation on the objects that it creates so that it can perform a 3-way diff to merge local changes into the live config without erasing other items such as the status.

Steps to reproduce:

Use `kubectl apply -f` to create a deployment using this config:

``` yaml
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80 
```

Update the config spec adding

``` yaml
strategy:
    type: "Recreate"
```

Apply the new config.

Result:

``` sh
The Deployment "nginx-deployment" is invalid.
spec.strategy.rollingUpdate: Forbidden: may not be specified when strategy `type` is 'Recreate'
```

This is caused because the server defaults spec.strategy.rollingUpdate but this is invisible to the client and cannot be differentiated from other changes made by the server that the client should ignore (e.g. status changes).

This can be seen for any field whose default is derived from another field such as Deployment labels and selectors (derived from the PodTemplate labels).

Solving this will require at least some changes on the server side.  One possible solution would be to:
1. Have the server record which derived fields that it adds / updates
2. Have the client then merge these changes into the last-applied-config used by diff patch so they are deleted
3. Have the server re-perform defaulting / normalization on the resulting object from the PATCH

Thoughts / Comments / Suggestions?

title: Have "kubectl drain" use eviction subresource

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
Documented here
http://kubernetes.io/docs/admin/disruptions/

Also we need to add some kind of "force" flag to say drain the machine even if it would violate pod disruption budget. If you use this flag, "kubectl drain" will use regular pod deletion rather than eviction subresource.

Another issue to consider (unrelated to eviction subresource/disruption budget) is whether to wait until all the pods have been deleted before returning (so e.g. if you call `kubectl drain` in a loop, you won't start draining the next machine until the pods have been deleted. this isn't as good as waiting for the pods to reschedule but it's better than just returning immediately, since graceful deletion could delay the actual deletion for an arbitrary amount of time. I don't think kubectl drain currently waits for the pods to be deleted before returning, but I can't remember. Note also that kubectl drain has a --grace-period flag that lets you override the per-pod grace period settings presumably with a lower value.)

cc/ @mml

title: AWS: Instances briefly deregistered from service ELB after replacement of single controller instance

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
**Is this a request for help?**: No.

**What keywords did you search in Kubernetes issues before filing this one?**: ELB, Elastic. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/26362 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/11002 may be related, but are not identical.

---

**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**: Bug report.

**Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`): 1.4.0

**Environment**:
- **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**: AWS
- **OS** (e.g. from /etc/os-release): Debian Jessie
- **Kernel** (e.g. `uname -a`): `Linux ip-172-20-63-176 3.16.0-4-amd64 #1 SMP Debian 3.16.7-ckt25-2 (2016-04-08) x86_64 GNU/Linux`
- **Install tools**: kubernetes/kops@5871b24b320b1c336c5d5096a456d1f94c82c2e7
- **Others**:  `kops create cluster $NAME --node-size m3.large --zones us-east-1a`

**What happened**:

On a single-controller 1.4.0 cluster launched with kops, requests to an existing service's ELB sometimes fail for a short duration after the termination of a controller instance and the creation of a replacement instance. In situations where requests are observed to fail, the newly-launched controller instance contains entries similar to the following in `/var/log/kube-controller-manager.log`:

```
I1006 18:28:35.971327       5 aws_loadbalancer.go:419] Instances removed from load-balancer a0bb431bd8bef11e692940a24a820d1a
I1006 18:30:15.130235       5 aws_loadbalancer.go:408] Instances added to load-balancer a0bb431bd8bef11e692940a24a820d1a
```

All requests failed to this service's ELB in the time between these two log events. CloudTrail records an `DeregisterInstancesFromLoadBalancer` request being made at the time of the first entry that removes all of the running minions from this ELB, and a corresponding `RegisterInstancesWithLoadBalancer` call that adds them back at the same time as the second entry.

**What you expected to happen**:

I expected the failure of a controller instance in a `kops` launched cluster to not negatively impact the ability to access a service through it's configured ELB, as a replacement instance is started with the same `etcd` state as existed on the previous controller instance.

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):

I'm able to reproduce this failure about 30% of the time by following this procedure:
- Create a kops cluster with the version and arguments provided above.
- Create the following resources:

``` yaml
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: http-echo
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: http-echo
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: http-echo
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: http-echo
        image: kennship/http-echo
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - name: http
          containerPort: 3000

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: http-echo
  labels:
    app: http-echo
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: http-echo
  ports:
  - port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: http
```
- Wait until an ELB is created: `kubectl get service http-echo -o jsonpath="{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}"`
- Confirm that a request to this ELB returns a successful result.
- Terminate the running controller instance.
- Send sustained traffic to the service's ELB.
- Observe that requests to this service fail after the newly-launched controller instance's controller-manager process deregisters minion instances from the service's ELB.
- Observe that requests to this service succeed a short while later as the controller manager re-registers the same instances.

**Anything else do we need to know**:

I'm able to re-run the simulation that triggers this situation and gather additional information anytime if there's anything in particular that would be useful.

/cc @justinsb, who spoke briefly with me about this in #sig-aws. Thanks again!

title: Re-enable "Feature" e2e tests to avoid regressions like Gluster not working on GCI

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
Gluster volumes don't work on GCI (issue?), which is an unintended regression in v1.4.

We _do_ have a [working e2e test for gluster](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/volumes.go#L402) that should have picked up that regression, but it has been (i.m.o. incorrectly) [disabled](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/volumes.go#L349) as a ["Feature"](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/d6258a0d9b0f85d4a1cd01886ad485f116baeeb8/jenkins/job-configs/kubernetes-jenkins/kubernetes-e2e-gce.yaml#L73) in all of our CI tests (as far as I can tell).

In general I think that all e2e tests that can be run reliably and automatically should be run regularly to detect these sorts of regressions.

@kubernetes/sig-testing @kubernetes/sig-storage @saad-ali @thockin @matchstick fyi

body:
As described here - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/31071#issuecomment-250933234

``` shell
KUBERNETES_PROVIDER=aws federation/deploy/deploy.sh deploy_federation
```

exits because the provider isn't gce/gke. However, the deployment mechanism itself should work on all the providers. We shouldn't exit, but just branch out to kubeconfig check instead.

cc @owenhaynes @kubernetes/sig-cluster-federation

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
I noticed that the master node is now added to NodePort and to AWS ELBs, now that the master is registered as a Node.

I think we probably don't want to do this, as we don't want to be bouncing traffic through the master, for performance reasons.  Also the master doesn't always run kube-proxy.

We should either use the external client library everywhere or (better) define an internal pod object for kubelet and all its internal modules, including volume plugins, and use the internal version consistently.
If we do not address this soon enough, the codebase will become very confusing for contributors.

title: openapi/swagger needs to be summarized across the cluster

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
The `kube-apiserver` now includes the aggregator and the default openapi information is accessible via delegation, but we should really be building it based on the specific group versions being aggregated by the aggregator.

This is not as simple as just including all the available API groups from a given server, since a server can reasonably host more GroupVersions than are exposed.  Common reasons for doing this would be servers that can handle delegated authentication or authorization checks.  This would be common for someone plugging in a new webhook (only aggregate the kube-apiserver check, but the kube-apiserver could delegate out) or cases where the aggregated API server wants to support operations like `kubectl auth can-i`.

Client-side validation will not function well for aggregated API servers until this work.

@mbohlool @kubernetes/sig-api-machinery-misc

title: scheduler and storage provision (PV controller) coordination

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

body:
There are several ongoing discussion threads related to this topic, so open this one to summarize all the relevant discussions and hope to reach a conclusion.

Currently pod scheduling and PV controller (PVC/PV binding and dynamic provisioning) are implemented in completely separated controllers. This separation has some benefits such as enabling scheduler pluggable, better isolation, and better performance since PV/PVC binding can be performed asynchronously before pod scheduling. But both controller makes decisions independently without considering the other's choice so that the node/zone selection might conflict.

The goal is to still keep this separate controller design largely and make necessary modification to overcome the problem of conflicting decisions. There are four scenarios we need to consider.

1. Single Zone, network attached storage
In such case, PV/PVC is not tied to any node selection. The binding can be performed interdependently. No change is needed from current code.

2. Single Zone, local storage
In this case, PV is tied to a specific node. Once a PVC is bound to a PV, it is bound to the node. The decision might not be compatible to pod scheduler's decision. Normally pod scheduler ranks nodes based on some predefined policies and picks the node with the highest score. PV controller is also trying to search and find the best match to bind PVC and PV. 
 
3. Multiple Zone, network attached storage
Pod scheduler gives each zone a score which is used to rank nodes. But PV controller itself does not consider zone information when choosing PV for PVC and it uses the same way of choosing PV for a given PVC. Only for dynamic provisioning, user might specify zone information and PV will be created in that zone. In such case,  pod scheduler has a predicate which picks nodes only from the zone where the PV is. For statefulsets, a hacky way to make sure volumes are spread across zones when creating the volumes by using PVC name as an indicator of statefulset. In this situation, it is possible that PV controller picks a zone in which no node has enough resources (CPU/memory) for a pod. See more discussion at #41598

4. Multiple Zone, local storage
PV controller could find PV candidates from different zones and nodes. It is similar to case 2. PV controller might picks up a zone and node that does not have enough resources for the pod. 

To solve these problems, I think it would be good for storage, scheduling, and workload team to get together and agree on the outcome we want to deliver.

Proposal:
[@vishh] Move the binding selection and decision from PV controller to scheduler. The PV controller will still be around to take care of dangling claims and/or volumes, rollback incomplete transactions (necessary when a pod requests multiple local PVs), reclaim PVs, etc.

title: Deprecate / remove alpha.kubernetes.io/fluentd-ds-ready annotation

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: sig/instrumentation
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Instrumentation.

body:
PR #32088 introduced an annotation for fluentd migration from static pod to the daemonset to avoid two instances of fluentd on a single node during the transition stage. I didn't read the pr carefully, but based on the code at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/32088/files#diff-6b0808bd1afb15f9f77986f4459601c2R199, every node object has one label be default: 
"alpha.kubernetes.io/fluentd-ds-ready". I think this is wrong. 1) Not everyone use fluentd as the logging agent. 2) It is hard-coded in Kubelet code as part of kubelet_node_status. No matter running fluentd as a static pod or a daemonset on the node, Kubelet shouldn't treat it different from other pods. The right approach is introducing an external controller to apply this cloud-provider / kubernetes vendor (i.e. GKE) specific label to the node. 

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Node
metadata:
  annotations:
    node.alpha.kubernetes.io/ttl: "0"
    scheduler.alpha.kubernetes.io/taints: '[]'
    volumes.kubernetes.io/controller-managed-attach-detach: "true"
  creationTimestamp: 2017-02-25T01:50:12Z
  labels:
    alpha.kubernetes.io/fluentd-ds-ready: "true"                                                        <======================
    beta.kubernetes.io/arch: amd64
    beta.kubernetes.io/instance-type: n1-standard-8
    beta.kubernetes.io/os: linux
...
```

cc/ @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs @mikedanese

I'd like all of the in-flight workload APIs (ReplicaSet, Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet) to advance to v1 together as a group, sometime this year.

Related issues:
* Deployment v1 issue: #20130
* DaemonSet v1 issue: #15310

I'd like to see at least:
* ~~Server-side cascading deletion (GC) by default (e.g., #23252, #40014)~~
* ~~Controller ref (#24946) to provide mutual exclusion even across controller types, but also ensure that orphaning and adoption work as expected~~

* ~~Scale subresource for all controllers for which it makes sense~~

* Documentation completed (e.g., #18465)
* Double-check validation and defaults (e.g., #42479)
* Fix/cleanup taint/toleration support in DaemonSet (#29738), affinity/anti-affinity (#29276), schedulability (#26810), scheduling on master nodes (#29108), durability (#29193), etc.
  * Maybe via DaemonSet use of scheduler (#42002)

Bugs:
* ~~Scaled-down Deployments don't identify old ReplicaSets (#42570)~~

Maybe:
* Finish UnavailableReplicas (#41789)
* ~~Disallow activeDeadlineSeconds (#38684)~~
* Rollout strategy update improvement (#24198, #34292, #35345)
* ConfigMap rollouts (#22368, #31701, #43112, ...)

* Make controllers aware of namespace deletion (#38612, #36891)
* Disallow label changes in status updates (#20978)
* Derive DaemonSet pod names from nodes (#41977)

Desirable, but can probably be done later:
* ~~Implement observedGeneration (#7328)~~

* Ensure the controllers generate the desired events, such as events when they can't create pods (#21912)
* Graceful degradation (e.g., #33041, #2529)

Definitely should not block v1/GA:
* Factor out common functionality (#37563)
* Support relabeling (#36897)
* Scale down gradually (#23885)
* PodDisruptionBudget completion (#12611)
* Critical pod hack cleanups in favor of general priority/preemption (#22212, #40573)
* Easier image/tag updates (#29097) / image triggers 
* Hooks (#14512)
* Image tag resolution (#1697)
* Bulk quota (#25146)
* In-place updates (#9043)
* Rolling restart (#13488)

* Selector overlap detection (#43321, #19830, #2210)
* Failure-domain awareness (e.g., #4301, #41394)
* Federation support (#37570)
* Service generation (#14956)
* Blue-green deployments (#33462)
* Min/max replica counts (#33843)
* Cron/batch jobs that run on every node (#17182, #36601)

TBD:
* Better history support (#28373)
* Kill specific pods (#36868)
* Deleted controllers in limbo (#24934)

We also should triage related issues that have been filed, though I did a quick triage through deployment and daemonset issues.

title: GCE Ingress (GLBC) needs improved federation handling at ingress deletion time

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/multicluster
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Multicluster.

body: While GLBC has been coaxed to handle duplicate Ingress objects at creation time, it needs more logic to correctly handle deletion of federated ingresses. Currently, deleting one of the ingress objects outside of  federation will cause the entire ingress to be torn down. Eventually the federated controller re-creates the ingress object but the downtime should be omitted altogether. Possible solutions include some form of adhoc refcounting mechanism or augmenting GLBC to notice that there are more than one relevant forwarding rules attached to an ingress object at deletion time. Details and design to be hashed out still.

body:
To reproduce error:
Install latest Docker release..

first terminal:

sudo PATH=$PATH KUBERNETES_PROVIDER=local EXPERIMENTAL_CRI=true CONTAINER_RUNTIME=docker hack/local-up-cluster.sh

second terminal:
cat /tmp/kubelet.log|grep illegal

E0303 10:36:09.811626    1592 container_manager_linux.go:90] Unable to parse docker version "17.03.0-ce": illegal zero-prefixed version component "03" in "17.03.0-ce"

note docker version
Client:
 Version:      17.03.0-ce
 API version:  1.26
 Go version:   go1.7.5
 Git commit:   60ccb22
 Built:        Thu Feb 23 11:02:43 2017
 OS/Arch:      linux/amd64

Server:
 Version:      17.03.0-ce
 API version:  1.26 (minimum version 1.12)
 Go version:   go1.7.5
 Git commit:   60ccb22
 Built:        Thu Feb 23 11:02:43 2017
 OS/Arch:      linux/amd64
 Experimental: false


**Kubernetes version**:
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"7+", GitVersion:"v1.7.0-alpha.0.746+1d97472361e611-dirty", GitCommit:"1d97472361e61106a1da1ce33da97f243e4d0441", GitTreeState:"dirty", BuildDate:"2017-03-02T22:50:43Z", GoVersion:"go1.8", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}

**Environment**:
- local, vm developer environment:
- "Ubuntu" "16.04.2 LTS (Xenial Xerus)"
- Linux mike-VirtualBox 4.4.0-65-generic #86-Ubuntu SMP Thu Feb 23 17:49:58 UTC 2017 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux

So the code is correctly reporting a semantic versioning error based on the rule that none of the segments should have a leading zero. But we don't own Docker's versioning. So... should we call ParseGeneric vs ParseSemantic (in pkg/util/version/version.go) to disable semver testing, or do we PR docker and limit the number of versions we're compatible with based on this test, or do we change this to a warning or info level information in the parse routine? Seems like overkill to error on a leading zero.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Multicluster.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
This is a follow-up to #41267.

Currently, the service account created in a joining cluster by `kubefed join` has role-based access to all APIs and all resources in all namespaces. We should determine if there is a tighter reasonable subset, or decide that this is conceptually OK. Making a tighter subset will be a small maintenance burden, and will potentially cause issues if people are trying to use older versions of kubefed with newer versions of the control plane.

title: [Federation] Decide whether or not to reintroduce support for non-RBAC Federated clusters in kubefed join

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/multicluster
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Multicluster.

body:
This is a follow-up to #41267.

#42042 removed support in `kubefed join` for clusters that don't support RBAC. Based on a discussion between me, @csbell and @madhusudancs, we need to decide Kubernetes cluster versions Federation will support. If we want to support pre-RBAC clusters, we need to reintroduce the old mechanism, with noisy warnings that the user should update for better security; if not, than this issue can be quickly closed.

title: Fix StatefulSet volume provisioning "magic"

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
**Feature Request** 

**tldr** 
Currently the volume [utilities](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/util.go#L287) used by the GCE and AWS cloud providers attempt to spread the Pods of StatefulSest across zones by detecting PVCs whose names conform to the StatefulSet naming scheme and round robin provisioning the required PVs across AWS and GCE zones. Aside from introducing “magic” for StatefulSet, which makes it not forkable, it does not currently work as documented, and its interaction with Pod Anti-Affinity will probably be, at best, surprising to users.

**Details**
StatefulSet creates PVCs prior to creating its Pods. For many Cloud Providers, the PVs, which are bound to the StatefulSets PVCs, are zonal resources. In order to achieve a high availability deployment, and to ensure the durability of data in the event of a zone failure, the PVs that correspond to PVCs requested by the StatefulSet controller are provisioned across zones in a round robin fashion by Volume Plugins for those environments.  After this, the Pods of the StatefulSet are bound to the zones where the PVs have been provisioned.
1. Zonal anti-affinity will not work as described for the Pods of a StatefulSet on cloud providers that have zonal PVs (i.e AWS, GCP, GKE). Once the PVCs are bound to a PV in a particular zone, the StatefulSet Pod must be scheduled in that zone. Specifying a hard, zonal anti-affinity can still be used to ensure that users will never have more than one Pod per zone, but soft zonal anti-affinity can not be used to achieve spreading across zones. 
2. The implementation will not correctly collocate PVCs from the same StatefulSet Pod in the same AZ/Zone. This causes the victim Pod to be unschedulable #35695.
3. The current implementation applies round robin spreading to any PVCs that end with -id, where id is a number. This will not exclude PVCs that were not generated by a StatefulSet. Given the naming constraints of PVC, it is impossible that users will use names like my-app-pvc-1, my-app-pvc-2, etc.
4. Attempts to fix 2. by grouping by the Pod name and spreading on the ordinal can not be successful in the general case #40910. PVCs created by StatefulSet Pods can not be identified by name. The current construction is ambiguous.
```raw
. Ordinal -> [0-9]+
. Subdomain ->  [a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?(\.[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?)*
. SetName -> Subdomain
. ClaimName -> Subdomain
. StatefulSetClaimName -> ClaimName-SetName-Ordinal
```
The legal name foo-bar-foo-bar-1 admits a variety of valid parses. Also, even if we take this approach, we are really only adding more StatefulSet "magic"

At a minimum, we need to document the current behavior. In general, as the relationship between storage affinity/anti-affinity and cluster topology (e.g. host, zone, rack, power domain) will become even complicated and critical with [local PVs](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/306), a more robust solution is probably necessary.

title: kubelet log lines are dropped at times

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: help wanted
labels.description: Denotes an issue that needs help from a contributor. Must meet "help wanted" guidelines.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
While debugging some failures on GCI (COS), a few people have noticed that some log messages that should've been there were missing in the output of `journalctl -u`. 
One very likely cause is that journald rates limits the log messages of individual services and drops messages accordingly.

The configuration is in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` and by default the limits are set to
```
RateLimitInterval=30s
RateLimitBurst=1000
```

If journald has dropped messages, one can check the log of the journald (`journalctl -u  systemd-journald`) and see messages such as
```
Feb 14 19:59:53 e2e-test-yjhong-minion-group-g3gr systemd-journal[27521]: Suppressed 23 messages from /system.slice/docker.service
Feb 14 19:59:55 e2e-test-yjhong-minion-group-g3gr systemd-journal[27521]: Suppressed 17 messages from /system.slice/kubelet.service
Feb 14 20:00:03 e2e-test-yjhong-minion-group-g3gr systemd-journal[27521]: Suppressed 21 messages from /system.slice/docker.service
Feb 14 20:00:05 e2e-test-yjhong-minion-group-g3gr systemd-journal[27521]: Suppressed 22 messages from /system.slice/kubelet.service
```

Missing log lines makes debugging test failures unnecessarily difficult.  We should check whether the limits are enough for kubelet (e.g., when creating/deleting 100 pods), and if not, whether to adjust the limits or reduce the log noise in general in kubelet. I believe this is less of a problem for production clusters which have lower log verbosity setting, but that needs to be confirmed.


/cc @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs @Random-Liu @dchen1107

title: Kubelet failure to umount glusterfs mount points

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
<!-- Thanks for filing an issue! Before hitting the button, please answer these questions.-->

**Is this a request for help?** (If yes, you should use our troubleshooting guide and community support channels, see http://kubernetes.io/docs/troubleshooting/.):
No

**What keywords did you search in Kubernetes issues before filing this one?** (If you have found any duplicates, you should instead reply there.):
glusterfs, umount
---

**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?** (choose one):
BUG REPORT
<!--
If this is a BUG REPORT, please:
  - Fill in as much of the template below as you can.  If you leave out
    information, we can't help you as well.

If this is a FEATURE REQUEST, please:
  - Describe *in detail* the feature/behavior/change you'd like to see.

In both cases, be ready for followup questions, and please respond in a timely
manner.  If we can't reproduce a bug or think a feature already exists, we
might close your issue.  If we're wrong, PLEASE feel free to reopen it and
explain why.
-->

**Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`):
`Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"5", GitVersion:"v1.5.2", GitCommit:"08e099554f3c31f6e6f07b448ab3ed78d0520507", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2017-01-12T04:57:25Z", GoVersion:"go1.7.4", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"5", GitVersion:"v1.5.2", GitCommit:"08e099554f3c31f6e6f07b448ab3ed78d0520507", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2017-01-12T04:52:34Z", GoVersion:"go1.7.4", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}`


**Environment**:
- **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**: aws
- **OS** (e.g. from /etc/os-release): ubuntu 16.04
- **Kernel** (e.g. `uname -a`): Linux hostname 4.4.0-59-generic #80-Ubuntu SMP Fri Jan 6 17:47:47 UTC 2017 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux
- **Install tools**: terraform/ansible
- **Others**:


**What happened**: 
Kubernetes allows users to delete a glusterfs pvc before it is has been umounted from all kubelets. This leaves orphaned mount points on the kubelet boxes and the kubelets looping trying and remove them.

**What you expected to happen**:
The kubelet should successfully remove the mountpoints.

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):

Example deployment with with a heketi/glusterfs storageclass.

gluster-test.yml:
```
---
kind: "PersistentVolumeClaim"
apiVersion: "v1"
metadata:
  name: "test"
  annotations:
    volume.beta.kubernetes.io/storage-class: "gluster"

spec:
  accessModes:
    - "ReadWriteMany"
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: "4Gi"

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  replicas: 10
  selector:
    role: test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        role: test
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: server
        image: nginx
        volumeMounts:
          - mountPath: /var/lib/www/html
            name: test
      volumes:
        - name: test
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: test
```

To reproduce :

kubectl create -f gluster-test.yml
<wait for all containers to come up>
kubectl delete -f gluster-test.yml

This will cause heketi to remove the glusterfs volume before some of the pods have umounted it. All mount points still online will error with: 'transport endpoint is not connected'

These can still be umounted, however the way the code is written it will try to "stat" the mount point before trying the umount. This will error with something like the following:

```
Feb 08 16:00:50 hostname hyperkube[20686]: E0208 16:00:50.484167   20686 nestedpendingoperations.go:262] Operation for "\"kubernetes.io/glusterfs/7915ad66-ee16-11e6-b43a-0a6fac4f1177-pvc-78f6b82d-ee16-11e6-b43a-0a6fac4f1177\" (\"7915ad66-ee16-11e6-b43a-0a6fac4f1177\")" failed. No retries permitted until 2017-02-08 16:01:06.484141794 +0000 GMT (durationBeforeRetry 16s). Error: UnmountVolume.TearDown failed for volume "kubernetes.io/glusterfs/7915ad66-ee16-11e6-b43a-0a6fac4f1177-pvc-78f6b82d-ee16-11e6-b43a-0a6fac4f1177" (volume.spec.Name: "test") pod "7915ad66-ee16-11e6-b43a-0a6fac4f1177" (UID: "7915ad66-ee16-11e6-b43a-0a6fac4f1177") with: Error checking if path exists: stat /mnt/secure/kubelet-root-dir/pods/7915ad66-ee16-11e6-b43a-0a6fac4f1177/volumes/kubernetes.io~glusterfs/pvc-78f6b82d-ee16-11e6-b43a-0a6fac4f1177: transport endpoint is not connected
```
This will prevent the umount and pod cleanup.


**Anything else we need to know**:


The code looks something like this:

```
func UnmountPath(mountPath string, mounter mount.Interface) error {
	if pathExists, pathErr := PathExists(mountPath); pathErr != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("Error checking if path exists: %v", pathErr)
	} else if !pathExists {
		glog.Warningf("Warning: Unmount skipped because path does not exist: %v", mountPath)
		return nil
	}

	notMnt, err := mounter.IsLikelyNotMountPoint(mountPath)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if notMnt {
		glog.Warningf("Warning: %q is not a mountpoint, deleting", mountPath)
		return os.Remove(mountPath)
	}
	...
```


```
// PathExists returns true if the specified path exists.
func PathExists(path string) (bool, error) {
	_, err := os.Stat(path)
	if err == nil {
		return true, nil
	} else if os.IsNotExist(err) {
		return false, nil
	} else {
		return false, err
	}
}
```
```
func (mounter *Mounter) IsLikelyNotMountPoint(file string) (bool, error) {
	return IsNotMountPoint(file)
}

func IsNotMountPoint(file string) (bool, error) {
	stat, err := os.Stat(file)
	if err != nil {
		return true, err
	}
	rootStat, err := os.Lstat(file + "/..")
	if err != nil {
		return true, err
	}
	// If the directory has a different device as parent, then it is a mountpoint.
	if stat.Sys().(*syscall.Stat_t).Dev != rootStat.Sys().(*syscall.Stat_t).Dev {
		return false, nil
	}

	return true, nil
}
```

I realise the importance of checking to see if a mountpoint is still up before removing it.

My first thoughts were to restrict the stat checks to only error if the mount point didn't actually exist.

Also checking /proc/mounts seems like a more reliable method for checking if something is mounted on linux.

title: NewSelfClientConfig assumes certs are valid for bind IP / localhost

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
NewSelfClientConfig assumes that the server's TLS certificates will be valid for the bind IP or (in the case of binding to 0.0.0.0) will be valid for localhost.

If there is not a valid certificate for the bind IP or localhost, the client built by NewSelfClientConfig will fail with TLS errors, and the server bootstrap will fail.

title: fluentd-gcp container does not send journal logs to cloud-logging (on master branch)

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/instrumentation
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Instrumentation.

body:
Some of the recent changes in HEAD broke the systemd plugin in fluentd-gcp container and as a result, logs from system journal are not uploaded to GCL anymore on GCI/COS. 
(specifically, since PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/37681 and PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/40017) 

**What happened**:
Because of removal of libsystemd setup inside the fluentd-gcp container, the fluentd systemd plugin stopped working and logs from system journal for various services (like kubelet.service and docker.service) are not sent to cloud-logging anymore.

**What you expected to happen**:
logs from system journal for interesting services are sent to cloud-logging.

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):
Start a cluster from master branch (`hack/dev-build-and-up.sh`) on GCP. Look at logs from nodes & master in Cloud Logging Logs Viewer. Docker & Kubelet logs are missing.

**Anything else we need to know**:
* Issue is only on the master branch. Release branches (1.4.x & 1.5.x) does not seem affected.
* The e2e test (`Cluster level logging using GCL should check that logs from containers are ingested in GCL`) does not seem to catch this breakage.

cc/ @piosz @Crassirostris @kubernetes/goog-image @dchen1107
