labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
**What happened**:
As an example `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/register.go` - `AddToGroupVersion()`:
```go
// AddToGroupVersion registers common meta types into schemas.
func AddToGroupVersion(scheme *runtime.Scheme, groupVersion schema.GroupVersion) {
	scheme.AddKnownTypeWithName(groupVersion.WithKind(WatchEventKind), &WatchEvent{})
	scheme.AddKnownTypeWithName(
		schema.GroupVersion{Group: groupVersion.Group, Version: runtime.APIVersionInternal}.WithKind(WatchEventKind),
		&InternalEvent{},
	)
	// Supports legacy code paths, most callers should use metav1.ParameterCodec for now
	scheme.AddKnownTypes(groupVersion,
		&ListOptions{},
		&ExportOptions{},
		&GetOptions{},
		&DeleteOptions{},
	)
// ERROR RESULT IS IGNORED BELOW
	scheme.AddConversionFuncs(
		Convert_versioned_Event_to_watch_Event,
		Convert_versioned_InternalEvent_to_versioned_Event,
		Convert_watch_Event_to_versioned_Event,
		Convert_versioned_Event_to_versioned_InternalEvent,
	)

	// Register Unversioned types under their own special group
	scheme.AddUnversionedTypes(Unversioned,
		&Status{},
		&APIVersions{},
		&APIGroupList{},
		&APIGroup{},
		&APIResourceList{},
	)

	// register manually. This usually goes through the SchemeBuilder, which we cannot use here.
// ERROR RESULT IS IGNORED BELOW
	scheme.AddGeneratedDeepCopyFuncs(GetGeneratedDeepCopyFuncs()...)
// ERROR RESULT IS IGNORED BELOW
	AddConversionFuncs(scheme)
// ERROR RESULT IS IGNORED BELOW
	RegisterDefaults(scheme)
}
```
The function should probably propagate that error as a return value.

Another example is `init()` in the same file:
```go
func init() {
	scheme.AddUnversionedTypes(SchemeGroupVersion,
		&ListOptions{},
		&ExportOptions{},
		&GetOptions{},
		&DeleteOptions{},
	)

	// register manually. This usually goes through the SchemeBuilder, which we cannot use here.
// ERROR RESULT IS IGNORED BELOW
	scheme.AddGeneratedDeepCopyFuncs(GetGeneratedDeepCopyFuncs()...)
// ERROR RESULT IS IGNORED BELOW
	RegisterDefaults(scheme)
}
```
`init()` should probably panic on error.

Client-gen produces scheme construction code that also misses error handling. For example:
`staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes/scheme/register.go`:
```go
// After this, RawExtensions in Kubernetes types will serialize kube-aggregator types
// correctly.
func AddToScheme(scheme *runtime.Scheme) {
// EACH FUNCTION CALL BELOW RETUNS AN ERROR THAT IS IGNORED
	admissionregistrationv1alpha1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	appsv1beta1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	appsv1beta2.AddToScheme(scheme)
	authenticationv1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	authenticationv1beta1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	authorizationv1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	authorizationv1beta1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	autoscalingv1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	autoscalingv2alpha1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	batchv1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	batchv1beta1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	batchv2alpha1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	certificatesv1beta1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	corev1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	extensionsv1beta1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	networkingv1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	policyv1beta1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	rbacv1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	rbacv1beta1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	rbacv1alpha1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	schedulingv1alpha1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	settingsv1alpha1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	storagev1beta1.AddToScheme(scheme)
	storagev1.AddToScheme(scheme)
}
```

**What you expected to happen**:
Proper error handling.
Also, maybe some of the functions can be changed to not return `error` because they always return nil?

/kind bug
/sig api-machinery

body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:
/kind bug

**What happened**:
I created a `LimitRange` with the following spec:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: mem-limit-range
spec:
  limits:
  - default:
      memory: 512Mi
    defaultRequest:
      memory: 256Mi
    type: Container
```

Now,
- When I create a pod without specifying both requests and limits. It gets request=256Mi and limit=512Mi. Working as expected.
- When I create a pod with limit=x and unspecified request, it gets created with limit=x and request=x. Working as expected.
- When I create a pod with request=x and unspecified limit, it gets created with request=x and limit=512Mi. This is okay when x is less than 512Mi. **But when x is greater than 512Mi, I get an error**:
  ```
  The Pod "blah" is invalid: spec.containers[0].resources.limits: Invalid value: "512Mi": must be greater than or equal to memory request
  ```

**What you expected to happen**:
The default limit should not act as the max limit. It should have allowed me to create a pod with request greater than the default limit. I am not sure what limit value LimitRanger should set in this case, we can either set it equal to request or we can keep it unspecified.

However, if this is expected behavior, I should get a better error message that clearly says that if I am only specifying request, I need to specify it less than the default limit.


body:
Spinning up a discussion from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/48561

> It would be nice to identify the server that sent the audit event, i.e. the aggregator vs. an end-user apiserver.

It can be implemented right now by adding a parameter to the webhook address on the deployment stage and process this parameter later in the pipeline. However, it's (relatively) easy to add information to the API and we want to make sure that the information we currently have is in the right state before going to beta / GA.

One thought is that it probably doesn't make sense to have this information in the event object, because events from different sources rarely mix up (until the backend anyway) and it would just mean the same information copied all over the request to the webhook. WDYT about adding this information to the EventList object?

title: Optimize the periodic API discovery of the garbage collector

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Currently every 30s, the garbage collector pauses all its workers, invalidates its discovery cache,  re-discover the API, waits for all the informers to be synced (i.e., waits for informers finish initial LIST), then resumes working. The process is expensive, costs 10~30 seconds according to the logs of presubmit tests (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/49966#issuecomment-319505816). 

Ideal mechanisms that won't make 1.8:
* One way to optimize it is to only redo the discovery if the API actually changes. After the ETag supports in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/47353 gets accepted, every 30s, the garbage collector could query if the swagger spec has changed, and only continues the rediscovery if the apiserver indicates the client cache is stale.
  * Blocking issue: custom resource is not in the openapi https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/47426
* Or we can use the watchable discovery API (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/45659, https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/617), but they are not going to be ready for 1.8

Temporary solution:
* similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/49966#issuecomment-319681399, use another goroutine to periodically re-discover, and resets the garbage collector if there are changes.

-->

**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**: Bug Report

/kind bug

**What happened**: When a Pod fails to initialize due to lack of system resources, none of the Conditions say anything about the reason the Pod failed to initialize. Instead, an Event is emitted with a plain english description of the error. For manual `kubectl` execution, this description is fine. But for interaction programmatically, via something like `client-go`, this seems fragile.

**What you expected to happen**: As per the description on the [kubernetes/autoscaler FAQ](https://github.com/kubernetes/autoscaler/blob/master/cluster-autoscaler/FAQ.md):

> A pod is unschedulable when the Kubernetes scheduler is unable to find a node that can accommodate the pod. For example, a pod can request more CPU [than] is available on any of the cluster nodes. Unschedulable pods are recognized by their PodCondition. Whenever a kubernetes scheduler fails to find a place to run a pod it sets "schedulable" PodCondition to false and reason to "unschedulable".

Basically, I was hoping for any kind of definitive error code or something in the Pod's Conditions that told me why the Pod failed to start. This is important to me as I'm trying to define some custom scaling logic for when there aren't enough system resources.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:  In a relatively low-power Kubernetes cluster (I used the default settings in GKE), create a deployment as follows:

```yaml
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
    name: mult
spec:
    replicas: 100
    template:
        metadata:
            labels:
                app: mult
        spec:
            containers:
                - name: mult
                  image: gposcidonio/mult
```

Feel free to use any image with high CPU usage (the one I listed there is an image I built that just multiplies two random numbers together over and over again). Upon doing so, you will see that some of the created Pods enter a `Running` state, but most of them remain in `Pending`.

Issue a `kubectl describe pod` on one of the `Pending` Pods and you will see that the Pod's Conditions simply state:
```
Conditions:
  Type          Status
  PodScheduled  False
```

At the bottom, you will see an event that says something like:

```
Events:
  FirstSeen     LastSeen        Count   From                    SubObjectPath   Type            Reason                  Message
  ---------     --------        -----   ----                    -------------   --------        ------                  -------
  24m           0s              89      default-scheduler                       Warning         FailedScheduling        No nodes are available that match all of the following predicates:: Insufficient cpu (3).
```

- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):

title: kube-proxy clears conntrack for all IPs when it cleans up a nodePort

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
When we clean up a node port, we run `ExecConntrackTool(execer, "-D", "-p", "udp", "--dport", strconv.Itoa(port))`.  This will clear ALL addresses, but what we really want is just NodePort addresses.

I'm not sure what the right way to express this is.  Consider that we use NodePort 30123 for service A and service port 30123 for service B.  When service A goes away, service B will have its state cleared.

This is very low impact.  The NodePort range is intentionally obscure, and unlikely to actually collide with real Services.  This only affects UDP connections, which are not common.  UDP is typically truly connectionless, so it shouldn't matter if the client gets a new backend.

This would have to have a UDP service be deleted while another UDP service uses the same port and has active "connections" that it needs to stay with the same backend.

Maybe a comment in the code would be sufficient, with a TODO to re-explore this if it ever becomes an issue?

@m1093782566

body:
The original issuse for feature ***federated pod autoscaler*** is [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/38974), and the feature is being tracked [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/features/issues/257). This issue is to track and follow up pending items from the first phase of implementation especially items chosen to defer in the first phase of implementation [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/45993).

1 - Make the replica nums offered (both min and max) and in turn increased or reduced from an existing cluster local hpa, configurable. Right now the value is kept to a pessimistic low of 1 at a time.
2 - Optimise the algorithm such that if there are clusters which need the replicas, they can first be taken from those clusters that have capacity to offer more.
3 - Implement hard limit based min/max preferences per cluster from the user.
4 - Contemplate usage of weighted distribution of replicas based on the weights applied on per cluster hpas by the user.

body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:

/kind bug
@kubernetes/sig-scalability-bugs 
@kubernetes/sig-api-machinery-bugs 
/priority important-longterm

**What happened**:

In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/56714#issuecomment-352756379 I killed `kube-apiserver` process in a 5000 node cluster under load (in the middle of replication controllers for a total of 150k pods ramping up).

It is not able to recover. It seems that:
1. (presumably) its caches are cold, so
2. it is no longer able to respond to all requests (most responses in its log are 429s), I also see some 5xxs, so
3. its container liveness probe is failing, so it is being periodically killed by kubelet, so
4. it is not able to stay alive long enough to rebuild its caches, so - back to (1)

**What you expected to happen**:

It should have enough breathing room to recover. Probably by a combination of:
1. bumping the `initialDelaySeconds` in its `livenessProbe`
2. clients (in particular kubelet) using exponential backoff

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

Bring up a 5k-node cluster, start sig-scalability density test. When the number of running pods reported by the test reaches 100k, kill the `kube-apiserver` process on the master.

labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
cAdvisor is becoming an implementation detail of Kubernetes, and may even be removed entirely in the future (or pushed down into the CRI layer). The Kubelet's stats API has been available for a long time as the prefered way of gathering stats, and there are a number of solutions (e.g. [influxdb+grafana](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/cluster/addons/cluster-monitoring/influxdb)) for cluster-level monitoring.

As such, we should begin the process of deprecating and removing the cAdvisor API surface. As a first step, I propose that we ~~default the cAdvisor port to 0 (disabled), starting with Kubernetes 1.10, and add a deprecation warning to the flag.~~
EDIT: We should add the deprecation warning in 1.10 along with a release note, but not change the default. The notes should warn that the default will change in 1.11. We disable the flag by default in 1.11, and remove it entirely in 1.12 or 1.13.

If **you** currently depend on the UI or the API, speak up! Going forward, the recommended way of taking advantage of those features will be to run cAdvisor as a DaemonSet.

/cc @kubernetes/sig-node-proposals @philips @dashpole

body:
Currently, for memory allocatable evictions, we sum the memory usage of pods in order to calculate allocatable memory usage.
We can get more accurate metrics by monitoring the kubepods cgroup, which contains all pods and their processes.  This has a few benefits:

1. It makes calculation of allocatable usage more accurate.
2. It makes the eviction manager simpler
3. After on-demand metrics are implemented in cAdvisor https://github.com/google/cadvisor/pull/1779, we can also collect metrics from this cgroup on-demand, which will make memory allocatable evictions more responsive, and able to prevent OOMs on the /kubepods cgroup more effectively.

cc @kubernetes/sig-node-feature-requests 

/priority longterm

body:
### Background:

We are adding extension mechanisms to the Kubernetes control plane, initializers and admission webhooks. If e.g. the webhooks are configured but not actually running in the cluster, then the cluster is broken until an administrator can fix it. To make it possible to avoid this situation, we're going to let the webhook be gated on a selector matching the labels on the namespace containing the item under consideration. This should make it possible to construct a set of labels on namespaces that will allow the namespaces hosting the critical webhooks to be operational when the webhooks aren't running. (I will add a link to the design when it is published.)

### What we need:

We're looking for documented best practices around this. We imagined building a "run level" system in labels on namespaces out of this. A complete solution should
* Cover how many run levels there are
* Cover what components go in which run level
* Analyze the functionality of the current controller-manager; it may need to be split into binaries or modes that are in different run levels
* Draw some inspiration from Brian's [layers doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1XkjVm4bOeiVkj-Xt1LgoGiqWsBfNozJ51dyI-ljzt1o/edit). 

We think cluster lifecycle SIG is probably the best place for this to be worked out.

(This is from a meeting between myself, @cheftako, @deads2k, @smarterclayton, @liggitt, @caesarxuchao, and @jagosan. )

body:
The scripts https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/generate-groups.sh and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/generate-internal-groups.sh were created to provide a standardized way of calling the generators for 90% of the CRD and UAS usa-cases. The command-line interface is simplistic, driven by the bash implementation rather than stability and extensibility in mind:

```shell
$ generate-groups.sh <generators> <output-package> <internal-apis-package> <extensiona-apis-package> <groups-versions> ...
```

I.e. the options are positional without flags syntax. Adding another option is impossible. Because https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/53449 should go into 1.8 as early as possible to give CRD users a tool to create especially deepcopy funcs easily, a proper Go implementation was out of reach because it is needs more changes, e.g. in Gengo (now merged). But mid-term we probably want to convert this to Go.

It was also suggested to turn k8s.io/code-generator into a Docker container to make it even easier to 3rdparties to generate code for Kubernetes style api types:

```shell
$ docker run -v $GOPATH:/go k8s.io/code-generator:1.8 generate-group github.com/foo/bar example:v1
```

Another line of thought is the question how and whether to use this also in Kubernetes itself instead of our pretty complex `Makefile.generated_files` mechanism.

**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:

/area cloudprovider

**What happened**:

There are two goroutines that can modify load balancer services in the service controller. The first is the worker that consumes events from the informer via the workqueue. The second is the worker that attempts to sync nodes and update load balancers when the nodes have changed (say one is cordoned now). 

As seen below in the logs, it's possible to have the node syncer and the queue worker updating the same service at the same time. The node syncer calls a method called [lockedUpdateLoadBalancerHosts](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/service/service_controller.go#L668); however, there is no mutex that prevents concurrent modification of a given service other than the queue contrary to what the comments say on the method. 

```
I1004 21:52:32.920417      48 service_controller.go:633] Detected change in list of current cluster nodes. New node set: [<host>]
I1004 21:52:32.920487      48 load_balancer.go:383] Attempting to update load balancer 'k8s-poc-7e8ab7fd-a94b-11e7-b2d8-0000170136cc'
I1004 21:52:34.072576      48 load_balancer.go:246] Applying `update` action on backend set `TCP-80` for lb `<lbid>`
I1004 21:52:34.202269      48 service_controller.go:736] Service has been deleted kube-system/kube-proxy-lb
I1004 21:52:34.202319      48 load_balancer.go:419] Attempting to delete load balancer with name `k8s-poc-7e8ab7fd-a94b-11e7-b2d8-0000170136cc`
I1004 21:52:35.502980      48 load_balancer.go:475] Deleting load balancer `k8s-poc-7e8ab7fd-a94b-11e7-b2d8-0000170136cc` (OCID: `<instanceid>`)
I1004 21:52:55.657560      48 service_controller.go:641] Successfully updated 3 out of 3 load balancers to direct traffic to the updated set of nodes
I1004 21:53:13.258233      48 load_balancer.go:487] Deleted load balancer `k8s-poc-7e8ab7fd-a94b-11e7-b2d8-0000170136cc` (OCID: `<instanceid>`)
```

**What you expected to happen**:

I expect that the update would happen followed by the delete, but not at the same time. 

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

1. Create a load balancer service
2. Cordon a node
3. While the backend is being updated delete the service

**Anything else we need to know?**:

I propose we solve this by submitting each service to the queue to be reprocessed if the known hosts change in the node sync loop. This way each service is guarded by the work queue.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.8
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration**: OCI


cc @luxas @andrewsykim @wlan0 @prydie

title: service controller can leave orphaned load balancers after services are deleted

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: sig/cloud-provider
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cloud Provider.

body:
/kind bug
/area cloudprovider

**Current**

The [service controller](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/service/service_controller.go#L735) fetches the service from the apiserver to sync. If the service no longer exists, then the load balancer is deleted. If the deletion fails (say networking issues or something), then the service key will be added back to the queue to be retried later. This works well until the service controller is restarted while a delete is in process or queued to be processed. At that point, the new service controller that takes over will never see the deleted service since the service has been deleted from etcd. 

**Proposal**

The service account controller should be a [finalizer](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/58b1c30d95719749068497ba35dfe4c64b21aa72/contributors/design-proposals/api-machinery/garbage-collection.md#orphaning-the-descendants-with-orphan-finalizer) on all services. Then we can ensure that the load balancer is successfully deleted prior to the service being deleted. That will make the delete process resilient to restarts / changes in leadership. 

cc @andrewsykim @wlan0 @luxas @prydie

There are almost no mention of using HOMEDRIVE and HOMEPATH, but authoritative information on the subject is hard to find.

title: Provide a solution for instance-specific Kubelet configuration

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
Certain flags, like `--hostname-override` are instance-specific, and thus won't play nice with shared configmaps under dynamic Kubelet config.

We should still have a solution to expose these parameters via a versioned Kubelet config API, rather than command-line flags.

A simple solution could be:
- Add a `KubeletInstanceConfiguration` object to `kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1`.
- Like `KubeletConfiguration`/`--config`, serialize to a file and provide via `--instance-config`.
- This object is not configurable via dynamic Kubelet config, as it contains parameters that should be deployed with the node.

It strikes me that `KubeletInstanceConfiguration` could also be a natural place for any fields that describe local topology maintained by the Kubelet, e.g. `--dynamic-config-dir` and `--root-dir`. Importantly, these are places the Kubelet should *manage* stuff on the node, *not* places the Kubelet should *get* stuff; the latter should be dynamically configurable so that the *stuff the Kubelet gets* (e.g. `kc.StaticPodPath`) is also deploy-able via dynamic config in the future, if we so desire.

body:
> /kind bug

**What happened**:

I setup custom metrics based autoscaling with multiple metrics.  One of those metrics was not available.  HPA reports all metrics as "unknown" (even the ones that are still available) and refuses to operate.

```
Metrics:                                               ( current / target )
  "sockjs_sessions_current" on pods:                   <unknown> / 500
  "ddp_method_calls" on pods:                          <unknown> / 25
  "http_requests" on pods:                             <unknown> / 25
  resource cpu on pods  (as a percentage of request):  <unknown> / 60%
Conditions:
  Type           Status  Reason               Message
  ----           ------  ------               -------
  AbleToScale    True    SucceededGetScale    the HPA controller was able to get the target's current scale
  ScalingActive  False   FailedGetPodsMetric  the HPA was unable to compute the replica count: unable to get metric ddp_method_calls: no metrics returned from custom metrics API
Events:
  Type     Reason               Age                  From                       Message
  ----     ------               ----                 ----                       -------
  Warning  FailedGetPodsMetric  1m (x1052 over 17h)  horizontal-pod-autoscaler  unable to get metric ddp_method_calls: no metrics returned from custom metrics API
```

**What you expected to happen**:

Pods would be automatically scaled based on metrics that were available, ignoring missing metrics (treating them as zero).

A partial failure in the metrics system should not prevent auto-scaling from proceeding with the data that it has.  For example, CPU % metrics come from the k8s metrics server whereas the other metrics come from the prometheus adapter.  If the prometheus adapter goes away we can still use the CPU metric as a lower bound on the number of replicas.

If you consider, e.g. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e99ec245958f82acb2404f8597844d62b8f459c9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L242 , instead of aborting the whole metric gathering process there, it could have stored a placeholder or zero metric value when it fails to fetch the metric.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

Setup a custom metrics server and tell HPA to scale based on several metrics, one of which is not actually available.

**Environment**:

kops 1.8 on AWS

title: Common approach for delegated pod admission & policy

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: sig/architecture
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Architecture.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
There are a number of features that apply policies to pods. However, this is challenging since pods are not typically created by users - they are typically created by a controller instantiating some pod template. Each policy addresses this in their own way:

- **PodSecurityPolicy** - policy is checked against the pods service account, in addition to the creating user. It is not intuitive to give the pod SA the permission to create itself. From a security standpoint, this is similar to namespace level, since we don't have special authorization for using a service account in a namespace.
- **NetworkPolicy** - a podselector determines the pods to apply to, but it's hard to guard or require use of the policy since pods can be created with any label (see next item). NetworkPolicy is namespaced, so a catch-all selector can require all pods in a namespace to comply.
- **ImagePolicy** - limits access to images in pod specs. No first-party story, delegates decisions to an external webhook. Review request includes image name (registry, name, tag, sha), pod annotations (matching prefix), and namespace.
- **LimitRanger, ResourceQuota** - limits resource requests, limits, and usage. Policies applied at namespace level (i.e. all pods in a namespace)
- **Toleration & NodeSelector restrictions** - namespace level, defined on the namespace object
- [Proposal for validated annotations](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/1604) and [Proposal for restricting label access](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Ql_Y-DRbvPCSA-o36CLOs3t4tQUoSvbQxtVEI4FCtEo/edit#heading=h.tx3ialsfu4bx) - Both face a similar problem of validating a pod.

Options for dealing with delegated policy application:

1. **Apply policy at the namespace level** - The most widely used approach right now, but we should standardize the API. This approach has the advantage that it is consistent with authorization (e.g. RBAC), where create permissions are granted at the namespace level. Disadvantages are that policies can't be applied more granularly in a namespace, and managing policy across namespaces needs to be handled.
2. **Apply policy on the pod's service account** - The approach PSP takes. This is counter intuitive, and doesn't really elevate security over the namespace approach, since service account access is not subdivided.
3. **Applied to requester, checked against PodTemplates** - Under this approach, the policy would be checked when a create ReplicaSet/Controller, Job, Deployment, DaemonSet, StatefulSet, etc. are created, matching the policy to the PodTemplate. To handle the delegation issue, controllers that create the pods according to the template are granted unrestricted access. This approach has an intuitive user experience, but a lot of problem including:
    - Dealing with CRDs & third party controllers is challenging
    - Large attack surface, if you can get control of a controller's credentials (particularly a problem for non-built in controllers)
    - Policy isn't checked against initializer values & mutating admission controllers that kick in at pod creation. Less of a problem if those apply to the podtemplates, but that has its own set of issues.
    - Not all policies can reasonable be applied at template creation time (e.g. ResourceQuota)
    - Updating a policy does not retroactively apply
4. **Delegated auth** - Same as above, but rather than granting unrestricted access to the controllers, grant them access to act as the user that initially created the template. This still faces a lot of the same problems as (3), but also introduces the challenge of determining if a Pod matches a template (which might be intractable, I can't come up with a good answer).
5. **??** - Suggestions wanted!

/kind feature
/sig auth
/priority important-longterm

Healthchecking of Tunneler is part of healthz of apiserver. However, that seems to be a bit broken:

This condition should be much less conservative.

body:
Back in 1.5, sig-node defined a set of node conformance tests (i.e., tagged `[Conformance]`). However, there lacks follow-up efforts to maintain the set of conformance tests. IMO, except for a specific set of features which depend on the OS distribution, container runtime, and/or are still under development, most features/tests should be included in the set of node conformance tests. To maintain the set of the tests and to actually utilize the fact that we have "conformance" tests, I think we can start from the following items.

 * Run only the conformance tests in presubmit (`pull-kubernetes-node-e2e` suite) should focus only on the conformance tests.
 * The regular post submit node e2e suite should focus only on the conformance tests.
 * Any new node e2e test added should either be tagged as `[Conformance]` or `[Feature: XXX]`.
 * We should add a dedicated CI test job for features.

If a new test does not have any such tag, it will not be run anywhere in CI. This gives the feature owner some incentive to categorize and promote tests for their features.

*Prerequisite for doing this:*
- Scan and promote/demote tests from the conformance suite.
- Ensure each test is assigned a tag.

*Some potential improvements (details TBD):*
 - It should be able to optionally trigger feature-specific test jobs for a given PR.
 - Define a set of common tags such as `[Feature: Performance]`.

Thoughts? @kubernetes/sig-node-proposals @dchen1107 @derekwaynecarr 
/cc @abgworrall

title: Request to add namespace name and namespace UUID to metadata of on-disk log file

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to adding, removing, or otherwise changing an API

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Instrumentation.

labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

body:
/kind feature

We assert that a log file on-disk (via CRI-O, or docker's json-file logging driver) should have metadata associated with that log file to describe the UUIDs _and_ names of the container, pod, **and** namespace associated with the log output to avoid k8s API calls later.  Today it does not _appear_ to include the namespace UUID or name (see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6caf34389b865be8b41811dc7c130c1006995d8a/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/helpers.go#L220).

Ideally (and arguably), a log collection system *should not be required* to query the Kube APIs about the log data in order to find the UUIDs of the k8s resource hierarchy associated with a container.  Only _optional_ metadata that decorates or enriches the log data would necessitate API calls to fetch that metadata; e.g., if one wanted to decorate logs with one or more labels or annotations from a pod or namespace.  A log collection system should be able to properly disambiguate and group logs accurately without additional API calls which might cause undo burden on the API server.  Since any metadata needed to be fetched via API calls is optional, it can be dropped when inconvenient or added later as a post-processing step.

The "location" of a container in a single k8s cluster is fully described by four pieces of information:

 * hostname
 * container UUID (and name)
 * pod UUID (and name)
 * namespace UUID (and name)

With the above information, understanding the origin of one or more log entries in an aggregation of logs can be accomplished unambiguously with respect to k8s in one cluster.  Today, it appears that k8s provides 3 of the 4 pieces of data, hostname (implicitly), container, and pod, when constructing the symlink for the log file path.

Can we consider adding namespace UUID and namespace name as well?

**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:

/kind bug

**What happened**:
Cloud provider was having issues, so a newly provisioned node was not found shortly after creation. As soon as the node registers itself to apiserver, controller-manager immediately deletes it. This leads to error loops in kubelet on the new node as it doesn't expect itself to be deleted asynchronously, and also prevents pods from being scheduled, despite the node being perfectly healthy.

**What you expected to happen**:
controller-manager should wait for `node-startup-grace-period` to give the node a chance to come up  and the cloud provider to update its state. This allows the node to come up as expected, irrespective of the state of the cloud provider.

**What happened**:

Since #29378, kubelet rewrites container's resolv.conf for setting DNS servers and search domains. This is because Docker 1.12 contains feature "The option --dns and --net=host should not be mutually exclusive", while Docker 1.11 doesn't allow this operation.

title: Validation Tightening is not Generally Possible

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

labels.name: wg/api-expression
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to WG API Expression.

body:
I have made this comment on a few PRs so maybe it's time to document and/or build a mechanism.

You cannot generally make validation tighter, because any existing objects that violate the new rule will not be able to be updated, and in many cases, deleted (because deletions involving finalizers require a sequence of updates).

This is because, to validate updates, we validate BOTH the transition, AND the final state of the object. It's this last part that is problematic.

It should be possible to address this by adding a new class of validation function that ONLY gets called on new objects, but then we have these problems:
* When is it safe to promote the logic into the main validation function? There's no way to know.
* This solves the problem for apiserver, but not for any clients that were sending invalid objects. Especially automated clients will suddenly and without recourse be quite broken.

Even at version boundaries it's hard to tighten validation, since objects have to be round-trippable and there are still old objects in the system.

So, new API authors: start out with restrictive validation; it's easier to relax than to tighten.

Existing API authors: prepare to write defensive clients.

/kind bug
/sig api-machinery

body:
Now it's possible to configure third-party auth providers using `kubectl config set-credentials` command with `--auth-provider` option.

It's nice to have the same possibility for the recently added `exec` [plugin](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authentication/#client-go-credential-plugins). 
Example: To specify the executable path we can run `kubectl config set-credentials k8s_user --exec-command="/path/to/the/executable"`

This will generate a new config for the user:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
users:
- name: k8s_user
  user:
    exec:
      command: "/path/to/the/executable"
      apiVersion: "client.authentication.k8s.io/v1alpha1"
```

Various auxiliary configuration options are also could be added. For instance: 
- `--exec-arg` to define an argument for the executable;
- `--exec-env` to set an environment variable;
- `--exec-api-version` to specify a desired API version.

/kind feature

title: Following container logs can leave processes running and open inotify watches

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:

/kind bug
/sig node

**What happened**:
If a container log is followed using kubectl or other API client, when the client disconnects, the process watching for changes in the logs does not die.

The process only dies when a new log line is received from the container (which may not happen) and the log process tries to send it to the client and then fails.  Furthermore, a inotify watch is also left open, which can potentially cause the OS to run out of watches and eventually results in `failed to create fsnotify watcher: too many open files` when the next container log is followed.

**What you expected to happen**:
When the client disconnects, the process watching the logs should die within a short time, and the inotify watch should be closed.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
This is simplest to reproduce using a single node instance of K8S e.g. minikube
Steps:

1. Create a pod that does not constantly produce log output e.g.
```
kubectl run log-test --image ubuntu:xenial --command sh -- -c 'date; sleep infinity'
```
2. With `kubectl` watch the pod logs (for the pod just created) and leave running:
```
kubectl logs log-test-78ddcd7d6f-7p7hr  -f
```
3. On the node that has the pod check the number of inotify watches from kubelet
```
 sudo lsof -p `pidof kubelet`  2> /dev/null | grep inotify | wc -l
```
4. Press ctrl-c to kill the `kubectl` watch started in (2)
5. Check the number of inotify watchers again by repeating (3).  The number has not decreased, and will never decrease until either the kubelet is restarted, a log line is received from the pod or the pod terminates.

**Anything else we need to know?**:
I believe the problem lies in how the `ReadLogs` function works here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/logs/logs.go#L269
Unfortunately this has no way of knowing if the client has disconnected until it tries to send a new log line via the `writer`, which will then fail, close the inotify watcher (via the `defer`) and exit.

A container producing no log output will therefore leave the process running.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version: both 1.9.7 and 1.10.3
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: VMWare
- OS (e.g. from /etc/os-release): Ubuntu Xenial
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): 4.4.0-122-generic

title: Wire ConfigFlags as RESTClientGetter across commands

body:
Now that most of the functionality provided to commands via the cmdutil.Factory has been decoupled from it via https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/64106, commands should no longer depend on the factory.

- Commands should mimic the pattern established by [NewCmdWait](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/64034/files#diff-6b69c44761e2a603e92ab44a6bc16d4fR67), receiving a `genericclioptions.RESTClientGetter` in place of the `cmdutil.Factory`.

- Commands should also make use of the "CmdFlags" struct pattern ([as demonstrated here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/64034/files#diff-6b69c44761e2a603e92ab44a6bc16d4fR42) in order to bind their own flags, and provide a way to retrieve [an options struct from them](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/64034/files#diff-6b69c44761e2a603e92ab44a6bc16d4fR98)).

- Further, commands should no longer make use of the `f.NewBuilder` method in order to retrieve a resource builer. Rather, they should make use of the new [ResourceBuilderFlags#ToBuilder](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/64034/files#diff-6b69c44761e2a603e92ab44a6bc16d4fR103) method.

If a command requires the use of a REST client, they should no longer use the factory to retrieve one, but rather the methods provided by the `RESTClientGetter` [as seen here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/64034/files#diff-6b69c44761e2a603e92ab44a6bc16d4fR108).

cc @soltysh 

/sig cli

title: kubelet's calculation of whether a container has changed can cause cluster-wide outages

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: help wanted
labels.description: Denotes an issue that needs help from a contributor. Must meet "help wanted" guidelines.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

body:
Updated 2020-11-09 by @liggitt:

In 1.16+, the kubelet hashes the serialized container spec:

1. API server sends data
    * Defaults for added fields will modify this data
    * If an alpha field that is not defaulted graduates to adding a default in beta, an API server upgrade from alpha->beta will modify this data
    * https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5f1e5cafd33a8863c5dfe9f36c9cba836f0e981b/pkg/apis/core/v1/defaults_test.go#L165-L167
2. Kubelet decodes that data into its v1.Container struct
    * If the kubelet is older than the API server, this means it will drop fields added in newer API server versions
3. Kubelet encodes that v1.Container struct to JSON and hashes that data
    * https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5f1e5cafd33a8863c5dfe9f36c9cba836f0e981b/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L98-L108

This mechanism is used by the kubelet in `containerChanged` and `getStableKey`, which means an API server upgrade that starts defaulting a container field graduating from alpha will instantly modify the computed hash and trigger a container restart. This results in simultaneous restart of all containers across all pods of a replicaset and can cause outages.

The kubelet should limit the fields it considers in the container hash to the ones it expects to be able to change in ways that would affect the running container (currently just `image`, I think). The pod uid is already included in `getStableKey` so a delete/recreate of the entire pod would already compute a different key.

Changing this mechanism on a minor version boundary (to improve the interactions with the API server changes in 1) is acceptable, because pods are expected to be drained as part of that upgrade (xref https://github.com/kubernetes/website/issues/12326#issuecomment-704469840)


-----------

Original description:

Kubelet hashes the container spec and store it with the container so that it can detect whether the container meets the current spec. If the hashes do not match, kubelet would kill the container and create a new one. The most notable side effect of this mechanism is that if a new field is added to the container spec in the 1.x kubernetes version, and kubelet is upgraded to 1.x from 1.x-1 version, all containers created by the 1.x-1 version kubelet will be killed.

This issue has come up quiet a few time before (see #53644), and discussed extensively in #23104. It was punted a few times because 1) in-place upgrade of kubelet was not officially supported, and 2) upgrading docker used to require restarting all the containers too. Now that upgrade is managed by the installers (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/6099#issuecomment-359331190) and docker supports live-restore, we should consider fixing this in kubelet.

There are related discussions/suggestions the #57741 PR already. Creating this issue as a centralized place for discussions and suggestions.

/cc @kubernetes/sig-node-feature-requests 
/cc a couple of folks who have expressed interests in this issue: @dixudx @kevin-wangzefeng @wackxu

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
/kind feature

I think eventually we will be asked to add a proto encoding for CRDs. It's very non-obvious how to do this, so I think we should start talking about it now.

I can think of two approaches off the top of my head:
1. Require the user to supply a proto spec as part of the CRD object.
2. Add x-proto-field-number extensions to OpenAPI spec documents. Require the user to set them in the CRD's `validation` field (which we should really rename, but that's another issue). (We'd also have to add type information, or define a strict mapping between the types we express in the spec and proto types.)

1 has the benefit of being very obvious, and probably less work. But I think I prefer 2, because it lets us expose the proto format for built-in types in exactly the same way.

title: Allow use of $ref in in CRD validation schema

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
(combined with https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/76965)

### `$ref` scenario 1:

In go types, we can define a type and use it in several other types. When generating CRD from this go types, we want to use reference for that type in the validation so that the schema has better readability. 
```
package v1beta1

import (
    metav1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
)
type DataType struct {
  Value int `json:"value,omitempty"`
}
type MyKindSpec struct {
  Data []DataType `json:"data,omitempty"`
}

type MyKindStatus struct {
  Data []DataType `json:"data,omitempty"`
}

// +genclient
// +k8s:deepcopy-gen:interfaces=k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime.Object

// MyKind
// +k8s:openapi-gen=true
// +resource:path=mykinds
type MyKind struct {
    metav1.TypeMeta   `json:",inline"`
    metav1.ObjectMeta `json:"metadata,omitempty"`

    Spec   MyKindSpec   `json:"spec,omitempty"`
    Status MyKindStatus `json:"status,omitempty"`
}
```
**What you expected to happen**:
In the CRD for this type, we expect to see the validation as
```  
     spec:
          properties:
            data:
              items:
                $ref: '#/definitions/<...>.DataType'
```

### `$ref` scenario 2:

Original type information is lost when CRD authors [expand their openapi definitions](https://github.com/ant31/crd-validation/blob/eab5f7e90b2c/pkg/convert_types.go#L81-L89). `openapi-gen`[-based operator code is similarly affected](https://github.com/coreos/prometheus-operator/blob/master/example/prometheus-operator-crd/alertmanager.crd.yaml). CRDs forbid `$ref` (implicit GVK link) and `x-*` properties (GVK hints).

_This information enables early, developer-friendly policy checks and useful manifest transforms_. Our CICD automation extends the base k8s schema with custom policy and relies on the schema's `$ref`-erential knowledge to inspect and operate on target resource types, anywhere they appear, eg. deeply nested **or embedded within custom resources**. Prior to validation, a simple callback might first:

**ObjectMeta**
- Require teams set `app.kubernetes.io/*` labels.
- Require teams set org-specific cost/usage/alert aggregation labels.
- Back and forward compat handling, eg. `app`, `app.kubernetes.io/name`, `team`, ...

**Container**
- Inject dynamic ENV and volumes.
- Resolve string properties with templates.
- Require several `resources.limits.*` are set.

**PodSpec** ... **PodSecurityContext** ... **Volume** ...
**Deployment** ... **CronJobSpec** ... **JobSpec** ...
**ServiceSpec** ... **SecurityContext** ... _**(many more)**_ ...

`$ref` expansion makes CRDs opaque to our automation. A pre-processing step is required to repair the type information and restore visibility into CRDs. Options considered are:

- Import all golang-based `openapi-gen`'ed CRDs _directly_ (wherever they write `openapi_generated.go`) and call each `GetOpenAPIDefinitions` function. Merge all results.
- Run `openapi-gen` on k8s and CRD sources ourselves. Avoids multiple `GetOpenAPIDefinitions` calls and potential linking problems.
- Use `kube-apiserver`. Run `hack/update-openapi-spec.sh` with extra CRDs "builtin" and enabled so `GET /openapi/v2` simply returns what we need.

I'd love `$ref` support, but I understand why that could be difficult or undesirable. Alas, if CRDs permitted a known property, eg. `x-kubernetes-group-version-kind` (or similar), CRD libraries can set it accordingly for _each unique `$ref` expansion_ (no need to nest GVK hints), allowing consumers (or even k8s itself) to restore this relationship if and when useful.

Are there options we can move on?

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Security.

body:
**Overview**

I get a lot of questions about how to setup mutual authentication for node-level cluster plugins. Examples include:

- Local volume provisioning
- Device plugins (modify node object)
- Device metrics (scraping)
- CRI Streaming
- _Are there others I'm missing?_

For the general case, our recommendation has been to use a service mesh (such as Istio), or NetworkPolicy (although this isn't really a full solution). But as both of those are optional features on Kubernetes, I don't think they are sufficient for core functionality.

We need some general guidelines for plugins, and may need to build some additional capabilities or libraries to support them.

The architecture we need to target includes:
- A central control component, running as a deployment in the cluster. Let's call this the "CCC".
- A DaemonSet that handles node operations, and communicates back to the controller. Let's call this the "DSP" (DaemonSet Pod).
- K8s API server

Things we might need to solve:

1. CCC -> apiserver (solved)
  a. [x] server (apiserver) authn -- cluster CA
  b. [x] client (CCC) authn -- Use service account tokens
  c. [x] authz -- RBAC
2. CCC -> DSP
  a. [ ] server (DSP) authn
  b. [x] client (CCC) authn -- Service account tokens + TokenReview
  c. [x] authz -- RBAC + SubjectAccessReview
3. DSP -> CCC
  a. [ ] server (CCC) authn
  b. [ ] client (DSP) authn
  c. [ ] authz
4. DSP -> apiserver
  a. [x] server (apiserver) authn -- cluster CA
  b. [ ] client (DSP) authn
  c. [ ] authz

Optionally, we could only solve one of (2) and (3), and just require communications to happen in a single direction (i.e. pull or push). We also might be able to avoid (4) by delegating to the CCC (i.e. require all DSP requests to the apiserver to go through the CCC).

/kind technical-debt
/sig auth

/cc @dashpole @vishh @davidz627 @Random-Liu

body:
This issue is meant to track all feature requests that fall into the category of improving existing compute resource APIs.
Some of the initial reasons for improving compute APIs are:
1. Providing per-device quota while not-compromising workload portability across compatible devices.
2. Enabling per-device billing while not-compromising workload portability across compatible devices.
3. Enabling compute resource consumption via metadata of resources like "minimum CPU version", "minimum GPU memory", etc.

[This doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Lpuw-tjm252W4oGqBvcFAFUZkwFlpZ2i0EgpCwialN0/edit?usp=sharing) provides more use cases for improving compute APIs.

This was discussed in the most recent [Resource Management Working Group meeting](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Df6uGCzGleAhRQYZ20v55U1YCBLfxV4PJh0CIWcMHkk/edit#heading=h.2ltjzba8ef5v).

The most promising design as of now is that of introducing separate API objects one to represent a concrete compute resource and the other to represent policy/grouping around concrete objects (similar to Storage classes). This design is yet to be fully spec'd out.

Design docs: 

* [Resource Class Proposal](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1qKiIVs9AMh2Ua5thhtvWqOqW0MSle_RV3lfriO1Aj6U) 
* [Alternate Resource Class Proposal](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1666PPUs4Lz56TqKygcy6mXkNazde-vwA7q4e5H92sUc)

There are other features that could in theory be a part of the Resource APIs design:
1. Cluster level resources - This could be a separate type of concrete compute resource that is different from Node level concrete compute resources. https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/1400 attempts to tackle cluster level resources differently. This feature is yet to be fully understood. 
2. Network Resources - Kubernetes is currently attempting to introduce support for additional networks via the [Network plumbing WG](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/kubernetes-sig-network/ANAjTyqVosw). Certain use cases for networking have node level devices (Infiniband) along with scheduling restrictions which could possibly be represented via the new resource APIs. This is a very early idea lacking rigorous thinking.
 
As of now the priority is to focus on the initial use cases of quota, chargeback and developer productivity as mentioned in the [use cases doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Lpuw-tjm252W4oGqBvcFAFUZkwFlpZ2i0EgpCwialN0/edit?usp=sharing). 

cc @kubernetes/sig-node-feature-requests @kubernetes/sig-scheduling-feature-requests

body:
/kind cleanup

Today many of in-tree volume plugin's dependencies are injected through the VolumeHost interface, but there are several pain points:
* It's difficult to see a list of dependencies for each plugin.
* Volume plugins have to embed nil checks for their VolumeHost dependencies directly in the code path that uses them. This makes plugins more prone to bugs.
* If a particular dependency is missing, there is no way to explicitly configure whether initialization of the caller component (e.g. kubelet, controller manager) should fail, or just skip plugin initialization. For different caller situations either option is possible.
  * Today, returning an error in the volume plugin's `Init()` call when a dependency is missing causes the caller component to fail.

Investigate whether it makes sense to improve this dependency injection mechanism.

/priority important-longterm

body:
### Background
In 1.12, the kubelet exposes a number of sources for metrics directly from [cAdvisor](https://github.com/google/cadvisor#cadvisor).  This includes:
 * [cAdvisor prometheus metrics](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/blob/master/docs/storage/prometheus.md#prometheus-metrics) at [`/metrics/cadvisor`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/server/server.go#L277)
 * [cAdvisor v1 Json API](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/blob/master/info/v1/container.go#L126) at [`/stats/`, `/stats/container`, `/stats/{podName}/{containerName}`, and `/stats/{namespace}/{podName}/{uid}/{containerName}`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/server/stats/handler.go#L111)
 * [cAdvisor machine info](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/blob/master/info/v1/machine.go#L159) at [`/spec`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/server/server.go#L291)

The kubelet also exposes the [summary API](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/apis/stats/v1alpha1/types.go#L24), which is not exposed directly by cAdvisor, but queries cAdvisor as one of its sources for metrics.

The [Monitoring Architecture](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/design-proposals/instrumentation/monitoring_architecture.md) documentation describes the path for "core" metrics, and for "monitoring" metrics.  The [Core Metrics](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/design-proposals/instrumentation/core-metrics-pipeline.md#core-metrics-in-kubelet) proposal describes the set of metrics that we consider core, and their uses.  The motivation for the split architecture is:
 * To minimize the performance impact of stats collection for core metrics, allowing these to be collected more frequently
 * To make the monitoring pipeline replaceable, and extensible.

### Current kubelet metrics that are not included in core metrics
 * Pod and Node-level Network Metrics
 * Persistent Volume Metrics
 * Container-level (Nvidia) GPU Metrics
 * Node-Level RLimit Metrics
 * Misc Memory Metrics (e.g. PageFaults)
 * Container, Pod, and Node-level Inode metrics (for ephemeral storage)
 * Container, Pod, and Node-level DiskIO metrics (from cAdvisor)

Deprecating and removing the Summary API will require out-of-tree sources for each of these metrics.  "Direct" cAdvisor endpoints are not often used, and have even been broken for multiple releases (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/62544) without anyone raising an issue.

### Working Items
 * [x] [1.13] Introduce Kubelet `pod-resources` grpc endpoint; KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/2454
 * [x] [1.14] Introduce Kubelet Resource Metrics API
 * [x] [1.15] Deprecate the "direct" cAdvisor API endpoints by adding and deprecating a `--enable-cadvisor-json-endpoints` flag
 * [x] [1.18] Default the `--enable-cadvisor-json-endpoints` flag to disabled
 * [ ] [1.21] Remove the `--enable-cadvisor-json-endpoints` flag
 * [ ] [1.21] Transition Monitoring Server to Kubelet Resource Metrics API ([requires 3 versions skew](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/67829#issuecomment-416873857))
 * [ ] [TBD] Propose out-of-tree replacements for kubelet monitoring endpoints
 * [ ] [TBD] Deprecate the Summary API and cAdvisor prometheus endoints by adding and deprecating a `--enable-container-monitoring-endpoints` flag
 * [ ] [TBD+2] Remove "direct" cAdvisor API endpoints
 * [ ] [TBD+2] Default the `--enable-container-monitoring-endpoints` flag to disabled
 * [ ] [TBD+4] Remove the Summary API, cAdvisor prometheus metrics and remove the `--enable-container-monitoring-endpoints` flag.

### Open Questions
 * Should the kubelet be a source for any monitoring metrics?
   * For example, metrics about the kubelet itself, or DiskIO metrics for empty-dir volumes (which are "owned" by the kubelet).
 * What will provide the metrics listed above, now that the kubelet no longer does?
   * cAdvisor can provide Network, RLimit, Misc Memory metrics, Inode metrics, and DiskIO metrics.
     * cAdvisor only works for some runtimes, but is a drop-in replacement for "direct" cAdvisor API endpoints
   * Container Runtimes can be a source for container-level Memory, Inode, Network and DiskIO metrics.
   * NVidia GPU metrics provided by a daemonset published by NVidia
   * No source for Persistent Volume metrics?

/sig node
/sig instrumentation
/kind feature
/priority important-longterm
cc @kubernetes/sig-node-proposals @kubernetes/sig-instrumentation-misc

body:
I am experimenting with CRD is `k8s.io/api`. I put my `types.go` to `staging/src/k8s.io/api/csi` and run `hack/update-codegen.sh`*. Such generated client(s) are part of the usual `clientset.Interface` with core Kubernetes APIs.

In kubelet and controller-manager, I can use the clientset to list my CRs  without any issues:

```go
client.Csi().CSIDrivers().List(meta.ListOptions{})
```

In kubelet and controller-manager, I can **not** use the clientset to **watch** CRs:
```go
w, err = client.Csi().CSIDrivers().Watch(meta.ListOptions{ResourceVersion: "0"})
if err != nil {
	glog.Infof("Watch error: %s", err)
	return
}
ch := w.ResultChan()
for {
	obj, ok := <-ch
	glog.Infof("watch got ok: %t, obj: %+v", ok, obj)
	if !ok {
		glog.Infof("watch closed")
		break
	}
}
```

`Watch()` returns just fine. But the returned channel `ch` closes immediately with this message in log:
```
E0820 14:55:10.279927   13837 streamwatcher.go:109] Unable to decode an event from the watch stream: got short buffer with n=0, base=851, cap=2688
```

It seems to be related to timing, sometimes the channel closes just like above, sometimes it's open, but never delivers any event, even if I create/delete CRs.

Everything gets working if I run controller-manager with `--kube-api-content-type="application/json"`, the channel reports all events as expected. It must be something with protobuf used for most of the API and json used for CRDs.


*) I had to hack `hack/update-codegen.sh` to work for API in `staging/src/k8s.io/api` without its internal counterpart in `pkg/apis`. I'll fill a separate issue/PR for it.

labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
Currently, if an intermediate CA is used to sign certs, the csr signing controller does not include the intermediate chain in the CSR status. This means that anything requesting a cert via the CSR API has to know the intermediates themselves (unlikely) or anything interacting with a component presenting or serving using an intermediate-issued cert must know about the intermediate issuer.

Ideally, we would have a way to:
1. indicate to the signing controller an optional intermediate bundle to include
2. include intermediates in the CSR status (appending to the existing `Certificate` field, having a separate `Intermediates []byte` field, etc)

/sig auth
/cc @mikedanese

body:
As a follow up to #62576 I was investigating other large packages.  In Go 1.10 it looks like `github.com/vmware/govmomi/vim25/types` is the next largest - it was ~ 23M compiled (by itself) and defines roughly 6k structs, and also preserves very large maps of type information as well as individual init functions to create that map.  When compiling `hyperkube` with the vmware packages commented out, total binary size dropped by roughly 23M as well.  Link-time-optimization won't work against a package like this since all type info in the package is included in the map.  It looks like the init functions alone are 1.5M, while the hash functions and eq functions for each struct are roughly 200-300b

@kubernetes/vmware has this ever been reported or investigated in the client library?  I suspect breaking the package up into multiple imports (one per group of APIs) and then allowing those sub packages to be directly imported or aggregated would allow more selective usage, but it's possible that the Go compiler is missing opportunities to more efficiently handle this package.  If we know what the surface area of the calls are, could we be more selective in the imports?

Once https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/62692 merges, we should add support for audiences to the Kubelet's token review.

This is important as part of the node isolation efforts, as the node could otherwise use tokens sent with requests to the nodes endpoints (e.g. stats requests) to send requests to other nodes.

I think the node should accept 3 types of audiences:

- legacy (no audience) - required for backwards compatibility
- `system:nodes` - token used for all nodes
- `system:node:<nodeName>` - per-node token, preferred

title: Sweep for calls to delete that result in orphaning dependents

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.description: Denotes an issue that needs help from a contributor. Must meet "help wanted" guidelines.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
**What happened**:

Several resources default to orphaning dependents for backwards compatibility:
* daemonsets in extensions/v1beta1, apps/v1beta2
* deployments in extensions/v1beta1, apps/v1beta1, apps/v1beta2
* replicasets in extensions/v1beta1, apps/v1beta2
* statefulsets in apps/v1beta1, apps/v1beta2
* jobs in batch/v1
* cronjobs in batch/v1beta1, batch/v2alpha1
* replicationcontrollers in v1

Calls made via client-go to delete these resource via these versions which do not specify a deletion propagation policy default to orphaning dependents. For controller-deleted resources, this is almost always not what we want.

A specific example of this was https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/71772 that deleted jobs and accidentally orphaned pods.

We should sweep controller calls that delete the resources/versions listed above without specifying a deletion propagation policy and decide what policy is expected. In general, I would expect controllers to use background deletion propagation.

title: Create/Update of custom resources returns wrong error code for bad requests, 500 instead of 4XX

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
**What happened**:
POST or PUT to a custom resource with a JSON body missing "kind" results in a 500 error:
```json
{
    "kind": "Status",
    "apiVersion": "v1",
    "metadata": {},
    "status": "Failure",
    "message": "Object 'Kind' is missing in 'object has no kind field '",
    "code": 500
}
```
A missing "apiVersion" also results in a 500 error:
```json
{
    "kind": "Status",
    "apiVersion": "v1",
    "metadata": {},
    "status": "Failure",
    "message": "Internal error occurred: Object 'apiVersion' is missing in 'object has no apiVersion field'",
    "reason": "InternalError",
    "details": {
        "causes": [
            {
                "message": "Object 'apiVersion' is missing in 'object has no apiVersion field'"
            }
        ]
    },
    "code": 500
}
```
Then with both "kind" and "apiVersion" defined we get the normal 4XX return codes.

**What you expected to happen**:
All bad inputs for create and update requests should be 4XX return codes.
E.g. Creating a `Role` with body of `{}` results in the 422 error:
```json
{
    "kind": "Status",
    "apiVersion": "v1",
    "metadata": {},
    "status": "Failure",
    "message": "Role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io \"\" is invalid: metadata.name: Required value: name or generateName is required",
    "reason": "Invalid",
    "details": {
        "group": "rbac.authorization.k8s.io",
        "kind": "Role",
        "causes": [
            {
                "reason": "FieldValueRequired",
                "message": "Required value: name or generateName is required",
                "field": "metadata.name"
            }
        ]
    },
    "code": 422
}
```

**How to reproduce it**:
Create a CRD or use a cluster that already has a one prepared (GKE 1.11.0+ clusters have the CRD `cloud.google.com/v1beta1` `backendconfigs` installed which you could test against). HTTP `POST` to that custom resource with a JSON body of `{}`.

E.g. 
```sh
curl -d '{}' -H "Content-Type: application/json" -X POST http://CLUSTER/apis/cloud.google.com/v1beta1/namespaces/default/backendconfigs
```

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.11.2
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: GKE
- OS (e.g. from /etc/os-release):
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`):

body:
Setting `--delete-namespace-on-failure=false` is often used to keep objects in test running when the failure occurs, to help with debugging. However, many storage e2e tests, including CSI tests, clean up test pods and PVCs in a `defer` statement and AfterEach. As a result, even if the flag is set to false, everything gets cleaned up anyway.

One option is to put cleanup functions at the end of each test, as regular function calls rather than deferred calls, but this defeats the purpose of `AfterEach`.

What we might need is a --cleanup-on-failure` flag that enables/disables `AfterEach`

/sig storage
/sig testing

body:
The kubelet uses a [versioned, kubernetes-style configuration](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go#L62).  As part of this migration, folks in sig-node [removed using the global flag set](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/57613) in favor of explicitly defining the flags the kubelet accepts.  Environment variables similarly share a global, unversioned namespace.

The kubelet should call `os.Clearenv` when it starts up to maintain control of its api surface and thereby ensure we follow api compatibility guarantees.  If there are environment variables we need, we should parse them before `os.Clearenv`, and pass them as explicit configuration to the consumer.

/area kubelet

title: Transition ServiceAccount admission controller to improved service account token volumes

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: kind/feature

labels.name: sig/auth

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
Over the next N releases, we would like to transition the ServiceAccount admission controller to injecting service account token volumes based on the TokenRequest API and volume projection designed here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/design-proposals/auth/bound-service-account-tokens.md
https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/design-proposals/storage/svcacct-token-volume-source.md

I propose we use the feature mechanism, with plenty of lead time and noisy announcements, to phase this change in.

### Proposed Plan

*This following is pretty close to what the announcement will look like.*

With the enablement of a new feature, SecureServiceAccountTokenVolume, we will switch the service account admission control to injecting service account token volumes that use the new TokenRequest API to provision tokens. We will loudly announce a new feature that will be Alpha in 1.13 called SecureServiceAccounTokenVolume. 

The new service account token volumes are preferred over the old volumes because:

* Tokens provisioned into the new volumes are only valid for a short TTL and are rotated automatically, minimizing the impact of a token exfiltration.
* Tokens provisioned into the new volumes are bound to the pod, which greatly reduces the difficulty of a forced credential rotation. Operators need only redeploy their application (e.g. trigger a deployment rolling update). This operation is complex to execute without application disruption with the old volumes, and we don’t have any official guidance on the process.
* Tokens provisioned into the new volumes are audience bound to the API server which should dissuade integrators from accepting them as identity proof elsewhere, thus improving the security posture of authentication to the Kubernetes API server.
* Tokens provisioned into the new volumes do not depend on data stored in Kubernetes secrets and are not persisted in any database, reducing the impact and value of a read compromise of the secrets API.
* Tokens provisioned into the new volumes do not depend on data stored in Kubernetes secrets that must be replicated per service account instance which will solve long standing scalability issues with the implementation of service accounts once the migration is complete. See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/48408
* Tokens provisioned into the new volumes are not referable in environment variables via the Downward API.
* Tokens provisioned into the new volumes have stricter file permission. They must be either `0600` or `0640` when using the "fsGroup" feature. They do not allow overrides to more permissive permissions.

The SecureServiceAccounTokenVolume feature will:

*Switch the service account admission controller to using a projected volume (with a token projection) to implement the old service account volume’s filesystem API.
* Make --service-account-issuer a required flag thus requiring that TokenRequest will be enabled.

Users who use the alpha release track to canary what’s coming down the pike will encounter this and will notice that:

* Their API servers won’t start until they add the flags required to enable TokenRequest
* In-cluster clients of the kubernetes apiserver that don’t reload service account tokens will start failing an hour after deployment. They will need to update these clients. (Partial fix in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/commit/d62f9c9df4e0c3f4dc71a6bb900f619cadc5f9a5)
* PodSecurityPolicies that allowed secret volumes but not projected volumes will no longer be usable with newly created pods that auto-mount service account volumes. They will need to allow projected volumes now. 
* Pre-1.11 Kubelets (assuming they also enable alpha features) will no longer run new pods that mount service account volumes.
* ~~Pods running as non root need an fsGroup or they will not have permission to read the token.~~

We will continue to announce this new behavior each release. We will leave this feature in alpha for a release or more then graduate it to beta and enable it by default. At this point, users will either have to make the changes to upgrade or explicitly disable the beta feature. After a long deprecation, we will promote the feature to GA and remove the ability for clusters to opt out.

### Notified Parties

* sig-apimachinery to consult on plan
* sig-arch to consult on plan
* kubernetes-dev to notify of intent to make this change
* kubernetes-announce to notify of intent to make this change

/kind feature
/sig auth
/sig api-machinery

@kubernetes/sig-auth-feature-requests 
@kubernetes/sig-api-machinery-feature-requests 
@kubernetes/sig-architecture-feature-requests
@liggitt @tallclair @cjcullen @smarterclayton
