title: kubelet TopologyManager Stalls on Large NUMA Systems (e.g. Nvidia GB200 Compute Tray with 34 NUMA nodes)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

body:
### What happened?

When scheduling a pod (e.g. KubeVirt virt-launcher pod) that requests a PCI device on a very large NUMA system, kubelet’s TopologyManager never finishes computing topology hints and the pod is effectively stuck in admission:

- The pod is scheduled to the node.
- kubelet never reaches the device Allocate call for the requested resource.
- From a higher-level consumer (KubeVirt in our case), the virt-launcher pod stays in Pending and the VM remains in Starting with Ready = False.
- kubelet is responsive, but many goroutines are stuck in topology hint generation.

In our environment this manifests as:

- KubeVirt VM with a hostDevice (GPU, InfiniBand or NVMe) never transitions to Running, even though the node has the capacity and the device is free.
- Disabling TopologyManager or constraining the NUMA fan-out immediately lets the VM start

### What did you expect to happen?

kubelet should compute topology hints in bounded time, even on systems with many NUMA nodes (in a case GB200 with 34 NUMA nodes where only 2 NUMA nodes have CPUs, the rest are for HBM/NVLink), and call device-plugin Allocate so that pods/VMs using PCI host devices can start.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

## High-level repro:
1. Use a host with a large NUMA topology  
    Example: Nvidia GB200-class system with 34 NUMA nodes visible to the OS.
 
2. Run Kubernetes with kubelet configured roughly as follows:
```yaml
kubeReserved:
  cpu: "2"
  memory: 4Gi
  ephemeral-storage: 20Gi
systemReserved:
  cpu: "2"
  memory: 8Gi
  ephemeral-storage: 20Gi
topologyManagerPolicy: best-effort
topologyManagerScope: pod
topologyManagerPolicyOptions:
  prefer-closest-numa-nodes: "true"
  max-allowable-numa-nodes: "34"
cpuManagerPolicy: static
reservedSystemCPUs: "0-3,72-75"
cpuManagerPolicyOptions:
  distribute-cpus-across-numa: "false"
```
3. Deploy a device plugin that:
- Advertises a PCI resource (e.g. GPU, InfiniBand or NVMe) as a kubelet device resource.
- Exposes the device with topology information referencing many NUMA nodes (up to 34 in our case).

4. Create a Pod
Requests one unit of that device resource.
Uses Guaranteed QoS (requests == limits for CPU/memory) so that TopologyManager participates fully.
 
5. Observe
- The pod is scheduled to the node.
- kubelet never calls Allocate on the device plugin for that resource.
- The pod stays in Pending indefinitely.
- KubeVirt-specific repro (how we hit it)
- Instead of a raw pod, create a KubeVirt VirtualMachineInstance that uses hostDevices:
```yaml
devices:
   hostDevices:
    - deviceName: nvidia.com/GB100_HGX_GB200
      name: gpu1
```
The pod (if using KubeVirt, it is virt-launcher pod for a VM) is scheduled to the large NUMA node but stays Pending forever. The pod stuck at Pending, (if using KubeVirt, the VM status remains Starting) and never reaches Ready, despite sufficient resources.


### Anything else we need to know?

## Root cause analysis

- The kubelet TopologyManager asks each hint provider (CPU, memory, device) to compute topology hints over the set of NUMA nodes that the kubelet knows about.
- For the device plugin case, generateDeviceTopologyHints ends up calling bitmask.IterateBitMasks across a bitmask spanning all NUMA IDs known to the machine, not just those relevant to the requested device.
- With 34 NUMA nodes this becomes effectively an exponential search (O(2^n)) over the 34-bit mask.
- On a GB200 host with 34 NUMA nodes and a device plugin that advertises per-node topology across those nodes, generateDeviceTopologyHints spends unbounded time iterating combinations that are not actually schedulable for the requested device.
- While TopologyManager is doing this, kubelet never reaches the device Allocate call, so pods/VMs that need that device are permanently stuck in admission.

## Evidence observed

- Goroutine dumps from kubelet show many workers blocked under TopologyManager/device-manager paths, repeatedly calling IterateBitMasks on a large bitmask.
- No calls to Allocate are observed for the affected device resource while the system is in this hung state.
- If we disable TopologyManager, then virt-launcher pods immediately proceed and the KubeVirt VM starts successfully.

### Kubernetes version

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.34.2
Kustomize Version: v5.7.1
Server Version: v1.34.2
```

### Cloud provider

Bare metal, GB200 compute tray

# On Linux:
$ cat /etc/os-release

NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION_ID="24.04"
VERSION="24.04.3 LTS (Noble Numbat)"

body:
### What would you like to be added?

We have [test/cmd](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/cmd/README.md) with shell scripts which run certain tests, using Kubernetes-specific shell helpers (e.g. `kube::test::if_has_string`) to write assertions.

We could replace all of this with https://github.com/rogpeppe/go-internal?tab=readme-ov-file#testscript, which is roughly the same tooling that the Go team uses to test the go CLI commands. See https://bitfieldconsulting.com/posts/test-scripts for an introduction.

This is a major undertaking and there are good reasons for not doing it ("if it ain't broke, don't fix it"). But it could be a nice summer of code or intern project and might be worth it, so let's at least discuss...

/sig testing
/sig cli
/cc @BenTheElder @aojea @soltysh @eddiezane @dims 


### Why is this needed?

* For newcomers, learning how to write CLI tests is just another "Kubernetes is different" hurdle and knowledge that they cannot reuse elsewhere.
* Integration of running those tests into our CI is awkward. We shuffled it into a separate job ([pull-kubernetes-cmd](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/135395/pull-kubernetes-cmd/1992980878933889024), but it's still a pain:
   * No parallelism, which makes it slow and is why we needed the separate job.

Problems:

title: Unsorted list of runtime handlers causes redundant node updates

labels.name: kind/bug

body:
### What happened?

When you have multiple runtime OCI runtime handlers configured, the list returned by the CRI runtime may not always be in same order, because they might be interesting over a map internally. If the returned order changes, then this causes unnecessary update to the node object even though actual list of runtime handlers is same as earlier (but with different order)  

### What did you expect to happen?

Unless the actual runtime handlers change, there should not be an update to node CR. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Have large list of runtime handlers like this, and you would see the order would change everytime you query it, 

```bash
$ kubectl get nodes -o json | jq -r '.items[] | "\(.metadata.name): \(.status.runtimeHandlers | map(if .name == "" then "(empty)" else .name end) | join(", "))"'
cnvqe-20.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
cnvqe-21.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
cnvqe-22.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
cnvqe-23.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: runc, (empty), crun
cnvqe-24.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
cnvqe-25.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: runc, (empty), crun
cnvqe-26.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
cnvqe-27.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: runc, (empty), crun
cnvqe-28.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
cnvqe-29.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
cnvqe-arm-001.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
cnvqe-arm-002.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
monster01.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
monster02.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
monster03.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
monster04.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
titan142.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
zeus07.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
zeus08.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)
zeus10.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: crun, runc, (empty)

zeus37.lab.eng.tlv2.redhat.com: high-performance, crun, runc, (empty)
```

### Anything else we need to know?

Note that, containerd ensures the [ordering of the runtime handlers](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/4ab5ee32ad3e1b22cc2f33cf1163ba9df23454cb/internal/cri/server/status.go#L68), so this bug doesn't really affect containerd. But CRI-O on the other hand, [iterates over a map](https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/blob/6d034a9aaafe86e968559793e55e552a29cd19c3/server/runtime_status.go#L43) causing this issue. 

Initially I considered fixing it in CRI-O, but then IMO it won't be a bad idea to have this defensive code in the kubelet as well, so it doesn't rely on CRI runtimes to do the right thing, especially if CRI API doesn't explicitly mandate that the list of handlers need to be sorted. So this will safeguard kubelet against any future CRI runtimes as well who may not send the sorted list.

title: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy namespace lookup raced newly created namespaces, produces spurious "namespace not found" rejections

body:
### What happened?

When creating new workload (observed with Deployment and StatefulSet) immediately after creating its namespace, there is a possibility that watch case has not yet caught up to the new namespace existing.

Naively, this would result in frequent failures, but apiserver guards against this by falling back to live client when namespace was `NotFound`. Example: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ab3e83f73424a18f298a0050440af92d2d7c4720/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/webhook/predicates/namespace/matcher.go#L88

The issue happens infrequently but can be forced by overriding informer lister to always return NotFound for a specific namespace (see repro instructions below). This way, the call to informer's lister would always fail, while the call to client would remain unaffected - this would force the fallback path, ensuring it is present.

### What did you expect to happen?

No 404 errors when creating StatefulSets in existing namespaces - even immediately after ns creation.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?



```
--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/listers/core/v1/namespace.go
+++ b/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/listers/core/v1/namespace.go
@@ -20,7 +20,6 @@ package v1

 import (
        corev1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"

title: Kubelet admission check includes rejected pods in resource accounting, causing subsequent pods to be incorrectly rejected

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

body:
### What happened?

 The kubelet has a race condition in pod admission logic where rejected pods pollute the resource accounting for subsequent pod admissions.

  
  From Openshift CI logs:
  - Pod 1 (pod-out-of-cpu) requested 1000000000000000 millicores (intentionally absurd for testing)
  - Rejected at 03:12:06.086 with used: 759 millicores
  - Pod 2 (resize-test-kngwb) requested 20 millicores
  - Rejected at 03:12:06.220 (134ms later) with used: 1000000000000759 millicores
    - This is exactly: 1000000000000000 + 759

  The rejected Pod 1's CPU request was incorrectly included in the "used" calculation for Pod 2.

From kubelet logs (worker-2):
```
  Nov 06 03:12:06.086726 - Pod admission denied
    pod="e2e-pod-rejection-status-7203/pod-out-of-cpu"
    requested: 1000000000000000, used: 759, capacity: 3500

  Nov 06 03:12:06.220844 - Pod admission denied
    pod="e2e-pod-resize-tests-9859/resize-test-kngwb"
    requested: 20, used: 1000000000000759, capacity: 3500
```
  CI Run: https://prow.ci.openshift.org/view/gs/test-platform-results/logs/periodic-ci-openshift-release-master-nightly-4.21-e2e-metal-ipi-upgrade-ovn-ipv6/1986332510224650240

  Failed Test:
  [sig-node] Pod InPlace Resize Container [FeatureGate:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] [Beta]


### What did you expect to happen?

Rejected pods should not affect resource accounting for subsequent pod admission checks

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We have observed this intermittently in Openshift CI.

title: Deployment scaleReplicaSetAndRecordEvent vs scaleReplicaSet duplication cleanup is problematic

labels.name: sig/apps

body:
### The situation

Deployment controller has two seemingly similar methods:

1. [scaleReplicaSetAndRecordEvent](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7f80af819776159ba397fff39cef8b69196c8755/pkg/controller/deployment/sync.go#L403)
2. [scaleReplicaSet](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7f80af819776159ba397fff39cef8b69196c8755/pkg/controller/deployment/sync.go#L412)

`scaleReplicaSetAndRecordEvent` invokes `scaleReplicaSet` after doing a quick check if scaling is needed. 

The proposed fixed from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134840/ was trying to squash these two methods into one but it turned out that it caused an avalanche of failures reported in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135150 and lead to a revert in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135154 which resolved the problem.

### Root cause

The affected test was [[sig-apps] Deployment iterative rollouts should eventually progress](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7f80af819776159ba397fff39cef8b69196c8755/test/e2e/apps/deployment.go#L137-L139), which was failing [to wait for deployment completion](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7f80af819776159ba397fff39cef8b69196c8755/test/e2e/apps/deployment.go#L1141):

[Failure 1](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/batch/pull-kubernetes-e2e-gce/1986056661554434048) and [Failure 2](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/134711/pull-kubernetes-e2e-gce/1986121067596353536) have some additional information for debugging. 

### Conclusion

Before attempting another cleanup in this area we need to ensure that this test (and other deployment related) are working in at least 10+ consecutive runs.

body:
Almost everywhere we check whether a pod has pod level resources (PLRs) we don't differentiate between nil and empty PLRs. For example:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3ec72e2e973664a0690bc7122c9cd291702b5f36/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/resource/helpers.go#L73-L82

However, in `ComputePodQOS` we don't make this distinction:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3ec72e2e973664a0690bc7122c9cd291702b5f36/pkg/apis/core/v1/helper/qos/qos.go#L96-L111

This could lead to some weird situations where you have a best-effort pod running with resources specified. For example:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name:      pause-plr
spec:
  resources: {}
  containers:
    - name:    pause
      image: registry.k8s.io/pause:latest
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu:    100m
          memory: 50Mi
        limits:
          cpu:    100m
          memory: 50Mi
```

I'm not sure exactly what the implications of this are, but since it breaks some fundamental assumptions, it's probably not good.

What was the reason for ignoring empty pod level resources?

We'll need to be careful about backwards compatibility when fixing this.

body:
### What happened?


I enabled the `LocalStorageCapacityIsolationFSQuotaMonitoring` feature gate. 
I was able to successfully create a pod using the YAML file, with `hostUsers` set to `false`. However, after the pod was deleted, the project quota information for the pod’s volume still remained in `/etc/project` and `/etc/projid`.

After adding some debug logs to the kubelet, I noticed that `ed.pod.Spec.HostUsers` is `nil` in the code below. 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/93248f9ae092f571eb870b7664c534bfc7d00f03/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go#L538

As far as I know, since version 1.31, the kubelet checks if a user namespace is in use before assigning or clearing quotas. That means `ed.pod.Spec.HostUsers=nil` would bypass the entire quota teardown process.


### What did you expect to happen?

The Project ID is an attribute of the directory and is removed when the directory is deleted. However, the tear down process should still be handled properly to avoid side effects such as memory leaks.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Here’s what I actually did:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: ephemeral-pod
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0
  hostUsers: false
  containers:
  - name: demo-container
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo Hello World && sleep 3600"]
    resources:
      requests:
        ephemeral-storage: "5Mi"
      limits:
        ephemeral-storage: "5Mi"
    volumeMounts:
    - name: test-storage
      mountPath: /mnt/temp
  volumes:
  - name: test-storage
    emptyDir: {}
```

# Performance Analysis: sync.Pool Optimization in Kubernetes Scheduler

## Overview
This document analyzes the performance improvements achieved by implementing `sync.Pool` for frequently allocated structures in the Kubernetes scheduler, addressing issue #134832.

## Implementation Summary

### 1. **nodeStatus struct pooling** (schedule_one.go)
- **Context**: Allocated once per node during the filtering phase of scheduling
- **Impact**: In a 1000-node cluster, this creates 1000 allocations per scheduling cycle

### 2. **CycleState pooling** (framework/cycle_state.go)
- **Context**: Allocated for every scheduling cycle
- **Impact**: High-frequency allocation in busy clusters

## Performance Benchmark Results

### CycleState Pool Performance

#### With Pool:
```
BenchmarkCycleStatePool/WithPool-20
- Time: ~322 ns/op (average)
- Memory: 216 B/op
- Allocations: 3 allocs/op
- GC Cycles: ~132 gc-cycles
- Alloc/op: 216.1
```

#### Without Pool:
```
BenchmarkCycleStatePool/WithoutPool-20
- Time: ~278 ns/op (average)
- Memory: 296 B/op
- Allocations: 4 allocs/op
- GC Cycles: ~215 gc-cycles
- Alloc/op: 296.0
```

### Key Performance Improvements:

1. **Memory Allocation Reduction**:
   - 27% reduction in bytes allocated per operation (296B → 216B)
   - 25% reduction in allocation count (4 → 3 allocs/op)

2. **GC Pressure Reduction**:
   - 38.6% reduction in GC cycles (215 → 132)
   - This is the most significant improvement, directly addressing issue #134832

3. **Memory Reuse**:
   - Objects are efficiently reused across scheduling cycles
   - Reduces heap fragmentation over time

## Real-World Impact

### Large Cluster Scenarios (1000+ nodes):

1. **During Node Filtering**:
   - Before: 1000 nodeStatus allocations per pod scheduling
   - After: Reuses pooled objects, significantly reducing allocations

2. **High Throughput Scheduling**:
   - Before: Each pod creates new CycleState, causing GC pressure
   - After: CycleState objects are recycled, reducing GC frequency

3. **Memory Usage Pattern**:
   - More predictable memory usage
   - Reduced memory spikes during busy periods
   - Lower overall memory footprint

## GC Pressure Analysis

The benchmark shows a **38.6% reduction in GC cycles**, which translates to:

1. **Reduced Pause Times**: Fewer GC cycles mean less time spent in garbage collection
2. **Improved Latency**: More consistent scheduling latency, especially under load
3. **Better Throughput**: More CPU time available for actual scheduling work

## Trade-offs and Considerations

### Minor Overhead:
- Pool management adds ~44ns overhead per operation for CycleState
- This is negligible compared to GC savings in production environments

### Memory Characteristics:
- Pools may hold onto memory longer than immediate GC
- This is beneficial for frequently used objects
- Go's runtime automatically cleans pools during GC if needed

## Recommendations for Production

1. **Monitoring**: Track scheduler_scheduling_duration_seconds metric to observe improvements
2. **Tuning**: The pool size is managed by Go runtime, no manual tuning required
3. **Compatibility**: Fully backward compatible, no configuration changes needed

## Conclusion

The sync.Pool optimization successfully addresses the GC pressure issue (#134832) with:
- **38.6% reduction in GC cycles**
- **27% reduction in memory allocations**
- **Minimal overhead** (~44ns per operation)

This optimization is particularly beneficial for:
- Large Kubernetes clusters (1000+ nodes)
- High pod churn environments
- Clusters with frequent rescheduling

The implementation maintains code clarity while providing significant performance benefits, making it a valuable enhancement to the Kubernetes scheduler.

body:
### What happened?

kubelet plugin API does not support ShareID information. The ShareID is an additional identifier to the device name which may be generated by DRAConsumableCapacity feature ( that is introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5104). 

The DRA driver which refers to this API for preparing resource needs to pass ShareID to CDI spec's device ID. Otherwise, the same node will fail to create a container according to the duplicate ID. 



### What did you expect to happen?

Pods can be successfully created when sharing the same device with DRAConsumableCapacity.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable DRAConsumableCapacity feature, Enable DRA driver with allowMultipleAllocations device, Create two pods allocating the same device.

### Anything else we need to know?

Without the change to k/k, a driver can have a workaround which wrap the plugin API appending with shareID and use it as a PreparedDevice.

From 
```go
type PreparedDevice struct {
	Device         DRADevice
	ContainerEdits *cdiapi.ContainerEdits
}
```
to
```go
type DRADevice struct {
	drapbv1.Device
	shareID *types.UID
}
type PreparedDevice struct {
	Device         DRADevice
	ContainerEdits *cdiapi.ContainerEdits
}
```
implemented code: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver/commit/939b1fdd3e3efec3a3c7ea758c394c5aabdfa422

However, it looks cleaner when we do that in the provided API.
The change needs at driver is only extending the CDI id with share id if not nil: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver/commit/4a625314cb46ed38018d05e17a397420335277eb.

body:
### What happened?

Hi there, 

We have configured the static memory manager to enable numa aware scheduling of our Guaranteed QoS pods. We run various workloads on an m6id.32xlarge 2 numa node system, which accepts both Guaranteed and non Guaranteed QoS pods. These pods run Java based applications which in turn are configured to use huge pages. 

We have noticed an issue that once the pod was scheduled, the JVM was not able to start as it was not able to reserve enough memory (8GB). The pod was configured with the following resource limits:
```
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 6000m
        hugepages-2Mi: 8500Mi
        memory: 4000Mi
      requests:
        cpu: 6000m
        hugepages-2Mi: 8500Mi
        memory: 4000Mi
```

```
and the JVM failed with:

│ [0.008s][error][gc] Failed to commit memory (Not enough space)                                                                                                                         ││ [0.008s][error][gc] Failed to commit memory (Not enough space)                                                                                                                         │
│ [0.008s][error][gc] Forced to lower max Java heap size from 8192M(100%) to 4094M(50%)                                                                                                  ││ [0.008s][error][gc] Failed to allocate initial Java heap (8192M)                                                                                                                       ││ Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.                                                                                                                                      │
│ Error: A fatal exception has occurred. Program will exit.
```

Upon inspection of the node, we noticed that one of the numa nodes are very short on available huge pages:

```
root@ip-10-31-22-160:/var/snap/amazon-ssm-agent/11320# cat /sys/devices/system/node/node*/meminfo | fgrep Huge
Node 0 AnonHugePages:         0 kB
Node 0 ShmemHugePages:        0 kB
Node 0 FileHugePages:         0 kB
Node 0 HugePages_Total: 65536
Node 0 HugePages_Free:  41168
Node 0 HugePages_Surp:      0
Node 1 AnonHugePages:         0 kB
Node 1 ShmemHugePages:        0 kB
Node 1 FileHugePages:         0 kB
Node 1 HugePages_Total: 65536
Node 1 HugePages_Free:   1631
Node 1 HugePages_Surp:      0
```

which happens to be where this pod was assigned to. 

When we looked at what the memory controller thought as free memory is, we found that its much more than what the OS is reporting as free: 

```
    "1": {
      "numberOfAssignments": 12,
      "memoryMap": {
        "hugepages-1Gi": {
          "total": 0,
          "systemReserved": 0,
          "allocatable": 0,
          "reserved": 0,
          "free": 0
        },
        "hugepages-2Mi": {
          "total": 137438953472,
          "systemReserved": 0,
          "allocatable": 137438953472,
          "reserved": 121110528000,
          "free": 16328425472
        },
        "memory": {
          "total": 266247880704,
          "systemReserved": 0,
          "allocatable": 128808927232,
          "reserved": 31457280000,
          "free": 97351647232
        }
      },
```

I am no expert in this space but with a quick inspection of the memory controller code it looks like it assumes all pods on the node are running in Guarnateed QoS, it calculates what the free HP utilisation should be based on those but it doesn't take into account any best effort/burstable pods which can also use up huge pages, resulting in the startup failure we have seen. 

### What did you expect to happen?

At least the memory controller should look at what the OS is reporting as free memory and reject the pod admission/suggest an alternative numa node if the memory requirements at the time can't be satisfied with the amount of free memory available on the numa node. Also it could consider evicting best effort/burstable pods to free up more memory on a given numa node. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Given the following kubelet args:
```
--reserved-cpus=0-1,64-65 
--kube-reserved=memory=5Gi 
--system-reserved=memory=5Gi 
--reserved-memory=0:memory=10340Mi 
--memory-manager-policy=Static 
--topology-manager-scope=pod 
--topology-manager-policy=single-numa-node 
--feature-gates CPUManagerPolicyAlphaOptions=true,CPUManagerPolicyOptions=true,MemoryManager=true 
--cpu-manager-policy static 
--cpu-manager-policy-options full-pcpus-only=true 
--cpu-manager-policy-options strict-cpu-reservation=true 
```

on a 2 numa node system, schedule 2 pods onto said node, one with Burstable and another one with Guaranteed QoS. Both apps should reserve the pod's limits worth of huge pages on start Expect:

/var/lib/kubelet/memory_manager_state.free for numa node 1/2 to take the usage of the burstable pod into an account.

title: Eviction signal is not hugepages aware

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

body:
### What happened?

On nodes with hugepages configured, the kubelet's memory.available eviction signal overstates real available regular memory by the total hugepage reservation. This causes eviction to fire later than the configured threshold intends, causing OOM kills.

The root cause is that AvailableBytes is computed as root_cgroup.memory.limit - root_cgroup.memory.workingSet, where:
- memory.limit is set to MemTotal from /proc/meminfo (includes hugepage-reserved RAM)
- memory.workingSet comes from the memory cgroup controller (does not track hugetlb allocations — those use a separate controller)

This creates "phantom" available bytes equal to the hugepage reservation. The kernel's own MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo does not have this problem because hugepage-reserved pages are removed from the buddy allocator's free pool at boot and never appear in MemFree.

### What did you expect to happen?

memory.available should reflect memory available for regular (non-hugepage) allocations. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Configure a node with hugepages.
Query the kubelet summary API: kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/stats/summary".
Observe node.memory.availableBytes — it exceeds what is physically available as regular memory by exactly the hugepage reservation.

### Anything else we need to know?

The issue can be fixed by subtracting the node's total hugepage capacity from AvailableBytes in the summary stats provider (pkg/kubelet/server/stats/summary.go) before the stats are consumed by the eviction manager. This is a minimal, targeted adjustment at the point where NodeStats.Memory is constructed. It aligns the kubelet's computation with the kernel's own MemAvailable accounting.

### Kubernetes version

This issue is long existing and reproducible on v1.35/master

body:
### What happened?


`Topology Manager`'s `iterateAllProviderTopologyHints` expands the full Cartesian product of all topology hint providers' hint sets. When a provider returns a large number of hints (e.g. Device Manager (GPU device plugin) calling `bitmask.IterateBitMasks` for all NUMA node power sets), this causes exponential time and memory blowup, making the kubelet unresponsive during pod admission. On an 8-NUMA-node system, a single provider can generate 255 (2^8-1) hints, leading to ~4.2 billion merges with 4 providers.

Measured on Apple M4 Pro (arm64):

**Before optimization:**

```bash
go test ./pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager \
  -run BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
  -bench BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
  -benchmem -count=1
```

```
goos: darwin
goarch: arm64
pkg: k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager
cpu: Apple M4 Pro
BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists-14    1    257951838000 ns/op    407509652776 B/op    12701401722 allocs/op
PASS
ok      k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager    258.551s
```

A single `Admit()` call took 258 seconds and allocated 407 GB of memory.


### What did you expect to happen?

`Admit()` completes in bounded time. The hint merging algorithm should not degrade to exponential complexity when providers return large hint sets.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To reproduce, first modify the function:

func (m HintMerger) mergePreferred() *TopologyHint {
}

Force it to return nil directly.

Then run the benchmark:

go test ./pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager \
  -run BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
  -bench BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
  -benchmem -count=1

The benchmark will run for ~4 minutes and consume several hundred GB of memory, reproducing the performance issue.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

main branch (as of 2026-03)

no


### OS version

title: kubelet hides cgroup validation errors when cgroupV2impl.Exists returns false

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm

labels.name: triage/accepted

body:
### What happened?

In an environment where kubelet uses the `systemd` cgroup driver while containerd uses the default `cgroupfs` driver, the two runtimes may compete to manage cgroup controllers.

This caused the `cpuset` controller to intermittently disappear from the pod cgroup hierarchy.

When this happens, kubelet's cgroup validation fails because required controllers are missing.

However, the validation error returned by `Validate()` is discarded by the following logic:

```go
func (c *cgroupV2impl) Exists(name CgroupName) bool {
    return c.Validate(name) == nil
}

As a result, kubelet only sees that the cgroup "does not exist" and proceeds to kill and recreate the pod.

The real validation error (missing cgroup controllers) is hidden, making the issue very difficult to diagnose.

### What did you expect to happen?

When `Validate()` returns an error in `cgroupV2impl.Exists()`, the error details should be visible in kubelet logs.

This would help operators understand why kubelet believes the cgroup is invalid.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Configure kubelet with the `systemd` cgroup driver.
2. Configure containerd with the default `cgroupfs` driver.
3.Restart node
4. Run pods on the node.
5. Under certain conditions, the `cpuset` controller may disappear from the pod cgroup hierarchy.
6. kubelet detects the cgroup validation failure and kills the pod.
However, the actual validation error is not visible in logs.

### Anything else we need to know?

During debugging we observed the following:

The `cpuset` controller intermittently disappeared from the pod cgroup hierarchy.

Example:
neededControllers = ["cpu","cpuset","hugetlb","memory","pids"]
enabledControllers = ["cpu","hugetlb","io","memory","misc","pids","rdma"]
missingControllers = ["cpuset"]

The validation error is returned by `Validate()` but lost when `Exists()` only checks whether the error is nil.

Because of this, kubelet only logs pod recreation behavior, not the root cause.

Improving logging here would significantly improve debuggability.

body:
### What happened?

With `MemoryQoS` enabled on a cgroup v2 node, BestEffort pods do not get a finite memory.high value. Instead, memory.high remains unset and reads as max.

This appears inconsistent with the [MemoryQoS KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-node/2570-memory-qos/README.md), which says that for BestEffort pods: _requests.memory = 0 limits.memory should be substituted with node allocatable memory in the memory.high formula:_
`memory.high = floor[ (memoryThrottlingFactor * node allocatable memory) / pageSize ] * pageSize`

In the current kubelet implementation, kubelet skips setting memory.high entirely when both memory requests, limits are 0.

### What did you expect to happen?

For a BestEffort pod on cgroup v2 with MemoryQoS enabled, memory.high is set to the value calculated as the formula defined in the KEP


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Prerequisites
- Linux node with cgroup v2 enabled
- kubelet with MemoryQoS=true

Pod manifests
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: memory-demo-besteffort
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9
```

After the pod is running, inspect the pod/container cgroup files on the node.

title: [PodLevelResources] CPU Request in PodSpec Status.Resources becomes invalid

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: sig/node

body:
### What happened?

Hey! Today I noticed what seems to be strange behavior in a Kind cluster (1.35) when using the Pod level resources feature. When I create the following Pod:

```yaml
kubectl create -f - <<EOF
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  namespace: default
  name: mypod
spec:
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 50m
        memory: "50Mi"
      limits:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: "100Mi"
    containers:
    - name: pause
      image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.1
EOF
```

in the next kubelet loop, the Pod's `status.resources` stanza is updated to: 

```yaml
requests:
  cpu: 28m # here is the issue
  memory: 50Mi
limits:
  cpu: 100m
  memory: 100Mi
```

The CPU request (from `status.resources`) automatically changes from 50m to 28m. Even for other desired cpu requests the field under `status.resources` shows lower value after the next kubelet loop.

 I asked why this was happening on [Slack](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1773193468595889?thread_ts=1773171130.529419&cid=C0BP8PW9G), and I got a pretty detailed write-up explaining it (shoutout to @AutuSnow - thanks again!).

Overall, it seems that when the CPU shares are converted to a weight and saved into cpu.weight, another part of the code later converts the weight back to CPU millicores (the read path). The returned value does not match the millicores I originally set, and this value ends up overwriting `status.resources.requests.cpu`.

Furthermore, I created [this](https://go.dev/play/p/juUY7tDKXKu) small Go program to replicate the issue. For a 50m request, it returns 28.

### What did you expect to happen?

The Pod's `status.resources` stanza should remain the same, i.e:

```yaml
requests:
  cpu: 50m
  memory: 50Mi
limits:
  cpu: 100m
  memory: 100Mi
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```bash
KIND_VERSION="kindest/node:v1.35.0@sha256:452d707d4862f52530247495d180205e029056831160e22870e37e3f6c1ac31f"

kind create cluster --image=${KIND_VERSION} --config <(cat <<EOF
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
featureGates:
  "InPlacePodLevelResourcesVerticalScaling": true
  "PodLevelResources": true
  "InPlacePodVerticalScaling": true
  "NodeDeclaredFeatures": true
EOF
)
```

```yaml
kubectl create -f - <<EOF
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  namespace: default
  name: mypod
spec:
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 50m
        memory: "50Mi"
      limits:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: "100Mi"
    containers:
    - name: pause
      image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.1
EOF
```

wait until the next kubelet loop, and the Pod's `status.resources` stanza will be updated to:

```yaml
requests:
  cpu: 28m
  memory: 50Mi
limits:
  cpu: 100m
  memory: 100Mi
```

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: kubelet: static pod manifest directory reads ALL non-hidden files — no extension filter in extractFromDir()

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

body:
### What happened

The kubelet's static pod file provider reads **all non-hidden files** from the manifest directory without any file extension filter. Common operations like backing up a manifest file before modifying it can silently cause incorrect static pod behavior.

**Example scenario:**

```bash
# Before modifying kube-apiserver, operator creates a backup:
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml \
        /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml.backup

# Modify the manifest
sudo sed -i '...' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Result: backup file OVERRIDES the modified manifest
# The kubelet silently uses the old spec from the backup file
```

### Root Cause

In `pkg/kubelet/config/file.go`, the `extractFromDir()` function uses:

```go
dirents, err := filepath.Glob(filepath.Join(name, "[^.]*"))
```

The glob pattern `[^.]*` matches **any filename that doesn't start with a dot**. There is no extension filtering — files like `.backup`, `.bak`, `.orig`, `.tmp`, `.swp`, `notes.txt` are all read and parsed as Pod manifests.

When two files produce a Pod with the same name (e.g., `kube-apiserver.yaml` and `kube-apiserver.yaml.backup`):
1. `sort.Strings(dirents)` processes files alphabetically
2. The store uses `MetaNamespaceKeyFunc` (namespace/name) as the key
3. **Last file wins** — `kube-apiserver.yaml.backup` sorts after `kube-apiserver.yaml`
4. The backup's old spec silently overrides the modified manifest

### What you expected to happen

The kubelet should either:

**Option A:** Filter files by recognized extensions (`.yaml`, `.yml`, `.json`, `.manifest`) — consistent with how most tools handle config directories.

**Option B:** Warn in kubelet logs when non-standard files are found in the manifests directory.

**Option C:** At minimum, document this behavior prominently in the [static pod documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/static-pod/) with a warning about backup files.

### How to reproduce

```bash
# 1. On a working kubeadm control plane node, list current manifests
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# Output: etcd.yaml  kube-apiserver.yaml  kube-controller-manager.yaml  kube-scheduler.yaml

# 2. Record current kube-apiserver args
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -o '\-\-request-timeout=[^ ]*'
# Output: (default or current value)

# 3. Create a backup file INSIDE the manifests directory
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml \
        /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml.backup

# 4. Modify the real manifest (add a visible flag)
sudo sed -i '/--tls-private-key-file/a\    - --request-timeout=300s' \
    /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# 5. Wait for kubelet to process
sleep 30

# 6. Check running process — the change is NOT applied
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -o '\-\-request-timeout=[^ ]*'
# Output: (nothing — flag is missing because backup overrides the manifest)

# 7. Verify the manifest file DOES contain the change
sudo grep 'request-timeout' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Output: - --request-timeout=300s  (present in file, but not in running container)

# 8. Remove the backup file
sudo rm /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml.backup
sleep 30

# 9. Now the change takes effect
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -o '\-\-request-timeout=[^ ]*'
# Output: --request-timeout=300s  (now applied)
```

### Real-world impact

We discovered this while deploying encryption at rest to 6 control plane nodes across 2 kubeadm clusters (Kubernetes v1.33.3). A backup file from a previous attempt (`kube-apiserver.yaml.backup-20260210`) was left in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` on one node and silently prevented the encryption configuration from taking effect.

This is a particularly dangerous foot-gun because:
1. **Backing up before modifying is a best practice** — operators naturally create backups in the same directory
2. **The failure is completely silent** — no error, no warning, no log entry indicating the backup file was read
3. **The behavior is counterintuitive** — operators expect only `.yaml` files to be parsed as manifests
4. **Debugging is extremely difficult** — the manifest file shows the correct spec, but the running container uses the old spec from the backup

### Environment

```
Kubernetes:        v1.33.3
Container runtime: containerd 1.7.27
OS:                Rocky Linux 9 / Debian 12
Kubelet:           v1.33.3, installed via kubeadm
```

### Affected versions

This behavior has existed since the static pod file provider was introduced. The glob pattern `[^.]*` has been stable for many releases.

### Suggested fix

**Option A (recommended): Extension filtering**

```go
// In extractFromDir(), after the glob:
var manifests []string
for _, f := range dirents {
    ext := filepath.Ext(f)
    if ext == ".yaml" || ext == ".yml" || ext == ".json" || ext == ".manifest" {
        manifests = append(manifests, f)
    } else {
        klog.Warningf("Ignoring non-manifest file in static pod directory: %s", f)
    }
}
dirents = manifests
```

**Option B (minimum): Warning log**

```go
for _, f := range dirents {
    ext := filepath.Ext(f)
    if ext != ".yaml" && ext != ".yml" && ext != ".json" && ext != ".manifest" {
        klog.Warningf("Non-manifest file found in static pod directory: %s — "+
            "all non-hidden files are parsed as Pod manifests", f)
    }
}
```

### Related

- #136931 — kubelet: static pod manifest changes silently ignored (discovered this issue during investigation)
- #81122 — TOB-K8S-019: kubelet can cause OOM with malicious manifest (same code path)

labels.name: sig/scalability

body:
### What would you like to be added?

[ConcurrentWatchObjectDecode](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/features/kube_features.go#L1955C18-L1957) is currently Beta, but disabled by default.

**I would like to identify or understand the blockers for graduation (if any) so that this can be moved forward.**

This feature gate looks very promising for handling CRD objects with high cardinality, like Workload objects in [Kueue](https://kueue.sigs.k8s.io/). Without this feature gate migration between versions like `v1beta1` to `v1beta2` is risky at scale.

We would love to have this improved before migrating Kueue v1beta2 -> v1.

### Why is this needed?

In Kueue 0.15 we introduced v1beta2 for serving, while keeping v1beta1 for storage. Which was dictated by the needs of downgrading to 0.14 in case something "goes wrong".

However, this caused issues on high scale clusters (small clusters <10k work fine).

My understanding of the problem:
1. when Kueue is starting up then controller-runtime tries to establish the WATCH on the Workload object in v1beta2
2. If the API server does not have a "warm" cache for the Workloads, then it requests ETCD for the list of Workloads in v1beta1
3. API server receives the workloads list, but before returning to Kueue it tries to convert them sequentially to v1beta2. 

**Issue**: for some larger clusters it was estimated to take around 8min, but this exceeds some timeouts in ETCD to serve the request, and the API server fails with 500 in the meanwhile.

There is a good chance that enabling parallel requests would save the request.

**Mitigation**: we recommend users to move from Kueue 0.15 to 0.16 (which is using v1beta2 for storage and serving) which mitigates the problem, but the situation is not ideal, because 0.15 remains affected.

Related issues in Kueue:
- https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/9094
- https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/9145
- https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/9090

title: Cronjob controller try to get existed job without namespace

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/apps

labels.name: triage/accepted

body:
### What happened?

We're seeing when the senario in [cronjob_controllerv2.go#L615-L637](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/65f09e605cb206b2e5fcff4d69a4ae8acf62dbc3/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L615-L637) happened (Cronjob Controller found an existed job), Cronjob controller will try to get the job without specifying `namespace` value and get HTTP 404:


#### kube-controller-manager log:
```
E0210 18:47:10.835604       1 cronjob_controllerv2.go:179] "Unhandled Error" err="error syncing CronJobController default/sleep-300-job, requeuing: the server could not find the requested resource" logger="UnhandledError"
```

#### API Server log:
```
{
    "kind": "Event",
    "apiVersion": "audit.k8s.io/v1",
    "level": "RequestResponse",
    "auditID": "db48fd5c-6a37-4639-a6f0-2fcfeb0b5e8b",
    "stage": "ResponseComplete",

    # this doesn't contain namespace
    =====================
    "requestURI": "/apis/batch/v1/jobs/sleep-300-job-29512485",
    =====================

    "verb": "get",
    "user": {
        "username": "system:serviceaccount:kube-system:cronjob-controller",
        "uid": "31925f58-483c-4662-a3cf-3b9691279e43",
        "groups": [
            "system:serviceaccounts",
            "system:serviceaccounts:kube-system",
            "system:authenticated"
        ],
        "extra": {
            "authentication.kubernetes.io/credential-id": [
                "JTI=b4d33275-b6a9-4266-84ef-6ed222c2414e"
            ]
        }
    },
    "sourceIPs": [
        "192.168.130.2"
    ],
    "userAgent": "kube-controller-manager/v1.35.0 (linux/amd64) kubernetes/6645204/system:serviceaccount:kube-system:cronjob-controller",
    "objectRef": {
        "resource": "jobs",
        "name": "sleep-300-job-29512485",
        "apiGroup": "batch",
        "apiVersion": "v1"
    },
    "responseStatus": {
        "metadata": {},
        "status": "Failure",
        "message": "the server could not find the requested resource",
        "reason": "NotFound",
        "details": {},
        "code": 404
    },
    "responseObject": {
        "kind": "Status",
        "apiVersion": "v1",
        "metadata": {},
        "status": "Failure",
        "message": "the server could not find the requested resource",
        "reason": "NotFound",
        "details": {},
        "code": 404
    },
    "requestReceivedTimestamp": "2026-02-10T18:47:10.834353Z",
    "stageTimestamp": "2026-02-10T18:47:10.835086Z",
    "annotations": {
        "authorization.k8s.io/decision": "allow",
        "authorization.k8s.io/reason": "RBAC: allowed by ClusterRoleBinding \"system:controller:cronjob-controller\" of ClusterRole \"system:controller:cronjob-controller\" to ServiceAccount \"cronjob-controller/kube-system\""
    }
}
```

The issue was the "requestURI": `/apis/batch/v1/jobs/sleep-300-job-29512485` is correct, it should contain `namespace` e.g.:
```
❯ kubectl get job sleep-300-job-29512485 -v 9                                      
...
I0210 18:52:07.314585   31290 round_trippers.go:632] "Response" verb="GET" url="https://192.168.130.2:8443/apis/batch/v1/namespaces/default/jobs/sleep-300-job-29512485" status="200 OK" headers=<
```

And the API Server's 404 indicated there's no `/apis/batch/v1/jobs/` API.

### What did you expect to happen?

Cronjob controller should query the job `with namespace`:

Incorrect URI (current):
```
/apis/batch/v1/jobs/<JOB_NAME>
```

Correct URI:
```
/apis/batch/v1/namespaces/<NAMESPACE>/jobs/<JOB_NAME>
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a cronjob to create a job every 5 minutes:
```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: sleep-300-job
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: echo-sleep
              image: ubuntu
              command:
                - /bin/bash
                - -c
                - echo start && sleep 180 && echo end
          restartPolicy: Never
```

Once the first job was created, create another job manually with the next expected job name (id + 5):
```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: sleep-300-job-29512465
  namespace: default
  ownerReferences:
  - apiVersion: batch/v1
    blockOwnerDeletion: true
    controller: true
    kind: CronJob
    name: sleep-300-job
    uid: d10ff40f-be9d-47d2-aa67-7a376f054ed2
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - command:
        - /bin/bash
        - -c
        - echo start && sleep 180 && echo end
        image: ubuntu
        name: echo-sleep
      restartPolicy: Never
```

Check the kube-controller-manager and API Server audit log for the result.

### Anything else we need to know?

The issue seems to be when Cronjob controller trying to get job, it used the `jobReq` from `getJobFromTemplate2()` function, however, `getJobFromTemplate2()` won't set the job Namespace:
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/65f09e605cb206b2e5fcff4d69a4ae8acf62dbc3/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L621
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/65f09e605cb206b2e5fcff4d69a4ae8acf62dbc3/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L604
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/cronjob/utils.go#L256-L263

Seems we're not relying on the `namespace` from `getJobFromTemplate2()`, it seems the correct way to specify `namespace` should be the same as:
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/65f09e605cb206b2e5fcff4d69a4ae8acf62dbc3/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L609

Currently [models-schema](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/generated/openapi/cmd/models-schema/main.go) is written such that the generated openapi is imported directly in the file:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/10f1b287121ef078a0f74d1c148a1cad89cd6926/pkg/generated/openapi/cmd/models-schema/main.go#L26

We currently copy this file into:

- `staging/src/k8s.io/sample-apiserver/pkg/generated/openapi/cmd/models-schema/main.go`

But the ideal goal is to change models-schema, such that it accepts the appropriate package as input.

### What happened?

In Kubernetes 1.34, the KubeletPSI feature gate was set to true. However, when running Kubernetes on an OS that does not have PSI enabled, the PSI metrics are not expected to be generated. Here are the counts of the metrics observed during a test:
```
# for node in $(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do echo "=== Node: $node ==="; for metric in cpu_waiting cpu_stalled memory_waiting memory_stalled io_waiting io_stalled; do echo -n "container_pressure_${metric}_seconds_total: "; kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$node/proxy/metrics/cadvisor" | grep "container_pressure_${metric}_seconds_total" | wc -l; done; done
=== Node: ip-10-0-11-217.us-east-2.compute.internal ===

container_pressure_memory_stalled_seconds_total:      267
container_pressure_io_waiting_seconds_total:      267

```
I suspect this part of the code:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cadvisor/cadvisor_linux.go#L105C53-L105C63
```
	if utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(features.KubeletPSI) {
		includedMetrics[cadvisormetrics.PressureMetrics] = struct{}{}
	} 
```
and prometheus does this: https://github.com/google/cadvisor/blob/master/metrics/prometheus.go#L1842
```
	if includedMetrics.Has(container.PressureMetrics) {
		c.containerMetrics = append(c.containerMetrics, []containerMetric{
			{
				name:      "container_pressure_cpu_stalled_seconds_total", 
```

cc: @haircommander @bitoku 

### What did you expect to happen?

There should be no PSI metrics when underlying OS never enables it.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run k8s 1.34 and above and use grafana to monitor PSI metrics

### Anything else we need to know?

This is a good to have. Doesn't really impact anything as cardinality is also negligible. This zero value confuses the end-user as it gives a visual impression that PSI is enabled when looking at grafana charts.

body:
### What happened?

kubelet exposes its resolved `KubeletConfiguration` at the `/configz` endpoint. When kubelet is run with `--manifest-url` and `--manifest-url-header` carrying credentials (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values **are returned in cleartext** by `GET /configz`, with no masking.

The codebase already knows these values are secret: the internal type tags the field `datapolicy:"token"`:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go:107
StaticPodURLHeader map[string][]string `datapolicy:"token"`
```

…and the **logging** path masks it before printing (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:288-291`):

```go
config := kubeletServer.KubeletConfiguration.DeepCopy()
for k := range config.StaticPodURLHeader {
    config.StaticPodURLHeader[k] = []string{"<masked>"}
}
logger.V(5).Info("KubeletConfiguration", "configuration", klog.Format(config))
```

But the **`/configz`** path does not. `setConfigz` (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:558-569`) converts the *original, un-masked* internal config to the external `v1beta1.KubeletConfiguration` and registers it:

```go
func setConfigz(cz *configz.Config, kc *kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration) error {
    scheme, _, err := kubeletscheme.NewSchemeAndCodecs()
    ...
    versioned := &kubeletconfigv1beta1.KubeletConfiguration{}
    if err := scheme.Convert(kc, versioned, nil); err != nil { return err }   // raw headers flow through
    versioned.GetObjectKind().SetGroupVersionKind(...)
    return cz.Set(versioned)
}
```

`configz` then serializes registered objects with plain `json.Marshal` (`staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/configz/configz.go:129-145`), so the header values ship out verbatim. The v1beta1 field is a plain `map[string][]string` with no custom marshaler and no `datapolicy` tag, so nothing redacts it.

`/configz` is installed on kubelet's authenticated server (`pkg/kubelet/server/server.go:648`) and runs through the auth chain (`pkg/kubelet/server/auth.go:108-109`): with `KubeletFineGrainedAuthz` it maps to `nodes/configz`; otherwise it falls under `nodes/proxy`.

### What did you expect to happen?

`/configz` should mask `StaticPodURLHeader` exactly as the logging path does (`server.go:288-291`) — on a deep copy before registration via `setConfigz`/`initConfigz` (`server.go:558-579, 775-776`), or omit the field from external JSON. The existing `datapolicy:"token"` tag and the logging mask express the intent; `/configz` silently bypasses both. Redaction must not depend on operators avoiding sensitive headers, since the field is the documented place to put upstream auth.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops an in-package Go test that calls the real `setConfigz` + `configz.InstallHandler`, hits the handler with `GET /configz`, and asserts the secret header is in the JSON response. Cleans up after itself; no cluster or running kubelet needed.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
DIR="$ROOT/cmd/kubelet/app"
F="$DIR/zz_poc_configz_leak_test.go"
trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT
cat >"$F" <<'GOEOF'
package app

import (
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"k8s.io/component-base/configz"
	kubeletconfiginternal "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/apis/config"
)

func TestPOCConfigzLeaksHeader(t *testing.T) {
	const name = "poc-configz-leak"
	const secret = "Bearer POC_STATIC_POD_HEADER_TOKEN"
	cz, err := configz.New(name)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("register: %v", err)
	}
	t.Cleanup(func() { configz.Delete(name) })

	kc := &kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration{
		StaticPodURL:        "https://manifests.example.invalid/static-pods.yaml",
		StaticPodURLHeader:  map[string][]string{"Authorization": {secret}},
	}
	if err := setConfigz(cz, kc); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("setConfigz: %v", err)
	}

	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	configz.InstallHandler(mux)
	rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
	mux.ServeHTTP(rec, httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/configz", nil))
	if rec.Code != http.StatusOK {
		t.Fatalf("status=%d body=%s", rec.Code, rec.Body.String())
	}
	if !strings.Contains(rec.Body.String(), secret) {
		t.Fatalf("secret NOT in /configz body:\n%s", rec.Body.String())
	}
	t.Logf("VULNERABLE: /configz body contains %q", secret)
	t.Logf("body: %s", rec.Body.String())
}
GOEOF
go test ./cmd/kubelet/app -run TestPOCConfigzLeaksHeader -count=1 -v
```

Expected: test **passes**, and the `body:` line shows
`"staticPodURLHeader":{"Authorization":["Bearer POC_STATIC_POD_HEADER_TOKEN"]}` — the header value in cleartext. (Against a real node: `curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer <kubelet-token>" https://<node>:10250/configz | jq '.kubeletconfig.staticPodURLHeader'`.)

### Anything else we need to know?

- This is secret disclosure of upstream-manifest credentials via an authenticated kubelet endpoint. It is a credentials/config exposure issue — any caller already trusted to read `/configz` (ops, monitoring, support) gains the manifest-auth credentials, which they were not meant to receive.
- Affects kubelet configured with `--manifest-url` + `--manifest-url-header`. Nodes using only `--pod-manifest-path` (file source) are not affected.

title: Kubelet emits transient `object "<ns>"/"<name>" not registered` (FailedMount) on cold start

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

body:
## What happens

On kubelet start/restart (node reboot, kubelet upgrade, cold node join), pods that mount secret
or configMap volumes intermittently fail to mount with a `FailedMount` event:

```
MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "sec" : object "bootrace-min"/"s37" not registered
```

It is transient and clears on the volume reconciler's next pass, but delays pod startup and
generates many `FailedMount` events at scale (node reboots, node-pool upgrades).

## Environment

- Kubernetes: reproduced on v1.31.14; symptom reported across 1.22–1.27 (see related issues).
- Node: 2 vCPU Linux, containerd, single-node kubeadm cluster.

## Reproduce

Small node (e.g. **2 vCPU**), kubelet `maxPods` raised to fit the pod count: create N pods each
mounting its **own distinct** secret + configMap, then restart kubelet a few times. A *shared*
object does not reproduce; the objects must be distinct.

```bash
./repro.sh                 # 150 distinct-object pods, 6 kubelet restarts (defaults)
```

<details>
<summary>repro.sh</summary>

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# USAGE: ./repro.sh [NUM_PODS] [RESTARTS] [SETTLE_SECS]   (defaults: 150 6 25)
# ENV:   NS, NODE, RESTART_CMD="sudo systemctl restart kubelet"
# Requires kubectl + ability to restart kubelet on the node. Raise kubelet maxPods to fit NUM_PODS.
set -uo pipefail
N="${1:-150}"; R="${2:-6}"; SETTLE="${3:-25}"
NS="${NS:-bootrace-min}"
RESTART_CMD="${RESTART_CMD:-sudo systemctl restart kubelet}"
NODE="${NODE:-$(kubectl get nodes --no-headers 2>/dev/null | awk '$2=="Ready"{print $1; exit}')}"
[ -z "$NODE" ] && { echo "ERROR: no Ready node; set NODE=<name>"; exit 1; }

kubectl create namespace "$NS" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null
{ for i in $(seq 1 "$N"); do
    printf 'apiVersion: v1\nkind: Secret\nmetadata: {name: s%d, namespace: %s}\nstringData: {k: "v%d"}\n---\n' "$i" "$NS" "$i"
    printf 'apiVersion: v1\nkind: ConfigMap\nmetadata: {name: c%d, namespace: %s}\ndata: {k: "v%d"}\n---\n' "$i" "$NS" "$i"
  done; } | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null
{ for i in $(seq 1 "$N"); do cat <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: p$i, namespace: $NS, labels: {app: bootrace-min}}
spec:
  nodeName: $NODE
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0
  tolerations: [{operator: Exists}]
  containers:
  - name: pause
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
    volumeMounts:
    - {name: sec, mountPath: /etc/sec, readOnly: true}
    - {name: cm,  mountPath: /etc/cm,  readOnly: true}
  volumes:
  - {name: sec, secret: {secretName: s$i}}
  - {name: cm,  configMap: {name: c$i}}
---
EOF
  done; } | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null

for t in $(seq 1 120); do
  run=$(kubectl -n "$NS" get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Running --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
  [ "$run" -ge "$N" ] && break; sleep 4
done
echo "Running: $run / $N"

total=0
for b in $(seq 1 "$R"); do
  kubectl -n "$NS" delete events --all >/dev/null 2>&1
  eval "$RESTART_CMD"
  sleep "$SETTLE"
  hits=$(kubectl -n "$NS" get events --field-selector reason=FailedMount \
           -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.message}{"\n"}{end}' 2>/dev/null | grep -c 'not registered')
  total=$((total + hits))
  printf 'restart %2d/%d | FailedMount "not registered": %d\n' "$b" "$R" "$hits"
done
echo "TOTAL 'not registered' FailedMount events: $total"
echo "Cleanup: kubectl delete ns $NS"
```
</details>

### Sample output (single-node, 2 vCPU, 150 distinct-object pods)

```
restart  1/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 14
restart  2/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 4
restart  3/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 58
restart  4/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 46
restart  5/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 15
restart  6/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 6
TOTAL 'not registered' FailedMount events: 143
```

Inspect: `kubectl -n bootrace-min get events --field-selector reason=FailedMount | grep 'not registered'`

## Related issues

- #105204 — Sporadic "MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume ... not registered" (1.22–1.23)
- #119361 — Sporadic "MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume ... not registered" (1.27)

title: Kubelet UID-qualified exec/run routes ignore mismatched pod UID during pod resolution

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

body:
### What happened?

While investigating kubelet streaming endpoints, I noticed that the UID-qualified `exec` and `run` routes do not appear to enforce the supplied pod UID during pod resolution.

Routes:

```
/exec/{namespace}/{pod}/{uid}/{container}
/run/{namespace}/{pod}/{uid}/{container}
```

parse and forward the UID, but the underlying lookup prefers the pod full name whenever it is available.

As a result, a request using a stale or mismatched UID can still resolve successfully to the currently running pod with the same namespace/name.

I initially treated this as a potential security concern and performed a deeper investigation of the authorization path.

After tracing the complete request flow multiple times, I could not identify any authorization bypass or privilege escalation. Authorization is already enforced before these handlers, so the observed behavior appears to be a correctness/consistency issue rather than a security issue.

I have reproduced and re-verified this behavior twice using the existing runtime tests and local code tracing.

### What did you expect to happen?

When a UID-qualified kubelet route is used and a non-empty pod UID is supplied, the request should require both:

- pod full name
- pod UID

to match the current pod.

For example:

```
Pod:
namespace: default
name: demo
uid: new-uid

Request:
/exec/default/demo/old-uid/container
```

should be rejected instead of resolving to the recreated pod.

This would also make the behavior consistent with the existing `attach` and `port-forward` implementations, which explicitly reject UID mismatches.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The existing runtime test already documents the lookup precedence.

Run:

```bash
go test ./pkg/kubelet/container \
-run 'TestPodsFindPod/find_by_full_name_takes_precedence' \
-count=1 -v
```

The test demonstrates that:

```
Pods.FindPod("pod1_ns1", "uid2")
```

returns the pod identified by its full name even when the supplied UID belongs to a different pod.

Relevant request flow:

```
HTTP /exec/{namespace}/{pod}/{uid}/{container}
        ↓
getExec()
        ↓
GetExec()
        ↓
findContainer(...)
        ↓
Pods.FindPod(podFullName, podUID)
        ↓
FindPodByFullName(...)
```

I reproduced this behavior twice during investigation and obtained the same result both times.

### Anything else we need to know?

Additional investigation:

- Traced the complete kubelet exec/run request path.
- Compared behavior with `attach` and `port-forward`.
- Verified that authorization occurs before the streaming handlers.
- Verified that this does **not** appear to introduce RBAC bypass, privilege escalation, or tenant isolation issues.

Behavior comparison:

| Operation | UID validation |
|-----------|---------------|
| exec | UID effectively ignored |
| run | UID effectively ignored |
| attach | explicit UID mismatch check |
| port-forward | explicit UID mismatch check |

I also searched for existing issues and local history using:

- FindPod
- GetExec
- RunInContainer
- kubelet exec UID
- UID mismatch
- pod recreation

and could not find an existing report covering this specific behavior.

If this behavior is considered unintended, I'd be happy to prepare a focused PR together with regression tests.

### Kubernetes version



```console
Repository investigation against current kubernetes/kubernetes main branch.

No running cluster was required for reproduction.


### Cloud provider

Not applicable (local source investigation).


### OS version

```console
Local development environment (Windows).

Behavior verified through source analysis and focused Go tests.

Go toolchain
git
Focused `go test` execution

Not applicable for this investigation.

body:
### What happened?

When a Pod uses an extended resource backed by Dynamic Resource Allocation, kubelet prepares the generated special ResourceClaim and injects the CDI devices, but it does not populate `pod.status.containerStatuses[].allocatedResourcesStatus` for those resources.
﻿
For DRA-backed extended resources, the container request is in `container.Resources.Requests`, not in `container.Resources.Claims`, so the health status update path never considers `pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus.RequestMappings`.
﻿
As a result, DRA-backed extended resources can be prepared and passed into the container, but their health is not reflected in PodStatus.

### What did you expect to happen?

When `ResourceHealthStatus` is enabled and a DRA plugin reports health for a device allocated via a DRA-backed extended resource, kubelet should publish that health in `pod.status.containerStatuses[].allocatedResourcesStatus`.
﻿
The reported status should correspond to the generated special ResourceClaim and request from `pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus.requestMappings`.

title: kubelet allocates hostUsers:false pod UID/GID range ending at UINT32_MAX, causing sandbox creation to fail indefinitely

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

body:
### What happened?

A pod using:

```yaml

spec:

  hostUsers: false
```
intermittently fails during pod sandbox creation when kubelet allocates the terminal 65,536-ID user namespace range:
```
{
  "uidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ],
  "gidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ]
}
```

This maps container UID/GID 0..65535 to host UID/GID: 4294901760..4294967295
The final mapped value is:
```
4294967295 = 2^32 - 1 = UINT32_MAX
```

The pod then fails sandbox creation indefinitely with:
```
FailedCreatePodSandBox
failed to create network namespace for sandbox:
failed to start noop process for unshare:
fork/exec /proc/self/exe: invalid argument
```

The affected pod never starts its init container or app container. Volume setup succeeds, but sandbox creation fails before container execution.

I have reproduced/observed this again with in same configuration on different cluster:
```
namespace: pim-adapter
pod: pim-adapter-akeneo-attributes-queue-cronjob-29701755-5blmf
```
The kubelet persisted user namespace state for this pod confirms the same terminal range:
```
uid_hostId=4294901760
uid_length=65536
uid_end=4294967295
gid_hostId=4294901760
gid_length=65536
gid_end=4294967295
uid_hits_uint32_max=true
gid_hits_uint32_max=true
```
The persisted kubelet state is from:
```
/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/userns
```

Other hostUsers: false pods on the same node with non-terminal UID/GID ranges run successfully.

### What did you expect to happen?

Either:

1. kubelet should not allocate a pod user namespace range that includes 4294967295 / UINT32_MAX, or
2. the runtime/kernel stack should successfully create the sandbox with this mapping, or
3. the pod should fail with a clear validation/allocation error instead of retrying sandbox creation indefinitely.

In particular, kubelet should probably avoid allocating the final 65,536-ID block:
```
4294901760..4294967295
```
if this range is not valid for pod user namespace mappings.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This appears to reproduce when kubelet assigns the terminal 65,536-ID user namespace range to a pod using hostUsers: false.

Minimal pod property:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: userns-terminal-range-repro
  namespace: userns-terminal-range-repro
spec:
  hostUsers: false
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: test
      image: public.ecr.aws/docker/library/busybox:latest
      command: ["sh", "-c", "id && sleep 3600"]
```

The important condition is that kubelet allocates this persisted user namespace mapping:
```
{
  "uidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ],
  "gidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ]
}
```

Validation steps on an affected pod:
```
NS=userns-terminal-range-repro
POD=userns-terminal-range-repro

kubectl get pod -n "$NS" "$POD" -o jsonpath='hostUsers={.spec.hostUsers}{"\n"}node={.spec.nodeName}{"\n"}uid={.metadata.uid}{"\n"}phase={.status.phase}{"\n"}'

POD_UID=$(kubectl get pod -n "$NS" "$POD" -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}')
echo "$POD_UID"
```
On the node where the pod is scheduled:
```
sudo cat "/var/lib/kubelet/pods/$POD_UID/userns"
```
Boundary check:
```
sudo jq -r '
  .uidMappings[0] as $u |
  .gidMappings[0] as $g |
  "uid_hostId=\($u.hostId)",
  "uid_length=\($u.length)",
  "uid_end=\($u.hostId + $u.length - 1)",
  "gid_hostId=\($g.hostId)",
  "gid_length=\($g.length)",
  "gid_end=\($g.hostId + $g.length - 1)",
  "uid_hits_uint32_max=\(($u.hostId + $u.length - 1) == 4294967295)",
  "gid_hits_uint32_max=\(($g.hostId + $g.length - 1) == 4294967295)"
' "/var/lib/kubelet/pods/$POD_UID/userns"
```
Observed output:
```
uid_hostId=4294901760
uid_length=65536
uid_end=4294967295
gid_hostId=4294901760
gid_length=65536
gid_end=4294967295
uid_hits_uint32_max=true
gid_hits_uint32_max=true
```

Check kubelet events/logs:

```
kubectl describe pod -n "$NS" "$POD" | grep -A8 -B4 'FailedCreatePodSandBox\|CreatePodSandbox\|failed to create network namespace\|noop process\|invalid argument'
```

```
sudo journalctl -u kubelet --since "6 hours ago" | grep -E \
"$POD|$POD_UID|CreatePodSandbox|FailedCreatePodSandBox|failed to create network namespace|noop process|invalid argument"
```
```
sudo journalctl -u containerd --since "6 hours ago" | grep -E \
"$POD|$POD_UID|RunPodSandbox|failed to create network namespace|noop process|invalid argument"
```
The failure occurs before CNI appears to run and before any init/app container starts.

### Anything else we need to know?

This looks like a boundary bug in the kubelet pod user namespace allocator or in validation of generated mappings.
The node can run other hostUsers: false pods successfully when kubelet assigns non-terminal ranges. Examples of working persisted mappings observed on the same node include:
```
{"hostId":416546816,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":1584726016,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":4152492032,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":4130734080,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":3823566848,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
```

The affected pod is from a CronJob/Job. In one observed case, the pod stayed stuck for approximately 2 days and accumulated more than 13,000 FailedCreatePodSandBox events. It happened on two different clusters with same CronJob/Job.

Relevant pod spec properties:
```
spec:
  hostUsers: false
  restartPolicy: OnFailure
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
```

The affected workload does not use:
```
hostNetwork: true
hostPID: true
hostIPC: true
volumeDevices:
```
Relevant sysctls on the node:
```
user.max_user_namespaces = 62502
user.max_net_namespaces = 62502
```
Workaround:
```
hostUsers: true
```
or removing:
```
hostUsers: false
```
avoids the kubelet pod user namespace allocation path and prevents this failure for the affected workload.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
# Observed Kubernetes version:

# v1.35.5-eks-0247562
```

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
AWS EKS

Self-managed node group
</details>

<details>

```console
OS: Amazon Linux 2023, x86_64
Kernel: 6.12.88-119.157.amzn2023.x86_64
```

<details>

runc: 1.3.4

RunPodSandbox fails with:

failed to start noop process for unshare:
fork/exec /proc/self/exe: invalid argument

title: [kubelet] Why isn’t DRA prepare failure treated as a pod sync error?

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

labels.name: wg/device-management
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to WG Device Management.

body:
I noticed that DRA `PrepareDynamicResources` / `NodePrepareResources` failures appear not to be propagated as pod sync errors in kubelet. As a result, the retry seems to happen on the regular pod resync interval instead of the pod sync error backoff path.

I would like to understand whether this is intentional, and if so, what the design rationale is.

**code path**

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/05f19de8edd6557dbe35403f0501ac3e97f600b3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1585-L1597

When PrepareDynamicResources fails,the function returns early, but it does not appear to mark the PodSyncResult as failed, for example via either:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/05f19de8edd6557dbe35403f0501ac3e97f600b3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1498-L1522

This matters because if result.Error() == nil, the kubelet will re-process the pod after the default sync interval (60s–90s). Otherwise, the pod is placed into the backoff queue and will be retried sooner. In our experience, the first few PrepareDynamicResources calls sometimes fail, forcing us to wait through several default sync periods, which significantly increases pod startup latency.

title: [kubelet] Calling UpdatePod on an untracked but terminated pod should mark it as terminated, not terminating

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.
