labels.name: wg/device-management
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to WG Device Management.

body:
### What happened?

**TL;DR:** the device-taint eviction controller (`pkg/controller/devicetainteviction`) only discovers which
claims a pod is using by reading `pod.Spec.ResourceClaims`. A pod that got its device through the newer
Extended Resource Backed by DRA path (KEP-5004, `DRAExtendedResource`) has its claim reference in
`pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus` instead — a field this controller never looks at. Both
`DRADeviceTaints` and `DRAExtendedResource` are Beta and **default-on since v1.36**, so this affects any
cluster running a stock 1.36+ apiserver/controller-manager with a DRA driver installed — no unusual
configuration required.

Live-reproduced on a `kind` cluster (full steps and output below): two pods, each holding one device from the
same driver, then a single `NoExecute` `DeviceTaintRule` applied against that driver:

| Pod | Requests its device via | Claim reference lives in | Result after `NoExecute` taint |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pod-to-be-evicted` | `ResourceClaimTemplate` | `pod.spec.resourceClaims` | Evicted within ~10s (correct) |
| `pod0` | plain `resources.limits` extended-resource request | `pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus` | **Still `Running`, untouched** — the bug |

The `DeviceTaintRule`'s own status confirms only one pod was ever considered:
`"1 pod needs to be evicted in 1 namespace"` → `"1 pod evicted since starting the controller"`.

**Scope note, to save a maintainer the round-trip:** this is specifically about the *post-allocation eviction*
path. Allocation-time taint enforcement (a **new** pod being blocked from a `NoSchedule`/`NoExecute`-tainted
device it doesn't tolerate) is unaffected and works correctly for both request styles. The bug is
narrowly in the separate, already-allocated-pod eviction controller.

**Couple of affected use cases**
- GPU health-triggered auto-remediation. A node-health/GPU-health controller (e.g. something reacting to Xid/ECC errors, similar in spirit to NVIDIA GPU Operator's health checks) detects a failing GPU and applies a NoExecute DeviceTaintRule to force workloads off it before quarantining or repairing the device. Any pod still using the classic nvidia.com/gpu: 1-style request — which is the majority of existing GPU workloads, since KEP-5004's entire purpose is letting them keep working unmodified under DRA — is never evicted, and keeps running on a known-bad GPU instead of being cleanly rescheduled. Worst case: silently corrupted training/inference output rather than a clean failure.
- Targeted single-device maintenance on a multi-GPU node. An admin wants to service or replace one GPU on a node without draining the whole node (disruptive to the node's other GPUs/workloads), so they taint just that device NoExecute instead of cordoning the node. Any pod holding that device via an extended-resource request keeps running through the "drain," so the device can't actually be safely pulled for maintenance without an admin separately hunting down and manually killing those pods — defeating the point of device-level (vs. node-level) maintenance tooling.
- Clusters mid-migration from device plugins to DRA. KEP-5004 exists specifically so clusters can adopt DRA drivers without immediately rewriting every pod spec — meaning a long transitional period where legacy extended-resource-requesting Deployments/Jobs and newer ResourceClaim-based workloads coexist on the same devices. During that period, any device-taint-based enforcement (decommissioning a device, isolating a suspect one) only works for the already-migrated minority of workloads, silently failing for everyone else — undermining the mechanism cluster-wide for as long as the migration takes, which for large fleets could be months.

### What did you expect to happen?

A `NoExecute` device taint should evict every pod actually consuming the tainted device, independent of which
API surface the pod used to request it. An admin tainting a failing/draining GPU for maintenance has no way to
know (and shouldn't need to know) whether a given consumer pod requested it via a `ResourceClaim` or via a
classic `resources.limits` extended-resource request — both end up running on the same physical device via
the same DRA driver and the same underlying `ResourceClaim` object. Today only one of the two is actually
evicted.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reproducible deterministically on a `kind` cluster with no real GPU hardware, using
[kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver) (a maintained,
public example DRA driver that simulates GPUs). All manifests below are the driver's own unmodified example
manifests (`demo/examples/device-taints-tolerations/device-taint-pod-noexecute/` and
`demo/examples/extended-resource-request/`), just applied side by side.

**Prerequisites:** Docker, `kind` v0.20+, `helm` v3.7+, `kubectl`.

```bash
# 1. Create a kind cluster with the required feature gates and API version.
#    (DynamicResourceAllocation and DRAAdminAccess are already GA/locked-on by v1.36 and are
#    omitted; DRADeviceTaints/DRAExtendedResource are Beta+default-on in 1.36 but included
#    explicitly for clarity; DRADeviceTaintRules is Beta+default-OFF in 1.36 and must be set.)
cat > kind-config.yaml <<'EOF'
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
featureGates:
  DRADeviceTaints: true
  DRAExtendedResource: true
  DRADeviceTaintRules: true
runtimeConfig:
  resource.k8s.io/v1beta2: "true"
containerdConfigPatches:
- |-
  [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri"]
    enable_cdi = true
nodes:
- role: control-plane
- role: worker
EOF
kind create cluster --name dra-repro --image kindest/node:v1.36.1 --config kind-config.yaml --wait 3m

# 2. Install the example DRA driver (8 simulated GPUs, no real hardware, default values).
git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.4.0 https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver.git
helm upgrade -i --create-namespace --namespace dra-example-driver dra-example-driver \
  dra-example-driver/deployments/helm/dra-example-driver
kubectl -n dra-example-driver wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app.kubernetes.io/component=kubeletplugin --timeout=90s

# 3. Control pod: requests a GPU via a ResourceClaimTemplate (pod.spec.resourceClaims).
kubectl apply -f dra-example-driver/demo/examples/device-taints-tolerations/device-taint-pod-noexecute/1-basic-resourceclaimtemplate.yaml
kubectl apply -f dra-example-driver/demo/examples/device-taints-tolerations/device-taint-pod-noexecute/2-pod-to-be-evicted.yaml
kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate wait --for=condition=Ready pod/pod-to-be-evicted --timeout=60s

# 4. Treatment pod: requests a GPU via the classic extended-resource field. The scheduler
#    satisfies it via DRA and records the claim in pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus instead
#    of pod.spec.resourceClaims (confirmed with the jsonpath check below).
kubectl create namespace extended-resource-request
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  namespace: extended-resource-request
  name: pod0
spec:
  containers:
  - name: ctr0
    image: ubuntu:22.04
    command: ["bash", "-c"]
    args: ["export; trap 'exit 0' TERM; sleep 9999 & wait"]
    resources:
      limits:
        deviceclass.resource.kubernetes.io/gpu.example.com: 1
EOF
kubectl -n extended-resource-request wait --for=condition=Ready pod/pod0 --timeout=60s
kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='{.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='spec.resourceClaims={.spec.resourceClaims}{"\n"}'

# 5. Taint the whole driver's devices NoExecute — both pods' devices are in scope.
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1beta2
kind: DeviceTaintRule
metadata:
  name: example
spec:
  deviceSelector:
    driver: gpu.example.com
  taint:
    key: gpu.example.com/unhealthy
    value: "true"
    effect: NoExecute
EOF

# 6. Observe.
sleep 15
kubectl get devicetaintrule example -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate get pod pod-to-be-evicted   # expect: NotFound (evicted+deleted)
kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o wide           # expect: still Running
```

**Actual output, captured just now:**

```
$ kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='{.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus}'
{"requestMappings":[{"containerName":"ctr0","requestName":"container-0-request-0",
"resourceName":"deviceclass.resource.kubernetes.io/gpu.example.com"}],
"resourceClaimName":"pod0-extended-resources-v77pc"}

$ kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='spec.resourceClaims={.spec.resourceClaims}'
spec.resourceClaims=

$ kubectl apply -f device-taint-rule.yaml
devicetaintrule.resource.k8s.io/example created

$ kubectl get devicetaintrule example -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'
# immediately after creation:
[{"lastTransitionTime":"2026-08-10T07:34:42Z","message":"1 pod needs to be evicted in 1 namespace.",
"observedGeneration":1,"reason":"PodsPendingEviction","status":"True","type":"EvictionInProgress"}]

# ~10s later:
[{"lastTransitionTime":"2026-08-10T07:34:52Z","message":"1 pod evicted since starting the controller.",
"observedGeneration":1,"reason":"Completed","status":"False","type":"EvictionInProgress"}]

$ kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate get pod pod-to-be-evicted
Error from server (NotFound): pods "pod-to-be-evicted" not found

$ kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -3
28s   Normal   DeviceTaintManagerEviction   pod/pod-to-be-evicted   Marking for deletion
28s   Normal   Killing                      pod/pod-to-be-evicted   Stopping container ctr0

$ kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o wide
NAME   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   NODE
pod0   1/1     Running   0          69s   dra-repro-worker

$ kubectl -n extended-resource-request get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
# Scheduled / Pulled / Created / Started only — zero eviction-related events, ever.

$ kubectl get resourceclaim -A
NAMESPACE                   NAME                            STATE
extended-resource-request   pod0-extended-resources-v77pc   allocated,reserved
# (pod-to-be-evicted's generated claim is gone — cleaned up along with the deleted pod)
```

Only one of the two pods using tainted devices from the same driver was ever evicted. This reproduces every
time; there is no timing dependency.


### Anything else we need to know?

### Where this happens in the code

Traced against tag `v1.36.3` and confirmed unchanged at master HEAD `94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f`;
live-reproduced above on `kindest/node:v1.36.1` (closest publicly available `kind` node image to `v1.36.3` at
time of testing — same code, confirmed by reading).

**1. The eviction controller enumerates claims from exactly one field.**

`pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device_taint_eviction.go`, `podEvictionTime`
([current source](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device_taint_eviction.go)),
is the *only* place this controller determines which claims a pod uses:

```go
func (tc *Controller) podEvictionTime(pod *v1.Pod) *evictionAndReason {
    if pod.Spec.NodeName == "" {
        return nil
    }
    var eviction *evictionAndReason
    for i := range pod.Spec.ResourceClaims {
        claimName, mustCheckOwner, err := resourceclaim.Name(pod, &pod.Spec.ResourceClaims[i])
        ...
    }
    return eviction
}
```

Grepping the full 1691-line file for `ExtendedResource` returns zero matches, on both the tag and master.

**2. The sibling `resourceclaim` controller already had to solve this exact problem.**

`pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller.go`, `enqueuePod`:

```go
// Check if pod has any resource claims to process.
// Extended resource claims are stored in pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus,
// not in pod.Spec.ResourceClaims, so we need to check both locations.
hasResourceClaims := len(pod.Spec.ResourceClaims) > 0
hasExtendedResourceClaims := pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus != nil
...
// Without this, extended resource claims would never be cleaned up when
// pods complete, causing device resources to remain allocated indefinitely.
if hasExtendedResourceClaims {
    claimName := pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus.ResourceClaimName
    ...
}
```

The device-taint eviction controller never received the equivalent treatment.

**3. Both contributing feature gates are Beta and default-on as of this release**
(`pkg/features/kube_features.go`):

```go
DRADeviceTaints: {
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.33"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Alpha},
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.36"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta},
},
DRAExtendedResource: {
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.34"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Alpha},
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.36"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta},
},
```

So this isn't an edge-case opt-in combination — it's the default state of a stock 1.36+ cluster with any DRA
driver and `DeviceTaintRule` usage.

**4. No test coverage exercises this interaction.** `test/integration/dra/device_taints.go` and
`pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device_taint_eviction_test.go` (2926 lines) both have zero hits for
`ExtendedResource`.

**5. Allocation-time taint enforcement is unaffected (see "Scope note" above)** —
`staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go`,
`taintPreventsAllocation`, is reached identically for extended-resource and explicit-claim requests, since
`extendeddynamicresources.go` builds an in-memory claim for the extended-resource path before `Filter` runs.
Included here to preempt the natural "does this mean extended-resource claims ignore taints entirely?"
question — they don't; only post-allocation `NoExecute` eviction is blind.

### Suggested fix direction

Mirror the `resourceclaim` controller's dual-location check into `podEvictionTime` — i.e. also resolve
`pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus.ResourceClaimName` when present, using the same claim lookup/ownership
logic already used for `pod.Spec.ResourceClaims`. This looks like a contained, well-scoped fix; happy to
attempt a PR once a maintainer confirms this is the intended approach (rather than, say, deprecating the
implicit extended-resource path's exemption from eviction on purpose — which seems unlikely given point 2
above, but worth confirming).

Live reproduction (above): `kindest/node:v1.36.1`, vanilla upstream via `kind`. Code paths involved confirmed
identical at tag `v1.36.3` (latest stable at time of this report) and master HEAD
`94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f` by direct source comparison.

title: CPU manager exclusive allocation metrics drifts

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

body:
### What happened?

The static policy in CPU Manager maintains the `CPUManagerExclusiveCPUsAllocationCount` and `CPUManagerSharedPoolSizeMilliCores` gauges by applying per-event deltas, and updates `CPUManagerAllocationPerNUMA` only for the NUMA nodes present in the current allocation. This drifts away from the actual allocation state in several scenarios:

1. Init container CPU reuse is double counted (container scope). When an app container reuses the CPUs of a non-restartable init container, `allocateCPUs` returns the full allocation including the reused CPUs, which stay assigned to the init container too. The allocation path adds the full size of both allocations, counting the reused CPUs twice. The release path correctly subtracts the sibling-adjusted sets, so after the pod is removed the gauge keeps a permanent positive residue equal to the number of reused CPUs. The shared pool gauge has the mirrored problem: the allocation delta subtracts CPUs which have never been taken out of the default CPU set.

2. Fresh allocations and restarts disagree. During a kubelet run the exclusive allocation gauge accumulates deltas with the duplicates described above, while after a restart `initializeMetrics` recomputes it as the union of the checkpointed assignments (no duplicates). The same node state can therefore report two different values before and after a kubelet restart.

3. Pod-level (pod scope) allocations can leak on partial failure. `allocatePodForAdd` updates the metrics and stores the pod-level CPU set, but a failure while partitioning the bubble among the containers (takeByTopology) returns an error without releasing anything: the bubble stays out of the default CPU set, the gauge stays inflated, and nothing can ever clean it up, because `RemoveContainer` returns early for a pod with no container assignments and `removeStaleState` only iterates over container assignments.

4. Pod-level releases can drift the gauge below the real value. `RemoveContainer` subtracts the whole pod-level CPU set when the last container assignment is removed, but after a kubelet restart `initializeMetrics` only accounts the union of the remaining container assignments, which is smaller than the bubble if some containers have already been removed before the restart. Releasing a pod which died while the kubelet was down then over-subtracts the difference.

5. `initializeMetrics` ignores the pod-level CPU sets. After a restart the gauge is seeded only from the container assignments, so the part of a pod-level bubble not covered by any container assignment is not counted, even though it is excluded from the default CPU set.

6. `CPUManagerAllocationPerNUMA` never drops back to zero. The update loop only writes the NUMA nodes present in the current allocation, so once the last exclusively allocated CPU of a node is released, the node keeps reporting its last non-zero value forever. The metric is also fed only with the container assignments, making a pod-level bubble invisible at allocation time, because the container assignments are stored later than the pod-level CPU set.

### What did you expect to happen?

Metrics always present valid current state of exclusive CPUs allocations.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The scenarios are described in issue.
They are also fully covered by unit tests.
Running unit tests without changes to the code will reveal the problems.

body:
### What happened?

When using CPU Manager with `static` policy and both of the following options enabled:
- `distribute-cpus-across-cores=true` (distributes CPUs evenly across NUMA nodes)
- `align-by-socket=true` (prefers NUMA nodes within the same socket)

CPUs may be allocated across multiple sockets instead of staying within a single socket. This violates the socket affinity guarantee that `align-by-socket=true` is supposed to provide.

For example:
- Socket 0: NUMA 0-3 (126 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 0: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 1: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 2: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 3: (30 CPUs available)

- Socket 1: NUMA 4-7 (126 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 4: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 5: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 6: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 7: (30 CPUs available)

Result: CPUs are allocated from NUMA 0,1,3,6 across both sockets.

### What did you expect to happen?

With `align-by-socket=true`, the 120 CPUs should be allocated entirely from Socket 0 (NUMA 0,1,2,3) (which has 126 available CPUs).


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Configure kubelet with:
--cpu-manager-policy=static
--cpu-manager-policy-options="distribute-cpus-across-cores=true,align-by-socket=true"

Set the available CPUs as above example, and create a pod with 120 CPUs.

title: DRA: a negative device consumesCounters value is accepted and over-commits a shared counter set

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

labels.name: wg/device-management
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to WG Device Management.

body:
### What happened?

A device's `consumesCounters` value may be negative. ResourceSlice validation accepts it, and the
structured allocator subtracts it from the counter set, so a negative consumption inflates the set's
available capacity and admits an allocation that over-commits the set.

`validateDeviceCounter` (`pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation.go`) returns nil for any parsed
quantity, with no sign check:

```go
func validateDeviceCounter(counter resource.Counter, fldPath *field.Path) field.ErrorList {
	// Any parsed quantity is valid.
	return nil
}
```

The allocator subtracts each allocated device's consumption from the set (`existingCounter.Value.Sub(c.Value)`
in `checkAvailableCounters`); a negative `c.Value` raises the available value instead of lowering it, so a
device consuming a large positive amount then fits against the inflated available.

The sibling consumable-capacity path already guards exactly this class. `CmpRequestOverCapacity`
(`.../structured/internal/experimental/consumable_capacity.go`) rejects a negative resolved capacity with
`errNegativeCapacity` (`if consumedCapacity.Sign() < 0`), and its comment notes a negative "can reach the
allocator from a stored ResourceSlice ... which admission does not re-check." The counter path has no such
guard — that asymmetry is the bug.

### What did you expect to happen?

Either ResourceSlice validation should reject a negative counter value (mirroring the capacity path's
stance that a negative is invalid input), or the allocator should fail closed on a negative consumption
rather than subtracting it into a larger available.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Publish a CounterSet of 8Gi, a phantom device consuming `-100Gi`, and a real device consuming `100Gi`:

```yaml
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceSlice
metadata: {name: nc-counters}
spec:
  driver: nc.example
  pool: {name: nc-pool, generation: 1, resourceSliceCount: 2}
  allNodes: true
  sharedCounters:
  - name: mem
    counters: {memory: {value: 8Gi}}
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceSlice
metadata: {name: nc-devices}
spec:
  driver: nc.example
  pool: {name: nc-pool, generation: 1, resourceSliceCount: 2}
  allNodes: true
  devices:
  - name: phantom
    consumesCounters: [{counterSet: mem, counters: {memory: {value: -100Gi}}}]   # negative, accepted
  - name: real
    consumesCounters: [{counterSet: mem, counters: {memory: {value: 100Gi}}}]
```

The slice is accepted (`resourceslice ... created`; the `-100Gi` is stored). A ResourceClaim requesting
`count: 2` from `nc-pool` allocates **both** devices (Pod `Scheduled`), because the aggregate consumption is
`-100Gi + 100Gi = 0 ≤ 8Gi` — even though the `real` device alone consumes `100Gi` from an `8Gi` set. Without
the phantom device, a `count: 1` claim for the `100Gi` device is refused (`100Gi > 8Gi`). Observed on a real
v1.36.2 cluster.

### Anything else we need to know?

The straightforward fix is a sign check on counter values in `validateDeviceCounter` (fail closed on a
negative), matching `errNegativeCapacity` in the consumable-capacity path; an allocator-side guard on a
negative consumption is a defensive complement. Threat model: a negative reaches the allocator from a DRA
driver's ResourceSlice, or from a slice stored before stricter validation — the same model the capacity
path's guard already accepts.

`DRAPartitionableDevices` (shared counters) is Beta and enabled by default since v1.36.

/kind bug
/sig node
/wg device-management

title: Memory Manager pod-scope restore compares container blocks with the pod request

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

body:
### What happened?

With pod-scope Topology Manager, after a kubelet restart, Memory Manager finds a restored container allocation and calls `regenerateHints` with that container's blocks and the whole Pod memory request.

For a multi-container Pod, those values differ, so `regenerateHints` returns no hint instead of restoring the Pod's previous NUMA hint. This can cause an existing Pod to fail admission under `restricted` or `single-numa-node`.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod-scope hint restoration should use the restored pod-level allocation and preserve the previous NUMA hint.

### How can we reproduce it?

Use a Guaranteed Pod with pod-level memory resources and two containers, allocate it with static Memory Manager, restart from the checkpoint, then call `GetPodTopologyHints`. The current code returns no regenerated hint because it compares one container's blocks with the Pod request.

title: CPU Manager AllocatePod re-allocates restored pod CPUs after kubelet restart

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

body:
### What happened?

With pod-scope Topology Manager and `PodLevelResourceManagers` enabled, static CPU Manager is not idempotent across kubelet restart.

After restart, pod-level CPU assignments are restored from the checkpoint. Existing Pods then go through admission again, and Topology Manager calls `AllocatePod(AddOperation)`. In `allocatePodForAdd`, the pod-scope path does not check whether a complete pod-level allocation was already restored. It allocates again from the default CPU set and overwrites the restored pod assignment.

This causes two deterministic failure modes:

- If the remaining default CPU set cannot satisfy the same request again, kubelet rejects an existing Pod after restart.
- If enough CPUs remain, CPU Manager assigns a second CPU set and overwrites the restored pod assignment, while the original CPUs stay removed from the default set, effectively leaking exclusive CPUs.

Examples with 1 reserved CPU and a Pod requesting 2 CPUs:

```text
4 CPUs:
restored pod cpuset:     1-2
restored default cpuset: 0,3
readmission error:       not enough cpus available to satisfy request: requested=2, available=1

6 CPUs:
pod cpuset:              1-2 -> 3-4
default cpuset:          0,3-5 -> 0,5
readmission error:       <nil>
```

The current path is here: [`allocatePodForAdd`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5f91251764f106ba06c25a612d646ff612392e35/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/policy_static.go#L397-L440). It calls `allocateCPUs` and `SetPodCPUSet` without consulting the restored pod allocation.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod-level CPU Manager allocation should be idempotent across kubelet restart.

If a complete pod-level allocation was restored from checkpoint, post-restart admission should preserve the restored pod CPU set, container assignments, and default CPU set. It should not allocate a second CPU set or reject the existing Pod because of its own restored reservation.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A deterministic unit test can extend `TestCPUManagerRestoreState`:

1. Enable `PodLevelResources` and `PodLevelResourceManagers`.
2. Configure static CPU Manager with pod-scope Topology Manager, 1 reserved CPU, and either 4 or 6 single-threaded CPUs.
3. Create a Guaranteed Pod with pod-level request/limit of 2 CPUs and 1 container.
4. Start CPU Manager and call `AllocatePod` once.
5. Add the container so the pod/container assignments are checkpointed.
6. Recreate CPU Manager with the same checkpoint dir to simulate kubelet restart.
7. Verify the pod CPU set, container assignment, and default CPU set were restored.
8. Call `AllocatePod(AddOperation)` again.
9. Verify the restored state is unchanged.

Observed results:

- On 4 CPUs: `not enough cpus available to satisfy request: requested=2, available=1`
- On 6 CPUs: the restored pod CPU set changes from `1-2` to `3-4`, and the default CPU set changes from `0,3-5` to `0,5`

### Anything else we need to know?

This is the CPU Manager counterpart of #140906.

This is separate from #129078 / #129079. Those concern the older container-level `full-pcpus-only` SMT validation path. This reproducer does not enable `full-pcpus-only`; it exercises the pod-level allocation path introduced by #134768.

`PodLevelResourceManagers` was promoted to Beta and enabled by default for Kubernetes 1.37 in #140573.

### Kubernetes version

`master` commit `5f91251764f106ba06c25a612d646ff612392e35`

Body

Hitting this on kubelet-gce-e2e-swap-ubuntu-serial - pretty sure this is the same flake as 
#136546/
#138527, just came back.

Testgrid: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-kubelet#kubelet-gce-e2e-swap-ubuntu-serial

A few sub-tests under Ensure Credential Pulled Images ... [FeatureGate:KubeletEnsureSecretPulledImages] are failing, all through the same shared BeforeEach helper (tempRemoveImagePulledRecord in test/e2e_node/util_kubeletconfig.go):

util_kubeletconfig.go:133] Unexpected error: the file with the pulled record for the image ID never appeared:
<context.deadlineExceededError>: context deadline exceeded
Quick rundown of what that helper does: it polls every 1s for up to 5s waiting for kubelet to write an ImagePulledRecord at /var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled/sha256-<hash>, then moves it aside so a later step can check kubelet's behavior when the record's missing. If nothing shows up in 5s, it just fails.

#138527 got closed by 
#138642, but looking at that PR, it only added debug logging to this wait loop - didn't touch the 5s timeout or actually figure out why the record's sometimes missing. So this was never really fixed, just made easier to see happening.

And that's actually how I found something new - the extra logging from 
#138642 caught this in a recent run (2026-07-25, ~12:40 UTC) that wasn't visible back when 
#138527 was filed:

util_kubeletconfig.go:116] failed to stat file ".../pulled/sha256-c0a25c4ccec43320c35febdf68a46e03b3f9323eada881535d78d91aa9962741": ... no such file or directory
util_kubeletconfig.go:128] contents of "/var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled": map[
  .../pulled/sha256-fbeb66043fabeed6f125049e44aef32e0b8f9e657a240b5a2091b292bab530f2:
    {"kind":"ImagePulledRecord", ..., "lastUpdatedTime":"2026-07-25T14:26:20Z", ...}
]
So at the moment it fails, the pulled/ directory isn't actually empty - there's a record in there, just for a different image, written ~23 minutes earlier by (presumably) an earlier sub-test in the same run. The record this specific check is waiting for just never shows up in the 5s window.

That makes me think this isn't pure slowness - more likely kubelet just doesn't write a new ImagePulledRecord at all when the image's already cached from an earlier sub-test in the same run, and the poll is timing out waiting for something that was never coming. Would be good to get sig-node's take on whether that's expected - if so, the fix is probably on the test's assumptions, not the timeout.

Checked the last 10 Testgrid columns for this job (~07-24 to 07-26) - failed 3/10 times, 6/20 over a longer window, so it's a real recurring thing, not a one-off. One specific run if useful: prow job 2080994746846679040 (2026-07-25, ~12:40-14:49 UTC), 2 sub-tests failed with this exact error.

title: Memory Manager AllocatePod re-applies restored pod allocations after kubelet restart

labels.name: kind/bug

body:
### What happened?

With pod-scope Topology Manager and `PodLevelResourceManagers` enabled, the static Memory Manager restores pod-level assignments from its checkpoint when kubelet starts. The existing Pods then go through admission again, and Topology Manager calls `AllocatePod` with `AddOperation`.
﻿
`AllocatePod` does not check whether the Pod already has a restored allocation. It calculates the request again and applies it to a machine state which already includes that Pod's reservation.
﻿
Depending on the remaining capacity, this can:
﻿
- reject an existing Pod during post-restart admission because its own allocation is no longer considered free;
- extend or change the previously selected NUMA affinity;
- reserve the same memory a second time, reducing `Free` and increasing `Reserved` and `NumberOfAssignments` again.
﻿
The Pod and container block entries are overwritten, but the additional machine-state accounting remains and is checkpointed.
﻿
﻿

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod-level Memory Manager allocation should be idempotent across kubelet restart.

When a complete allocation for the Pod has been restored from the checkpoint, post-restart admission should preserve the existing pod allocation, container assignments, NUMA affinity, and machine state. It should not consume capacity again or reject the Pod because of its own reservation.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A deterministic unit test can extend `TestMemoryManagerRestoreState`:

1. Enable `PodLevelResources` and `PodLevelResourceManagers`.
2. Configure static Memory Manager with pod-scope Topology Manager.
3. Create a Guaranteed Pod with pod-level memory requests and limits and one container.
4. Start Memory Manager and call `AllocatePod` once.
5. Save the pod blocks, container blocks, and machine state.
6. Recreate Memory Manager with the same checkpoint directory to simulate kubelet restart.
7. Start the new manager and verify that the state was restored.
8. Call `AllocatePod` again with `AddOperation`, as post-restart admission does.
9. Verify that the call succeeds and all restored state remains unchanged.

With the current implementation, step 8 either accounts the Pod again or fails when there is not enough unreserved capacity to satisfy the same request a second time.

Using a single-container Pod keeps this reproducer separate from pod-scope hint regeneration behavior for multi-container Pods.

### What happened?

As mentioned in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137050#discussion_r3615804000 by @jpbetz, we should fix a race where a different controller can race the main controller to do illegal state initialization during the first sync.

> I think the first sync can bypass the anti-spoofing machinery. This gate only applies when oldStatus != nil, and none of the time checks below require state == Active, so the initializing write can pre-populate startTime and completionTime on Inactive entries too. With completionTime already set, the heartbeat deadline check is skipped on each later flip, so a single actor with status write can walk the whole responder chain to Completed in seconds without any responder acting, then set the final conditions.



### What did you expect to happen?

Should the first sync require non-Active entries to be name and priority only instead of setting the whole struct? A test would be valuable.

Fast controller tries to race the evictionrequest-controller

TestVolumeAttachLimitExceededCleanup

### Since when has it been flaking?

Since commit `954ac21c6c8b2bc77666373d5c4f5b68603a8e50` (2025-09-03), which introduced the test in PR #133357.

### Testgrid link

https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140657/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master/2079304403352817664

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The test creates 500 pods and expects all of them to reach `PodFailed` state within a 30-second timeout. On Windows CI this is insufficient due to:

1. **Mutex contention** — `FakeRuntime.GetPod` and `FakeRuntime.GetPodStatus` are called via `fakeCache.GetNewerThan` for each pod, each acquiring the `FakeRuntime` mutex. With 500 pods this results in ~1000 serialized lock acquisitions.
2. **Status manager contention** — `SetPodStatus` is called twice per pod (once for `PodPending`, once for `PodFailed`), each acquiring the `statusManager` mutex (~1000 acquisitions).
3. **Disk I/O** — `makePodDataDirs` performs 3 `os.MkdirAll` calls per pod (1500 total mkdir operations), which is slower on Windows CI.

The 30s timeout is exceeded before all 500 pods can be processed through the `podWorkerLoop` → `SyncPod` → `rejectPod` → `SetPodStatus(PodFailed)` pipeline.

title: CPUManager distribute-cpus-across-cores relies on CPU numbering order instead of topology

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

body:
## What happened?

The `distribute-cpus-across-cores` CPU manager policy option (KEP-4176, alpha since v1.31) does not correctly spread CPUs across physical cores on systems where sibling thread CPU IDs are contiguous (e.g., core 0 = CPUs 0,1; core 1 = CPUs 2,3).

The spread algorithm in `sortAvailableCPUsSpread()` sorts CPUs numerically within each socket:

```go
func (a *cpuAccumulator) sortAvailableCPUsSpread() []int {
    var result []int
    for _, socket := range a.sortAvailableSockets() {
        cpus := a.details.CPUsInSockets(socket).UnsortedList()
        sort.Ints(cpus)
        result = append(result, cpus...)
    }
    return result
}
```

This assumes that numerically-sorted CPU IDs naturally interleave across physical cores. That assumption holds on systems where the BIOS/firmware enumerates all first threads before second threads (e.g., core 0 thread 0 = CPU 0, core 1 thread 0 = CPU 1, ..., core 0 thread 1 = CPU 8, core 1 thread 1 = CPU 9), but fails when sibling threads have contiguous IDs (e.g., core 0 = CPUs 0,1; core 1 = CPUs 2,3).

With contiguous siblings, `sortAvailableCPUsSpread()` produces the same CPU order as `sortAvailableCPUsPacked()`, and the spreading has no effect — both allocate sibling threads together.

## How to reproduce

On any system with contiguous sibling CPU IDs (common in VMs/QEMU, and some bare-metal configurations):

```
$ lscpu | grep Thread
Thread(s) per core:  2

$ cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/topology/thread_siblings_list
0-1
$ cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu2/topology/thread_siblings_list
2-3
```

Enable the CPU manager with `distribute-cpus-across-cores`:
```
--cpu-manager-policy=static
--feature-gates=CPUManagerPolicyAlphaOptions=true
--cpu-manager-policy-options=distribute-cpus-across-cores=true
```

Create a Guaranteed pod requesting 4 CPUs. The allocated cpuset will be contiguous (e.g., `1-4`), hitting only 2-3 physical cores instead of spreading across 4 separate cores.

The kubelet logs confirm the option is active:
```
"created with configuration" options={"DistributeCPUsAcrossCores":true,...} cpuGroupSize=2
```

## Expected behavior

Requesting 4 CPUs on a system with 8 cores × 2 threads should allocate 1 thread from each of 4 different physical cores (e.g., CPUs 0, 2, 4, 6), regardless of whether sibling IDs are contiguous or non-contiguous.

## Root cause

The algorithm uses `sort.Ints()` on CPU IDs as a proxy for topology-aware spreading. It should instead use the core topology information already available in `cpuAccumulator.details` to explicitly round-robin across cores:

```go
func (a *cpuAccumulator) sortAvailableCPUsSpread() []int {
    var result []int
    coresCPUs := make(map[int][]int)
    maxThreads := 0
    for _, core := range a.sortAvailableCores() {
        cpus := a.details.CPUsInCores(core).SortedList()
        coresCPUs[core] = cpus
        if len(cpus) > maxThreads {
            maxThreads = len(cpus)
        }
    }
    // Round-robin: pick thread 0 from all cores, then thread 1, etc.
    for t := 0; t < maxThreads; t++ {
        for _, core := range a.sortAvailableCores() {
            if t < len(coresCPUs[core]) {
                result = append(result, coresCPUs[core][t])
            }
        }
    }
    return result
}
```

This approach works regardless of CPU numbering because it explicitly iterates cores and picks one thread per core before doubling up.

## Additional context

- The KEP-4176 example topology assumes non-contiguous siblings (CPUs 0 and 6 as siblings), which is common on many server BIOSes that enumerate all thread-0 CPUs before thread-1 CPUs, but is not guaranteed.
- QEMU/KVM always produces contiguous sibling IDs (thread ID in lowest APIC bits), making this feature untestable in virtual environments.
- The Linux kernel topology documentation notes the "alternative enumeration" (non-contiguous siblings) depends on BIOS MADT ordering and explicitly states "we do not trust BIOSes to enumerate packages in a consistent way."
- Tested on Kubernetes v1.35.6 with `DistributeCPUsAcrossCores: true` confirmed in kubelet logs.

body:
/sig node
/kind feature

### Problem: KEP-2570 `memory.min` Introduces Node Stability Risks & Bin-Packing Regressions

The current Memory QoS (KEP-2570) implementation brings vital cgroups v2 protections, but enforcing `memory.min` as the default, one-size-fits-all solution for Guaranteed pods creates severe operational risks for mixed workloads.

Mapping memory requests to the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) is structurally necessary to satisfy node-local agents (NRI plugins, telemetry daemons) without injecting synchronous HTTP calls to the `kube-apiserver` during pod startup. However, the chosen cgroup primitive (`memory.min` for Guaranteed) fundamentally breaks node elasticity.

#### 1. The `memory.min` Bin-Packing Problem

The KEP assumes all Guaranteed pods require strict, kernel-level memory locking. In reality, users often set requests equal to limits solely to prevent Kubelet eviction (e.g., for ML inference or periodic batch jobs). These workloads might allocate a large heap but sit idle for long periods. When mapped to `memory.min`, the kernel is legally forbidden from reclaiming their idle page cache. Locking unused memory behind a hard wall destroys the node's ability to safely maximize resource utilization and share capacity with neighboring pods.

#### 2. Behavioral Shifts and Starvation

Because the Kubelet applies this logic universally by default via `TieredReservation`, existing cluster behavior will change drastically. When Guaranteed pods hoard idle cache behind a node-wide `memory.min` wall, the node exhausts shareable memory much faster. During memory pressure, instead of gracefully and proportionally reclaiming page cache, the kernel hits a hard wall and is forced to immediately OOM-kill BestEffort and Burstable pods.

#### 3. Node-Level Enforcement Breaks Mixed Workloads

Relying exclusively on node-level configurations forces a single profile onto all workloads. Administrators cannot safely run a latency-sensitive database (requiring strict `memory.min` protection) alongside an elastic web application on the exact same machine. Applying `memory.high` globally means a large workload might be aggressively throttled well before it consumes its physical free capacity. This node-level rigidity defeats the purpose of high-density Kubernetes colocation.

---

### Proposed Solution: The Tiered Protection Architecture

We propose modifying the Memory QoS architecture to establish `memory.low` as the global default baseline, while allowing opt-in escalation for hard protections via node-level flags or per-pod APIs (DRA).

#### 1. The Baseline: Map All Requests to `memory.low` (Soft Protection)

Instead of forcing Guaranteed pods to `memory.min`, the Kubelet should map all pod memory requests (Guaranteed and Burstable) to `memory.low` by default.

* **Maximum Elasticity & Bin-Packing:** This protects memory during normal operations, but during a catastrophic node-level emergency, the kernel retains the flexibility to reclaim idle cache rather than hitting a hard boundary that triggers artificial OOM kills.
* **Industry Validation:** This matches the `fbtax2` architecture utilized at scale by Meta, which explicitly favors `memory.low` because it is "work-conserving" and safely handles system memory overcommit without thrashing.
* **CRI Visibility:** Mapping to `memory.low` successfully populates the CRI payload, satisfying local node agents instantly without API server queries.

**Action Item:** Expand `memoryReservationPolicy` to include a `SoftReservation` mode (or update the default behavior of `TieredReservation`) where all requests are mapped to `memory.low`.

#### 2. Node-Level Hard Protection (Explicit Opt-In)

For specialized, dedicated hardware pools (e.g., dedicated database nodes), administrators should be able to explicitly toggle `memoryReservationPolicy: HardReservation` to universally map Guaranteed workloads to `memory.min`.

* **Action Item:** Ensure that even when `memory.min` is enforced, the Kubelet redundantly populates `memory.low` with the same value in the CRI payload so node daemons retain a uniform schema regardless of the enforcement mechanism.

#### 3. Long-Term Vision: Per-Pod Memory QoS via DRA

Because Kubelet-level enforcement is too blunt for hybrid clusters, fine-grained hard memory locks (`memory.min`) and custom proactive throttling thresholds (`memory.high`) should be managed via **Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA)**.

* **Industry Validation:** Organizations like Alibaba Cloud already recognize the upstream limits of KEP-2570, resorting to external Koordinator agents and custom annotations to inject per-pod Memory QoS policies.
* **Action Item:** Transition application cgroup routing out of Kubelet defaults. The Kubelet should focus on protecting the node (`kube-reserved`), while users request strict memory isolation via DRA `ResourceClaims` that instruct the container runtime to append `memory.min` or `memory.high` on a per-pod basis.

---

### Discussion Request for SIG-Node (July 7, 2026)

We would love to get SIG-Node's feedback on:

1. Shifting the baseline cgroups v2 mapping strategy from `memory.min` to `memory.low` for Guaranteed & Burstable workloads to prevent aggressive OOM starvation.
2. The viability of expanding `memoryReservationPolicy` to give administrators explicit `SoftReservation` / `HardReservation` choices in the upcoming beta cycles.
3. The long-term roadmap for offloading specialized, per-pod Memory QoS configurations (like hard locking and custom throttling factors) to Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA).

body:
### What happened?

When kubelet runs an HTTP liveness/readiness/startup probe, it logs probe parameters at verbosity `-v=4` — and the logged fields include the raw `HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders` values taken directly from the PodSpec:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go:160-173
case p.HTTPGet != nil:
    req, err := httpprobe.NewRequestForHTTPGetAction(p.HTTPGet, &container, status.PodIP, "probe")
    if err != nil {
        logger.V(4).Info("HTTP-Probe failed to create request", "error", err)
        return probe.Unknown, "", err
    }
    if loggerV4 := logger.V(4); logger.Enabled() {
        port := req.URL.Port()
        host := req.URL.Hostname()
        path := req.URL.Path
        scheme := req.URL.Scheme
        headers := p.HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders              // <-- raw PodSpec headers
        loggerV4.Info("HTTP-Probe", "scheme", scheme, "host", host, "port", port,
            "path", path, "timeout", timeout, "headers", headers, "probeType", probeType)  // <-- sink
    }
    return pb.http.Probe(req, timeout)
```

`headers := p.HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders` is the user-supplied header list with **no redaction**, emitted into the `"headers"` structured field.

### What did you expect to happen?

The kubelet prober should not log raw probe `httpHeaders`. The `"headers"` field should be dropped or redacted (e.g. log only header names, or omit the value) in the `HTTP-Probe` line at `prober.go:173` — matching how other secret-bearing probe fields are handled. As written, attacker/operator-supplied credential headers are emitted verbatim into verbose logs.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops a same-package Go test under `pkg/kubelet/prober`, sets `-v=4`, builds an HTTP liveness probe with `Authorization: Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token`, calls the real `(*prober).runProbe`, and the fake HTTP prober returns `Success` — proving the leak happens **before** the request executes and does not require probe failure. Cleans up after itself; no cluster needed.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
F="$ROOT/pkg/kubelet/prober/zz_poc_probe_header_leak_test.go"
SECRET="Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"
trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT
cat >"$F" <<'GOEOF'
package prober

import (
	"context"
	"flag"
	"net/http"
	"testing"
	"time"

	v1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/intstr"
	kubecontainer "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/container"
	"k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/probe"
	"k8s.io/klog/v2"
)

type pocSuccessHTTPProber struct{}

func (pocSuccessHTTPProber) Probe(_ *http.Request, _ time.Duration) (probe.Result, string, error) {
	return probe.Success, "ok", nil // probe SUCCEEDS — leak is pre-request, not failure-only
}

func TestPOCHTTPProbeHeaderLogLeak(t *testing.T) {
	if flag.CommandLine.Lookup("v") == nil {
		klog.InitFlags(nil)
	}
	if err := flag.Set("v", "4"); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}

	pb := &prober{http: pocSuccessHTTPProber{}}
	_, _, err := pb.runProbe(
		context.Background(),
		liveness,
		&v1.Probe{ProbeHandler: v1.ProbeHandler{HTTPGet: &v1.HTTPGetAction{
			Path: "/healthz",
			Port: intstr.FromInt32(8080),
			HTTPHeaders: []v1.HTTPHeader{
				{Name: "Authorization", Value: "Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"},
			},
		}}},
		&v1.Pod{},
		v1.PodStatus{PodIP: "127.0.0.1"},
		v1.Container{Name: "app"},
		kubecontainer.ContainerID{Type: "test", ID: "container"},
	)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	klog.Flush()
}
GOEOF
OUT="$( cd "$ROOT" && go test ./pkg/kubelet/prober -run TestPOCHTTPProbeHeaderLogLeak -count=1 -v 2>&1 )"
printf '%s\n' "$OUT" | grep 'HTTP-Probe' || true
if printf '%s\n' "$OUT" | grep -F "$SECRET"; then
  echo "VULNERABLE: kubelet HTTP probe Authorization header leaked into verbose logs"
else
  echo "NOT VULNERABLE: secret header not observed in logs" >&2; exit 1
fi
```

Expected: a `prober.go` `HTTP-Probe` log line containing the secret in the `headers` field, followed by the `VULNERABLE` confirmation:

```text
I0702 11:32:34.631974 2674209 prober.go:173] "HTTP-Probe" scheme="http" host="127.0.0.1" port="8080" path="/healthz" timeout="0s" headers=[{"name":"Authorization","value":"Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"}] probeType="Liveness"
VULNERABLE: kubelet HTTP probe Authorization header leaked into verbose logs
```

### Anything else we need to know?

- This is secret disclosure of probe-configured credentials to kubelet verbose logs. It is a duplicate of the same finding already recorded internally as `kubelet_prober_http_probe_header_log_leak`.
- It is **distinct** from the recorded `kubelet_http_probe_header_log_leak` (sink `pkg/probe/http/http.go:119`, failure-only). This report's sink is `pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go:173` (pre-request), so successful probes leak too. Both are already separately recorded in the knowledge base.
- Affects HTTP liveness/readiness/startup probes; requires kubelet `-v>=4`. `TCP`/`Exec`/`GRPC` probes do not carry `httpHeaders` at this sink.

title: kubelet logs --manifest-url-header credentials (Authorization / API keys) to runtime logs

labels.name: kind/bug

body:
### What happened?

When kubelet is configured with `--manifest-url` and credential-bearing `--manifest-url-header` values (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values are written to kubelet runtime logs at startup, in cleartext.

At static-pod source init, `makePodSourceConfig` copies the config map into a plain `http.Header` and logs it directly:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go:372-393
manifestURLHeader := make(http.Header)
if len(kubeCfg.StaticPodURLHeader) > 0 {
    for k, v := range kubeCfg.StaticPodURLHeader {
        for i := range v {
            manifestURLHeader.Add(k, v[i])          // values copied into a plain http.Header
        }
    }
}
...
if kubeCfg.StaticPodURL != "" {
    logger.Info("Adding pod URL with HTTP header", "URL", kubeCfg.StaticPodURL, "header", manifestURLHeader)  // <-- sink
    config.NewSourceURL(logger, kubeCfg.StaticPodURL, manifestURLHeader, ...)
}
```

The codebase already knows this field is secret and masks it elsewhere:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go:107
StaticPodURLHeader map[string][]string `datapolicy:"token"`
```

…and the *config-dump* path redacts it before logging the full `KubeletConfiguration` (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:287-290` masks the map to `<masked>`). But `makePodSourceConfig` logs the **runtime `http.Header` copy**, not the config map — so neither the `datapolicy:"token"` tag nor the logging-mask applies, and the header values ship out verbatim. (`datapolicy` only fires on a strongly-typed field argument; here the value has been flattened into an `http.Header` passed as a generic `"header"` argument.)

### What did you expect to happen?

`makePodSourceConfig` should not log the header values. The `datapolicy:"token"` tag and the `server.go:287-290` config-mask both express the intent that `StaticPodURLHeader` is secret; this code path bypasses both by logging a runtime copy. The sink should mask/drop the `header` field (e.g. log only that headers are present, or redact like the config-dump path does). Redaction must not depend on operators avoiding sensitive headers, since the field is the documented place to put upstream auth.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops a same-package Go test under `pkg/kubelet` that calls the real `makePodSourceConfig` with a custom `logr` sink capturing klog output, sets `Authorization: Bearer static-pod-url-secret`, and asserts the secret appears in the captured logs. Cleans up after itself; no cluster or running kubelet needed.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
F="$ROOT/pkg/kubelet/zz_poc_staticpodheader_logleak_test.go"
trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT
cat >"$F" <<'GOEOF'
package kubelet

import (
	"bytes"
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"strings"
	"testing"
	"time"

	"github.com/go-logr/logr"
	metav1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
	kubeletconfiginternal "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/apis/config"
	kubeletutil "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/util"
	"k8s.io/klog/v2"
)

type pocSink struct{ buf *bytes.Buffer }

func (s *pocSink) Init(logr.RuntimeInfo)          {}
func (s *pocSink) Enabled(int) bool               { return true }
func (s *pocSink) Info(_ int, msg string, kv ...interface{}) {
	fmt.Fprintln(s.buf, append([]interface{}{msg}, kv...)...)
}
func (s *pocSink) Error(err error, msg string, kv ...interface{}) {
	fmt.Fprintln(s.buf, append([]interface{}{msg, err}, kv...)...)
}
func (s *pocSink) WithValues(kv ...interface{}) logr.LogSink { return s }
func (s *pocSink) WithName(string) logr.LogSink              { return s }

func TestPOCStaticPodURLHeaderLogLeak(t *testing.T) {
	var logs bytes.Buffer
	ctx := klog.NewContext(context.Background(), logr.New(&pocSink{buf: &logs}))

	const secret = "Bearer static-pod-url-secret"
	kubeCfg := &kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration{
		StaticPodURL:        "http://127.0.0.1:1/static-pods.yaml",
		StaticPodURLHeader:  map[string][]string{"Authorization": {secret}},
		HTTPCheckFrequency:  metav1.Duration{Duration: time.Hour},
	}
	deps := &Dependencies{PodStartupLatencyTracker: kubeletutil.NewPodStartupLatencyTracker()}

	if _, err := makePodSourceConfig(ctx, kubeCfg, deps, "node-a", func() bool { return true }); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("makePodSourceConfig: %v", err)
	}
	if !strings.Contains(logs.String(), secret) {
		t.Fatalf("secret NOT in logs:\n%s", logs.String())
	}
	t.Logf("VULNERABLE: static pod URL header secret written to kubelet logs\n%s", logs.String())
}
GOEOF
( cd "$ROOT" && go test ./pkg/kubelet -run TestPOCStaticPodURLHeaderLogLeak -count=1 -v 2>&1 | grep -E 'VULNERABLE|Adding pod URL|PASS|FAIL|ok ' )
```

Expected: printed lines show the secret in the kubelet log output, then `PASS`:

```text
VULNERABLE: static pod URL header secret written to kubelet logs
    Adding pod URL with HTTP header URL http://127.0.0.1:1/static-pods.yaml header map[Authorization:[Bearer static-pod-url-secret]]
--- PASS: TestPOCStaticPodURLHeaderLogLeak (0.00s)
ok  	k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet
```

i.e. the `Authorization: Bearer static-pod-url-secret` value is logged verbatim by `Adding pod URL with HTTP header`.

### Anything else we need to know?

- This is secret disclosure of upstream-manifest credentials to kubelet logs, at default verbosity. It is a duplicate of the same finding already recorded internally as `kubelet_staticpodurlheader_log_leak`.
- Distinct from `kubelet_configz_staticpodurlheader_leak` (the `/configz` JSON path, different sink and code path) — both leak the same `StaticPodURLHeader` field but via different endpoints; both capitalize on the fact that `makePodSourceConfig`/`setConfigz` bypass the `datapolicy`/config-mask that `server.go:287-290` applies.
- Affects kubelet configured with `--manifest-url` + `--manifest-url-header`. Nodes using only `--pod-manifest-path` are not affected.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ git describe --tags
v1.37.0-alpha.2-121-ga0b6070d29d   # current master; reproducer verified at a0b6070d29d
```

</details>

title: EmptyDir volume tmpfs mounts should have the correct selinux context set

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
Tmpfs mounts done by the `EmptyDir` volume plugin will by default receive a different security context than the kubelet root dir.  This results in AVC denials on reads from the container's selinux context while selinux is enforcing.  We should change the EmptyDir volume plugin to set the `rootcontext` option of the mount based on the selinux context of the kubelet rootdir.

Eventually this will touch the [security context work](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/design/security_context.md).

body:
_update : i closed this issue, maybe we can follow up with the etcd folks and just use their smoke tests_

This is optional, and I'm open to opinions on wether or not we should/shouldn't have an etcd soak test.  I found it useful in an experiment this week, so im happy to PR it if we like the idea.

Given that erroneous  etcd deployments can  lead to  nodes being split brained (not an etcd issue necessarily, just a general distributed systems issue that can crop up due to network partitions or other infrastructure problems) , we can add an etcd soak test to optionally run periodically on kube clusters...  I have one such test psuedo code is below...

```
//TEST: That each the WRITE from any server is READABLE from any OTHER server.
//given an integer n, which is the # of writes to test.
for each i in n
   write key $i to etcd to a random server

for each i in n
   for each server s
       read key $i from s
       if key not there, fail.

for each i in n
   delete key
//pass test.
```

concretely, 

```
for etcd servers s1, s2, s3
if n = 7
write 
  server1->(k1,k1)
  server2->(k2,k2)
  server2->(k3,k3) 
  server3->(k4,k4) and so on, until we write k7,

then 
  on server1
      read k1,k2,k3,....k7 (fail if one is unreadable)
  on server2
      read k1,k2,k3,....k7 (fail if one is unreadable)
   ... and so on
```

The basic node upgrade mechanisms (#6099, #6088) will be out-of-band, e.g. run on a user's desktop. We might instead want to have the master run the node upgrade process. title: Node upgrades: in-place upgrades

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
See issue #6079 as the roll-up for node upgrades.

This issue is to do an in-place upgrade of the kubelet and kube-proxy binaries while a node is running. Docker and the kernel/OS are not changed. This upgrade can only be performed if the requested new version of kubelet and kube-proxy are compatible with the existing Docker and kernel/OS version; see #4855 for more details on versioning.

We simply want to download the new (kube*) node binaries, stop the old ones, and start the new ones (#1573). That way, the pods continue to run, and we don't have to migrate any storage. Possible complications include:
- #3333 leftover state or configuration of the VM will cause unwanted side effects after the upgrade is complete
- the configuration of the node (environment variables, flags passed to kube_, something salt does) might change between kube_ versions
- when kube\* binaries are stopped, the master might think the pods are all gone, and schedule new copies of the pods elsewhere throughout the cluster

The following requirements follow:
- smart salt stanzas: idempotency, can run on a previously salted node
- must have an upgrade grace period where the pods are considered alive even if they cannot be health-checked by kubernetes

The tests for this feature are tracked in #7256.

References:
- #4855 cluster versioning
- #3333 lively debate about kubelet & kube-proxy upgrades, specifically in-place _vs_ fresh-node
- #1573 online kubelet upgrades; the original issue for this work item

1. Kind-based filtering on object streams -- only operate on the kinds of objects specified. This would make directory-based kubectl operations much more useful. Users should be able to instantiate the example applications using `kubectl create -f <example-dir> ...`
1. Create services before other objects, or at least before objects that depend upon them. Namespace-relative DNS mitigates this some, but most users are still using service environment variables. [#1768](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/1768)

Simple version is done, more complex version needs work.

```

  1. Rollback (make rollingupdate reversible, and complete an in-progress rolling update by taking 2 replication controller names rather than always taking a file)
  1. Rollover (replace multiple replication controllers with one, such as to clean up an aborted partial rollout)
  1. Write a ReplicationController generator to derive the new ReplicationController from an old one (e.g., `--image-version=newversion`, which would apply a name suffix, update a label value, and apply an image tag)

```

Done, now that readiness corresponds to Running and is tracked by Kubelet status if the readiness hook is set?

title: Namespace directory nodes are not removed from etcd

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

body:
The resource paths for each object in etcd follow a convention like the following:

```
/registry/pods/namespace1/pod1
/registry/pods/namespace1/pod2
/registry/pods/namespace2/pod1
/registry/pods/namespace2/pod2
```

The same pattern follows for all other namespace scoped resource types.

When we delete a namespace, we are properly deleting the individual resources (pod1 and pod2), but in etcd, we still get a directory node that represented what used to be that namespace's content directory.

For example, if we delete namespace1, we end up with the following empty directory in etcd.

```
/registry/pods/namespace1
```

We should develop a solution to purge these empty directories from etcd to maintain system performance over time.

We could do this at a lower-level:

1) some controller that purges empty dirs from etcd
2) or some other convention in our registry to ask that the folder node for a namespace is deleted as part of namespace termination

The remaining folders cause no end-user impact, but just result in unnecessary folders left in etcd repo.

title: Apiserver proxy rewriting not useful for intra-cluster links

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Forked from #4440.

The apiserver proxy uses httputil.NewSingleHostReverseProxy. This rewrites URLs to a fixed scheme, host, and base path. This is not smart enough to facilitate translation of links to other (intra-cluster) services, pods, and nodes, which are all proxy-able directly. In fact, if someone puts the correct proxy links into their pages, the links are munged and broken by the reverse proxy.

Internally, we don't rewrite links. Applications use intra-cluster names (DNS and our internal NS) and addresses, and we have a few different mechanisms to route those to the reverse proxy.

If we want to stick with the rewriting approach, the proxy should recognize and translate intra-cluster names and addresses. #3481 proposed proxying by IP address in addition to resource path.

cc @enisoc @lavalamp @smarterclayton

title: Unnecessary killing of the pod infra container.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Currently, we evaluate whether the `pod infra container` should be killed by computing each container's hash and compare them with the running container's hash. If any of them has changed, then we mark the `pod infra container` to be killed.

Instead, how about just comparing the expecting pod infra container's hash with the running one's? If nothing has changed, then we don't need to bother with the `pod infra container`. If the hash does have changed, then we restart it before in ahead. 

By doing this, I think we can simplify the kubelet's syncPod loop a lot. And also this can make it easier to migrate to new container runtimer interface (e.g. We can let `RunContainerInPod` to test and compare the hash).

Hope to hear from your opinions:) Or questions? Thank you!

@dchen1107 @vmarmol

Today, we only look at the Port Number and a result, are over-aggressive in disallowing a pod from being run on a node.

For e.g if pod1 is using udp on port 8080, and pod2 is using tcp on port 8080, both pods can go on the same host and hostIP.
But today, pod1 and pod2 would not be scheduled on the same node.

body:
On a cluster running 0.13.2, I ran `kubectl get pods`, picked out the name of a pod that only contains a single container, let's call it foo, and then ran `kubectl log foo`. It prints nothing other than the message "Unexpected path for command running". If I add on the container name (`kubectl log foo container`), then it prints nothing, presumably because the pod has no logs.

The docs for kubectl log say that the container name is optional if the pod only has one container, so I wouldn't expect this response.

title: Updating system date and time on master/nodes kills pods

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
It seems that updating the date and time on a single master/node host kills all the running pods.

I haven't had time to properly debug this and identify what actually triggers the issue (master or node side), and if anything can be done to fix this.

In general there could be multiple things to consider here:
1. in general it's better not to use date/time for timeouts but rather using monotonic system time
2. where the monotonic system time cannot be used (rate) because the value is persisted/shared among machines (future multiple master?)  then UTC should be used
3. changing the hosts timezone should not affect the timeouts

I haven't tested or checked these 3 items but I am mentioning them here for future reference.

I'll investigate them as soon as I'll have time to figure out what's going on (any info that would make my debug session faster is welcome!)

title: Make the status.Replica count useful to watchers

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
Currently the status.Replica count is not very useful to watchers (like stop rc, which actually doesn't watch but should):
1. Its updated `fillCurrentState` style: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/registry/etcd/etcd.go#L114
2. If we remove that (we should, in any case), it will only get updated once in 10 seconds.

The quick and dirty solutions are:
- Decreasing the polling interval: will probably lead to load on the apiserver.
  - We can probably tolerate a quicker interval if we just list pods once in the manager, instead of listing in each rc.
- Wait on the  goroutines that create/delete replicas, assume a 200 response means the request was a success, and update the count then and there: If a pod just keeps dying (stuck in a create->death loop), the status.Replicas would never reflect this because we can always create the pod (and hence update Status.Replicas), it just dies. So the watcher won't be aware of it.

@lavalamp thoughts on just watching the status field of all pods in the manager through the controller framework? I feel like we either need to do that, or list once in the manager and decrease the poll interval.

title: First timer tick for a pod status update takes too long

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
It appears that the first pod status update tick is fired on average 1/2 pod status frequency duration.  This is unnecessarily long - I don't know if we have an existing issue to cover this, but it makes many small, simple pods take up to a minute to report ready (on their first time).  @vmarmol added a note to convert this to a better mechanism, but I wanted to make it obvious.

Some thoughts:
- The first transition between Pending and Running is the one that should fire with minimal latency - we should look to send these ASAP, in preference over all other status updates
- Subsequent updates can come at lower priority
- We should probably poll/check/update pod status at different intervals (inversely proportional to their age up to a cap), since most failures will happen in the first seconds of launch

title: generic etcd should surface ctx/obj namespace mismatches

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Currently its hard to surface a mismatch context in an update via generic etcd. If I do something like:

```
obj.Namespace = "valid"
update(api.WithNamespace(ctx, "invalid"), obj)
```

it will fail in the `get` with whatever go-etcd error, because the path /invalid/objname doesn't exist; and if i do:

```
obj.Namespace = "valid"
update(api.WithNamespace(ctx, "valid_different"), obj)
```

it will fail with a resource version mismatch (so `NewConflict`), because the get will return the object in `/valid_different/objname`, but its resource version is different.

Ideally both these cases should fail with a `NewBadRequest`. This would happen if the validation flow reaches `BeforeUpdate`, but it fails due to the mentioned checks earlier in the callstack. To catch both cases we probably need to refactor the namespace checking out of `BeforeCreate` and `BeforeUpdate` into a common location and call it from generic/etcd.update.

title: Move from `cmd/e2e` runner to native Ginkgo runner

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
This is an off-shoot of https://github.com/onsi/ginkgo/issues/146#issuecomment-83699596. I actually think that the structure of the existing `cmd/e2e` runner is wrong, and that we need to work towards getting the native Ginkgo runner working with our suite(s). This has the following advantages:
- Right now, we pretty much just generate [one suite](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/driver.go#L83). We really want to target at least a second group, a stress group. We could do this hackily with `--ginkgo.focus`, but we should have a better tool.
-  We've extended our own runner a couple of times just to add things the base runner already has. We should stop doing that.
- We're eventually going to want things the normal runner already has, like parallelism.

I'm not as well versed in the blockers. I remember part of it is as simple as the command-line flags: we take a host of flags to the tests and didn't want to take them as environment variables, but I think this one was easily solved? But I think the other blockers were just someone taking the time to actually do the work.

title: Proposal to create a stress and fault injection tool

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
While the codebase contains unit tests and some e2e tests, I think there's a need for some tool and/or framework to do some stress/reliability testing (with some fault injection as well). This is akin to ChaosMonkey, but lighter and targeted to k8s. The need for this type of tool arose during my planning for master process recovery, but it'd be a useful tool to have in general.

The outline of the design is fairly straightforward. The major components could be broken down as:
- Stress driver - the main process that runs and coordinates all the various tests and remote agents.
- Stress agents - remote processes running on the master and minion nodes. Used to trigger faults (i.e. killing processes, misconfiguring networks, etc) and to provide a side-channel back to the stress driver.

Within the stress driver, it'd have to be able to:
- Setup a k8s cluster.
- Install test app into a cluster. Includes setting up the network for external traffic.
- Make requests to test app to verify it's functional.
- Tear down all k8s resources.
- Trigger various actuators that inject fault into various parts of the cluster (i.e. kill process, fill up disk space, misconfigure etcd, misconfigure network, etc).
- Allow different types of test cases to be written to test specific functionality.
- Allow pseudo-random variations of the various test cases.
- Provide a continual reporting and logging ability. Also be able to halt testing during faults for investigations.

The scope of this task could also expand fairly easily, since the tool has a lot of requirements that overlap with other areas of the product. Namely, it seems to have rather similar requirements as the e2e testing (with the added thing that it must be able to do some operations in parallel). As such, it feels like it'd be good to integrate those efforts and come up with either a common framework to be used by both, or better, to have the ability to use the same or slightly modified test cases for both e2e and stress testing. Things like cloud provider abstractions (to enable multiple cluster creation, SSH communications, etc) also seem like common needs in k8s.

A more detailed design proposal and some initial code should be available shortly, but I'd like to start the discussion of:
1. Is this a useful task and should it be funded?
2. What are the type of functionality needed?
3. What is the proper scope of this task, vis a vis the rest of the e2e testing and other k8s stuff?

Thanks.
