title: Kubernetes master freezes when the etcd leader is unreachable

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
While doing some perturbation tests, I noticed that the Kubernetes master breaks if we loose the machine hosting the etcd leader.

Here is the test (I’m using the libvirt-coreos cluster)
### Suspend any non-leader node
- Start a cluster with a multi-node etcd cluster and a multi-node kubernetes cluster

```
$ ./cluster/kube-up.sh
```
- Issue a `get minions` query:

```
$ ./cluster/kubectl.sh get minions
NAME                LABELS              STATUS
192.168.10.2        <none>              Ready
192.168.10.3        <none>              Ready
192.168.10.4        <none>              Ready
```
- Suspend a VM which is a kubernetes node and an etcd node:

```
$ virsh suspend kubernetes-minion-2
Domain kubernetes-minion-2 suspended
```
- Issue a `get minions` query:

```
$ ./cluster/kubectl.sh get minions
NAME                LABELS              STATUS
192.168.10.2        <none>              Ready
192.168.10.3        <none>              Ready
192.168.10.4        <none>              Ready

$ ./cluster/kubectl.sh get minions -o yaml | grep lastProbeTime
      lastProbeTime: 2015-03-18T09:48:08Z
      lastProbeTime: 2015-03-18T09:46:42Z
      lastProbeTime: 2015-03-18T09:48:08Z
```

**`get minions` answers and we see that the `lastProbeTime` of the frozen VM is not refreshed anymore. This is what is expected**

Now, the issue:
### Suspend the the VM hosting the etcd leader
- Start a cluster with a multi-node etcd cluster and a multi-node kubernetes cluster

```
$ ./cluster/kube-up.sh
```
- Issue a `get minions` query:

```
$ ./cluster/kubectl.sh get minions
NAME                LABELS              STATUS
192.168.10.2        <none>              Ready
192.168.10.3        <none>              Ready
192.168.10.4        <none>              Ready
```
- Suspend the VM which is the etcd leader:

```
$ for i in {1..4}; do ssh core@192.168.10.$i journalctl -u etcd; done | sort | egrep "state|leader"
…
Mar 18 09:51:14 kubernetes-minion-1 etcd[560]: [etcd] Mar 18 09:51:14.004 INFO      | kubernetes-minion-1: leader changed from '' to 'kubernetes-minion-1'.
Mar 18 09:51:14 kubernetes-minion-1 etcd[560]: [etcd] Mar 18 09:51:14.004 INFO      | kubernetes-minion-1: state changed from 'follower' to 'leader'.
…

$ virsh suspend kubernetes-minion-1
Domain kubernetes-minion-1 suspended
```
- Issue a `get minions` query:

```
$ ./cluster/kubectl.sh get minions
F0318 10:55:11.503734   17913 get.go:67] Error received from API: 501: All the given peers are not reachable (Tried to connect to each peer twice and failed) [0]
```
- Test that etcd is still responsive on the master:

```
$ ssh core@192.168.10.1 ps ax \| grep kube-api
/opt/kubernetes/bin/kube-apiserver […] --etcd_servers=http://127.0.0.1:4001 […]

$ ssh core@192.168.10.1 etcdctl ls
/registry
/coreos.com
```
- Check that etcd elect a new leader:

```
$ for i in {1..4}; do ssh -o ConnectTimeout=2s core@192.168.10.$i journalctl -u etcd; done | sort | egrep "state|leader"
[…]
Mar 18 09:54:32 kubernetes-master etcd[575]: [etcd] Mar 18 09:54:32.939 INFO      | kubernetes-master: leader changed from 'kubernetes-minion-1' to ''.
Mar 18 09:54:32 kubernetes-minion-2 etcd[568]: [etcd] Mar 18 09:54:32.874 INFO      | kubernetes-minion-2: leader changed from 'kubernetes-minion-1' to ''.
Mar 18 09:54:33 kubernetes-minion-3 etcd[565]: [etcd] Mar 18 09:54:33.135 INFO      | kubernetes-minion-3: leader changed from 'kubernetes-minion-1' to ''.
Mar 18 09:54:33 kubernetes-minion-3 etcd[565]: [etcd] Mar 18 09:54:33.135 INFO      | kubernetes-minion-3: state changed from 'follower' to 'candidate'.
Mar 18 09:54:33 kubernetes-minion-3 etcd[565]: [etcd] Mar 18 09:54:33.137 INFO      | kubernetes-minion-3: leader changed from '' to 'kubernetes-minion-3'.
Mar 18 09:54:33 kubernetes-minion-3 etcd[565]: [etcd] Mar 18 09:54:33.137 INFO      | kubernetes-minion-3: state changed from 'candidate' to 'leader'.
```
- But Kubernetes doesn’t recover:

```
$ cluster/kubectl.sh get minions
F0318 11:16:18.822576   19360 get.go:67] Error received from API: 501: All the given peers are not reachable (Tried to connect to each peer twice and failed) [0]
```

**The kubernetes master is streaming logs saying: `501: All the given peers are not reachable (Tried to connect to each peer twice and failed) [0]` and all kubectl commands answer with the same reply.**

The etcd cluster could be secured on a set of dedicated VMs, but still: the loss of a single VM of a cluster can completely break Kubernetes if we are so unlucky that the lost VM was the etcd leader.

Would anybody be aware of a such a kind of issue and possible mitigation?

title: cache selector results

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
This is a proposal to implement caching selector result. https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/4817#issuecomment-76495394

AFAIK, currently only [two components](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/labels.md#api) use selector to group their members: `service` and `replicationController`, and they get list of their members by matching seletor against all pods' label every time.

Here I propose a way to cache seletor result in etcd.

Define a new registry in etcd: selector.

Whenever a `service` or `replicationController` is created, generate [uid](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/identifiers.md#uids) for its selector, and register selector with that uid in etcd. While creating `service` or `replicationController`, it watches that selector in etcd to wait updates on result of selector. We should add pre-existed matched pods to its result of course.

And whenever a `pod` is created, matches its label with all selector under its namespace (assuming we forbidden selector select object in another ns, which I not quite sure), and add that pod to selector result if match. Update or delete a `pod` should also update all selectors' result under its ns.

When a `selector` and `pod` is created at same time, we should use some kind of mutex to avoid race condition.

Any comment?

title: Proposal: IP addresses as a opaque counted resource

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
## IP addresses as a opaque counted resource

Currently Kubernetes scheduler is not aware of number of IP addresses available on a single node. We do have some assumptions about network masks, from which a number of available IPs can be inferred, but this is not general or configurable in any way. We want to create a simple counted resource published by kubelet and visible for scheduler, which will allow finer grained configurations to be used.
## Resources in Kubernetes

Resource validation in Kubernetes is performed as one of FitPredicates of Scheduler, namely ResourceFit predicate check. Available resources are computed by reading resources from NodeInfo, and subtracting resources of Pods currently bound to the given Node. The data comes (indirectly?) from etcd in a form of API Node > Spec > Capacity struct.

Capacity is a part of NodeStatus periodically updated by Kubelet in tryUpdateNodeStatus method (even though Capacity is a part of the NodeSpec). As of now, all Node capacity data is read from cAdvisor MachineInfo struct. During Node creation NodeController fills up Capacity in some way (either statically or get it from the cloud provider), but later on it’s overwritten by data provided by cAdvisor. IUUC Kubelet is the only entity which triggers modifications of Node entries after they are created. 
## IPs as resources

Introducing IP addresses as resources is straightforward: we need to add them to ResourceList/ResourceName and related places, and modify PodFitResources method in Scheduler. In current model it is assumed that we have one IP per Pod model, hence there’s no need of introducing additional scheduling requirements/usage info. In the future if we’d want to loosen this assumption changes to make will be pretty straightforward.

On top of those simple changes we need to decide how to keep the configuration. As it resides in NodeSpec, which is written by both Kubelet and NodeController it can be a part of any one of configurations (Node or Kubelet). If it were a part of Kubelet, then we’d need to wait for first “syncNodeStatus” call before setting it up. On the up side doing it in Kubelet will make the change of the IP number in runtime more robust (Kubelet is and will be overwriting Specs, so if anything else were to modify the value race condition would be possible).

title: Race condition updating events for compression

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
There is a race condition in event compression logic in `pkg/client/record/event.go`. If the same event is created in rapid succession it is possible that ResourceVersion used to update one of the events becomes out-of-date and the update fails due to `Conflict`.

The fix for the race condition can not be implemented on the client side, because it requires doing an atomic increment operation: no client can control/guarantee the behavior of any other client and thus no client can implement an atomic increment operation using separate read/write REST calls.

The correct fix for this is to expose a new REST call on the API Server that can take an event key and `LastSeen` timestamp, and do the following operations atomically:
  1) Read the event object for the given event key
  2) Write the event object back with an incremented count and new `LastSeen` timestamp (timestamp should only be updated if it is more recent then the existing timestamp).

While this race condition exists in theory,  in practice it is unlikely to be triggered by our code because it requires either another client to do an update on an existing event object that it did not create or multiple threads on the same client doing the exact same operation on the exact same object in rapid succession and create an event for it--our code is mostly synchronous and does no identical event generating operations in parallel.

I am marking this bug as P2 because of the unlikely nature of it occurring in normal operation and the work required to implement the correct solution.

Branched from #5327 (even though this doesn't cause that issue, it needs to be tracked).

Today we have server, client, and test binaries. We expect the server ones to only build in Linux, but the client and test ones we expect to be able to build and run in Linux, Mac OS X, and Windows.

Server binaries:
- kube-proxy
- kube-apiserver
- kube-controller-manager
- kubelet
- hyperkube
- kube-scheduler

Client binaries:
- kubectl
- kubernetes (busybox)

Test binaries:
- e2e
- integration
- gendocs
- denman

title: Not all clusters support the same security model

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
There are two cluster security models in use today in getting started guides
1. Auth-based: 
   - nginx proxy is exposed to the internet.
   - nginx proxy does basic auth of users.
   - kube-apiserver does authentication and authorization of users
   - kubelets/kube-proxy use tokens to auth to apiserver
   - the salt-based distros use this model 
2. Network-based:
   - if you can reach the apiserver, then you are authorized
   - apiserver (hopefully) not expose to the internet.  Either only serves on local machine, for single-physical machine clusters, or you have to tunnel/vpn to reach the cluster network.
   - Other distros, such as CoreOS-based ones, use this model.

For now, having the more relaxed Network-based model for some distros is fine.  At some point, we will want to bring all distros listed on our site up to a common standard of security.  This issue is a reminder to do that.

Also, I will add some documentation about this current state of affairs.

title: Replication controller doesn't reject updates with a modified resourceVersion

labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Setting the resource version to something arbitrary will fail the CAS, but doing something like:

```
for i := 10; i < 100; i++ {
  controller.ResourceVersion = strconv.Itoa(i)
  rc.Update(controller)
}
```

Will work if the latest version is < 100. Fix:
1. Teach `ValidateObjectMeta` to overwrite the resource version like it does creation timestamp
2. Modify the rc's Update method to call `ValidateReplicationControllerUpdate` with the current version of the object (it currently calls `ValidateReplicationController` with just the update).

This should tie in well with moving the entirety of rc validation into a strategy (https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/4973).

title: upgrade: Rolling system updates via delete/re-create nodes

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
I'm looking for a way to make kubernetes to do rolling system updates of node machines. I'm targetting the kernel and operating system levels, though kublet would come along for the ride. 

My thought is that do an "update" of a node you simply turn up a new node, and then tear down the old one. This model is simple and easy to reason about, much easier than in-place update. We want kubernetes to know that a node is gone immediately though, so downtime of containers on that node is small. I think this is consistant with current plans? (e.g. https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/4855)

Here's my proposal:
- Add kubectl (and API) functionality to add and remove nodes from the cluster dynamically, also ensuring the state gets exported to the "spec" for that node (I think what's needed  is already in the status).
- Within the kube shell scripts, refactor the startup and shutdown functions a little so they use lower-level functions that spin up a new machine and remove an old one using the kubectl calls. Add direct access to these new functions via something like kube-removenode and kube-addnode scripts. These scripts can poll the status and spec, and block until the change is complete (or error out if the spec changes).
- The "rolling" part of the update can then be done with another small shell script in the kubernetes codebase, or by a user script.

I'm with Meteor, the folks running kubernetes on AWS, and my intention is to implement this myself within about 2 months if it looks like a good direction to go. I don't want to step on anyones toes, and after I do this work I'd really like to upstream it, so I'm trying to ensure that this is compatible with the rest of the project.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
@ArtfulCoder has pending PR to run etcd_server in a pod, which is pretty much ready to go any minutes. 

Now we want to have other master components running inside a pod / pods. For GKE, this should be easy since it only upgrades to a proper release, from which we could build docker image and push to some repository. But there are the issues for dev cluster. @ArtfulCoder and I discussed this, and now we have two proposals on the table, and both have pros and cons:

**Idea 1:** Build docker images for each release build and tag it with kubernete-dev version bit, and push those images tar file through salt:

pros: 
- The same building process could be re-used for GKE and other cloud provider for production release.
- We can use salt to push docker image directly to master node without complicated feature supported in kubelet.

cons: 
- Everytime when we build a development release, we have to update manifest file for those mater component with new image tag from version bit. 
- More dependency on salt which we want to get rid of

**Idea 2:** Build docker images on master node at runtime. Kubelet is watching a managed directory, and get inotify on changes. When new binary is pushed to master node, kubelet is notified, and create image from scratch, and tell docker to reload newly created image, then restart containers.

pros:
- No update to manifest file for master components for each build

cons:
- It is pretty complicated when I were typing the idea. 
- It requires some special code in kubelet and other components. 

Any more ideas? or suggestions? or objections? 

cc/ @alex-mohr @bgrant0607 @thockin @davidopp

title: Need a general design for varying storage media and volumes

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
From #4602 

I do want to offer a tmpfs EmptyDir.  The obvious thing to do is to add a
tmpfs plugin.  But WAIT.  It's identical to EmptyDir in pretty much every
way except a call to mount() instead of mkdir().  I expect that eventually
I will want a local SSD EmptyDir too - do I again fork it and just hardcode
the concept?  What about when phase change and NVM and whatever new space
age storage tech emerges?

And what about things like the GitRepo?  I want to make that go away, but
the replacement will need similar concepts.  Do I make N copies of that for
disk, SSD, NVM, PCM, quantum, etc?

Stick with me, I am going somewhere, I think.

In a sense, WHAT you store and WHERE you store it are orthogonal.  But not
REALLY because the full matrix doesn't make sense - we don't want to offer
secrets on disk, and what does it even mean to map PD or NFS or iscsi onto
tmpfs?  That's a nonsensical question.

In a sense, what you want to ask for is a QoS of storage or a set of
attributes that must be met.  For example secrets requires a volatile
storage medium, but it doesn't care much about perf.  Someone who cares
about perf might ask for IOPS > x or throughput > y MB/s.  It seems that an
API like:

``` json
    source: emptyDir{ requirements: [ "IOPS >= 1000" ]}
```

...is a better way to express performance.  This happens to be similar to
what @markturansky is pushing with pet storage, but I can't help but thing
that is TOO exact, and not good UX.  But if we HAD such an API, I would
argue that secret volumes are essentially hardcoded to "Volatile"
requirements.

So the question I offer is this: Is it worthwhile to take a swing at this
now, and implement secrets in terms of it?  Or should we punt on this and
just make a kubelet-global tmpfs (which we might want for other things
eventually) and then carve slices off of that for secrets?

I think the latter is probably more expedient but messier.  The former is
going to take longer, but has a better chance of lasting, IMO.

And then a second question: Is secrets really just a special case of
GitRepo, which is just a special case of "run this side-car container" ?
In other words, could we get rid of the secrets volume plugin and instead
just run a container which syncs some Secrets objects into files?  The
ServiceAccount tie-in makes me think maybe not, but i wanted to put it on
the table.

This is not a critical issue for Secrets - I am fine offering a tmpfs-centric solution for now and migrating to this once we have it.

There's also some overlap with the of plugin-wrapper plugins (e.g. secrets is literally a wrapper around an emptydir(medium=tmpfs) plugin instance).

Filing this issue so we can consider it independently.

body: Currently the replication controller update routine validates each update as it would a create. Before we can add subresources to a replication controller (https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/4909), we need a way to validate updates as incremental changes,  by comparing the current and proposed versions of an object. We can achieve this by moving the update validation into a strategy and directly calling `BeforeUpdate`. This will also bring rc validation inline with the implementation in generic/etcd, making it easier to merge the two.

title: Scheduler spreading using services vs replication controllers

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
Creating a separate issue since the PR (https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/pull/4674) in which this discussion was initiated is merged and this merits a second look.

I had raised the question of why we used services instead of replication controllers for identifying peer pods for spreading by the scheduler. The argument is that services might not be needed and could be avoided in some cases, whereas replication controller will most likely always be there.

@bgrant0607 's initial response: why use services instead of replication controllers for identifying peer pods for spreading. Discussed in #1965 and #2312. Replication controllers are associated with deployments. We expect there to be multiple per service: canaries, rolling updates, multiple release tracks, etc. What people want is spreading of the whole service. Custom spreading is discussed in #4301 and #367.

While I agree that there can be multiple replication controllers per service, I still believe that spreading of pods should still happen independently for the replication controllers. Also, we have customer use cases where the services are not created at all and routing/load balancing to a group of pods is being handled by custom middleware.

Rolling updates: the new pods coming in should be scheduled on the best possible minions and should not be combined with the existing older pods for achieving a good spread. Eventually, when all the older pods are removed and only the new ones remain, its the spreading of the new pods that really matters.

Canaries: This one is slightly different, but in general the same argument applies here as for rolling updates.

Multiple release tracks: shouldn't we have a good spread within each release track to ensure HA for each release track? Why would we want to jointly consider the pods for different release tracks for a good spread?

When I changed the value of `publicIPs` to an actual IP address, the `iptables` rules on the minions were successfully created.

This leads be to believe there should be some validation of the `publicIPs` field to make sure that actual IP addresses are provided.

body:
There are pitfalls when using the watch + list pattern. Many of our controllers use this pattern, and we expect many future pieces of code to use this pattern. Therefore, we'd like to provide a framework/example which lets you fill out three functions (list, watch, and process) to get a shiny new bug-free (at least the list+watch part) controller.

This can be modeled after/mostly copied from the scheduler.

title: Versioned clients

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Right now, pkg/client auto-converts everything to our internal, unversioned format. This is convenient for kubernetes components, but not so convenient for any 3rd party users. (The whole point of the versioning system is so that we can make changes to the unversioned structs without affecting downstream users.)

So we should maintain versioned clients.

It is possible that this is as easy as copying pkg/client and replacing the `"pkg/api"` imports with `api "pkg/api/v1beta1"`. If so, we should do this soon. If it turns out to be much more complex than that, we can defer this change until after 1.0, I think.

When we deprecate an old client version, we should be nice and provide people a list of gofmt rewrite rules which will switch them to the next client version.

title: PodInterface should support Watch

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

body:
PodInterface should have Watch method behaving in the same way as ServiceInterface.Watch does.

Use case: a monitoring system (namely Prometheus) expects to get the list of monitored servers performing a  DNS-SD query. Special service (similar to kube2sky shipped with Kubernetes) mirrors status of running Pods into etcd, which is in turn monitored by SkyDNS server and exported as DNS-SD. Schematically the data flow looks like this: Kubernetes -> kube2sky -> etcd -> SkyDNS -> Prometheus.

The biggest challenge is to deliver list of all running pods from Kubernetes to kube2sky. Currently kube2sky can only poll Kubernetes with PodInterface.List() each N seconds, which is not efficient. Having a Watch method would be much better.

title: Expose secrets to containers in environment variables

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
Now that #4126 and #4514 have landed, it should be possible to expose secrets to containers as environment variables.  While this is arguably not the optimal way to consume secrets, it will be important to users taking their first steps into a cloud environment, and we should offer this feature to enable a good experience for users who need it.  For what it's worth, we consider this to be an important use-case for users of [OpenShift](https://github.com/openshift/origin).

Let's start with getting all the requirements and challenges on the table:
1.  How should this be modeled in the API?
2.  What limits are reasonable to place on secrets exposed to containers this way?  For example, there are different upper limits on aspects of environment variables on different platforms.
3.  Secrets are not static but environment variables are.  Should the consuming containers be restarted when a secret value changes?
4.  Should environment variables containing secrets be exposed via `docker inspect`*?
5.  Environment variables that contain secrets should not be captured by `docker commit`*

*Applies to future equivalencies in other supported container runtimes

On all aspects of the problem mentioned above, we should take into account possible cross-cuts with:
1.  Pass pod info to container (#560)
2.  Dynamic configuration (#1553)
3.  Sundry other things collected under the downward/upward API aggregator (#386)

```
 Running: cluster/../cluster/gce/../../_output/local/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl resize --replicas=1 rc my-nginx
 F0220 17:34:02.420311    4984 resize.go:66] replicationController "my-nginx" cannot be updated: 101: Compare failed ([188 != 189]) [189]

labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
We may want to rotate keys/certs periodically for things that use pkg/client.
- we might rotate the master's certs when they expire.  don't want clients to fail during that transitition
- Pod using automatically generated credentials in a secrets volume.  
- kubelet/kube-proxy using a per-node token or x509 keypair

Suggest we assume that whatever key rotation plan is used (out of scope of this bug), that old and new tokens/keypairs will always have overlapping lifetimes.  If not, we'd need to teach .kubeconfig to have a list of creds and teach pkg/client to retry.  (I prefer the former option).

Suggest pkg/client watches the .kubeconfig file and any file mentioned by it, using inotify.

title: Consider moving events out of etcd

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
We've discussed this in person a few times.

Events account for the overwhelming majority of our etcd write volume, which is causing a variety of performance and stability problems (#3853, #3329, #2298, #3521, #4073). 

Since we GC events, they can't be relied upon as a messaging mechanism. Distributed control components should be watching status instead. Also, we support hooks to facilitate user extensions, so events are (arguably) not needed for that case, either, provided we add the necessary hooks. 

Therefore, the main purpose of events is to inform users of relevant occurrences. Given that, we could consider a different delivery mechanism for the events.

One proposal is to treat them as log messages. That has a certain appeal. We do "log" all such events into our equivalent of BigQuery internally, to facilitate searching, filtering, sorting, etc. 

We'd need to find a way to make the logs/events accessible via the CLI and UI, and we'd need a non-BigQuery implementation for other platforms. We could probably use fluent as the plugin mechanism. There's also an [amqp fluent plugin](https://github.com/restorando/fluent-plugin-amqp), which would facilitate pushing the events into a message queue.

@lavalamp @brendandburns @saad-ali @smarterclayton

title: Retry handling in queue-based controllers is flawed

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
## Fee-FIFO-fum

The Kubernetes `plugin/scheduler` follows a pattern which has become canonical downstream in OpenShift. The pattern employes the `api/cache` package thusly:
1. Combine a `Reflector` with a `FIFO` to drive a state reconciling controller
2. Handle a single unit of work in the controller, where the work unit is a single resource returned from the `FIFO`
3. Defer errors to a handler

This pattern is dependent on the event compression characteristics of `FIFO`: newer resources added to the queue will be compressed with an existing older resource in the queue, so that the result of the add operation is a single, newer queue entry.

The semantics of `FIFO` presents error handling challenges in the context of the state reconciling controller pattern described. If a recoverable error occurs when processing a resource from a `FIFO`, it's almost always desirable to retry processing (according to some policy: for the sake of this discussion, we'll assume the policy is to retry forever).

The most intuitive approach to implementing a retry is to simply re-queue the resource into the `FIFO`; however, simply re-queueing the resource can lead to undesirable interactions with the compression behavior. For example, consider this timeline:
1. Given a queue, `Q=[A.1, B.1, C.1, D.1]`
2. Controller consumes `A.1`, `Q=[B.1, C.1, D.1]`
3. Concurrently, a `Reflector` receives an update to `A` , now `Q=[B.1, C.1, D.1, A.2]`
4. Controller fails to process `A.1` and re-queues, now `Q=[B.1, C.1, D.1, A.1]`

The `A.2` state has been lost and will not be processed until the controller is restarted (which will result in the `FIFO` being initially seeded with the latest state of all resources).

To account for the compression interaction, there's a small fix (demonstrated in [the Scheduler factory](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/scheduler/factory/factory.go#L225)): Prior to re-queue, the resource (`A` in the example) is re-acquired from a client call. This ensures that:
1. Any older resources still enqueued will be (desirably) updated during re-queue
2. Any changes to the re-queued but yet-to-be-processed resource will be (desirably) updated to a newer state

At a glance, this neatly solves the original problem. However, the fix itself introduces another problem: the retry logic itself can fail. The retry logic now has an external/volatile dependency in the re-acquisition call. I believe I've established it's unsafe to re-queue a stale resource, and that any retry logic must itself be able to retry failures (to retry).
## Solutions

One possible approach (not very well thought out) is to introduce the notion of versioning into the `FIFO` to allow the rejection of stale resources, which would alleviate the need to refresh the resource prior to a re-queue. The `Add` would no-op if a "newer" resource already exists in the queue. This seems like even more complexity to a set of structures which are rapidly growing (e.g. key functions, indexing). My fear is introducing more subtle bugs.

Another approach is to sidestep the problems by replacing the use of `FIFO` with periodic `Store` reconcilers. Taking the scheduler as a convenient example: if a `Store` of all Pods were periodically reconciled, then any Pods which failed to process on the previous iteration would simply be re-processed using the latest resources obtained during the next interval's list. One drawback is a loss of efficiency as the controller potentially churns through no-ops for most of the Pods in the `Store` which were successfully processed last time; however, there's room for optimization at this level (for example, by tuning the `ListWatcher` implementation to only provide un-bound Pods). Are there gaps in this approach?

I'd like to discuss whether the current or future `FIFO` is the appropriate construct to use in this class of controller.

title: Scheduler input should be taken when reducing replicas

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: kind/feature

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
When the replica count is increased, the new pod(s) are assigned to hosts by the scheduler based on policies defined by the selected predicates/priorities. However, during scale-down (reducing the replica count), the scheduler does not come into the picture potentially resulting in a violation of the scheduling policies. It is irrelevant whether the scale-down is automatic or manual.

Consider the case that there are 5 pods being spread across 3 machines, with 2 pods on each of the two machines and 1 pod on the third machine. If the replica count is reduced to 4, we shouldn't remove the single pod from the third machine (assuming the scheduler policy is to achieve greatest possible spread). To address this, we need to involve the scheduler in the workflow to figure out which pod(s) to get rid of. 

Also, see https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/3948 for some other concerns related to determining which pods are removed when the replica count is reduced.

I do not have a proposed solution for this would like to invite some discussion and feedback on this issue.

title: Kubernetes should support cross-zone cluster

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

body:
Most applications should be running in multiple zones to increase availability. Kubernetes should support it. I imagine this to work in the following way:
1. User sets up cluster in a region in a way that minions are spread evenly across all available zones
2. User creates replication controller for the application with size > 1
3. Scheduler spreads pods within the same replication controller across available zones

That way user gets regional availability for free.

AFAIU this will mostly require changes in how we create cluster and how we schedule pods.

cc @wojtek-t

body:
I started a new deployment of kubernetes cluster, and I noticed that an idle kubelet, to which no pod has been bound yet, writes the following error log in every second:

```
Feb 05 10:27:56 node01 kubelet[3359]: E0205 10:27:56.753081    3359 etcd.go:64] etcd failed to retrieve the value for the key "/registry/nodes/node01/boundpods". Error: 100: Key not found (/registry/nodes/node01) [22]
Feb 05 10:27:57 node01 kubelet[3359]: E0205 10:27:57.753844    3359 etcd.go:64] etcd failed to retrieve the value for the key "/registry/nodes/node01/boundpods". Error: 100: Key not found (/registry/nodes/node01) [22]
Feb 05 10:27:58 node01 kubelet[3359]: E0205 10:27:58.754592    3359 etcd.go:64] etcd failed to retrieve the value for the key "/registry/nodes/node01/boundpods". Error: 100: Key not found (/registry/nodes/node01) [22]
Feb 05 10:27:59 node01 kubelet[3359]: E0205 10:27:59.755346    3359 etcd.go:64] etcd failed to retrieve the value for the key "/registry/nodes/node01/boundpods". Error: 100: Key not found (/registry/nodes/node01) [22]
Feb 05 10:28:00 node01 kubelet[3359]: E0205 10:28:00.836717    3359 etcd.go:64] etcd failed to retrieve the value for the key "/registry/nodes/node01/boundpods". Error: 100: Key not found (/registry/nodes/node01) [22]
Feb 05 10:28:01 node01 kubelet[3359]: E0205 10:28:01.837324    3359 etcd.go:64] etcd failed to retrieve the value for the key "/registry/nodes/node01/boundpods". Error: 100: Key not found (/registry/nodes/node01) [22]
```

After pod is scheduled to the kubelet, it stops writing this error. Then when every pods are unassigned from the kubelet, and it becomes idle again, the above logs do not appear again.

The reason is most probably that the general node information is stored under `/registry/minions/{node name}` in etcd right after setting up the cluster (starting kube-controller-manager with `--machine` option), while information about bound pods is stored under `/registry/nodes/{node name}/boundpods` key when the first pod is scheduled on the given node.

```

    "action": "get",
    "node": {
        "createdIndex": 26,
        "dir": true,
        "key": "/registry/nodes/node01",
        "modifiedIndex": 26,
        "nodes": [
            {
                "createdIndex": 26,
                "key": "/registry/nodes/node01/boundpods",
                "modifiedIndex": 32,
                "value": "{\"kind\":\"BoundPods\",\"creationTimestamp\":null,\"resourceVersion\":26,\"apiVersion\":\"v1beta1\",\"host\":\"\",\"items\":[]}"
            }
        ]
    }
}
[root@node00 ~]# curl -L -s http://node00:4001/v2/keys/registry/minions/node01 | python -mjson.tool
{
    "action": "get",
    "node": {
        "createdIndex": 8,

body:
I spun up a k8s cluster on CoreOS using [https://github.com/pires/kubernetes-vagrant-coreos-cluster](this vagrant setup). I was able to create & list Pods, but the Pod containers would never get launched. The kubelet log showed what looks like an issue with an etcd watcher. Note the 'key modified index' is much lower than the cluster index (cluster: 26286, key: 19255), meaning the watch will never get triggered. I understand this is a known issue in etcd, and it cannot be fixed correctly without major changes to the data model. To work around this, the kubernetes watchers need to be using the cluster index when creating watchers rather than the key's modified index.

Manual Workaround: "touch" the etcd key by doing:

etcdctl get /registry/nodes/172.17.8.102/boundpods | etcdctl set /registry/nodes/172.17.8.102/boundpods
```

title: Binding annotations should be preserved alongside Host assignment

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Recap of related tangent in #2483 follows.

Use case:  I need to implement mesos task reconciliation in the kubernetes-mesos scheduler. If it crashes and then restarts, I want to be able to recover things like taskID, slaveID, offerID, etc. so as to rebuild the internal state of the scheduler. Once state is recovered, I can reconcile the against the tasks that the mesos master knows about.

If I can't use binding annotations for this, then I need to store state some other (super inconvenient) way. Currently the etcd registry assignPod() implementation drops binding annotations on the floor. It should not, and instead they should be preserved for later access.

Proposal: Store binding-related annotations in a new field: Pod.Status.Annotations
- When setting Pod.Status.Host="{some-host-name}" via assignPod(), binding annotations are copied in from Binding
- When cloning Pod.Status.Host in UpdatePod() (for an already-scheduled pod), the Pod.Status.Annotations are also cloned.

I don't think /bindings has to be a readable apiserver endpoint, as long as the binding metadata is exposed some other way, as proposed above.

I'd also like to propose that once binding annotations are "bound" to Pod.Status they become read-only. So they're essentially write-once, just like Pod.Status.Host is meant to be.

cc @smarterclayton @bgrant0607 @erictune 
xref https://github.com/mesosphere/kubernetes-mesos/issues/73

body:
Every node on GCE by default has cAdvisor, fluentd-es running as pod. We are going to put etcd server into a pod soon, and other master components into pods later. Those pods are pre-provisioned, and not through apiserver, and scheduler, I called them "static" pods. 

Today, kubelet does generate events related to those static pods, and push them to etcd. But there is no way to query those pods config from clients, and static pods in crashloop cannot be detected easily  because apiserver doesn't aware of them. 

Also those pods do consume resources, and without awareness of static pods on a node, scheduler might overcommit a node easily. 

We should have a mechanism defined for kubelet to sync back to master with those static Pods. 

cc/ @bgrant0607 @thockin @brendandburns

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

body:
What are the intended capitalization rules for labels? I wouldn't be surprised if it's that both the keys and values should be all lower case, but I don't see it defined anywhere, unless it's assumed that the identifiers.md doc about names applies to them as well.

I bring this up because the validation applied to labels on pods seems to be more strict than that applied to labels on nodes. I was able to attach a label "diskSize: massive" to a node, but got errors (very unhelpful ones, at that) when trying to attach the same label to a pod or in a pod's nodeSelector:
`ERROR: F0203 13:18:17.236041    6515 create.go:78] pod "nginx" is invalid: spec.nodeSelector: invalid value 'diskSize'`

I think there's 3 things to do here:
1. Pick a capitalization policy and document it - presumably in one of the two labels docs.
2. Improve the error message for users not following the policy.
3. Ensure it's validated consistently for different resource types.

title: Remaining work for using tokens instead of basic auth

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
#2328 is about having a flow for issuing new tokens and new users.

In addition to that, we also need to just be able to accept a bearer token for the "admin" user, rather than basic auth.  Not sure that #2328 is planning to encompass that, and at any rate @jlowdermilk may be interested in getting something going with bearer tokens before that PR lands.

So, here is what I recall needed to be done:
- there is already a function called get-admin-token in master/cluster/gce/util.sh that generates a token.  Not sure what calls that if anything.  But it looks good to use.
- In kube-up in that file, it calls get-passwd to get or generates a password, and makes a htpasswd file.  We don't need that anymore.  .  We need to call get-admin-token in place of get-passwd and stick that into a file somewhere that the apiserver can read.
- cluster/saltbase/salt/kube-apiserver/default is where we tell the apiserver where the token file is.  That should be fine as is. 
- cluster/gce/templates/create-dynamic-salt-files.sh is where we generate the token for the kubelet and stick it into the tokens file, which is just a csv file.  We'd want to have, at a minimim, one line for the kubelet token and another line for the admin token, in that file  So you need to work out how to get both in there, and the kubelet one to the kubelet and the admin one to the user.  
- currently, the apiserver sits behind the nginx proxy.  Nginx doesn't support bearer tokens, afaics, and anyhow we want the apiserver to handle the token so it can map the token to a user and apply policies.   And we want apiserver to terminate SSL because that is how the code is currently written to work.  so:
  - we need to get rid of nginx altogether
  - change the apiserver so that it serves on port 443, with authentication enabled.  That means setting --auth_port to 443 instead of 6443 in cluster/saltbase/salt/kube-apiserver/default.  You will then have to change the kubelets so that they talk to port 443 instead of  6443.
  - Ideally, we do the same for AWS and Azure kube-ups too, and ask someone to test them.

@jlowdermilk FYI

body:
kubectl decodes a json file and encodes it again before sending out the request to the API server, i.e.,
`versioned json-> versioned api object -> internal api object -> versioned api object -> versioned json`
The API server then decodes the versioned json and converts it to the internal API object. 

It is debatable whether kubectl needs to perform the round-trip conversion, since the API server would perform the similar process immediately after receiving the request. Can we simplify this?

title: Remove --auth-path from kubectl

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Since the .kubeconfig file was introduced, there is a new way to describe the information contained inside of the existing .kubernetes_auth format.  .kubernetes_auth combined information that described how to recognize the api-server with information about how to authenticate the user to the api-server.  .kubeconfig separates those two concepts into discretely re-useable chunks, but --auth-path was kept for backwards compatibility.

If .kubernetes_auth is eliminated, there will be one way to express that information and that will simplify the explanation of how the information is built.  Right now, allowing references to .kuberentes_auth and defaulting to looking at the ~/.kubernetes_auth makes it harder to describe exactly where authentication information is coming from.

This would be a breaking change that has ripples affecting e2e tests, so I'd like to be sure there is agreement to the concept before starting a change.

/cc @jlowdermilk @smarterclayton @liggitt

title: Resolve the form of special "verbs" in the api for v1beta3

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

body:
Currently, we support custom "verbs" such as proxy, redirect, and watch. These prefix the object paths, such as /api/v1beta1/watch/... (Note that proxy doesn't follow the actual path convention: api/v1beta1/proxy/minion/minion1:10250 -- note that minion is singular, and the port number.) See #3548 and #3612 for more examples. 

More verbs are proposed, such as stop (#1535), resize (#1629), and clone (#170).

In order to be more compatible with REST/OO style, to simplify auth, and to facilitate discoverability and shardability, I propose we change these to SUFFIX api paths, in the standard collection/instance pattern. Something like: _object_path_/methods/verb_name. Note that some "verbs" (e.g., resize) require the ability to GET as well as POST, which is somewhat different than our REST objects.

@smarterclayton @lavalamp

title: GCE: Reduce the frequency of calls to "compute.instances.get" API

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
The current default free quota for requests to the GCE API is 250,000 requests/day.

We're finding that we easily exceed that when attempting to run a k8s cluster with 20 or more minions.

Some numbers for reference (pulled from the GCE console):

20 minions ~ 3.2 /sec ~ 276K requests/day to "compute.instances.get", which exceeds the daily quota
12 minions ~ 2.1 /sec ~ 181K requests/day

We're running k8s v0.8.1 FWIW.

The number of calls to the other GCE API methods pales in comparison, with compute.instances.get making up ~95% of all the API traffic:

| method | count | % |
| --- | --- | --- |
| compute.instances.get | 960,002 | 95.2% |
| compute.instances.list | 33,347 | 3.3% |
| compute.zones.list | 6,050 | 0.6% |
| ... | ... | ... |

We've scaled down the number of minions for now, until we either request a quota increase, or the API call frequency is reduced somewhat.

title: Volume that overrides a Dockerfile VOLUME doesn't mount into container

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
I'm trying to start a MongoDB container which overrides the default data volume /data/db (specified by the image's [Dockerfile  VOLUME directive)](https://github.com/docker-library/mongo/blob/master/2.6/Dockerfile).

Kubernetes fails to mount the overridden volume from the path configured for the pod. Docker inspect shows that the volume is actually mounted from /var/lib/docker/vfs/dir/xxx, i.e. the default path.

For comparison, mounting another data volume with a different path in the same container works just fine. Also, running a similar container manually with Docker CLI works fine and mounts /data/db properly. SELinux doesn't seem to affect this but I've tried with "setenforce 0" just in case. My environment is Fedora 21 Atomic which uses Docker 1.4.0.

These are the relevant portions from "docker inspect" when the container is running:

```
"HostConfig": {
    "Binds": [
        "/var/lib/data/mongodb/data/db:/data/db",
        "/var/lib/data/mongodb/data/db2:/data/db2"
    ],
    "VolumesFrom": null
},
"Volumes": {
    "/data/db": "/var/lib/docker/vfs/dir/d0064b45422af35e836b39256233e616fb7909803e621e6a4006914c5b769ead",
    "/data/db2": "/var/lib/data/mongodb/data/db2"
},
"VolumesRW": {
    "/data/db": true,
    "/data/db2": true
}
```

The pod configuration looks like this:

```
apiVersion: v1beta1
kind: Pod
id: mongodb
labels:
  name: mongodb
desiredState:
  manifest:
    version: v1beta1
    id: mongodb
    volumes:
      - name: mongodb-data
        source:
          hostDir:
            path: /var/lib/data/mongodb/data/db
      - name: mongodb-data2
        source:
          hostDir:
            path: /var/lib/data/mongodb/data/db2
    containers:
      - name: mongodb
        image: mongo:2.6.6
        command: ['mongod', '--smallfiles']
        volumeMounts:
          - name: mongodb-data
            mountPath: /data/db
          - name: mongodb-data2
            mountPath: /data/db2
```

labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
The general question of upgrades is discussed in #2524 

The question of version skew between the master and components that use the API is discussed in #3560.

With the closing of #3376, only the apiserver needs to talk to its storage (etcd).  User may want to upgrade the apiserver version while keeping the storage intact.  We need to define how far apart the old version and new version of apiserver can be.   

Two issues:
1. new apiserver supports a new api version.  Can't upgrade, create new object, and then roll back without upgrading them.  
2. new and old have the same api versions, but hidden details of the storage format have changed (directory structure, etc).

For item 1, propose that users should do upgrades in stages:
- upgrade to new apiserver version but don't expose new api version.
- test it, commit to it.
- flip flag to expose new api version.  
- if a bug is exposed by that, then newly created object will need to be manually fixed up.

For item 2, propose:
- we plan to support upgrades and reverts across, say, 1 minor revision (e.g. v0.7.1 to v0.8.4).  Do multiple upgrades if you are further behind.

So with a schema like:

id: cloud-delivery-test
labels:

desiredState:

        containers:
        - name: cloud-delivery-test
          image: quay.io/littlebits/cloud-delivery-test:latest
          ports:
          - name: cloud-delivery-test
            containerPort: 7654
          env:
          - name: PORT
            value: 7654
```

It fails when used like so:

```
⧑  kubectl rollingupdate cloud-delivery-test -f kubernetes-v1beta2/replicationController.yaml                                                      

Continuing update with existing controller cloud-delivery-test.
F0113 23:31:57.503427   57607 rollingupdate.go:99] Missing/unexpected annotations for controller cloud-delivery-test: map[]
```

If I try a `v1beta3` schema that looks like:

``` yaml
kind: ReplicationController
apiVersion: v1beta3
metadata:
  name: cloud-delivery-test
  labels:
    name: cloud-delivery-test
    version: 0.5.0
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    name: cloud-delivery-test
    version: 0.5.0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        name: cloud-delivery-test
        version: 0.5.0
    spec:

      - name: cloud-delivery-test

        - name: PORT

then the error is:

⧑ kubectl rollingupdate cloud-delivery-test -f kubernetes-v1beta3/replicationController.yaml                                                      

F0114 09:43:17.497021   58006 resource.go:302] no object named "ReplicationController" is registered
```

The error generation comes from: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/6e242739378fd830a62afb1375c80ad24254a85b/pkg/kubectl/rolling_updater.go#L154-L155

title: Revist design of Annotations currently stored in docker container name

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
We currently only supports one annotation (container source), and it is stored as part of the docker container name ([pkg/kubelet/types.go#L73](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/types.go#L73)):

``` GO
// GetPodFullName returns a name that uniquely identifies a pod across all config sources.
func GetPodFullName(pod *api.BoundPod) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("%s.%s.%s", pod.Name, pod.Namespace, pod.Annotations[ConfigSourceAnnotationKey])
}

// ParsePodFullName unpacks a pod full name and returns the pod name, namespace, and annotations.
// If the pod full name is invalid, empty strings are returend.
func ParsePodFullName(podFullName string) (podName, podNamespace string, podAnnotations map[string]string) {
    parts := strings.Split(podFullName, ".")
    expectedNumFields := 3
    actualNumFields := len(parts)
    if actualNumFields != expectedNumFields {
        glog.Warningf("found a podFullName (%q) with too few fields: expected %d, actual %d.", podFullName, expectedNumFields, actualNumFields)
        return
    }
    podName = parts[0]
    podNamespace = parts[1]
    podAnnotations = make(map[string]string)
    podAnnotations[ConfigSourceAnnotationKey] = parts[2]
    return
}
```

Example Kubernetes Docker container name:

```
/k8s_mynginx1.18b0b73d_ca4e7148-9ab9-11e4-924c-f0921cde18c1.default.etcd_ca4e7148-9ab9-11e4-924c-f0921cde18c1_7b81f5b7
  ^     ^       ^           ^                                                 ^                                   ^
  |     |       |           |                                                 |                                   |
 prefix |    hash       full pod name                                       uuid                          rand.Uint32()
      container name
```

The delimiter is "`_`", so the full pod name is:

```
ca4e7148-9ab9-11e4-924c-f0921cde18c1.default.etcd
  ^                                   ^        ^
  |                                   |        |
pod name                     pod name space    |
                                           pod source
```

The delimiter is "`.`", and so the source is:

```
etcd
```

Questions to consider:
- Will we ever have more then one annotation?
- If so, should annotations be stored in the docker container name, or elsewhere?
- If the annotations should be stored in the container name, what would the key value pairs/delimiters look like (keep in mind that "." is already used as a delimiter for the pod name fields and "_" is used as a delimiter for the container name fields)?
- If the annotations should be stored in the container name, what validation, if any should be done on key/value pairs to avoid parsing errors?

title: Rev Travis GoFmt version

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Travis currently runs GoFmt only on Go v1.3 builds not 1.4. This is because GoFmt rules for 1.3 and 1.4 can conflict: for example, Go v1.4 no longer requires assignment in for-range loops, so the GoFmt optimizations differ for both versions (i.e. v1.3 expects `_ = range blah` 1.4 expects just `range blah`).

This causes issues for those of us running 1.4 locally, because running GoFmt locally produces code that fails Travis 1.3 builds. And if we use v1.3 syntax, local commits are blocked because v1.4 GoFmt won't be happy (which can be overridden but is still annoying).

Recommendation: modify Travis to Run GoFmt on Go v1.4 builds instead of v1.3 builds.

title: Proposal: deouple networking for segmentation and other use cases

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

body:
The Kubernetes network design works great for interconnecting containers and build services construct to avoid ports-conflict ,etc. I am capturing some use-cases that, in my opinion, are not supported due to the current network design (https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/design/networking.md).
### Use-Case 1: Multi-tenancy - multiple disjoint container networks:

Today, a container can talk to another container as long as it knows the IP and port (or perhaps it can scan the entire range). Supporting isolation between multiple container networks will disallow unintended communication, especially if a user is running application developed by third party. This is a fundamental need for multi-tenant deployment. It also allows separation needed for accidental (non malicious) inter-connectivity/communication between a set of apps, for example a development app server can’t accidentally connect to a production db, etc. The separation also allows for overlapping IP address space in disjoint networks (see IPAM comment below), secure PaaS infrastructure, and flexible rules using which these apps can communicate with each other.
### Use-Case 2: Bridged/L2-connectivity

Bridged connectivity at layer2 between applications/containers will help enable following sub use-cases:
- Applications that rely on multi-destination services (e.g. mDNS for auto-discovery, or broadcast for DHCP based IPAM), will benefit from this support.
- Applications that require communicating with non-container applications at l2 level. Say a infrastructure provider has a hardware-accelerated firewall device and require that all traffic exiting a given l2-domain (aka bridged network) must traverse through the firewall.
- Applications that require their peers apps to be in the same subnet. While I understand there are very few apps that still talk non-IP, but apps that cluster together do use some basic form of adjacent l2 reachability (e.g. Jboss clusters) to discover/interact with each other. Today, since an entire subnet belongs to one host this is not possible. With some changes to flannel (or equivalent overlay), it should be possible to support this with host routes advertisements and install these routes upon receiving updates from others (think scale!). On other hand use of services for this is neither needed, nor desired (for scale and indirection).
### Use-Case 3: SDN applications

Most of the SDN apps manage the life-cycle of various flows by applying rules to which the communication between apps need to abide by to get the advantage of software defined network in very unique ways. Allowing POD’s IP/network and eventually flow manipulation (iptables in linux-bridge or openflow rules in ovs) will allow Kubernetes controller to be used in such deployments to schedule jobs and all rest of the goodness. Perhaps flow manipulation can be done outside Kubernetes (pardon my ignorance, I am still catching up on the code), certainly IP/MAC allocation, subnet-reachability and hooks thereof are the ones tied in closely.
### Use-Case 4: Multicast Applications

Applications that use IP multicast (PIM-SM/SSM, or PIM-BIDIR), for example to to stream video-webcast, will benefit from container deployment. The network model of kubernetes needs to change to allow applications to join (igmp) the multicast-tree or become a source of multicast tree by allowing to send multi-destination traffic within the network (stated above the need for multi-destination apps in deployment).
Then there are clustering application that rely on multicast to discover the peers (but that discovery is usually done within a bridged domain, which ties into previous use case stated earlier).
### Use-Case 5: IPAM integration with current tools

For infrastructure users that use somewhat sophisticated IPAM policy, for example CNR, (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IP_address_management), it will allow backward compatibility to current suite of tools, if the IPAM is decoupled from scheduling/replication-controllers in kubernetes.
### Summary

Kubernetes is a great tool; decoupling networking code, and exposing them as APIs, would allow more use cases. To that extend, the proposal is asking to:
- Keep the current networking model as default (i.e. no change to the user experience), but decouple networking from rest of the functions (aka scheduling/replication-controllers/services)
- Allow others to plug-in or enhance kubernetes itself to support the above use cases. 
- It will also fit in the plugin model for network that is being worked upon and proposed in docker and coreos community (https://github.com/docker/docker/issues/9983 and https://github.com/coreos/rocket/issues/273)

If people agree this is worth a shot, then along with the community, I can work on the code changes and submit it back to the community for review towards this initiative.

`Disclaimer: I work for Cisco`

title: Discussion: Version skewed e2e tests

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
There is a somewhat heavy dev burden to pay if the tests in `hack/e2e-suite` have to run against old cluster versions. Take the issue fixed in #3314. Was @thockin supposed to run e2es against all released versions of the code? Questions here:
- Do we even want to support version skewed e2e tests?
- What's the line? What GKE supports? (That seems arbitrary.) The official k8s upgrade matrix (when we resolve that)? What?
- If we don't, how are we planning on supporting cross-version testing? We could potentially do something where we're grabbing new binaries and running old tests, but then we could just be running crappy tests. The tests at head also represent improvements to the test.

We may also be overthinking the dev burden. I think the problem here:https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/commit/e045c6ce2fd81b85637894a1655a90bc367b90f7#commitcomment-9206336 (fixed in #3314) may actually be mitigated by abstracting the "shoot things in the head" pieces into a library. We could then test the library against all dev releases, and ask everyone to run e2e tests against HEAD, and if you add one of these "muck with cluster internals" things, only then do you need to add a version specific piece and do it cross-versioned. I think there's definite room for refactoring here.

Other relevant reading includes:
- https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wwh569PwAWvEZcLc0gHSrO1xr-N-T5cnKjepjc0dXvI/edit#heading=h.20sqp7sxyy7q
- https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/2953 (to help with how to actually accomplish shooting things in the add during development, as we're adding features)
- ... and I'm probably missing some.

cc @thockin @roberthbailey @lavalamp

title: Add default config file lookup pattern

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
When `kubectl` is given a CRUD command for a resource (`pod`, `replicationController`, `service`), if it is not explicitly given a path to a config file, it should try a systematic file system lookup pattern for a config file for that resource.

Presumably these CRUD commands are being issued for a project and therefore I think the lookup pattern would not go beyond the `cwd`. _However_... it would be interesting if the command could be issues within any directory inside a project. `git` for instance gets away with this because it assumes the project root has a `.git` folder.

Some sketchy ideas:
1. per-resource config files like `.kubernetes-pod.yaml`, `.kubernetes-replicationController.yaml`, etc.
2. single config file like `.kubernetes.yaml`
3. directory like `.kubernetes` with per-resource config files therein like `pod.yaml`, `replicationController.yaml`, etc.
4. directory like `.kubernetes` with single config file like `config.yaml`

A `.kubernetes` _folder_ seems somewhat interesting:
- A folder space for additional meta files and other resources; Perhaps a place for plugins/higher-level-tools to add functionality in a standardized way
- A folder that provides the aforementioned ability for `kubectl` to detect the "project root"

Do not necessarily take this idea too literally, its just a sketch for a general feature-characteristic. Lots of ways this could be skinned/go. The goal is ultimately:
1. A way to streamline defaults (e.g. auto-discovered config files)
2. A standard way for extensions to plant themselves

title: kubectl get pods says REASON, but reason for what?

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
Example output from my cluster:

```
$ kubectl get pods
NAME                      READY     REASON                                  RESTARTS   AGE
cpuhog                    0/1       ExitCode:127                            0          1h
frontend                  0/2       Pending                                 0          1h
frontend2                 0/1       Running                                 12         48m
frontend3                 0/1       Running                                 11         39m
frontend4                 0/1       Pending                                 0          18m
frontendbig               0/2       Pending                                 0          16s
kube-dns-v3-hzdfg         3/3       Running                                 2          3d
memhog                    0/1       OOM Killed                              0          5m
private-image-test-2      0/1       Running                                 12         3d
private-image-test-3      0/1       Error: image foo/private:v1 not found   0          3d
```

What is the REASON column a reason _for_?
It looks like it is the reason for being terminated if terminated, otherwise it is showing `status.phase`, except when `status.phase == "Failed"`, in which case it shows one of the `.status.containerStatuses[].state.terminated.reason`.

I think it would be clearer to show phase and then reason, so that it is clear that the reason about why it is in that phase.

For example:

```
$ kubectl get pods
NAME                      READY     PHASE    REASON                                  RESTARTS   AGE
cpuhog                    0/1       Failed   ExitCode:127                            0          1h
frontend                  0/2       Pending                                          0          1h
frontend2                 0/1       Running                                          12         48m
frontend3                 0/1       Running                                          11         39m
frontend4                 0/1       Pending                                          0          18m
frontendbig               0/2       Pending                                          0          16s
kube-dns-v3-hzdfg         3/3       Running                                          2          3d
memhog                    0/1       Failed   OOM Killed                              0          5m
private-image-test-2      0/1       Running                                          12         3d
private-image-test-3      0/1       Pending  Error: image foo/private:v1 not found   0          3d
```

I get that we are trying to save screen width.  It costs 8 columns to separate Phase.
We could recover 3 columns by narrowing the READY column
and another 3 by renaming "RESTARTS" to "TRIES".

title: Improve scheduler event messages

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
Scheduler event:

```
Events:
  FirstSeen  ... Reason                    Message
  ...              ...  failedScheduling    Error scheduling: For each of these fitness predicates, pod frontend failed on at least one node: PodFitsResources.
```

Problems with this event message:
1. It says `Error`, but having pods fail to schedule is a common event in a system, and "Error" is too alarming a term.
1. It says `scheduling`, but the event makes it clear that this is about scheduling in both the `From` and `Reason` fields.
1. it says `For each of these fitness predicates .. failed on at least one node:` but there is only one predicate in this case.  Lets be concise and to the point where possible.  Maybe when only one predicate failed, say: `No node satisfied rule PodFitsResources`.
1. the message contains the string `pod frontend`, but that information is already present in the event object.  Save space by removing this.  Also, it reduces the cardinality of the set of distinct message strings, which facilitates grouping of events.

An improved output looks something like this:

```
Events:
  FirstSeen  ... Reason                    Message
  ...              ...  failedScheduling    No node found where PodFitsResources.
```

body:
Here's the question I want to answer: when I use kubectl, what cluster am I talking to?

As a developer with several clusters, this is a really important question to me.

I was looking through `kubectl config --help` and I saw the options are:

```
  view            displays Merged kubeconfig settings or a specified kubeconfig file.
  set-cluster     Sets a cluster entry in kubeconfig
  set-credentials Sets a user entry in kubeconfig
  set-context     Sets a context entry in kubeconfig
  set             Sets an individual value in a kubeconfig file
  unset           Unsets an individual value in a kubeconfig file
  use-context     Sets the current-context in a kubeconfig file
```

Only asking @jlowdermilk did I learn that `kubectl config view --minify` was what I wanted. This seems kind of crazy! `--minify`? To see my current context?

@bgrant0607 how would you feel about one of the following options?
1. Top-level "GET" analogs for the "PUT" methods (get-cluster, get-credentials, get-context, ...)
2. Have `kubectl config view` output _only_ the current context by default, and have a flag like `--full` for the full config (rather than having to pass `--minify` for the current context).

(Leaving this for oncall and @bgrant0607 to determine priority.)

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
In docs/resources.md we state that cpu is actually in units of KCU, which is normalized CPU.
But, on GCE/GKE we don't do that.  Nor on Vagrant, or anything else.
As @justinsb points out, the AWS cloud provider is reporting cores in ECUs (amazon's normalized core).
GCE is reporting actual cores.
GCE used to have GCEUs but it seems the documentation for that is gone.

So, we need to do something.  Some options:
1.  kubernetes.io/cpu resource is implementation defined.  
- Can continue to use ECU on amazon
- Can continue to use absolute on GCE
- Remove mention of KCU from docs.
- Config is portable, but performance varies.
  1. kubernetes.io/cpu resource is cores on all cloud-providers.
- Change Amazon
- Fixup docs  
- Config is portable, but performance varies
  1. kubernetes.io/cpu resource is normalized for all platforms, and ostensibly comparable across cloud-providers
- put actual core count as a new field on nodes, in case anyone cares
- define values for GCE, other platforms
- Let the battle begin over who's cores are better 
- Constantly update a table of (processor type, core) to KCU mappings, as there are vastly more types of cpus in the wide world than there are just on amazon and GCE.
- Config is portable, and performance varies less
  1. Each platform can define its own normalized unit, with cores as a fallback
- kubernetes.io/ecu means AWS ECUs
- cloud.google.com/kcu means some normalized unit for GCE processors
-  Config is not portable, and you are forced to think about performance when porting.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

milestone.title: v1.2-candidate
milestone.description: Things to consider for next minor release.

body: Using iptables commands directly on a system managed by firewalld can result in problems. Currently all documentation recommends turning off firewalld before using kubernetes. Instead, like docker, we should send commands to firewalld instead of directly via exec of iptables. This removes the race issues where they both try to operate at the same time and removes problems where our rules are removed for no apparent reason.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

body:
Currently, tests are built based on "apiserver_request_latencies_summary" which is SummaryVec.
The drawback of this approach is that SummaryVec is considering only request from the last X minutes to be valid ones - for more details see:
https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/860

By default this is 10 minutes (which is reasonable for tests taking less than 10 minutes). However, for tests taking 30 minutes (capacity load) we are measuring something not well defined.

Probably the easiest fix for now is to increase the maxAge (which I'm going to do now), but we should rethink it deeper after 1.0.
