labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Currently it is possible in a kubeconfig file to do:

``` yaml
users:
- name: kubelet
  user:
    client-certificate: /etc/kubernetes/certs/kubecfg.crt
    client-key: /etc/kubernetes/certs/kubecfg.key
```

But it is not possible to do:

``` yaml
users:
- name: proxy
  user:
    token: /etc/kubernetes/token/proxy.token
```

This means that certificates and kubeconfig files can be decoupled and distributed separately, but kubeconfig files and tokens MUST be managed together.

Not sure if it's possible to distinguish, so maybe a "token_file" option?

title: Sort yaml/json fields more helpfully when printing objects

labels.name: priority/backlog

body:
When I do `kubectl get foo/bar -o yaml`, I see things like this:

```
apiVersion: v1beta3
foo: blah     <------------- why is this before kind and metadata?
kind: bar
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: 2015-06-24T21:09:17Z  
  name: myregistrykey  <----- why isn't this first because it is the most important metadata.
  namespace: default
  resourceVersion: "1497"
  selfLink: /api/v1beta3/namespaces/default/secrets/myregistrykey
  uid: 46703fde-1ab5-11e5-b558-42010af0cf71
zlist:
  - property: foo   
    name: bar   <---------- why isn't name always first?
```

It appears that tags are sorted alphabetically.
I'd rather always see fields that are in all objects at the top, so `apiVersion`, `kind`, and `metadata` should come before any kind-specific fields. (In the above example, field `foo` comes before `metadata`).

And I'd rather see `name` as the first property in a list for which name is the merge key.

Maybe this is just my opinion.

body:
2 issues:
1. node controller pod eviction
2. kubelet restarts by monit

The nodecontroller can send an event when it decides to evict pods from a node for 1 and we already have a kubelet restart event we can watch. Useful things to list out when one of these happens:
1. Running pods (via the master proxy, getting this before the pods are gone would be nice)
2. High latency node operations, eg: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/density.go#L373
3. Node resource info: Should be a way to get it out of cadvisor, otherwise an on demand ad-hoc ps debug endpoint?

This will also flag deadlocks (i.e if monit restarts the kubelet but all latencies/resource utilization look normal). 

/ref https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/10282

title: Issues with GCE and service type LoadBalancer

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/support
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as a support question.

body:
Now that publicIPs have become deprecatedPublicIPs, and is on its way out. I have found a couple of issues dealing with service type LoadBalancer.
1. It doesn't support UDP (if I recall correctly this is being addressed)
2. Doesn't support static IPs on GCE. I can't seem to find a way to create a LoadBalancer service on kubernetes, and then assign an existing static IP you already have on GCE to it. So if you delete the service and create it again, there is no way to go back to the old IP you had, even if you still own that IP (GCE) and is free to be used.
3. It creates a target pool per each service. So if I have 70 services and I scale the cluster, I have to manually go thru all 70 backends and update its members. It will be nice if LoadBalancer type had a way to pass which backend to use, if it doesn't exists create it, otherwise reuse it. At the end all backends point to the same set of minions, why create one per each service?

Use cases:
- DNS: this applies for 1 and 2
- Any service that requires an static IP, lets say a company web site: this applies for 2
- If you have a lot of services and decide to scale the cluster... have fun: applies for 3.

The way I used to deal with those use cases was to manually create the forwarding rules on GCE using only one backend and then create a service clusterIP with publicIP set to the GCE loadbalancer IP. This solves 1, 2 and 3.

Am I looking at this from the wrong angle and missing something? Is there anyways to deal with those issues without publicIPs / deprecatedPublicIPs ?

title: Improve e2e test coverage of services

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
What's currently included in the services e2e test:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/service.go
1. Services should serve a basic endpoint from pods
2. Services should serve multiport endpoints from pods
3. Services should be able to create a functioning external load balancer
4. Services should be able to create a functioning NodePort service
5. Services should be able to change the type and nodeport settings of a service
6. Services should release the load balancer when Type goes from LoadBalancer -> NodePort
7. Services should prevent NodePort collisions
8. Services should check NodePort out-of-range
9. Services should release NodePorts on delete
10. Services should correctly serve identically named services in different namespaces on different external IP addresses

What's not yet covered (and there are surely more than what's in the following list):
- [x] Multiport TCP services (this seems false given item 2 above - update the comments).  https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/service.go#L67
- [ ] Spreading of traffic across backends appropriately (round robin etc).  @satnam6502 had an indirect test somewhere for this AFAIK, but we should perhaps factor it into a narrow service-specific test.
- [ ] LiveNessProbes (perhaps belongs in Kubelet e2e tests, but it would be good to make sure that they are usable and work properly in the use case of providing a highly available service).
- [ ] ReadinessProbes (comments as above)
- [ ] General high availability of services in the presence of pod or network failure. Inject pod, node and network failures, and verify that the service remains available, within the published specs.
- [ ] More... ??

title: Clean up excessive volume mounts for SSL

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
According to https://golang.org/src/crypto/x509/root_unix.go, the list of places that golang looks for root certificates is:

```
    13      "/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt",     // Debian/Ubuntu/Gentoo etc.
    14      "/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt",       // Fedora/RHEL
    15      "/etc/ssl/ca-bundle.pem",                 // OpenSUSE
    16      "/etc/ssl/cert.pem",                      // OpenBSD
    17      "/usr/local/share/certs/ca-root-nss.crt", // FreeBSD/DragonFly
    18      "/etc/pki/tls/cacert.pem",                // OpenELEC
    19      "/etc/certs/ca-certificates.crt",         // Solaris 11.2+
```

We don't care about OpenBSD, FreeBSD, or Solaris yet.
So, the only possible paths are:
- `/etc/ssl/...`
- `/etc/pki/tls/...`

Currently, the Pods for apiserver, scheduler, and controller-manager also mount these dirs:
- `/usr/share/ssl`
- `/var/ssl`
- `/usr/local/openssl`
- `/etc/openssl`
- `/usr/ssl`
- `/usr/lib/ssl`

Go won't search any of these.  So, they should be removed from the Pod spec.

Also, all these directories are empty on a GCE debian node (except `/usr/lib/ssl` which holds hard links to the files in `/etc/ssl/`.

title: Proposal: Network Labels for pods (e.g. for security-groups), libnetwork remote driver

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
# libnetwork

Docker has got a new network stack: [libnetwork](https://github.com/docker/libnetwork)
libnetwork supports external logic to manage container networking via a remote driver API.
When starting up a container libnetwork asks the remote driver to create one or more network endpoints, set them up and attach them to the container. It is possible to provide user defined options in form of key-value pairs to the driver. After the driver has created and attached the endpoints Docker will execute the container.
# Proposal

The idea is to add network-labels to the Kubernetes pod manifest. These labels will be propagated through Docker into the libnetwork remote driver. The remote driver will configure the container's network according to the given labels.
This allows to realize some interesting things: For example you can attach a container to multiple separated networks. Or you can realize security groups.
## Multiple Networks

You could separate pods via different networks. E.g. tenantA would have an other network than tenantB.
## Security Groups

Security groups may work like this:
You have an application-server pod and add a network-label `security-groups=http-server,db-client`. Further you have a database pod with the network-label `security-groups=db-server`.
When starting the pods Docker will provide these labels to the libnetwork remote driver. The driver creates the network endpoints and configures iptables with rules defined by the security groups.
E.g. the security group `db-server` may look like this:

```
allow incoming traffic from sec-group 'db-client' to TCP port 3306.
allow outgoing traffic to sec-group 'db-client' from TCP port 3306.
```

and `db-client` could look like this:

```
allow outgoing traffic to sec-group 'db-server' to TCP port 3306.
allow incoming traffic from sec-group 'db-client' status ESTABLISHED,RELATED.
```

whereas the group `http-server` would allow incoming http traffic:

```
allow incoming traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 to TCP port 80.
allow outgoing traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 from TCP port 80.
```
# Difficulties
## Service IPs

The DNAT used by kube-proxy could be a problem to identify the container the traffic is coming from. The source IP should not be altered by the NAT.
# Tasks
## Docker

Docker still has to add support for remote libnetwork drivers. At the moment it can only use the internal libnetwork drivers.
## Kubernetes
### Pod Manifests

The pod manifest would need to support network-labels
### Security-Groups

There would have to be a place where you define the security group rules.
### Remote Driver

We would need to create a libnetwork remote driver that supports the described features.

body:

The problem exists for reverting iptables filter and may be in other places.

This should be cleaned up. It would also be good to review other e2e tests where this may occur.

cc @lavalamp, @quinton-hoole

title: Density should cleanup better

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
In cases where one wants to run multiple iterations of density back to back, we really need to make sure a pervious iteration's load doesn't leak into this one. 2 main culprits are:
1. Deleting the namespace will return in a moment, when really it takes like ~15m to delete all events (~20,000 events for 3000 pods). These deletes actually have a bad effect on the next run.
2. We should make sure the pods are actually gone on the kubelet before staring a new run by using the proxy to poll /pods or something. Otherwise we're effectively putting > 30 pods on a node and the kubelet is known to be slow during pod deletes.

This is obviously not a problem if we tear down the entire cluser between iterations.
@gmarek

title: Record pod StartTime when we receive a watch notification on the kubelet

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Forked from: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/9792#issuecomment-113213791, https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/pull/7868#issuecomment-99706316

Proposal for StartTime modification:
1. Initialize StartTime, once, when the kubelet gets an add notification for the pod
2. If something else modifies it via the apiserver the kubelet will ignore the modification (we can probably evolve this to have the kublet correct any meddling)
3. If the pod is deleted and re-added, the timestamp will change, but not otherwise
4. If the kubelet is slow in dealing with a watch notification (eg: because of pod deletes) the StartTime will include that.

Such a timestamp would be helpful in measuring apiserver -> node watch latencies as well. Node team, thoughts? 

Fyi we can approximate the time it's currently recording as StartTime by sorting the startedAt timestamp of the containers of the pod.

title: Allow Service NodePorts on low ports

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

body:
To capture some of the discussion.

Gripe: Service NodePorts can only be in a "special" port range (apiserver flag).  This is annoying for people who want to expose a service on port 80 (for example) but instead have to use something like 30986.

Rationale for this behavior:
1. We don't want service node ports to tromp on real ports used by the node (e.g. 22). 
2. We don't want service node ports to tromp on pod host ports.
3. We don't want to randomly allocate someone port 80 or 443 or 22.

Proposed compromise:  Allow NodePorts on low ports with a bunch of caveats.

To address rationale points (1) and (2): Make kube-proxy open (and hold open) ports that it is using.  This will prevent it from using port 22 (for example) for a service node port.

To address rationale point (3): Use the flag-configured range for random allocations, but allow users to request any port they want.

Caveats and analysis:

1) Error reporting is not good.  We do not know about what non-container stuff is using ports on the host and we do not have an easy way for the API server to allocate ports between pods and services.  Not easy to resolve.  The implication of this is that port-in-use errors will only be detected by kube-proxy when it tries to open the port on the node.  Sending events for this is possible, but not great (one event from every node) and no other node-level error gets a kube-proxy event.  Net result: user asked for a service on node port 22, and it just doesn't work and they have no idea why.

2) Doing dual-ranges (use the flag range for allocations but allow the whole range to be used) is non-trivial and has to be plumbed through more code than I am comfortable with at this point.  The implication of not doing this is that sometimes people will get allocated a port that happens to be 22 and can never work.  Combined with caveat (1) this is really unpleasant.  We could do some REALLY hacky things like just retry the random allocation if it is not in the flagged range.  This avoids plumbing the dual-range logic down, but is embarassingly ugly.  I am ashamed to have suggested it.

3) Holding ports open is pretty easy and we should do this anyway.  The error reporting properties are still not good.

Summary: I am unconvinced that this is worthwhile to rush into v1.  We still have the option of baking a container that receives traffic on a HostPort and redirects it to a service.  I have a demo of using socat to do this (simulating a pod manually):

```
root@kubernetes-minion-nnx6:/home/thockin# docker run -d --dns=10.0.0.10 --dns-search=default.svc.cluster.local -p 8080:93 thockin/hostport-to-service 93 hostnames2:80
1dcc1e94c30834290ae243ac298c6699b2a3348fc014b4b77ae34c13ead44854

root@kubernetes-minion-nnx6:/home/thockin# curl localhost:8080
hostnames2-gxt4f
```

title: Clarify label prefix guidance

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
I just found in 
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/labels.md

that:

Valid label keys have two segments: an optional prefix and name, separated by a slash (/). (...)
If the prefix is omitted, the label key is presumed to be private to the user. System components which use labels **must specify a prefix**. The kubernetes.io/ prefix is reserved for kubernetes core components.

I found that cluster addons specify "k8s-app" and "version" label with no prefix:

```
    k8s-app: heapster
    version: v2
    kubernetes.io/cluster-service: "true"
```

I wonder if we should rename it to:

```
    kubernetes.io/k8s-app: heapster
    kubernetes.io/version: v2
    kubernetes.io/cluster-service: "true"
```

or rather update the doc about labels.

I ask because I need to disable it for Mesos testing (minion nodes do not exist until pods have been created). Disabling via `-check_cluster_size=false` in e2e.go makes sense. Disabling with an env var in bash could work too, but is messy. Having to disable both is just silly.

title: Multiple schedule policies for different pods.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: area/admin
labels.description: Indicates an issue on admin area.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
In production, we need multiple schedule policies to meet the requirements of different pods. For instance, some pods may prefer a schedule policy in which ServiceSpreading is considered to be import, while some other pods just want themselves to be deployed on the nodes with more free resources regardless of the ServiceSpreading. To meet these "conflict" requirement, different schedule policies should be allowed when kube-scheduler is up.

How should we do this? 

An initial discussion at https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/google-containers/wyn8dNXq6xI.

title: Salt does not do well with systemd

labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
- It requires lots of module.reload (#9860).
- Salt (at least our version) is entirely broken on Ubuntu 15.04 (it just doesn't see our services)
- We have lots of comments in our salt code where we say "this doesn't work" around service restarting

In order to work around this, I created a simple script that does the systemctl management directly: https://github.com/justinsb/kubernetes/commit/37005c14700fd6cc52ce49bc70675106d2f5a1e7

Is this reasonable?  Or does someone want to take on making systemd & Salt work together :-) ?

(Background: for AWS, Ubuntu Vivid Vervet is the only system I've found that has a sufficiently modern kernel and doesn't need a reboot either to upgrade the kernel or change kernel boot params.  Vervet though uses systemd, and our current Salt scripts assume that Redhat <=> systemd.  I have fixes ready to work with theoretical-Salt, but bugs with real world salt have reduced me to the patch I've linked above)

body:
Rewriting relative URLs breaks paths which are loaded into the browser at a different path from where they are served, as is the case with angularjs templates. Since relative paths should already be relative to the proxy path prefix, the solution is to simply not rewrite those paths.

This issue is blocking #9674

title: Specify PersistentVolumeClaimSource by Selector, not Name

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
My understanding is that when we want a cluster of e.g. 3 pods with persistent storage, the best we can do today is to launch 3 RCs, specifying a different persistent volume for each.   We can still group those into one service.

I think it would be nice to be able to just specify one RC, and have it map to a group of persistent volumes.

One way to do that would be to specify a list of persistent volumes in the RC, with some sort of parameterization to say "this PV is for pod 1, this PV for pod 2, etc"

An alternative which would be "more k8s" would be to allow specifying a selector, which would match labels on our PersistentVolumeClaims.  The "identity" of a pod would be determined not by the rc passing down an identifier to the pod, but by whatever PV it ended up with.

For unaware databases, this might require a smarter management process in the pod, but I'm thinking about that separately ;-)

One downside would be that it would be hard to specify groupings; for example we might want a data-volume and a log-volume to be assigned together.  We could specify a further list of fields that must match across all volume allocations to a single pod, but there may be neater solutions (and this may not be that important).

Is this a good idea?  Or is there a trick I am missing to do this today?

body:
Testing containerized Kubelet and seeing:

```
W0611 21:27:27.828300       1 container_manager_linux.go:68] [ContainerManager] Failed to ensure Docker is in a container: failed to find pid of Docker container: exit status 1
```

This is normal because Docker isn't in the pid namespace of the kubelet - but either cAdvisor needs to use the same pid namespace escape tricks that the kubelet uses for mounts, or we need to run the kubelet outside of a pid namespace, which makes other things regarding the container much harder.

Started with https://github.com/google/cadvisor/issues/770 then @rjnagal explained this was in container-manager.

From Rohit

---

This bit of code is in kubelet. It creates a new cgroup and tries to move docker processes there.

I think the problem is that kubelet is execing pidof docker to find docker processes. In cadvisor, we mount system root at /rootfs and use that to proxy process listing.

kubelet can do the same with chroot /rootfs pidof docker

Three lines of change, but needs to go in kubelet :)

Are the namespaced kubelet changes getting in? I can make the kubelet change if someone is willing to merge it in.

---

Answers no, this was us testing in OpenShift in preparation for enabling containerized workflows.  Not a huge deal on our end, this is mostly for development and kick the tires workflows.

body:
### **Proposal**

After finishing with #9032, we can also add resource labels as extra columns when we print resources. 

The user could define in a flag `--label-column=` or `-l` the names of the labels that he wants to print, and then **kubectl will append extra columns in the end of each resource row**. 

The extra column will use:
- as header-column name --> the label name
- as per row value --> the label value for each resource

For labels:
- names can be both in lowercase or uppercase
- non-recognized labels will return `<n/a>` to explicitly declare that this label is not available in this resource _(as labels are strings, we can differentiate empty string "" with non-existing label)_ **???**
- declaration order on the command reflects on printing
### **Example**

```
$ kubectl get pods --label-column=version,deployment
NAME             READY     REASON    RESTARTS   AGE  VERSION  DEPLOYMENT
my-nginx-00jsd   0/1       Pending   0          ~1m  v1       2016-01-01
my-nginx-7kqqp   0/1       Pending   0          ~1m  v1       2016-01-01
my-nginx-fb2s6   0/1       Pending   0          ~1m  v2       2016-01-02

title: Image access control is not multi-tenant.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/feature

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

body:
Docker does a credential check when pulling images, but not when using them. It will let you run an image that is already pulled even if you don't present credentials.

That is reasonable behavior from the standpoint of the docker tool since it is not trying to be multi-user.

However, it makes it hard to make Kubernetes multi-user. If an image is already pulled, (e.g. using `imagePullSecrets`, then anyone else can use that image by setting pull policy to `IfNotPresent`, even if they lack proper credentials.

 We could try to fix this by disallowing `IfNotPresent` pull policy on all pods, thus forcing a docker pull before each docker run, and failing the pod if the docker pull failed.  We would need to implement and e2e test that.

title: `events_cache` should not be a singleton

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Discovered while debugging #9453

**Problem:**
The `events_cache` used by `pkg/client/record/event.go` is created as a singleton in `pkg/client/record/events_cache.go`. That means all sinks created by `StartRecordingToSink` in `event.go` end up using the same LRU cache.

**Impact:**
This is unlikely to cause issues since all our components (kubelet, scheduler, service controller, node controller, replication controller) use only 1 sink (kube client). Only our tests specify other sinks (logs, etc.).

**Suggested solution:**
Create a new `event_cache` object instance for each new sink (every `StartRecordingToSink` call).

v1.0 triage needed.

- /etc/kubernetes/config ``` # Comma separated list of nodes in the etcd cluster KUBE_ETCD_SERVERS="--etcd_servers=http://centos-master:4001" # logging to stderr means we get it in the systemd journal KUBE_LOGTOSTDERR="--logtostderr=true" # journal message level, 0 is debug KUBE_LOG_LEVEL="--v=0" # Should this cluster be allowed to run privileged docker containers KUBE_ALLOW_PRIV="--allow_privileged=false" # How the controller-manager, scheduler, and proxy find the apiserver KUBE_MASTER="--master=http://centos-master:8080" ``` - /etc/kubernetes/kubelet ``` ### # kubernetes kubelet (minion) config # The address for the info server to serve on (set to 0.0.0.0 or "" for all interfaces) KUBELET_ADDRESS="--address=0.0.0.0" # The port for the info server to serve on KUBELET_PORT="--port=10250" # You may leave this blank to use the actual hostname KUBELET_HOSTNAME="--hostname_override=centos-minion1" # location of the api-server KUBELET_API_SERVER="--api_servers=http://centos-master:8080" # Add your own! KUBELET_ARGS="--cluster-dns=10.254.100.10 --cluster-domain=kubdomain.local" ``` - /etc/sysconfig/flanneld ``` # Flanneld configuration options # etcd url location. Point this to the server where etcd runs FLANNEL_ETCD="http://centos-master:4001" # etcd config key. This is the configuration key that flannel queries # For address range assignment FLANNEL_ETCD_KEY="/coreos.com/network" # Any additional options that you want to pass #FLANNEL_OPTIONS="" ``` - Content of flannel subnet.env in centos-minions is apparently ok, for example in centos-minion1 ``` [root@centos-minion1 ~]# cat /run/flannel/subnet.env FLANNEL_SUBNET=18.16.98.1/24 FLANNEL_MTU=1450 ```

processes running in minions

``` /usr/bin/kube-proxy --logtostderr=true --v=0 --master=http://centos-master:8080 /usr/bin/kubelet --logtostderr=true --v=0 --api_servers=http://centos-master:8080 --address=0.0.0.0 --port=10250 --hostname_override=centos-minion1 --allow_privileged=false --cluster-dns=10.254.100.10 --cluster-domain=kubdomain.local /usr/bin/flanneld -etcd-endpoints=http://centos-master:4001 -etcd-prefix=/coreos.com/network /usr/bin/docker -d --selinux-enabled --bip=18.16.37.1/24 --mtu=1450 ``` And now the problem: I can ping ips to other pods within the same minion but when I pinging from pods in different minions: ping from busybox1-59sm9 in centos-minion1 (pod ip 18.16.98.21) to busybox2-zoisy in centos-minion2 (pod ip 18.16.37.39) ``` [root@centos-minion1]# docker exec -ti 04d53905fc4b ping 18.16.37.39 PING 18.16.37.39 (18.16.37.39): 56 data bytes ^C --- 18.16.37.39 ping statistics --- 8 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100% packet loss ``` I'm not sure what else I can try, I'm a bit lost with all the different guidelines in the documentation but not sure which one is more accurate and what can be failing in my setup. Any clue what can I check, thanks!

title: int fields should probably not set omitempty

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
In v1beta3, ReplicationControllerSpec.Replicas is defined as:

```
Replicas int `json:"replicas,omitempty" description:"number of replicas desired"`
```

In v1, it is:

```
Replicas *int `json:"replicas,omitempty" description:"number of replicas desired; defaults to 1"`
```

omitempty means a value of 0 will not be serialized in v1beta3 (see http://play.golang.org/p/INjWh33QnH).

Removing a user-set value of 0 when building v1beta3 API responses, and treating the absence of that value as a different default in the next version of the API is surprising. The conversions handle the cases correctly, but I would expect this to trip up users.

title: Downward API does not work inside of list object

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Trying to use the [Downward API](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/downward_api.md) inside of a list object results in an error when trying to create the objects:

> Error: ReplicationController "backend-rc" is invalid: [spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[0].valueFrom.fieldRef.fieldPath: invalid value 'metadata.name': error converting fieldPath, spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[1].valueFrom.fieldRef.fieldPath: invalid value 'metadata.namespace': error converting fieldPath]

Example:

``` yaml

---
apiVersion: v1beta3
kind: List
items:
- kind: ReplicationController
  metadata:
    name: backend-rc
    labels:
      type: backend-type
  spec:
    replicas: 3
    template:
      metadata:
        labels:
          type: backend-type
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: backend-container
          image: gcr.io/google-samples/env-backend:1.1
          imagePullPolicy: Always
          ports:
          - containerPort: 5000
            protocol: TCP
          env:
          - name: POD_NAME
            valueFrom:
              fieldRef:
                fieldPath: metadata.name
          - name: POD_NAMESPACE
            valueFrom:
              fieldRef:
                fieldPath: metadata.namespace
- kind: Service
  metadata:
    name: backend-srv
    labels:
      type: backend-type
  spec:
    ports:
    - port: 5000
      protocol: TCP
    selector:
      type: backend-type
```

Taking the replication controller out of the list and running `kubectl create -f` with just the RC works fine:

``` yaml

---
apiVersion: v1beta3
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  name: backend-rc
  labels:
    type: backend-type
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        type: backend-type
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: backend-container
        image: gcr.io/google-samples/env-backend:1.1
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5000
          protocol: TCP
        env:
        - name: POD_NAME
          valueFrom:
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: metadata.name
        - name: POD_NAMESPACE
          valueFrom:
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: metadata.namespace
```

title: kube2sky should do smart updates including not deleting-recreating for each update

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

body:
To do a DNS update, kube2sky currently deletes all records related to a service and then recreates them.
1. For unchanged records: This is not desirable since there is a brief interval where valid records that did not need to be changed, are unavailable (since they are being deleted and re-created)
2. For modified records: instead of deleting and recreating entries, it should be possible to simply overwrite the etcd entries for the modified records since the etcd key strings are stable.
3. For records that are new or being deleted, no work needs to be done. 

@thockin

body:
I'm not really sure what to call this PR since it touches so many things.  Suggestion receptacle open if anyone can think of a better name.  I have been thinking about this for a while and want to open discussion while I'm thinking about it.

TL;DR: when there's a multi-platform dashboard for E2E described in #6605, one of the things on that dashboard should be a run of e2e on at least one platform that is done with SELinux enforcing.

We need this for a couple of reasons:
1.  We need to validate that the core-use cases tested by the E2E tests are operationally solvent when SELinux is enforcing
2.  We have SELinux-specific features related to security context that cannot be effectively tested without SELinux enforcing.

I have been running local E2E runs when making changes that can touch SELinux but that isn't sustainable long-term.

title: By default, merge more .kubeconfig files

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
By default, kubectl should have access to all clusters, users and contexts defined in any .kubeconfig files in any of the following locations:
- Any files or directories specified by KUBECONFIG
- /etc/kubernetes/config/*
- ~/.kube/*

(Today kubectl only loads from ~/.kube/config, or only KUBECONFIG or --kubeconfig if specified.)

This would allow me to do a few things that I can't easily do today:
- /etc/kubernetes/config/*: Use puppet/ansible/chef/etc. to drop separate credential files for each of our clusters into /etc/kubernetes/config/\* to make it really easy for developers to run kubectl --context=<some-cluster> on any server and always get to the right cluster without any configuration on the developers part. (And if there's only one cluster, just run kubectl <cmd> and have it work automatically with no configuration.)
- ~/.kube/*: Download a .kubeconfig file and have access to it immediately just by moving it into ~/.kube/. Today I have to either manually merge the files or specify KUBECONFIG or --kubeconfig (which would then ignore all Preferences in my ~/.kube/config file).
- KUBERNETES_CONFIGS/--kubeconfig: I can download a zip of kubeconfigs, unzip it, and point at it, without losing access to my kubeconfig preferences/current context.

The convention I would follow is that files in any of the above locations would not contain Preferences or CurrentContext to prevent any merging headaches (which is what caused much anger in #4428); those two .kubeconfig fields should only be specified in ~/.kube/config. I would prefer to move them to a different file altogether, but that is a separate discussion.

body:
Forked from #8087.

We intended to get rid of LegacyHostIP when we created the NodeAddresses field, but I don't think we have an adequate replacement yet, as we found when we tried to switch ResourceLocation to use an internal IP in #9155.

What we need to know is at least:
1. At which address/name the master/bastion can reach the node, for /proxy, /portforward, /redirect, kubectl exec, kubectl logs, etc.
2. Which address/name is in the node's cert. Ideally this is the same as the above.
3. At which address/name external load balancers can reach the node. 

InternalIP and ExternalIP don't tell us either of these. Only Openstack and AWS even set InternalIP. Openstack and AWS also set ExternalIP, as does GCE. 

LegacyHostIP is set in a variety of ways in different cloudprovider implementations. AWS sets LegacyHostIP to the InternalIP. In the case of Mesos, Ovirt, Vagrant, and Rackspace, they only set LegacyHostIP.

In the case of no cloudprovider, the --hostname-override flag in Kubelet sets LegacyHostIP.

In most of these cases, we don't know whether the LegacyHostIP is internal or external.

We could just rename LegacyHostIP to IPForMaster, ProxyIP, BastionIP, or something similar. InternalIP and ExternalIP would be optionally populated by the cloudprovider. Which address should be used by the external load balancer could be cloudprovider-specific, as it is now.

NodeHostName is defined, but neither set nor used, AFAICT.

I think this change can be made in a backward-compatible manner, so it doesn't absolutely have to be done for 1.0.

cc @krousey @cjcullen @dchen1107 @roberthbailey @ncdc

body:
kubernetes-server-linux-amd64.tar.gz is 71 MB; that seemed bigger than I remember it being.

Focusing on kube-scheduler...

`tar tzvf kubernetes-server-linux-amd64.tar.gz` shows e.g.

```
-rwxr-xr-x root/root  17781624 2015-06-03 22:27 kubernetes/server/bin/kube-scheduler
-rw-r--r-- root/root  20449792 2015-06-03 22:27 kubernetes/server/bin/kube-scheduler.tar
```

Expanding kube-scheduler.tar, the big layer (for me) is one where the JSON says has 
`Cmd":["/bin/sh","-c","#(nop) ADD file:1921730b6a5704e5144432383579662ef9b1a97e9361f7a3cf276544f4ac349c in /usr/local/bin/kube-scheduler"]`

And untaring layer.tar shows that the only file is `usr/local/bin/kube-scheduler`

Checksum indicates the files are identical.

I think this is repeated for kube-apiserver & kube-controller-manager.

Excluding the repeated files and re-tarring drops the size from 71MB to 54MB.

I believe we aren't using these files other than in the Docker containers (?)

body:
In `pkg/kubelet/kubelet,go` in `getClusterDNS(...)`, it appends cluster DNS nameserver and search paths to the ones in the host resolv.conf.

A user reported trying to add skydns nameserver address and kubernetes search paths to the host resolv.conf.  Not what the instructions say to do, but a reasonable thing to do.  Very reasonable if you want to be able to resolve service names while debugging from the root UTS namespace.

This wasn't working for the user.  One thing I think would go wrong here is that if the node has 1 or 2 search paths, and then the user added the 3 for kubernetes, that is 5.  Then when kubelet adds 3 more (duplicate) entries, you get 8, which exceeds the limit of 6.  

Would it be better if the code filtered duplicate search entries?

title: Kubectl delete should handle stopping an rc while it's starting replicas

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Since kubectl stop currently polls status.Replicas, if one creates an rc and stops it soon after there's a chance the polling hits status.Replicas=0 when in fact the rc has not updated status.replicas yet. 

An elegant solution to this problem probably involves kubectl _not_ deleting the rc, but somehow signaling to the rc manager that it wants the rc gone. A halfway solution involves kubectl not deleting the rc while it's working. One solution is as follows (hacks like defaulting status.replicas to -1 aside):

The current stop flow is:
1. resize
2. poll on status.Replicas
3. delete rc

At the time of the resize, the rc could be in 3 states:
- `stable` (status.Replicas == spec.Replicas)
- `dormant` (waiting on watch events from previously created/deleted replicas)
- `working` (currently creating/deleting replicas)

It is not safe to poll status.Replicas while the rc is in `working`. If we create it in working and move it to dormant/stable after updating status.replicas, we can add a stage between 1 and 2 that blocks till this happens.

title: Hide IaaS-specific DNS search paths

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
On a GCE VM (created by GKE):

```
$ cat resolve.conf
domain c.some-project-123.internal.
search c.some-project-123.internal. 987654321.google.internal. google.internal.
nameserver 169.254.169.254
nameserver 10.240.0.1
```

Kubernetes will append:
`$NAMESPACE.svc.$CLUSTER_SUFFIX svc.$CLUSTER_SUFFIX $CLUSTER_SUFFIX`
to the search line where `$CLUSTER_SUFFIX` defaults to `cluster.local`, but cluster admins can redefine.

Pods which depend on resolving these special dns names will not be portable to other cloud providers, or potentially even across projects/clusters/zones within the same cloud provider.  We should strive to avoid things which reduce portability of pods.   
- Exposing the project name and other details about the underlying node goes against the kubernetes philosophy of abstracting the hardware from the application. 
- Encourages addressing nodes directly (e.g. foo.c.some-project-123.google.internal) rather than using pods and services, which undermines kubernetes networking abstractions.
- It limits the flexibility of the cluster admin to chose which nodes comprise a cluster.
- Enterprises may want to ensure that they keep their pods portable for various reasons.  Hiding nonportable APIs like this is one way to do that.  

Suggest that
- kubelet has a flag that causes it to pass a certain resolve.conf to docker when creating a pod..
- kubelet setup has per-cloud-provider algorithm for filtering non-essential info from the node's resolve.conf.
- If anyone asks for it, provide an escape hatch, e.g. `hostResolveConf` option on Pod Spec, default false.  Not clear this is needed.  Pods that want to talk to the metadata server can just skip DNS and use its IP address.

Suggest filtering as follows on GCE:
- remove `domain` since it mentions project (and does nothing when search is specified)
- remove `c.some-project-123.internal. 987654321.google.internal. google.internal` from the search path.  
- remove `nameserver 169.254.169.254`, which is just used for GCE metadata requests.

Related:
- conserve limited search and nameserver entries (#9079)
- hide metadata from pods, which contains secret information (#8867)

title: Generate API documentation for Kubernetes using Swagger

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
I'm in the process of generating AsciiDoc / Markdown from swagger specs.  General goals:
1. Generate documentation files suitable for inclusion into formal docs (OpenShift uses AsciiDoc -> DocBook)
2. Generate tables and examples for all objects that correctly represent the action
3. Have richer descriptions for each object and operation than we currently include, so that users understand what the object does (not just its fields).

Primary angle of attack is https://github.com/RobWin/swagger2markup
### Issues encountered
- [swagger-parser](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-parser) doesn't handle the "TRACE" verb - going to open a pull to fix that
- PATCH documents don't properly document their body parameter model type (no schema) - should be "any" which we can probably make happen with `map[string]interface{}`.  Also, the return type should be versionedObject
- We don't have descriptions on our path parameters for individual types, so any descriptions have to be external (swagger2markup supports external descriptions but this should come from the type).
- Our top level API objects don't have title or description (description really needs to be a long description - it's the description of the API)
- Our model objects don't have descriptions
- Our operations don't have descriptions
- go-restful ApiDeclaration doesn't have "Info" which contains title and description, used by the generator to frame the document
- Our paths should have descriptions like "Use this path to operate on lists of Pods", "Use this path to operate on individual Pods", "Use this path to control the status of a Pod"
- Our operation descriptions should be capitalized - those are used as headers and TOC lines in doc
- Our dates and times are missing format "date-time"
- runtime.RawExtension should be documented more like "any" - RawJSON is not actually exposed.  May need to set JSON struct tags on it.
- Swagger model order is random because ApiDeclarations.Models is a map[string]Object.  We need to convert it to a `[]...` in the swagger serialization format.

title: DNS: If nodes use 3 nameservers or > 3 search records -- trouble

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body: Linux's libc is impossibly stuck ([see this bug from 2005](https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=168253)) with limits of just 3 DNS `nameserver` records and 6 DNS `search` records.  Kubernetes needs to consume 1 `nameserver` record and 3 `search` records.  This means that if a local installation already uses 3 `nameserver`s or uses more than 3 `search`es, some of those settings will be lost.  As a partial workaround, the node can run `dnsmasq` which will provide more `nameserver` entries, but not more `search` entries.

title: Inconsistent use of service-accounts, .kubeconfig, and kube-addons secrets.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Making a serviceAccount causes automatic creation of a secret with an apiserver authn token.  But it does not generate a kubeconfig file holding the token.

kube-addons.sh makes secrets with tokens AND kubeconfigs.  But it does not make a ServiceAccount.  It also does not run on non-GCE platforms.

Our addons (logging, monitoring, dns) rely on secrets with secrets from the second category. 

We should stop manually generating secrets in kube-addons.  Instead, we should POST service accounts and let the automation make the secrets.  There should not be specific logic in kube-addons to make the service-accounts.  That should be part of the yaml for each addon.

This means we need to automatically generate kubeconfig in the TokenController, or change the client code for (dns, monitoring, logging) to understand how to read the bare token from its default location.

body:
CoreOS does not have an equivalent to "kube-addons.sh", and so there are not system secrets created when the cluster is created.   So, when some of our CoreOS users run things like the Hazelcast example, or the elasticsearch example, they currently rely on kubernetes-ro to reach the apiserver.  When kuberenetes-ro support is removed (#8155), these examples will still work on GCE, because they can use the kubeconfig in their associated secret.  But, on CoreOS, it seems they will break.

Possible fix alternatives:
1. Change #8155 to not remove support for the --readonly_port feature, but default it to off for GCE.
2. Change all known examples to include instructions on how to generate a secret when setting up the example.
3. Extend CoreOS cluster setup to include the kube-addons.sh secret-creation functionality.
4. @lavalamp has a plan that uses a proxy in a sidecar.

Option 1 is nice because it allows us to defer fixing the problem until after 1.0 freeze.

title: kubectl rolling-update should not exitcode=0 when resumes an update

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Consider this:

```
> kubectl rolling-update A --image a:v2
```

Control-C half way through update

```
> kubectl rolling-update A --image a:v3
Found existing update in progress (X), resuming.
Continuing update with existing controller (X).
Update succeeded. Deleting old controller: X
Renaming X to X
```

So the update to v3 succeeded (I think), but the update was actually to v2.

I think it should update to v3; ideally by co-opting the existing rolling-update and repointing to v3.  If we can't do that, it should completing the existing rolling-update, then rolling-update to v3.  If we can't have that, it should exit-code != 0.

body:
Our current rolling update scheme requires deleting a pod and creating a replacement. We should also have rolling "in-place" update, of both containers and pods. There are two kinds of in-place update
1) [only applies to container update] pod stays in place, but container doesn't - for example, change container image without killing pod
2) [applies to pod or container update] pod stays in place, and container stays in place - for example, resource limit updates (IIRC we don't implement this yet, or at least don't implement it in-place)

The motivation is that there's no reason to kill the pod if you don't need to. The user may have local data stored in it that they don't want blown away due to update.

title: active log streaming times out after 5 minutes

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
I noticed that if I'm following a pod log that is being actively written to it will timeout after 5 minutes.  However if the pod is not writing logs the request will not timeout.  In that case the request will remain open seemingly indefinitely.

I can change the behavior by modifying this line of code:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/server.go#L68

To make it happen faster you can set the value lower.  I've been testing with 1 minute.

Steps to reproduce:
1. Launch cluster
2. Create the nginx pod in `examples/pod.yaml`
3. In another terminal generate log output by hitting the pod: `while :; do curl 172.17.0.22; sleep 0.5; done` (you'll need to change the ip).
4. Watch the logs: `time curl -ivs --raw "http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1beta3/namespaces/default/pods/nginx/log?container=nginx&follow=true&previous=false"`

In this case whenever the WriteTimeout is reached curl will receive the zero sized chunk and the connection will be closed.  If you leave out step 3 curl will continue seemingly indefinitely.

This behavior definitely seems odd.  Is the usage of WriteTimeout correct here?  A quick search shows that others have been confused by the intention of WriteTimeout which is why I ask.

body:
Based on the discussion on the mailing list [https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/google-containers/j0QR971KtJc] i'm opening a feature request.

We have the following scenario in our application. On each container we run a multi-tennat java app. For each tenant we're using using 2 NFS volumes . One is used to store the tenant's files (inputs for processing,reports and other data we can't loose) and another one is to store temp data used for short lived temporary stuff. The reason why we're using NFS is that we need that to grow dynamically so here NFS/Gluster us handy as based on the space usage alert we can increase it automatically up to some predefined limit, again without restarting the container. The ability to grow the data volume is also a requirement.

Our tenants also move from one container to another when being upgraded. We move the tenant to another container because that runs a newer version of the app, however since moving them means a service interruption we can't always move all the tenants to a new version so we need to do it selectively without affecting the existing ones . When moving them we also need to unmount the volumes associated with the tenant and mount them on the new container.

title: kubectl exec by pod label

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

body:
I often find myself wanting to exec commands on single-container pods, and since pod names are not "stable", I use some wrapper script to avoid constantly updating pod names:

```
kubectl exec -p $(get_current_pod_name) my_script.sh
```

My `get_current_pod_name` returns the name of the first pod matching a label, and that covers the case when I want to execute the script on any one and only one container.

For fetching server logs of different pods/containers, for example, I'm currently giving an argument to `get_current_pod_name` to actually give me the _n-th_ pod from the list of matches, but that's kind ugly... and no multiplexing.

I found this [comment](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/8448#issuecomment-103235025) by @brendanburns on #8448 which led me to believe that there might be more people who'd like "-l" argument support:

> I would think to do that we'd actually want to use label syntax, e.g.
> 
> ```
> kubectl exec -l stage=production,user=bburns or whatever.
> ```

Would it be reasonable to add label filtering + some way to say "run in any one container" or "run in all containers" (in this case, maybe no support for "-it" flags...)?

body:

```
resource := "pods/status"

```

Right now, it results in:

```
resource := "pods"
kind := "Pod"

title: status doesn't work for kube-addons and for kube-master-addons daemon

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
`kube-addons` and `kube-master-addons` are created as (bash) daemons. 

The status command for neither of them works. For `kube-addons`, this is how we check if the process is running:

```
KUBE_ADDONS_SH=/etc/kubernetes/kube-addons.sh
SCRIPTNAME=/etc/init.d/$NAME
...
        ps --no-headers ${pid} | grep ${SCRIPTNAME} > /dev/null || exit $?
```

while the process that is started is `$KUBE_ADDONS_SH`, not `$SCRIPTNAME`:

```
root@kubernetes-master:/home/biskup# ps --no-headers 21476 | grep kube-addons
21476 pts/1    S      0:00 /bin/bash /etc/kubernetes/kube-addons.sh
```

Similarly for kube-master-addons.

`kube-addons` does this when it starts:

```
# We stay around so that status checks by salt make it look like
# the service is good. (We could do this is other ways, but this
# is simple.)
sleep infinity
```

while `kube-master-addons` does not.

I suggest also to make `kube-addons` and `kube-master-addons` consistent, i.e. both should `sleep infinity` or both should not. Or, if a different behavior is needed, please comment in the code.

As bash scripts can get easily broken, I suggest also to write a test for the status command (just invoke `service kube-addons status` and `service kube-master-addons status` at start of some e2e test).

title: Room for optimizing rc stop operations

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
We haven't really profiled how long it takes to stop a large rc and I suspect there's a lot of room for improvement. At the kubectl level we should do: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/8572. At the rc manager level:
1. Resize rc to 0 -> "real time" (or as fast as the watch anyway)
2. Rc deletes pods -> rate limited to 20qps over all rcs (this connection is shared with node and endpoints controller), so however long it takes (probably as long as it takes to spin up the rc)
3. Update status.replicas -> "real time" (as the watch delivers notifications for each pod deleted)

Here is at least 1 corner case where updating status.Replicas can take upto 30s extra: 
when the pods controller does a relist (once in 5m) in between when the rc has fired off a bunch of deletes, these deletes have hit the apiserver, but before the watch has delivered those deletes to the rc manager. The relist will not have those pods but the store will. We do not differentiate this case from  dropped deletes: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/replication_controller.go#L247 

One way to fix this would be for the informer to embed the deleted object instead of just the key, into the tombstone entry.

title: Clarify strange kubernetes behaviour (bugs or features)

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Hi, in order to find most suitable way(for us) to zero-downtime cluster updates i do some research of kubernetes behavior and found it very strange, so we need to know what things are bugs and what are features, what may changes in future and what not.
All for Kubernetes v0.15.

I have two nodes, and start pod on node1 then i delete node via REST delete /nodes/node1 but didn't stop any services like kubelet, docker, kube-proxy.

Results:
1) Pod still running, more than a hour... works fine, and even restarted by kubelet if it fails. No evicting process happens on this node(bug or feature?).
2) Pod has status "running" even if i stop kubelet and docker on this node.
3) After restarting pod on node (simulated fail via docker stop\kill) new containerID is updated on Master, updated pod ip. Service for this pod update his endpoints and emits events. But why? Node is even not a member of a cluster...
4) If i delete pod via kubectl on Master it will be deleted on removed node too.
5) If add this node to cluster again - pods will works fine and wouldn't be deleted during kubelet resync process.
Same behavior even for replicated pods.

What we like in this behavior is:
1) No evicting after 4 min. This gives us more time to update node. No pods will be stopped during update process.
2) We can add this node to cluster again and all pods will continue to work.

Best way for us is to control evicting behavior. May be there any way to do this? For example temporary disable it for update process and then enable at the and.
Maybe some thing like this?

``` bash
kubectl update nodes $NODENAME --patch='{"apiVersion": "v1beta3", "spec": {"unschedulable": true, "evicting_policy": "off or 0min or 2hour"}}
```

title: API: frequent ResourceVersion changes (from status updates) cause false conflicts

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
I've noticed that the `resourceVersion`of a resource will update even if only the `status` section has changed. I get that technically the RESTful resource _has_ changed and this is needed to trigger events. However this is problematic when you need to update a resource during a period of frequent status changes, b/c the `resourceVersion` in PUT requests must be in sync with the API server's version. The status could be changing so quickly that the roundtrip required for a GET then PUT will almost always be too slow.

A simple way to reproduce this:
1. Kill some of the kubelets in the cluster.
2. Create an RC with a simple pod template & set the Count to a sufficiently high number.
3. Wait a little, then attempt to update the Replication Controller.

The RC will constantly try to fulfill its desired count. Most of the pods will fail to run b/c they get scheduled to dead kubelets. This causes the RC's `status.count` to flap constantly, in turn increasing the `resourceVersion` every time. This makes it nearly impossible for the operator (or other components) to reliably update the RC b/c as soon as the resource is retrieved it's outdated very shortly after.

Related to: #2726

title: Service config validation error: "spec:ports" ...

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/support
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as a support question.

body:
Running `kubectl -f some-service.yaml` (or JSON) file, fails with following error:

> Service "some-service" is invalid: spec.ports: required value

I have two config files. One for **pod** and other for **service**. I'm able to deploy **pod** without any problem.

**pod:** `rabbitmq-pod.yaml`

``` yaml
apiVersion: v1beta3
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    mq: rabbit
    role: master
  name: rabbitmq-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: rabbitmq
      image: tutum/rabbitmq
      ports:
        - containerPort: 5672
          name: main-port
          protocol: tcp
        - containerPort: 15672
          name: admin-port
          protocol: tcp
```

**service:** `rabbitmq-service.yaml`

``` yaml
apiVersion: v1beta3
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: rabbitmq-service
spec:
  ports:
    - port: 5672
      name: main-port
      targetPort: 5672
      protocol: tcp
    - port: 15672
      name: admin-port
      targetPort: 15672
      protocol: tcp
  selector:
    name: rabbitmq-pod
```

The error is reproducible with `kubectl` 0.17.0 and Mac OS X.

body: I'm very afraid that we forget to validate fields over time.  I'm a big fan of testing these things automatically.  Idea: make each validation function take a function, which it must call with the name of each each field it considers.  In real binaries this is a no-op function.  Then we can have a test that provides a function which uses reflection to map out structs and ensure that every field was validated.  This is half-baked but I wanted to file it before I forgot.

title: Move validation to be per-API-version

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
Validation as it exists today is pretty wrong - it tracks internal types.  Once we have long-term support for v1 API and are deep into v2 rework, the validation errors that are produced for v1 will be less and less useful.

We've gone back and forth about this but have not yet come up with a good answer on how to do this generically.  I propose we just move it to be per-version, same as defaulting.

Given that v1beta[12] are on the block right now and v1beta3 will be soon, this is the right time.  The same day we delete v1beta3 we should move pkg/api/validation into v1 and make it use versioned types.

Yes, it will be tedious to make changes, but I think that is the cost of having multiple versioned APIs in support cycles.

title: Should provide better information on how to select multiple labels

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
Abstractly, what you want to do is this:
  1) pod template in your first replication controller gives the pods it creates the label "version=v1"
  2) pod template in your second replication controller gives the pods it creates the label "version=v2"
  3) your service uses label selector "version=v1 OR version=v2"
However, we don't currently support OR in label queries. Therefore you need to do something like this:
  1) pod template in your first replication controller gives the pods it creates the labels "service=foo" and "version=v1"
  2) pod template in your second replication controller gives the pods it creates the labels "service=foo" and "version=v2"
  3) your service uses label selector "service=foo"

When we originally implemented get, the first column was the type, i.e. "POD", not "NAME".  Over time others implemented "NAME" as the primary column in other printers.

One benefit of "<TYPE>" is that the output (if saved or pasted or viewed later) gives a clue about the type.  A downside is that the column width can be much longer - i.e. "SERVICE ACCOUNT".

We should make a decision and be consistent (change Pod, or change everything else).

title: Incorrect aws cli parameters format in doc

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

body:
It looks like the parameters in the doc of [aws coreos getting-started-guides](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/getting-started-guides/aws-coreos.md) doesn't works properly.

I'm using the latest aws cli released [v1.7.27](https://github.com/aws/aws-cli/releases/tag/1.7.27), and the create stack command in the doc keep popping error of "missing parameters" to me.

```
$ aws --version
aws-cli/1.7.27 Python/2.7.6 Darwin/14.3.0

$ aws cloudformation create-stack --stack-name kubernetes --region ap-southeast-1 \
  --template-body file://$(pwd)/cloudformation-template.json \
  --parameters "ParameterKey=KeyPair,ParameterValue=<Key_id>" \
  --parameters "ParameterKey=ClusterSize,ParameterValue=3" \
  --parameters "ParameterKey=VpcId,ParameterValue=vpc-<id>" \
  --parameters "ParameterKey=SubnetId,ParameterValue=subnet-<id>" \
  --parameters "ParameterKey=SubnetAZ,ParameterValue=ap-southeast-1b"

A client error (ValidationError) occurred when calling the CreateStack operation: Parameters: [KeyPair, SubnetId, VpcId] must have values
```

I had a glance into the `aws cloudformation create-stack help` content, it tells parameters need to **separated by space**:

```
--parameters (list)
  A list of Parameter structures that specify input parameters for the stack.

  Shorthand Syntax:
     Key value pairs, with multiple values separated by a space.
     --parameters ParameterKey=string,ParameterValue=string,UsePreviousValue=boolean ParameterKey=string,ParameterValue=string,UsePreviousValue=boolean
```

Then I tried below commands, and now it works!

```
$ aws cloudformation create-stack --stack-name kubernetes --region ap-southeast-1 \
  --template-body file://$(pwd)/cloudformation-template.json \
  --parameters ParameterKey=KeyPair,ParameterValue=<Key_id> \
  ParameterKey=ClusterSize,ParameterValue=3 \
  ParameterKey=VpcId,ParameterValue=vpc-<id> \
  ParameterKey=SubnetId,ParameterValue=subnet-<id> \
  ParameterKey=SubnetAZ,ParameterValue=ap-southeast-1b

{
    "StackId": "arn:aws:cloudformation:ap-southeast-1:<id>:stack/kubernetes/<id>-<id>-<id>-<id>-<id>"
}
```

Looks like the `--parameters` option should only be use once, the command in doc is incorrect.

title: Copy of binary to GCS for GCE kube-up.sh fails silently

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
I was running get.k8s.io, and somehow got in a state where the the salt gz/sha1 were in my GCE bucket, but not the server gz/sha1.  This meant the cluster never came up and it hung the client script.

In gce/util.sh, we're pretty careful about how this works.

upload-server-tars calls copy-if-not-staged, which calls already-staged to see if the if the file has been staged, otherwise copy-if-not-staged will gsutil the file up to GCS.

I think this weirdness can happen if...
- we get into copy-if-not-staged and echo the server hash into the .sha1
- the file upload hit a glitch, and the gsutil - m -q -h command doesn't in fact pass the hash check.  then GCS deletes the uploaded files (the policy for files that don't hashcheck), but we don't note the error

Then the master/nodes will try to install k8s from GCS, but never find it.

Even worse, if you ctrl-c, then bring the cluster down and back up, it fails again
- it looks like already-staged is comparing to the local .sha1 that was generated last time.  This will pass, since the hash was generated and still does match - it's that GCS never got the file

So, if I'm right about the above, I think the best fix is to compare the hash of the local binary to the saved hash in GCS, not just assume that the presence of the local hash file means that everything is in GCS.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
kube-apiserver should use the sd_notify() systemd API, either directly, or by reimplementing it (since it's trivial).

http://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/sd_notify.html

The sd_notify() systemd API tells systemd that the service is ready to accept connections. systemd will track its status correctly. 

In particular `systemctl start kube-apiserver.service` should not return until kube-apiserver is ready to accept connections. This allows other services, tests or consumers of kube-apiserver to deterministically depend on it.

title: Do we need consistent reads of etcd?

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
I am looking and looking at the code for pkg/registry/service/ipallocator/controller/repair.go, and I am having a hard time proving to myself that it is correct.

We have etcd configured to read in 'weakly consistent' mode.  As @smarterclayton and @lavalamp  previously explained to me (thanks!) that is not a problem, because any writes are done as a CAS with the version.  We might see stale data, and derive stale data from that, but we won't ever be able to write stale data.

However, I am worried that I can construct what appears to be possible etcd-partition states that an inconsistent read won't catch.  I'm basing this on this issue https://github.com/coreos/etcd/issues/741, in particular that raft/etcd allows a node to believe itself the leader while another leader has been elected.

For example, support I have one service, s1, with one IP at t0: 1.1.1.1  Then I change s1's IP at t1: 2.2.2.2.  So our IP allocation map should go from (1.1.1.1) -> (2.2.2.2)

But suppose we had a partition event in etcd just before t1.  At t0, node 1 believes itself to be the leader.  At the partition event, nodes 2 and 3 elect node 2 to be the leader.  Node 1 still believes itself to be the leader at t1 (though its days are numbered), and will answer inconsistent reads.  But Node 1 has not seen s1's change from 1.1.1.1 -> 2.2.2.2.

Now, at t2 the repair process does the following:

Reads the services from node 1: { s1=(1.1.1.1) }
Reads the node map from node 2: { (2.2.2.2) }
Builds a new node map: { (1.1.1.1) }
Writes the new node map back to node 2: { (1.1.1.1) }
And now (2.2.2.2) can be re-allocated to another service, despite the fact that s1 has it allocated.

Moreover, I think that not only can this happen with a double-leader partition, but it can happen simply if node 1 is lagging (no partitions behind the leader) when go-etcd is doing weakly consistent reads.

In short, I think we need etcd do consistent reads.  And then we _also_ need to do further checks to detect partitions: I think the partition scenario could be caught because the node map in node would be newer than the newest service.

Is this in fact possible?  Or is there some etcd/versioning mechanism I am missing?

labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
http://onsi.github.io/ginkgo/#focused-specs

Right now, GinkgoRunner returns 1 if there are any programmatically Focussed, Skipped or Pending tests, so Jenkins reports all tests runs as failed, when they should be considered passed.

Adding the Focussed, Skipped and Pending tests to Ginkgo's command line (which overrides programatic settings) within the Jenkins (and in fact any Continuous Integration environment), will cause the CI to report successes and failures correctly.

title: Create UI roadmap

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

body:
Going forward, what do we want out of the UI? We need a roadmap so that people know how to contribute.

This was discussed at the Kubernetes contributors meeting in December.

First of all, visualization/dashboard is more important than actuation. The CLI (kubectl) is expected to be the main tool for controlling the system and applications running on it. Table-friendly views should also be incorporated into kubectl, not just a GUI. I want to ensure that we maintain a common look and feel and functionality with kubectl for analogous table views and use cases -- the primary use cases and essential information are identical. That's not to say it shouldn't support actuation, but that creates additional issues, such as SSO auth.

With respect to visualization/dashboards,  we need views that are customized to the most common use cases:
1. Understanding the system architecture and/or application topology: diagram view that shows interconnection between objects
2. Deployment status: what images/versions are deployed, what deployments are in progress, what pods deviate, health by deployment version, provenance info
3. App debugging: for devs -- what’s failing most recently / most often, why, how often, logs, events
4. System debugging: dashboard w/ system and node health, uptime, versions, config, status events, change history, surface logs (from builds, containers or container failures), what’s where (node-centric view: example visualization: http://azure.microsoft.com/blog/2014/08/28/hackathon-with-kubernetes-on-azure/)
5. Resource usage analysis: how much resources  (mem, cpu, disk) are being used (current/historical, individual/distribution), usage relative to quota or limits, why did my thing run out of resources, top (sort by decreasing usage)
6. App dashboard / launchpad: status overview, launch links to app-domain, custom app dashboards, links to cadvisor and/or kubelet GUIs, links to elasticsearch and heapster (logging and monitoring dashboards), etc.

Some functionality is probably lacking in order to support all these views at the moment (e.g., stats collection).

Presentation guidelines:
- timeseries graphs: single-column, all same time-scale, for easy correlation
- text:
  - dense (information density)
    - multi-column tables
    - alternate colors of rows/columns rather than introduce whitespace
  - highlight high-value content
    - sort by “most important” information for the view (e.g., priority, scale, recency, eventful)
    - color to highlight important/abnormal details
    - don’t show fields in tables by default that are almost the default/boilerplate values
- flexible grouping (e.g., tree view), filtering, sorting, searching, aggregating
  - by namespace
  - by labels
  - by reverse label lookup
  - by image
  - by phase

Come up with recommended semantic labels/annotation keys and meanings:
- env (dev, test, stage, prod)
- source/containing object/provenance
- responsible party (name, email, etc)
- links (urls to app-specific dashboards, GUIs, web UI, etc)
- html (arbitrary html to inject link, description, status)
- workload type (web frontend, database, etc.)

Other issues:
- simplify user experience of dealing with multiple API objects (e.g., replication controller, template, pods)
- summarization of large numbers of pods
- event/status history
- change history
- latency
- similar views in CLI
- help
- customizable user preferences
- bookmarkable view URLs
- carry filter/context across views
- need to show information that’s most relevant to most people by default

Finally, there are others building UIs. We've discussed building the UI such that pieces can be reused with different chrome, etc.

cc @lavalamp @jackgr @smarterclayton
