body:
It's clear we're not going to be able to make all the changes we'd like in the v1 API (#7018), so this issue is to track/brainstorm things we might want in the v2 API.

Last updated 6/19/2015

API/client overhaul:
- Top-level API object plugins: #991, #3201, #1744, #703, #6923
  - Convert ReplicationController to a plugin #3058, rename it to ReplicaSet #3024, and recursively delete pods by default (see graceful termination #1535, below)
  - Daemon #1518
  - Job #1624
  - Deployment #1743
  - ConfigData #6477, #1553, #1627, #2068, #5582
  - Rename PersistentVolumeClaim to PersistentVolume, PersistentVolume to StorageVolume (or similar) as per [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/14095/files#r39791183)
- Subobject plugins: discussed in #7203 and lots of other places
  - I'd also like to consider replacing annotations with a list of plugins #12226
  - volume sources should be converted to plugins
- Multiple API prefixes/groups, including an experimental API prefix: #3806, #6363, #10009, #635, #1490
  - API group in addition to kind and apiVersion: #7111, #10009, #12951 
  - Modular API: #1744, #3481 (API subsets), https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/9633#issuecomment-113712917 (separate client objects from API objects)
  - Provider/domain field (e.g., kubernetes vs. docker) -- https://github.com/projectatomic/atomicapp
  - Some hypothetical API groups:
    - end-user execution objects: pod, pod template, secret, config data, persistent volume claim
    - end-user networking-related objects: service, ingress
    - end-user app deployment objects: replica set, deployment
    - end-user batch objects: job, scheduled job
    - app admin objects: namespace, limit range, resource quota
    - identity/auth objects: service account, user (future)
    - system / tooling objects: event, endpoints, component status, resource metrics
    - infrastructure / cluster admin deployment objects: daemon set
    - infrastructure / cluster admin infrastructure objects: node, persistent volume
    - experimental apis and plugins
- Binary encoding: #3338, #8132 (proto)
- Split objects in etcd to mitigate false conflicts: #8625
- API support for apply: #17333
- Restructuring: #1451, #2306, #2742, #4851, #5660, #6210, #7111, #7311, #7337, #7584, #3933
- Client versioning: #3955, #4874
- Fork versioned client on every breaking change
- Versioned validation: #8550, #3084
- Strict validation: #5889
- Tag-driven, swagger-documented validation: #8116
- Fine-grain versioning: #4855, #2953
- Return more info on failure: #6132
- Fix syntax for field validation errors: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/12035/files#r36374661
- API test fixtures: #5121, #4894
- Cleanup object references and selfLink: #6596, #2797, #1490, #4651, #4549
- Kubelet to use apiserver: #2098
- REST best practices and HTTP correctness: #4187, #5672, #6387, #656
- Swagger correctness: #6842, #6167, #2968, #2971, #4700, #3714
- Swagger 2.0: https://github.com/emicklei/go-restful/issues/157
- Form and client generation: #6487, #4210, #3685
- Improved API documentation: #10933, #5331 
- Change all fields to pointers for uniform detection of unspecified fields
- Scale to 1000 nodes / 50k pods

API feature changes:
- Finish subresource work, such as #2726, #4909, #8337, #10043
- Bulk API: #9633, #3279
- Initializers: #3585
- Dependencies and graceful termination for all objects: #1535
- Per-object generation numbers for all objects: #7328
- Generalized label selector: #341
- Generalized field selectors: #1362, #4476
- Reverse label lookup: #1348
- Get by uid: #4817
- Get subset of fields: #1459, #2740
- Generalized image representation: #8702
  - ACI images: #7203

title: Volumes require filesystem clients and utilities on host

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
The various filesystem plugins currently work by mounting a filesystem on the host then passing that mounted dir to the pod for access.  This requires that the host system has the filesystems client & utils installed and configured.

I would like to containerize the filesystem client pieces and run it as a sidecar to the POD requesting the volume.

Hi,

I recently did a [lesson](https://bulletproofmeteor.com/architecture/deploying-meteor-apps-into-a-kubernetes-cluster) on kubernetes for BulletProof Meteor. I want my users to play around with Kubernetes and learn about Kubernetes. Frankly, deploying a cluster your own is not yet easy. GKE is nice, but I want them to try using any cloud.

So, I built kube init: https://github.com/meteorhacks/kube-init

It's a way to run Kubernetes cluster on a single server. (it's based on hyperkube. may be we don't need hypekube at all). It also comes with the skydns configured too.

Then I ask users to create a SOCKS proxy into the box and they can access pods and services locally.

This is never meant to be a production cluster. But, users could experiment with the cluster without worrying about deploying and configuring a cluster.

Hope this helps.

title: Run services as non-privileged users

labels.name: priority/backlog

labels.description: Denotes an issue that needs help from a contributor. Must meet "help wanted" guidelines.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
At the moment most services in kubernetes run as root. This includes (from glancing at ps aux on a minion):
- etcd
- kube2sky
- td-agent
- ~~skydns~~ (no longer exists in addons)
- elasticsearch
- ~~heapster~~ (removed in 31fb04fa98e34773e18bd32d5aa4dfc554a9b83e)

It's best practice to use non-root user accounts for services that don't need them. E.g. elasticsearch had remote code execution vulnerabilities in the past.
Even though docker's root has a capability bounding set applied so it doesn't translate to a real root on the host, the attack surface for privilege escalation attacks is still increased.

title: Proposal: configurable proxyPort for kube-proxy

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Currently the addServiceOnPort invocation specifies a random port.

https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/release-0.16/pkg/proxy/proxier.go#L431

When running on Mesos we need to account for all server (listening) ports. I'd like to propose a PortAllocator interface that we can leverage for this purpose:

``` go
interface PortAllocator {
  AllocateNext() (int, error)
  Release(int)
}
```

A default implementation for allocating a `proxyPort` would simply have AllocateNext() always return 0 and Release() as a noop, maintaining current behavior. A range-based implementation would be configured with one or more port ranges and allocate from those. This would be configurable via kube-proxy flag.

It looks like someone has already started down the path of port allocation, albeit for portals.
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/pull/6684

title: Grouping a list of unknown containers into a pod for container/image management

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
The container runtime interface in kubelet sticks to the pod-level abstraction for most of the functions. There are two components that do not handle this interface well:
- `containerGC`: It needs access to all containers managed by kubelet in order to determine whether or not to remove them. This includes all containers starting with the `k8s_` prefix. Note that these containers may not have a valid pod name due to changes to the naming convention that are incompatible.  
- `imageManager`: It needs to know all the containers running on the node, whether managed by kubelet or not (e.g. if a image is used by any container, it cannot be removed).

The easier solution is to support retrieving a list of containers in the container runtime interface, but this is not clean. @vmarmol suggested that `GetPods` should return a single pod encompassing all the unknown containers. Based on the two requirements above, we'd need at least two different kinds of unknown pods (one for `k8s_` containers, and the other for the rest of the unidentified containers). If we go with this route, what UID/name should we use for the pods? We don't want naming conflict that'd affect user-created pods. Thoughts?

/cc @vmarmol, @dchen1107, @yifan-gu

title: Accessing the apiserver from a container

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
I want to access the apiserver from a container and I don't want to use the soon to be deprecated read only port so I will need to provide auth information. I only need to read state information -- I don't need to PUT/POST anything -- I just need to list the running pods in the same namespace as the pod modulo label filters. So it seems like my best bet is to use secrets? I could store either the basic auth or the bearer token or the cert information in a secret. Every time I bring up a cluster I would have to manually create a secret which contained the clusters auth information. Furthermore, since secrets live in a namespace and can only be used in that namespace I would have to perform this step N times for N namespaces where I needed containers that have to make apiserver calls.

This seems odd to me. If I can issue a `kubectl` command to get a list of pods why can't I launch a pod that has a container that lists the pods running in its own namespace? I feel that access to the apiserver (even for reading information in the same namespace) ought to be easier than this.

One way to do this might be to automatically create a secret in the default namespace which has the cluster auth information and allow this to be accessed by pods running in any namespace?

body:
There are a couple in-progress items currently that are going to touch the image pull with secret story, so I'm creating this issue to get everyone on the same page and hopefully do some productive design and factorings in front of the implementation work that will need to happen.

Our long-term goal is to be able to use secrets to enable pull from private image repositories.  Those secrets will definitely come from service accounts; it seems possible to me that we'll want to enable a use-case where a secret can also be explicitly referenced in a pod's spec to enable image pull as well.

One key thing to figure out is exactly how we want to model this inside the kubelet.  Currently the container manager has a `Pull` method that simply takes the container's `image` field as input.  I think, regardless of how the kubelet ultimately models associations between credentials, pods, and images, that this signature will need to change to include:
1.  Information about the pod
2.  The credentials to be used for the pull

Some random questions I can think of that we will need to sort out:
1.  Say that two different pods are set up to pull that same image from the same private registry using different credentials.  If the kubelet pulls the image on behalf of pod X, and then pod Y is scheduled onto the same node, and the image is already present on the node, do we still have to test pod Y's credentials somehow?  I would say the answer is yes, but I don't believe there's a way to dry-test a set of credentials with a docker registry at this point.  Please correct me if I'm wrong -- I would love to be wrong about this.
2.  Presumably the problem in (1) applies to each auth mode, credential type, registry type.
3.  Will credentials be cached on the node?  If so we need to have tmpfs storage for these, since they shouldn't be allowed to come to rest on the node's fs.

@liggitt @yifan-gu @smarterclayton @vmarmol 

Trying to keep the tagging minimal, feel free to tag your friends and coworkers.

body:
After several conversations with CoreOS, we've settled that the current usage of the client library is incorrect.  https://github.com/coreos/etcd/issues/2677

1.) The client is technically **not** thread safe, and round-robin rotation will never occur because we share the client (EtcdHelper).  The intended usage was a client per context, and would rotate operations across the quorum. 

2.) If we want keepalives we will need to option enable on the transport and pass to the etcd-client.   
#5589 , #6559

I don't see an easy work-around for this

title: Cluster Controller

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
This is my post 1.0 vision for how cluster upgrades happen. Writing it up since it's been mentioned a few times.

cluster-controller
- A new cluster component.
- Runs in a pod, with admin privileges.
- Takes over from the bootstrapping process when a new cluster is started.
- Keeps a desired cluster state object, stored in the system with other api objects. This includes:
  - The desired node configuration.
  - The desired master component versions & configurations.
- Runs a sync loop, observing cluster state, and changing it to match desired state.
  - Important: rate limited!
- Provisioning a new node and/or reinstalling an existing node is pushed into the cloudprovider interface.
  - We add a declarative node configuration so we can say "make node X look like {config}" or "make a new node like {config}". We could start out with this being the salt script we currently use.
- Cluster upgrades and rollbacks are done by pushing a new desired state.

title: Migrate PV binding from PV.Spec.ClaimRef to Binding subresource

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
@bgrant0607 this is a breaking API change.

@thockin @smarterclayton 

From #6105 

> This should use a "binding" sub-resource, as with pods. We've drawn the analogy of claims and PVs being like pods and nodes - we should follow the same pattern. That seems like a significant change, so I am willing to proceed on this path as long as we have a strong promise to fix it ASAP. This is, strictly speaking, an API change (albeit constrained to ~1 consumer - you).
> 
> As per our IRC chat, there are a lot of things this might change:
> 
> Do we bind the Claim to the PV or vice-versa?
> Do we move the Claim.VolumeRef to Spec?
> Do we allow users to ask for a specific PV?

and 

> As per the binding sub-resource discussion, I sense that we have this backwards. PersVolume.Status should host a ClaimRef and PersVolumeClaim.Spec should host a VolumeName (not ref, I think).

Per @thockin's questions above...

I think the PersistentVolume should own the binding.  It is 1:1 with Claims and it is more natural to query for volumes and see what's bound than to traverse all namespaces to see if a claim exists for a given volume.

Claim.Status.VolumeRef (potentially changed to VolumeName, since Namespace is unneeded) can stay where it is.  That status is reconstructable by observing the bound volume.

Allowing users to ask for a specific PV breaks the separation between them.  We can steer users towards some volumes (through admission control that retains some types/sizes of volumes to certain namespaces) but still not give them the exact volume.

I can add the Binding subresource similar to pod, but I need some help understanding how to use it effectively.  It looks like Pod's use of Binding is still in flux (see https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/scheduler/factory/factory.go#L294).

Technical advice and guidance is required :)

If another process is altering iptables rules at the time k8s attempts to add iptables rules it will fail with a locking error. k8s should use -w and retry after a delay.

Below, an external process (openshift-sdn-node) modifies iptables at roughly the same time and k8s fails without retrying.

```
...
Apr 27 11:40:20 ose3-master.example.com openshift-sdn-node[2058]: + iptables -I INPUT 2 -i lbr0 -m comment --comment 'traffic from docker' -j ACCEPT
Apr 27 11:40:21 ose3-master.example.com openshift-node[2237]: E0427 11:40:21.661746    2237 proxier.go:337] Failed to initialize iptables: error checking rule: exit status 4: Another app is currently holding the xtables lock. Perhaps you want to use the -w option?
Apr 27 11:40:21 ose3-master.example.com openshift-node[2237]: E0427 11:40:21.661912    2237 node.go:245] WARNING: Could not modify iptables.  iptables must be mutable by this process to use services.  Do you have root permissions?
Apr 27 11:40:22 ose3-master.example.com openshift-node[2237]: I0427 11:40:22.147405    2237 failing_service_config_proxy.go:19] Failed to properly wire up services.  This can happen if you forget to launch with permissions to iptables.  Access to the following services will be impaired: "kubernetes-ro, router, database, frontend, ruby-example, docker-registry, kubernetes"
```

Related to https://github.com/openshift/origin/issues/1922

title: Rep. Controller encodes created-by annotation incorrectly

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
pkg/controller/replication_controller.go uses `json.Marshal(createdByRef)` at one point to record a reference to a pod's creator in an annotation. This is incorrect because it's serializing an unversioned object.

Additionally, the rule should probably be "objects in annotations should be serializied in the same version as the parent object", but it's hard to see how we can enforce that without a very expensive trek through the annotations in every encode/decode call.

title: Document best practices for Kubernetes users

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
We should document best practices for using Kubernetes, especially within the context of creating new examples (#4926), so that reviewers can check for the issues. This is a successor to #1603.

Off the top of my head:
- Use the latest stable API version (currently v1)
- Use YAML rather than JSON (more user friendly for config)
- Group related objects together in a single file. This currently requires a List object in YAML, but it's still better than separate files. Almost nobody knows about this feature.
- Create service before corresponding replication controllers so that the scheduler can spread the pods comprising the service. #11144 (or, create the RC without specifying replicas, create the service, then scale up the RC, which may work better in an example using progressive disclosure and may have benefits in real scenarios also, such as ensuring one replica works before creating lots of them)
- Use `kubectl create -f <directory>` where possible. Another little-known feature.
- Don't use hostPort unless absolutely necessary (e.g., for a node daemon). Use the apiserver proxying or port forwarding for debug/admin access, or a service for external service access. Though #1487 was closed, hostPort is still in several examples.
- Don't specify default values unnecessarily. Now that we default the selector and labels in RC, it should get slimmer. Eventually we'll need a user's guide that can cover more advanced topics, but we want examples to look simple, in general.
- We should establish a convention other than "name" for label keys. (#3394) Probably some combination of "app", "component", ... I put some examples in labels.md.
- Service should use a subset of the labels used by the replication controllers whose pods it targets. #8524
- Use kubectl run and expose where appropriate, at least presented as an alternative
- Use headless services where appropriate
- Use kubectl bulk operations (via files and/or labels) for get and delete
- Use kubectl delete rather than stop
- No naked pods, except for RestartNever scenarios. (A minimal Job is coming. #1624)
- Use Deployment (#1743) for RestartAlways services rather than RC directly, when we have that.
- In the meantime, put a version number or hash as a suffix to the name and in a label on a ReplicationController, to facilitate rolling update, as we do for [--image](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/072137764665182394975e1e1459ade58ee25719/pkg/kubectl/rolling_updater.go#L112)
- Put object description in an annotation

cc @smarterclayton @thockin

title: Pod API Clients, Certificates, and Pod External API Clients

labels.name: kind/design

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Some requirements:
- Pods that need to reach the APIserver need to know where it is.  
- The method should support multiple apiservers.
- The client needs to know what name to expect on the cert that the master presents.
- The client needs to know what root CAs it trusts for the master's cert when setting up TLS with the master.
- The client needs to know what root CAs it trusts when establishing TLS with external services, like cloud.google.com, github.com, etc.

Some master discovery options:
- static list of master IPs 
  - doing that in #7055
- via a kubernetes serviceIP
- via DNS
  - requires that all K8s distros have a way to put the kubernetes service into DNS.  

How do pods get root certs to verify identity of external remote service:
- Use Node OS root certs, like in #6916?  
- Use Container Image root certs (should gcr.io provide a curated base image with trusted root certs, like https://registry.hub.docker.com/u/centurylink/ca-certs/ 
- Assume people use a OS distro with root certs as their base image

How do pods get root cert to verify identity of self-signed cert on master?

title: Shared Pod Storage (e.g. Config Storage)

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
I am working on a Kubernetes extension that would run in its own pod but would like to store some information (e.g. configuration) that has similar requirements as the data stored in API Server.  In particular it would be nice if the storage had the following properties:
- **Durable:**  Survives pod restarts, migrations, and upgrades.
- **Consistent:**  Even if there are multiple pods writing the same resource concurrently, consistency is maintained.
- **Addressable:**  When a pod starts it can find the storage allocated for its application.
- **Isolated:**  Different applications don't accidentally write over each others data even if they use the same names, paths, keys, etc.
- **Semi-structured:**  Something like JSON-store would be fine.
- **Service Oriented:**  Ideally this is provided as a simple RESTful service such that it is accessible from any operating environment and doesn't require linking any specific client library.
- **Timestamped:**  Each resource has a logical-clock timestamp (i.e. eTag) that can be used for optimistic concurrency control.  Ideally without imposing any particular versioning scheme or strategy on the resources themselves.
- **Watch Support:**  It is possible to watch or be notified of updates to resources (or even small set of resources, e.g. subfolders). 
# Possibilities:
## Use Volumes

Applications can always mount a volume and write their own storage to files.  This is not ideal for a few  reasons: 
- It requires a lot of reimplementation for each application.  
- Disks that survive cluster and pod restart are not a guaranteed part of all Kubernetes deployments making apps more difficult to deploy and move between Kube environments.
- PD can have undesirable limitations (e.g. how many pods can mount them simultaneously).
## Have applications run their own storage as a pod

Running your own etcd cluster is an obvious choice.  However, running storage as a pod is actually quite tricky.  Durability and consistency are difficult to provide and are often better maintained by a dedicated team that knows about backup and recovery.  Durability itself requires some off pod storage which brings you back to volumes.  Storage pods that are restarted need to rediscover and reattach the persistent storage used by a previous instance even though their identities are not related in any way (see Nominal Services).
## API Server's Etcd Cluster

The etcd server used by the API Server provides almost all of these features with the exception of isolation.  One possibility would be to expose a thin shim service at the API Server that wraps its underlying etcd cluster and re-exposes scoped portions of its namespace to pods.  The shim would enforce scoping and authorization.  The shim could also provide some adaption of the etcd watch interface to be more consistent with the semantics exposed by the API Server itself.

Pros:  This possibility unifies the problems of durability, consistency, addressability with the API Servers almost identical requirements.  Since any deployment must already solve these issues for API Server it doesn't create any additional burden.  In hosted environments (e.g. GKE) the host provides Etcd and its durable storage in a way that is independent of the Kubernetes model allowing for backup, restore, and survivability to be implemented in ways that would be difficult if run directly as a pod.  API Server already implements a sophisticated RESTful web service endpoint with authentication, authorization, timestamping, and watch support.  This logic could be shared by the shim without addition complexity or duplication.

Cons: Opening up the API Server's Etcd server (even if the shim correctly implements isolation) to third-party applications will create additional load on both API Server and Etcd.  This would affect the responsiveness of API Server and scalability in ways that may be difficult to predict.  Bugs in the shim or Etcd might expose the data from either the master or other applications to corruption or deletion.

title: kube-proxy: use sysctl route_localnet to simplify logic

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
FAO @thockin (and any other networking gurus)

Currently kube-proxy normally listens on 0.0.0.0 or on the eth0 IP, which causes potential problems with port conflicts when using externally accessible services vs internal kube-proxy services.

It would be great if we could listen on 127.0.0.1, but this doesn't work:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/96bcb56f1065bfcba5ce42c3fa727bdc99dda9f6/pkg/proxy/proxier.go#L740-L741

This seems to be the reason why those packets disapper:  http://superuser.com/a/807612

By setting `sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.route_localnet=1`, I was able to get DNS to resolve inside a container - running kube-proxy with bind_address=127.0.0.2 to bypass the localhost test :-)

This is apparently only in kernel >= 3.6.  Is this something we would want to consider anyway?

If not, maybe we could listen on 10.244.x.1, and avoid allocating that IP to a pod.  That seemed to "work for me" also.

If we did this, I think we avoid all the problems with conflicts between internal & external ports, allowing us to do all the things we've been discussing in the ELB patch & #6684 cleanly.

title: Add port annotations to know what protocols a port will support for pods, maybe services

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Service Catalog.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
There are several use cases where knowing what protocols a port on a container in a pod actually supports would affect information presented to end users.

Ex 1:
I have a container in a pod exposing port 8080, do we show a clickable link in the GUI?  Right now we have to assume it exposes http(s) and always show the link, or never show a link.  If the port was annotated to say that it supported http(s) we would know for sure.

Ex 2:
I have a container in a pod exposing port 8080, I don't have any services routing to the pod.  Should I recommend to the end user that they create a service?  If the port were annotated to say that it exposes http(s) then we would be more likely to suggest they create a service than if it was annotated to expose a different protocol.

```
    mapper, typer := f.Object()
```

GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes#6380 introduced a change where  **/healthz** stoped being found at port 10250 and is now (by default) at port 10248. due to this kube-register now fails. a quick & dirty fix was provided by me to upstream [here](https://github.com/kelseyhightower/kube-register/pull/15) and i'm using it on my own [here](https://github.com/AntonioMeireles/kubernetes-vagrant-coreos-cluster/commit/d45687c992ddd44c5ffa218e7ba541b56d9b662e) without afaict any visible issue.

title: Avoid thundering herd of relist

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
We currently relist for at least 2 reasons:
1. Correctness, aka recovering from random issues we can't explain
2. Etcd's watch window

This could lead to a thundering herd  because all our major watch clients open up connections at around the same time. A quick and dirty way to avoid this is to pick a random timeout server side (or  set the sever timeout to 10m and allow every reflector started without a relist period to pick a random number between 5-10).

Arguments for server side:
- It is easier to generate pseudo randomness from a single server process than n clients

Arguments for client side:
- We already have a relist timeout idiom on client, this needs to integration with the server setting
- It feels like the clients should control when they relist, and the server should control when the connection is dropped, but I'm willing to compromise on the SoC for the sake of simplicity.

@lavalamp

title: Deleting containers holds up the update bus on kubelet

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
This might just be WAI. We currently have something like (people who know better please correct):

```
apiserver
   |
reflector
   |
|(1) api  --(listen)>|                                 
|(1) file --(listen)>|(merge)->(compress) ->[update BUS (50)] ->syncLoop
|(1) http --(listen)>|                                  
```

Where (x) is a channel of capacity x
1. We can only get watch events as fast as we can compress in MergeState (which takes the lock on the pod storage and iterates through all its pods https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/config/config.go#L337)
   
   But still, that's mostly been _ok_ in the little profiling I've done.    
2. It's fairly easy to fill up that update bus with a few tries of:

```
cluster/kubectl.sh create rc --replicas=30
<wait for pods to start running>
cluster/kubectl.sh stop rc
cluster/kubectl.sh create rc --replicas=30
```

Bump replicas to 100 on a 3 core system  and it'll happen sooner :)

The stop and second create will fill the bus with 50 podupdates while SyncPods is still destroying containers from the delete. This causes merge to stall for the 51st update, which causes the reflector to stall. So essentially everything is held up on delete, which feels kind of backwards, because I usually don't care about deleted pods anymore?

title: Probe back off settings

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
While using a liveness probe on a pod that must initialize itself with multiple configuration files we found that the liveness probe delay was not always sufficient without making it a large value.  https://github.com/openshift/origin/issues/1504#issuecomment-87824041

It seems likely that we may run in to a scenario where the initial delay is unpredictable but a probe is still desired.  The use cases I can think of are:
1.  An application that must perform N amount of work before initializing.  For example, an application that must read in configuration before starting the processes that will enable the probe to complete.  The configuration may be a single, variable sized file, multiple files, retrieving and writing data from master, etc.  
2.  At scale in a prod environment, resource jitter may delay what was a good probe initial delay setting in dev/test environments.

An initial delay with a back off for failures seems appropriate in these use cases in order to give an adequate amount of time between probes before killing and restarting the container.

title: Create a cache in apiserver to improve its performance

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

body:
## Background

 While running Kubernetes on 100-node cluster, the main bottleneck is the apiserver.
For example, starting a replication controller with 3000 pods (100 nodes, 30 pods per node) on the empty cluster lasts almost 20 minutes, and the CPU of 4-core master is 100% saturated for all that time.

 Looking at the profiles, more than 50% of CPU is spent on decoding objects coming from etcd (i.e. decoding jsons). I don't think we can do much with decoding itself, but what we can do is to limit the number of decodings we perform.

 For example, imagine a 100-node cluster and say one pod has just changed. What happens currently (which I think is reasonable) is that all Kubelets are listening to pods that are assigned to them. This however translates to opening watch for all pods, and filtering them at the apiserver based on the label/field selectors. This means that the particular change of a pod will be read from etcd 100 times, each time we independently decode it, apply labels and send it (to at most one Kubelet).
 Note that we're decoding the same pod read from etcd 100 times, which is a clear waste of resources.
# PROPOSAL

  My proposal is to create some kind of cache in the apiserver. The approach I am suggesting is:
1. The cache is used only for reading (writing doesn't read or modify cache)
2. The cache is storing decoded api objects (whether we will be storing all objects or just objects of some particular types is TBD) together with their etcd index (ModifiedIndex)
3. The cache is storing at most one version of the object with a given key (the newest one).
4. When we read an object from etcd (either via Get or Watch) we:
- send a request to etcd
- if the returned version (response contains ModifiedIndex value as an explicit field) is the same as currently stored in cache, we don't need to decode it and simply return the value from the cache
- if the returned version is newer (ModifiedIndex is monotonically increasing) we decode it an update the cache with the new version (the old version)
- if the returned version is older, we simply have a cache miss and decode it without using cache

What do you think about this proposal? If you think that's worth doing I'm happy to run some experiments to check how much it would help (I think the gain would be huge for bigger clusters).

@thockin @smarterclayton @fgrzadkowski @davidopp @lavalamp @timothysc

title: Proposal: Upstream Kubernetes-Mesos framework

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
## Overview
### Goals
1. It should be super-easy for any k8s user to deploy a k8s cluster on Mesos.
2. Immediate (developer) awareness of divergence between existing k8s core and k8s-mesos integration.
3. [k8s-mesos](https://github.com/mesosphere/kubernetes-mesos) integration no longer vendors k8s, but is a _part of_ the k8s distribution.
4. Compatibility with existing cluster integration tooling
5. Phase 1 (see below) integration complete as of k8s 1.0
### Dependencies / Assumptions
1. "mesos" cloud provider implementation has been merged into k8s core
2. k8s-mesos has achieved adequate test coverage
3. k8s-mesos has adopted Google's Go code style/standards
## Core Integration
1. Packaging alignment
   - [k8s-mesos](https://github.com/mesosphere/kubernetes-mesos) isn't really an add-on, it's the basis for an alternate distribution/deployment
2. Releases will consist of the current k8s core components, as well as the k8s-mesos framework
   - Larger distribution size
   - Current k8s-mesos dependencies merged into k8s dependencies (e.g. k8s will vendor mesos-go, et al.)
   - Platform builds will fail upon divergence between k8s core and k8s-mesos framework
3. Phased approach
   - Phase 1: Build & Deploy + Framework
   - Phase 2: Cluster Provider + Salt
   - Phase 3: Wish List
### Build & Deploy

``` shell
$ git clone https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes k8s
$ cd k8s
$ export KUBERNETES_PROVIDER=mesos:gce              # s/:/--/ for hier providers
$ hack/dev-build-and-push.sh                        # (unchanged)
$ cluster/kube-up.sh                                # phase 2: bring up mesos/gce cloud w/ k8s
```
### Framework

```
github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/plugins/third_party/mesos
    doc.go                # what is this stuff?!
    pkg/
        scheduler/
        executor/
        offers/
        ...               # additional, utility classes
    cmd/
        km/               # unified framework binary, can run either as mesos scheduler or executor
```
### Cluster Provider

```
github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/cluster/mesos--gce
    util.sh        # provide some additional configs for mesos cluster config,
*(other).sh        # but mostly delegate to gce provider.
                   # probably set DISABLE_CORE_K8S (see Salt below)
                   # domain = kubernetes.mesos
```
### Salt

```
github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/cluster/salt
    ...         # k8s scheduler plugin isn’t started (via DISABLE_CORE_K8S)
                # kubelet isn’t started (via DISABLE_CORE_K8S)
                #    - no static pod support
                # use existing kube-apiserver support
                # use existing controller-manager support
                # use existing kube-proxy support
                # zk started on master node
                # mesos-slave system service started on all minions
                # mesos-master system service started on master node
                # km framework is deployed to mesos (--run_proxy=false)
                #    - this provides both the scheduler and executor components
                # kube-addons should still function if deployed by kubectl
```
### Wish List
1. [mesos-dns](https://github.com/mesosphere/mesos-dns) integration (to resolve services in .kubernetes.mesos domain)
   - This would likely become an add-on
2. Hierarchical cloud provider support for the “mesos” cloud provider API implementation
   - To expose the more feature-rich underlying cloud provider impl, like GCE

cc @bgrant0607 @davidopp @guenter @timothysc @ConnorDoyle

title: Reflector shouldn't leak io watcher on error events

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

milestone.title: v1.0
milestone.description: Issues that need to be resolved for v1.0 of Kubernetes.

body:
This is more of a reminder for myself to follow up with investigations and fix a resource leak. Currently the reflector forgets to close the streamwatcher when it receives a watch event with an error: 
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/client/cache/reflector.go#L167

This means the stream watcher will remain dangling until the connection expires; could lead to problems when the error rate spikes: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/tools/etcd_helper_watch.go#L171

@lavalamp


This result includes updates for services "kubernetes", "kubernetes-ro", "redis-slave", "redis-master", etc.  Even though the requesting URL indicated only "guestbook" updates were to be watched.

This seems to only occur when no resourceVersion is specified and the most recent resourceVersion has fallen off the etcd watch window.
# Expected Behavior

The expected behavior when resourceVersion is not specified I would think should be either:
1.  an initial update with the latest version of the resource, followed by filtered updates.
2.  nothing, followed by filtered updates.

Though I'm not sure which of these is actually the spec.  I would prefer (1) since it allows you to do a resource watch without having to first do a separate GET.  But (2) coupled with a preceding GET would yield the same results.

title: Multi-container pod fate sharing issue

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
I have a pod with an InfluxDB database container and a Kafka consumer container. The Kafka consumer imports data from Kafka into InfluxDB. 

Recently, the Kafka consumer container experienced an error, causing it to crash and preventing it from properly starting up again. However, the InfluxDB container was still running fine.

The issue is that Kubernetes removed the endpoint for the service I created for the pod, which I assume is because it didn't deem the pod healthy or ready. However, this prevented other pods from accessing the InfluxDB database.

I am wondering if this type of fate sharing among containers in a pod is a good design? I assume that had I set "ClusterIP: None" in the service (i.e., no proxy/LB), InfluxDB would still be accessible. Maybe it is better to to create an endpoint as long as at least one container is running in the pod? Or, at least make this configurable.

I think it is a common deployment pattern in Kubernetes that you have a side-car container that performs some simple, but non-critical task (like backups, or configuration updates, etc.). A failure in one of these side-cars shouldn't bring down an otherwise functioning service.

labels.name: priority/backlog

Conformance Tests are using a skip regex, which means that every time someone adds an e2e test that isn't skipped, it's automatically added to the Conformance Tests on master:HEAD.

While this does mean that our conformance tests provide very good coverage, it also makes them an ever-moving target, which is nearly impossible to meet.

I propose we change them to a whitelist.

This will still require evaluating every new e2e test to determine if it should be in the Conformance Tests, but it makes them much more controlled and hard to accidentally break.

- [ ] tag experimental tests
- [ ] tag smoke tests

title: Audit and evaluate apiserver client usage in kubelet

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
The current apiserver client QPS for kubelet is the default 5.0, which is not high for kubelet. When batch creating pods, the startup latency is completely dominated by the QPS (e.g. see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/14554#issuecomment-143829191, events consumed most of the bandwidth). Moreover, the _perceived_ kubelet performance may be affected by slight change in kubelet's behavior, due to the QPS limitation (e.g., https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/14554#issuecomment-143898216).

We should audit our apiserver client usage and re-evaluate whether to bump the QPS, or to clearly surface any increase in the client usage.

Major consumers for the apiserver client includes:
- events
- pod status
- node status (relatively low)

The breakdown of starting a pod of N containers (when there is no failure):
- (N+1) \* 3 events  (for each container, including the infra container, there are pulled, created, and started events)
- 3 pod status update (the initial pending, running, and finally the running+ready status). This may increase once we let user control per-container probing period.

For starting 30 single-container pods on kubelet, the pods along would generate ((1+1)*3+3)*30= 9*30=270 requests.
This would take kubelet 270/5 qps = 54 seconds to send out.

/cc @kubernetes/goog-node

title: Have an option to keep Pod around for debugging

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
We received an interesting suggestion today which has multiple layers to it but basically the use case was that they would like us to keep Pod state around for debugging in the case where a Pod is "moved" to another machine. This would presumably be an option in the Pod, rather than default behavior, since in the normal case people probably only care about the logs and not the full state.

[Please read "move" here in the proper cattle-centric way, meaning "kill old Pod and create a fungible replica on a different machine"] 

Today IIUC the only scenario where we "move" a Pod to a new machine is if the machine fails. So the feature request is that when the machine comes back up, we want it to still have logs, containers, host directories, Pod-scoped directories, etc. still intact. I guess this is somewhat related to the Borg critical data concept, although for a very different purpose.

In the future I imagine we will want some other scenarios to trigger the Pod to "move" -- for example there is a restart loop (kubelet keeps restarting the container locally due to repeated OOM or something else that boils down to "the Pod is just not going to work here, but might work in another machine"). In this case you'd want to also keep the same state from the old Pod around despite creating a replacement replica elsewhere.

The last use case that was brought up was debugging deadlock. There would be an option to start a new replica on another node while keeping the deadlocked Pod/container running so that you can attach a debugger to the process that is deadlocked. Of course you'd also like to keep the same state we've been talking about for the other cases (logs, containers, host directories, Pod-scoped directories).

@mikedanese does this sound like a fairly accurate description of the request? Anything I left out?

title: RFC: Allow perm-failed deployments

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
There are times when the deployment system can infer that the latest deployment state has no reasonable chance of being realized (e.g. a bad or unpullable image). The current deployment controller design will continue to try reconciling indefinitely regardless of the possibly of success. If based on inference or user constraints (e.g. timeout conditions specified in an enhancement to the deployment API #1743) the system is ready to give up its best-effort attempt, the deployment could be somehow marked as "permananently failed" for a given spec hash so that the system won't continue thrashing on a doomed deployment.

There is a bit of functional overlap with inert deployments (#14516) in that both concepts result in the deployment controller "ignoring" a deployment whose state still needs realized, but inert deployments as described don't seem to capture all the context users would want in this case (i.e., it's not enough to just mark a doomed deployment intert without more context about why, and without UX safety nets to distinguish the repurcussions of re-activating the suddenly inert deployment vs. a permafailed deployment.)

The new deployment API (#1743) specifies some out of the box strategies (recreate, rolling) which will be implemented inside the deployment controller. It's possible these strategies may not cover all deployment needs for end users, or for downstream users (such as OpenShift). The deployment system should enable:
1. Users to define their own deployment strategy logic in a custom Docker image.
2. Downstream systems to define deployment strategies in a delegate controller.

title: Proposal: Affinity Priority for pods of different RC/services

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
When deploying a multi-layer application, a typical model is to spread the pods of same layer while placing pods of different layers together.
Currently the scheduler can spread pods from the same RC and/or Service, but cannot affiliate a pod to another.

This proposal is to support the affinity priority between pods of different RC/services.

As a first step, we use label selector to implement. When scheduling, the scheduler compares affinitySelector with all pods’ labels on each node. Nodes with pods(that have particular label values) running on will get high score.

The initial version will be in a followup PR, thanks to have a look and let me know.

**Here is a example of usage**  
The definition of Redis:  

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  name: redis-rc
  labels:
    name: redis-rc
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    service: redis
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        service: redis
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: redis-container
        image: redis
```

The definition of application that accesses Redis:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  name: nodejs
  labels:
    name: nodejs
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    name: nodejs
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        name: nodejs
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-container
        image: nodejs
      affinitySelector:
        service: redis
```

title: Node becomes unstable when overcommit on memory qos, does not always recover

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
I can reproduce a situation where the node can become unstable and never recover from a NotReady status using either the Vagrant or GCE based Kubernetes setups.

```
$ export KUBERNETES_PROVIDER=vagrant || gce
$ export NUM_MINIONS=1
$ export KUBE_ENABLE_CLUSTER_MONITORING=none
$ export KUBE_ENABLE_CLUSTER_DNS=false
$ export KUBE_ENABLE_CLUSTER_UI=false
$ cluster/kube-up.sh
```

Assuming you are using GCE, let's spin up the following:

```
$ cluster/kubectl.sh run mem-guaranteed --image=derekwaynecarr/memhog --replicas=2 --requests=cpu=10m --limits=memory=600Mi --command -- memhog -r100000 500m
$ cluster/kubectl.sh run mem-burstable --image=derekwaynecarr/memhog --replicas=2 --requests=cpu=10m,memory=600Mi --command -- memhog -r100000 100m
```

At this point, the Node is stable, and we have 2 guaranteed memory containers allocating 500MB of memory and writing to it repeatedly.  We also have 2 burstable memory containers allocating 100MB of container and writing to it repeatedly.  Both containers are using `memhog` utility.

The node is stable, and all is good.

If I do the following:

```
$ cluster/kubectl.sh run mem-besteffort --replicas=10 --image=derekwaynecarr/memhog --requests=cpu=10m --command -- memhog -r10000 500m
```

Where you may choose to scale the above based on replica size, the pods startup and each try to write 500MB of memory, and a `SystemOOM` event is triggered as expected.  

The Node may or may not remain stable at this point.  After some time, I found that even though we put the containers in a `CrashLoopBackoff` ultimately, the `Kubelet` ceased to report status back to the `kube-apiserver` for over 5 minutes and as a result, its status was reported as `NotReady`.  I was unable to SSH into the GCE box to debug (it was locked out).

The only way I could get the node to fix itself was to kill the replications controllers in the cluster.  

After some time, it appeared the Node recovered and went back into a `Ready` state.  What I would prefer to have seen is that the Node remained `Ready`, and only the `BestEffort` containers found themselves quarantined in a longer back-off period without affecting the other system processes from reporting status.

I looked at the logs for the 5 minutes that I encountered the NotReady status on the Kubelet and see messages like the following (using GCE):

```
/proc/2892/net/dev: open /proc/2892/net/dev: no such file or directory
```

title: Persistent Volume health checks / reconciliation with provider

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
The introduction of volume.Creater allows new volumes to be created dynamically in the storage provider.  PVs are then created that point to the volume.

Errors can occur in between creation of the resource (say an EBS volume in AWS) and the creation of the PV pointing to that resource.  This leaves the EBS volume orphaned and without a PV.

Each volume created in the infrastructure requires, at a minimum, the namespace/name of the claim for which the volume was created.  The cloud provider API should be able to query for all volumes and retrieve whatever tags are applied.  Those volumes earmarked for the cluster must be reconciled with the existing PVs in the cluster to ensure they match.

GCE PD API allows a text description on a PD.   EBS volumes can have tags applied.  Cinder likely has an equivalent.

@thockin @saad-ali @kubernetes/rh-storage

title: APIGroupVersion smashes discrete fields

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/13945 made `APIGroupVersion.Root` (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/apiserver/apiserver.go#L81) a combined field when called from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/master/master.go#L988.  

This ends up making the field ambiguous, since `APIPrefixes` are allowed to contain slashes (at least my knowledge).  Even if they aren't allowed to contain slashes, it hard to make a case for combining two logically discrete fields into a single field that later requires parsing to distinguish.

We need to refactor this into discrete fields to make it easier to reason about.

Implementation problem of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/12951

title: vspere cloud provider fails if multiple ESX networks are present

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
When attempting to create a Kubernetes cluster using KUBERNETES_PROVIDER=vsphere, I get the following error:

```
$ cluster/kube-up.sh 
... Starting cluster using provider: vsphere
... calling verify-prereqs
... calling kube-up
Starting master VM (this can take a minute)...
Error: default network resolves to multiple instances, please specify
```

Following the thread a bit, this is because the instructions don't mention that you need to set the `GOVC_NETWORK` flag if your vcenter manages multiple networks (similarly, it omits the GOVC_DATACENTER flag which was also necessary in my case to upload the kube.vmdk file).

Setting the `GOVC_NETWORK` env variable (using the output of `govc ls /<datacenter name>/network`) has got me past this issue.

title: GKE: Kubernetes semi-manual upgrades

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/provider/gcp
labels.description: Issues or PRs related to gcp provider

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
Currently, upgrading involves something like:

```
gcloud container clusters upgrade NAME --cluster-version 1.0.6
```

which will re-create all nodes one by one.

While this is a great feature to have, we are running [Vault](https://vaultproject.io) on top of our cluster, which requires a manual _unseal_ of each running Vault instance after it restarts, for enhanced security.

This means that, for truely zero-downtime upgrades, we'd need a way to:
1. mark a node as [unschedulable](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.0/docs/admin/cluster-management.md#maintenance-on-a-node)
2. upgrade that single node
3. make sure at least _one_ instance of Vault is running on that node
4. unseal Vault
5. we are now ensured of one unsealed vault being available during the next steps
6. upgrade all other nodes at will

Is this possible? In effect, I am trying to manually reproduce the "Node Upgrades" [documentation](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.0/docs/admin/cluster-management.md#node-upgrades):

> Node upgrades for GKE and GCE-OSS again use a Managed Instance Group, each node is sequentially destroyed and then recreated with new software.

_As mentioned elsewhere, running two clusters could solve this problem, but that's a bridge too far right now, in terms of engineering effort and costs_

title: Setting credentials in 1.1.0-alpha.1 on AWS

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
We're working on upgrading from 1.0 to 1.1.0-alpha.1. Before spinning up a cluster with kube-up, we set the credentials:

``` sh
kubectl config set-credentials aws_kubernetes --username=myusername --password=mypassword
```

This works as expected on 1.0. With 1.1.0-alpha.1, though, we saw that these credentials (myusername:mypassword) are overwritten with values created in `gen-kube-basicauth` (admin:randomstring). These credentials from `gen-kube-basicauth` are stored in `.kube/config` and are used in the cluster.

If we comment out `gen-kube-basicauth` in `cluster/aws/util.sh` and set the following env variables, the credentials are set on the cluster as expected:


title: Authz interfaces/implementations don't support API groups

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

body:
API group support was added without updating the corresponding pieces needed for authorization.

Because resource names are no longer unique across API groups, authorization must have the group information from the request in order to make a authz decision. Changes needed:
- The `authorizer.Attributes` interface needs a way to get the API group (e.g. `GetAPIGroup`)
- `apiserver.requestAttributeGetter` needs to plumb the API group into the attributes
- `APIRequestInfoResolver` needs to parse group info from the request URL into the returned `APIRequestInfo`
- `abac.policy` needs a way to indicate which API group a rule applies to (and decide how to handle existing rules which do not specify a group... match all? match no group (e.g. v1))

labels.name: priority/backlog

body:
Instance storage is dependent on the instance type, and this is tricky for users:
- some types include adequate free instance storage (m3.large is 32GB)
- some types include small free instance storage (m3.medium is 4GB)
- some types automatically deploy a backing EBS volume (t2.micro has a 32GB EBS volume)
- some types do not include any instance storage by default (m4 family)

(at least I think that's the case).

We should figure out a sensible approach here that ensures users have sensible storage.  This may turn out to be primarily a docs issue.

title: Indexed Job

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
Allow a Job to optionally be a  _Indexed_ Jobs by setting `.spec.nominal = true`. 

EDITED: _Indexed_ was previously called _Nominal_.

If `indexed` is true, when each Pod is created, manager decides which "completion index" that pod is going to work on.  Manager ensures that there is one completion for each index from 0 to `completions - 1`.  We make it possible to expose that index via the downward API.  Pods can specialize themselves based on their index.  For example, by indexing into bash-array env var. 

Examples of podTemplates in _Indexed Jobs_:

```
spec:
  containers:
    - name: foo
      env:
        - name: N
          valueFrom:
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: metadata.completionIndex
      cmd: [ "/bin/sh", "-c", "myprogram --work_unit=$N" ]
```

or

```
spec:
  containers:
    - name: foo
      env:
        - name: N
          valueFrom:
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: metadata.completionIndex
      cmd: [ "/bin/sh", "-c",
             "files_to_process=(foo bar); myprogram --work_unit=$files_to_process[$N]" ]
```

body:
1. (COMPLETE) set a deadline and kill the job after that deadline . This was called ActiveDeadlineSeconds in the original proposal.  I argued for removing it for now and it was dropped during review.  @bgrant0607 argues that we have tried (on Borg) offering users many options for managing/throttling failures, and none of them worked well for users except deadlines for non-serving jobs. 
2. automatically throttle creation of new pods when failures are frequent.
3. distinguish between "application failures" and "cluster failures" (e.g. machine-level OOM, node failure) in reporting failures, and in throttling. 
4. consider interaction of Pods of a Job with Vertical Autoscaler.  That is, I should be able to start a job with an initial prediction of memory usage, and then if it OOMs, modify the request and retry.  
5. ensure that successful pods are not automatically deleted before the Job finishes (because then the Job Manager will forget about the success).  Either mark the pod as do-not-garbage-collect, or else record the success somewhere else.
6. Show relevant pod events in Job describe output.
7. Ensure graceful deletion works when reducing parallelism
8. Indexed Job feature: when each Pod is created, manager decides which "completion index" it is trying to do.  Ensures one completion for each index from 0 to `completions - 1`.  Expose that index via the downward API.  Pods can pick up pod-specific options by e.g. indexing into bash-array env var.  #14188

title: Node in NotReady status after kernel upgrade and reboot on Ubuntu Vivid (15.04) due to Docker service failure (no aufs)

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
Hi. I'm writing this partially because I want to start a discussion and to leave some trails for others potentially affected.

I started my journey with Kubernetes just a few days ago. I downloaded the 1.0.6 release (now I know this a only a pre-release and I should've downloaded the 1.0.4 release but this doesn't seem to be related to my particular issue).

I brought up a tiny k8s cluster with the following config:

```
export KUBERNETES_PROVIDER=aws
export KUBE_AWS_ZONE=eu-west-1a
export NUM_MINIONS=3
export MINION_SIZE=t2.micro
export AWS_S3_REGION=eu-west-1
export AWS_S3_BUCKET=xxx
export KUBE_AWS_INSTANCE_PREFIX=xxx
```

My cluster was created properly and after a bit of playing I left it in a good shape.

The next day I wanted to investigate some DNS related issue on k8s nodes so I logged in on one of the minions. I noticed `*** System restart required ***` in the MOTD. I ignored it for a moment and investigated the DNS matters (some `nslookup`s, nothing dangerous). Then I rebooted the machine.

Once the machine was up again I found out that `kubectl` reported it as `NotReady`. I started digging and investigating. It took me some time to find out that the Docker service on the node was not running:

```
$ sudo docker info
FATA[0001] Get http:///var/run/docker.sock/v1.18/info: read unix /var/run/docker.sock: connection reset by peer. Are you trying to connect to a TLS-enabled daemon without TLS?
```

```
$ sudo journalctl -u docker -f
-- Logs begin at Fri 2015-09-18 08:06:53 UTC. --
Sep 18 08:09:49 ip-172-20-0-149 systemd[1]: docker.service failed.
Sep 18 08:09:51 ip-172-20-0-149 systemd[1]: docker.service holdoff time over, scheduling restart.
Sep 18 08:09:51 ip-172-20-0-149 systemd[1]: Started Docker Application Container Engine.
Sep 18 08:09:51 ip-172-20-0-149 systemd[1]: Starting Docker Application Container Engine...
Sep 18 08:09:51 ip-172-20-0-149 docker[3397]: time="2015-09-18T08:09:51Z" level=info msg="+job serveapi(fd://)"
Sep 18 08:09:51 ip-172-20-0-149 docker[3397]: time="2015-09-18T08:09:51Z" level=info msg="Listening for HTTP on fd ()"
Sep 18 08:09:51 ip-172-20-0-149 docker[3397]: time="2015-09-18T08:09:51Z" level=fatal msg="Shutting down daemon due to errors: error intializing graphdriver: driver not supported"
Sep 18 08:09:51 ip-172-20-0-149 systemd[1]: docker.service: main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
Sep 18 08:09:51 ip-172-20-0-149 systemd[1]: Unit docker.service entered failed state.
Sep 18 08:09:51 ip-172-20-0-149 systemd[1]: docker.service failed.
```

Further investigation led me to a conclusion that the problem arose from the fact that before the reboot the kernel was upgraded to 3.19.0-28, which no longer by default supports AUFS module which Docker uses as its storage driver.

Looks like the solution is to install the `linux-image-extra-virtual`, as concluded from docker/docker#10859 and other sources, and reboot the node. After reboot the node got back to the `Ready` state.

Moreover, I guess an upgrade to a newer Docker version, using the official install command `curl -sSL https://get.docker.com/ | sh` would solve the problem as the most recent install script already installs `linux-image-extra-virtual` as per docker/docker#10860, although I'm not sure how Docker was installed on the k8s node, so I don't know if it's safe to upgrade it this way.

So I have a number of questions:
1. should k8s provide a workaround / fix for this particular issue?
2. or is it left to a cluster admin as it's an issue of a particular provider/env/configuration?
3. why is k8s using Docker v1.6.0 which is pretty old?
4. is it safe to use k8s in production on a setup in which Docker uses AUFS storage driver which seems to be deprecated by the Ubuntu team and thus dropped from the main kernel image?

Note that I haven't done anything unusual, just installed fresh k8s on AWS using the default Ubuntu release. Hence I believe it's important to fix it somehow in k8s.

Possible duplicate: #9779.

title: Enable deployment strategies to tolerate concurrent external scaling events

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

milestone.title: v1.2-candidate
milestone.description: Things to consider for next minor release.

body:
The rolling updater should be tolerant of external scaling events concurrent with the update, but  lacks the required context to reevaluate its internal state. As a result, updates can conflict with manual scaling and the autoscaler in unpredictable ways.

The rolling updater computes the desired replica count for the target replication controller only once during initialization based on a snapshot of the the target replication controller state. If during the rolling update the target replication controller `spec.replicas` is modified externally (via scale operations), the rolling updater is unable to deduce the intent of the replica count change in order to recompute the target desired replica count for the replication controller.

A new replication controller field such as `spec.trendingToReplicas` could be added and  considered a formalization of the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/desired-replicas` annotation. This field would provide a means for deployment strategies and scaling systems to set a desired replica count for the replication controller itself in the context of replication controller transitions (such as a rolling update).

The rolling updater (and any other strategies) would drive the replication controller `spec.replicas` towards `spec.trendingToReplicas`. Any changes to `spec.trendingToReplicas` could safely result in recalculating the scaling internals.

Scaling systems and other API calls which ultimately want to mutate `spec.replicas` could then work safely with deployment strategies: If `spec.trendingToReplicas` is set, update `spec.trendingToReplicas` and cause rolling updates (or other deployment strategies) to adapt. If `spec.trendingToReplicas` is unset, directly update the RC `spec.replicas`.

cc @nikhiljindal @bgrant0607 @smarterclayton @kargakis

title: API server is not accessible via VirtualBox/docker-machine after getting started instructions

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/docs
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Docs.

body:
The (awesome) getting started guide for docker includes support for running on VirtualBox and suggests using docker-machine to manage that. While the provided commands do get the kubernetes cluster up and running /within/ the VirtualBox VM, the cluster's API server is not accessible from /outside/ the VM without further hackery.

The `master.json` file configures the API server to listen on 127.0.0.1:

``` json
    {
      "name": "apiserver",
      "image": "gcr.io/google_containers/hyperkube:VERSION",
      "command": [
              "/hyperkube",
              "apiserver",
              "--portal-net=10.0.0.1/24",
              "--address=127.0.0.1",
              "--etcd-servers=http://127.0.0.1:4001",
              "--cluster-name=kubernetes",
              "--v=2"
        ]
    },
```

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd5f970679e81c4c4338788f0458f0f17b6a1095/cluster/images/hyperkube/master.json#L25

The following commands instead reconfigure kubelet to create API servers listening on all addresses (assuming the kubelet container is named `kubelet`):

``` console
docker exec kubelet perl -pi -e 's/address=127.0.0.1/address=0.0.0.0/' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/master.json
docker restart kubelet
```

With this adjustment, everything works as expected and a user can connect to the API server on the VirtualBox's IP address:

``` console
$ kubectl -s $(docker-machine ip dev):8080 get nodes
NAME        LABELS                             STATUS
127.0.0.1   kubernetes.io/hostname=127.0.0.1   Ready
```

Based on the above, I'd suggest modifying `master.json`'s API server configuration to listen on 0.0.0.0. I can imagine that this might feel icky from a security perspective, but I would hope users are not simply running these images in production without modification. Further, the other containers described in the guide listen on 0.0.0.0 (including etcd), so it seems no less secure (and more useful) if the API server does as well.

Thanks!

Reference:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8de12acc3d3ac391f28c4854f557421dac5cbcea/docs/getting-started-guides/docker.md#step-two-run-the-master

title: RFC: Handling logs in the future

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: sig/instrumentation
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Instrumentation.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Having to handle logs at the node level complicates disk management considerably. 
- Currently logs are stored in the context of containers. The lifetime of logs is tied to the lifetime of container instances. 
- Disk usage accounting for logs is tricky since log files are handled by docker daemon, which provides no disk accounting.
- Containers store log files onto root filesystem at times, leading to uncontrolled disk usage.
- The existing implementation of logs APIs requires keeping old container instances around, which hinders efficient disk utilization.
- System level logs (kubelet, docker daemon, kube-proxy) have to be rotated quickly to avoid taking up too much disk space.

Since we have a cluster level logging infrastructure, we can redirect the `logs` endpoints to the logging infrastructure. This might require building a new component that can proxy logs requests to various logging backends like elasticsearch, Google Cloud Logging, etc. 

Another alternative is to not support `logs` in our APIs and require users to use their cluster logging infra to access all their logs.

GCE PD Volume attach/detach code issues [`attachDisk`](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/reference/latest/instances/attachDisk) and [`detachDisk`](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/reference/latest/instances/detachDisk) REST calls.

A HTTP 200 response to these calls simply indicates that the operation was successfully queued for asynchronous execution.

The GCE PD code currently assumes that the request succeeded and polls the `/dev/disk/by-id/` directory on the instance to verify the PD was successfully attached or detached.

Sample `attachDisk` request/response:

```
POST https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/myproject/zones/us-central1-c/instances/instance1/attachDisk
{
  "deviceName": "myPD",
  "source": "https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/myproject/zones/us-central1-c/disks/myPD",
 "kind": "compute#attachedDisk"
}
---------------------
200 OK
{
  "kind": "compute#operation",
  "id": "2212687535833054933",
  "name": "operation-1441821490584-51f5439c699c1-e9730079-76ced44a",
  "zone": "https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/myproject/zones/us-central1-c",
  "operationType": "attachDisk",
  "targetLink": "https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/myproject/zones/us-central1-c/instances/instance1",
  "targetId": "14974812993638556205",
  "status": "PENDING",
  "user": "***",
  "progress": 0,
  "insertTime": "2015-09-09T10:58:10.755-07:00",
  "startTime": "2015-09-09T10:58:11.232-07:00",
  "selfLink": "https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/myproject/zones/us-central1-c/operations/operation-1441821490584-51f5439c699c1-e9730079-76ced44a"
}
```

Instead of assuming that the request succeeded, GCE PD code should issue follow up [`zoneOperations/get`](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/reference/latest/zoneOperations/get) requests to track the status of the attach/detach calls until the operation `status` is `DONE` and check the completed operation response for errors that may have occurred during processing of the operation.

Sample `zoneOperations/get` request/response:

```
GET https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/myproject/zones/us-central1-c/operations/operation-1441821490584-51f5439c699c1-e9730079-76ced44a
---------------------
200 OK
{
 "kind": "compute#operation",
 "id": "2212687535833054933",
 "name": "operation-1441821490584-51f5439c699c1-e9730079-76ced44a",
 "zone": "https://content.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/myproject/zones/us-central1-c",
 "operationType": "attachDisk",
 "targetLink": "https://content.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/myproject/zones/us-central1-c/instances/instance1",
 "targetId": "14974812993638556205",
 "status": "DONE",
 "user": "***",
 "progress": 100,
 "insertTime": "2015-09-09T10:58:10.755-07:00",
 "startTime": "2015-09-09T10:58:11.232-07:00",
 "endTime": "2015-09-09T10:58:32.747-07:00",
 "selfLink": "https://content.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/myproject/zones/us-central1-c/operations/operation-1441821490584-51f5439c699c1-e9730079-76ced44a"
}
```
