milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
I believe AWS, GCE, bare-metal and vagrant rely on our [salt file](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cluster/saltbase/salt/docker/init.sls) to ensure docker installation. Non-RedHat distribution downloads and install a [deb package](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cluster/saltbase/salt/docker/init.sls#L102). The deb package used to (<=1.7.1) contain a static docker binary. Docker announced two months back that all distributions'd get dynamic binaries.
https://blog.docker.com/2015/07/new-apt-and-yum-repos

Now that we don't have a deb file with a static binary anymore, we need to augment this salt file significantly for each distros/version for docker upgrade. Some initial concerns are:
- It is not very clear what distros/versions we need to support
- The salt file is hard to read as it is, and this would only make it worse.

We should figure out what we want to support, what level of control we want (i.e., a specific version or just the existence of docker) and how to continue doing it.

cc @justinsb for AWS setup/support

cc @dchen1107

body:
I want to revisit the resource requirements for kube-addons now that we have qos.

All of the `kube-addons` that are added to the cluster are guaranteed qos for the cpu and memory enumerated resources.  I would like to reduce the amount of resource required by the `kube-addons` if possible so I can spin up a smaller sized cluster and still deploy some basic things without needing multiple nodes.

- Can we set requests to half the limits?

Thoughts?

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
```
$ ./kubelet --version
Kubernetes v1.0.3
```

The implementation of HashContainer is sensitive to the `name` of a volume in the `volumeMounts` section, and not the actual volume. This means that a change to a volume will not result in containers being restarted.

Eg, changing the `hostDir` path from `/tmp/dir` to `/tmp/another-dir` will not result in the kubelet recreating the container for the spec below.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pause
```

title: Add support for Quotas on Running Pods

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: area/admin
labels.description: Indicates an issue on admin area.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
This is a continuation of a discussion started in the #sig-scheduling kubernetes slack channel between @davidopp, @smarterclayton, and @quinton-hoole.

Fundamentally the quota system prevents the 'creation' of pods but has nothing (as far as I can tell) to do with the 'running' of pods.  There are lots of reasons why a pod can't get get to the 'Ready' state especially in a resource constrained cluster.  What a 'running' quota would do is not penalize a given user/namespace for having pods that can't be scheduled.

A simple example would be a namespace with a quota of 4 pods that current has 2 ready/scheduled pods and 2 pods that can't be scheduled and may not be able to for quite a while.  Given a the current quota system a new pod could not be created in this namespace.  With a running quota system of 4, however, 2 additional pods could get scheduled.

I believe that this is the time to address this functionality because the addition of the JobController, and support for batch workloads in general, will increase the potential of a given Kubernetes cluster to be resource constrained.

title: Container garbage collection should define MinAge as age since the container termination

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
The definition of `MinAge` in Container GC:

```
// Minimum age at which a container can be garbage collected, zero for no limit.
MinAge time.Duration
```

It determines a container's age by looking at its "Created" time. Even if a container has just died, as long as the container was created `MinAge` before, it would be eligible to be GC'd.
This seems arbitrary to me. What we should be looking at is "how long since the container died", so that other components in kubelet has a chance to look at the dead container before it's GC'd.

/cc @vishh @pwittrock

title: Rolling restart of pods

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
`kubectl rolling-update` is useful for incrementally deploying a new replication controller. But if you have an existing replication controller and want to do a rolling restart of all the pods that it manages, you are forced to do a no-op update to an RC with a new name and the same spec. It would be useful to be able to do a rolling restart without needing to change the RC or to give the RC spec, so anyone with access to kubectl could easily initiate a restart without worrying about having the spec locally, making sure it's the same/up to date, etc. This could work in a few different ways:
1. A new command, `kubectl rolling-restart` that takes an RC name and incrementally deletes all the pods controlled by the RC and allows the RC to recreate them.
2. Same as 1, but instead of deleting each pod, the command iterates through the pods and issues some kind of "restart" command to each pod incrementally (does this exist? is this a pattern we prefer?). The advantage of this one is that the pods wouldn't get unnecessarily rebalanced to other machines.
3. `kubectl rolling-update` with a flag that lets you specify an old RC only, and it follows the logic of either 1 or 2.
4. `kubectl rolling-update` with a flag that lets you specify an old RC only, and it auto-generates a new RC based on the old one and proceeds with normal rolling update logic.

All of the above options would need the MaxSurge and MaxUnavailable options recently introduced (see #11942) along with readiness checks along the way to make sure that the restarting is done without taking down all the pods.

@nikhiljindal @kubernetes/kubectl

title: Monitoring and managing the quota size of containers and local volumes

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Today no process on the node manages the amount of storage in use for:
- Container CoW layers (the container's writable directory)
- Empty dir volumes
- Docker volumes created implicitly on startup of the container

Since neither Docker nor the host operating system can totally manage this, I think it should be possible to have a management loop in / around the kubelet to control the total usage of these elements.  Today, it's possible to write to the empty dir until you fill the filesystem, at which point all pods fail.  You _could_ set quotas (if the uids of the processes are different), but that requires all your pods to be running unique uids (or set quota to a multiple of the count of the pods with the same UID which doesn't protect against bad actors).

I would propose the following
- Add something to cAdvisor to track top layer CoW usage where possible for the filesystems that can provide it 
  - Docker today does not expose this - we could potentially add an abstraction endpoint there, or do the checks directly against devmapper / overlay
- In the Kubelet, honor a resource limit for usage of emptyDir (per mount / pod?) as well as the cow filesystem with a simple check loop.
  - In situations where the container CoW layer has exceeded the maximum, restart the container gracefully (this is hard to do outside of the kubelet today)
  - In situations where the emptyDir has exceeded size... do something??
- Report the volume and cow metrics up through cAdvisor
- Support read only containers through docker as a pod setting and allow it to be controlled via pod policy or similar (user cannot set non-readonly containers)
- Be able to deny emptyDir volumes via pod policy or forcibly limit them to a specific size.

title: Pod-to-self networking require hairpin mode

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Linked to #3760, when using the iptables proxy instead of userspace, a pod can connect to a service IP it serves, looping back to itself. In this case, the Linux bridge implementation stops the packet from being processed because it then has the same input and output interfaces. 

The solution to this problem is to enable the hairpin of each port of the virtual bridge where the pods are connected. It should be equivalent to the following shell script:

```
# To get traffic from a pod to itself via a service:
for intf in $(ip link list | grep veth | cut -f2 -d:); do brctl hairpin cbr0 $intf on; done
```

/cc @thockin

title: Endpoint watchers cannot assume Ready pods are "Ready" in the presence of process restarts

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
If a pod process dies and is restarted by Kube (triggering the ready flag to be reset), there's no guarantee a load balancer watching endpoints sees the pod go back to not ready (kubelet updating status -> endpoints controller -> load balancer watcher) prior to the pod starting to listen on its port.  For any process that opens its TCP port before being ready, this means when a process dies and is restarted, load balancers will continue to hit the endpoint before its readiness check passes.  

One solution is to have your load balancer include the readiness check - but that only works a) if your load balancer supports it, or b) if you chose http or tcp (load balancers can't use the exec check).  Most load balancers do support ready checks, although not all support the same set of options.

One possible fix for the exec check is to expose on the kubelet an endpoint that can be a readiness proxy for the process - `https://kubelet:10250/v1/pods/<pod name or maybe pod ip>/readinesscheck` that uses the internal ready bool to return.  This would put slightly higher load on the kubelet, and mean the kubelet restarting would result in load balancers thinking the pod is down.

- The inconsistent docker root due to a potential race between kubelet and docker.

title: kubelet should clean up more reliably

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
kubelet offloads most of the pod-specific work to the per-pod workers (goroutines). This includes creating pod directories and mounting volumes, and killing containers in some cases.
On the other hand, the main kubelet loop performs global cleanup/housekeeping such as unmounting and removing volume/pod directory, and killing containers in some cases.

This creates race conditions that lead to transient errors or often something worse. We should let the pod worker does all the cleanup and let kubelet only garbage collects unused resources. The first step is to teach pod worker to understand the notion of "deletion" and try to clean up their own pod if possible, and retries on errors.

@kubernetes/goog-node, @saad-ali, any thoughts?

title: Proposal: Record which user created an object

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

body:
Currently no creator information is recorded at the time an object is created. The creator may be:
- an end user calling the api (authenticated via the Authenticator interfaces)
- a controller calling the api (authenticated via Authenticator)
- a core controller locally invoking the storage interfaces (bypasses authentication)
- someone directly editing etcd (repair process or object created in the past).

It is a common requirement to record audit information with objects that allow UIs and administrators to determine the actor involved in a transaction. The information may be recorded in a side channel (an audit log), but end users may also wish to understand who created a particular object.

Use cases:
- Allow clients to determine which user made a change
- Allow an administrator to reconstruct an audit record for who created which resources were created in the system

In the first two scenarios above, the user is clearly identified (`GetUserName()` on the user resolved by the authenticator, which rest.Storage has access to).  In the third, this is effectively what we call a "system" user, and could be assigned an arbitrary username that does not collide with real user names, or left blank.  In the last case there is probably a user name, but no mechanism whereby it is provided.
### Considerations
#### Inferential attribution
- Actions may not be undertaken by a user, but on behalf of a user
  - the replication controller process creates pods on behalf of the user who created a replication controller, but if another user edits the replication controller, both users may have a causal relationship to the pods created
  - a virtual resource may run as elevated privileges against another api and allow a user to create a resource they normally don't have permission to create - both the end user and the api process have a causal relationship to the underlying resource
  - a higher privilege user may request to run as another user via **impersonation** - the actor is the higher privilege user, but they are explicitly wishing to be recorded as acting as the impersonated user
- Actions may be separated in time and space from their cause
  - a user may delete a node, which results in a pod being deleted, which results in a pod being created by a replication controller

Recommendation: we should scope the attribution of creation to the caller (direct creator), and ensure that an external "audit log" could be constructed that can infer chain of attribution for complex cases.
#### Creating child resources

In general, it may be desirable for high level constructs (deployments, scheduled jobs) that create lower level resources (replication controllers, jobs) to propagate creation attribution. However, that raises a security risk that the creating component can lie about the source of a creation. Since an audit trail can be reconstructed between parent and subordinate resources by observing API changes, it is not necessary to propagate that info.
#### Referencing a user

We currently define a `user name` as a string that represents a unique user. That value is expected to be stable over the time periods the admin desires (only admin action would result in a user name changing). Under the covers, the user name may refer to many different types of users - the [authentication design](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/design/access.md) identifies two:
- User
  - ServiceAccount - a namespaced resource that represents a unique automated identity
    - In the future, this account may be backed by an external user
  - ExternalUser - via an external system
    - May be a human or an external service account

In addition, we have an implicit type:
- SystemUser - created implicitly in the infrastructure to represent distinct process identity prior to bootstrapping of service accounts or external users
  - Which user represents the code in the master that creates the default service account?

The `Authenticator` interface requires all of the above users to be mapped into a single user name string before filtering through the system. This string is the `userName` and must be unique across all sources of authentication.

It is assumed that the audit system and other client systems understand the mapping between the various authentication sources and `userName`.  These mappings may differ between different installations.  It should be possible for a client or third party to provide a `userName` and retrieve an object (or objects?) representing the source of the user name. 

As an example, Kube must overlay the service account user identifier onto the external authenticator source. Today, that is enforced via a unique prefix `system:serviceaccount:` that is reserved. In the future, we may map `ServiceAccount` to an external user, in which case the unique prefix may not be needed. OpenShift, which needs to manage users internally as well as externally, uses a further system of subdivision of namespace to assign a `userName` via indirection.
### Proposed change

When objects are created through rest.Storage, record the identifying user info onto the object. Add `creationUserName string` to `ObjectMeta` and assign it the `GetUserName()` value provided by the Authenticator. This value may not be changed, but may be unset if authentication is disabled.

Implications for clients:
- Clients will want to show "pretty" names to end users (`userName` may be email, but may also be a unique identifier or LDAP DN or short name). Clients that wish to do that will need a way to map `userName` to a useful value efficiently and in bulk (it's assumed that the "pretty name" for a user changes at very infrequent intervals)
- Clients may be tempted to assume the `userName` can be parsed. This limits the admin's ability to change this value. Instruct clients not to assume the `userName` value will be human readable or that it follows a parseable pattern.

Other implications:
- Clients should not be allowed to set the `creationUserName`. 
- Administrators may wish to migrate old data to assign a `creationUserName`.

body:
`kubectl version` used to print the client version before it attempted to get the server version, which means even if the server is unavailable you can still see the client version. That seems to be broken now, and instead you just get an error when the server is unavailable:

```
$ kubectl version
error: couldn't read version from server: Get http://localhost:8080/api: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: connection refused
```

Instead, the client version should print before going to check the server version (which should still print an error if the connection fails).

title: Issue with livenessProbe

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Hi, i spot weird issue with livenessProbe. You can see pod description here https://gist.github.com/roman-shuhov/d5d6c230bb3b86b639be .

I tried to create this pod and it kept restarting, and kubectl describe showed the following error:

`
Liveness probe failed: Get http://website-example-a:80/watcher.html: dial tcp: lookup website-example-a: no such host
`

So, looks like if "host" value is specified in livenessProbe (as in the example above), kubernetes is trying to fetch url http://<host>/<path> instead of sending host as a HTTP header. 

You can actually see this logic in the source code - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L205

The problem is that in this case this request go to the random pod (because it goes through load balancer), so if kubernetes have a bad pod it may kill a healthy one instead.

I think this logic should be changed, because i don't see any reason to make http://<host>/<path> request for the livenessProbe.

title: Client negotiation is too aggressive, makes disconnected operation hard

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Negotiation is only required when the server doesn't support the requested client version.  The requested client version is always known (whether default from code or specified by the user).  We should probably only negotiate in the presence of a failure to access an endpoint that should exist, or during a client action that mimics "establish config to new server".  On high latency connections, this may double the perceived delay for users which is also a usability concern.

Copied from comment on #9762

---

I totally missed the implications here when reviewing this change, but this makes it difficult to run kubectl in a disconnected mode.  That's a significant usability issue (I can't run kubectl commands that deal with local files and can output content without contacting the server on a plane, for example).  Once we add export or other temporary working tools this becomes even more irritating.  OpenShift has more generate level commands (above and beyond run) that can work in dry run which now require a running server to work.  

We can work around it in individual commands (defer .Client until later()) but there may be a better way to solve it.

One option is to have negotiation only invoked when negotiation is required.  If the user specifies a version, negotiation isn't required unless the server doesn't support the version.  If the user has recorded a preferred version, negotiation also isn't required unless the server supports the version.  Those could be handled by a fallback pattern on error.  At minimum, we could negotiate lazily on the first connection.  However, we have code that uses the api version prior to connect.  If we wanted to do aggressive negotiation we could do it on a login or config create action.

title: Enumerating options on Load-balanced apiservers.

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Over time we've discussed several options regarding how we wish to provide active-active HA on the api-servers.  Currently "we"/Red Hat support this by updating the apiservers to use a common virtual IP(VIP) that is used by both an external load-balancer and is referenced by the kube-proxy and kubelet.  

However, in the past we have discussed other options, including leveraging a discovery service.

The goal of opening this ticket is to enumerate some of the ideas and to determine a common path forwards provided it makes sense. 

@lavalamp, @davidopp, @rrati, @wojtek-t

title: Clean up: stop making pre-service-account tokens.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

body:
Currently, a cluster created with salt gets a bunch of secrets automatically created.
You can see them here:

```
$ kubectl get secrets --namespace=kube-system
NAME                              TYPE                                  DATA
default-token-flvj5               kubernetes.io/service-account-token   2
token-admin                       Opaque                                1
token-kube-proxy                  Opaque                                1
token-kubelet                     Opaque                                1
token-system-controller-manager   Opaque                                1
token-system-dns                  Opaque                                1
token-system-logging              Opaque                                1
token-system-monitoring           Opaque                                1
token-system-scheduler            Opaque                                1
```

Ignore `default-token-flvj5`, which is fine.

The others (`token-*`) were added to the cluster turnup process prior to the existence of service accounts.  The intent was to have different accounts for each component that accesses the apiserver, to allow for giving them least privilege.  However, this has yet to be implemented, and if we did implement it today, we'd use custom service accounts for each component, which would generate their own tokens.  So, we wouldn't do it this way.

It looks like approximately nothing in github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes or github.com/kubernetes/contrib is referencing the `token-*` secrets.  So, we can remove the code that creates them.

The code that creates the secrets is here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/185b5af26f069d34e3cfab653fdabfc3d22f7915/cluster/saltbase/salt/kube-addons/kube-addons.sh#L190

We also don't need to put most of those tokens in the known-tokens.csv file.
That happens in these places:
- [AWS](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a171d2e4fb81f3422a561f9a21d7b1632dab1494/cluster/aws/templates/create-dynamic-salt-files.sh#L111)
- [GCE](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a171d2e4fb81f3422a561f9a21d7b1632dab1494/cluster/gce/configure-vm.sh#L322)
- [Rackspace](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a171d2e4fb81f3422a561f9a21d7b1632dab1494/cluster/rackspace/util.sh#L148)
- [Vagrant](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a171d2e4fb81f3422a561f9a21d7b1632dab1494/cluster/vagrant/provision-master.sh#L224)

We still want the kubelet and kube-proxy tokens in that file, but we don't need those to become API tokens.

title: Feature request: dynamic cluster addon resizer

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
People create clusters at a wide range of sizes. People then resize clusters to a wide range of sizes. Our cluster addons are configured statically, and do not respond to such changes in size. This causes problems in some cases:
1. The default addons don't all fit on sufficiently small clusters (e.g. create a cluster with a single f1-micro on GCE, prepare to feel the pain) 
2. The default addons waste a large proportion of resources on small clusters -- does my two node cluster 300MiB for heapster? Will it ever need more than one DNS pod?
3. The default addons don't scale properly to large clusters - heapster with 300MiB of memory isn't going to cut it on even some medium sized clusters, let alone clusters with a hundred nodes ([example](https://groups.google.com/d/topic/google-containers/LlXw0xJqWMI/discussion)). More than one DNS pod will be useful for availability.

Some really simple control logic should be able to make the situation better by listing the nodes in the cluster and updating the addon RCs using a few basic rules. It could be part of the node controller, or be a very small container that runs on the master or even in the user's cluster (but it better be very small to justify its benefits).

Forked from #11368.

Openshift has an "export" command that strips out fields typically set automatically by the system, or at least would be different for different instances of a resource, such as status, nodeName, clusterIP, etc.:
https://github.com/openshift/origin/blob/master/pkg/cmd/cli/cmd/export.go
https://github.com/openshift/origin/blob/master/pkg/cmd/cli/cmd/exporter.go

This would be useful for creating "clean" config files from live state, for cloning resources, and for creating replication controllers from pods (#11490).

I'd prefer to do the resource munging in the apiserver rather than in the client, either by adding subresources or query params.

body:
The GCE LoadBalancer implementation creates fw rules with tags where it assumes that 
- Instances all contain the same prefix followed by a "-" and a random 5 characters
- Instances all contain tags with the prefix

This causes unnecessary constraints on instance names and forces hostname+tags that match this pattern, even in a non-GKE environment.

title: Make it possible to disable collection of kubelet/docker logs

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
When I run Kubernetes cluster on GKE, it generates a lot of system logs coming from docker and kubelet. Even if my cluster runs just a few pods, I can see dozens or hundreds of log entries per second available in Google Cloud Logging in docker and kubelet logs. This makes the actual logs from my application get lost among them, if I do not set appropriate filter. Also, I am afraid that collecting massive amounts of logs imposes unnecessary workload on fluentd pod in my cluster.

It would be good if I could just disable collection of kubelet/docker logs (and potentially other Kubernetes system logs) assuming that I do not want to have these logs exported.

title: Exposing services with load balancers should allow either existing load balancer names, existing static IPs for load balancers or assignment of DNS records to load balancers

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Currently when you an expose a service, there's no way to guarantee that the service is exposed on a certain IP address.  It looks as if the `publicIPs` setting is now ignored (it does nothing when specified), and when you use `--create-external-load-balancer=true` it will result in the creation of a new load balancer for the same named service if the cluster has been destroyed and recreated (e.g. when upgrading the VM size on Google Cloud Compute).

To ensure that automated deployments come back up with the same configuration, one (or more) of the following should be supported:
- Allowing the specification of an existing load balancer with an IP address already assigned (via `--attach-external-load-balancer=name`).
- Allow specifying the IP address the newly created load balancer should use (via `--external-load-balancer-ip-address`).  This option should also take into account reassigning the IP address if it's currently in use by another load balancer (since in this case we often want to replace it).
- Allow specifying a DNS record which is set up or configured in Google Cloud DNS to point to the Ephemeral IP address assigned to the load balancer.

title: Restructure SyncPod in kubelet

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
This is forked from #12540.

Proposal #12802 adds a pod lifecycle event generator. This requires pod workers in kubelet to know what events to expect in from the actions of `SyncPod`.

**Background**: [`SyncPod`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/runtime.go#L56) is the all-encompassing function defined in the container runtime interface to drive pod states to match the spec. `SyncPod` can perform millions of tasks, but all of them are hidden from kubelet. The reason behind the abstraction level is that the container runtimes (docker and rkt) are so different, and it is simpler to push all the implementation details down to individual runtimes. The downside, however, is that the code is hard to profile and reason about. 

Here are a few options that we can do.

**Option 1: Keep SyncPod as a black box**
Kubelet remains unaware of what's going on in `SyncPod`, but `SyncPod` would return a list of expected events to for pod worker to wait on.
Pros [+] and cons [-]:
- [+] No change to the container runtime interface or the main kubelet code. Individual runtimes can divert naturally.
- [-] Still need to restructure the code in docker/rkt packages.
- [-] `SyncPod` remains a monolithic function.

**Option 2: Define clear control flow and expectations in kubelet**
Break `SyncPod` into a couple of functions in the container runtime interface and define expected events for each of them. E.g.,

``` go
func SyncPods(....) {
    if !runtime.NetworkIsUp() {
        runtime.SetupNetwork()
        // Record the NetworkSetupCompleted event in expectations
    }
    if ! runtime.containerIsRunning() {
        runtime.StartContainer()
        // Record the ContainerStarted event in expectations
    }
    ...
}
```

Pros [+] and cons [-]:
- [+] The overall control flow is clear in kubelet.
- [-] It's hard to come up with a control flow that would work both for rkt and docker (e.g., docker would need to kill all containers if POD infra container needs to be restarted).

**Option 3: Define a generic execution plan at the runtime-level abstraction**

This is a compromise between option 1 and 2. Instead of forcing a control flow in kubelet, we'd ask each runtime what the execution plan is, and calls individual functions to complete this plan. E.g.,

``` go
type ExecutionPlan struct {
        TearDownNetwork   bool
        SetupNetwork      bool
        ContainersToKill  []string
        ContainersToStart []string
}

func GetExecutionPlan(api.Pod, kubecontainer.Pod) (*ExecutionPlan, error)
...
```

Based on the plan, we can augment the container Runtime interface to include new actions.

| Plan | Action | Expected events |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TearDownNetwork | SetupNetwork() | NetworkSetupCompleted |
| ContainersToKill | KillContainersInPod() | ContainerTerminated |
| ContainersToStart | CreateContainersInPod() | ContainerCreated |

Pros [+] and cons [-]:
- [+] The overall execution plan is clear in kubelet.
- [-] Need to come up with a generic ExecutionPlan understood by both runtimes.

---

I am leaning towards option 3 at the moment. The example I use is still more docker-centric, and needs to be worked on more for rkt.
@yifan-gu, what do you think about this?

title: RBD volume on CoreOS require udev rules.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body: RBD driver requires rbd device path in format `/dev/rbd/<pool name>/<image name>` while latest kernels places it under `/dev/rbd{number}`. Driver should check dev name by executing "rbd showmapped" command.

title: JSONPath output needs a quote operator to safely generate arguments

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Since we're likely to want to use JSONPath output with bash, we need to have a way to ensure that output can be safely escaped for use with scripting.  Go templates support quoting and encoding, but we have no JSONPath equivalent.

E.g. `oc get -o jsonpath -t 'echo {.metadata.annotations[foo]}'` could contain spaces and thus makes it difficult to safely encode.  The `strconv.Quote` function is an effective tool in this space.

    - It does not say anything about how to setup service account (private) key file which is needed by the newer version of kubernetes
5, Users cannot specify the version of kubernetes(and its dependencies such as etcd) they want to install.

What do you think about it?

title: encrypt secrets when in etcd.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

labels.name: sig/service-catalog
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Service Catalog.

body:
We should limit access to secrets when in etcd.

Initially discussed in #11937.

Although we discourage it, people seem to want to build their own clusters where etcd is used by both Apiserver and by other components, to store configuration.  Secrets want to have Kubernetes access controls on them, and not to be widely readable.  Other types of configuration wants to be widely readable. 

We could do this in a couple of ways:
1. use etcd ACLs to limit access to the etcd keys that hold secrets.
1. encrypt some or all of the secret data when stored.

@liggitt @pmorie 
thoughts?

labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
It is normal for services within a cluster to require TLS & hence keys/certificates are required. Managing this is normally manual & time-consuming. I'd like to be able to generate keys/certificates on (authenticated) request & provide these to the relevant pods via secrets. This a common problem in a microservice architecture - great blog post on it [here](https://blog.cloudflare.com/how-to-build-your-own-public-key-infrastructure/).

I have a working prototype building on top of [cfssl](https://github.com/cloudflare/cfssl). The basic idea is to watch secrets as they are added & if annotated correctly to update the sceret with generated keys & signed certificates via a cfssl pod (cfssl is bound to localhost so no external connectivity). These are then mounted inside pods that require them in the normal way.

Obviously this is very insecure at the moment as there is no idea of authorization, or of revocation, or of ... well anything other than simply usability. I am not advocating the approach I currently have, just explaining what I've done so far to start discussion.

This is related to some other issues around secret/token generation such as #11070 & #8866, but separate IMO, perhaps just a special case, but one that justifies it's own discussion.

title: Some thoughts about the pod/container abstraction in kubelet

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
This is purely food for thought, as others may not agree and this probably wouldn't be prioritized anytime soon :-)

Kubelet defines [`Pod`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/runtime.go#L117) in the container runtime, which has and a list of [containers](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/runtime.go#L170) and an [`api.PodStatus`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/runtime.go#L131) object which includes all the container statuses. This seems counter-intuitive to me because `Pod` is supposed to be a representation of the running pod in the system, i.e., it is essentially the pod status/states (so we have status nested in the status?) It is also not necessary for the container runtime to talk `api.PodStatus` because kubelet has to [fill extra information later on to complete it](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2326-L2370). 

The abstraction is a bit hard to digest alone, and the types seem to center around the implementation details (retrofitting?). Moreover, we pass Pods often without any valid pod/container status. You have no way to tell after-the-fact that whether a container in the pod is running or dead. I'd prefer a flatter struct reflecting the status of the containers/pods, and let kubelet interprets and translates the status into `api.PodStatus`.

A simple example would be:

``` go
type Container struct {
    ID  types.UID
    Name string
    Image string
    Hash uint64
    State ContainerState
    Ready bool
        ...
}
type Pod struct {
    ID types.UID
    Name      string
    Namespace string
    Containers []*Container
    PodIP string
}
```

/cc @yifan-gu

title: Conversion and deep-copy evolution

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
With the introduction of the experimental api prefix, we introduce large amounts of duplicate code for our autogenerated conversions and deep-copy functions. This increases the size of our binaries, and is not elegant. For simplicity, I will only talk about deep-copies, but everything that follows should also apply to conversions. I propose that we eliminate the duplicates as follows:
- We remove all autogenerated deep-copy functions from the source tree whenever we generate new deep-copy functions (or use a [build tag](https://golang.org/pkg/go/build/) to hide them from the go compiler)
- We check whether the Scheme has a deep-copy function for the target type already registered, if not, we generate a deep-copy function
- Whenever we a see that a deep-copy function has already been generated, we do the copy by calling into the conversion.Cloner

(In the case of handwritten conversions, we will need to make them switch to using the conversion.Scope instead of calling autogenerated functions directly).

Assuming that we create the deep-copy functions in the order following the import dependency tree, we should not have any duplicate deep-copy functions. However, this approach brings with it some overhead.

For both cleaning up our deep-copy functions and increasing performance in the face of this overhead, I propose we take the following steps:
- Profile the apiserver to measure what time is spent doing deep-copies
- Create some microbenchmarks to use as a baseline (initial work can be found [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...uluyol:dedup))
- Create a new method DeepCopyTo and pass pointers to avoid needless copies
- Switch to exception handling within the deep-copies (elaborated below)
- Change autogenerated functions to use generic signatures instead of per-type ones i.e. instead of `f(a, b *T) error`, we have `f(a, b interface{})` and use type assertions. This lets us reduce the amount of reflection that we use in exchange for boxing

In Go, exception handling is typically discouraged, but it is completely reasonable to use it so long as it doesn't cross an API boundary. For example, [here](https://golang.org/src/encoding/json/encode.go#L258) it is used within the standard library. When we see an error during a copy, the copy operation cannot recover. This is the prime use-case for exception handling. We can similarly catch errors within Scheme.DeepCopy, and instead of doing explicit error checking all over the place, simply panic and convert it into an error in DeepCopy. We can also create a new function, MustDeepCopy, which does not catch the error for use within the deep-copy functions.

@wojtek-t @nikhiljindal

title: emptyDir Volume sometimes not populated (race condition?)

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

body:
I have a pod which consists of two containers, an application "build" container with application code and a "runner" container which executes the application.

In order for the two to share the data, the build container copies over the application code to an `emptyDir` volume on startup, which is also mounted in the runner container. The runner container polls for the existence of a magic file in the volume and, when found, executes the application.

Roughly 50% of the time, even after the build container successfully copies over the data, the runner container can't see it. Using a shell via `docker exec` I can verify that the data is copied to the correct location from the perspective of the build container, however i can also see that it is an empty directory from the perspective of the runner container.

The pod template is equivalent to this:

``` yaml
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app-runner
          image: foobar/app-runner:latest
            - containerPort: 3000
              protocol: TCP
          volumeMounts:
            - name: app-build-volume
              mountPath: /opt/k8s-build
        - name: app-build
          image: foobar/app-build:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: app-build-volume
              mountPath: /opt/k8s-build
      volumes:
        - name: app-build-volume
          emptyDir: {}
```

The build container does this on startup:

``` bash
rm -rfv /opt/k8s-build/* || exit 1
cp -v -R /opt/build/* /opt/k8s-build/ || exit 1
```

This is what the volume looks like from the runner:

``` bash
$ ls /opt/k8s-build/foobar/
application-name
$ ls /opt/k8s-build/foobar/application-name/
$
```

I usually have to delete and restart the controller once or twice before the volume succeeds. This is k8s 1.0.1 on CoreOS in AWS.

Any ideas how I can troubleshoot further?

body:
In https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/proposals/resource-qos.md, we have defined the QoS of CPU/Memory resources. Based on the description, I think it would make more sense to use requested resource instead of resource limit when prioritizing the node with respect to free resources. That is, free resource on a node should be measured by `capacity - sum_of_requested_resource`.

Besides, limits are replaced by requests in the corresponding predicate function `CheckPodsExceedingFreeResources()`, so I think it is necessary that we make similar changes in prioritizer function. 

What do you think? I would be happy to implement this if you think it is OK.

@davidopp @AnanyaKumar 

> update 2015.08.14:

In fact, as mentioned by @AnanyaKumar in the comments, we should use request instead of limit when scheduling. So, basically we need to change almost every limit in all priority functions. I will handle them carefully and send PR sooner. We can have further discussion based on the PR.

title: Collect logfiles inside the container

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
## Logs to stdout/stderr

Currently, it's ok to collect container's logs which are printed to `stdout/stderr`.
According to [kubernetes/fluentd-eslasticsearch](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/tree/master/pkg/volume) addon, kubelet links the docker containers' log to  `/var/log/containers`,

```
/var/log/containers/<pod_full_name>_<container_name>-<container_id>.log -> /var/lib/docker/containers/<container_id>/<container_id>-json.log
```

then fluentd tails the logfiles in `/var/log/containers`, and add the tag `<pod_full_name>_<container_name>-<container_id>`to log record by parsing the path.
## Logs in files

Now want to collect the logfiles inside the container. 
Firstly, should use volume mount the logdir , 
### HostPath Volume

Mount the logdir(/log) by HostPath Volume, like:

```
/var/log/pods/<pod_name> => /log
```

Use `/var/log/pods/<pod_name>` to persist the logs, it's configured manually, so fluentd can distinguish the logs file also.
But all the pod's instances will use the same HostPath(/var/log/pods/<pod_name>), this can cause conflict.
## EmptyDIr Volume

Mount the logdir(/log) by EmptyDIr Volume, like:

```
/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod_id>/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/log-storage => /log
```

fluentd can tail the logfiles in `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod_id>/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/log-storage`,  but the path only include `pod_id`,   pod_id changes when pod migrates, so I don't think it's ok to be the tag.

Any better solution?

title: The 24 character Service limit

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Can this be removed? It's really annoying limit.

**Description of problem**

_If you type any service name that's more then 25 characters (and I assume other naming rules also apply) you will get something like the following error:_

```
The Service "a-25characterslongstring" is invalid:metadata.name: invalid value 'a-25characterslongstring': must be a DNS 952 label (at most 24 characters, matching regex [a-z]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?): e.g. "my-name"
```

RFC 952: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc952

So why is 24 characters long a problem? Let's say you have a cluster, and you have many projects on that cluster and you have many services per cluster and you also have different stages to development that also sit on said cluster. Ok so, given all that if you say have "project1" and two services "www" and "api" and you have a stage in development called "testing" you now have a service name that might look like this "project1-testing-www-svc" (25 characters, so illegal). I find it not being able to handle such a _extremely simple_ name quite a bit troublesome.

I don't know where and how exactly RFC 952 applies to the service name (is this just for some future compatibility?), but as far as I'm concerned if I write "project1-testing-www-svc" then I'm writing it for myself and other developers; I'm not writing it for some network table. The network table can have it as "asdjasjkfghajks" for all I care.
## 

Assuming RFC 952 compatibility here is relevant, can we have something like "metadata.alias" which would support at least 255 characters long names and just automatically generate a unique 24 character id. Any sort of getters would report the alias with the actual name in parenthesis, eg.

```
project1-testing-www-svc (qn37txumha6tfmm19gokei3w)
```

For me personally even something like just a little mark would be enough (eg. `project1-testing-www-svc*` or `@project1-testing-www-svc`). The real ID can be hidden under a flag 99% of the time.

Hi all..
I have recently started looking into kubernetes project and strongly willing to contribute to the project. I have environment set up of Kubernetes on CoreOS baremetal servers. 
It seems to me that scheduler is not considering the current state of resources(cpu/memory) of hosts while taking decisions.

I performed following steps:
1. There are 2 hosts(slaves), host1 and host2. And one host0(master) which consists of scheduler and apiserver.
2. I started creating pods , in the kubernetes cluster by just changing the "name" field in pod template everytime. 
[I did not mention cpu and memory limits in the pod template.
Pod had just one simple container (ubuntu image).]
The scheduler was nicely putting pods on different hosts one by one.
3. Then I intentionally exhausted the cpu of host1 by starting some processes on host1 via pod.
4. Now on adding new pods, the scheduler was still scheduling the pods on the host1 as if it is not considering its current cpu status, while it should put new pod on host2 which is a better decision.

I understand it may possible that in near future the cpu usage may go down in host1 . There may be other issues as well. 
But , I think scheduler should consider the current status of cpu/memory while scheduling the pod. I am not sure but scheduler can utilize the data from cadvisor.
Please let me know if I am missing something.

title: Proposal: Allow anonymous inline claim in pod definition

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
If you have a replicationcontroller with a pod that uses claims for persistent storage you currently have a hard time to scale them up. The name of the claim is part of the pod definition, so if you try to scale up every pod will try to use the same claim. If you have a scalable application where each pod needs its own storage this is not what you want.

If you can add an anonymous claim as part of the pod definition, a new pod would automatically be assigned with a new claim for his storage. If you scale down that claim get deleted and the claimed storage gets freed up.
Also, the claim must be reassigned to a new pod in case of a rolling update without getting cleared.

title: Read flags from environment variables

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
In order to simplify configuration of the Kubernetes components, each component should parse its own flags from the constructed environment, setting its flags based on the variables it finds. This will simplify configuration of Kubernetes components under complex init systems such as systemd, where it is a common pattern to overlay several files on one another to allow both the operating system vendors, the packagers and the end-users to jointly override the configuration options for a given service.

github.com/coreos/pkg/flagutil#SetFlagsFromEnv [0] provides an example of the code needed to achieve this, and the corresponding tests demonstrate its usage [1]. The code walks through each flag in a given flagset and parses a corresponding value from the environment prefixed with a configurable string.

As for a practical example, the kubelet could be vendored into an operating system like this, setting the default bind address to 127.0.0.1:

```
# /usr/lib64/systemd/system/kubelet.service
[Service]
Environment= KUBELET_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1
ExecStart= /usr/bin/kubelet
```

Then an end-user deploying a cluster could override the value to make the kubelet routable:

```
#/etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/20-address.conf
[Service]
Environment= KUBELET_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0
```

One alternative here would be to initialize a KUBELET_OPTS env var, but that pushes more complexity onto the user and doesn't allow a clean way to selectively override a single flag. Another option would be to maintain a custom set of environment variables, but that pushes a lot of complexity onto the OS vendor and packager, forcing them to chance new flags exposed by the Kubernetes components over time.

[0] https://github.com/coreos/pkg/blob/master/flagutil/env.go#L16
[1] https://github.com/coreos/pkg/blob/master/flagutil/env_test.go#L9

title: Need fencing in HA recovery process

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Some apps, usually those need access to shared data or legacy apps, need to make sure that there are at least one (HA) and only one (fencing) instance running. Otherwise, if one instance is detected to be down, but still accessing data (e.g. network issue or responsiveless); the second instance is boot up, accessing data too. Data will be corrupted.

The fencing, in above case, need to make sure the first instance is "fully dead" or totally isolated from any access to data. Fencing is commonly used in active-passive HA such as Pacemaker.

One walkaround is to implement leader selection for the app, using etcd/zookeeper. However, it may happen that: instance1 acquires leader => instance1 keep writing but responsiveless => heartbeat timeout and instance2 acquires leader => instance1 still writing => instance2 writes => data corruption. Besides, in may use case, modifying existing apps is not feasible.

Another walkaround is to implement a distributed lock using shared FS (file lock) or etcd/zookeeper. Beside the added overhead of locking every write operation, it has the similar problem: instance1 acquires lock => instance1 becomes responsiveless but still writing => lock timeout => instance2 acquires lock => instance1 still writing => instance2 writes => data corruption.

The code of the app would look like

```
# Enter the app
distributed_lock.lock()

do_things1()
do_things2()
...
do_thingsK()    # lock is acquired by instance2 at this time
do_thingsK+1()    # I'm still writing, so data corrupts
...
do_thingsN()

# Exit the app
distributed_lock.unlock()
```

However, if the app keeps checking lock too frequently, say every heartbeat, the overhead would be unfeasible, yet hard to write the correct code.

So, my point is that the best place to implement fencing is the underlying cluster manager, i.e. k8s.

Related discussion: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/coreos-dev/ZCAywIDVyys

title: Collecting and publishing cluster configuration

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
This issue captures the results of a conversation between @satnam6502 , @vishh and @jackgr regarding the use of [cluster-insight](https://github.com/google/cluster-insight) to collect and publish cluster configuration for the [graph tab](https://github.com/kubernetes-ui/graph) developed for the Kubernetes UI. See also the related discussion in #8716.

cc: @vasbala, @EranGabber, @supriyagarg, @rimey, @bgrant0607 
# Overview

The graph tab provides a visualization of a running cluster based on the [d3 force layout](https://github.com/mbostock/d3/wiki/Force-Layout), showing all of the objects in the cluster and the relationships between them. It also provides two detailed views of the properties of a selected object: a summary view on the main page that displays a few properties, and a complete view on a child page that displays all of the properties.

The information presented includes:
- objects and relationships exposed by the Kubernetes api server (e.g., nodes, pods, replication controllers, services, namespaces, etc.), 
- objects and relationships exposed by the Docker daemon on each cluster node (e.g., containers, processes, images), and 
- relationships among all of the objects that can be inferred (e.g., between a replication controller and its pods, between a service an its pods, between a container and its processes, etc.).

Rather than attempt to collect, analyze and organize all of this information on the client, we chose to write a Kubernetes service that does that work on the server side. Using a service has several advantages, such as:
- simplifying the client by allowing it to focus exclusively on presentation, 
- hiding details from the client that might change over time by providing the cluster configuration information as an untyped JSON document, 
- reducing load on the cluster from multiple clients by caching the information and making it available on demand, and 
- separating the collection and publication of cluster configuration from the graph tab or any other client, so that it can be used for a variety of purposes.
# Cluster Insight Design

Cluster insight is a set of python scripts that run inside a vanilla python container. (See [the docker file](https://github.com/google/cluster-insight/blob/master/collector/Dockerfile) for details.)

As revealed by the docker file, it runs in one of two modes: 
- in minion mode, it acts as a read only proxy for the local Docker daemon, providing read only access to the data it exposes, and 
- in master mode, it acts as an aggregator and cache, collecting information from the Kubernetes api server and from the minions, processing it, storing it, and returning it on demand in response to queries.

Two aspects of this design were cause for concern in the discussion on #8716:
- In order to read from the Docker daemon, the python script must run as root, or as a member of the docker group, and
- In order to retrieve information about Docker running on every node, the script must run in minion mode on every node.
# Alternative Solutions

In practice, these issues may not be as severe as suggested by the discussion on #8716, since:
- most containers commonly run their processes as root, 
- cluster-insight has a very small memory and cpu footprint in minion mode, and 
- cluster-insight does not provide write access to the Docker daemon.

Nevertheless, it was agreed that we should investigate the possibility of using cadvisor, which already runs on every node within the kubelet, to collect and publish configuration information, in addition to the information it already collects and publishes, which is primarily performance oriented, but does reveal some aspects of configuration.
# Use Cases

In order to support focused discussion about alternative solutions, it was agreed that we should enumerate the key use cases for the configuration collection and publication service. The following use cases were identified and discussed:
- Collecting the current actual configuration and making it available in response to queries, in order to support visualizations and other consumers.
- Collecting the most recently supplied configuration, so that it can be compared with the current actual configuration to determine whether or not the latter contains values that deviate from the intended values.
- Collecting the most recently supplied configuration, so that it can be used to provide defaults when updates do not specify values for all possible parameters, since it captures user preferences from previous configuration updates.
- Collecting historical information about configuration changes, so that it can be correlated with events, logs and monitoring data to support anomaly detection and other forms of programmatic analysis.
# Issues

The following issues were identified and examined during the discussion:
- We should consider the general problem of collecting and publishing cluster configuration information in a holistic way, instead of focusing on the needs of a specific client or use case.
- Configuration information collected by this service might overlap with similar information maintained by the api server, or as annotations on objects stored in etcd, and should perhaps be combined with it to reduce storage overhead.
- It might be possible to collect the most recently supplied configuration directly from the deployment process by pushing new configuration to a configuration store, rather than to the api server, and then starting processes to make the actual configuration conform to it.
- Different container engines may expose different configuration values, despite efforts to standardize their interfaces and configuration formats. We do not want to choose which container engines to support and which to ignore, or to keep up with changes in container engine APIs that have historically evolved rapidly and may continue to do so for some.
- Some of the information already collected by cadvisor may overlap with some of the information currently collected by cluster-insight. We need a pass over the two information sets to reconcile them. In the process, we might also want to make some judgements regarding the value of specific configuration values, in order to reduce the number of values we collect, store and publish.

title: Union authenticator may send credentials to all authentication providers

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
In `plugin/pkg/auth/authenticator/request/union/union.go` it tries each of the authentication methods in order.  This means that if you pass the admin token using basic auth, then it sends the basic auth information to all configured auth providers.  So, for example, if the admin is authorizing with the cluster's csv-file-based admin token, that password might also be sent to a configured OpenID identity provider (#10957), who didn't previously know my admin password, but could now learn it.  

In all the practical cases I can think of, I trusted the various authentication providers about the same amount.  But I think it is unexpected behavior and it makes me a little uneasy.

A minor improvement would be to document this behavior.  

A bigger improvement would be for the client (kubectl) to include a header saying which authentication provider the password or token were intended for.  

@liggitt what are your thoughts.

title: Generate unique label for Replication Controller, Job

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

body:
Currently, the user is responsible for ensuring that a replication controller has a selector which will be disjoint from all other replication controllers.  Job will have the same issue.

I expect some users will think carefully about their labels and not have a problem ensuring this uniqueness property for their rcs/services.  I expect other users will not be as careful, and may forget to do this.  If they forget it will be hard to debug.  

I expect this problem to be worse for Job because Jobs are run in a more ad-hoc manner, so with less thought, and don't last as long, perhaps making debugging of conflicts more difficult.  Also, while RCs often need to adopt existing pods, jobs need to be able to do this less often (but maybe in some cases?).

The solution seems to be to have a way to request that the Job or the ReplicationController will pick a unique label for the pods it creates.    Something like `kubernetes.io/job-uid=$UID_OF_JOB` or `kubernetes.io/rc-uid=$UID_OF_RC`.   This might be via a boolean flag like `generateSelector`.  When `generateSelector` is false, then the user is assumed to have provided a selector which provides the necessary uniqueness, either via the spec.selector, or via defaulting from the pod template.  If true, then the system adds another selector and adds another label to the pods which is unique per Job/RC.

We probably want as much as possible the same behavior for Job and ReplicationController.  
However for Job, it would be nice to have generateSelector default to true, so people can write succinct specs, and default to false for RC for backwards compat. 

@bgrant0607 said that it should always be possible for users to disable creation automatic creation of the system label.

```
Get http://localhost:8080/version: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: connection refused
```

I did some investigation/a lot of `debug.PrintStack()` and `fmt.Println(...)`, and I have found out that everything basically gets messed up here: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/ded48a376107a66abb374e38ec6fc1d48e66678e/pkg/client/clientcmd/client_config.go#L296 which is due to `mergo.Merge` only merging unfilled values, and https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/ded48a376107a66abb374e38ec6fc1d48e66678e/pkg/client/clientcmd/client_config.go#L36 already having filled in the host. So this seems wrong to me, I can't figure out a better way.

Here's where things get really weird though:

I've gotten kubectl from the following sources (I'll reference the numbers below):
1. From gcloud and put on my path per the GCE docs, at `${HOME}/google-cloud-sdk/bin/kubectl`
2. From releases, at https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-release/release/v1.0.1/bin/darwin/amd64/kubectl
3. From checking out tag `v1.0.1` and doing `make all WHAT=cmd/kubectl GOFLAGS=-v`
4. From checking out tag `v1.0.1` and doing `go get -d -v -t ./cmd/kubectl/... && go install ./cmd/kubectl`
5. From `master` and doing `make all WHAT=cmd/kubectl GOFLAGS=-v`
6. From `master` and doing `go get -d -v -t ./cmd/kubectl/... && go install ./cmd/kubectl`

(1), (2), (3), and (5) all work:

```
# sample output from (5)
$ ./_output/local/bin/darwin/amd64/kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"1+", GitVersion:"v1.1.0-alpha.0.1279+ded48a376107a6", GitCommit:"ded48a376107a66abb374e38ec6fc1d48e66678e", GitTreeState:"clean"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"0", GitVersion:"v1.0.1", GitCommit:"6a5c06e3d1eb27a6310a09270e4a5fb1afa93e74", GitTreeState:"clean"}
```

(4) and (6) do not work:

```
# sample output from (6)
$ ~/go/bin/kubectl version
error: couldn't read version from server: Get http://localhost:8080/api: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: connection refused
```

So,
- What gives? I'm assuming it's something to do with a dependency, but that actually makes no sense unless it's mergo.
- The docs for how to use kubernetes from golang don't work/having to rely on the Godeps dependencies when this is a library gets wonky.

Any thoughts? Am I missing something huge and about to have egg on my face (probably)?

**Situation**: `kubectl get pods` gives you all pods, including the failed/succeeded ones.

body:
Proper functioning of the kubelet and node depends upon an expected version of whatever container runtime the kubelet uses.  For example, the proposal for QoS tiers being explored in #12035 will rely on the CPU quota feature introduced in docker 1.7, and I believe there is some code that depends upon docker 1.6. Should we have a version check in the kubelet for each container runtime to ensure the minimum usable version is present, and at least warn the user if not?

title: Suggested staging of Disk Space work

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
From conversations with @wojtek-t @fgrzadkowski @jszczepkowski @gmarek @davidopp @bgrant0607 @mwielgus @piosz @vmarmol 

First round of disk space changes (target v1.1):
1. kubelet has flags that user can set to specify desired amount of disk space of main disk to set aside for inactive images and logs from terminated containers
2. kubelet measures usage of idle images and terminated container's volumes by asking docker.  
3. kubelet triggers GC of images and containers using flag provided max as a high-water-mark.

User benefit:
1. users can avoid running out of disk space

Second round (post v1.1):
1. kubelet gets capacity of the one local disk of the machine and reports it in its node
   1. we won't support multiple local disks.  If you have these then you can either merge them into one big disk with lvm/md or you can have a storage daemon pod access them via hostDir
2. pods and volumes may specify a disk space request (setting on container not recommended)
   1. there is no enforcement or measurement of the actual usage of disk space. (this is hard to do, so we don't do it at first)
3. kubelet reports a "shadow pod" for the system which has a container that has a disk resource request equal to the flag provided high-water mark for cached images and old container logs.
4. users may optionally set a request for disk space on each container.  
   1. if there are multiple containers per pod with shared image or volume disk usage, the user needs to figure out a way to apportion this total usage among his containers.
5. the scheduler uses the node capacity and the sum of container limits (including shadow container) to do scheduling.
6. no measurement or enforcement of disk space limits on containers.

User benefit:
- users with well behaved containers with varying disk needs can get the scheduler to do disk-space aware scheduling.

Third round:
1. figure out how to do disk space measurement and enforcement 
2. decide whether to add a per-pod overall resource limit and to only do disk space limit and usage there (sum for pod and its volumes) or to break down further.
3. for measuring usage see: https://github.com/appc/spec/issues/198

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

body:
On certain cloud providers like digital ocean the public interface has multiple addresses, one of which is a link-local address that points to a metadata server. The node is supposed to come up and contact the metadata server to bootstrap the public interface with a real address. At this point, the interface has 2 addresses, eg (from irc debugging): https://dpaste.de/T8s0/raw. 

Looks like we create the kubernets endpoint using the first, link-local address and it always gets rejected. The kubernetes master service creation can keep failing (and re-checking for a valid public ip) when this happens because it knows link-local is not allowed: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/master/controller.go#L97

title: AWS: Figure out workaround for non-atomic tag creation

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Because we create tags non-atomically on AWS, there is often/always a window in which things can be in inconsistent states, where we have created the resource but not tagged it.  The consequence could be resource leakage, or (more rarely) infinite loops (see e.g. #11324).

We may be able to find a procedure, for example by searching for untagged resources and trying to recover from failed creates.  But this is hard because we don't want to go around deleting/claiming a user's non-k8s resources.

Retrying tagging will also help (#11029), but we still have a problem if we crash before we are able to tag the resource.

title: Prometheus auto discovery

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

body:
The current Prometheus config in contrib requires up front configuration via env vars to select which service to scrape metrics for. I've submitted a PR to Prometheus for initial kubernetes discovery of nodes & services to scrape - https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/905. 

Nodes & services are watched & scraped metrics are labeled using the kubernetes labels to make it easy to reuse kubernetes labels across both systems. Nodes are automatically scraped so api server, kubelet & container cgroup metrics are ingested into Prometheus.

Discovery of services to scrape is done by watching services & checking that appropriate annotations (`prometheus.io/*`) are set to start scraping the service endpoints, which are also watched as they come & go. Again, metrics are labeled using the kubernetes labels. This gives clusters automatic ingestion of their application metrics of they expose Prometheus formatted metrics (pretty easy to do with the various Prometheus exporters available).

I'm waiting on a review of the Prometheus PR but was wondering if this is something the kubernetes community would be interested in. If so, I'd love to hear what people would like to see, either on this issue or on the Prometheus PR linked above.

title: Validate PV AccessModes

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
A PV can be created with any string as an AccessMode.  It can match a PVC asking for the same string, regardless of that string being a real AccessMode constant.

See  https://github.com/openshift/origin/issues/3891  (2nd point)

The API server should validate that only real AccessModes are being assigned in PV and requested in PVC.

title: Support multiple schedulers

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
Forked from #9920, #11470, and other issues.

Kubernetes should multiple schedulers, including user-provided schedulers. The main thing we need is a way to not apply the default scheduling behavior, perhaps by namespace, using some sort of "admission control" plugin. I want that to be a fairly generic mechanism, since I expect to need it at least for horizontal auto-scaling and vertical auto-sizing, as well, if not other things in the future. This is related to the "initializers" topic (#3585).

A custom scheduler would then need to be configured for which pods to schedule. This probably requires adding information of some form to the pods. We should take that into account when thinking about the general initializer mechanism.

The custom scheduler should then be able to watch all pods and nodes to keep its state up to date, but I imagine we could add more information, events, or something to make this more convenient, as requested in #1517.

cc @davidopp

There are a couple of functions in plugin/scheduler which I don't think belong there. For example:

CheckPodsExceedingCapacity
PodFitsResources

If fact, the kubelet calls CheckPodsExceedingCapacity in the scheduler. I don't think the Kubelet should depend on functions in scheduler. I think these functions belong in the Kubelet - the scheduler could have separate versions of them if it needs to approximate whether a pod fits.
