body:
I think we want to support the following:
- when the service account controller makes a service account, it delegates creation of a credential to a  plugin. 
  - when the service account controller makes a service account, it delegates creation of policy for that new service account to a plugin. 
  - in both cases, compiled-in plugin is fine.  E.g. in the style of authorizer.Authorizer and authenticator.Request.
  - in both cases, default one would work the way things work now, but users could substitute a different one.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
I've been looking into getting a cluster-local docker registry up as a cluster addon (#1319) and the problem comes down to creating the certificate for the registry and trusting it. The apiserver CA cert is already visible from every node and every pod, so signing the registry certificate with the apiserver CA would eliminate any CA cert distribution issues.

Right now, we create the CA and apiserver certificate and key in a number of places (we have provider-specific ways to create them or use one of two scripts in salt). We don't copy over the CA key which is needed to sign new certificates.

One approach to fixing this is copying the CA key (might as well copy all of the pki/ directory used by easyrsa), but I'm not sure that this is a good idea. Alternative, we could add creation to every instance where the CA cert is created, but this is tedious and error prone.

title: Refactoring Kubelet Source Tree

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
I started working on the Kubelet recently, and I think we need to refactor the way the files and directories are organized. For example, there are a bunch of utilities functions scattered around in various files in the main kubelet package, which can be better aggregated into relevant packages. Besides being messy and confusing, having utilities lying around in the main kubelet package also seems prone to cyclic dependencies (kubelet.go uses kubelet/subpackageA, but kubelet/subpackageA/pods.go might want to use kubelet/types.go). There are many other issues, for example there's a kubelet/util.go and kubelet/util/format.go, both of which mostly contain functions that extract information from pods.

Refactoring all the files in one pass is very tedious, but I think it's useful to lay out a directory structure we're aiming for. As we add features to the Kubelet, we can extract functions with a desired directory structure in mind. For example, in my current project, I’m adding functions which extract information from a pod, so I’m trying to aggregate “pod information” functions into a package.

Here’s a proposed structure:

container
- generic
- docker
- rkt

pod
- podinfo
- podworkers

managers
- disk
- image
- pod
- container
- volume
- status

statistics
- cadvisor
- prometheus

setup
- envvars
- config

types

mirrorclient

network

oom

healthcheck
- prober.go

run
- runonce.go
- runtime_hooks.go

server

lifecycle

leaky

I believe this handles most files except kubelet/util.go and kubelet/util/format.go. There are 5 functions between these 2 files:

util.go:
canRunPod (move to pod/podinfo)
allowHostNetwork (move to pod/podinfo)
CapacityFromMachineInfo (I'm not sure where to put this)

util/format.go has 2 functions that format pod information, and can go to either pod/format.go, or a new package format in kubelet (if we think we might want to format other objects in the future).

I think the proposed structure better organizes the Kubelet code by functionality. Also, since most code is in it's own package (as opposed to having a giant kubelet package with lots of files), cyclic dependencies won't pose a problem, and it's easier to identify the file a function is defined in. Any thoughts?

title: Implement Resource Consumer

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

labels.name: sig/autoscaling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Autoscaling.

body:
_This is @socaa's intern project._
## Background

We are working on autoscaling for Kubernetes in 3 dimensions:
- cluster size autoscaling
- horizontal autoscaling of pod - changing the size of replication controller #2863
- vertical autoscaling of pod - changing its resource limits #10782

We need a tool which will help us to test e2e those kinds of autoscaling.
## Resource Consumer

Resource Consumer will consist of two parts: container consuming resources and library managing this load.
### Container

The container which consumes specified amount of resources (cpu/mem). Docker container, uploaded to Google Container Registry, open sourced, possibly written in go (it’s not a requirement, but it’s strongly encouraged). The resources to consume should be set and mutated by sending appropriate http request to the container.

The interface should allow to consume the given amount of cpu/mem for the given period of time. It should consist of the following methods:

```
ConsumeCPU(milicores, duration_sec)
ConsumeMem(megabytes, duration_sec)
GetCurrentStatus()
```

Each http request will be handled by spawning a new process which will consume given amount of resource and exit after given timeout.The request cannot be cancelled. 
#### Consuming CPU

Consuming the whole core can be done easily. The problem is how to consume some part of it. One of possible ways to achieve it is to split time into small quants, then perform heavy compute operation during some percentage of quants and sleep during the other ones. It is a part of the task to figure out the best way to consume CPU.
#### Consuming memory

There are few possible ways how to handle memory consumption. We want to make sure the memory can be correctly freed. The only problem is that the container use some memory itself, so that this amount should be considered in calculations as well. It is a part of the task to figure out the best way to consume memory.
### Library

Client side library written in go will be linked with e2e tests and should consist of two kinds of methods: static consumption of resources and dynamic one.
#### Static consumption

This part of library should allow to consume constant amount of resource over time:

```
ConsumeCPU(node, percentage)
ConsumeMem(node, percentage)
CreateConsumingPod(node) : PodID
ConsumeCPU(pod, percentageOfRequest)
ConsumeMem(pod, percentageOfRequest)
```
#### Dynamic consumption

This part of library should allow to create service on top of replication controller, and then request to consume the given amount of resources by all replicas together based on service level load balancing. It can be implemented with sending a lot of consumption request for short period of time and small amount of resources. The interface should consist of:

```
CreateConsumingService() : RcID
ConsumeCPU(rc, milicores)
ConsumeMem(rc, megabytes)
```

In both cases there might be an option to add possibility to modify/stop consumption if needed.
## Use cases
#### Cluster size autoscaling
1. consume more resources on each node that is specified for autoscaler
2. observe that cluster size increased
#### Horizontal autoscaling of pod
1. create consuming RC and start consuming appropriate amount of resources
2. observe that RC has been resized
3. observe that usage on each replica decreased
#### Vertical autoscaling of pod
1. create consuming pod and start consuming appropriate amount of resources
2. observed that limits has been increased
## Milestones
- [x] Resource Consumer application
  - [x] http API skeleton server #12076
    - [x] define API
    - [x] implement mock methods which just return theirs names
  - [x] implement cpu consumption #12517
  - [x] implement memory consumption #13789
  - [x] figure out how to verify that the resource consumer works correctly and do it
  - [x] create Dockerfile, build and deploy Docker image #12257
  - [ ] [optional] accept resource.Quantity style strings in request
- [x] Client library for e2e test
  - [x] static consumption #14167
  - [x] dynamic consumption using Kubernetes service based load balancing #13243, #14036
- [x] Implement few e2e test for autoscaling using Resource Consumer to prove it is useful
  - [x] port horizontal cluster autoscaling tests #14275
  - [x] horizontal pod autoscaling based on cpu #13640
  - [x] horizontal pod autoscaling based on memory #14036
- [ ] Ensure that tests are not flaky.
- [x] Document how to use Resource Consumer #14645
- [x] Final presentation
#### Dropped ideas
- [optional] add possibility to specify initial consumption request
- [optional] add a status page

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| 9/15/15 | beta | `gcr.io/google_containers/resource_consumer:beta` | Feature complete |

title: Kubelet does not enforce pod.spec.nodeSelector if APIServers list is empty

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/pull/9759 added a short-circuit to `checkNodeSelectorMatching` which allows all pods if the kubelet thinks it is in standaloneMode.

`standaloneMode` defaults to `true` if the Kubelet's initial APIServer list is empty. This means it is very easy to put a kubelet in a state where it is not enforcing `pod.spec.nodeSelector`, which is a major component of securing which nodes a pod can be run on.

title: kubelet should set readiness to true as soon as possible for containers without readiness probe defined

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
Forked from #11007

kubelet set readiness for containers when checking container health in SyncPod. For containers that are created for the first time, the readiness of the containers would only be set in the next sync (~10s or less). This applies to containers with _NO_ readiness probe defined, so that they'd stay as not ready until the next sync. Instead, kubelet could perform an extra probe right after the container creation to make sure the readiness is set correctly as soon as possible.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

body:
cc @smarterclayton 
As I understand it, the nickname for each operation should be unique[1]. I searched the open issues, and could not find an open issue relating to this, however my apologies if this is a duplicate. 
Since the introduction of 'namespaced' apis (`/api/v1/services` v.s.`/api/v1/namespaces/{namespaces}/services`), there are operations with duplicate nicknames [2][3].
This means when we try to consume APIs via their swagger definition, the client overwrites the namespaced version of the API with the non-namespaced version. 
Maybe `listService` and `listServiceByNamespace` might be the convention to go by? 

Thanks @webron for the help in IRC confirming this

[1] https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-spec/issues/64
[2] https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/api/swagger-spec/v1.json#L9961
[3] https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/api/swagger-spec/v1.json#L10863

title: Show logs from updated pods during rolling update

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
This is a suggestion from one of our users.

During rolling update, we are informed about replication controller changes:

```
biskup@cathedral:~/go/src/github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes$ kubectl rolling-update update-demo-nautilus --update-period=10s -f examples/update-demo/kitten-rc.yaml
Creating update-demo-kitten
At beginning of loop: update-demo-nautilus replicas: 3, update-demo-kitten replicas: 1
Updating update-demo-nautilus replicas: 3, update-demo-kitten replicas: 1
At end of loop: update-demo-nautilus replicas: 3, update-demo-kitten replicas: 1
Stopping update-demo-nautilus replicas: 3 -> 0
Update succeeded. Deleting update-demo-nautilus
update-demo-kitten
```

But even if replication controllers are scaled properly, we don't know if the pods actually started and are well. A way to check pods is to get logs from each of them and check if they printed a certain message like `service started`. Currently to achieve it, we have to list pods, identify which ones belong to the new RC and get logs from them. It would be nice to show logs from pods **during** rolling update, so that the admin could see how the update goes.

Ways to proceed:
1. fetch and print pod logs by `kubectl rolling update` (this was the suggestion).
2. improve our examples and show an equivalent (and easy) way to accomplish the same.

title: kubelet's MASQUERADE support is insufficient

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

body:
Today kubelet sets up an iptables MASQUERADE rule for any traffic destined for anything except 10.0.0.0/8.  This is close, but not even correct on GCE, and certainly not right elsewhere.

First GCE.  We probably want something like:

```
iptables -t nat -N KUBE-IPMASQ
iptables -t nat -A KUBE-IPMASQ -d 10.0.0.0/8 -j RETURN
iptables -t nat -A KUBE-IPMASQ -d 172.16.0.0/12 -j RETURN
iptables -t nat -A KUBE-IPMASQ -d 192.168.0.0/16 -j RETURN
iptables -t nat -A KUBE-IPMASQ -j MASQUERADE
iptables -t nat -I POSTROUTING -j KUBE-IPMASQ
```

This catches all traffic to RFC1918 ranges and masquerades it.  We can probably optimize with CONNMARK or something so we only consider packets from containers.  This is probably still imperfect, but better, for lack of project-wide NAT for egress.

For other environments, we really have no idea what the correct policy for this is.  It is closer to "your nodes must handle this" than "we can handle this for you".  It's debatable whether we should even try.

Either:
a) We teach kubelet a lot more and let people pass flags to nearly=arbitrarily configure this
b) We tell people to configure this as part of their node setup

This popped up when I realized GKE allows users to set up 172.\* clusters - any traffic between containers in one of these will get masqueraded - not correct behavior!!  This is not a huge deal right now because kube-proxy has the same effect when traversing services.  As we fix kube-proxy in the wake of 1.0, masquerade will be a bigger deal, especially for micro-segmenting.

Additional considerations: VPNs have bizarre and very custom needs.  Every such thing has an as yet unmeasured perf implication.  This also pops up in our GCE firewall thing that @ArtfulCoder is working on.

title: make ServiceAccounts easier to work with - post1.0

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Having spent some time working with service accounts downstream, there are a few enhancements I'd like to see post-1.0
1. Make it easier to get a valid token for a service account.  The long-lived, but fully revocable aspect of SA tokens makes it desirable to use them for machine accounts, but it is really painful to describe to a user how they can get the SA token outside of a pod.  While I recognize that we'd like everything to be a pod, the world hasn't fully changed yet.
2. Make it easier to create a new token for a service account.  Related to the first point, but I'd like to be able to allow a user to create a new token for a single service account without giving them rights to create or get tokens in general.  Currently, there's no way to do that.  Also, it's really hard to describe to someone how to perfectly craft a secret to a token automatically filled in.
3. Allow user to rotate a service account token, without granting delete rights to secrets.  Right now, the only way to rotate an SA token is to delete the secret.  The power to delete arbitrary secrets is more significant than the power to rotate an SA token.
4. Create separate field for `AutomountedSecrets`.  The auto-mounting feature for service accounts is really nice, but sometimes I only want to use service accounts for things like pull secrets and I don't want them to handle their credentials out to ever pod they're attached to.  Rather than place the burden on an RC or a Pod to create a conflicting volume mount, I'd like to be able to explicitly choose which secrets get automounted.  This would also allow someone to describe additional secrets that get automounted.

title: Generate static, object-focused documentation of types

body:
Users should not have to read our go code to get documentation of the API types.  They could use swagger-ui.  But the swagger-ui is also not a good presentation because:
- It presents too much info about REST that is not relevant to most users:
  - it talks about POST, etc.  However, people are mostly going to use either Kubectl or pkg/client.  Those don't use the word POST.  Kubectl uses "create" and pkg/client uses "Create()".
  - it talks about the URLs.  However several parts of the url (api version, namespace) are not things that users normally need to think about when they are using Kubectl.  Mostly they just want to know what fields can be used and what they mean.
  - you have to click several times to find the schema on the swagger-ui page.
- It is not as accessible as markdown documentation
  - I don't think that the swagger-ui schema blurbs will be indexed in same way that github.com markdown docs are.
  - is is a different style than the markdown docs.
  - swagger inlines all subtypes in each object's schema.  This makes the schema overwhelming and defeats the grouping of related things that can be ignored as a group like SecurityContext or various volume plugins.  I'd rather there were links to subobjects. 

Therefore, we should generate markdown docs for the API types (but not the REST endpoints).
We could maybe generate this using a go program that reflects the struct tags from all the types in pkg/api/v1/types.go.

body:
If the kubelet can't retrieve machine info from cadvisor for some reason (or cadvisor really returns 0 cpu/mem), it reports node capacity as 0. If the scheduler comes across a pod with 0 capacity, it short circuits the fitness check.

In reality getting machine info from cadvisor is really straight forward and there's no reason it should fail, but the scheduler sholdn't assign pods to nodes that have 0 capacity. I suspect this is because we _don't_ want the kubelet to start rejecting pods if cadvisor can't figure out capacity.

body:
When trying to get Kubernetes running on top of Mesos, the docker image pulled from quay.io/coreos/etcd:v2.0.12 (as referenced in the getting started guide) doesn't expose its ports correctly or is misconfigured. 

When the container is running and you run the following command to test, the connection is refused from the server: 

`curl -L http://${KUBERNETES_MASTER_IP}:4001/v2/keys/`

The current work-around I found is to install the standard coreos/etcd image, which was in the guide previously:

`sudo docker run -d --hostname $(uname -n) --name etcd -p 4001:4001 -p 7001:7001 coreos/etcd`

 I noticed the image to run was changed 23 days ago in dc7a9c87926723dd7dfde6c1f2f8f608c4e2646c.

title: Cluster monitoring configs don't work with startup-time InfluxDB

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
After `./hack/dev-build-and-up.sh`, heapster is working fine and grafana shows all the panels correctly. If I take down the heapster and replace it with the influxdb monitoring config, the panels with `label 'name:heapster'` start complaining that there are no datapoints.

This is how I replaced heapster:

``` bash
$ kubectl delete rc monitoring-heapster-v5 --namespace=kube-system
$ kubectl create -f cluster/addons/cluster-monitoring/influxdb/heapster-controller.yaml
```

Editing the panels to use the `k8s-app:heapster` instead of `name:heapster` gets them to work again.

title: Integrate Red Hat stack + e2es into jenkins run

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/testing
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Testing.

body:
For some time now we have maintained a bare-metal RHEL-Atomic cluster on our end which served two primary purposes. 
1. Evaluate performance & HA, and feedback issues upstream.
2. Verify stack sanity by running e2e gauntlet on our stack.  

#2 has proven to be untenable, as we seem to eat a large number of changes that break for various reasons, and we're left hunting to feedback what has broken the system. 

Going forwards, we would like to add the automated startup and provisioning of our stack to run the e2e-tests and to red-flag commits before it reaches us downstream. 

The goal of this issue is to rationalize how we intend to solve this and integrate with upstream.  

/cc @eparis @jayunit100 @rrati @pmorie 
/cc @quinton-hoole @roberthbailey @ixdy

EDIT: 

Solution to the logging problem found: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/google-containers/D6RdGOqxKP4

---

I am running a kubernetes cluster on the GCE, cluster has a pod running a nodejs server. I can see the logs for the server with `kubectl logs podName`, however I cannot see the web server logs on the console. The web server creates logs with `console.log()`. The pod is managed by a replication controller, and I created the rc after I created the respective service.

Edit: Further testing: If I create a new cluster in a separate project and create a 'counter' pod as specified in the [getting started guide for logging](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/getting-started-guides/logging.md), then I am able to see the logs in the console under Monitoring>logs. It is also the case that if I run the webserver on the other project, I can see the logs in the console. 

Note: I am the owner of the project where I can see the logs. However I am not the owner of the project where I can not see the logs. The project where I can not see the logs has multiple instances running, each with multiple pods, and I need to be able to see the logs for everything. But in the console it does not give me the option to look at the logs for any of the instances. Instead the only type of log I can see is info, even though I select "any log level."

title: GCE/GKE: test/e2e/restart.go - MIG rolling update with identical template will not restart nodes

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/testing
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Testing.

body:
test/e2e/restart.go, func restartNodes, assumes that MIG rolling update on GCE will cause node restart.

However, there is a feature of MIG rolling update (currently broken) that skips update if the new instance template is the same as the old one.
The feature is supposed to work quite soon, so the test will not test anything (reboot will not be performed).

A workaround may be to create an identical instance template with a different name.

By the way, the current name `restartNodes` is misleading. It should be `recreateNodes`.

cc @mbforbes @quinton-hoole

title: Unclean container garbage collection

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/support
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as a support question.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
I'm conducting PoC about distributed build using Kubernetes.
Jenkins master distribute jenkins slave pods through Kubernetes API Server.
When build is done, jenkins slave pod is also deleted by kubernetes API Server.
But, kubernetes didn't delete container. (Pod is deleted well)

After searching, I found kubelet’s containerGC option.
So, I adjusted below options to kubelet.

--minimum-container-ttl-duration=0s
--maximum-dead-containers=0

After adjusting both 2 options, container was deleted, too.
But, kubernetes containerGC didn’t delete host volume path.
(/var/lib/docker/vfs/dir/..)
Due to aufs’s low performance, I used data volume of host instead of container inside.
So, data volume was accumulated and host's inodes was fulled, too.

Is there any solution to clean the containers wreckage?

My environment was..
Docker: v1.6.2
Kubernetes: v0.18.2 (container based multi clustering)

body:
I am trying to setup a test cluster on a few fresh Ubuntu trusty64 VMs using the docker multi-node getting started guide but at the very first stage on the master node, etcd fails to startup with the provided parameters and gives an error:

`2015/07/06 13:20:39 etcd: listen tcp: lookup localhost: no DNS servers`

 Even after I got it up and running with the following changes to parameters:

```
docker -H unix:///var/run/docker-bootstrap.sock run -d \
          --net=host \
          -p 4001:4001 \
          -p 2380:2380 \
          --name etcd \
          -v /opt/etcd:/opt/etcd \
          -v /usr/share/ca-certificates/:/etc/ssl/certs \
          -e "SERVICE_2380_NAME=_etcd-server._tcp" \
          gcr.io/google_containers/etcd:2.0.9 \
          /usr/local/bin/etcd \
          -data-dir /var/etcd/data \
          -name coremaster-01 \
          -listen-client-urls http://172.17.8.100:4001,http://127.0.0.1:2379 \
          -advertise-client-urls http://172.17.8.100:4001 \
          -listen-peer-urls http://172.17.8.100:2380 \
          -initial-advertise-peer-urls http://172.17.8.100:2380 \
          -initial-cluster coremaster-01=http://172.17.8.100:2380 \
          -initial-cluster-state new
```

`etcdctl` still cannot connect to it on the same VM and gives this error:

`Error:  cannot sync with the cluster using endpoints http://127.0.0.1:4001, http://127.0.0.1:2379`

Is this supposed to work the way I am trying to use it or have I completely missed something?
@brendandburns Any ideas?

Thanks in advance.

title: Cherry pick process

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
After 1.0, we've talked about the timeline for minor releases being longer (circa ~1mo), which means we'll be putting out more patch releases (1.0.1, 1.0.2, etc.) in the interim. Outside of developers, people are probably going to be running something closer to the `release-X.Y` branch, so release validation (#10676) is going to be very important as well.

Our current cherry pick "process" is very loose. We cobble together a list using an issue, or a label, and then we blast all of those commits together all at once as the patch version commit (e.g. #10559).

With a small amount of scripting, we can change this so that cherry picks are just proposed pull requests to the release branch. They can be completely automated, as a single commit with a small justification for the cherry pick. We could then decide on a group of people that were responsible for triage over the release branch (and maybe a small set with fastpath triage for hot stuff.)

This also has the added advantage that cherry-picks can just be trickled into the release branch gradually, and we would then either cut patch releases on cadence (i.e. "patch Tuesday") or immediately for a breakfix - and in the latter case we'd already know from validation that the other patches in the release branch are safe to ship as well.

The importance of this is also higher if the cadence of the minor releases is slower because the cherry picks will undoubtedly hit more and more conflicts towards the end of the cycle - validation after conflict resolution is doubly important.

c.f. #10709 (I'd update releasing.md after this)

cc @alex-mohr @goltermann @thockin @brendandburns @quinton-hoole

labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
I've seen a variety of bugs stemming from the use of strings as types in internal API's where more specialized types could have been more appropriate, and enabled our compiler rather than our users to pick up programming errors.

https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/pull/10699 is one particular example, where node names and host names got confused, as they are both passed around as strings.  I have seen several other similar bugs which were picked up at much greater expense by users than if our compiler had simply errored.  Name vs namespacedName is another recurring theme.  internalName vs externalName.  The list goes on.

Lets create more specilized types for these and plumb them throughout the system.

More specific sub-issues still TBD - creating this placeholder in the mean time so that it gets done.

body:
The condition on task for checking if the cert is created only checks the file. We need to name the file something so we can know when to force the task to create a new cert on IP change. 

https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/contrib/ansible/roles/kubernetes/tasks/gen_certs.yml#L20
### Issue

Kubelet can then not reconnect to apimaster

```
Jul 02 23:54:56 node-1.vms.local kubelet[12850]: E0702 23:54:56.092537   12850 reflector.go:136] Failed to list *api.Service: Get https://172.10.1.100:443/api/v1/services: x509: certificate is valid for 10.0.2.15, 10.254.0.1, not 172.10.1.100

title: Better PV matching

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Currently, the PV binder matches claims with the exact access modes on the volume and claim.  For example, a GCEPD with RWO+ROX will bind only to a claim that requests RWO+ROX.

Matching should be loosened to allow users to request fewer modes but possibly get more than they asked for.  A user can request RWO in a claim but get a GCEPD with RWO+ROX.

Getting more than requested follows storage, which matches on at least the amount requested (5Gi) but could be more (the volume actually has 10Gi).

title: kubectl describe - undocumented feature: resources are matched by prefix

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
There is an undocumented feature in "kubectl describe": If we give two arguments, for instance

```
kubectl describe node e2e-test
```

and the name is not found, kubectl searches for resources whose name starts with the given prefix (here: nodes with names starting with e2e-test

This feature doesn't work if we use / to separate the resource type:

```
kubectl describe node/e2e-test
```

What needs to be sorted out:
1. document (or not) this feature
2. unify (or not) the behavior for space-separated and /-separated parameters
3. document what return code is returned if resource is not found - people may be confused if they get success if node name is not matched, but is matched to another node with the given prefix.

If we want to leave this undocumented function as it is, I suggest to include comments in the go sources explaining why we have it.

title: Some volumes mix "what" and "how" in API

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

body:
The GCE PD volume (and several others) have a `ReadOnly` flag alongside all of the fields that identify a PD.  This works fine in plain old "mount a volume" mode - the user specifies in their pod just what they want (a specific PD) and how they want it (read-only vs read-write).

The problem arises with PersistentVolumes - they also hold the same VolumeSource struct with the PD name and the ReadOnly flag.  This is wrong because the ReadOnly flag is not an attribute of the Pers.Vol., it is an attribute of the Claim (which indeed has a ReadOnly flag).
#10424 plumbs that down, but I find it to be a bit clumsy still.  This is an area the API can get better.  Maybe something like moving ReadOnly out of each volume and into the `Volume` struct (making it `{Name, ReadOnly, VolumeSource}`)

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

body:
@davidopp 

We have a need to be able to label pods with the 'primary' user in order for our custom scheduler to make better decisions during periods of resource contention.  Additionally we would like to have our users belong to one-to-many groups representing an organizational hierarchy such that our group base scheduling decisions can be made.  I think that native representation of organizational groups and users would be generally beneficial to other schedulers, user interfaces, and reporting solutions that integrate with Kubernetes.  To meet our needs the following would be required:

1) An admission controller that sets the 'user' based on the authenticated user making the API call on controllers and pods when a 'human' user is making the request and copies the 'user' object from the parent controller on pods created by controllers.  Additionally the controller would prevent direct modification or explicit setting of this field.
2) Provide an easy method to select all of the pods of a given user
3) Provide an easy method to select all of the pods owned by users in a given group
4) Handle the change of user group membership on existing resources

The following describes a possible implementation

1) Add 'user' and 'group' as top level objects.
2) A 'user' object represents a person who is responsible for the object
3) A 'user' object minimally has a name and a primary 'group' that could be null.
4) A 'group' object has a list of user objects and a list of groups that belong to the group.
5) Add 'user' to ObjectMeta

This would allow for complex hierarchies and an easy way to get all of the users in a given group or branch of the tree.

Why labels aren't enough...
- Doing all of the above with labels would require complex API queries to get all pods that belong to all users in a group when dealing with hierarchies.  
- Simply relying on labels also would require the complete relabeling/reannotating of all objects when organizational configuration changes.

title: Remove the concept of "unversioned" types and replace it with common server types and type reuse

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
The unversioned concept is not needed.  Every object demonstrably has a schema that constitutes a single version (there is no object without a version).  Unversioned is a limited concept intended to solve two cases - api objects that are not retrieved in the context of a locked version (/apis/, /api/, Status errors encountered outside a scheme), and the reuse of objects across versions.  The latter is better served by type aliasing (declaring that v1beta1 Status has the equivalent to schema of v1 Status) or type duplication (copy v1 Status into v1beta1 and register it).  The former still has a schema that requires exposure through swagger, and for which certain code that already handles versioned code is directly better.  The contract of backwards compatibility for unversioned API endpoints requires that we not deliver backwards incompatible schemas to clients, but that does not limit us to the exposure of new API groups on different server implementations that have newer implementations of status.

The unversioned package should be changed:
- We should create a "v1" unversioned package (indicating these are versioned types) that contains everything in "v1".  
  - The parent package name should be renamed to "common" or "server"
  - No backwards incompatible changes are allowed in this package (same statement as today)
  - We can put common types into here that individual implementations of APIs get to pick from - for instance, an API can choose to take v1 Status or v2 Status
- API status, when returned by an API versioned url path (`/apis/group/version/*`) should be versioned - the Go type `common/v1/Status` should be registered into each API version under the name `Status`, and the returned group and version of the object from the API would be the group and version they are under
- Top level, non-version-lockedAPIs should return `kind: "Status", version: "v1"` which is backwards compatible with what we launched with.  That means they obey the schema registered under "version 1" which is in the legacy group.
- Any new top level object returned from a non-locked API today should return version "v1" (APIGroup, others)
  - In the future, when we have to add incompatible objects, we will rev the whole server endpoint (`/apis.2/` etc)

The changes above mean that there is no need for internal versions to know about "unversioned" - they always have an API group they serve from (unversioned is v1).  Encoding will properly fail if the type is not registered and locked into a type.  We will declare that any object retrieved outside of a versioned endpoint must be added to the `common/v1` package, and otherwise requires no special handling.

Examples:
- `/api/` returns `v1 Status`
- `/apis/` returns `v1 APIGroupList`
- a 403 error on `/api/` returns `v1 Status`
- a 403 error on `/api/v1/foo` returns `v1 Status`
- a 403 error on `/apis/extensions/v1beta1/foo` returns `v1beta1 Status`
- Swagger returns `v1beta1 Status` for extensions that has the same schema as `v1 Status`

title: WIP: Add pod-to-rc cache for RC/Job/DaemonSet/Endpoint

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: needs-sig
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `sig/foo` label and requires one.

body:
K8s use Labels and Selector to couple pods and the ReplicationController, currently, when find the rc for a pod, k8s will traverse all rcs to find the matching one, which is not efficiency.

Some optimization could be done to improve the look up time, such as:
1. add namespace index, so that filter first on namespace and then search in that namespace for a match. see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/17277
2. add a "equivalent pod" cache: usually, a rc will have a replica number 3-5, which means there are 3-5 pods will have same labels(and thus same  rcs), so there is no need to search the matching rc for every "equivalent" pods. We can search the matching rc for the first pod, and cache the result. ControllerManager could watch the update/delete of rcs, and marks a cached value as dirty. When need find the matching rc for  a new pod, check to see if the search result for an equivalent pod is already cached. If so, re-search the matching rc just for the "dirty" values

body:
Following the example for
http://kubernetes.io/v1.1/examples/spark/README.html

The worker-controller json file
http://kubernetes.io/v1.1/examples/spark/spark-worker-controller.json

Utilizes  "hostPort": 8888 which is incorrectly specified, this should be removed as all the replicas started will try to occupy the port 8888 (unless you change replicas: 1). After following the example and using kubectl get pods, only 1 worker will have been started.  The others will fail with the reason below.

```
kubectl get events

title: Further evaluate client backoffs for Rest clients in chaos scenarios.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
The new clients exp. backoff functionality is now merged, but , needs to be evaluated on a cluster, to make sure that (when configured) it is actually backing off the way we expect it to.
- Measure how many requests are created when etcd goes down (thundering herd) without the exponential backoff policy.
- Does the "thundering herd" of requests back down when we trigger a backoff policy w/ > 0 seconds base?
- If not, move backoff to client scope, and redo this experiment.

To close this issue we should attach evidence that the backoff is working the way we want it to in chaos scenarios we are concerned about. this may require updating the backoff to act at a more global scope (doing so is a very minor modification to rest_client.go).

cc @krousey @timothysc

Right now we set `KUBE_GCE_INSTANCE_PREFIX` separately from `INSTANCE_PREFIX` (which we set to `E2E_CLUSTER_NAME`), but in `cluster/gce/config-default.sh` and `cluster/gce/config-default.sh` `INSTANCE_PREFIX` gets overwritten with `KUBE_GCE_INSTANCE_PREFIX` anyway. body:
# Problem statement

Some images require pull secrets in order to be used by the Kubelet. Pull secrets are per namespace. Imagine the following scenario:
1. If a pod in namespaceA has valid pull secrets for `foo/bar:stable`, when it is scheduled to a given node, the Kubelet uses the pull secrets to pull the image to the node
2. If a pod in namespaceB also refers to `foo/bar:stable` but does not have valid pull secrets for it, if it happens to be scheduled to the same node as the pod in step 1, the Kubelet respects the image pull policy
3. Because the image already exists on the node, if the pull policy is Never or IfNotPresent, the Kubelet runs the pod, even though namespaceB shouldn't be able to use that image.
# Proposed solutions
## Option 1 - Kubelet flag to ignore pull policy and always try to pull

Add a flag to the kubelet, `--always-pull-images` (or something similarly named) that, if true, would force the Kubelet to attempt to pull every image prior to running a pod, regardless of the image's pull policy.

Pros:
- Easy to implement
- Guarantees that a namespace is allowed to use an image

Cons:
- Overrides user-specified intent in image pull policy
- Requires remote registry to be online to check authorization
- Introduces small amount of latency to pod startup time (because of the additional network requests to the registry)
## Option 2 - Keep an in-memory cache of which namespaces are allowed to use which images

After an image has been successfully pulled, record the mapping from namespace to image in an in-memory cache in the Kubelet. Subsequent attempts by pods in the same namespace to use the same image would respect the image pull policy. Any attempts by pods in other namespaces to use this image would ignore the image pull policy and instead force a pull attempt.

Pros:
- Doesn't override user-specified intent in image pull policy
- No added latency to pod startup time

Cons:
- Doesn't handle authorization revocation; if the credentials to pull an image have changed in the remote registry, there is no way to evict an entry from the cache, possibly allowing access to an image that would otherwise fail with option 1. This could be mitigated if the entries in the cache have a TTL.
# Suggested path forward

Looking for feedback from the community on this one. I'd like to implement option 1 in the short term, with the default being false (so image pull policy is respected) to keep the status quo. If we can come to an agreement on option 2, I'd like to move to that eventually.

@kubernetes/goog-node @kubernetes/rh-cluster-infra @kubernetes/sig-node

title: Proposal: Split issue Priority into Importance and Urgency

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
cc @thockin @goltermann @bgrant0607 @smarterclayton
# Status Quo

Currently we apply a single **Priority** label to every issue, and (somewhat inconsistently) use that as a work queue mechanism for the project.  Each person in theory tries to work on a priority/P0 issue, and if there are none of those, or they're all already being worked on, or the person does not have the required skills to work on any of the P0 issues, they try to work on a P1 issue, P2 issue, etc.
# Problems with this approach

The core problem with that approach is that the two orthogonal concepts of **Urgency** (how soon we'd like something done), and **Importance** (how important we think it is in the long term that something gets done) are munged together into a single **Priority** value, and in the process we lose a very important signal.  

More specifically, without explicit steps to avoid this, it becomes too easy to focus too much attention on supposedly urgent issues and not enough on truly important, but less urgent issues.  Sometimes a similar distinction is made between **tactical** and **strategic** work.

This phenomenon has been well documented elsewhere, and is pretty main-stream thinking in management science, e.g. [Covey's Time Management Grid](http://www.usgs.gov/humancapital/documents/TimeManagementGrid.pdf).

Another practical problem with a combined **Priority** value is that it tends to be more volatile than the the individual **Importance** and **Urgency** values (when we get time to work on a P2 issue, it becomes a P1 issue. When a P1 issue starts blocking other important stuff like merge-bot it becomes a P0 issue etc, etc).  So priority values need to be updated a lot, and easily become inaccurate over time.  So while the Priority method involves fewer labels, and is therefore theoretically easier to understand, and less work to maintain, in practise people get very confused by it (is this thing a high priority because it's urgent, or because it's important?  Why are you working on this thing that is not a top priority?  Because we think it's strategically important. etc).  And they spend a lot of time prioritizing and re-prioritizing things, rather than getting things done.
# Proposed Alternative

Assign independent **Importance** and **Urgency** values to each issue.  This places every issue in one of 4 quadrants:
- **Quadrant 1: Import and Urgent** - clearly these should be worked on in preference to all else.  If we apply enough effort to important stuff in advance of it becoming urgent, it tends not to end up in this quadrant.  In a happy world this quadrant is empty.
- **Quadrant 2: Important but not Urgent** - this is the stuff that often doesn't get done, and causes big problems down the line.  Make sure that we do it in preference to the stuff below wherever practical.
- **Quadrant 3: Urgent but not Important** - time-pressured distractions.  These are often fallout from not doing enough important stuff in quadrant 2 above.  
- **Quadrant 4: Not Important and not Urgent** - just ignore this stuff - it's of low value.

In practise I think that we need more than binary values for Importance and urgency.  A scale of 0..3 as we use for priorities seems sensible, although we could possibly reduce this to 0..2.
# Migration Plan

Given the number of issues that we already have that have a priority label assigned to them, it could be a real pain to have to manually apply a the proposed new Importance and Urgency labels to them instead (and deprecate the Priority labels). But there is a potential short-cut as follows:
1. Use the existing priority label to automatically assign an Importance label to each issue.  So high priority items become important items in the new world.
2. Assign low urgency labels to everything by default.

Over time, new issues will get the right labels, and old issues will have their importance and urgency labels corrected (e.g. increase an issue's importance or urgency to get it into a release).

Thoughts? Unless anyone has objections, I'll implement it after appropriate consultation.

title: Standalone cAdvisor for monitoring

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
As of Kubernetes v1.1, and possibly v1.2 as well, cAdvisor is linked into kubelet.
Kubelet groups detailed cAdvisor metrics into pods and nodes and exposes them via REST endpoints (`/stats`)

Monitoring is resource intensive. There are currently several issues filed against kubelet around resource usage which are mostly related to cAdvisor's resource consumption.
Support for custom metrics adds significant resource overhead to kubelet.

Not all users of kubernetes need cAdvisor for monitoring.

Kubelet will need just a few metrics for its functionality. Specifically, cpu usage, memory usage, and filesystem usage for now. These metrics are needed for scheduling and other cluster functionalities.

By separating out cAdvisor monitoring agent from kubelet, users can choose to run cAdvisor as a standalone container and get a lot more detailed metrics. 
This split will let us optimize resource impact of kubelet and cadvisor independently.
cAdvisor can expose potentially expensive metrics as well.

For the basic metrics that kubelet needs, it will embed specific libraries from cAdvisor and compute those metrics internally.

cAdvisor needs to be enhanced to support pods. To make this easier, kubelet should expose the pods that it is currently managing via some API. (#9473 talks about one such API)

for scheduler, 

```
latency * throughput = 1
```

as scheduler has just one loop to process all pods

but for kubelet

```
latency * throughput = n(count of nodes)
```

maybe the latency of kubelet is near or slow than scheduler, but there are many kubelets run in system. If `latency(scheduler) == latency(kubelet)`, and there are 500 nodes, the `throughput(kubelet) == 500 times of throughput(scheduler)`. this explains the different result of these 2 tests.

**When cluster scale, the throughput gap between scheduler and kubelet/apiserver will be bigger.**
**So it is necessary to make scheduler parallel across pod.**

title: Compartmentalize secrets between service accounts

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
A key use case for service accounts is compartmentalization of secrets.

In other words:

> As a user, I can create serviceAccounts/A, whose pods have access to secrets/A, but not secrets/B; and serviceAccount/B whose pods can access secrets/B but not secretsA.

A specific use case raised by a Kubernetes user was:

> The e-commerce pods can access Stripe API keys, but the email-sending pods can't.

These use cases as possible, but currently hard to get right

---

The way you could do the second use case currently is:
1. create secret "stripekey" with the Stripe API keys.
2. create Kubernetes Service Account called "ecommerce".
3. Add a reference from "serviceAccounts/ecommerce" to "secrets/stripekey".
4. create Kubernetes Service Account called "email".
5. create e-commerce pods/rcs with .spec.serviceAccount=ecommerce.  Mount the stripe secret in the pod.
6. create email pods/rcs with .spec.serviceAccount=email. 
7. ensure that pods with serviceAccount=email cannot GET  "secrets/stripekey".

Actions needed
- [ ]  This entire procedure needs to be well documented.  (e.g. in docs/user-guide/service-accounts.md).
- [ ] There needs to be e2e testing which ensures compartmentalization of secrets. 
- [ ] step 7 above needs to be easier, preferably happening by default rather than requiring action.

Step 7 deserves more detail:

Currently, a newly created service account has `root`-like API permissions.   There are two ways to reduce these permissions:

The first is to block the service account from accessing the API entirely.  Ways to do this are discussed in #16779.  The current way is a hack.  You have to put a certain `volumeMount` on each container in each pod of that service account, which in turn blocks the service account token from being mounted.  Issue #16779 suggest the alternative of having a flag on each service account that blocks creation of an API token entirely.  

The second is to edit the authorization config for each service account.  Currently, only "ABAC" authorization is supported, and requires manually editing a file read by the apiserver.  This doesn't work at all on GKE.

Both of these options requires specific action from the user to get the behavior they most likely want.  We should look at changing the defaults.  For example, we could change the default when creating a new service account to not have an API token.

body:
The `kubectl create secret generic` command let's a user specify a type for the secret.  It defaults to `opaque`.  

The kube server supports a set of known secret types with specific behaviors.  The client could support checking that the user specified secret type is one of the known types that are specified in `kubernetes` by default, and if it is not, require the client to pass a ``--confirm` flag to ack that they were not just making a typo.
- Pros
  - makes user less prone to fat fingering the type
- Cons
  - third-parties may define new types of secrets so central management of names may not be desirable

title: PHP on guestbook example is setting its include_path and using short tags.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
We've found these issues after trying to run the guestbook example with a different set of containers. The issues are located at the file `kubernetes/examples/guestbook/php-redis/guestbook.php`, on the following lines:

```
<?

set_include_path('.:/usr/local/lib/php');
```

Although the Guestbook example works on the container referenced in the example (`gcr.io/google_samples/gb-frontend:v3`), it exposes some bad practices that binds that code to the specific configuration of that particular container. If you try to run the same code with a different configuration, it will fail because of that.

First, it is using PHP short tags, which won't work if the short_tags is disabled on PHP's configuration. It should use `<?php` instead, which is the recommended approach. Some references at http://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-1/ or http://pear.php.net/manual/en/standards.tags.php

Also, it sets a new `include_path` which binds the code to a specific directory configuration, and it's not required by default. Its default value will point to the PEAR packages directory, so it should be left untouched and everything should continue to work.

title: Pluralizing rest resource names in APIs is a mistake

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
The pluralization of rest resource names in URL paths is mostly human conceit that complicates every interaction from clients and leads to little practical benefit for end users.  In addition, it's an arbitrary transformation that cannot lead to predictable results.

The use of pluralization is entirely historical, and is not based on any pattern other than making readable urls for bookmarking in a web browser.  That is not the same use case as a well constructed API - the set of end users who create urls against our API are extremely limited.  

I believe for v2 versions of our APIs and new API resources we should abandon pluralization in our URL paths.  We can continue to support the old paths as aliases throughout each published API version, but removing the arbitrary process of generating a plurals will allow future api logic to be simpler.

Ie:

/api/v1/namespace/foo/pod/bar/subresource

title: [Component Registration] Phase 1 - Simplify Endpoints

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Architecture.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
Phase 1 of [phased changes](https://github.com/mesosphere/kubernetes/blob/component-registration-proposal/docs/proposals/component-registration.md#phased-changes) from the Component Registration proposal: #13216
1. Add a new API resource (ExternalServiceProvider) that represents a non-pod service provider
   - Require specification of a network route (host[:port])
   - Allow specification liveness and readiness probe methods
   - Allow storage of the last known status (list of conditions)
2. Add (or modify) a controller (e.g. EndpointsController) to probe ExternalServiceProviders and update their status
3. Update EndpointsController to manage Endpoints based on both Pod and ExternalServiceProvider status
4. Update kubectl to allow management of ExternalServiceProviders

Endpoints should continue to be reverse compatible. It must continue to be possible for users or automated agents to specify Endpoints. However, the primary usage pattern going forward should be for users/agents to create ExternalServiceProviders instead and let an automated process (controller) handle updating Endpoints from the ExternalServiceProviders.

One primary goal for this change is to allow the distinction between Spec and Status when inquiring about external endpoints, and the robustness and extensibility of multiple Spec permutations and Status conditions that that design enables. The Endpoints API resource has an "clever" design for its original purpose, but it's become evident trying to extend it that it is now both confusing and hard to use, as-is. We would like to transition Endpoints to being primarily a read-only resource from the user's perspective, generated and updated by k8s components/controllers/addons.

Another primary goal of this change is that with the increased flexibility that ExternalServiceProvider provides, it can be used to represent k8s components that are not hosted on k8s. This would be done with labels, and will be pursued in subsequent Component Registration phases.

As a secondary goal, the addition of ExternalServiceProviders allows users to generate lists of ExternalServiceProviders and Pods with similar labels. This will be useful for bootstrapping, especially, as components may be initially deployed as ExternalServiceProviders and then migrate to being Pods. Having these resources be similar in API makes this kind of process easier. In a later phase, it will also enable improving the expressiveness of the Service API to represent both internal and external service providers more dynamically (e.g aggregate status).

title: Rolling updates should fail early if a pod fails to start

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
In 1.0.x, rolling update didn't block, so we could check things like a failed pod while waiting for the update to complete.

In 1.1.x, rolling update does block up to the timeout amount. This is great since we had to script it externally before. However it waits the entire timeout even if the update fails immediately. For instance, if you specify a non-existent image the pod will report a `PullImageError`. At that point the rolling update could abort immediately. Instead it blocks for the 5 minute timeout. When frequently developing and deploying this 5 minute timeout becomes painful.

I suggest rolling-update fails immediately if any of the new pods are not in a 'Pending' or 'Running' state. Not sure if there is a set of non-error states we can use.

title: Refresh Tokens

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
A little ways back, support was added to the APIServer for authenticating with JWTs obtained from OpenID Identity Providers ( #10957 ). However, these tokens tend to be short-lived, so we'd like to add support for refresh tokens.

The obvious place for this at first glance is `kubectl`, but that presents a number of problems: a refresh token request requires a client ID and secret; surely we don't want to distribute the API Server client secret to every user who want to use the command line?

So should the APIServer instead be able to consume Refresh tokens? If that's the case, it would seem that it would need to have an endpoint where someone can go to obtain one in the first place (eg., they navigate to some URL, do the OAuth2 dance with their OIDC IDP, end up back at the APIServer on a page that displays the refresh token, which they can then embed in their kubectl config file. Does this approach make more sense?

Thanks! 

Bobby

title: Reject overly precise resource values

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Currently, ResourceMemory and ResourceStorage will accept non-whole-number values (e.g. a Pod can request 10 mlli-bytes). This doesn't make sense, so we should reject (in validation) non-integer values for these. Along similar lines, ResourceCPU accepts and blindly rounds up values with sub-milli-core precision (rounding up to nearest milli-core). Rather than rounding, we should reject these values.

These changes are **breaking** changes to the API.

This is all a really long winded way to say, what's the real recommended way to run multiple API servers?

title: scheduler: Relaxed randomization

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
From borg paper:

```
It is wasteful to calculate feasibility
and scores for all the machines in a large cell, so the
scheduler examines machines in a random order until it has
found “enough” feasible machines to score, and then selects
the best within that set. This reduces the amount of scoring
and cache invalidations needed when tasks enter and leave
the system, and speeds up assignment of tasks to machines.
```

This seems to be easy enough to implement for generic scheduler without a lot of complexity. But we need a way to define `enough`. Probably configurable percentage of all nodes for generic scheduler?

There is a small issue with current implementation for adding this too.

Scheduler have additional extenders that will try to filter out feasible nodes again. And it is done in a batch (The current extender is a HTTP implementation. Probably we want to reduce latency.) 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/scheduler/generic_scheduler.go#L145

So if we send the "enough" nodes to extenders in a batch, we might end up with no feasible nodes. But in reality, there are feasible nodes that outside the "enough" set. This might affect scheduling correctness. Do we want to ensure "correctness" at scheduler level? 

Any idea?

/cc @hongchaodeng @davidopp @HaiyangDING

Spun off from #18130.  I haven't tried to reproduce this, but I think what is happening is that our caching strategy is keyed only off of build version, but not off of how the server is configured.

I had initially set up my cluster without daemnsets enabled.  Later, I rebuilt the server using the same build but with daemonsets turned on.  Unfortunately, kubectl had cached an old version of the schema and wouldn't let go of it.  Until I manually mv'd ~/.kube/schema out of the way, I would get

title: Needed: field-level extension mechanism

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

body:
We don't have a good mechanism for plugging extension fields into objects. That is, suppose we have an Autoscaler type, and we want user on FooCloud to be able to set some extra fields in Autoscaler.FooExtensions for the FooCloudProvider to make use of.

Currently, we do this by letting everyone add a *FooCloudOptions variable into the Autoscaler type. The downside of this is that people have to modify things in our code base, and that these options appear whether or not they actually exist on the cluster.

Another alternative is adding a `CloudProviderOptions RawExtension` (e.g., []byte) and letting people dump whatever options they want there. This has the downside that apiserver can't validate or document the contents of that field, nor can it convert it between versions, etc. Using an annotation is basically the same thing.

So my idea here is to leverage federated API servers. Basically, you'd make a new apiserver (which should be very easy in the future) and drop-in a Autoscaler type. This would be exactly the same as the main Autoscaler type, except for the addition of your custom fields. (We'd have to make some rules so this can work correctly.) Then we point /apis/scale/autoscalers at your apiserver instead of the main apiserver.

The downsides:
- depends on incomplete features.
- Only one such override per resource per cluster would be possible.
- Only possible for resources that don't have custom apiserver logic (which should be everything)

But the good part is that we'd be able to deliver the validation, documentation, conversion features users expect.

body:
The [quickstart](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/user-guide/quick-start.md) is likely where a lot of people new to Kubernetes jump in, and I feel like its current content is not necessarily doing us any favors.  IMO we should give an example at a bit higher level of abstraction and more declaratively (e.g. create a simple 'all-in-one' file that starts up an nginx RC + service), instead of running a command that will look to a new user like they're just starting up some containers. (We can swap in a Deployment object example a bit down the road).  This page should also, IMO, include a lot more links to the descriptions of the various introduced concepts.

I could take a stab at this change, but there are probably lots of opinions as to what this page should contain, so I want to make sure there's some buy-in on the general idea before I do that.

title: scheduler: using inefficient math library causes significant slowdown

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
We did a few benchmark and profiling tests for the scheduler for 1000 nodes cluster.

We found the scheduler component is the bottleneck of starting pods. And it spents most of the time in an external pkg (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/api/resource/quantity.go#L27) that handling math operations.

Profiling result for schedule 1000 pods over 1000 nodes:
https://storage.googleapis.com/profiling/org.svg

By giving the library a closer look, I found it does too many unnecessary allocations and causes GC pressure.

By mocking an efficient version of rounding function (do not handle overflow), we reduced nearly 50% of the latency for secluding 1000 pods(23s vs 53s). As we scheduled more pods, the effect getting more significant since it generates more objects per schedule.

New profiling result for schedule 1000 pods over 1000 nodes:
https://storage.googleapis.com/profiling/fix.svg

Any suggestion on how we should improve this?

/cc @hongchaodeng @lavalamp @philips

title: ContainerState may be set to Terminated when it should be Waiting.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
In kubelet/dockertools/manager.go:

In [`SyncPod()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/dockertools/manager.go#L1911-L1956), when a container fails to be restarted, we'll store the error reason in the reason cache, and set the container to `Waiting` state in `GetPodStatus()`.

But in [`GetPodStatus()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/dockertools/manager.go#L519-L531), when there are historical containers (which means that the corresponding `statuses` will be set in the loop above), only container with `kubecontainer.ErrCrashLoopBackOff.Error()` is set to `Waiting`, while the container fails with other reasons will be set to `Terminated` because of the historical exited containers.

Is this the expected behavior?

/cc @yujuhong @dchen1107

title: Consider adding a Pod phase called PodAssigned

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
It would go between PodPending and PodRunning. It means the Pod has a NodeName but has not yet been acknowledged as started by the Kubelet.

I know there's generally strong opposition to adding new Phases but I think this would be very useful and it's easier to do it now than a year from now when it's even more obvious how useful it is. I'm not sure it causes a significant backward compatibility problem because every Pod would still go through PodPending and PodRunning. (I realize it causes a backward compatibility problem for people who wrote code that expects exactly the phases we currently have, and only those phases.)

In general even if we are reluctant to add new phases, surely there must be some way we can add them; it doesn't seem reasonable to lock ourselves into exactly the phases we have forever. I guess we could say we have to wait until we rev to v2 of the API, but it would be nice if we could make minor changes like this without having to wait for a major API version change.

title: Namespace deletion should respect grace of resources

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
It is non-intuitive (to me) that a namespace with default grace, containing a pod with grace, seems to delete the pod immediately. Try:

``` yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: test

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: simple
  namespace: test
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 600
  containers:
  - image: bprashanth/sigtest:0.0
    imagePullPolicy: Always
    name: sigtest
```

followed by:

```
$ kubectl --namespace=test logs simple --follow
$ kubectl delete ns test
```

The pod just waits for sigterm, then loops forever printing time since. You'll observe that we don't get 600s of grace. This is most likely because we're imposing the namespace grace on all resources: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/namespace/namespace_controller.go#L429. 

@derekwaynecarr kubectl delete ns test --grace-period=0 should hammer it, everything else should respect grace?

body:
The vagrant recipes spin up clusters and verify scheduler, controller manager.

**Background**
The current vagrant recipes use a containerized salt stack that pulls containers for various core components, like the proxy itself.  Some of these containers might fail pulling for a variety of reasons, even though the other services (etcd, controller-manager, ...) are working.  

The trend towards "total bootstrapping" of kubernetes and the increasing importance of add-on / system containers, means that we will be in a rat-race to keep up with the amount of stuff you need to verify in a clutser.

**We should just make vagrant validate at the same granularity as E2Es**

Possibly a better / complimentary validation to run after "up" on a new cluster: would be the same one which e2e tests run: Making sure that all the pods in `kube-system` are transitioned into `Running` state before starting. .  This should hep us bring the vagrant validation to parity without having to continually maintain it, since introspecting what needs to run in kube-system is an automated task.

tl;dr  this is just proposing we add validation of all kube-system pods to be in "Running" state to the cluster validation.

body:
I always use `kubectl create -f pod.yaml` to create a pod, but if something wrong happened , **I can just get the state of POD is `pending`**, though there are **many kinds of internal error** objectively exists. For example:
- The URL of images is invalid
  
  Kubernetes just return the state `pending` to users. Unless you run `kubectl get pods -ojson`, you can get the real error:

```
"API error (500): repository name component must match \"[a-z0-9]+(?:[._-][a-z0-9]+)*\"\n"
```
- failed to schedule
  
  when resource of all nodes is limit, if you run `kubectl create -f pod.yaml`, the state of pod will also be `pending`. Until you run `kubectl describe pod ***` , you can get the real error 

```
{scheduler } failedScheduling Failed for reason PodFitsResources and possibly others
```

BTW, there are five states of PODs in kubernetes:

``` golang
type PodPhase string
const (
    PodPending PodPhase = "Pending"
    PodRunning PodPhase = "Running"
    PodSucceeded PodPhase = "Succeeded"
    PodFailed PodPhase = "Failed"
    PodUnknown PodPhase = "Unknown"
)
```

It can not represent the phase of PODs clearly enough.
So, should we add some **another phases** or **some different status code(or error code)** to   signify more states of PODs for users?
