title: Proposal: Authorizing use of a PodSecurityPolicy via the "Use" verb

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
## Summary of proposal
- a pod has a pointer to a serviceAccount.  (this is currently the case)
- a user must be authorized to **use** a serviceAccount in order to create a pod that has that serviceAccountName. (proposed new check)
- a user must be authorized to **use** a podSecurityPolicy in order to create a serviceAccount that points to that podSecurityPolicy. (proposed new check)
- a serviceAccount has a pointer to a PodSecurityPolicy  (proposed new field)
- a pod's PodSecurityContext and each of its container's SecurityContext must match the Pod's serviceAccount's PodSecurityPolicy. (proposed new check)
## Longer Version
- (prerequisite) @deads2k's proposal #12209 is implemented, in particular so that:
  - the Authorization interface knows the specific verb (e.g."create" or "logs") used.
  - the Authorization interface knows the name and namespace of the referenced object.
- (prerequisite) @pweil-'s proposal #7893 for PodSecurityPolicy is merged, except the `User` and `Groups` fields are dropped from it.
- (new thing) "serviceAccount" gets a new verb called "use".  The endpoint does not do anything, it is just for authorization purposes.
- (new thing) when a pod is created or updated by user U, and the pod has a serviceAccount S, then, in addition to our existing authorization checks, there is a new, second, authorization check that checks whether user U is allowed to "use" serviceAccount S.
  this check happens after an empty ServiceAccount is defaulted to "default".
- (new thing) serviceAccounts gain an objectReference to a PodSecurityPolicy.  
  (new thing) an admission controller enforces that a pod's securityContext(s) and podSecurityContext must match the podSecurityPolicy of its serviceAccount.
## Detailed design
### Pod Creation Detailed Steps
1. request authenticated
2. modify authenticated user using "acting-as", if requested, for e.g. controller managers (see #16933, not strictly needed for this proposal but included to show all steps in eventual system)
3. check whether authenticated user U (in groups G) is allowed to create pods, in the general case, via `authorizer.Authorize(user=U, groups=G, verb="create", kind="pods", namespace=N, …)`
4. LimitRanger admission controller runs (per #17097, this may someday set security-sensitive fields, hence we ought to re-authorize after defaulting)
5. SecurityContextDeny plugin no longer used
6. ServiceAccount plugin may set default serviceAccount
7. Note: this marks the end of "mutating" admission controllers.  All further admission controllers are not allowed to modify the object from the request body.  Since the object is in its final form, the next step(s) can do final authorization of the object.
8. New UseServiceAccount admission controller checks whether authenticated user U (in groups G) is allowed to use the pod's service account S, via  `authorizer.Authorize(user=U, groups=G, verb="use", kind="serviceAccount", objectName=S, ...)` 
9. New PodSecurityPolicyCheck plugin compares the pod's securityContext(s) and podSecurityContext with the pod's serviceAccount's podSecurityPolicy, and rejects if not matching
10. DenyEscalatingExec is not needed anymore, since it is covered by UseServiceAccount check.
11. Quota admission controller runs.
### The "UseServiceAccount" admission controller
- for "create", "update", "exec", and "attach" verbs, it checks that the requesting user is authorized to "use" the serviceAccount of the Pod in question.
- for "logs", it does not make this check.  reasoning here is that sensitivity of logs (PII or not) is somewhat independent of the privileges of the pod that is doing the logging.   So, don't require the check. 
- for "portforward", "proxy" verbs: TBD
- for "status" verb, no check.
### Use cases from #7893
##### Use case 1

As an administrator, I can create a namespace for a person that can't create privileged containers AND enforces that the UID of the containers is set to a certain value

steps to implement use case:
- create namespace N1
- create PodSecurityPolicy P1 specifying desired UID.
- create service account S1 in N1, pointing to P1.
- allow user U1 to "do anything to pods in N1" and to "use S1".
##### Use case 2:

As a cluster operator, an infrastructure component should be able to create a pod with elevated
privileges in a namespace N where regular users cannot create pods with these privileges or execute
commands in that pod.

steps to implement use case:
- create totally permissive PodSecurityPolicy P2 which can create privileged pods.
- create special purpose service account S2 which references P2
- give cluster operator user U2 permission to use S2
- do not give any other users permission to use S2.  Create S2 in a namespace other than N2 if needed.
- U2 creates Pod with service account S2, and any security context desired.

Note that the cluster admin can (1) make a powerful service account and make a pod using that account or (2) make a pod that runs as any existing service account, with that service accounts limitations, but the cluster admin cannot make a powerful pod that runs as an existing weak service account.  This is the same as Unix.  Root is powerful when running as root, and can su to any other user, but it not powerful when su'ed to a weak user.
#### Reasons I like this approach
- We will need to add code that checks whether a user can read a secret before allowing creation of a pod that mounts it.  The pattern for that will be quite similar to this.  If we do  #7893 as proposed, then we end up with two quite different patterns.
- It will be easier to teach an existing outside-of-kubernetes authorization system that something called a "serviceAccount" has a "use" verb, than it will be to teach it about the exact format of a PSP object and its users and groups fields.
- Keeps users and groups (which belong to "object-level authorization") separate from  field-level authorization (see #17549).  
- The "use" verb idea is very similar to the "acting-as" header proposed in #16933 to avoid confused deputy problem.
- By putting a reference to PodSecurityPolicy into a serviceAccount, it allows you to know the maximum set of things that a serviceAccount can do from inspecting just that serviceAccount object.  Otherwise, you can have a privileged pod run by a serviceAccount that you don't expect to be privileged.
- Once the pod's service account has been determined, further policy checks need not make any reference to users or groups.  This should simplify pod policy.
- Rather than needing to check all the PSPs a user has access to, the correct PSP is known from the pod's SA.

erictune commented:
We are going to want to have kubelet-computed labels, as well as labels that a user puts into a file on the kubelet and the kubelet automatically syncs to the node. We should think about how those two sets of labels interact.

Specifically, if a user is running on bare metal, and the user does not have a cloud provider to get the zone info from, the user are going to want to set the zone label via the file method.

title: Request Authorization vs Field Authorization

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
This issue is about defining a pattern we already have.

Proposed definitions:
- **object authorization**: deciding if a request is allowed based only on a limited set of attributes which are common to all Kubernetes-style objects and requests.
- **field authorization**: deciding whether creating or updating an object _with specific values in specific fields_ is authorized.

Reasons why it make sense to treat these as separate things:
1. _one needs to be pluggable but the other does not_.   Object authorization is a pretty generic concept.  It has been done many times before.  Therefore, people have opinions about it and existing systems they want to tie into.  So, it needs to be pluggable.  Field authorization is very specific to our types, such as Pod.  So, people are going to look to us on how to do it.  And their existing systems are not going to have support for it.  So, it is not clear that it needs to pluggable.
2. _need to happen at different times_: Object Authz should happen as early as possible, so we can reject totally unauthorized request as early as possible.  Since object authz ony depends on attributes found in the request path and HTTP headers, it can happen before the body is parsed.  Then if it it passes the Object Authorizer, then we parse it.  Then we should run admission controllers which do defaulting of fields.  Then, after that is done, we should do field authorization.  Doing it after most admission controllers run makes it less likely that the admission controllers are confused deputies.  Some admission controllers, like Quota, need to run after field authz, but that should be a small set.
3. _third party apiservers_: if I run a third party apiserver, I probably want to delegate object authz to be the same as whatever the first party apiserver uses.  Object Authz is generic.  But since Field Authz is specific to particular objects, it can be hard-coded into a third-party apiserver, for the types of objects it provides.

title: Need simple kubectl command to see cluster resource usage

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

body:
Users are getting tripped up by pods not being able to schedule due to resource deficiencies.  It can be hard to know when a pod is pending because it just hasn't started up yet, or because the cluster doesn't have room to schedule it.  http://kubernetes.io/v1.1/docs/user-guide/compute-resources.html#monitoring-compute-resource-usage helps, but isn't that discoverable (I tend to try a 'get' on a pod in pending first, and only after waiting a while and seeing it 'stuck' in pending, do I use 'describe' to realize it's a scheduling problem).

This is also complicated by system pods being in a namespace that is hidden.  Users forget that those pods exist, and 'count against' cluster resources.

There are several possible fixes offhand, I don't know what would be ideal:

1) Develop a new pod state other than Pending to represent "tried to schedule and failed for lack of resources".

2) Have kubectl get po or kubectl get po -o=wide display a column to detail why something is pending (perhaps the container.state that is Waiting in this case, or the most recent event.message).

3) Create a new kubectl command to more easily describe resources.  I'm imagining a "kubectl usage" that gives an overview of total cluster CPU and Mem, per node CPU and Mem and each pod/container's usage.  Here we would include all pods, including system ones.  This might be useful long term alongside more complex schedulers, or when your cluster has enough resources but no single node does (diagnosing the 'no holes large enough' problem).

title: Narrow down object listing in the deployment controller/utils

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

body:
Forked from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/17398/files#r45286341

After https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/17398 merges, there will be a couple of places in the deployments code where we can narrow down the list operations to just the objects we care about instead of fetching everything and filtering.
1. `util.GetNewRC` lists all rcs and filters based on the desired template. Instead we can filter based on the podTemplateHash label and list just that rc we want. (what if the user has specified not to use it though?)
2. `util.GetOldRCs` lists the pods that have the desired labels based on the deployment selector and all rcs, iterates through all pods and tries to pick the rcs that own these pods (ie. those owned by the deployment). It would be much simpler if every rc owned by a deployment would have a label like `kubernetes.io/owned-by`:`deployment.name` and filter the rcs directly. We can probably avoid the listing operation in 1. altogether by fetching all the rcs for a deployment here and separate the new from the olds in just one step.
3. The deployment controller cache fetches all objects (pods, rcs) w/o caring about labels. We could instead have one more even more general label than the one in 2. (something like `kubernetes.io/owned-by`:`deployment`) that would denote that these pods and rcs are owned by deployments and filter directly based on that label.

labels.name: priority/backlog

body:

title: Deploying applications to Kube should take into account security and the permissions necessary to accomplish their goals

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to design.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: sig/service-catalog
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Service Catalog.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
We are starting to discuss formalizing / defining how an application is deployed onto Kube (via config files, examples, deployment-manager, Helm, and OpenShift templates).  Many of those applications are going to be isolated with no external dependencies.  That's the easy problem.

The next problem is how those applications (or Kube extensions running as extensions) are:
1. Authorized to talk to the Kube API or extension API to:
   1. ... read resources in their namespace (cassandra example reading service endpoints)
   2. ... change resources in their namespace (pod that updates status of resources, like a local controller)
   3. ... read resources across all namespaces (heapster and logging integrations need to read pods)
   4. ... change some resources across all namespaces (controllers running in pods)
2. Authorized to talk to other namespaces
   1. ... via the network
   2. ... via a proxy endpoint
3. Are given secrets that allow them to securely connect to other services in Kube, in other clusters, or outside of clusters
   1. We can inject secrets, but we don't make it easy to tie secrets and config to services and access them via apps in a way that is not "copy your secrets to every other place"
4. Are given secrets that allow them to securely serve for other services to connect to
   1. ... it is hard to run an app that protects itself via SSL on the cluster (requires certs that are generated, but the certs need to be signed by the proper authority, but the cluster controls internal DNS, but the external DNS is not visible to the cluster today for ingress or load balancers)
5. Are properly authorized to do dangerous things on the cluster, including but not limited to:
   1. ... accessing hostPath (root access on node)
   2. ... accessing pid / net / ipc / privileged flags (root access on node in some cases)
   3. ... defining arbitrary volumes in their pod spec which can mount any AWS / GCE / Azure host in the cluster (because the node has permissions to attach disks to itself, and the kubelet accepts the pod, the kubelet is a confused deputy)
   4. ... running images that other containers have access to (by specifying PullIfNotPresent and guessing the other images name) or that come from arbitrary sources (unscreened code)

Currently, Kube has limited protection / solutions for any of the above.  A few are being added today as a result of work done in OpenShift or in the community:
- PodSecurity policy protects clusters from random pods getting root on boxes #7893
- Authn/z in the cluster would define a way for applications to request 1 #17440
- Network isolation is being discussed in #15465
- Service accounts are in the code, which allow roles to be assigned to pods to enable 1, but you can't assign roles
  - Service accounts can control what secrets are visible to containers via an optional admission controller
- Discussion of generating secrets for apps automatically

To properly deploy applications to Kube, we will need to separate the "what" of the thing being installed cluster with the "what is it allowed to do".  Running random code from an upstream repo on your infrastructure that also has access to your internal network generally leads to bad results.  Extension components to Kube also need this clarity - it is insufficient for them to expect to run as root on the cluster.

We should formalize:
- How applications request and are granted the permissions they need to operate on the cluster
- How applications request and are granted the access to other applications on the cluster
- How extension applications (logging, metrics, extension API groups) differ from regular applications
- How our clients know which actions are escalation actions (make kubectl confused deputy) and which are not
- How simple applications can be given complex permissions without requiring the details of each cluster to be defined

We should make all of the above items easy to layer _on top_ of application definitions.

@bgrant0607 @erictune this is my tracking issue for "it's not enough to just deploy apps, they have to not take root on your cluster when they do it".

title: Kubernetes application definition

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/service-catalog
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Service Catalog.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Forked from #17027.

Currently, there is no way to define higher level types in Kubernetes. For example, there's no way to abstractly define a Redis cluster, consisting of a Redis master, which consists of a service and replication controller, plus a set of Redis slaves, each of which consists of a service and replication controller pair, with appropriate wiring between the master and slaves.

Granted, one can easily instantiate the replication controllers and services, as demonstrated by [the guestbook example](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/22e527fe2577e2ee29d557681ee388b2d10b91a6/examples/guestbook). Likewise, the Redis slaves in that example have a priori knowledge of the name of the Redis master service, and the port it's using. All fine for something hard wired.

However, these mechanisms don't generalize well. There's no programmatically discoverable information that identifies the pieces as part of a Redis cluster, or which exposes the role that each one plays.

Yes, there are labels, such as `app:redis` and `role:slave`. But those are ad hoc strings, not clearly related to each other or described by any form of type definition. Consequently, there's no way to programmatically determine what labels to use when creating a Redis cluster, or more importantly what labels were used to create a Redis cluster and its components.

Likewise, the dependencies between services are not defined in a discoverable way. How then can one assemble an application from multiple standalone services which didn't know a priori that they would be used together in that specific configuration?

We have opportunity at this point to move beyond configuration format discussions, and define a firmer notion of application for Kubernetes. While an application will likely be defined by one or more types or templates, it also needs metadata that tools and controllers can use to reason about it... e.g., metadata that:
- describes its monitoring, logging and alerting configuration,
- allows it to be listed in a marketplace,
- helps Ubernetes schedule it and/or its constituent components, etc.

Ultimately, we need to make it easy to answer questions like:
- What applications are running in this Kubernetes cluster?
- What components comprise a given application and how are they organized?
- How is component X configured and what other components does it use?
- What Kubernetes resources comprise component X?
- How is a Redis (Cassandra, RabbitMQ, Storm, Kafka) cluster defined?
- What are its configuration points?

The purpose of this issue is to start a discussion about what constitutes applications and components, and how they are defined/expressed.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

body:
In order to
1. An example of external authorizations / authentication in the upstream Kube repo that can provide more sophisticated behavior than the simple checked in code
2. To prove that we can integrate 3rd party extension APIs in a clean way that do not live in the Kube codebase (via reuse of a shared 3rd party library, verify discovery works, prevent refactorings from breaking 3rd parties)

We're looking to split the Origin policy engine (supporting full namespace auth and user facing apis) and Origin user/group resources (supporting LDAP, integration with 3rd party github, etc) into their own project that can be easily integrated with Kube.

To do this, there are some up front questions that need to be answered:
1. Do we want to encourage Kube ecosystem pieces to be in the `kubernetes/` GitHub organization?
   1. How do we add ecosystem pieces to a regular flow (build, test, e2e) without being in the org and having some control?
   2. How do we appropriately label contributions that may overlap?
2. Do we want to encourage Kube ecosystem pieces to be focused on usefulness, or on clear decomposition?  Put another way, how willing are we to accept ecosystem parts that may be coupled (like any UAA server) together, but which breaking up may not make technical sense?

One plan might be
1. Ensure the upstream apiserver libraries are present for easily building a new client api server
2. Create a `kubernetes/kubernetes-uaa-server` project that contains the extracted components from OpenShift, marked as "ecosystem project", reusing those libraries and exposing a set of new apigroups to Kube
3. Add a kubernetes plugin for authz/authn to the Kube repo and e2e tests that validate that kubernetes-uaa continues to run and serve auth even when we iterate on Kube
4. Manage the `kubernetes-uaa-server` project as one possible way to run auth, integrated with Kube, documenting and describing it but making it clear that it is not part of the core.  Develop a set of processes for curating projects like this that are not part of the core, but reuse the same tools and patterns.

body:
**Scenario:**
controller X has a WATCH against kube-api-server on resource Y
client A creates a new Y
1. kube-api-server creates a resource Y in etcd
2. etcd acknowledges create and responds with Y, Y createdIndex/modifiedIndex mapped to ResourceVersion
3. kube-api-server is notified via a WATCH event from etcd that Y exists
4. controller X is then notified that Y exists

**Goal:**
Measure the time between when the kube-api-server knows the resource was created (step 2) and when it is retold that the resource was created via a watch notification from etcd (step 3).  I think we could track this by recording the local kube-api-server time with the resource creationTimestamp for watch where the nodeAction is create.

There have been a few issues where as the number of keys in etcd grows to N, the time it takes to get notified in the api-server for N+1 resource appears to grow even when inside an etcd watch window, having a metric would make it easier to debug, but have encountered some issues where latency appears to ~20s in some cases where if reported could provide a dump of some metrics endpoint, it would have been easier to isolate the issue.

**Caveats:**

I am most interested in measuring the time when inside of an etcd watch window; so I think it's fine if we ignored the metric on LIST+WATCH scenarios.

body:
These are described in section 3.4 of the Borg paper.

There are a lot of ways to do this. One simple way is
1) When you apply the predicate and priority functions to a pod, cache the results (namely, for each machine, whether the pod is feasible on that machine, and the priority value for the pod on that machine)
2) Scheduler watches for bindings and unbindings and node changes, and marks a cached value as dirty whenever there is a change that invalidates a cached value. (For example, if the labels on a node change, or a new pod gets bound to a machine, then all cached values related to that machine are invalidated.) In the future when we have in-place updates, some updates to pods running on the machine would also cause the node to be marked dirty.
3) When scheduling a new pod, check to see if the scheduling result for an equivalent pod is already cached. If so, re-evaluate the predicate and priority functions just for the "dirty" values (i.e. not for all machines), and update the cache.

labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
With #17197 (multiple schedulers), I see the third instance (load-balancers and storage being the others) of an API pattern and I want to pin it down.

The pattern is that of a "claim" being filed (pod, ingress, pvclaim) that is to be satisfied by some semi-abstract "service class", which is implemented by a process or pod somewhere in the cluster.

For load-balancing this manifests as "what kind of load balancer will you get", and for storage it manifests as "what kind of persistent volume will you get".  In both cases we have an open question as to whether the varying classes of service are reflected anywhere in the API or whether they simply understood to exist in the abstract.  Now that we have a third example (what scheduler will I get), I'd like to iron this out.

API:
- PRO: allows users to "go shopping"
- PRO: allows the system to verify that a requested class of service is valid (producing an error instead of pending)
- CON: more API objects
- CON: more complex (are they namespaced or global?  How to vary QoS by namespace?  What happens if a class is removed while claims are live?  How do we indicate that a class is "healthy"?)

Abstract:
- PRO: simpler
- PRO: scoping of policy (namespaced or not) are decided by the implementor
- CON: typo'ed claims get stuck pending without a clear reason
- CON: informal, harder to comprehend "current state"

title: Implement dedicated nodes using taints and tolerations

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: area/admin
labels.description: Indicates an issue on admin area.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
This is really a meta-feature; it can be built from other features that we already have or plan to have.

The requirements are
- nodes are partitioned into groups
- administrator can specify a policy that forces pods meeting particular criteria to only run on machines in one of these groups
- optionally, the policy can say that pods that do _not_ meet the criteria can _not_ run on those machines

One possible implementation that meets these requirements is
- each node optionally has a label with key 'dedicated' and some value denoting a group name
- an admission controller has a table mapping namespace name to label value, and adds the corresponding <"dedicated", value> node selector to a pod if its namespace is in the table (ideally this is done in a way that the end-user cannot later modify, but I don't think we have that ability yet)
- not sure yet about how to implement the third bullet from the requirements; #14573 has some discussion.

(I guess this could be done with annotations instead of labels.)

The user who requested this feature also requested the following: kube-proxy on a node in the dedicated machine group belonging to namespace A should not know about any of the services outside of namespace A (except system services of course). Of course this only makes sense if the policy in the admission controller assigns pod to dedicated machine group based on the pod's namespace.

This is closely related to the discussion in #14573, but here I'm trying to capture the exact feature that was requested from a user in-person recently.

There is of course a "preferred" variant of this that acts as a preference rather than a hard constraint.

title: Clarify (and perhaps loosen) our version-skew policy between master and Kubelet

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Per #16961, it seems there are needs for running Kubelets at versions ahead of masters.  This is not currently recommended in [our versioning policy](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/design/versioning.md#upgrades).

There are a number of considerations here, (not the least of which is the feasibility of guaranteeing and testing version skews,).  This issue is meant to be a place to discuss community needs around master/Kubelet version skews.

(cc @bgrant0607, @brendandburns, @a-robinson, @zmerlynn)

From #16961, we've already seen:

@quinton-hoole:

> Agree on not supporting bidirectional version skews, unless someone comes up with a legitimate use case for that. My preference would be to eliminate version skew to the maximum extent possible (e.g. mandate a strict ordering of master upgrade before node upgrade, and restrict version skew in that case to a maximum of one minor version difference, purely to allow asynchronous upgrades). But there are currently legitimate use cases (e.g. GKE), where we need to support node updates that lag many versions behind master.

@aaronlevy:

> CoreOS currently ships the Kubelet as part of the OS image, and the scenario I was testing against is an updated kubelet (1.1) shipping with a new OS version, while the master components remain unchanged.
> 
> If this type of use case isn't supported, it means an automated global update of the kubelet in the OS image requires a manual step by all CoreOS/Kubernetes users. For example, all users would need to have updated their masters prior to the OS updating with a newer kubelet (and this is not possible to guarantee). Alternatively, it would mean CoreOS couldn't ship updates to the kubelet as part of the OS image.

@philips:

> I think a very reasonable use case for version skew is simply being able to roll back a cluster upgrade midstream. Imagine I upgrade to kubernetes 1.1 and then start upgrading my kubelets. Then I find that kubernetes 1.1 control plane has a bug/performance problem/etc and so I rollback to kubernetes 1.0 control plane until I can solve the issue in 1.1.
> 
> I agree we should minimize version skew but I think it is fairly practical to allow for rollback and compatibility on both sides of the system.

title: apiserver and kubelet don't agree on what names to use in TLS verification

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
The kubelet will generate its own self-signed TLS certificates if none exist, and it uses the public IP of the server as the identifier.

apiserver, however, will attempt connections using hostnames where possible. This can cause a mismatch, such as when using `kubectl exec`, where an error will be thrown in the form of:

```
Nov 12 19:49:42 master kube-apiserver[985]: E1112 19:49:42.117202     985 errors.go:62] apiserver received an error that is not an api.Status: x509: certificate is valid for 10.1.24.65@1446839265, not ip-10-1-24-65.us-west-1.compute.internal
```

The kubelet should probably attempt to determine its hostname via reverse lookup to generate its cert, or the two should know to do identity checks via IP address, so that this doesn't happen.

Run once pods are not well accounted for by the current quota system, because run-always pods can absorb the quota and prevent jobs from running (builds, scheduled tasks).  We discussed today a "pods per unit time" measure with "max run once pods" that allow for users to run short jobs in parallel or over a longer time.

title: JSON clients have trouble with ints >= 53 bits

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
There are several fields in the API that use int64 types (uid, gid, etc). Any int >= 53 bits will not be preserved when read using some JSON clients that treat all JSON numbers like float64s (notably, browsers).

That means web clients cannot create items containing ints >= 53 bits (it will serialize them as floats, which will lose precision at best, and break go decoding at worst)

We should investigate converting uid/gid (and other int64 fields) to IntOrStrings, or adding validation to restrict int64 values to (at most) `-9007199254740991 <= x <= 9007199254740991`

References:
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Number/MAX_SAFE_INTEGER

title: Pods on AWS with native networking can't access Amazon provided DNS

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
When using native networking in in AWS (i.e. with options `cloud-provider=aws`, `cluster-name=<cluster_name>`, `allocate-node-cidrs=true`, `cluster-cidr=<pod_network>`, `configure-cbr0=true`, `bridge=cbr0`, `iptables=false`, and `ip-msq=false` as appropriate to `kube-apiserve`r, `kube-controller-manager`, `kubelet`, and `docker`), everything works except that Pods, including kube-dns, can't make DNS queries to the Amazon provided DNS server in the subnet.  That means Pods can't resolve external hostnames.

It appears that the Amazon provided DNS server won't respond to queries with an address other than one within the subnet.  The solution to the problem is to masquerade traffic from the Pod network to the Amazon provided DNS server in the subnet.

`sudo  iptables --table nat -A POSTROUTING -s <pod_cidr> -d <dns_ip>/32 -j MASQUERADE`

Arguably this should be done by `kubelet`when it is passed the `configure-cbr0` option alongside the `cloud-provider=aws` option.

title: Feature request: test dashboard to view results/history for all test runs across jenkins jobs and branches

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Right now visibility is the biggest problem we have with e2e tests. We have too many jenkins jobs to keep track of test history for each one manually, and with test filters becoming increasingly targeted, there is no easy way to know what job a particular test is running in. Moreover, because test filters are shared across jobs, changing them can result in a set of tests that _should_ be running on a particular provider/branch/job becoming silently disabled and no one is the wiser, as the test still looks green.

Case in point, filter updates caused reboot tests to be skipped on [gke-ci-reboot](http://kubekins.dls.corp.google.com/view/GKE/job/kubernetes-e2e-gke-ci-reboot/). So the job is green but it isn't even testing what it's meant to.

In order to avoid this kind of confusion and get proper visibility into what tests are running, it would be immensely helpful to have a single test dashboard that aggregates latest test results across all jobs for every defined e2e test in one big grid. Ideally it would also make results viewable by provider (GCE, GKE) and release name.

title: (Tracking Issue) Ubernetes (Federation) Lite

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
This issue is to track progress on Ubernetes (Federation) Lite.

Ubernetes Lite is a single k8s cluster running across multiple availability zones (AWS) or zones (GCE).  Other clouds & bare metal will also be possible, but won't be implemented as part of this proposal.  (But much of the infrastructure should be the same, e.g. for bare metal, if you tag nodes & volumes correctly the scheduler constraints should "just work")

I have this working on my branch, and I am cleaning up code and PRing chunks.  The 'end result' can be seen on my branch:  https://github.com/justinsb/kubernetes/tree/multizone_with_labels

There are various elements to the plan (this is the AWS track):
- [x] MVP changes to kube-up so that it can create nodes in multiple zones for AWS (MVP done in #16735, better support depends on e.g. #16199)
- [x] Make any needed changes to the AWS cloud provider (believed to be none)
- [x] Change kubelet to label new nodes with Zone information (#16866)
- [x] Change the scheduler to be spread across zones as a preference (PoC https://github.com/justinsb/kubernetes/commit/d8d8ec2b548abf040a93db52a8c9012b5d7fe20d).
- [x] Add zone labels to persistent volumes (using an admission controller?  PoC https://github.com/justinsb/kubernetes/commit/8c2a87a3a183ad9c2aeee7e6ae7cfc0a979fe2f6)  Likely only for PersistentVolumes initially.
  [ ] Use volume zone labels as a hard-constraint on pod scheduling (PoC https://github.com/justinsb/kubernetes/commit/670c033b2cf85e49fedaa226f0597f80c752719f)

In parallel we do GCE:
- [x] Change kube-up so that it can create nodes in multiple zones for GCE (PoC of MVP level: https://github.com/justinsb/kubernetes/commit/173b17aeba21c7cb59a65593e01839d0b852993b)
- [x] Change GCE cloud provider to be multi-zone aware.  It looks like this will likely require a feature flag because of changes to the semantics of zone awareness (PoC https://github.com/justinsb/kubernetes/commit/f54943bdf873041af8dd969804ab69bc4d67aa72)

That is the intended initial scope of the initial Ubernetes Lite work.  In particular, we're not planning on implementing things like HA master or zone awareness in the kube-proxy as part of this effort.  But, if HA master is implemented we can enhance it to make it multi-zone.  Or if kube-proxy adds node-locality routing, then maybe we can add zone-locality routing also.  Otherwise, the answer for more advanced functionality is likely to be "that will be done in Ubernetes Proper".

title: RFC: Where to put official Kubernetes packages / templates / etc.?

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
We're starting work on building more baked, fully formed sets of resources and images running on Kubernetes (see #16517, which is still very much in pre-alpha, but defines an epoch to get Spark to a respectable place). Right now, we (the Kubernetes team) have been checking the pieces for this into the `examples/` directory into the main https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes repo. That's starting to feel wrong for a few reasons:
- The collection of resources and images for "apps" might use advanced features that only exist on `master`, but typically are designed to work back to old versions. If they _do_ use advanced features, typically I would suggest templatizing it somehow (more on that in a bit).
- There's a fundamental difference between teaching examples, and packages. For instance, you might use `nginx` to teach Services, but an `nginx` package may actually look pretty different (it should include a `ConfigResource`, once it exists, and more metadata in general). Teaching examples don't have to be full-blown apps, and full-blown apps don't have to teach.

In addition, we've now got both [Deployment Manager](https://github.com/kubernetes/deployment-manager), [Helm](https://github.com/deis/helm) and [OpenShift Templates](https://docs.openshift.org/latest/dev_guide/templates.html) as interesting targets to write templates/packages for. It'd be nice to package this metadata in one place with the package. ~~(Unfortunately, helm (unlike DM) can't point at an alternate git path, so that one is actually tricky/possibly wasteful to consolidate under our repo as well. This is possibly a temporary limitation, though.)~~

**Current Proposal**:
- Create a https://github.com/kubernetes/application-dm-templates repo to host Deployment Manager templates, satisying https://github.com/kubernetes/deployment-manager/issues/82, splitting it from https://github.com/kubernetes/deployment-manager for all the reasons laid out in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/17027#issuecomment-157785896.
- Create a https://github.com/kubernetes/application-images repo to host image build content for containerized applications: Dockerfiles, startup scripts, config files, etc.

Both of these can be maintained by (separate) teams with fairly open memberships.

If there is interest in an additional repository to host Helm charts, we can create such a repo, but for the upstream https://github.com/helm/charts is the obvious spot. Similarly, if there is interest in hosting OpenShift templates, we can create such a repo, but the upstream https://github.com/openshift/origin/tree/master/examples is the obvious spot. We will link there in the k8s docs as well.

title: NsenterWriter is an arbitrary shell-execution / path traversal attack waiting to happen

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
EDIT: This is not a vulnerability right now, but it is a potential one.

While fixing #16969 we noticed that NsenterWriter has the potential for arbitrary shell-execution if a caller doesn't validate their paths.  We need to ensure that is impossible by invoking `filepath.Clean` on the passed input, and then using `%q` to verify that the shell we generate cannot be escaped.  However, we may need to go even further (since bash + escaping == epic disaster).

Docker 1.10 _should_ have a mount propagation setting which allows --shared mount, at which point this code should die and be totally removed.  We should leave the containerized code in experimental and put big security warnings around it until we have that.

I'd also like to figure out how we can have much stronger review policies around places where we execute bash code in the node, by requiring it go through a strict review process, and having specific helpers.  I'd also like to put some automation in place to ensure we do not execute shell except through whitelisted paths.

title: Cannot use dash in environment variable names in a pod definition

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
It's not possible to define a container with an environment variable containing dash. For example:

``` yaml
...
containers:
        - name: my-name
          image: gcr.io/id/name:v1
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: SOMETHING_WITH-DASH
              value: Something
...
```

yields the following error:

``` bash
The ReplicationController "rc-name" is invalid:spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[0].name: invalid value 'SOMETHING_WITH-DASH': must be a C identifier (matching regex [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*): e.g. "my_name" or "MyName"
```

So why is this needed? 

I'm trying to deploy an existing [Spring Boot](http://projects.spring.io/spring-boot/) Java application running inside a Docker container. Spring boot allows you to inject configuration using this approach:

``` java
@Value("${something.with-dash}")
private String mySomething;
```

Spring Boot allows you to [externalize the configuration](http://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/docs/current/reference/html/boot-features-external-config.html) in various different ways. For example it maps environment variables like this:

> If you use environment variables rather than system properties, most operating systems disallow period-separated key names, but you can use underscores instead (e.g. SPRING_CONFIG_NAME instead of spring.config.name).

So in this case I need to use an environment variable called `SOMETHING_WITH-DASH` in order for spring to pick it up and map it to `something.with-dash`. 

This works when using tools like [Docker Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/). In bash it works when you do like this:

``` bash
env 'SOMETHING_WITH-DASH=Something' myprogram
```

It's even more common when using Clojure and the popular [environ](https://github.com/weavejester/environ) library that deals with properties. Since Clojure uses Lisp syntax it's very common to name keys using dashes.

Without support for this it'll be harder for me (and presumably others) to sell Kubernetes to my company since we have to make code changes in several projects/services.

I'm using Kubernetes 1.0.6 on Google Container Engine.

title: Schedule a group of pods all at once (aka coscheduling, sometimes known as gang scheduling)

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Like many other schedulers, k8s scheduler is a sequential scheduler handles pods one by one.
This makes the architecture and algorithm simpler, but in some cases a sequential scheduler could make worse decisions than a scheduler which takes a group of pods into account, The sequential scheduler is like a “greedy algorithm” framework for pods placement.

I would like to suggest adding “group scheduling” support for the scheduler, and an ”all-or-nothing” result is reasonable I think.
Please share your thoughts.
Thanks!

@davidopp

title: Taking network bandwidth into account for scheduling?

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
Currently k8s scheduler only takes memory and cpu into account but since network bandwidth oversubscription widely exists in current data center networks, and the host itself has even higher oversubscription ratio when more and more number of pods run on a host, bandwidth contention could be a big problem for bandwidth sensitive applications.

Some thoughts about this problem:
1.  By adding pod bandwidth into request/limits factors as well the proper algorithms, it could solve the problem introduced by the host level oversubscription
2.  If we want to guarantee those special applications won’t get blocked anywhere in a cluster, we’ll probably need a full picture of the whole cluster network topology and take which into account in the algorithms of scheduler (e.g. nonblocking and blocking aggregate switches lead to different placements)

I’m looking to get opinions and ideas from the community.
Thanks!

@davidopp

title: Evaluate the benefits of adopting docker event stream

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
In #12540, docker event stream was proposed as part of the pod lifecycle event generator (PLEG) to reduce number of docker operations.

However, even without adopting the docker event stream, we can still implement a PLEG solely by periodically relisting the containers. The generic PLEG in #13571 is an example. 
This would still improve the average resource usage of kubelet and docker because only one goroutine queries docker at a higher frequency (as opposed to all pod workers). The drawback, on the other hand, is that kubelet's reaction time to container events would be equal or greater than the relist period. We should try to understand the limit of pure relisting by running some micro-benchmark using docker, so that we know how much benefits the container event stream can bring us.

Metrics:
- latency
- cpu usage percentiles

Parameters to vary:
- op: list, inspect
- period
- number of containers
- GCE machine size

The next step would be benchmarking the docker event stream.

/cc @kubernetes/goog-node

title: Need CR to get first prompt after kubectl run

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
When you run an image with kubectl run, it prints a bunch of `Waiting lines like this:

```
./kubectl run -i --tty temp2 --image busybox
Waiting for pod default/temp2-7ob5w to be running, status is Pending, pod ready: false
.. lots more lines ...
Waiting for pod default/temp2-7ob5w to be running, status is Pending, pod ready: false
```

Once it is done waiting, it doesn't print anything else, and it does not show the command prompt.  You have to hit enter to get a command prompt.  Users may not realize this.

Suggest at the end of the `Waiting...` loop, we print a line like `Hit enter for prompt` or else figure out what is wrong with the terminal or shell settings that it isn't happening immediately.

title: HPA type should accept a resource

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to adding, removing, or otherwise changing an API

milestone.title: v1.2-candidate
milestone.description: Things to consider for next minor release.

body:
The HPA type currently has a `kind` field.  While sometime unambiguous, the HPA contract is actually with a `group, resource` tuple.  You can see the expression of this in the Scaler client, where they map the `kind` to a `resource`.  Unfortunately, that construct requires that the kube process be aware of and have registered the `kind` and associated a `resource`.  In the general case, that won't happen.

`kind` should still be an option, but a `resource` (mutually exclusive to kind) should be allowed.

title: More flexible way of setting external address

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Currently one can set external address of the master either via a specific IP or rely on very opinionated _default interface_ selection mechanism (`util.ChooseHostInterface()`). It would be very handy to override this via exact interface name as well as DNS.

There are currently two flags, `--advertise-address` and `--external-hostname`. It is a little surprising that setting `--external-hostname` still doesn't affect what the external address will be, however may be all that's needed is `--external-interface`...

I am running apiserver in a container on Weave and it's Docker's `eth0` that `util.ChooseHostInterface()` currenly favours, as that's what has the default route, but that's not my cross-host network. Weave adds `ethwe` interface and I'd like to use whatever IP that gets. Right now I have to add a wrapper which gets IP of `ethwe` and passes it to `--advertise-address`,  which is in fact just a call to `hostname -i` (see weaveworks/weave#68). Perhaps, a simple mechanism, like `hostname -i`, is what would work more like other programs out there?

title: Static pod Lifecycle Formalization (was: Decide fate of mirror pods)

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

labels.name: area/pod-lifecycle
labels.description: Issues or PRs related to Pod lifecycle

body:
I would like to open a discussion on how and whether we should continue support mirror pods, given that 1) mirror pods need to be treated differently in multiple places in kubelet, making them brittle, and 2) there are some limitations about mirror pods that may cause confusion (e.g., what to expect if user modifies mirror pods)?

_Background_
kubelet watches a few sources for pods: apiserver, http, and files in a local directory. We support non-apiserver sources for several main use cases:
- Standalone kubelets
- Schedule one pod per-node (e.g., fluentd). This will soon be deprecated in favor of DaemonSet of controller.

These pods are sometimes called _static pods_ in the codebase.

For pods from non-apiserver sources, kubelet would create a corresponding _mirror pod_ in the apiserver and continues to update the status. These mirror pods serve two main purposes:
1. Allow users to inspect the pod status through kubectl.
2. Allow scheduler to account for resource usage.

Note that currently the mirror pods may not reflect truthfully what's been running on the node because apiserver can apply default (or cluster-specific) values to certain fields in the mirror pod, but kubelet will adhere to the original pod spec obtained from the source.

**[Option 1]: Deprecate mirror pods completely.**
- The majority use case is covered by DaemonSet.
- For resource accounting, kubelet can report *AllocatableResources" to the scheduler, which already excludes resources occupied by static pods.
- Mirror pods are meaningless for standalone kubelet users.
- The downside would be that if user wants to use static pods, they would not be able to inspect them from the apiserver.

**[Option 2]: Only allow the use of static pods in standalone kubelets.**
- This eliminates the need of mirror pods at the cost of user flexibility.

**[Option 3]: Continue supporting mirror pods, but mark them readonly (non-updatable) in apiserver**
- User won't be allowed to modify the mirror pods arbitrarily.
- Mirror pods could still have values that are different than its static pod.
- We still need to treat mirror pods different in the kubelet codebase.

**[Option 4]: Continue supporting mirror pods, and kubelet should sync to the mirror pods**
- If apiserver is present, kubelet will first create a mirror pod, and then sync to the pod when it receives the mirror pod through watch.
- If apiserver is not present, kubelet will sync the static pods as well.
- Mirror pods will reflect the truth since kubelet syncs to the mirror pod, and apiserver can supply any additional values in the pod spec.
- Mirror pods are read-only.
- Increased code complexity in kubelet.

**[Option 5]: Option 4 + updatable mirror and static pods**
- If a user updates the mirror pod, kubelet would overwrite the file-based static pod.
  - What if the static pod is from an http source or the directory is not writable?
  - What if user updates the static pod at the same time?
    This is my least preferred option since we'll need to resolve conflicts and handle all corner cases. I think it's reasonable to have a single source of truth.

**[Option 6]: Maintain status quo**
- Static pod is the single source of truth. Users can modify the mirror pods arbitrarily, but kubelet would ignore all the modifications as long as the annotation kubelet uses remains unchanged.
- If the mirror annotation changes in the mirror pod, kubelet recreates the mirror pod.
- If the static pod changes, kubelet recreates the mirror pod.
- Mirror pod may not reflect the true status of the static pod due to apiserver settings, as mentioned before.

/cc a couple folks who have expressed opinions about mirror pods: @bgrant0607 @thockin @davidopp @kubernetes/goog-node

body:
[Config best practices](../tree/fe6b15ba/docs/user-guide/config-best-practices.md) says:

```
Create a service before corresponding replication controllers so that the scheduler can spread the pods comprising the service. You can also create the replication controller without specifying replicas, create the service, then scale up the replication controller, which may work better in an example using progressive disclosure and may have benefits in real scenarios also, such as ensuring one replica works before creating lots of them)

It also says:

```
Use kubectl create -f <directory> where possible. This looks for config objects in all .yaml, .yml, and .json files in <directory> and passes them to create.

services/spark-master

title: apiserver: CORS only works in insecure mode?

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
I am writing a client-side AngularJS app that uses XMLHttpRequest trying to talk to the apiserver. The apiserver was brought up with the following flags, especially with `cors-allowed-origins` hoping to allow CORS.

```
--cors-allowed-origins=.* 
--insecure-bind-address=127.0.0.1 
--insecure-port=8080 
--bind-address=0.0.0.0 
--secure-port=443
```

and I configured apiserver to support basic auth with https.

However, the pre-flight OPTIONS request failed with 401. Below is my rationale:
- For CORS to work, the client will always first send a pre-flight OPTIONS request to the api endpoint
- When the apiserver runs in the secure mode (with authn), for each request the master will use ["m.Handler"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go#L597) to process the request; whereas an ["m.InsecureHandler"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go#L650) will be used if running in insecure mode
- The m.InsecureHandler will handle CORS [correctly](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/52136bdb68d7ac34a702f9d962e141664a31ec0f/pkg/master/master.go#L720) without performing any auth.
- In comparison, the m.Handler will add authn functionality _before_ CORS, as shown [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/52136bdb68d7ac34a702f9d962e141664a31ec0f/pkg/master/master.go#L731), where the [handlers.NewRequestAuthenticator](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/52136bdb68d7ac34a702f9d962e141664a31ec0f/pkg/master/master.go#L727) will add auth _before_ the InsecureHandler that handles CORS. In short, in the secure mode, we _first_ authenticate _all_ requests (including OPTIONS) _before_ detecting if it is an OPTIONS request
- Meanwhile (unfortunately), as the OPTIONS request cannot carry any auth headers (by w3c standards), the OPTIONS requests will _always_ fail the authentication.

Is this expected behavior or did I miss anything? If it is expected, then what is the recommended way to allow CORS with authn on? I am thinking of using a proxy in front of the apiserver

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
Kubernetes 1.0.3
Watch api is not clear and almost useless. Also it does not comply documentation. Will try to explain by examples:

```
curl localhost:8080/api/v1/pods?watch=true
```

Returns only one latest object for each pod with:
...
"resourceVersion":"41195"
...
"resourceVersion":"43383"
...
Then:

```
# with any resourceVersion lower the last at least by 1 or more returns
curl localhost:8080/api/v1/pods?watch=true\&resourceVersion=43300
```

``` json
{"type":"ERROR","object":{"kind":"Status","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{},"status":"Failure","message":"401: The event in requested index is outdated and cleared (the requested history has been cleared [95462/43300]) [95461]"}}
```

At the same time for nodes(which is updated every few seconds) same approach is works:

```
curl localhost:8080/api/v1/nodes?watch=true
# few objects with
"resourceVersion":"95466"
```

```
curl localhost:8080/api/v1/nodes?watch=true\&resourceVersion=95000
# returns 466 object entries as expected
```

Why whis happens? resourveVersion is a global counter for all `kind`'s in kubernetes? If yes, where this is described, and how this api can be useful? I read https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/devel/api-conventions.md#concurrency-control-and-consistency but it's said nothing about this(or i missed this).
So how i can retrieve any changes for pods if counter always in future (for pods or any infrequently changed objects)? Node's changes will almost always "shadow" any others.

According to the swagger docs (http://kubernetes.io/third_party/swagger-ui/#!/api%2Fv1/watchServiceList):

```
resourceVersion:

When specified with a watch call, shows changes that occur after that particular version of a resource. Defaults to changes from the beginning of history.
```

But this is also not true! When resourceVersion is omitted it returns only last changes, not `from the beginning of history` as described in docs, and this even confirmed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/13969

title: Duplicate swagger param name "path"

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
In the swagger api spec, in the proxy methods:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/api/swagger-spec/v1.json#L6670

There are many such entries like this:

``` js
       {
        "type": "string",
        "paramType": "query",
        "name": "path",
        "description": "Path is the URL path to use for the current proxy request to pod.",
        "required": false,
        "allowMultiple": false
       },
       {
        "type": "string",
        "paramType": "path",
        "name": "namespace",
        "description": "object name and auth scope, such as for teams and projects",
        "required": true,
        "allowMultiple": false
       },
       {
        "type": "string",
        "paramType": "path",
        "name": "name",
        "description": "name of the Pod",
        "required": true,
        "allowMultiple": false
       },
       {
        "type": "string",
        "paramType": "path",
        "name": "path",
        "description": "path to the resource",
        "required": true,
        "allowMultiple": false
       }
```

As you can see, the name "path" is used twice here. Despite the `paramType` being different, this causes `swagger-codegen` to create invalid code:

``` cs
ConnectOptionsNamespacedPodProxy_6 (string _namespace, string name, string path, string path);
```

As the name is there twice, path is a duplicate variable, causing errors.

Although this isn't necessarily a kubernetes issue - duplicate names should be handled properly in swagger-codegen - I think it would be wise to not use the same name twice in these methods.

body:
GCE PD attach/detach logic uses the `pkg/util/keymutex/keymutex.go` package to keep track of which PD attach/detaches are in progress. The underlying map grows indefinitely as the kubelet encounters more and more unique PDs (until kubelet binary is restarted).

Although in practice this is unlikely to be an issue unless someone is attaching/detaching millions of unique PDs (which is unlikely since they'd probably hit GCE quota issues first). We should still implement some sort of garbage collection to prune values that are not needed overtime.

title: Find alternative mechanism to resend pod status in kubelet

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
The pod status manager, when fails to update, [deletes the cached value to trigger the next update](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/165169ab1c18f0a6df60505a1bdc7783e56b303e/pkg/kubelet/status/manager.go#L262). This is not preferable because for the following reasons:
-  kubelet has grown organically to rely on the statuses in this cache. E.g., `git grep -n statusManager.GetPodStatus` shows

```
kubelet.go:1353:                        existingStatus, ok := kl.statusManager.GetPodStatus(podToUpdate.UID)
kubelet.go:1450:                        status, found := kl.statusManager.GetPodStatus(pod.UID)
kubelet.go:1573:                status, found := kl.statusManager.GetPodStatus(pod.UID)
kubelet.go:1660:                podStatus, ok := kl.statusManager.GetPodStatus(pod.UID)
kubelet.go:1680:        status, ok := kl.statusManager.GetPodStatus(pod.UID)
kubelet.go:2218:        podStatus, found := kl.statusManager.GetPodStatus(podUID)
kubelet.go:2695:        if existingStatus, hasExistingStatus := kl.statusManager.GetPodStatus(pod.UID); hasExistingStatus {
```

Arbitrarily deleting the values may affect access to such data from other components.
- This mechanism assumes kubelet would write pod status update periodically. This may no longer be true once we switch to the event-driven model (#12802), or at the least, the period would be much longer.

I suggest instruct status manager to use a different mechanism to requeue the update. Thoughts? @kubernetes/goog-node

title: Frequent logs about exceeded maxTries

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
I am seeing frequent kubelet logs like this:

```
E1022 04:12:32.944300    3663 manager.go:1933] Error running pod "rand-local-1ia25_e2e-tests-job-mfyjr" container "c": exceeded maxTries, some processes might not have desired OOM score
E1022 04:13:02.773880    3663 manager.go:1933] Error running pod "rand-local-1ia25_e2e-tests-job-mfyjr" container "c": exceeded maxTries, some processes might not have desired OOM score
```

I am running a cluster built from head on Oct 19th.

I trigger the logs by running this e2e test repeatedly:

``` console
$ e2e.test --host="https://104.197.70.187" --provider="gce" --ginkgo.v=true -ginkgo.dryRun=true --kubeconfig="$HOME/.kube/config" --repo-root="$KUBERNETES_SRC_PATH" -ginkgo.focus='Job.should.run.a.job.to.completion.when.tasks.sometimes.fail.and.are.locally.restarted
```

Then I look at the kubelet logs on my kubelets.

The `exceeded maxTries` string is from `pkg/util/oom/oom_linux.go`.

I think the problem is that the container run by this test exits very quickly, and so by the time we get to run this code, there are no pids in the container.

Would it make sense to detect when there are no pids in the container, and conclude that it has exited and not return an error?  Or would there be a race waiting for it to start?  But doesn't that race already exist?

body:
there is already --advertise-address which when set, is used as the public address in default `kubernetes` service endpoint. Can --advertise-port setting also be exposed ?
Currently, the secure port is passed along to master controller as the publicServicePort to be used in `kubernetes` endpoint. this will be helpful in multi apiserver setups using external loadbalancer for both external and internal cluster access, where the external loadbalancer port is different then the loadbalanced apiserver's secure port. 

advertise-address was added here https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/8649

body:

title: Remove ContainersNotReady conditions from a terminated Pod?

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
When a Pod without a readiness probe is running, we show a Condition like `status: "True" type: Ready`.
We document this behavior in `docs/user-guide/introspection-and-debugging.md`.
This seems reasonable.

However when a Pod without a readiness probe terminates in Phase Succeeded, we show it as not Ready.  Showing it as not-ready is confusing and noisy.   It looks like this:

```
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: 2015-10-22T17:54:57Z
    message: 'containers with unready status: [foo]'
    reason: ContainersNotReady
    status: "False"
    type: Ready
```

It is confusing because words like "False" and "ContainersNotReady" sound like bad things.  But, they are in fact expected since the Pod has reached a final non-running state.  And because it was ready before.

Also, it is visual clutter when you dump out the complete status of the pod.

Would it make sense to do one of the following:
1. remove the Ready condition entirely from terminated pods (or does it have some historical value?) 
2. not set a Readiness condition at all for Pods which do not have RestartPolicy = Always and do not have an explicit readiness probe, on the assumption they are not going to be part of services, and so don't need Readiness.

title: Add Metrics for RESTClients to kuberentes for all clients to optionally use via standard scrape (WAS: pushgateway but that is overkill)

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Recently @timothysc has suggested the idea of using backpressure for managing client connect storms through a LB endpoint.  

As a corallary to that end, we've dug in and saw that the RESTClient implementation has a mixture of timed backoff/throttle logic.  

As a way **to quantify requests and backoffs for requests into the apiserver, and also to determine what the real hotspots are, we can use a prometheus pushgateway in the RESTClient.**  This basically allows us to, for a given time frame, collect metrics on how the RESTClient is being used or abused by nodes, clients, applications and so on.    

Of course, this **could** be estimated from apiserver metrics, but only the clients themselves are tracking backoff rates.  

Right now, the RESTClient has some metrics, but they aren't necessarily going to be collected for every connection in a system.

I am doing this experimentally now just for data gathering.  I can open a PR if folks are interested in having it in the upstream.

title: Job: need parallel task-queue example

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

body:
We need a concrete example of how to write a parallel job that uses a task-queue.

One aspect is setting up a task queue.  We could use rabbitmq, e.g from examples/celery-rabbitmq/rabbitmq-controller.yaml.   Or do an example on GKE/GCE that uses [GCP task queue](https://cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/python/taskqueue/rest/).

Another aspect is getting a list of tasks (e.g. files to process, parameters to simulate, images to build, etc) into a task queue.  The task queue should be populated before Job is created, or else there is a race where Pods might see an empty queue and think they should terminate.  

A third aspect of is what Pods do when they are running.
Presumably, a Pod sits in a loop where it:
- tries to lease a task from the task queue
- works on task
- deletes task
- repeat

A fourth aspect is how pods exit and how this affects completion of the job. 
I think pods need to exit when there are no remaining tasks.  If all tasks
are currently leased, the task should not exit with success, but rather sleep and recheck.  Otherwise,
there could be a race as follows:
1. pod1 and pod2 each lease 1 task.
2. pod1 completes its task, deletes it, and exits with success. 
3. Job counts 1 completion is done.
4. pod2 completes its task, but then crashes before deleting it, but with lots of time left on lease.
5. pod3 started by Job to replace pod2.  
6. pod3 sees all tasks still leased (one task still leased to pod2), so exits with success
7. Job counts second completion, and so Job exits with success.
8. A task is not completed, yet the Job is done. Boo.

A fifth aspect is how scaling works.  Couple issues there:

If you try to increase parallelism greater than completions, then the controller currently won't start extra pods.  This means you need to set completion to the highest level of parallelism you might need (which is wierd, but should work okay -- you'll just have a bunch of pods that start, see an empty task queue, and then exit with success).  

If you try to decrease parallelism while it is running, pod will be terminated.  This needs to be unsuccessful termination if there are still incomplete tasks in the task queue.

title: Refactoring downward API ObjectFieldSelector

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
At the moment `ObjectFieldSelector` can only be used to access a handful of metadata fields belonging to a pod. Extracting a generic `ResourceSelector` would make downward API very flexible. 

For example, in #6477 we would be able to specify a mounted object field roughly as follows:

``` yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  name: ExampleReplicationController
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    app: busybox
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: busybox
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: busybox
          image: gcr.io/google_containers/busybox
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config-data-volume
              mountPath: /cfg
      volumes:
      - name: config-data-volume
        downwardAPI:
          items:
            - path: "config.yaml"
              resourceRef:
                from: pod-config-volume
                fieldPath: component_config
```

This is just one example but it applies to Secrets as well and also opens up possibilities for more.

There might be some concerns about allowing every API object to be accessible, but I believe that's in line with the purpose of the downward API

title: Consider writing last O(200 bytes) of container log output to pod status for terminated pods

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
A significant debugging obstacle to pod failures are easy access to the last snippet of logs.  We could potentially add the last few hundred bytes of stdout/err or the termination log to the status of a terminated container in order to enable better debugging ux.  As that could grow pod json by a significant percentage, we could restrict it to failed pods, or have it be a separate snippet recorded at a different etcd key.  However, it's likely that in most "new user" scenarios failures are frequent and represent a barrier to entry - enough that displaying some segment of logs during a pod describe should be considered

Another option is to add this logging to the event - pod exit is highly correlated with failure, and a pod termination event with log snippet is potentially more useful than a termination.

We believe this would reduce debugging load substantially, and enable better ux around pod status.
