title: Proposal: Service connection affinity

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/multicluster
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Multicluster.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
As of now connections to Services are either handled in a round robin fashion (the default) or can make use of client IP based affinity, where the endpoint for the initial connection to the service by a client is selected in a round robin fashion and subsequent connections will attempt to use the previously selected endpoint.

In some environments there is a need for a topographical or administrative prioritization of the Service endpoint selection.  For instance, a cluster may be comprised of multiple zones with Service endpoints spread across zones.  Latencies across zones may be low, yet still higher than intra-zone latencies.  There may also be financial costs associated to inter-zone traffic.  Thus, it is could be desirable for a number of reasons to prioritize endpoints for a Service within the same zone as that of Pods making connections to the Service.

Note that this proposal is distinct from that of #14484. #14484 proposes priority affinity when scheduling Pods (colocation).  I am proposing priority affinity of network connections to Services.

This could be implemented allowing the admin to specify a tag selector within the session affinity spec.  kube-proxy could then look up the tag on the Pod that initiated a connection and on any Pods that are endpoints for the Service.  It would prioritize endpoint Pods that a tag with a value that matches the value of the tag on the client Pod.  Partial matches be prioritized by the number of tags that match.

If multiple endpoints match at the same priority, then the selection of one of them can be performed in a round robin fashion, or ClientIP affinity could be applied optionally.

title: Watching a list of resource doesn't work

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
**Problem**:
`kubectl get -f <file> --watch` won't work if the file contains a list (api.List, api.ReplicationControllerList, etc). 

For example, if we want to watch a ReplicationControllerList with 2 rc:

``` console
$ kubectl get -f hack/testdata/multi-resource-rclist.json -w
CONTROLLER   CONTAINER(S)     IMAGE(S)           SELECTOR    REPLICAS   AGE
mock         mock-container   kubernetes/pause   app=mock    1          <unknown>
mock2        mock-container   kubernetes/pause   app=mock2   1          <unknown>
error: resource name may not be empty
```

Note that watch will first print the object being watched and then start watching. The object printed here should be but is _not_ retrieved from server, because the list doesn't have a "name" and therefore the code failed to refresh the object. 

**Solution**:
Since we don't support watching multiple resources, we should print an error message when we find the file contains a list. The above example should print:

``` console
$ kubectl get -f hack/testdata/multi-resource-rclist.json -w
error: watch is only supported on a single resource, but a list of resources is found
```

cc @bgrant0607 @smarterclayton

title: Reflector's call of WatchInterface.Stop() every resyncPeriod results in a new TCP connection to the apiserver each resync

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

body:
The Reflector is currently calling WatchInterface.Stop() each resyncPeriod to stop the watch, retrieve the full list of resources again, and then restart the watch.

Unfortunately, as indicated by https://github.com/golang/go/commit/8476d4cf2937fc261bbcf2890ba39d815bce3ae5, you have to read the response's body to completion before calling body.Close() if you want to reuse the TCP connection.

Because the watch response is chunked and of infinite length, there is no way to read the body to completion before calling close.

The end result is that each resyncPeriod, the TCP connection from the Reflector to the apiserver is closed, and a new one is opened.

title: kube-dns should be the only Nameserver for Pod with DnsPolicy=ClusterFirst

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/15303#issuecomment-146840698

With more than one NS on cluster-first pods, the problems are: 
1.  Faulty NXDomain Problem:
   If skydns were to fail, clients on a pod (with clusterDnsPolicy) will start getting NXDOMAIN for *cluster.local lookups instead of SERVFAIL(which could have signaled clients to retry), from the second NS
2. Faulty Resolution Problem:
   If skydns were to fail, clients on a pod (with clusterFirst DnsPolicy) might accidentally get the wrong IP.
   Consider that a k8s user has created a service called "mail".
   Assume that the search paths are "default.svc.cluster.local google.com"
   Ideally, the Query should be resolved by skydns for mail.default.svc.cluster.local.
   But since Skydns is down, the Query gets resolved by the fallback nameserver for mail.google.com

The Faulty Resolution Problem exists even if skydns is used in no-rec mode.
- We need to exercise caution while doing this because skydns needs to be robust enough.
  Otherwise ClusterFirst containers will be badly impacted with skydns being their only NS. 
  (skydns will be in recurse mode)
- We should have atleast 2 instances of kube-dns running for High Availability.
  (And also because kubelet has a backoff policy if any pod restarts too many times in a certain time window)
- SkyDNS will use the other NS for queries that don't end in ".cluster.local" (domain param of skydns)

title: Add clarity into container/image garbage collection in kubelet

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
We've received plenty of user questions asking whether their container or image GC routine functions correctly. There are two most likely causes:
1. Their GC settings are not aggressive enough. I usually point them to our [GC doc](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/80f2d89a79bee987e6c1553ff7617a7c71b977d9/docs/admin/garbage-collection.md) to check if varying the parameters would help (thanks to @dalanlan, @pwittrock and @vishh for the doc).
2. GC does not run correctly. This is harder to detect.

To provide more clarity for the second case, we can do:
1. Log more. This is the easiest solution, but reading `kubelet.log` may not be the best experience (for users) as it could be noisy. We also don't want to add more to our logs.
2. Similar to sync loop health check, we can ask each GC component to log a timestamp and fail the check if they are not responsive or haven't been able to successfully run recently.
3. Registers stats to Prometheus. We can ask the users to check the /metrics endpoint. We can also add a Prometheus pod to scrape the data in the future (#11858).

I am leaning towards option (3) since it's easier to customize the metrics we collect, and it's more user-friendly too.
Thoughts? @kubernetes/goog-node

title: --cert-dir flag can cause existing certs to be clobbered.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
The comments imply, to me, that specifying --cert-dir will cause the apiserver to look in --cert-dir for some appopriately named certs and will use those. This is in lieu of the user specifying --tls-cert-file and --tls-private-key manually.

Two problems: one, the flag descriptions don't tell the user what the cert/key need to be named for them to be auto-picked up. Two, the code doesn't actually look for those files in the --cert-dir. It just clobbers them with Kubernetes's own self-signed certificates.

Of course, it's also possible that I'm just misunderstanding the description of --cert-dir. In that case, I think it would be clearer if --cert-dir said "The directory where self-signed TLS certs are placed".

Relevant code: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go#L621-L622

(note, util.GenerateSelfSignedCert says in a comment that it will replace any existing certs)

title: [minor] controllers: clean up use of new.... s/xyz.NewXYZ()/xyz.New()

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
**problem**

The controllers in each package under controller have redundant camel cased `New...` methods... like 
- `NewDaemonSetController` (could be just `daemon.New`).  
  -`NewJobController` (could be `job.New` )

for example

```
286         go daemon.NewDaemonSetsController(kubeClient, s.resyncPeriod).
```

and here again...

```
289         go job.NewJobController(kubeClient, s.resyncPeriod).
```

and so on...

```
290             Run(s.ConcurrentJobSyncs, util.NeverStop)
291
292         podautoscaler.NewHorizontalController(kubeClient, metrics.NewHeapsterMetricsClient(kubeClient)).
293             Run(s.HorizontalPodAutoscalerSyncPeriod)
294
```
#### I think the below seems the right way to do this..

Each controller **subpackage** has a `New(...)` function...  We know the controller by looking directly at the sub package.

```
295         deployment.New(kubeClient).
296             Run(s.DeploymentControllerSyncPeriod)
297     }
298
```

Shall we replace these all accordingly? It makes
- the use of controllers a lot easier to grep for 
- the code easier to reason about 
- slightly simplifies/reduces the amount of code (trivial)  
- It also reinforces 1-1 ratio  controller-to-package, which appears to be the convention we're following.

tl;dr?  If each controller is going to have its own package,  lets have the New() create methods be named exactly the same.

body:
Right now runtime config can turn on or off group/version pairs. I want to extend this to allow turning on a group/version, and turning individual objects in that group/version off.

title: Proposal: Required, permitted, prohibited, and default label keys (and maybe values)

labels.name: priority/backlog

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Service Catalog.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
LimitRange enables administrators to make resource-related requirements upon pods created by users (including indirectly via controllers).

We could create a similar policy object that would enforce required, permitted, prohibited, and default label keys (and perhaps values) on all/selected resources within whatever scope such policies are enforced -- currently per namespace. In this case, per namespace makes sense because label selection is scoped by namespace.

The motivation: it's useful for cluster and app admins to be able to impose such restrictions in order to simplify management, monitoring, etc. For instance, if they know that every resource has an `environment` label key, then they could easily differentiate dev, staging, and production workloads.

title: Identify the configuration format

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Currently kubectl looks for files with extensions .yaml, .yml, and .json, and Kubelet reads .manifest files, at least by convention, for legacy reasons.

None of these extensions indicate that the files are Kubernetes-specific. Ironically, we don't even use the extensions to infer the encoding type -- a .json file could contain YAML, for instance.

As users build preprocessors and/or adopt higher-level orchestration tools (e.g., nulecule, terraform, deployment manager), they'll use config files of multiple formats, consumed by multiple systems. We should choose an extension that makes it clear that the files can be consumed by kubectl.

How about .kube?

Openshift uses the same format and tooling. Would it use .kube files, or choose a different extension, such as .os?  Or should we choose something more neutral, like .sic -- self-identifying config (contains apiVersion and kind)?

@smarterclayton

title: v1.List: should not use []RawExtension

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
RawExtension is intended for use where you have a two-phase unpacking, or want to pass arbitrary objects around.

v1.List should have _only_ v1 objects in it, and therefore can be unpacked in 1 pass; you don't have to defer the understanding of the object.

We need an object that is similar to RawExtension, but contains an internal runtime.Object, guaranteed to be a v1 object. It should be convertable, so conversions between v1.List and api.List types should work.

title: kubelet should treat each pod source independently

labels.name: priority/backlog

labels.name: area/pod-lifecycle
labels.description: Issues or PRs related to Pod lifecycle

body:
Right now kubelet waits until all sources are ready before deleting pods, so that it wouldn't accidentally kill desired pods from not ready sources (bug to-be-fixed by PR: #15167). 
What kubelet should do is to treat each source independently, i.e., if a source is ready, we can sync _and_ clean up pods from that source.
In order to do this, kubelet needs to be able to recognize which source the pod (container) even after restarting. There are two options:
- checkpointing: see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/15122#issuecomment-145926227 and the original checkpointing issue #489
- write it as a docker label (#15089); we'll need to do similar thing for rkt too.

/cc @dchen1107 @thockin

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
This is a problem we're going to run into as we're running 1.0 e2e tests against 1.1 clusters, (which we do because we need to make sure that 1.1 clusters still operate the way 1.0 clusters did).  If a test fails, but the failure is due to a bad test rather than a problem in 1.1, what do we do?

For example, Services/Nodeport e2es are failing on upgrade due to change in error message.  They fail when running 1.0 e2es against a HEAD master (in jobs kubernetes-upgrade-gke-step3-e2e-old and kubernetes-upgrade-gke-step5-e2e-old):
-  Kubernetes e2e suite.Services should check NodePort out-of-range

```
Expected
    <string>: Service "nodeport-range-test" is invalid: spec.ports[0].nodePort: invalid value '53127', Details: provided port is not in the valid range
to equal
    <string>: Service "nodeport-range-test" is invalid: spec.ports[0].nodePort: invalid value '53127': provided port is not in the valid range
```
- Kubernetes e2e suite.Services should prevent NodePort collisions

```
Expected
    <string>: Service "nodeport-collision2" is invalid: spec.ports[0].nodePort: invalid value '31641', Details: provided port is already allocated
to equal
    <string>: Service "nodeport-collision2" is invalid: spec.ports[0].nodePort: invalid value '31641': provided port is already allocated
```

@ixdy @quinton-hoole Any ideas about how to fix this?  This definitely isn't a regression, but it's probably not a good idea to just disable these tests.  My best thought is to cherry-pick the 1.1 test changes into 1.0, and somehow pull these tests HEAD of the 1.0 branch.  That's a lot of mucking around though, and I'm not sure it's worth it.

For now, I think we should punt on these specific tests until we have a better idea of how widespread this kind of version-skew problem is going to be.

title: Leverage docker labels to construct container statuses without consulting pod spec

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

milestone.title: v1.2-candidate
milestone.description: Things to consider for next minor release.

body:
Kubelet reconciles the difference between the pod status and the desired pod specs. When generating status for a pod (`GetPodStatus`), kubelet relies on several pieces of information from the apiserver:
- PodSpec:
  - container name
  - termination message path
- PodStatus:
  - container restart count

(_edit: this list may be incomplete_)

We can eliminate this dependency by writing the information as docker labels onto the container. The benefits of doing so include 1) kubelet can populate and maintain a container/pod status cache, representing what's running on the node, regardless of whether it has access to the pod spec yet or not; 2) this should simplify a lot of logic in pod spec.
(Note that `rkt` doesn't have this dependency as it writes relevant bits in the systemd unit file)  

Alternatively, kubelet can store a checkpoint of pods assigned to itself, and load the checkpoint when kubelet restarts. We may need to do this eventually, but in the meantime, docker labels seem like a good idea.

The original docker label issue: #3764

body:
We created the `runtime.Unstructured` to hold objects containing `TypeMeta` that we should be able to deserialize and inspect for other fields (`ObjectMeta` for instance) using common functions in the `runtime` package.  Using these types in validation (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/api/validation/schema.go#L99) would make for cleaner code and better re-use.

title: RFC: Coupled Services and Deployments

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Forked from #1743.

A number of systems (Borg, Aurora, etc.) use a single config blob to represent both the set of executing containers and the endpoints exposed to communicate with them. In Kubernetes, these are currently separate resources, such as a Service and ReplicationController:
http://kubernetes.io/v1.0/docs/user-guide/managing-deployments.html#organizing-resource-configurations
They can be specified in a single source file, but there are still multiple concepts, a few lines of boilerplate, and a small amount of redundancy, in the Service's label selector and port spec. 

Going forward, Deployment (#1743) is the persistent resource we expect users to create to manage their services, either imperatively or declaratively. It already generates other resources -- ReplicationControllers. For the common case of a single release track, it seems reasonable to autogenerate a corresponding Service by default. It should be optional, so that multiple Deployment resources could be covered by a single Service without creating unnecessary Service resources.

As Service becomes more complex, I wouldn't want to add all those knobs to Deployment. I think Deployment should stay simple and it's fine to require a separate Service for more advanced use cases (e.g., session affinity, public IPs). We probably at least need to support external load balancers and maybe nodePort.

cc @smarterclayton @ironcladlou @nikhiljindal @brendandburns @ghodss

title: Network plugin not informed of missing pods

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
I've noticed a case where the network plugin is not informed of pods which have gone missing.  Specifically, if Docker is restarted (or the node rebooted), any containers which had been running will be stopped.  The kubelet will notice this and re-create the pod infra container.

However, the network plugin will not have any knowledge that the previous infra container / pod are no longer running.  

I've specifically run into this issue in the context of IPAM:
- If the network plugin is performing IPAM, this can lead to leaked IP addresses, since the plugin does not know to un-assign the IP address from the previous pod.  
-  If the plugin is using Docker's IPAM, Docker will assign the same IP address to the new infra container.  From the network plugin's perspective, two pods now have the same IP address, which is a problem.

I'm not sure what the ideal fix is here.  I think one option would be to declare pod `tearDown` as idempotent, and whenever the kubelet detects that an infra container should be re-created (was running, is now missing) it calls the network plugin `tearDown` on the previous container before `setUp` on the new infra container.

@thockin - Any thoughts?

title: Allow Users to change labels using deployment

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

body:
Based on discussion with @bgrant0607 

Problem:
Deployment.Spec.Selector is used to select old pods (which are scaled down) and is also used as the selector for the new RC (that is scaled up).
Hence labels on both old and new pods must match Deployment.Spec.Selector. As a result, it is not possible to change the value of a label that is part of Deployment.Spec.Selector. It is however possible to add a label to the new pod.

Possible solution:
Introduce ObjectRef to keep track of parent objects (RCs will ref to Deployments) and allow RCs to be orphaned. Users get to choose what to do with orphaned RCs - they can be left as is or can be scaled down and deleted.
When user wants to change a label value, they change DeploymentSpec.Selector to match the new pod labels, so that deployment creates a new RC and scales it up. A different controller will handle orphanedRCs (RC is orphaned if it points to a deployment via its ObjectRef, but the Deployment's selector does not target that RC).

title: epic: Reducing network overhead and optimizing kubernetes control plane communications

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

body:
Per @quinton-hoole's request, I'm attempting to chart a well established path such that we can address some of the larger communications issues.  Hopefully this can serve as a jump point for the communications issues we wish to target in the 1.3 cycle. 
## Problem Statement

The **overhead** and data flow of the kubernetes control plane has led to a series of artificial limits, or **caps** (qps,max-inflight, etc), that have been placed on different system components.  These caps are an attempt to limit the system from overloading the api-server, and to ensure certain SLOs are met.  The core issue is not that the caps exist, but the fact that the interaction between the components can cause system overload in the first place.  

This epic, targeted for 1.3, is intended to help breakdown some of the different facets of this issue as we see them today, and address each aspect independently, provided there are resources available to do so.

The higher level objective would be to fix the system where possible, in order to prevent the degenerative case of overloading from occurring... at all.
## Breakdown

From operations and tests, we have witnessed the following issues which relate to this broader epic:

**P1:** There are a large number of connections in the system. (#21081) 
- _Worst offenders are not quantified?_
- **A1.1:** Analyze api-server metrics, and add metrics on who is creating the most connections, investigate their usage, and optimize their workflow.  Different solutions may exist depending on the situation, which in turn may become their own issues.  (This is a meta-problem).
- _Each new connection incurs an overhead in the system (TLS+kernel+application), and there isn't a single choke-point to throttle during overloaded situations._
- **A1.2:** Pursue http2 for internal communications, each component should have only 1, or 2 connections to the main api-server, as well as golang 1.6 for the decreased EC/TLS overhead.  

**P2:** Components do not properly back-off under extraneous load conditions. 
- _We can create a number of conditions which can cause the system to overload, e.g. fail-over, or aggressive loading._
- **A2.1:** Once we've addressed P1, and have a single choke-point it's relatively trivial to back-off during loaded situations. 

**P3**:  Enconding and decoding dominate api-server load 
- **A3.1:** We've known this for a long time, and there are a series of issues around protobuf and gRPC to address. @wojtek-t has an issue list. 

/cc @kubernetes/sig-scalability @jeremyeder

title: Kubectl expose service should change type on existing services

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

body:
I created a service of type ClusterIP. I later decide that I want to expose it externally. What's the correct way to do this in a 1.2 cluster, and where is it documented? I found nothing about it in our docs, and the approaches that came to mind first all don't work:

``` shell
# Creating the service without an external load balancer
$ kubectl create -f kubernetes/examples/guestbook/frontend-service.yaml
service "frontend" created
$ kubectl expose svc frontend
Error from server: services "frontend" already exists
# Modify the original config to set `type: LoadBalancer`
$ vim kubernetes/examples/guestbook/frontend-service.yaml
$ kubectl update -f kubernetes/examples/guestbook/frontend-service.yaml
W0330 15:51:21.625806    7556 cmd.go:187] update is DEPRECATED and will be removed in a future version. Use replace instead.
The Service "frontend" is invalid.
spec.clusterIP: Invalid value: "": field is immutable
kubectl replace -f kubernetes/examples/guestbook/frontend-service.yaml
The Service "frontend" is invalid.
spec.clusterIP: Invalid value: "": field is immutable
```

`kubectl expose` doesn't work because it only supports creating new services, not modifying existing services.

`kubectl update` and `kubectl replace` I'm not quite as sure about. The yaml file doesn't specify a `clusterIP` field, so kubectl is filling in the empty value for me. I seem to remember this working on older versions of kubernetes.

I assume you can craft a `kubectl patch` command that would do it, but there's a lot more friction in learning how to use `patch` than in running `update` or `replace`.

I feel silly even needing to ask about this, but it appears to be lacking from our docs.

cc @kubernetes/goog-cluster

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
The contrib/ansible project is focused on deploying kubernetes in a production-ready fashion. For example, [1] and [2] hard-code env variables meant for developer deployments. Here are a few proposals for improving the addon manifests:
1. If they must be hard-coded, then the manifests should support production deployment requirements by default.
2. Turn the yamls into templates (i.e. Jinja) and support a minimal number of parameters that meet dev/prod deployment use cases.

The addon manifests should be opinionated by default, but flexible enough to support *_common *_ production use cases such as how services get exposed (NodePort, ClusterIP, etc..). Otherwise contrib/ansible and potentially other projects that leverage addons need to maintain variations of the manifests to meet production deployment requirements. This can lead to less than optimal user experience.

[1] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cluster/addons/cluster-monitoring/influxdb/influxdb-grafana-controller.yaml#L56-L67
[2] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cluster/addons/cluster-monitoring/influxdb/grafana-service.yaml#L10-L12

body:
Forked from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/23430#issuecomment-202768265

The ubernetes scheduler needs to know the available resources in each cluster to be able to divide resources (such as replicasets) appropriately.

As per https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/design/federation-phase-1.md#cluster:

> In phase one it only contains available CPU resources and memory resources. The cluster controller will periodically poll the underlying cluster API Server to get cluster capability. In phase one it gets the metrics by simply aggregating metrics from all nodes. In future we will improve this with more efficient ways like leveraging heapster, and also more metrics will be supported.

There is also a proposal to provide cluster level metrics via apiserver: #23376, which we can start using whenever it is available.

We should allow two services in different k8s clusters to share an ELB, or to use an existing one that is created elsewhere.

One idea that was proposed was to use a "shared secret".  If two services are labelled with the shared "shared secret" for their loadbalancer on two different clusters (but the same AWS account), they would get the same ELB.

The implementation of this would be fairly straightforward: we would tag ELBs with the shared secret, and reuse an ELB with a matching shared secret.  This is not terribly secure, because anyone with API access can see the shared secret, but protects against mistakes and casual attackers.  

If we ran the shared secret through a hashing process we could make attacks a little harder.

We could also look at the set of registered nodes on the ELB, so that we could delete it cleanly when no cluster was using it.

It is unfortunate though that GCE doesn't have resource tags (I think).  We could use the name to encode the shared secret though I think.

cc @thockin @brendandburns because I know you want shared LB
cc @quinton-hoole because I think this is useful for Ubernetes

title: autoscaling/v1 groupversion does not work well with validation/edit/export

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: sig/autoscaling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Autoscaling.

body:
As noted here: https://github.com/openshift/origin/issues/8213

Attempting to create the following HPA:

``` yml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v1
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: test-autoscaler 
spec:
  scaleRef:
    kind: DeploymentConfig 
    name: frontend 
    apiVersion: v1
  minReplicas: 1 
  maxReplicas: 10  
```

We get the following error:

``` sh
$ kubectl create -f hpa.yaml
kubectl create --validate=false -f hpa.yaml
The HorizontalPodAutoscaler "test-autoscaler" is invalid.

* spec.scaleRef.kind: Required value
* spec.scaleRef.name: Required value
```

This doesn't make sense as the values that seem to be missing in fact are in the YAML -- the issue is that `scaleRef` is the name of the reference in the `extensions/v1beta1` groupversion, whereas `scaleTargetRef` is the name in `autoscaling/v1`.

Attempting `kubectl edit` and making any change to the HPA will result in:

```
$ kubectl edit hpa test-autoscaler
error: apiVersion should not be changed
```

even if no changes to `apiVersion` field were made

Furthermore, when exporting using `kubectl get -o yaml`, the groupversion emitted is `extensions/v1beta1` even if the HPA was originally created as `autoscaling/v1` - this may be the desired behavior but it is suprising nonetheless.

```
$ kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"1+", GitVersion:"v1.1.0-alpha.0.1588+e44c8e6661c931", GitCommit:"e44c8e6661c931f7fd434911b0d3bca140e1df3a", GitTreeState:"clean"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"2", GitVersion:"v1.2.0-36-g4a3f9c5", GitCommit:"4c91857", GitTreeState:"not a git tree"}
```

/cc @liggitt @DirectXMan12

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
I'm exploring the new `Deployment` resource in Kubernetes 1.2 and it seems it is not quite correct. It scales down the old replica set before scaling up for the new set. This is inconsistent with the rolling-update command which waited for new replication controller to scale up successfully first. As a result, deployment resource cannot be used for zero-downtime deployment in case of a single replica pod.

Please correct this to match the way `kubectl rolling-update` works which seems to be the right way.

title: Fixing scheduler benchmark

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
Even though existing scheduler benchmark showed almost linear scheduling rate, in kubemark density test we didn't see as huge improvement.

This is caused by the discrepancies between scheduler benchmark and density test in mostly two places:
- [ ] Replication controller: 
  - Scheduler benchmark creates pod one by one. See [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e664ef922fd3ecc2dcb692c8d012950cd4646af6/test/component/scheduler/perf/util.go#L115). Density test creates pods by using replication controller. See [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9a71dfe753b4e67016f306ac18d6a27698f4517b/test/e2e/density.go#L303). 
  - This affected how SelectorSpreadPriority made calculation and in Kubemark we saw it's the largest time consumer.
- [ ] Port: 
  - Scheduler benchmark creates pod without specifying port. Density test specifies ports. See [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4402e57588522d6d94870a86ed494e3c1fbd479e/test/e2e/util.go#L1833).
  - This affected how PodFitsHostPort() predicate made calculation and in Kubemark we saw it's the second largest time consumer.

Meanwhile, there is one left issue in scheduler benchmark we should fix:
- [ ] Avoid scheduling path in pod setup. In some benchmarks, we want to see scheduling behavior when  a number of pods have been scheduled. Currently the setup needs go through scheduling. See [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e664ef922fd3ecc2dcb692c8d012950cd4646af6/test/component/scheduler/perf/scheduler_bench_test.go#L57-L64). It's unnecessary and time consuming, and most importantly, stopping us from making large setup.

We are planning to fix these and improve scheduler performance in 1.3 timeline.

title: Dashboard is run by default, but could allow privilege escalation when used with custom authorization

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

body:
Dashboard is run by default (by virtue of the file: cluster/addons/dashboard/dashboard-controller.yaml).   Dashboard lets anyone who can connect to it view, edit, and delete objects.  
Kubernetes authorization plugins allow putting very flexible restrictions on what users can do what to which objects.

I plan to immediately edit Authorization docs, Addons docs, and 1.2 release notes docs to recommend that users who are using fancy Authorization should disable the Dashboard addon.

I'm not sure what the best long term solution is.  The best ones I can think of so far are:
1. implement [acting-as](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/16933) and dashboard uses that for all accesses to the API, and does no caching.
2. do not run dashboard by default, and leave it to users to decide if their authorization scheme is compatible with dashboard.

title: Using HPA in version autoscaling/v1 might return unexpected results in kubectl

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/autoscaling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Autoscaling.

milestone.title: v1.3
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/master/release-1.3/release-1.3.md

body:
In Kubernetes 1.2 HPA was graduated to GA, new types are available in `apiVersion: autoscaling/v1`.The previous version, `apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1`, is still supported for backward compatibility. Also all Kubernetes core components in 1.2 still use objects in `extensions/v1beta1`.

In `extensions/v1beta1` if `CPUUtilization` in `horizontalPodAutoscalerSpec` was not specified it was set to `80` by default while in `autoscaling/v1` HPA object without `targetCPUUtilizationPercentage` specified is a valid object. Pod autoscaler controller will apply a default scaling policy in this case which is equivalent to the previous one.

Due to the way how defaults are applied (during the conversion between versions) if you create HPA object using `autoscaling/v1` API without `targetCPUUtilizationPercentage` specified and read it using kubectl it will print default value as specified in `extensions/v1beta1` despite the fact the field is empty.

This should be fixed in 1.3 by migrating kubectl to use HPA in `autoscaling/v1`.

ref #22431, #22449

title: Getting started: "Running Kubernetes Locally via Docker" doesn't work on Max OS X

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
## Problem description

The "**Download kubectl**" section mentions the following:

> Create configuration:
> 
> ```
> $ kubectl config set-cluster test-doc --server=http://localhost:8080
> $ kubectl config set-context test-doc --cluster=test-doc
> $ kubectl config use-context test-doc
> ```
> 
> For Max OS X users instead of localhost you will have to use IP address of your docker machine, which you can find by running docker-machine env <machinename> (see documentation for details).

The `docker run` command doesn't publish any ports though, so the above does not work even if `localhost` is replaced with the correct IP address of the docker machine.

`kubectl get nodes` will then fail with:

```
The connection to the server 192.168.99.100:8080 was refused - did you specify the right host or port?
```

_Note: `192.168.99.100` is the IP of the docker machine that I configured as described_
## Hypothesis

It looks like the API server (?) port `8080` needs to be published.
## Workaround

A workaround is to keep using `localhost` in the configuration line above and to then set up an SSH tunnel:

```
docker-machine ssh $MACHINE_NAME -N -L 8080:localhost:8080
```

(where `$MACHINE_NAME` is the name of the docker machine being used, `docker-machine ls` can be used to list all running machines).

This is sufficient to make `kubectl get nodes` work as described.

title: AWS: API RequestLimit delayer was not triggering

labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
@benmcrae reported that while trying beta.0 he was hitting the AWS ELB rate limit exceeded error because of a security group tagging problem (`Error creating load balancer (will retry): Failed to create load balancer for service default/my-nginx: error creating AWS loadbalancer listeners: Throttling: Rate exceeded`).  However, he did not see `Inserting delay before AWS request (%s) to avoid RequestLimitExceeded: %s` in the kube-controller-manager logs.

The error isn't unexpected because the fix in 5b3bb56a4f851ce88d52d702e09a550e29802554 did not make beta.0 (it did make beta.1).

But, we would have wanted to see some AWS API throttling.  Possible solutions:

1) We have a single pool for all API requests per region, which isn't right I don't think.  We should probably have one for EC2 us-west-2, one for ELB us-west-2 etc.
2) We should probably log the current statistics whenever we hit a RateLimit error (perhaps at v=2).  This way we can tweak our statistic based upon what we see in the real world.

title: Ensuring only images are from approved sources are run

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
A customer has asked for a feature which would ensure that only certain "approved" binaries are run on the cluster.  This issue is to get feedback from other users on whether this would be useful, and to clarify requirements, and to see if some simple implementations would be sufficient.
## Background

The threat some users are trying to protect against is that an otherwise authorized user of a kubernetes cluster accidentally or intentionally creates a pod that runs a binary that was built from untrusted, possibly malicious, source code.  It might actually cause direct harm, or just require costly auditing after the fact.  Auditing requirements may be dictated by  [Service Organization Controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service_Organization_Controls).
## Requirements Questions
1. Is it sufficient to whitelist what image repositories are allowed? For example, allow only image names with prefixes `gcr.io/myproject/*` or `docker.io/library/ruby`.  Or is finer control, such whitelisting individual tags or tag patterns needed?  Or  even specific binary content hashes.  
   1. Docker supports specifying images at a specific checksum, like `docker pull someimage@sha256:d149ab53f8718e987c3a3024bb8aa0e2caadf6c0328f1d9d850b2a2a67f2819a`.  Is this allowed, and if so how would it work with a tag whitelist?
2. Should the whitelist check be intersected with Docker Content Trust tag signing checks?
3. Does it need to work for all container runtimes (docker, rkt, etc) or is just Docker enough for now?
4. Is a single, cluster-wide policy useful, at least as a first-pass.  Will we eventually will want policy for each user (to allow the cluster admin to run any image) or per namespace (to ensure each "tenant" in a multi-tenant cluster runs images from its own trusted build chain).  
5. Is a policy that is expresses as a flag useable enough?
6. Is the policy mandatory, or would after-the-fact auditing be sufficient for most users?  If it is mandatory, how easy does it need to be to override it in an emergency (e.g. docker hub is down, and our policy says only pull docker images, and we need to push a new image now due to a critical bug; how do I do that?)
7. Is image whitelisting useful by itself?  Or are restrictions on other parts of a Pod spec (volumes, configMaps, env vars) needed to meet auditing requirements?
## Implementation Ideas
1. [docker auth plugin](https://github.com/docker/docker/blob/HEAD/pkg/authorization/plugin.go) such as [twistlock](https://github.com/twistlock/authz) which only allows certain images to run
2. kubelet flag that contains an image prefix whitelist
3. admission controller that checks image strings in pods against a policy objects stored in the APIserver.
4. contributed controller that watches for pods with disallowed images and sends alerts somewhere.

Policy enforcement in the apiserver is easier to change and easier to surface errors, but probably more work to get something we all agree on working.  Policy enforcement or docker can apply to http and file source pods, and kubelet or docker are in better position to talk to a private registry, if more complex interaction is later needed.  A docker-based solution could be applicable to all users including non-kubernetes users.  A kubelet or apiserver solution would apply to multiple container runtimes.   Only the apiserver can easily have a per-user policy, since only it is aware what user is creating the object.  Only apiserver or kubelet can have a per-namespace policy, since docker does not know or care what a namespace is.
## Related Technology
### Docker Notary and Docker Content Trust

[Docker Content Trust](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/trust/content_trust/) checks the integrity of the image (e.g. to ensure it was not modified by a man-in-the-middle), and only allows images with signed tags to run.

Docker Content Trust uses Docker Notary.

[Docker Notary](https://github.com/docker/notary) is a general solution to compute checksums of collections of files, and publish signed checksums of those files.  Docker Notary could also sign things not in images, like configMaps, for example.

The docker client (CLI, or the go language docker client library, in the case of Kubelet) is responsible for setting whether trust should be enabled, and what notary server to use, on each call to docker.

Docker content trust only applies to image tags.  A user who asks for a specific content hash, e.g. `docker pull someimage@sha256:d149ab53f8718e987c3a3024bb8aa0e2caadf6c0328f1d9d850b2a2a67f2819a`, always succeeds.  

So, it isn't clear how to use Docker Content Trust by itself as a solution to prevent untrusted images from being run.
### rkt Trust

[rkt trust](https://coreos.com/rkt/docs/latest/subcommands/trust.html) works similarly to Docker Content Trust (and predates it.)  It controls which registries are trusted.
### Integrity Measurement Architecture

The Integrity Measurement Architecture (IMA) provides a way for parties to remotely verify the integrity of programs running on a machine. 
https://sourceforge.net/p/linux-ima/wiki/Home/#integrity-measurement-architecture-ima

It appears to be a quite complex system.  It requires a kernel that supports it, and I imagine it is complex to debug.  I am not considering it at this time.
### Openshift Builds and Imagestreams

Openshift provides an image build system and a private registry for each cluster, or each tenant of a cluster.   Having image builds happen on the same cluster as images run may be convenient in some cases, but do we need to mandate this to use this feature?  Some users have their own build system already setup
### Per-cluster registries

Kubernetes has an open issue to provide a per-cluster registry as an add-on (#1319). 
On GKE, clusters have access to a Project-wide Image registry.  However, some customers may have existing, private registries.   We should not require them to change that to take advantage of this feature.

title: intermittent DNS issues between containers

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### **Our understanding of k8s DNS**

on each node we have a kube-dns pod which contains a Sky DNS server running in one container (which answers the DNS queries) and etcd which provides the data, when you do a container-to-container call, say an http request from Buy service  to a Sell service we reference the other service using a regular DNS name.
### **Issue**

```
Error from server: Get https://node-1:10250/containerLogs/kube-system/kibana-logging-v1-x1hr3/kibana-logging: dial tcp: lookup node-1: no such host

Kubernetes master uses nodeName to fetch logs from kubelet, which doesn't always resolve.  There are two workarounds as I can think of:

body:
Guidelines for how kubectl run can satisfy:
http://martinfowler.com/bliki/InfrastructureAsCode.html

Off the top of my head:
- Always tag your image with a version-specific tag and don't move that tag to a new version. For example, use :v1234, v1.2.3, r03062016-1-4, or somesuch, rather than :latest.
- If the image is lightly parameterized, capture the parameters in a checked-in script, or at least use --record, to annotate the created objects with the command line.
- If the image is heavily parameterized, definitely check in the script.
- If features are needed that are not expressible via kubectl run flags, switch to config files checked into source control. Those files could be created using kubectl run --edit followed by kubectl get --export.
- Pin to a specific generator version, such as kubectl run --generator=deployment/v1beta1

title: Scheduler to continue if a predicate throws an error for a particular node

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

body:
Currently each node is passed through all the predicates to figure out whether the node is a match/fit to host the pod or not. The predicates are expected to return true/false without an error. However, if a predicate returns an error for a particular node, the scheduler throws an error and that pod that does not get scheduled.

Instead, I would suggest we continue on to other nodes to see if any of them can be a fit and clear the all predicates. This might make for a slightly sub-optimal scheduling decision (assuming that the node was expected to clear the predicate in the absence of the error), but at least the pod gets scheduled.

If this makes sense, I can quickly make this change and add test cases and submit a PR.

title: Consider using fluentd's buffer_queue_full_action setting to avoid dropping logs when the buffer is full

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
The setting was added late last year and we've just started using a version of fluentd that includes it. It sounds great, in that it causes the input half of fluentd to stop reading input whenever the output buffer is full (when normally the input half would just drop any input it reads during that time). Given that all our input comes from files on disk, this makes a lot of sense.

However, it's a pretty significant change to how the agent works, and the fluentd folks themselves don't seem very hot on the idea, so we should do some due diligence on it first before starting to use it. I tested it a bit this morning and at the very least it didn't cause fluentd to crash or hang when I filled up a buffer, but I didn't validate that it didn't drop anything.

title: Two more problems with Deployments

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

body:
We discovered these problems when I prepared for the demo.
The deployment config file I used:

```
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: deployment-demo
  namespace: demos
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
    type: RollingUpdate
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        demo: deployment
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: busybox
        image: busybox
        command:
        - sh
        - -c
        - while true; do echo "$(hostname) v1" > /data/index.html; sleep 60; done
        volumeMounts:
        - name: content
          mountPath: /data
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx
        volumeMounts:
          - name: content
            mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
            readOnly: true
      volumes:
      - name: content
```

The first problem occurs when I rolling update it with the following command:

```
cat deployment.yaml | sed 's/ v1/ v2/g' | kubectl --namespace=demos apply -f- --validate=false
```

**The problem is when the v1 rs scrolls down from 1 to 0, it gets scrolled up to 4 and then to 0.**

Then I use this command to roll back:

```
kubectl --namespace=demos rollout undo deployment deployment-demo
```

**The problem is the v1 rs get scrolled from 0 to 3 at once, and the v2 rs get scrolled from 3 to 0 at once.** @janetkuo and I had `watched` the events to confirm this was not caused by my bash scripts.

Output of `kubectl version`:

```
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"2+", GitVersion:"v1.2.0-alpha.8.877+2cf3c7809eac09-dirty", GitCommit:"2cf3c7809eac093f4ccbabbfac4640abde41d6b1", GitTreeState:"dirty"}

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
If I shut off my instance, it should receive an [ACPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Configuration_and_Power_Interface) shutdown signal, (e.g. [in GCE](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/stopping-or-deleting-an-instance#delete_timeout)). I'm branching this off of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/7351, because a node- or cloud provider-initiated shutdown is different from going through the API.

title: kubectl code cleanup: overhaul the resource alias introduced #6573

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/6573 introduces the alias for resources. As our code base evolves, this code needs overhaul. I've noticed several problems:
1. `aliasToResource` is a global variable, so every `DefaultRESTMapper` has the same alias map. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/api/meta/restmapper.go#L492
   (This hasn't caused any bug yet because the problem is hidden by `SplitResourceArgument`)
2. So far the only alias we have is "all", added in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/api/install/install.go#L119, which will be translated to `"rc", "svc", "pods", "pvc"`. I think this map needs to be updated. And I'd suggest use another alias, because kubectl also has a flag `--all`, which is confusing.

FWIW, I thought about using our ShortcutExpander to replace the alias code, but it doesn't seem to work because they are in different stages of the cmdline argument processing.

@kargakis @janetkuo

title: Notification of failed CronJobs

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
Chronos can notify users of failures of scheduled jobs via email.  In a discussion with a potential K8s user, the question came up whether K8s will have an email-notification feature.

About the Chronos Feature:
- [Chronos flags documentation](https://mesos.github.io/chronos/docs/configuration.html)
- option 1: HTTP notification on failure
  -  uses these flags: `--http_notification_credentials` and `--http_notification_url` on the Chronos server.
- option 2:  mail notification
  - uses these flags: `--mail_from`, `--mail_password`, `--mail_server`, `--mail_ssl`, `--mail_user`.

Questions for Kubernetes:
- Should we do this at all, or let the community build their own solutions?
- If we do build something, is it a one-size fits all solution that we own, or is there an example implementation, with ways for plugging in alternatives.
  - I think the answer is the latter, since alternative impls may have more features.   For example, Google Cloud Monitoring provides alerting via "via email, SMS, PagerDuty, HipChat and more". 
  - Similar to the way Google Cloud Logging can be used in place of elasticsearch logging? 
  - Setting up reasonable defaults here is the tricky part.
- Should we make email/http failure notification tightly coupled with ScheduledJob, like Chronos does, or create a generic mechanism for notifying about aribitrary events from controllers?  
  - I think the answer is generic, but care needs to be taken that the mechanism is not so flexible that configuring it is too hard.  Reasonable defaults are needed.
- Is it triggered off of events, or off of the conditions of Objects.
  - Events are nice because you don't have to discover new object types.
  - Conditions are considered a formal part of the API, while we have been fuzzy about events.

Possible implementations:
1. **nothing**: do nothing by default.  Assume users will use commercial (sysdig, Datadog, etc) solutions, and/or find examples on how to configure popular OSS to alert.
2. **De-novo**:  write a new go controller that has its own configuration object, and watches events (or conditions), and sends emails about matching events (or conditions).
   - drawback: users have to learn new monitoring configuration language
   - drawback: something else to support.
   - advantage: if we own the configuration language, we can set good defaults more easily when kube-up-ing?
3. **ELK**: shove some/all K8s events through ELK (elasticsearch/logstash/kibana) pipeline.  Include an alert line in the example logstash config to alert on ScheduledJob failures. 
   - advantage: builds on our existing ELK setup. and tell users to alert on ScheduledJob failures.
   - advantage: users of competing stacks will probably know how to mimic our example, as they will be used to mimic-ing ELK.
   - advantage: possibility of showing failure event in context with log output from the job that failed.
4. **HIG**: Write a go program that watches events or maybe directly watches objects, and exports the condition of objects, such as ScheduledJobs, as a time-series metric (e.g. failure-condition-count).   Have those stats be collected by the Heapster-InfluxDB-Grafana pipeline or a Prometheus pipeline, and users can write alerts on changes in the time-series metric.
   - disadvantage: prometheus supports email alerting, but we don't have a standard prometheus setup
   - disadvantage: HIG does not appear to support email alerting
   - disadvantage: not clear if time-series is the best representation for a "failure event".

I think I like 1 and 3.

title: Workqueue Jobs for long running processes in continuous deployment

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/support
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as a support question.

body:
Hi, we have been trying to implement a reliable continuous deployment on top of Kubernetes.  We originally looked in to replication controllers, but our services are streams that cannot be reconnected once started and the version of graceful termination for an rc is much less than what we need.

What we need is a way to keep an older service alive until the clients have disconnected from the stream, and then terminate the pod.  We assume that we will be able to steer new stream requests to newly deployed services.

Is it possible that workqueue based jobs could be utilized to bring up new service releases in this way?  Are there better patterns now or in the future planned?

I understand that when a workqueue job terminates successfully, all other pods must be ready to terminate as well.  Is there a way to modify the job to terminate unsuccessfully and not restart (and before the upgrade be set to restart on failure) or other solution to reduce the workqueue count to those only still serving clients?

We are interested in any solution that would automate in some form the draining of our stream servers.

Thanks!

body:
_Background_

Ginkgo skip and focus are not good at filtering tests at a high level, rather, they are built to focus on the tests' hierarchichal data model (Describe/By/It) themselves.

_Our goal_

We want to run upstream tests from a binary which 
- has both downstream and 
- also has upstream tests in it.

Wrap `It()` in the kube e2e framework as `KIt`, such that `KIt` automatically adds a Kubernetes specific annotation to every test.  We can even export the annotation as a public variable so downstream test runners can invoke upstream tests in a type safe way by adding the filter string programmatically in their wrappers to e2e.go.

title: can't delete a daemonset if an existing rc (with > 0 replicas) uses the same label for its pods

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Not sure if this will be considered a bug.
Suppose you create a RC with a given label selector for its pods (and > 0 replicas), then create a daemonset that uses the same label for its pods.

Then, if you try to delete that daemonset, the deletion will never terminate, since the termination process is waiting for the associated pods to shut down before it exits.  Things will just thrash back and forth-- the daemonset will shut down the pods and then the rc will re-create them...

(also, perhaps more obviously.. if the number of nodes in the cluster that the daemonset is mapping to, and the number of replicas in the rc are set to different values, they will thrash back and forth even prior to deletion :)

It seems like there ought to be some precedence ordering for these resources so that if they are playing chicken, one 'wins'.

body:
Esp. the Deployment controller.

When working on #21963 and #19299 we discovered a lot of suspect behavior in the expectation behavior.

Expectations are supposed to be used to await previous controller actions to be seen in watch.

However, there appear to be a number of issues:
- Can't distinguish unexpected events from controller actions. title: AWS: Fix cluster tag

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
We currently rely on a cluster tag called "KubernetesCluster".  This has two problems:
1. It doesn't follow the kubernetes.io namespacing pattern
2. It doesn't allow for something to be tagged with two clusters

While in general we have to be careful with something being owned/managed by two clusters (which is what the cluster tag implies), there are cases where it might be OK.  For example with a public subnet for your ELBs, when running k8s in private subnets.  That public subnet can be shared between clusters.

Instead of `KuberentesCluster=mycluster`, it could be `kubernetes.io/cluster:mycluster=1` or something like that.

Another alternative is to allow a comma-separated list of values.  We can't query this as efficiently though.

(Tag keys must be unique per resource)

Spawned from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/21497.

The implementation of the `BasicLongRunningRequestCheck` can be gamed by adding spurious query parameters. We can prevent this by doing a full request parse and interpreting the result to only allow things like watch, proxy, port-forward, and exec to be long running.  This is more expensive and more invasive than the change in the existing pull, but is probably more resilient to abuse.

title: Proposal to rework examples.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

body:
Today in @kubernetes/sig-testing we discussed the idea of improving the examples over time with a new policy, based on.
- a few, domain driven examples that are artfully curated by developers, i.e., less than 4.
- covering all features in the examples : rather than duplicating the core features using non idiomatic kube techniques.
- converting the existing examples which don't actually "tell a story" into a `blueprints/` directory which might be put into contrib.  
  - That way, if the mongodb community wants to curate their recipes upstream, they can easily do so, without us having to support then in the e2es.

I think this should be done slowly.  For now, I think its great for us to keep maintaining the examples/, as many people continue to use them.  We can work with the @kubernetes/sig-big-data @kubernetes/sig-api-machinery  and @kubernetes/sig-auth and other sigs to make sure the pedagogical elements are all addressed.

title: "Running Kubernetes locally via Docker" should address services opening ports on node's public IP

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

body:
The stated objective of [Running Kubernetes locally via Docker](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/getting-started-guides/docker.md) is to setup a **single node** Kubernetes cluster using Docker.

The instructions do produce a functioning installation on a single node via hyperKube.  

However, every service that is exposed for internal communication inside the single node is also made available on the node's public IP address (they are exposed because multi-node clusters would use those ports for load balancing) directly with no protection.   

In the case these instructions were followed on an internet facing server, kubernetes-master, skydns, cadvisor, and any database services could be attacked directly.  This makes for a very poor security posture.

Ideally, the instructions should mention a method of limiting the node's public ports to those used to administer the machine (i.e. ssh) + those allowed by the Kubernetes Ingress rules (i.e. a Ingress/LB controller on a designated port like http/80 or https/443).

At the very least, there should be a big fat warning on this document advising people not to use it on a server not behind a firewall for the reason outlined above.

title: We should sanitize mountPath

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

milestone.title: v1.2
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/wiki/Release-1.2

body:
A user made an error setting their mountPath - they set a docker-style mountpath `mountPath: /data/ldap/db:/var/lib/ldap`

However, the error that they got (and inspection of the code) indicates that we just passed that straight through to docker (`API error (500): invalid mode for volumes-from: /var/lib/ldap`).  Docker treats the 3rd argument as a mode flag.

We should sanitize the input, both to help users when they make mistakes, but also because if Docker allowed other options in its mounts this could become a security issue.

title: The servicecontroller loop is racy

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
In pkg/controller/service/servicecontroller.go, we start 10 goroutines that process service events: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/service/servicecontroller.go#L139-L141

Each of these workers then locks on a per-service mutex when processing events: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/service/servicecontroller.go#L225-L228

But I believe there is no guarantee that the order of lock acquisition is the same as the order of events.  Thus I think we might process events out of order when services change rapidly.

An alternative design might be to have a per-service goroutine with a per-service event queue.  This would mean that service events would be guaranteed to be processed in order.  It would also make caching of the previous state much simpler.  Finally, when we hit an error like a failure to create a LoadBalancer, we could simply sleep without risking exhausting our "thread pool".

body:
It would be very use for kubectl to be able to export all api objects in a namespace from a running cluster to JSON/YAML files, and import that state from files  to another cluster.

This fuctionality can currently be hacked out of kubectl for specific use cases by transforming the output of `kubectl get -o=json all`, switching contexts, and feeding the fixed-up JSON back into `kubectl create`. Your json transformer have to do things like discard the status sub-objects and the service-token secrets. Ideally kubectl would do this for you.

I'm envisioning something like this:

``` sh
#export
kubectl config use-context clusterA
kubectl --namespace=my_application export -o=json > my_application.clusterA.json

#import
kubectl config use-context clusterB
kubectl import < my_application.clusterA.json
```

title: Proposal: Required node selector labels for pod creation

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
## Problem statement

Sometimes you want to partition your nodes into different pools, because they have different properties. For example, they may have different networking setups, different hardware, or may be owned by different sub-divisions inside an organization. It's common to delineate these features with node labels. And it's common for an organization to have some policies regarding what kind of pods can be scheduled on which pools.

Right now there's no way for a cluster admin to enforce this kind of policies, for two reasons:
1.  If a pod creation request doesn't specify any NodeSelector, the scheduler will happily schedule the pod on any node.
2.  Even if the pod creation specifies NodeSelector to select a pool, there is no way to enforce policies regarding who can use which pool

This proposal aims to solve problem 1, with the assumption that problem 2 can be solved with a more beefed up ABAC solution than the current one.
## Proposed solution

We propose a new admission controller, RequiredNodeSelector. When using this admission controller, the cluster admin will provide a config file, specifying the list of required node selector labels, possibly with default values. It could be something like:

```
requiredNodeSelectorLabels:
  - name: pool
    default: default
  - name: arch  # no default means must explicitly specify
```

The RequiredNodeSelector admission controller will, for each label in `requiredNodeSelectorLabels`, check whether it's present in pod.Spec.NodeSelector.
- if present, the request is left alone
- if not, does the required label has a default?
  - if yes, add `$name=$default` to pod.Spec.NodeSelector
  - if not, deny the request

title: Client library should support update retries

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
By taking a function to check preconditions and apply changes. Every client doing Update needs to do this to deal with conflicts, timeouts, etc.

```
func updateRSWithRetries(rsClient unversionedextensions.ReplicaSetInterface, rs *extensions.ReplicaSet, applyUpdate updateFunc) (*extensions.ReplicaSet, error) {
 +  var err error
 +  oldRs := rs
 +  err = wait.Poll(10*time.Millisecond, 1*time.Minute, func() (bool, error) {
 +      // Apply the update, then attempt to push it to the apiserver.
 +      applyUpdate(rs)
 +      if rs, err = rsClient.Update(rs); err == nil {
 +          // rs contains the latest controller post update
 +          return true, nil
 +      }
 +      // Update the controller with the latest resource version, if the update failed we
 +      // can't trust rs so use oldRs.Name.
 +      if rs, err = rsClient.Get(oldRs.Name); err != nil {
 +          // The Get failed: Value in rs cannot be trusted.
 +          rs = oldRs
 +      }
 +      // The Get passed: rs contains the latest controller, expect a poll for the update.
 +      return false, nil
 +  })
 +  // If the error is non-nil the returned controller cannot be trusted, if it is nil, the returned
 +  // controller contains the applied update.
 +  return rs, err
 +}
```

title: Kubelet does not notice pod has completed

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
## Problem

Pod that should run quickly to completion almost always does, but at least one time, it did not, causing a test flake (#21169). 
## Symptoms

We see pod get to the point of pulling its image, according to events on apiserver, but we don't ever see "Created" or "Started" events, until test times out after 15 minutes.  Kubelet logs show ContainerStarted even according to PLEG, and shows volumes being cleaned for the pod again and again.  
## Logs

I've attached a kubelet log from an e2e test: [bad-kubelet.txt](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/133194/bad-kubelet.txt)

The pod of interest is called `fail-once-local-r6hqn` in namespace `e2e-tests-job-r1z3y`.

I've also attached a version of that log that just includes lines from the pod I am interested in (lines matching its pod name, uid, or docker container id):
[bad-kubelet-filtered.txt](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/133210/bad-kubelet-filtered.txt)
## Discussion

A similar pattern occured 3 times on a single node in a single e2e run, and not at all on the other nodes.  See #21169.  So, it might be a bad node or bad docker.  However, other many other containers ran successfully during the e2e test time frame.

The pod's command line is `if [[ -r /data/foo ]] ; then exit 0 ; else touch /data/foo ; exit 1 ; fi`.  This command will exit quickly, and so there could be a race where docker or kubelet doesn't notice that the container exited because it exited so fast.  However, this has to be a rare race because the test passes many times.

The pod gets as far as the `ContainerStarted` state according to PLEG.

```
I0212 15:08:11.894177    3890 kubelet.go:2324] SyncLoop (PLEG): "fail-once-local-r6hqn_e2e-tests-job-r1z3y(6e23f2c1-d19a-11e5-8e8a-42010af00002)", event: &pleg.PodLifecycleEvent{ID:"6e23f2c1-d19a-11e5-8e8a-42010af00002", Type:"ContainerStarted", Data:"5032a5cb8b882e6eb82ce7d8abba525c4bc9ce53c47dc342567de0d0b3712834"}
```

But there are no "Created" or "Started" events on the APIserver for the pod.   That seems odd.

After the `ContainerStarted` event from PLEG, the kubelet logs show kubelet considering unmountin the Pod's volumes every few second for the next 15 minutes, like this:

```
I0212 15:08:12.648445    3890 volumes.go:234] Making a volume.Cleaner for volume kubernetes.io~empty-dir/data of pod 6e23f2c1-d19a-11e5-8e8a-42010af00002
I0212 15:08:12.648493    3890 volumes.go:316] Used volume plugin "kubernetes.io/empty-dir" to unmount 6e23f2c1-d19a-11e5-8e8a-42010af00002/kubernetes.io~empty-dir
I0212 15:08:12.648525    3890 volumes.go:234] Making a volume.Cleaner for volume kubernetes.io~secret/default-token-kp0b0 of pod 6e23f2c1-d19a-11e5-8e8a-42010af00002
I0212 15:08:12.648561    3890 volumes.go:316] Used volume plugin "kubernetes.io/secret" to unmount 6e23f2c1-d19a-11e5-8e8a-42010af00002/kubernetes.io~secret
```

These log lines appear to be coming from getPodVolumesFromDisk.  I think these lines just mean that the Pod's volumes are still on disk and that they are still in use by a container.

title: Propagate "no container" error from attach/exec/logs up cleanly to the API server level

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Today, it's very hard to do proper error handling in the `attach`, `exec`, `logs`, and `run` commands for short running commands (those that run, print output, and then exit rapidly).  That is mostly due today to the Kubelet not returning structured, known errors back to the apiserver in these scenarios in a way that the caller can react to the pod terminating / restarting before the attach call completes.

We started stitching in the `logs` flag to allow attach to fetch logs instead of opening stdout - but we need to normalize and manage that from the attach client so that it's clear that the operation will succeed.

The end result today with these races is errors like:

```
F0215 16:46:02.580615   83601 helpers.go:104] error: error executing remote command: Error executing command in container: container not found ("mysql")
```

which aren't very useful to end users.
