title: Investigate how many time ReplicationManager/ReplicaSetController must wait before they start to work

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

body:
If ControllerManager restart, ReplicationManager/ReplicaSetController/DeploymentController could not start to work until the PodStore/RCStore has been synced, otherwise, they will make incorrect decision when sync ReplicationController/ReplicaSet/Deployment. 

Client of ControllerManager first list all Pods and put them into a `DeltaFIFO`, a Process route then pop the Pod one by one from the `DeltaFIFO` and put into `PodStore`, and call `ResourceEventHandlerFuncs`. For ReplicationManager/ReplicaSetController, `ResourceEventHandlerFuncs` need list all the RCs/RSs in RCStore/RSStore to find the RC/RS which control the Pod, and put it into workqueue. ReplicationManager/ReplicaSetController can not start work until the first batch of Pods inserted by the first list has been synced to PodStore.

When cluster size is large, ReplicationManager/ReplicaSetController may must wait a long time, since `ResourceEventHandlerFuncs` of ReplicationManager/ReplicaSetController is time-consuming(list all the RCs/RSs in RCStore/RSStore to find the corresponding RC/RS which control the Pod).

We need investigate how many time ReplicationManager/ReplicaSetController must wait before they start to work. If it take a long time to wait PodStore synced, we should optimize `ResourceEventHandlerFuncs`(`getPodController()`/`getPodReplicaSet()`) of ReplicationManager/ReplicaSetController. Speed up `getPodController()`/`getPodReplicaSet()` is also very helpful when relist occurs from the perspective of user experience(otherwise, a new created RC/RS may wait a long time when relist occurs).

title: Error out if a kubeconfig's current-context doesn't exist

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
In 1.1, if you specify "current-context: i-do-not-exist" in a kubeconfig, and there's no matching context by that name in the contexts, kubelet silently uses what I assume is either an empty or a default configuration.

This can result in hilarity like wondering why your kubelet isn't using the TLS settings you provided, and spending several hours debugging the whole stack only to discover that you typo'd current-context :).

It would be better if kubelet and other users of kubeconfig.yaml errored out on such a misconfiguration, to make the failure obvious and trivial.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/examples/mysql-wordpress-pd

The example doesn't follow best practices: #11361.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/user-guide/config-best-practices.md

Some of these practices are newer than the example, and it needs to be updated. For instance, it shouldn't use `name` as a label key.

More significantly, now that we have [persistent volume provisioning](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/examples/experimental/persistent-volume-provisioning), we should make it provider-independent. Perhaps we could put a GCE-specific PD example in the GCE getting-started guide.

The biggest problem with the example is that it creates a naked Pod, which isn't self-healing.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/user-guide/config-best-practices.md#naked-pods-vs-replication-controllers-and-jobs
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/user-guide/pods.md#durability-of-pods-or-lack-thereof

If we want to start with a pod for explanatory purposes, we need to follow up with an explanation of why that's not sufficient, and show the recommended solution. In 1.2, that will be to use a single-replica Deployment. In 1.3, it will probably be PetSet.

title: Conversion generation and registration order is not stable

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
The order that conversion functions are added to the scheme depends on the package initialization order in Go.  The name of a conversion function is used in other generated functions (for performance), but because the order of packages is not guaranteed stable any change in build order can result in conversions being generated in different orders.

The reason we have duplicate conversions is extensions/v1beta1 and v1 for Pods (of which most of the sub objects are identical).  We need to ensure that there is a predictable order for the public conversion name - because conversions overwrite each other in the scheme, the generator doesn't have access to all conversions, only the most recent.

title: Scale Deployments Proportionally

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Filed an issue to represent work started here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/20273
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/20696

The proposal was to scale the underlying RCs with non-zero replicas proportionally in order to mitigate risk. 

Otherwise, scaling up currently increases the size of the newRC and scaling down could decrease the sizes of the old ones, both of which would have the effect of hastening the rollout progress, which could produce a higher proportion of unavailable replicas in the event of a problem with the rolled out template.

cc @kargakis @janetkuo @mqliang @ironcladlou

body:
While working with a customer issue, customer had a 1.0.6 `kubectl` talking to a 1.1 cluster and sent it the equivalent of the following `ReplicationController` (note the `downwardAPI` volume):

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  name: api-sandbox
  labels:
    env: sandbox
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    name: api-sandbox
    env: sandbox
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        name: api-sandbox
        env: sandbox
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api-sandbox
          image: nginx:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: podinfo
              mountPath: /etc/podinfo

      volumes:
        - name: podinfo

            items:

title: ETCD becomes the bottleneck of cluster when we have 1K+ nodes

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

body:
ETCD becomes the bottleneck of cluster when we have 1K+ nodes. 

After close scrutiny, it's the 1K+ nodes frequently send PUT request to ETCD to update it's status(every 10s using default configure), which give ETCD  a big burden.

May I suggest, instead: 
**_Let NodeController initiatively do the health check. Thus we could significantly reduce the number of request sent to ETCD.**_

IIRC, in kubernetes v0.12, we make NodeController initiatively do the health check [DoChecks](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-0.12/pkg/cloudprovider/controller/nodecontroller.go#L344), but after v1.0, we make kubelet update it's status. Is there good reason for this change?@gmarek @fgrzadkowski 

By the way, I think may be it's time to think about make ETCD extensible.

We should either

body:
Hi,
I've deployed and tested `docker-multinode` a few times now. It worked, with a few issues
- `/dev/pts/ptmx` permissions is set with wrong permissions #18230
- A turndown script is missing, so one have to clean up by hand. Partially related: #19179
- If one runs e.g. `master.md` a few times, many `DOCKER_OPTS`-lines are created in `/etc/default/docker`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/19212#issuecomment-177497396

When I rebooted the computer though, the CPU usage was 100% on two of four cores.
It turned out five kubelets and kube-proxies had restarted, although I think I had `docker rm -f` them.
Two of them were zombies, one was running and I don't really know what the two other were doing.

I could kill three of them with `docker rm -f`, but then I had to reboot, `docker rm -f` one of them, reboot and finally kill the last one.
I had to reboot because the parent PIDs of hyperkube is 1 and of course I don't want to kill the whole system.

So I would say we should replace `--restart=always` with `--restart=on-failure`, because it's extremely annoying to not be able to `docker kill` those containers. Now and then they start when you least expect it.

And `on-failure` should do it's job.
I can make a PR for this.

title: Shortening long api group names when typing into kubectl.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

body:
# Problem

Need short way to type long resource type names.  Need to handle not only long Kind name (e.g. `replicationController`, but also the length of new API group names (e.g. `batch` which is proposed in #20120), and third-party resource types (e.g. `networkstartup.io/firewall`).
# TL;DR

We want user-defined short resource names — like `po` for `pods`, but user defined.
They go into a kubectl preferences file.  Until we have that feature, we will keep defining short names for our own types, as needed, once they graduate to v1 and out of extensions.
# Option 1: Matching

Allow user to type only the part of the type name after the slash.  For example, assuming `networkstartup.io/firewall` is an API group/kind, then you could type `kubectl get firewalls`.

In case of multiple matches,  there are two ways to resolve: a defined _sort order_ among api groups (suggested by lavalamp on #20120), or _error on multiple matches_.

Examples of a multiple matches are built-in `pod` vs `metrics.pod` (actual) and  `persistentVolumes` and `storagestartup.io/persistentVolume` (hypothetical).

This would extend the approach currently used by kubectl.  When you run `kubectl get jobs`, `kubectl` uses `RESTMapper.VersionAndKindForResource` to map the string `jobs` to  `(group: extensions/v1beta, kind:`Jobs`).  This approach is documented in [docs/proposals/api-group.md](docs/proposals/api-group.md).
# Option 2: Extensible Short Names

`kubectl` already maps `rc` to `replicationController`.  

We can keep hard-coding new mappings into kubectl for api groups that the project owns.
But, to support third-party resources, we need a way for others to add new short names.
# Comparison of 2 options

If we do _matching_, we may later want  _extensible short names_.  For example: `scheduledJob` is shorter than `jobs/scheduledJob`, but `sj` is even better.  But, if we do  _extensible short names_, do we really need  _matching_?

Extending `RESTMapper.VersionAndKindForResource` to include used-defined mappings exposes the user to reasoning about versions.  Also, that code is complex, and may not benefit from growing new responsibilities.

**Tenative Recommendation**: Implement _extensible short names_ for the third party use case with the mapping stored in a user preference file.

I'm not super confident in the recommendation because I don't understand `RESTMapper` well.
# Implementation of extensible short names

Mappings for project-owned resources can continue to be compiled in kubectl.

We will add a `.kube/preferences` file.  This will include a map from shortname to full type name.
Issue #1755 talks about storing prefs in a separate file from `.kube/config`.

The latter should take precedence.  That way, the core project can use new names without breaking user's third-party use cases.

Two third-parties might both want to use the same suffix (e.g. `faststorage.io/persistentVolume` and `cheapstorage.com/persistentVolume`).  K8s project should not be in the business of picking winners.  
Therefore, kubernetes project should not produce hard-coded aliases for third-party types.  This line may be a bit fuzzy.

Short-name mappings are separate from a more general user-defined aliases mechanism.  Issue #18023 talks about user-defined aliases.  It will presumably be like [git aliases](https://git.wiki.kernel.org/index.php/Aliases).  This is not a good choice because in order to map the short name `ba` to resource name `foo/bar`, you have to write several alias rules, e.g.:

```
# file: $HOME/.kube/preferences 
[alias]
        get ba = get foo/bar $*
        describe ba = describe foo/bar $*
        delete ba = delete foo/bar $*
        # ... and so on for all verbs
```

Therefore, we will need shortnames in addition to command aliases.

Scripts that use short names will not be portable.  This is okay.  There several `kubectl` command patterns that need to be avoided in portable scripts.  We will document these -- @bgrant0607 has a list of these rules somewhere.

With that said, expressing the short mappings as a user-defined preference makes it more clear to the user that a script is not portable to other users.   For example, you would not write a script that used your own git command aliases and expect it to work for another user.

title: kube-addon-update fails badly if api server is unavailable

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
`kube-addon-update.sh` does not check the status of the `get-addon-nsnames-from-server` call to fetch the list of installed addons.

if apiserver is unavailable (or if the request times out) this causes it to think the error message is the list of services and enter a loop of trying to remove imaginary services and re-create existing ones. 

i assume all of these just error out quickly but the retry policy means it ends up running all 60 retries x num addons which on a limited spec (eg the default aws t2.micro configuration) can amplify the original failure and help brick the master node (see #18975)

the simple fix to check status and abort (https://github.com/petermd/kubernetes/commit/4d4f1c645cbb75c444f7e33463b871c21da7890b) is enough to stop the problem, and any missing addons will be updated on the next iteration.

it _might_ be worth considering making the retry policy back off and/or not use the entire check interval as the retry period (otherwise you could potentially have multiple instances running trying to update the same service)

body:
kube-addons today identifies RC specs by only matching the prefix assuming that suffix will always be a version number ex:monitoring-grafana-v1. Ideally we should just check if the entire string matches both in server and on file and delete/create RCs as and when needed.

By placing two RC specs monitoring-grafana and monitoring-influxdb as a cluster addon, what happens is that monitoring-influxdb keeps getting deleted as the addons update script assumes that a newer version is available for update. This causes influxdb RC to be deleted and recreated periodically whenever the addon update script is triggered. Should we have mandate for version number to be present always in RC? We dont have that check in place for Service specs. Doing full string match should cover the use cases of: 
1) newer version of the RC being available if a version suffix is present.
2) delete RCs for whom the spec is no longer available
3) create RC for a newly available spec.

Also, for the rolling upgrade of RC specs, would it make sense if the versions can be pulled from something like labels within the RC spec instead of going for file names?

title: single-node restart: setup-files.sh generates new cert, breaking containers with "the old" ca.crt files

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Hello,

This might be rather unimportant, especially if single-node deployments are not meant to be durable at all, but I think fixing it is easy, and it'd help with developing things for/on a local node. (Especially with a containerized hyperkube, which is very easy to "turn up".)

If my assessment is correct, the problem is that killing all docker containers and then restarting the kubelet container basically results in a re-run of `master.json`, which means starting docker containers for k8s-master. And generating new certs. Which is a race condition. Usually the apiserver picks up the old cert, but then pods that should be running are started and they get the new cert.

Or if there are pods in /var/lib/kubelet kubelet starts them too (though my understanding of these parts of k8s is rather fuzzy), and they get their already existing ca.crt, but then new pods get a new one.

It seems simple enough to check if there are already files (token CSV and certs) in /data, and skip generating them if they are there.

Thanks for considering!

title: Explore ability to improve namespace deletion performance

labels.name: priority/backlog

labels.name: sig/scalability

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
The `Namespace` deletion process is complex and requires orchestration.
- `DELETE` `Namespace` marks it as `Terminating`
- controller observes `Terminating` `Namespace`
  - for each `Kind`
  - LIST `Kind`
  - DELETE `Kind` item by item

For `Event` objects we added support for `DELETE_COLLECTION`.  This operation does not reduce the number of operations to `etcd`, but it can reduce the number of requests to `kube-api-server`.

A few options to pursue:
- add `DELETE_COLLECTION` support for other `KIND`s (must do)
- explore keeping track of set of known `KIND` resources in a `Namespace`.  The list could grow during admission of new resources into the `Namespace`.  Orchestration of deletion could reference that information to know what `KIND`s are candidates to delete.
  - an annotation is not appropriate to hold this information since it is too easily editable and could cause the controller to leak data by never cleaning it up.
  - in practice, this is most likely an over-optimization that would only benefit our `e2e` setups, but noting it here.

title: Question about network resource management (especially for switch buffer)

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

body:
Hi Kubernetes people,

I have a question about the network management functionality of Kubernetes. Is there a plan for managing buffers of switches from Kubernetes?

Currently, a switch buffer doesn't have a mechanism for isolation that can be used from distributed systems easily. Therefore problems like [microburst](https://www.arista.com/assets/data/pdf/7148sx-ixnetwork-microburst.pdf) can happen. The problem can increase latency so it is critical for user facing interactive systems.

Although there are [some solutions for solving the problem](http://simula.stanford.edu/~alizade/Site/DCTCP.html), they don't seem to be widely used yet. Straightforward solution would be careful capacity planning that tends to produce a situation of over provisioning. In addition, it requires difficult engineering tasks (e.g. voluntary scheduling by applications and operators).

I think Kubernetes is a suitable component for controlling the buffer. If it is possible to add a new resource type of the buffer [like other network resources](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/design/resources.md#future-network-bandwidth), the management of switch buffer would be easier for application developers and operators. Fortunately, recent white box switches provides their SDKs for managing buffers. Connecting Kubernetes and these SDKs would be possible.

I'm very new to Kubernetes. I'm happy if I can hear your opinions.

title: Admission controller to restrict hard ("requiredDuringScheduling") anti-affinity to "node" TopologyKey

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
As discussed in the (anti-)affinity issue (#18265), "hard' anti-affinity is dangerous especially at large topology scopes, until we have some mechanism like priority/preemption. It could be used maliciously or by accident to block scheduling in an entire cluster, for example. The primary use case for hard anti-affinity is at the node level (give a pod exclusive access to a machine); we don't anticipate that larger topology scopes are urgently needed. So before deploying anti-affinity, we should build an admission controller that is enabled by default that prohibits anti-affinity with a TopologyKey other than "node."

title: should introduce a knob to enable quorum read of etcd for HA

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Copied from #19816 
@mqliang  said

> One problem is that we may need enable quorum read when apiserver send read request to etcd, otherwise ControllerManager/Scheduler/Kubelet may get old data.
> 
> we found that ControllerManager/Scheduler/Kubelet may get old data since apiserver doesn't quorum read etcd. To solve this problem we add an option to api-server to enable quorum read, but it make read less effective.
> 
> I am not sure such a solution is fine to community. I am glad to upstream this to community if it looks good.
> 
> There are two cases where we may read old data if we have multi api-server:
> 
> 1) When a etcd member is isolated from etcd cluster, we can still read from it(but all the write request sent to the isolated member will failed). If unfortunately nginx forward some read request to the isolated member, those read request will get old data.
> 
> 2) Consider the following case:
> 
> A write request(e.g. ?key=hello&value=world) was forward to apiserver-1 and then forward to etcd-1, etcd-1 will return 200 indicating the write request was succeeded if the data has been written to a majority of members.(for example, written to etcd-1 and etcd-2)
> Almost immediately, a read request(?key=hello) was forward to etcd-3, if api-server doesn't enable quorum read, this read request will failed(key not found) since the data has not been synced to etcd-3.

title: Don't allow updates of Node.PodCIDR except from "" to valid.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
As we move closer to using a net plugin for the default network, this came up.  Is Node.PodCIDR actually mutable?  What do we expect to happen if it changes for a Node which has running containers?

Options: 
a) allow updates and kill running containers (heavy)
b) allow updates but ignore them as long as any containers are running (inconsistent)
c) allow updates but ignore them except at reboot (inconsistent)
d) only allow updates from "" to valid CIDR (presumably by node controller)
e) don't allow updates (breaks nodecontroller)
f) only allow updates by a sub-resource, and choose one of a-d

Of all of these, I think (d) is the only sane and halfway reasonable option right now.  Longer term, we need to reconsider the role of this field in a more pluggable world.

title: kubectl apply should be able to delete objects missing from supplied config (aka prune)

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
The declarative configuration workflow described in #1702 implies that you can give kubectl apply a set of objects and all changes will be applied. One change that is trickier is to declaratively apply is the deletion of an object when a spec is missing. After all, how does kubectl apply know which objects to delete were previously created by kubectl apply and therefore should be deleted vs created by the system (e.g. pods from a replication controller) or other unrelated users?

The answer is the kubectl apply annotation itself. We should add a flag (`--prune`?) to kubectl apply which deletes all objects that (1) aren't in the list given to kubectl apply and (2) do have a kubectl apply annotation at `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration`.

Note that currently it's hard to give kubectl apply many objects at once but once #19767 and/or #19639 are finished it will be much easier.

cc @kubernetes/sig-config

body:
Our `kubectl get rc` output is extremely wide:

```
$ kubectl get rc
CONTROLLER                CONTAINER(S)                           IMAGE(S)                                                                                               SELECTOR                                                                                                                   REPLICAS   AGE
convert-mon-rc-dev        convert-mon                            docker-registry.dev.internal.box/sam/convert-mon:0.0.0-21.2015_12_31_22_37_37.56e95-image-16           box.com/app-id=convert-mon,box.com/env=dev,box.com/version=2015-12-13                                                      1          16d
convert-mon-rc-live       convert-mon                            docker-registry.dev.internal.box/sam/convert-mon:0.0.0-21.2015_12_31_22_37_37.56e95-image-16           box.com/app-id=convert-mon,box.com/env=live,box.com/version=2015-12-13                                                     1          16d

...
```

(Note the columns are wider than the text because I've omitted rows that have longer text in them.)

I would contend that when you are typically trying to list RC's, you're mostly looking for (1) which ones exist, (2) how many replicas they have and perhaps (3) the selector. Usually the name is enough to remind you what's inside of it, but if you want all the details of what specific containers and images it has you can do `kubectl describe rc <x>` or `kubectl describe pod <x>`. As such I suggest moving CONTAINER(S) and IMAGE(S) columns into -o wide only.

title: kubectl should process files recursively when given a directory

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
When given a directory, `kubectl apply -f <directory>` should search a directory recursively for any JSON|YAML files when given a directory. Currently it only finds the immediate children of the given directory.

I believe kubectl apply is exhibiting the same behavior as `kubectl create`, `kubectl delete`, etc., but to enable the original #1702 use case of a nested directory of configuration objects being reconciled with the server's state, kubectl apply especially should act recursively.

Current behavior:

```
$ ls pod/
pod2.yaml  pod.yaml
$ kubectl apply -f pod
pod "nginx-1" configured
pod "nginx-2" configured
$ cd pod
$ mkdir subpod
$ ls
pod2.yaml  pod.yaml  subpod
$ mv * subpod/
$ ls
subpod
$ cd ..
$ kubectl apply -f pod  # everything is now in pod/subpod/*.yaml
error: you must provide one or more resources by argument or filename (.json|.yaml|.yml|stdin)
$
```

Expected behavior:

```
$ kubectl apply -f pod  # everything is now in pod/subpod/*.yaml
pod "nginx-1" configured
pod "nginx-2" configured
$
```

title: Proposal: Allow easy secret manipulation from string data

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

body:
Secrets today have schema `Data map[string][]byte json:"data,omit empty"`.  The end result is a base64 string in JSON, which is hard to work with as a normal client on the cli.  It should be possible to pass string values for the data that are transformed into `[]byte`.  Since v2 is far away, this should be backwards compatible.
### Proposal

Add a new `StringData map[string]string` with json identifier `stringData` that is read during create and update and merged into `data`.  This is backwards compatible (new clients can send both fields and stringData takes precedence).  Clients always read `data`. `stringData` is not stored in etcd.
### Alternatives:
1. Add a second new map that is not merged - not backwards compatible
2. Add a subresource that takes data as strings - not easily sent via kubectl
3. Add a new top level resource `SecretMap` that is backed by `Secret` and has `data map[string]string`, but operations on `SecretMap`.  Not easily used (requires new client work), also has potential for confusion, and in the long run we need both binary and text data for secrets anyway.
   a. Variant 1 - add a new SecretMap that has both fields, or a deeper struct, and convince everyone to change away from secret.  SecretMap would be backed in etcd by Secret resources.  Problem: unable to have fields that are binary and fields that are string.

title: Kubernetes, Docker Machine and exposing the API and other services.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
Hi all,

I've been following these instructions to set up a local development environment that mimics a production environment: http://kubernetes.io/v1.1/docs/getting-started-guides/docker.html

I start by creating a docker machine using:

``` bash
docker-machine create --driver virtualbox kubetest
```

Get the host info:

``` bash
eval "$(docker-machine env kubetest)"
```

I am able to run containers directly by using my local docker client.

Now, I then try this:

``` bash
DOCKER_MACHINE_NAME=kubetest

docker stop $(docker ps -a -q) # Stop all running containers
docker rm $(docker ps -a -q) # remove all containers

# Run the following containers based on the instructions at 
# http://kubernetes.io/v1.1/docs/getting-started-guides/docker.html
docker run -d \
  --net=host \
  gcr.io/google_containers/etcd:2.0.12 \
    /usr/local/bin/etcd \
    --addr=127.0.0.1:4001 \
    --bind-addr=0.0.0.0:4001 \
    --data-dir=/var/etcd/data

docker run -d \
    --volume=/:/rootfs:ro \
    --volume=/sys:/sys:ro \
    --volume=/dev:/dev \
    --volume=/var/lib/docker/:/var/lib/docker:ro \
    --volume=/var/lib/kubelet/:/var/lib/kubelet:rw \
    --volume=/var/run:/var/run:rw \
    --net=host \
    --pid=host \
    --privileged=true \
    gcr.io/google_containers/hyperkube:v1.0.1 \
      /hyperkube kubelet \
      --containerized \
      --hostname-override="127.0.0.1" \
      --address="0.0.0.0" \
      --api-servers=http://localhost:8080 \
      --config=/etc/kubernetes/manifests

docker run -d \
  --net=host \
  --privileged \
  gcr.io/google_containers/hyperkube:v1.0.1 \
    /hyperkube proxy \
    --master=http://127.0.0.1:8080 \
    --v=2


docker-machine ssh $DOCKER_MACHINE_NAME -f -N -L "8080:localhost:8080"

until $(kubectl -s http://localhost:8080 cluster-info &> /dev/null); do
    sleep 1
done
```

After a few seconds I do see it running when I try this:

``` bash
kubectl -s http://localhost:8080 cluster-info
Kubernetes master is running at http://localhost:8080
```

Or this...

``` bash
kubectl -s http://localhost:8080 get nodes
NAME        LABELS                             STATUS    AGE
127.0.0.1   kubernetes.io/hostname=127.0.0.1   Ready     26m
```

I then run these to test that I can get a service working:

``` bash
kubectl -s http://localhost:8080 run nginx --image=nginx --port=80
kubectl -s http://localhost:8080 expose rc nginx --port=80
```

And then see it worked...

``` bash
kubectl -s http://localhost:8080 get svc nginx
NAME      CLUSTER_IP   EXTERNAL_IP   PORT(S)   SELECTOR    AGE
nginx     10.0.0.3     <none>        80/TCP    run=nginx   9m
```

Now, the whole thing being inside a docker-machine means I should be able to access things through the IP reported by `docker-machine ip kubetest` but when I try to curl that ip, I get:

``` bash
curl: (7) Failed to connect to 192.168.99.100 port 80: Connection refused
```

I get the same if I try localhost and 127.0.0.1 and other's I've tried.
### Questions
1. How do I expose the API service through the docker-machine's IP? I thought this would have worked with the steps that I am following.
2. Is there an environment variable I can set so i don't have to set the `-s` flag to every kubectl command I run? Ie: `kubectl -s http://localhost:8080 cluster-info`
3. When I run a service like nginx above, do I need to configure the external IP somehow? I've done that before using service configuration files on GKE but I'm not sure how to do it here and particularly when I'm not using service configuration files (.yml)?

Thank you so much for any help.

title: HA Kubernetes etcd configuration

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/multicluster
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Multicluster.

body:
I'm looking at setting up k8s with a HA master, and following along with the HA documentation at http://kubernetes.io/v1.1/docs/admin/high-availability.html

The k8s HA doc suggests using a discovery token.  However, the etcd documentation at https://github.com/coreos/etcd/blob/master/Documentation/clustering.md says:

> Moreover, discovery URLs should ONLY be used for the initial bootstrapping of a cluster. To change cluster membership after the cluster is already running, see the runtime reconfiguration guide.

I was thinking of running the masters in an AWS auto-scaling group, but this means that their IP addresses would change (I have some strategies involving grabbing disks to ensure that they have some notion of persistent identity though).

An alternative idea I had was to use static config, but to have a process that queried the cloud API, and located the instances, and then dynamically updated a hosts file with the IP addresses.  So for example etcd would be launched with

```
etcd -name node1 -initial-advertise-peer-urls http://10.0.1.10:2380 \
  -listen-peer-urls http://10.0.1.10:2380 \
  -listen-client-urls http://10.0.1.10:2379 \
  -advertise-client-urls http://10.0.1.10:2379 \
  -initial-cluster-token etcd-cluster-1 \
  -initial-cluster node1=http://node1:2380,node2=http://node2:2380,node3=http://node3:2380 \
  -initial-cluster-state new
```

And then the hosts file would look like

```
10.0.1.10 node1 
10.0.1.11 node2
# node3 not yet running
```

(I guess I could also use skydns rather than hosts files, but I am not sure about the bootstrapping there.  Or even Route53...)

Will discovery actually work and 'self-heal' as IP addresses change?  Is there a better alternative to dynamically updating DNS / host files?  @xiang90 I think you would know best here.

Also cc @quinton-hoole because I think you'll find this interesting...

title: Better script to bring up Kubernete cluster

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
If we run the `get-kube.sh` script using the following command and if this if the first time you run this script, then the create_cluster function will fail because the `kubernete` directory does not exist: 

``` Shell
$ export KUBERNETES_PROVIDER=aws; export KUBERNETES_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=yes; curl -sS https://get.k8s.io | bash 
```

If you look at the script to bring up Kubernete cluster (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cluster/get-kube.sh)

``` Shell
# Original
if [[ "${KUBERNETES_SKIP_DOWNLOAD-}" ]]; then
  create_cluster
  exit 0
fi
```

I propose the following

``` Shell
directory=kubernetes

if [[ "${KUBERNETES_SKIP_DOWNLOAD-}" ]]; then
  if [ -d "${directory}" ]; then
    create_cluster
    exit 0
  else
    echo "The directory ${directory} is not in current directory. Bailing out. "
    exit 5
  fi
fi
```

During the initial downward API implementation for environment vars, we decided to punt on exposing specific annotations/labels in environment variables because it would require container restart if those values changed, and we wanted to be able to change annotations/labels without restarting containers.  During an F2F meeting today, we decided to just implement this with the caveat that env vars are not updated, period.
This issue is to do that implementation.

Proposed syntax:

``` yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: dapi-test-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: test-container
      image: gcr.io/google_containers/busybox
      command: [ "/bin/sh", "-c", "env" ]
      env:
        - name: SOME_ANNOTATION
          valueFrom:
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: metadata.annotations[k8s.io/some-annotation]
        - name: SOME_LABEL
          valueFrom:
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: metadata.labels[some-label]
  restartPolicy: Never
```

title: Convert Go field and type names in autogenerated API docs

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
We autogenerate user-facing API documentation from types.go comments now. Most people tend to refer to Go field and type names in their comments as per typical godoc style. However, this isn't appropriate for user docs. I generally tell people to use the json field names instead of Go field names and English instead of type names, but it's been an uphill battle to enforce.

When generating documentation in WriteSwaggerDocFunc, we should try to automatically convert Go field and type names in the comments to json field names and English rather than type names. ParseDocumentationFrom keeps the json field names but discards the Go field names. In general, they should be the same except for capitalization of the first letter, but we could also just keep both in KubeTypes, and replace all occurrences of the Go field name with the json field name in the Doc string. For the type names, we could replace all occurrences of the Go type name with the type name split into separate words at capital letters. For example, `ReplicaSetSpec` would become `Replica Set Spec`. That's not ideal, but `Horizontal Pod Autoscaler List` would be better than `HorizontalPodAutoscalerList`.

title: Discovering, bookkeeping and isolating platform resources other than CPU time and main memory.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
## Overview

Users may want to schedule pods based on additional resources beyond the dimensions that Kubernetes already accounts and isolates. Any attempt at static enumeration would be incomplete, so this proposal discusses a plan for _discovering_, _bookkeeping_, and _isolating_ custom resource types.
### Discovery

Discovery involves enumerating available features and resources on the node so they are available to the scheduling coordinator (in Kubernetes, the API server and scheduler). This may involve being opinionated about how to represent the features.
### Bookkeeping

Bookkeeping or _schedulability_ captures making the user aware of the available features and allowing them to target their workload against nodes that have specific features. For Kubernetes, this includes the ability to target pod placements to nodes that meet certain criteria.
### Isolation

Isolation, or enforcing allocations, may range from simply ensuring exclusive access to a resource for a task, to fine-grained sharing between co-located tasks. For devices like FPGAs, MICs and GPGPUs, the user may want exclusive access. Features that offer a sharable capacity, such as Intel CAT, need to be accounted accordingly while actuating the necessary mechanisms to ensure that utilization does not exceed the allocated limits.
## Proposal

For a more in-depth discussion of the requirements, mechanisms and proposed changes please refer to (and also comment/edit) this shared document: [goo.gl/FjOkIe](https://goo.gl/FjOkIe).

After discussing and solidifying the ideas outlined in the document, we can add them to the `docs/proposals` and/or `docs/design` directories. Advice from maintainers on what belongs where is welcome.
## Upstream work items
- [#28311: Hardware feature discovery to add node labels with a unique prefix (e.g. `scheduler.alpha.intel.com/<feature-name>`).](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/28311)
- [#28312: Accounting and feasibility for custom integer resources in the API server and scheduler.](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/28312)
- [#28313: Support for isolating custom resources.](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/28313)

See also [#28315: Online resource oversubscription and external QoS control](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/28315)

@quinton-hoole @nikhiljindal 

One thing need to discuss with you about k8s services.
in single k8s cluster when users define service.spec.sessionAffinity=ClientIP, then the service will be session affinity, means if there are multiple calls from single clientIP, those calls will be redirected to the same pod, so the session context could be reused.

Per my understanding, in k8s, for the case that iptables is enabled, when a service being created, the iptable entry will be write to all nodes, so it is easy to find the target pod and redirect to it.

But if this concept is put to federation level, and if the global dns server is round robin, the service might be redirected to different cluster even sessionAffinity is specified. As a result, the service lost the sessionAffinity capability.

Any comments?

title: Allow reusing api deep copy functions without having to register all of them

labels.name: priority/backlog

body:
Right now, federation-apiserver depends on `pkg/api` (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2127a40596dfc08dfe95ed1a76034d00d17ef66e/federation/apis/core/deep_copy.go#L20) to reuse some of the deep_copy_generated funcs related to Service. As a side effect of that dependency, deep copy functions for _all_ v1 api resources are registered to the schema automatically: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec518005a89ea0b2094f3ae3e565eaa30816d8ce/pkg/api/deep_copy_generated.go#L35.
This is unnecessary. We need to register only the service functions in federation-apiserver.

As a result of this, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2127a40596dfc08dfe95ed1a76034d00d17ef66e/federation/apis/core/deep_copy.go is useless.

One way to fix this will be to move the code that auto registers deep copy funcs out of pkg/api into a sub package (similar to `pkg/api/install` or maybe reuse the same?).

cc @kubernetes/sig-cluster-federation @kubernetes/sig-api-machinery @thockin

This missed the cut due in the rush for 1.3, but exporting all of the journald fields is pretty excessive - most of them are unnecessary and just get in the way. For example, this is all the info that gets exported for a typical message (in addition to the metadata attached by fluentd):

```
structPayload: {
    SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER: "docker"      
    _HOSTNAME: "gke-arob-test-gci-default-pool-78709c83-sual"      
    MESSAGE: "time="2016-06-29T17:34:20.797624934Z" level=debug msg="Calling GET /v1.23/containers/json""      
    _SYSTEMD_UNIT: "docker.service"      
    PRIORITY: "6"      
    _TRANSPORT: "stdout"      
    _GID: "0"      
    _CMDLINE: "/usr/bin/docker daemon -s overlay --host=fd:// -p /var/run/docker.pid --iptables=false --ip-masq=false --log-level=debug --bridge=cbr0 --insecure-registry 10.0.0.0/8"      
    _PID: "1441"      
    _CAP_EFFECTIVE: "3fffffffff"      
    _EXE: "/usr/bin/docker"      
    _MACHINE_ID: "f63f0f17ff364194458987d2577404a0"      
    _BOOT_ID: "6050440b4553480b803a006469bae74e"      
    SYSLOG_FACILITY: "3"      
    _SYSTEMD_CGROUP: "/system.slice/docker.service"      
    _COMM: "docker"      
    _SYSTEMD_SLICE: "system.slice"      
    _UID: "0"      
  }
```

And since "MESSAGE" is capitalized, it doesn't get special cased by the log viewer as the main content to be displayed (as it would if it were just "message"), so it's tough to read any of the logs without digging into their details.

title: Everything but serviceaccount/token controller supports ECDSA

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Apiserver and kubeconfig all work using ECDSA keys for PKI but the service account controller supports only RSA because our jwt code assumes RSA although this is not a requirement of jwt in general:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/serviceaccount/jwt.go#L63

This produces a cryptic non-fatal error in the early controller-manager boot that could be easily missed and pods will fail to create assuming ServiceAccount admission controller is enabled (which it usually is).

```
E0628 02:31:57.135921       6 controllermanager.go:440] Error reading key for service account token controller: asn1: structure error: tags don't match (16 vs {class:0 tag:4 length:48 isCompound:false}) {optional:false explicit:false application:false defaultValue:<nil> tag:<nil> stringType:0 timeType:0 set:false omitEmpty:false} AlgorithmIdentifier @5
```

Is EC something that we want to support? If yes, we should enable it in the JWT parser. If no, we should explicitly validate against it.

cc @liggitt @erictune

title: Allow Kubelet Node Status to be updated on demand

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

body:
The kubelet volume manager depends on the `VolumesInUse` field of the node status being updated before it can proceed with attaching a volume. Since node updates happen periodically on kubelet it can take as much as 10 seconds before the field is updated.

Consider a force sync for the node status update code, something like:

``` GO
    select {
     case <- forceSync
     case <-time.After(10*time.Second)
     }
    tryUpdateNodestatus()
```

Where the `forceSync` channel can be passed to the volume manager to allow it to force updates faster than 10 seconds when needed.

title: kubectl replace: --force options is broken be design

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
When replacing an existing pod, the `kubectl replace --force` command fails as it tries to create a pod with a name that is still used by terminating pod.

How does the `--force` option works?
1. `kubectl replace` deletes a pod (e.g. mypod)
2. `kubectl replace` creates a new pod with the same name (mypod)

What happens? As the command tries to recreate the pod, it fails as the `mypod` is in `Terminating` state. Thus it can not be created.

The problem is the `kubectl replace` does not wait for a pod to be deleted.

**Reproducer**:
1. kubectl run mypod --image=yapei/hello-openshift  --generator=run-pod/v1
2. kubectl get pod mypod -o yaml > mypod.json
3. kubectl replace -f  mypod.json --force

The last command ends with:

```
pod "mypod" deleted
Error from server: pods "mypod" already exists
```

title: Update commented-out taint/toleration code to replace NoScheduleNoAdmitNoExecute with NoExecute

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
We can represent NoScheduleNoAdmitNoExecute with two separate taints, one NoScheduleNoAdmit and one NoExecute. Having a NoScheduleNoAdmitNoExecute taint effect is only beneficial if there are use cases where you could use one taint with the NoScheduleNoAdmitNoExecute effect instead of two taints (one NoScheduleNoAdmit and one NoExecute). But it seems such use cases do not exist. At least the most common use case, representing "bad machine," requires two taints, so that a pod can choose any of 
- don't schedule me there and evict me if I'm already running there
- don't schedule me there but leave me bound if I'm already running there
- schedule me there and leave me bound if I'm already running there

A single taint isn't sufficient because you can't get three separate behaviors with just a single taint.

Since we need two separate taints for this common use case anyway, it makes more sense for those taints to be called NoScheduleNoAdmit and NoExecute, rather than NoScheduleNoAdmit and NoScheduleNoAdmitNoExecute.

So, we should rename NoScheduleNoAdmitNoExecute to NoExecute.

title: iptables proxy times out when a request is made to a pod's hostIP

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

body:
If a pod makes a network request to a service endpoint matching its hostIP, for instance to read data from a service running in a different namespace on the same cluster, that request will time out.

Here's the scenario where we're seeing this behavior:
1. we have a backend service running in namespace "A", with a NodePort configured to listen on port 9123
2. we want to access this backend service in namespace "B", so we define a service in namespace "B" that has no selector, and add our kube node IP addresses to the endpoints for that service.
3. when a pod in namespace B accesses this external service, requests that get load balanced via a service endpoint into to the pod's own node will time out.

Here are the iptables rules:

```
ip-172-27-223-103 ~ $ sudo iptables -t nat -S KUBE-SVC-KGYXPATUVNKZMVSP
-N KUBE-SVC-KGYXPATUVNKZMVSP
-A KUBE-SVC-KGYXPATUVNKZMVSP -m comment --comment "statsd-demo/backend:http" -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.33332999982 -j KUBE-SEP-7RROIIUYDTARWBEO
-A KUBE-SVC-KGYXPATUVNKZMVSP -m comment --comment "statsd-demo/backend:http" -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.50000000000 -j KUBE-SEP-PJWPIY4U6IL5GHGZ
-A KUBE-SVC-KGYXPATUVNKZMVSP -m comment --comment "statsd-demo/backend:http" -j KUBE-SEP-AFRVQPFXWW24IO52

ip-172-27-223-103 ~ $ sudo iptables -t nat -S KUBE-SEP-AFRVQPFXWW24IO52
-N KUBE-SEP-AFRVQPFXWW24IO52
-A KUBE-SEP-AFRVQPFXWW24IO52 -s 172.27.223.103/32 -m comment --comment "statsd-demo/backend:http" -j KUBE-MARK-MASQ
-A KUBE-SEP-AFRVQPFXWW24IO52 -p tcp -m comment --comment "statsd-demo/backend:http" -m tcp -j DNAT --to-destination 172.27.223.103:9123
```

In the rules above, 172.27.223.103 is a kube node with a nodeport open on 9123.

If I ssh into a pod, direct requests to the host IP work:

```
ip-172-27-223-103 ~ $ docker exec -ti ffe784258a00 sh
/ # wget 172.27.223.101:9123 -O -
Connecting to 172.27.223.101:9123 (172.27.223.101:9123)
-                    100% |**************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************|    18   0:00:00 ETA
/ # wget 172.27.223.102:9123 -O -
Connecting to 172.27.223.102:9123 (172.27.223.102:9123)
-                    100% |**************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************|    18   0:00:00 ETA
/ # wget 172.27.223.103:9123 -O -
Connecting to 172.27.223.103:9123 (172.27.223.103:9123)
-                    100% |**************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************|    18   0:00:00 ETA
/ # exit
```

but using the cluster IP, a certain percentage of requests will time out:

```
ip-172-27-223-103 ~ $ docker exec -ti ffe784258a00 sh
/ # export
export BACKEND_SERVICE_HOST='192.168.1.209'
export BACKEND_SERVICE_PORT='9123'
export BACKEND_SERVICE_PORT_HTTP='9123'

/ # wget $BACKEND_SERVICE_HOST:$BACKEND_SERVICE_PORT -O -
Connecting to 192.168.1.209:9123 (192.168.1.209:9123)
-                    100% |**************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************|    18   0:00:00 ETA
/ # wget $BACKEND_SERVICE_HOST:$BACKEND_SERVICE_PORT -O -
Connecting to 192.168.1.209:9123 (192.168.1.209:9123)

title: When rolling update fails, new RC remains making another rolling update impossible and breaking our continous delivery

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

body:
If a rolling update fails (for instance, by rolling update to an image that doesn't exist), the new, as of yet unrenamed, RC remains in place. 

If you try another rolling update, it will fail because

```
[master] Running shell script
+ /var/lib/jenkins/kubernetes/kubectl-1.2 --kubeconfig=xxx rolling-update xxx --image=xxx/xxx:master-42-e4c7a5b
error: Found existing in-progress update to image (xxx/xxx).
Either continue in-progress update with --image=xxx/xxx or rollback with --rollback
See 'kubectl rolling-update -h' for help and examples.
```

Two things wrong:
  a) the message `Either continue in-progress update with --image=xxx/xxx` must be wrong, as that's exactly what we're doing
  b) This breaks our continuous delivery pipeline as the only way to recover is for someone to notice, then manually delete the new RC.

Kubernetes 1.2.4.

body:
Whenever I do a rolling update of a replication controller with an image, the originally deployed pod is kept alive on the cluster. For instance, if I deploy a new application, version 1 gets deployed. After a number of deployments, both original version 1 and version X are active.

Not only that, replication controllers seem messed up. If I describe the pods in question, they each are in a different replication controller (the original rc with the original pod, and a new one with the new pod). But if I go into the kubernetes kube-ui dashboard, the OLD rc is linked to the NEW pod.

Also, the describe command reckons the OLD rc and pod started AFTER the new one.

Old and new version are load balanced on the service, and clients are served 50% of the time from old code.

Quite a few things not right here. 

I'm roll-updating via `kubectl rolling-update rc-name --image=new/image:version`.

Kubernetes 1.2.4, deployed on AWS via supplied scripts. Images are built with docker 1.10 and stored at amazon's ECR.

title: Federation: Proposal: support snapshotting or mirroring persistent volumes between clusters

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: sig/multicluster
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Multicluster.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Reading the Ubernetes proposal and specifically with interest in Scenario 4:

"I want to be immune to any single data centre or cloud availability zone outage, so I want to spread my service across multiple such zones (and ideally even across multiple cloud providers)."

I would like to add scenario 5 to also include thinking which covers persistent volumes if these were available across both clusters (via some external storage replication mechanism). This would allow applications to retain state (subject to any asynchronous replication conditions of course) in the case of failover between sites.

Akin to DR and worrying about RTO/RPO.

Comments for @quinton-hoole  . Opening as an issue initially to discuss.

The scenario I have in mind is similar to 4, but it also includes PV/PVC which is replicated between two distant sites (for example London and New York).

I have three assumptions I am making:
1. There is something external to the clusters that is replicating storage between the locations.
2. I am putting the network fail-over out of scope, I am  also assuming that you do have service discover-ability external to the cluster.
3. There is a distributed Source Configuration Management system which is available in all locations and makes globally available deployment yaml files and container images.

So if we had a service which was discover-able externally via a DNS entry at one location where it normally ran:

service1.production.london.example.com

If there is a DR event and we need to restart the service in New York then I am going to assume for now that we could find it at a different location such as:

service1.production.ny.example.com

Assuming that some of the pods for this service are using persistent storage and we want to recover the state by attaching the replicated PV and creating a corresponding PVC at the remote site, then we may need to have a copy of the list of PV's at each location as well as some API call to the control plane that is replication storage to find out what identifier the replicated storage is using for the same PV at each site.

For example, if the PVC for the London storage was backed by a PV with an identifier of 12345, then we could ask the storage replication controller what the corresponding identifer would be in NY, which could be 54321. In this case we would want to update the pod definition to attach the correct PV as part of the deployment.

Thanks

Chris

title: `git describe` to semver translation wrong in hack/lib/version.sh

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
The line in question is https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/527cb50583a2599823e1784b0c35deb1e8ad763a/hack/lib/version.sh#L59

We built a custom version off of v1.2.4. The output of `git describe` is `v1.2.4-1-ge191e9760c2dbd`

After the translation, it became `v1.2.4.1+e191e9760c2dbd`.

It's not a valid semver. Node controller complained about this fact:

```
nodecontroller.go:364] couldn't parse verions "v1.2.4.1+e191e9760c2dbd" of minion: Invalid character(s) found in patch number "4.1"
```

One consequence of this is the node is presumed to not support graceful shutdown (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.2.4/pkg/controller/node/nodecontroller.go#L365), and every pod deletion resulted in forceful shutdown, which caused a bunch of problems for us.

title: RFE: Inter-pod signaling on cohort life-cycle events.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
**Motivation:** 
As a distributed systems designer who would like to create a "better batch" system atop of kubernetes, I would like to be able to create my own master-worker model using kubernetes concepts to sustain an overall higher throughput.

**Background:**
In traditional batch systems there is often the notion of "claim re-use".   Traditional batching will typically have a queue which can sometimes be several orders of magnitude greater then the resources provided, and in order to maximize overall throughput designers tend to avoid unnessary scheduling and other lifecycle events.  Other systems often refer to this as "claim-reuse".  Your job has been matched to a machine, and once it is finished another is ready to follow behind it without going through scheduling etc. 

**RFE Requirements:** 
Leveraging kubernetes co-scheduling, I would like to schedule a pod to a machine where one of the members of the pod is actually a worker to be executed.  I would like to denote via spec, that a given container should be signaled on life-cycle changes to any changes in the cohort, and could potentially augment some of the parameters of the next container to be run.    The specifics of both the events and interactions are still TBD. 

**High level example use cases:** 
- Large DAGs whose executions are pleasingly parallel
- Iterative machine learning

/cc @kubernetes/sig-node @jayunit100 @rrati @jeremyeder @sdminonne

title: kubectl run -it loses some lines of the log

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

body:
When running a command via `kubectl run -it` that immediately prints something, we might lose some lines of the log due to a race of the execution of the container and the `kubectl attach` used by `kubectl run` to attach to the terminal (compare comment https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/16670#issuecomment-199017681).

As a workaround for running an interactive shell we have this ugly `Hit enter for command prompt` now. The actual root problem though is that `docker attach` does not replay the logs. It looks like `docker run` is the only way to actually synchronously run a command, get all the output and attach to the process.

Right now when you get RS with `kubectl get rs`, they're ordered alphabetically by their name. title: RFC: Re-evaluating `kubectl logs` --since flags

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
Log management on the node has been discussed in #24677. @vishh proposed that containers should log directly to files, and kubelet should access the log files directly without going through the runtime.
(More discussion and details in the original issue #24677)
A main part of the idea is for kubelet to create a designated log directory (e.g., `/var/log/pods`), and ask the container runtime to store the stdout/stderr logs in the per-pod subdirectory (e.g., `/var/log/pods/<POD_UID>`) with a given file name. This approach has the following benefits:
- [node] This detaches log's lifecycle from container's -- making disk space accounting/management on the node easier. 
- [cluster] kubelet can provide any log collector (e.g., fluentd) a log directory (e.g. `/var/log/pods`), where pod/container metadata such as name/namespace/uid can be extracted easily from the file paths. This means that log collector only has to integrate with kubernete once, and it can support all container runtimes (provided that the collector understands the log format used by the container/runtime). This reduces one more integration pain point for new runtimes.

This solution assumes that kubelet treats log files as blobs, i.e., it does not need to know the logging formats (for a good reason).
On the other hand, although a good cluster logging setup is essential to production workloads, `kubectl` provides access to container logs for convenience.  kubelet not knowing the log format means that even though it can serve the raw log for `kubectl logs`, it will not be able to support flags to filter logs by timestamps.

So, here are the questions: How important is it to support the filtering feature in `kubectl logs`? Is it worth imposing a log format for runtimes (IMO, no) to support this feature? 

p.s., There are other workarounds but none of them look too appealing. E.g., kubelet (or a separate process) can parse the logs based on a few common known formats, etc.

EDIT: `kubectl logs` does **not** always works. The current implementation relies on `docker logs`, which only works with json and journald logging drivers.

/cc @kubernetes/sig-node @vishh @mtaufen 

Ref: The current `kubectl logs` usage:

```
Flags:
  -c, --container="": Print the logs of this container
  -f, --follow[=false]: Specify if the logs should be streamed.
      --include-extended-apis[=true]: If true, include definitions of new APIs via calls to the API server. [default true]
      --limit-bytes=0: Maximum bytes of logs to return. Defaults to no limit.
  -p, --previous[=false]: If true, print the logs for the previous instance of the container in a pod if it exists.
      --since=0: Only return logs newer than a relative duration like 5s, 2m, or 3h. Defaults to all logs. Only one of since-time / since may be used.
      --since-time="": Only return logs after a specific date (RFC3339). Defaults to all logs. Only one of since-time / since may be used.
      --tail=-1: Lines of recent log file to display. Defaults to -1, showing all log lines.
      --timestamps[=false]: Include timestamps on each line in the log output
```

title: isLikelyNotMountPoint() function needs refactored

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
CC @kubernetes/sig-storage 

Currently, isLikelyNotMountPoint() is implemented in mount_linux.go and nsenter_mount.go. They use different approach to determine whether a path is mounted or not.
1. mount_linux.go checks if the directory has a different device as parent, then it is a mountpoint.
2. nsenter_mount.go uses findmnt command result to check the mountpoint. This approach has issue: if the path is relatively long, findmnt execute output will truncate the last letter of the path. 

Open an issue here to investigate whether we need to different approaches for this function. Another related issue is that isLikelyNotMountPoint() is called by many places and served as two purposes, one is checking whether directory exists or not, the other is to check the mount point. Suggest to separate these two functions.

title: Copy logs from dead containers to local files to facilitate immediate GC of dead containers

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
One of the reasons for keeping dead containers around in kubelet today is to get access to logs from previous instances. Dead container instances can take up disk space via their root filesystem and result in disk pressure on the nodes. To alleviate disk pressure and improve the logging experience in kubernetes, kubelet can retrieve logs from dead containers and GC them right away once kubelet doesn't depend on metadata associated with old containers.
Specifically,
- Kubelet can retrieve logs from the runtime and store in a per-pod, per-container directory inside of `/var/log/` directory. For the docker runtime, this can be a simple move operation. For rkt, we will have to retrieve the logs remotely.
- The directory structure can be `/var/log/<podUID>/<ContainerName>/<InstanceNumber>_stdout.log`
- Update `kubectl logs -p` to return logs from the files instead of relying on the runtime for previous logs.
- These logs will be kept around on a best-effort basis and will be deleted whenever there is disk pressure.
- Kubelet can prefer keeping the first and most recent instances of a container around and aggressively delete other log files.
- All these logs will be accessible initially via the `/logs` REST endpoint. In the future, we can consider expanding `kubectl logs` interface to support an instance number or add support for the first attempt specifically.

title: Probe timeout ignored by ExecAction

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
I'm using a readiness probe that may take a long time to run, and I expected it to be interrupted after the specified timeout.

A probe defined like this:

``` json
"readinessProbe": {
  "exec": {
    "command": ["bash", "-c", "sleep 15"]
  },
  "timeoutSeconds": 5
}
```

Instead of timing out and failing, it is actually succeeding and ignoring the timeout.

I noticed that both `TCPSocketAction` and `HTTPGetAction` probes timeout according to the value of `TimeoutSeconds`, `ExecAction` on the other hand ignores it.

Looking at the code:

`if p.Exec != nil`, no reference to timeout:
[pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L146](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6ecfb4c8fad41156e1fbccf29ac9f5d98901e991/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L146)

`if p.HTTPGet != nil || p.TCPSocket != nil`, timeout is used:
[pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L163](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6ecfb4c8fad41156e1fbccf29ac9f5d98901e991/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L163)
[pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L171](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6ecfb4c8fad41156e1fbccf29ac9f5d98901e991/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L171)

title: Shard apiservers by resource type

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
## API server cacher should have some locality property

Currently, we have a cache layer in API server, which is responsible for serving WATCH and LIST requests. But the cacher will cache for ALl kinds of resources. IMO, since we have multi API server, the cacher should have locality property. Le me explicate it with an example, I have 3 API servers, and I configure the nginx/haproxy as: 
- API server A is dedicated for all Pod related requests by default, API server B and C are backups when A is unhealthy
- API server B is dedicated for all Node related requests, A and C are backups.
- API server C is dedicated for other requests, A and B are backups.

In such a case, It's fine that API server A just cache for Pod, right? Cache for ALL resources works though, it consumes much more memory and cpu, build more connections to etcd server. Hence, I suggest the cacher works as follows:
- Only start caching(list&watch form etcd) when server the first LIST/WATCH request. If it never server any LIST/WATCH requests about a resource, it does not need cache for it.
- Have expiration policy. For example, if it has not server any LIST/WATCH requests about a resource for a long time(this could be configurable), stop caching for that resource and free the memory it used.

Just my thoughts for discussion. I could also work on it if it sounds good.

title: Possible Bug: Deployment Rollout History Missing Deployments

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
## background

We're running deployments in a CI/CD context. Sometimes there will be two commits in rapid succession triggering nearly back-to-back deployments. When we observe the `kubectl rollout history` we are missing some deployments. These are likely caused when two deployments happen at/around the same time.
## the problem
- running `kubectl rollout history deployment <something>` does not show all deployments
- running `kubectl apply -f <deployment>` returns success and indicates success (e.g. `deployment "edge-router" configured`) even if it is not represented in the rollout history.
## our expectation
- if `kubectl` returns `deployment configured` then there should be a corresponding entry in the `rollout history` otherwise return an error
- ideally, `kubectl` should output the revision that was created e.g. `deployment "edge-router" configured (revision 1234)`
## how to reproduce
1. create a deployment resource
2. add a tag like `serial: $SERIAL`
3. use the following script

```
serial=0
while true; do
  serial=$(($serial + 1))
  echo $serial
  sed "s/\$SERIAL/$serial/g" /tmp/test-deployment.yml | kubectl apply -f -
done
```
1. inspect each revision (E.g. `kubectl rollout history deployment test --revision 1`, then check 2, 3, 4, 5)
2. Notice that at some point, a serial will be lost. It seems to get worse the longer the script runs.
## screenshots

Do a bunch of deployments. Output from `kubectl` indicates success. 
![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/52489/15793592/dd3171c0-2999-11e6-83fb-918d2917be94.png)

Check each revision. Notice that 7 & 8 are missing. If I continue iterating over the rest of the revision, I find even bigger gaps and no deployment for 7 or 8. In fact, I ran 100+ deploymemnts and the rollout history has only 33 entries. 

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/52489/15793572/bed71234-2999-11e6-810a-12713f6b172e.png)

title: Secret keys should allow underscores

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

body:
The [Secrets user guide](http://kubernetes.io/docs/user-guide/secrets/#creating-a-secret-manually) states that `The data field is a map. Its keys must match DNS_SUBDOMAIN, except that leading dots are also allowed. The values are arbitrary data, encoded using base64.`

This feels like an arbitrary restriction, and it definitely impacts usefulness of being able to mount secrets as volumes - disqualifying keys matching any filename that normally contains underscores (`id_rsa`, `id_dsa`, `authorized_keys`, `sshd_config`, `ssh_host_key`, etc. ad infinitum).

Please consider modifying the criteria for key names to something a bit less restrictive - these aren't URLs and the underscore is an incredibly pervasive character in many standard _UNIX_ filenames.

title: Some kubectl errors are hidden incorrectly

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/26425#issuecomment-222258484:

> Found a hidden issue here: if the output flag `-o` is specified, the "resource not found" error will not be exposed. 
> 
> ``` console
> $ kubectl get pods abc 
> Error from server: pods "abc" not found
> $ kubectl get pods abc -o name
> <no error>
> $ kubectl get pods abc -o template --template='{{if (exists . "status" "containerStatuses")}}{{range .status.containerStatuses}}{{if (and (eq .name "update-demo") (exists . "state" "running"))}}true{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}'
> <no error>
> ```

Why? In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubectl/cmd/get.go, the errors returned by `r.Visit` are appended to `allErrs` but then `return printer.PrintObj(obj, out)` is called and `allErrs` are dropped silently.

Also, the error returned by `sorting, err := cmd.Flags().GetString("sort-by")` isn't handled/returned either. 

Some of these are related to the changes made in #23673. This may happen to other kubectl commands too. 

cc @metral @kubernetes/kubectl

labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

body:
Forked from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/23591#issuecomment-203042820
Creating a new issue so I won't forget.

PLEG serially gets status for every pod, where at least one container has encountered a state transition. This becomes the bottleneck if a lot of containers changed in one relist period. We were aware of this problem and had come up with a few options before:
1. Add a new GetPodStatus variant to bypass the `docker ps -a` call since pleg already have this information. The downside is that this is a very docker-specific optimization and doesn't make sense for other runtimes.
2. Parallelize the process.
3. Do nothing. Assume docker is busy and process slowly.

I think we can do (2) with a small number of goroutines (e.g., 2) to speed up the time.
