title: Don't blindly trust cached state of load balancer resources in service controller

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Multiple users have been bit by some variant of the following problem: they delete a resource from their cloud provider that was created as part of a service's external load balancer. If they deleted it accidentally, they wonder why their load balancer stopped working. If they deleted it intentionally, they wonder why it comes back after an indeterminate amount of time (typically on the order of days or weeks).

This is caused by us caching the last observed state of the cloud provider resources in the service controller (with no TTL) rather than rechecking it periodically, such that it only gets rechecked when the controller manager process is restarted. This confusion isn't worth saving a few cloud API calls, particularly given that most clusters don't expose all that many external services.

We might want to include this as a bug fix in 1.3, but it's not absolutely critical. Happy to hear your thoughts on that.

@bprashanth @thockin @alex-mohr

title: Solution discussion for rebuilding federation service controller cache on restart

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/multicluster
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Multicluster.

body:
I am working on federation service controller, and there is a limitation on current cache, after had a call with @quinton-hoole, as it's not a common case, we will leave it as is in v1.3, and I open this issue to track the problem and to find out a more robust solution.

**Federation service controller behavior description:**
1. service controller watch federation apiserver for new services, create service map in the form of
`fedServiceMap: [serviceName]cachedService: {service info, endpointMap: [clusterName]int, serviceStatusMap: [clusterName]api.LoadBalancerStatus}`
endpointMap and serviceStatusMap have no element at this moment.
2. service controller create the service on all healthy clusters
3. service controller watches all healthy clusters for services and endpoints.
When new serviceStatus with LB info is returned, add it to serviceStatusMap and service info and update federation apiserver with the new LB info.
4. when new endpoint info returned, add it to endpoint map with flag 1 which indicates there is reachable endpoints

**Problem description:**
From above behavior description, we can see that serviceStatusMap is the only place to link clusterName and LB info, it is not persisted anywhere and it will go on service controller down.

So if during service controller down time, the service on any clusters is deleted, and after federation service controller being starts, the service will be rebuild on that cluster again, with different LB info, and as we lost the link between cluster and LB info, we do not know which old LB info in federation service was returned by from that cluster, as a result, we can add the new IP to federation service, but there is no way to remove the old one.

**One typical example**
Federation service:S1
Clusters: C1, C2
after S1 is created, it will be created in C1 and C2, with LB IP1, and LB IP2 assigned.
So after the a while S1 will changed to S1[LB:{IP1, IP2}]
serviceCache is same S1[LB:{IP1, IP2}]
serviceStatusMap [C1]S1[LB:IP1], [C2]S1[LB:IP2] , most import one, it links Ingress IP and clusters.
endpointMap [C1]1,[C2]1 

For the case that LB IP in C1 changed from IP1 to IP3
If we have the cache info, we know IP1 is from C1 previously, so we can remove it and add IP3.
But If Service Controller is restarted, we will lose the old LB IP info, we do not know which IP we should remove from Federation IP, and the ingress info will be changed to S1[LB:{IP1, IP2, IP3}]

body:
Filing this for future work.

pkg/volume/plugins.go defines a set of `*VolumePlugin` types that all implement small interfaces like `NewDeleter()`.  This started with `NewMounter()` and `NewUnmounter()` which plugins implement with different structs and are passed around.  It got cargo-culted into a half dozen other such interfaces that do not have the same restrictions, and generally are called like:

```
r := plugin.NewRecycler(name, spec)
r.Recycle()
```

Most of these interfaces could be reduced to:

```
plugin.Recycle(name, spec)
```

Relatively easy one for someone to jump on, but NOT going into the 1.3 milestone.

Additionally, `NewMounter()` and `NewUnmounter()` could be extracted to a `MountableVolumePlugin` type and `VolumeHost` could go through a similar fragmenting.

body:
The following PR is blocked by this problem (best I can tell)
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/25982

Change needed:

``` shell
$ mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system.conf.d
cat <<EOF >/etc/systemd/system.conf.d/kubernetes-accounting.conf
[Manager]
DefaultCPUAccounting=yes
DefaultMemoryAccounting=yes

```

To verify accounting is enabled, you should restart the kubelet and docker

``` shell
$ cat /proc/$(pidof docker)/cgroup
11:pids:/
10:cpu,cpuacct:/system.slice/docker.service
9:cpuset:/
8:devices:/system.slice/docker.service
7:hugetlb:/
6:memory:/system.slice/docker.service
5:net_cls,net_prio:/
4:blkio:/system.slice/docker.service
3:perf_event:/
2:freezer:/
1:name=systemd:/system.slice/docker.service
```

Where the important thing to very is that the cpu,cpuacct and memory have an entry that is not `/` and matches where the unit is launched.

I edit a pod with some metadata such as:

```
# Please edit the object below. Lines beginning with a '#' will be ignored,

# reopened with the relevant failures.
#
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod

Then I close the file and it pops back open with this message after I add `fun: true` label:

# Please edit the object below. Lines beginning with a '#' will be ignored,
# and an empty file will abort the edit. If an error occurs while saving this file will be
# reopened with the relevant failures.

    app: guestbook
    fun: true
```

Putting the error in the comment header is OK but I was very confused when this happened to me and didn't notice the errors at all. A few potential fixes:
1. Print out the errors and then ask the user to "press enter" to fix, then launch the $EDITOR again
2. Put the error message above the line that generated the error
3. Automatically quote true/false values before converting to JSON in fields like labels.

Given the three options 1 is probably easiest and would fix the issue well enough for now.

We have two challenges:

This is causing issue with testing and also releasing containers that are broken.  We do not have a e2e test cycle that will support this.

body:

rolling.go (has all functions/methods related to rolling deployments)
recreate.go (has all functions/methods related to recreate deployments)
rollback.go (has all functions/method related to rolling back)
scale.go (has all functions/method related to simple scaling events)
util.go (has all general-purpose utilities)

There are also a couple of utilities in pkg/util/deployments that use callbacks from the controller to do things. We should have those squashed in pkg/controller/deployment/util.go. Using callbacks between packages is very hard to follow.

Hopefully this refactor will reduce the barrier of entry into understanding the deployment controller.

body:
Service.spec.selector comments say "If empty, all pods are selected, if not specified, endpoints must be manually specified".

As far as I can tell this is not implemented, though.  While Go understands the different between a nil slice and a non-nil slice with no elements, JSON does not.  With an `omitempty` field, we get the field dropped in either case.

To actually achieve this semantic, we need the type to be a pointer, so omitempty applies to a nil pointer but not an empty map.  But at least protobuf codegen does not support this, either.  I think the right fix is to change the documentation.

- [ ] Document all possible status codes and returned object types: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/6167

title: Add Ready replica count to DaemonsetStatus

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

body:
Readiness is as relevant to daemonsets as deployments, but while DeploymentStatus has "AvailableReplicas" i.e. the number of pods ready for at least minReadySeconds, DaemonsetStatus does not have an equivalent count of replicas that are healthy/ready. Not only can services point at daemonset pods, making readiness relevant, but readiness can also be used to indicate general health. I suggest adding "readyReplicas" to DaemonsetStatus.

The main use case should be for kubectl, but I also would like to add a metric to [kubernetes/kube-state-metrics](https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-state-metrics/) reflecting ready replicas of a daemonset, as it exists for deployments.

body:
There are system components updating 
ObjectMeta.Finalizers, so it requires the three-way merge feature of the strategic merge patch.

ObjectMeta.Finalizers is a slice of string, but the strategicmerge package doesn't handle the merge patch for a slice of a base type. It only uniqifies the entries in the merged slice, but doesn't support removing an entry.

There are two possible solutions:
1. make ObjectMeta.Finalizers a list of structs;
2. define a strategic merge patch syntax to express the deletion of an entry in a slice of a base type. For example:
supposing originally Object.Fanalizers=["foo","bar"], after applying the patch

```
ObejctMeta
  $patch/finalizers: delete foo
  finalizers:
    - baz
```

It should become ["bar", "baz"]

title: Propogated errors missing context

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: help wanted
labels.description: Denotes an issue that needs help from a contributor. Must meet "help wanted" guidelines.

labels.name: sig/instrumentation
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Instrumentation.

labels.name: sig/architecture
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Architecture.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
## Problem

Our code is riddled with snippets that look like this:

``` go
if err != nil {
  return nil, err
}
```

These lines bubble errors up the call stack until someone decides to log them and move on:

``` go
if err != nil {
  glog.Errorf("Something failed: %v", err)
}
```

Which can yield an unhelpful error message like (fake, but not totally unreasonable):

```
E0426 01:02:59.506727    2740 manager.go:110] Something failed: unexpected EOF
```

And now we're tasked with trying to crawl through the code to figure out where that error actually came from.

We discourage logging an error that's also returned (duplicate log statements interwoven throughout the code can also be confusing), but if you (the person debugging) is lucky someone has attached a unique context message that can help you find the source (e.g. `Operation foo called on pod bar (441234) failed: %v`).
## Assumptions
- Errors are relatively uncommon - i.e. this doesn't apply to "not found" errors that should probably be `bool`s, or errors which can be generated in a tight loop
- Errors are ephemeral - that is, they are handled (e.g. logged) and then discarded (not stored anywhere)
- When an error is produced, it is not always possible to know how it will be handled, or even how severe it is
## Proposal

From the above assumptions, I get 2 guiding principles:
1. If returning an error, it is your job to provide the maximum amount of debugging information and context around that error.
2. If handling an error, it is your job to use the _appropriate_ context for the specific case (e.g. a critical failure should have more detail than something that is expected to occassionally fail and will be retried).

To this end, I'd like to create a kubernetes error package that we promote everywhere. The constructor could look something like (rough sketch, not final API):

``` go
func New(msg string, context ...Context) Error { ... } // Context TBD
func Wrap(msg string, err error, context ...Context) Error { ... }
```

In addition to the provided message, error, and context the constructors could automatically attach additional metadata such as: a full stack trace, timestamp, etc.

We would also provide formatting functions that could flatten the error objects and format them to various levels of detail for logging. Finally, to get the maximum benefit, we would want to discourage the pattern of returning a raw error without first wrapping it with extra context.

For implementation, there are already several projects which provide similar functionality:
- https://github.com/go-errors/errors ([blog](http://blog.bugsnag.com/go-errors))
- https://github.com/hashicorp/errwrap

X-ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/6461, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/23338 - This proposal is independent of which log library we use, we just need to provide functions to log the appropriate context in whatever format.

/cc @thockin @timothysc @pwittrock @bgrant0607

title: Weird quota and limitrange behavior

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
I'm using HEAD in the master branch with a simple 1 master + 1 slave setup. API server is started with the following flag: `--admission-control=LimitRanger,NamespaceLifecycle,ResourceQuota`.

To reproduce:

```
kubectl create namespace test
kubectl --namespace=test create -f docs/admin/resourcequota/quota.yaml
kubectl --namespace=test create -f docs/admin/limitrange/limits.yaml
kubectl --namespace=test run nginx --image=nginx:latest --requests="cpu=500m,mem=100mi"
```

Of course, no pods will be created because "cpu=500m" exceeds the default value of "cpu=300m". This is expected behavior. However, the unexpected part is when I do a `kubectl describe namespace test`, and the cpu usage was showing:

```
Resource Quotas
 Name:          quota
 Resource       Used    Hard
 --------       --- ---
 cpu            1500m   20
 memory         300Mi   1Gi
```

As each container was supposed to request 500m cpu, this looks like replicaset controller is trying to create more pods after previous ones were rejected, and this causes the quota usage to keep increasing. This will continue until the quota controller runs and reconciliates the actual information (by default it runs every 5 minutes). I'm wondering if this is the intended behavior, as this could cause all the quota to be used up very quickly until the quota controller runs the next time, and effectively, this blocks all the future pod creation.

title: Make API field defaulting and validation less error-prone

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
There are frequent errors in API field specification, such as:
- default vs inferred (e.g., `fsType`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/api/v1/types.go#L557); note that implicitly inferred is discouraged
- default vs required
- required/optional vs omitempty
- omitempty vs. pointers
- documentation vs actual defaulting and validation code

For examples of multiple errors in one type, see:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/18885#issuecomment-218376807

One way to make defaulting and validation less error prone would to be allow them to be specified declaratively, on API fields using tags or comments. Protocol buffers allow literal default values to be specified (though, unlike in Kubernetes, they aren't conveyed on the wire; non-literals, such as fields defaulted from other fields, can't be specified this way). Declarative validation, where possible (i.e., simple rules), was previously requested by #8116. 

Since omitempty and pointer rules are apparently non-obvious, I think we should require specification of required vs optional and then either verify that the other properties are consistent or autogenerate them. 

Auto-fixing field names in documentation is covered by #19319.

cc @lavalamp @thockin @kubernetes/sig-api-machinery

body:
I am seeing unexpected behavior from a user standpoint when `kubectl apply -f mydeployment.yml`

The existing Deployment has an HPA associated with it and the current replica count is 3. When the deployment is accepted, the number of replicas jumps to 9, then scales down to 6, the value in the deployment. Eventually, the new pods info starts flowing in and the HPA does its thing and scales back to satisfaction.

The behavior I expected is that the rollout would use the current replicas from the HPA and the strategy parameters from the Deployment to keep replica count in line with the current target set by the HPA.

```
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: Deployment
metadata:

spec:
  replicas: 6
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate

      maxSurge: "50%"
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: myapp
          image: "someimage"
```

```
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: mydeployment

spec:

title: RC shouldn't update observedGeneration with pending creates/deletes

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
The desired behavior is:
- Create spec.Replica pods
- As pods keep coming down watch, update status.Replicas, so users have pseudo real-time feedback
- If during this time someone submits a new update to spec.Replicas that bumps up the generation, _dont_ update status.Generation to match
- Update Generation when pending creates/deletes are observed

Without the third check, we could confuse a client who quicky scales up/down into thinking the current `observedGeneration` is for their spec (because spec will match status, but we still have pending creates/deletes). 

Observed in: https://pantheon.corp.google.com/storage/browser/kubernetes-jenkins/pr-logs/pull/24391/kubernetes-pull-build-test-e2e-gce/38289/artifacts/e2e-gce-builder-1-1-master/

body:
When a pod (or rep controller, or service) fails for reason like 'no corresponding docker image' or PodExceedsFreeCPU  we see this when we do  a "pod describe".  I have included the describe output for one of our test runs below.  Notice that the Status for the replication controller is  Pending -- however an event occurred whose corresponding 'Reason' code is FailedScheduling.  

I would argue this is an API usability bug.  The suggested fix would be to add a new enum value to the 'Status' attribute of  resources (like pods, rc's, etc) -- namely  "Failed".

This would make it much easier to manage K8s clusters via REST API's like fabric8.

In fact, I posted a stack overflow question asking how -- using the fabric8 API -- we could find out that a pod (or other resource)  failed to provision correctly. [ http://stackoverflow.com/questions/37020369/best-way-in-kubernetes-to-receive-notifications-of-errors-when-instantiating-res ].     If Kubernetes provided a  "Failed" status, the current implementation of fabric8 API would automatically work better.      And there would be less confusion for users who used kubectl to find out the status of provisioning a resource.

# RFC: Adding test cases to [e2e/persistent_volumes.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/persistent_volumes.go) and [integration/persistent_volumes_test.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/integration/persistent_volumes_test.go)
## Existing test cases
### [e2e/persistent_volumes.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/persistent_volumes.go)

This file creates an NFS PV with recycle policy and an PVC to claim the PV. 
After the PVC is bound, it is deleted and PV is recycled.
### [integration/persistent_volumes_test.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/integration/persistent_volumes_test.go)

This file creates a fake PV with Recycle policy, creates a PVC that binds to fake PV, deletes the PVC and triggers PV recycler, watches for the PV to be released then available.
In the second test, the PV is set Delete policy and binds to a PVC. After PVC is deleted, watches the PV to be deleted too.
In the third test, 100 PVCs are created, manually puts one of the PVC ref to a PV, watches PV is bound and verify PV is bound to the PVC.
## Existing Red Hat Tests proposed for transfer to Kubernetes E2E Test Environment

| Test Case | PR | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 |  |  |
| 2 |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |
| 4 |  |  |
### 1. Create Pod that uses multiple PVCs. Verify all PVCs are successfully bound and mounted.
- Setup. 
  - In the NFS server pod, creates 3 exports  
  - Create 3 PVs, with sizes 1GB, 2GB, and 3GB, these PVs map to the 3 NFS exports
  - Create 3 PVCs, with claim sizes 1GB, 2GB, and 3GB. 
  - Create a client Pod that uses the 3 PVCs
- Expected Result. The client Pod should mount all NFS PVs, each PVCs are bound to the PVs with the matching size.
### 2. Create one PV and multiple PVCs. Verify exactly one PVC bound while other PVCs are pending.
- Setup
  - Create 1 PVs with sizes 1GB
  - Create 3 PVCs, with claim sizes 1GB, 2GB, and 3GB. 
- Expected Result. 1GB PVC should be bound to the PV, 2GB and 3GB PVCs are pending.
### 3. Delete PVC and make sure PV changes to proper state given one of Recycle, Delete, and Retain policies defined in the PV.
#### Create PV with Delete policy
- Setup
  - Create 1 PVs with sizes 1GB and Delete reclaim policy 
  - Create 1 PVCs with claim sizes 1GB
  - Delete the PVC
- Expected result. After PVC is deleted, PV is also deleted
#### 4. Create PV with Retain policy
- Setup
  - Create 1 PVs with sizes 1GB and Delete reclaim policy 
  - Create a file on the PV
  - Create 1 PVCs with claim sizes 1GB
  - Delete the PVC
- Expected result. After PVC is deleted, PV still exists and the file on the PV also exists

title: [RFC] PVC recycle should wait for pod termination.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

body:
I know we have talked about this before but I wanted to get some discussion on the record as I think we discussed this in the context of protecting the binder state as opposed to user protection. I ran into a use case which exposes this problem.

The https://github.com/openshift/origin-metrics has a redeploy option which does a delete  of all pods and PVCs and recreates them. The issue is that the cassandra pod takes a while to shut down meanwhile the deletion of the PVC triggers recycling.

For NFS based volumes this creates a problem; when a file that is still open is deleted the NFS client renames it to .nfsXYZ (http://nfs.sourceforge.net/#faq_d2). The recycler sees those files and is unable to delete the directory.

I am not sure if there is a mechanism to do this but one possible solution would be to add the PVC to a list of things which are deleted when a pod is terminated.

title: Fix the "first pod problem" for inter-controller/service pod affinity like we did for same-controller/service pod affinity

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
In the pod affinity design we identified a problem (let's call it the "first pod problem") where the way you express the rule "run all the pods from service S in the same zone" is to say "each pod from service S should only run in a zone that is already running a pod from service S"; this works once there is one pod from S running, but the first pod from S will block forever if the rule is taken literally, so nothing will ever schedule. So we have a workaround where we identify this scenario explicitly, and allow the first pod to schedule anywhere.

It occurred to me that we have a similar problem if people use pod affinity to ensure that a group of pods co-schedule. For example, in #18450 one element of a possible solution is to say "X can only run on a machine with Y, and Y can only run on a machine with X" (so that if you kill X or Y, the other one reloads, once we implement that behavior). But such a rule will allow neither of them to ever schedule, since neither will be allowed to "go first."

Fixing this is not high priority.

cc/ @kevin-wangzefeng

body:
There are a few PRs in flight to use annotations to add extra features to the ELBs that k8s sets up (DNS, SSL, Proxy Protocol), and I've written up here what I think a consistent set of those annotations would be.  I think the PRs that we have are pretty close to what we have here.
### Proxy protocol support:
- `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-proxy-protocol=*`

This is required to get the client IP, but the service must be aware of the extra header bytes that are sent.  Likely our ingress controllers will turn this on and then set an HTTP X-Forwarded-For header, and also some advanced services might set it also to indicate they "speak proxy protocol".

cc @williamsandrew and cf #24569 
### SSL support at the ELB:
- `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-ssl-cert=arn:aws:acm:us-east-1:123456789012:certificate/12345678-1234-1234-1234-123456789012`
- `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-ssl-ports=*` (or e.g. `https`)

If the user wants the ELB to do SSL decryption, they should set these annotations.  ssl-cert specifies the certificate to use; ssl-ports specifies on which ports we should enable SSL.  ssl-ports can be optional and default to "*".  We need not implement ssl-ports right away, because the primary use for SSL and non-SSL is likely http and https for webservers, and they will likely use ingress, which will likely use SNI instead.  (But I do think some people will want direct-to-the-service http & https, so I bet we'll want it eventually..)

cc @therc and cf #23495 
### DNS support at the service level:
- `service.beta.kubernetes.io/hostname=myservice.myzone.com`

If set, Kubernetes will configure a DNS alias for the ELB.  Because this isn't specific to AWS, I don't think it gets an "aws-" prefix.

cc @chbatey and @quinton-hoole and cf #21397
### Sharing / reusing an ELB
- `service.beta.kubernetes.io/load-balancer-secret=some-sort-of-secret-value`

This allows an ELB to be (safely?) shared between two k8s clusters.  If set, k8s will look for an ELB with a tag derived from the secret.  If it finds one, it will use that ELB, otherwise it will create one (and tag it).  In this way, two k8s clusters with services with the same tag will share an ELB.  If the secret is kept reasonably secret then a user won't be able to "steal" someone else's ELB (this will be more realistic when we have RBAC etc).

cf #23483

body:
This has come up a bunch of times in conversations.  The idea is that some external orchestration is being performed and the user needs to signal (SIGHUP usually, but arbitrary) pods.  Sometimes this is related to ConfigMap (#22368) and sometimes not.  This also can be used to "bounce" pods.

We can't currently signal across containers in a pod, so any sort of sidecar is out for now.

We can do it by `docker kill`, but something like `kubectl signal` is clumsy - it's not clearly an API operation (unless we revisit
'operation' constructs for managing imperative async actions).

Another issue is that a pod doesn't really exist - do we signal one container?  Which one?  Maybe all containers?  Or do we nominate a signalee in the pod spec?

title: Improve Redis example

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

body:
A few points of improvement of the Redis example on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/examples/redis:
- Configuration files should include only fields that deviate from the [default](http://download.redis.io/redis-stable/redis.conf) in order to clarify. For example for `redis-master.conf` it could probably be (excluding comments) using [CONFIG GET](http://redis.io/commands/config-get) to check, or just use a single `redis.conf` like:
  
  ```
  save 900 1
  save 300 10
  save 60 10000
  dir /redis-master-data
  slaveof ${master-ip} ${master-port}  # only for slave, not when bootstrapping.
  ```
- Describe how to use in clients (should be to use the `redis-sentinel` host name but should be documented)
- Describe how to upgrade to newer versions of Redis, preferably using the `Deployment` Job.
- Could simplify [`run.sh`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/examples/redis/image/run.sh):
  - Use `cat some.config.template | envsubst > some.config` for both cases: `launchsentinel()` and `launchslave()`
  - Use Kubernetes `args: ["redis-server", "/redis-master/redis.conf"]` to start the master.
  - Use Kubernetes `args` to ask the `redis-master` Pod to start with master IP set to `$(hostname -i)`.
  - Possibly even remove completely `run.sh`
- Remove to describe `redis-proxy.yaml`

Extra question: Instead of `while true`, why not just let Kubernetes handle that? It seems useful to see pods restarting vs seeing them running. Of course one should include some probes (could be in the example as well), so that it'd get restarted anyway.

labels.name: sig/apps
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Apps.

body:
I have a deployment resource named: `helloworld`, with labels `app=helloworld,version=1`
I want to replace the deployment with a new version of image, but with an updated label, `version=2`

This seem to be impossible to do. If I do: `kubectl apply -f deployment-v2.yaml`, it'll tell me selector doesn't match template labels.

If I do `kubectl replace deployment helloworld -f deployment-v2.yaml`, it'll in fact replace the Deployment resource, and create a new ReplicaSet, and create new Pods with the new labels. But the old ReplicaSet and the old Pods with the `version=1` label are not removed.

Should the replace operation also remove any old ReplicaSet/Pods associated with the previous Deployment?

title: when finished rolling-update, couldn't know old pods names

labels.name: sig/apps

body:
Although we have elasticsearch to store pod logs, if one didn't list pods before rolling-update, it's a bit painful to find historical pod logs. It's better if we print old pods names and new pods names during rolling-update, so pod names can be traced.

For example, it's hard to find logs of my-nginx-xxxx in the following example.

```
root@master-1:/home/vagrant# /opt/bin/kubectl rolling-update my-nginx -f ./nginx-rc-new.yaml
Created my-nginx-v4
Scaling up my-nginx-v4 from 0 to 2, scaling down my-nginx from 2 to 0 (keep 2 pods available, don't exceed 3 pods)
Scaling my-nginx-v4 up to 1
Scaling my-nginx down to 1
Scaling my-nginx-v4 up to 2
Scaling my-nginx down to 0
Update succeeded. Deleting my-nginx
replicationcontroller "my-nginx" rolling updated to "my-nginx-v4"
```

If rolling-update output can list the names of the pods went down and the names of the pods going up, then we can check all the logs from the elasticsearch by pod name.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Hi,

I'm trying to get started (again, new machine, workplace bla bla) with Kubernetes but so far the experience if nothing short but confusing. I was expecting to have a clear documentation for how to start on a Ubuntu machine but in turn I can't find anything that correctly replicates the real life (especially since I can't remember what arcane stuff I've done the previous time to get it working).

I've spent more than an hour figuring out how to boot up the thing locally on my Ubuntu machine and I'm still not sure if I've understood how to do it.

I appreciate that the pace of development is fast and things move a lot but that's exactly why such a process must enforce that documentation matches what's in the code and the other way around.

If you look at other projects, the usually have a development period and a cool down period in which various features are documented and bugs are ironed out.

Also, any change that affects the users in terms of getting started should be accepted only if they provide the changes for the documentation as well.

Finally, no release should be done if there are still pending documentation issues that have not been sorted out as that leads to the current case where documentation is P2 or P3 or whatever P that's not critical for doing a release.

Please take a bit of time to improve experience for users as it's a pity to have an awesome project with a less than ideal documentation.

Thank you.

title: Add events for Volumes

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: area/admin
labels.description: Indicates an issue on admin area.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
I think it would be beneficial for debugging to add events about volumes in the system.  A couple examples:
1.  A PV should have an event recorded when it is attached / detached from a node.
2.  We should make an event when a mount happens (whether it failed or not)
3.  We should make an event when a volume is formatted (whether the format fails or not)

If a volume that requires a cloud provider attach is used directly in a pod, I suggest that event should be generated for that pod where applicable.  For example, detach may not be applicable since the pod will necessarily have been deleted or died.

For the record, I think this is probably more applicable to network storage than to things like secrets or configmaps, but it's not strictly PVs, since pods can use volumes directly without using PVs.

@kubernetes/sig-storage

Turns our that when running a container in host network, its `podStatus *kubecontainer.PodStatus` that is passed to dockertools.SyncPod() will always contain empty IP, as a result, the `PodIP` environment becomes empty.

Maybe we want to use the `apiPodStatus` instead of `podStatus` in this case to [determine the pod IP](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.3.0-alpha.2/pkg/kubelet/dockertools/manager.go#L1805-L1808) ? Since the apiPodStatus has the valid PodIP, which is [populated by kubelet](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.3.0-alpha.2/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L3271-L3278) when the container runs in host network.

Or just populate the podIP with hostIP in `dockertools.syncPod` when the container runs on host network.

Ref https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/22666

title: Quota not fully enforced in a HA setup?

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body: Reflectors are used extensively in Kubernetes to reduce the load on the etcd backend. In a non-HA setup, where there's only 1 apiserver, inconsistencies between what's in the local cache vs. what's actually in etcd probably doesn't matter as there's only 1 apiserver that's touching this data. However, in a non-HA setup, there's a higher chance of inconsistencies between local cache and etcd as multiple apiservers are in play. I could see there are corner cases that an apiserver could admit a pod to be created simply because its local cache is a bit behind the actual state. Could this happen? If so, are there anything put in place to mitigate such situation?

body:
One of the issues we face right now is that the various addons and cluster components have flags and parameters.  It's not at all clear which params apply to all settings, and which just apply to some, or what all the valid options are.  It strikes me as awfully similar to Linux's kconfig.

Imagine if things like network integrations and addons just registered themselves by existing in specific dirs with specifically named files.  Some `make config` process would walk the dirs, joining the input files into a tree of options, and then would allow you to configure your cluster turnup.  Once finished, it would generate a `cluster.yaml` or something which would be used by kube-up (or its successors) to set up the cluster.  That yaml could even find itsway into a config map.  This would be somethign users could check in to version control or share with colleagues or for support tickets.

This would be INFINITELY better than the existing config-default junk we have.

Obviously this is an idea, and not fully formed.

@mikedanese

title: kubectl third party resource race

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
When registering more than one ThirdPartyResource, there appears to be a race in kubectl for the ability to read the APIs. Note that all these commands are executed sequentially, and an empty response on the `get` is due to no objects being registered (this is an expected behavior). This is using kubectl at e81663c8242b54eafa9c97d947339a02b0d23780, which is after #18835 landed. 

```
$ cat tprs.yml
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
description: A foo
kind: ThirdPartyResource
metadata:
  name: foo.foo.example.com
versions:
- name: v1

---
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
description: A bar
kind: ThirdPartyResource
metadata:
  name: bar.bar.example.com
versions:
- name: v1
$ kubectl create -f tprs.yml 
thirdpartyresource "foo.foo.example.com" created
thirdpartyresource "bar.bar.example.com" created
$ kubectl get foos
error: unknown api group/version: foo.example.com/v1, Kind=Foo
$ kubectl get bars
error: unknown api group/version: bar.example.com/v1, Kind=Bar
$ kubectl get bars
error: unknown api group/version: bar.example.com/v1, Kind=Bar
$ kubectl get bars
$ kubectl get foos
$ kubectl get foos
error: unknown api group/version: foo.example.com/v1, Kind=Foo
$ kubectl get foos
$ kubectl get foos
$
```

I believe the fix is here, but I'm not in a position to properly test (although I did test a kubectl build by hand and it seemed to work). 

```
diff --git a/pkg/apimachinery/registered/registered.go b/pkg/apimachinery/registered/registered.go
index c1e1511..110ef1b 100644
--- a/pkg/apimachinery/registered/registered.go
+++ b/pkg/apimachinery/registered/registered.go
@@ -202,7 +202,7 @@ func AddThirdPartyAPIGroupVersions(gvs ...unversioned.GroupVersion) []unversione
        for ix := range filteredGVs {
                next[ix] = filteredGVs[ix]
        }
-       thirdPartyGroupVersions = next
+       thirdPartyGroupVersions = append(thirdPartyGroupVersions, next...)

        return skippedGVs
 }
```

title: Informer should not saturate workqueue with sync events

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

body:
Initial discussion is in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/24323
#### Problem:

When cluster is large and a periodic relist happens, a large number of RCs added by Sync event will block the work queue, thus RCs added by Added/Updated/Deleted event may have a long latency(those events are usually caused by users, they should be processed ASAP).

> I have done a benchmark about replication_controller: if we have 1000 namespace, each have 10 RCs, each RC have 10 replicas(so, 100, 000 pod in total), when periodic list happens, replication_controller need 20s to process the RCs added into work queue by relist, which means if a user create a new RC just at that time, it will be processed after 20 seconds. Users are always captious and impatient.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/23394 propose to distinguish relist and resync, but that's not enough:

> IIUC, use replication_controller as example:
> - Relist means "reflector send LIST request to etcd, replace local cache with items get form etcd, and put all deltas to a queue, then the controller framework pop deltas from the queue and put the RC need to process to work queue".
> - Resync means "go through the items in the local cache, put all RCs(in local cache) to work queue".
> 
> Since both relist and resync will add ALL RCs(all RCs from etcd when relist, all RCs from local storage when resync) to work queue, when cluster is large, a large number of RCs will block work queue for a long time. If a unfortunate user create a new RC just at that time, he will get a bad user experience.
#### Proposal

If my understanding of relist/resync is correct, I propose to let [work queue](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/replication/replication_controller.go#L93) respect priority: RCs added by Added/Updated/Deleted event(usually caused by users operation) will have a higher priority when pop, so they could be processed ASAP. RCs added by periodic relist/resync will have a relatively lower priority.

This proposal and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/23394 is not conflict, they are complementary actually.

title: Cassandra on Kubernetes - Seed Provider and Snitch

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
# Background

This project currently contains a custom [SeedProvider](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/examples/cassandra/java/src/io/k8s/cassandra/KubernetesSeedProvider.java) that allows for discovery within a kubernetes cluster.  This issue is covering design and improvements around this initiative.  Once stable these components are stable recommended that this code gets moved into the Apache Cassandra code base.  But since the code lives here ... This is where we start.
# Definitions
## Seed Provider / Gossip

https://docs.datastax.com/en/cassandra/3.x/cassandra/configuration/configCassandra_yaml.html?scroll=configCassandra_yaml__seed_provider

> When a node first starts up, it looks at its cassandra.yaml configuration file to determine the name of the Cassandra cluster it belongs to; which nodes (called seeds) to contact to obtain information about the other nodes in the cluster; and other parameters for determining port and range information.
> 
> seed_provider 
> The addresses of hosts deemed contact points. Cassandra nodes use the -seeds list to find each other and learn the topology of the ring.
> class_name (Default: org.apache.cassandra.locator.SimpleSeedProvider)
> The class within Cassandra that handles the seed logic. It can be customized, but this is typically not required.
> - seeds (Default: 127.0.0.1)
>   A comma-delimited list of IP addresses used by gossip for bootstrapping new nodes joining a cluster. When running multiple nodes, you must change the list from the default value. In multiple data-center clusters, it is a good idea to include at least one node from each data center (replication group) in the seed list. Designating more than a single seed node per data center is recommended for fault tolerance. Otherwise, gossip has to communicate with another data center when bootstrapping a node. Making every node a seed node is not recommended because of increased maintenance and reduced gossip performance. Gossip optimization is not critical, but it is recommended to use a small seed list (approximately three nodes per data center).

Snitches - https://docs.datastax.com/en/cassandra/3.x/cassandra/architecture/archSnitchesAbout.html

> A snitch determines which data centers and racks nodes belong to. They inform Cassandra about the network topology so that requests are routed efficiently and allows Cassandra to distribute replicas by grouping machines into data centers and racks. Specifically, the replication strategy places the replicas based on the information provided by the new snitch. All nodes must return to the same rack and data center. Cassandra does its best not to have more than one replica on the same rack (which is not necessarily a physical location).
# Tasks
- Document Current State - Document how the current provider operates, and is configured
- Asses Architecture - Are there any short term changes that are recommended
- PetSet - Determine architecture with future needs of the PetSet initiative
- Write code and drink much Scotch or Green Tea.
- Determine needs for allowing racks and multiple datacenter implementations.
# Current Challenges
- Documentation is lacking
- Current seed provider sets every C\* node as a seed ... not the best
- Code is not tested well
- Code is not built on correct version
- No multi rack support
- No multiple DC support

title: Amazon ELBs - ICMP and Network Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU)

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

milestone.title: v1.3
milestone.description: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/blob/master/release-1.3/release-1.3.md

body:
The firewall rules created on Amazon ELBs do not include ICMP. This means that issues can occur with PMTU. Please see below for more information.

When a HTTP/TCP request exceeds a certain payload size, with ELBs not allowing "ICMP request/reply", the request stalls. This is due to the ELB trying to send big packets to the client but the client dropping them since the MTU was higher than expected.

To avoid this ICMP traffic should be allowed on the ELB so they can negotiate the MTU:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Path_MTU_Discovery
- http://www.networkworld.com/article/2224654/cisco-subnet/mtu-size-issues.html
- http://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/network_mtu.html

When enabling ICMP traffic the client will be able to communicate with the ELB normally.

An example of what occurs when ICMP is not enabled.

```
$ time curl -v -O > /dev/null http://a8222e4ee025111e6a25d0a91ac3ee4d-1379358768.eu-west-1.elb.amazonaws.com/docs-api/swaggerui/lib/jquery.slideto.min.js
  % Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time    Time     Time  Current
                                 Dload  Upload   Total   Spent    Left  Speed
  0     0    0     0    0     0      0      0 --:--:-- --:--:-- --:--:--     0*   Trying 52.49.165.25...
* Connected to a8222e4ee025111e6a25d0a91ac3ee4d-1379358768.eu-west-1.elb.amazonaws.com (52.49.165.25) port 80 (#0)
> GET /docs-api/swaggerui/lib/jquery.slideto.min.js HTTP/1.1
> Host: a8222e4ee025111e6a25d0a91ac3ee4d-1379358768.eu-west-1.elb.amazonaws.com
> User-Agent: curl/7.43.0
> Accept: */*
> 
  0     0    0     0    0     0      0      0 --:--:--  0:00:29 --:--:--     0< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< content-length: 369
< content-type: application/javascript; charset=utf-8
< last-modified: Thu, 12 Feb 2015 14:06:22 GMT
< etag: "b849bafad46251cbced13d4b501694dd21bd7464"
< cache-control: no-cache
< accept-ranges: bytes
< Date: Thu, 14 Apr 2016 15:31:06 GMT
< Connection: keep-alive
< 
{ [369 bytes data]
100   369  100   369    0     0     12      0  0:00:30  0:00:29  0:00:01    85
* Connection #0 to host a8222e4ee025111e6a25d0a91ac3ee4d-1379358768.eu-west-1.elb.amazonaws.com left intact

real    0m29.547s
user    0m0.012s
sys 0m0.004s

```

Ideally security rules for ELBs should be allowed to be attached to an ELB via annotations and/or by default.

ICMP rules at a minimum to avoid this should cover:
- 0 - Echo Reply
- 8 - Echo Request

*\* Please note that this does not just affect Amazon ELBs, but in addition direct access to instances too.**

body:
When testing against rkt's prestop hooks support (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/23532),
I found that kubelet will try to kill pod more than once when deleting the pod. And the first when it kills, it calls rkt.KillPod() with a valid runningPod, and things work fine. But shortly after the pod is killed, it invokes rkt.KillPod() again. Not sure if this is a normal race case or a bug.

To reproduce:

```
$ cat /tmp/pod
# Copy of pod.yaml without file extension for test
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: busybox
  labels:
    name: busybox
spec:
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: busybox
    command:
    - sleep
    - "600"

apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1

apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: Deployment

body:
During writing container attach node e2e test, I found this.

Docker attach has an option called `Logs` (see [Docker Remote API](https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/api/docker_remote_api_v1.22/#attach-to-a-container)).
With this on, before each container attach docker will print the container log first (see [code](https://github.com/docker/docker/blob/5709f8e4227e0e1da333739c44003a3f47279bd5/daemon/attach.go#L77-L106))

The `Logs` option is supported in go-dockerclient (see [code](https://github.com/fsouza/go-dockerclient/blob/master/container.go#L1127)), while it is not supported in engine-api yet (see [code](https://github.com/docker/engine-api/blob/8924d6900370b4c7e7984be5adc61f50a80d7537/types/client.go#L14-L21)).

Before [switching to engine-api](#23506), the `Logs` option is **true** (see [old code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.2/pkg/kubelet/dockertools/manager.go#L1115)). While because engine-api doesn't support it, we don't set it now (see [code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/dockertools/kube_docker_client.go#L324-L331))

What is the expected behavior here? If needed, we could send a PR to engine-api to support it.

body:
I searched but didn't find this, so I'm going to propose it here.

Users should be able to easily 
- Mutate individual keys in a config map and secret
- Extract a configmap/secret to disk

This would enable simpler interaction in scripts that depend on it.

We should 
1. Add `kubectl set secret-data SECRET ...`
2. Add `kubectl extract secret/NAME [directory/file]`

Also, the `--from-literal` syntax makes me want to die a little on the inside every time I am forced to use it (for being the most common use case, it's about 12 characters too long to type).  It makes it too hard to mutate these fields.  We should at least consider how to apply the environment variable, annotation, and label syntax to these operations.

```
# create a secret
kubectl create secret generic foo --from-literal=PASSWORD=something

# extract the secret to disk in the current directory as a file "PASSWORD" with contents "something"
kubectl extract secret/foo

# mutate the secret
kubectl set secret-data foo --from-literal=PASSWORD=other
```

and similar operations for config.

title: Deleting in-use PVs and PVCs leads to erratic behavior

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Currently, Kubernetes places no restrictions on deleting PVs and PVCs.  Because of this, if users delete these resources in an unexpected order, strange and incorrect behavior can result.  There are essentially two parts to this issue, but they seem similar, so I'm grouping them in the same issue for now.
## Deleting bound PVs before PVCs

Suppose a user has a PV, `test-vol`, currently bound to a PVC, `test-claim`.  Then the following sequence of events happens:

```
    kubectl delete test-vol
    kubectl create -f test-claim2.yaml
    kubectl create -f test-vol.yaml
```

Once this is done, running `kubectl get pvc` will show both `test-claim` and `test-claim2` to be bound to `test-vol`.  Pods that reference `test-claim2` will be able to start successfully, while pods that reference `test-claim` will hang in the ContainerCreating state.
## Deleting PVCs in use by a pod

As long as the pod remains up, the pod will continue running successfully (assuming the storage underlying the PVC has not been deallocated).  However, if the pod crashes and is brought back up, one of two cases can happen:
- If no PVC with the name of the deleted PVC exists, the pod will enter CrashLoopBackoff (this should be expected.
- If a new PVC has been created with the same name, the pod will restart with the underlying storage for that PVC mounted.  This will occur even if the PVC has bound to a different PV.

Neither of these cases seem like urgent problems--they rely on users behaving badly--but they could easily lead to confusion or, in the case of in-use PVC deletion, they could enable attacks.  There may be other cases similar to these, but these are what I've noticed so far.

title: kubectl get all should show resource types in headers or column

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
When running `kubectl get all` I can see the different types of resources running in the cluster but if I want to delete/remove/get one of the resources I don't know what type it is.

e.g.

``` sh
$ kubectl get all --all-namespaces
NAMESPACE     NAME                DESIRED        CURRENT            AGE
kube-system   kube-dns-v9         1              1                  26m
NAMESPACE     NAME                CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP        PORT(S)         AGE
default            kubernetes          172.23.0.1     <none>             443/TCP         45m
kube-system   kube-dns            172.23.0.100   <none>             53/UDP,53/TCP   26m
NAMESPACE     NAME                READY          STATUS             RESTARTS        AGE
default       kube-proxy-node1   1/1            Running            0               35m
default       kube-proxy-node2   1/1            Running            0               33m
default       kube-proxy-node3   1/1            Running            0               32m
kube-system   kube-dns-v9-yoir3   3/4            CrashLoopBackOff   7               26m
```

But if I want to do anything with kube-dns-v9 I have to know what resource type it is.

The header row should say what type of objects it is listing so I can more easily get details about the objects.

e.g.

``` sh
(ReplicationControllers) NAMESPACE     NAME                DESIRED        CURRENT            AGE
kube-system   kube-dns-v9         1              1                  26m
(Services) NAMESPACE     NAME                CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP        PORT(S)         AGE
default            kubernetes          172.23.0.1     <none>             443/TCP         45m
kube-system   kube-dns            172.23.0.100   <none>             53/UDP,53/TCP   26m
(Pods) NAMESPACE     NAME                READY          STATUS             RESTARTS        AGE
default       kube-proxy-node1   1/1            Running            0               35m
default       kube-proxy-node2   1/1            Running            0               33m
default       kube-proxy-node3   1/1            Running            0               32m
kube-system   kube-dns-v9-yoir3   3/4            CrashLoopBackOff   7               26m
```

Or maybe it'd be helpful for interactive usage to leave off the headers and add a new column with TYPE

``` sh
NAMESPACE     NAME                DESIRED        CURRENT            AGE     TYPE
kube-system       kube-dns-v9     1              1                 26m       rc
```

This would make other cli tools (grep, awk) much easier to use with `kubectl` output because then I can do something like `kubectl get all --all-namespaces | grep rc` and get all of the replication controllers. I know I can use `kubectl get rc` but there are still more powerful cli tools that I may want like excluding rc ( `grep -v rc` ) or printing and looping on a specific column from the output (eg `kubectl get all | grep -v ing | awk '{print $2}'` )

title: Jenkins can create CI versions that release scripts don't like

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/release-eng
labels.description: Issues or PRs related to the Release Engineering subproject

body:
On the `release-1.2` build today, the builds started failing due to the version not matching required regular expressions.

The last passing build had version `v1.2.1-beta.0.42+60bda7b53ec344-dirty`.
Then the release version updated, making the next build have version `v1.2.2-beta.0-dirty`, and this failed:

```
!!! [0401 11:18:38] Invalid ci version: 'v1.2.2-beta.0-dirty', must match regex ^v(0|[1-9][0-9]*)\.(0|[1-9][0-9]*)\.(0|[1-9][0-9]*)-(beta|alpha)\.(0|[1-9][0-9]*)(\.(0|[1-9][0-9]*)\+[-0-9a-z]*)?$
```

It looks like the previous version worked because the `+[sha1]` part allowed the `-dirty` tag at the end to match. Without that sha1 appended, the `-` in `-dirty` was now disallowed.

I'm not familiar enough with our versioning scheme to know if the version generated is incorrect, or if the regex matching it is incorrect. (My personal opinion is that `-dirty` builds should always fail on Jenkins, though that's an aside.)

cc @kubernetes/goog-testing @david-mcmahon @ihmccreery

title: Kubernetes scheduler doesn't support N+1 fault tolerance in the presence of automated shutdowns and restarts of VMs

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
I experienced that the kubernetes scheduler doesn't redistribute pods of a service across multiple nodes after suspended or shutdown VMs come back on-line. This isn't a problem with clusters with high number of nodes but in small clusters with 2 or 3 nodes, it is a problem in the sense that N+1 fault tolerance is not guaranteed for services. I was able to arrive at situation where all pods of a service are placed on the same node, and there is no timeout handler that triggers the scheduler to relocate the pods. 

I have experienced the same scheduler behavior with Juju as Kubernetes Provider and also in Google Container Engine. In the latter environment, GKE shutdowns the single node were all pods of a service were located, leading to temporary unavailability of the service.

Below you find my findings in Juju and GKE
## Juju

I have an openstack environment with 3 kubernetes units, and a redis service deployed with 4 replicated pods

```
ubuntu@juju-openstack-machine-5:~$ kubectl get nodes
NAME            LABELS                                 STATUS    AGE
172.17.13.141   kubernetes.io/hostname=172.17.13.141   Ready     1d
172.17.13.144   kubernetes.io/hostname=172.17.13.144   Ready     1d
172.17.13.145   kubernetes.io/hostname=172.17.13.145   Ready     1d

ubuntu@juju-openstack-machine-5:~$ kubectl get services
NAME          CLUSTER_IP    EXTERNAL_IP   PORT(S)     SELECTOR                            AGE
kubernetes    10.1.0.1      <none>        443/TCP     <none>                              1d
redis-slave   10.1.2.166    <none>        6379/TCP    app=redis,role=slave,tier=backend   1d

ubuntu@juju-openstack-machine-5:~$ kubectl get rc
CONTROLLER    CONTAINER(S)   IMAGE(S)                                 SELECTOR                            REPLICAS   AGE
redis-slave   slave          gcr.io/google_samples/gb-redisslave:v1   app=redis,role=slave,tier=backend   4          1d
```

First when I suspend 2 machines in my openstack dashboard, all pods are placed on the remaining machine after a timeout of 5 minutes..

Then, when I resume the two suspended machines in my openstack dashboard,  the pods are not replicated across different machines to ensure fault tolerance of services
I thought the specification of scheduling entails that when you create a service and thereafter a replicacontroller, pods should always be placed on different machines if that is possible However, this behavior does not occur. Below you find some command output for the redis-slave service which have 4 replicated pods.  It shows that all 4 pods are placed on the same machine.

```
ubuntu@juju-openstack-machine-5:~$ kubectl describe pod -l app=redis | grep Node
Node:                           172.17.13.144/172.17.13.144
Node:                           172.17.13.144/172.17.13.144
Node:                           172.17.13.144/172.17.13.144
Node:                           172.17.13.144/172.17.13.144
```
## GKE

I found out that the reported behavior of Kubernetes Juju bundle also appears in Google Container Engine. See attached RAW file.

Below I describe the findings

This was my initial desired state:

```
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl get nodes
NAME                               STATUS    AGE
gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-7mmj   Ready     1m
gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-buym   Ready     1m
gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-demf   Ready     1m
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl run nginx --image nginx --port=80
deployment "nginx" created
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl describe pods -l run | grep Node
Node:           gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-7mmj/10.128.0.2
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl scale deployment nginx --replicas=0
deployment "nginx" scaled
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl expose deployment nginx
service "nginx" exposed
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl scale deployment nginx --replicas=3
deployment "nginx" scaled
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl describe pods -l run | grep Node
Node:           gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-7mmj/10.128.0.2
Node:           gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-demf/10.128.0.4
Node:           gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-buym/10.128.0.3
```

Then I suspended 2 machines via the google cloud engine dashboard. These machines were automatically restarted by google container engine

At a certain moment I reached the following state:

```
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl get nodes
NAME                               STATUS    AGE
gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-7mmj   Ready     1m
gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-buym   Ready     4m
gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-demf   Ready     22m
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl describe pods -l run | grep Node:
Node:           gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-demf/10.128.0.4
Node:           gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-demf/10.128.0.4
Node:           gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-demf/10.128.0.4
```

Then google container engine's behavior diverted from the kubernetes-core bundle. In fact google container engine did something very surprising: It suspended the machine where all 3 replicas were placed:

```
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl get nodes
NAME                               STATUS     AGE
gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-7mmj   Ready      5m
gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-buym   Ready      8m
gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-demf   NotReady   26m
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl describe pods -l run | grep Node:
Node:           gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-demf/10.128.0.4
Node:           gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-demf/10.128.0.4
Node:           gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-demf/10.128.0.4
```

At this point the nginx service was unavailable:

```
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl describe pods -l run | grep IP:
IP:
IP:
IP:
```

I think google container engine suspended 10.128.0.4 in order to trigger the replication controller (aka deployment manager) to redistribute the pods. Indeed after some time 

```
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl describe pods -l run | grep IP:
IP:             10.0.1.2
IP:             10.0.1.3
IP:             10.0.0.4
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl describe pods -l run | grep Node:
Node:           gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-7mmj/10.128.0.2
Node:           gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-7mmj/10.128.0.2
Node:           gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-buym/10.128.0.3
[centos@public-kubernetes-gw ~]$ kubectl get nodes
NAME                               STATUS     AGE
gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-7mmj   Ready      10m
gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-buym   Ready      13m
gke-cluster-1-09071288-node-demf   NotReady   31m
```
## Summary

I think there is an issue with Kubernetes. I had a look at how the scheduler of kubernetes is designed It is policy-configurable and extensible. 

The default policy of the scheduler corresponds with the policy below. As you can see, the scheduler policy would definitively change the situation where all pods of a service run a single node and the other nodes are idle. 
So the question is: why is the scheduler never invoked to change that situation in the Kubernetes-core bundle? 

In Google Container Engine scenario, a too drastic approach is taken to trigger the scheduler: Shutting down that single node in order to let the scheduler become active. 

```
{
    "kind" : "Policy",
    "version" : "v1",
    "predicates" : [
        {"name" : "PodFitsPorts"},
        {"name" : "PodFitsResources"},
        {"name" : "NoDiskConflict"},
        {"name" : "MatchNodeSelector"},
        {"name" : "HostName"}
    ],
    "priorities" : [
        {"name" : "LeastRequestedPriority", "weight" : 1},
        {"name" : "BalancedResourceAllocation", "weight" : 1},
        {"name" : "ServiceSpreadingPriority", "weight" : 1}
    ]
}
```

title: kubectl: auth failures on discovery give confusing message

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
`kubectl` often says something like this when the problem is your authentication token: `failed to negotiate an api version; server supports: map[], client supports: map[v1:{} batch/v1:{} componentconfig/v1alpha1:{}...`

Kubectl should detect the 401 and report a auth error, not this discovery error.

title: Docker build fails with 'could not find bridge docker0'

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

body:
*_BUG REPORT *_

When trying to run `docker build` inside a container with docker mounted into it the build starts of fine, but fails to create and endpoint on network bridge docker0 as soon as the build process hits the first RUN command.

```
Executing "docker build --force-rm=true --no-cache=true --file=target/docker/Dockerfile --tag=****:1.0.258 ."

Sending build context to Docker daemon 557.1 kB
...
Sending build context to Docker daemon 78.04 MB

Step 1 : FROM travix/base-debian-jre8
 ---> a130b5e1b4d4
Step 2 : ADD ***-1.0.258.jar ***.jar
 ---> 8d53e68e93a0
Removing intermediate container d1a758c9baeb
Step 3 : ADD target/newrelic newrelic
 ---> 9dbbb1c1db58
Removing intermediate container 461e66978c53
Step 4 : RUN bash -c "touch /***.jar"
 ---> Running in 6a28f48c9fd1
Removing intermediate container 6a28f48c9fd1
failed to create endpoint stupefied_shockley on network bridge: adding interface veth095b905 to bridge docker0 failed: could not find bridge docker0: route ip+net: no such network interface
```

The agents are deployed with the following manifest (leaving out a couple of envvars that don't seem relevant for sake of brevity):

```
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: gocd-agent
spec:
  replicas: 2
  strategy:
    type: Recreate
  revisionHistoryLimit: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: gocd-agent
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: gocd-agent
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: gocd-agent
        image: travix/gocd-agent:16.10.0
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        securityContext:
          privileged: true
        volumeMounts:
        - name: docker-sock
          mountPath: /var/run/docker.sock
        - name: docker-bin
          mountPath: /usr/bin/docker
        env:
        - name: "DOCKER_GID_ON_HOST"
          value: "107"
      volumes:
      - name: docker-sock
        hostPath:
          path: /var/run/docker.sock
      - name: docker-bin
        hostPath:
          path: /usr/bin/docker
```

Inside the container I make a _docker_ group and add the _go_ user that runs the build to that group so it works without sudo.

```
groupadd -g $DOCKER_GID_ON_HOST docker && gpasswd -a go docker
```

The interesting thing is that it used to work fine when running a vm based on the following image:
- https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/google-containers/global/images/container-vm-v20160321

With this container manifest:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: gocd-agent
spec:
  containers:
  - name: gocd-agent
    image: travix/gocd-agent:16.10.0
    imagePullPolicy: Always
    volumeMounts:
    - name: docker-sock
      mountPath: /var/run/docker.sock
    - name: docker-bin
      mountPath: /usr/bin/docker
    env:
    - name: "DOCKER_GID_ON_HOST"
      value: "107"
  restartPolicy: Always
  dnsPolicy: Default
  volumes:
  - name: docker-sock
    hostPath:
      path: /var/run/docker.sock
  - name: docker-bin
    hostPath:
      path: /usr/bin/docker
```

The big difference seems to lie in the networking setup for the container vm and the container engine cluster. We also tested it with host networking, but that didn't make a difference.

A couple of stats about the Kubernetes / Container Engine cluster that might help.

**Kubernetes version**

1.3.5 on Google Container Engine using the non-GCI host image. GCI fails in a different way and has a different gid for the _docker_ group.

title: clients: Make it obvious when you should call Update and when you should call UpdateStatus

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
Currently if you e.g. make changes only in the status of a resource and then call Update, the server appears to accept your request but doesn't actually make any changes. (This is intentional, because you should use UpdateStatus for status changes.)

This is probably very confusing the first time you encounter it. The easiest fix is just documentation.

Note that we can't make the server warn or fail your request if you change the status, because the point of the spec/status split is to not penalize clients with a lot of conflicts if a controller is rapidly updating the status. That is, the situation is exactly the same as if you didn't change status, but a controller did.

We could maybe get fancier, like make the server reject a request if it has _only_ status changes and no other changes.

Longer term, if the object that you sent in an update didn't include status at all, then it would be obvious that that was not supposed to work. But that's a much larger api change.

title: Kubelet volume manager fails to reconstruct volume information if global mount path is gone

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
## Problem:

If pod is deleted while kubelet is restarted, master might detach volume while it is not yet unmounted. In this situation, the following sequence might happen.
1.  Kubelet restarts, all information about mounted volumes are gone. Node updates its status indicating that no volume is mounted currently. (but the truth is that volume is still mounted)
2. Master deletes the pod, volume reconciler detaches the volume because it thinks the volume is not mounted anymore. 
3. On node, global mount path is gone because of detach. But the bind mount path for the volume is still there. Volume manager reconstruct process scans the directory but could not get the device path so fails to reconstruct the volume information. The kubelet cleanupOrphanedPodDirs will also fail to clean the pod directory because the bind mount still exists.
## Proposed solution:

Please refer to #33203. The root cause of this problem is master is trying to detach while volumes are still mounted. The global path is gone while bind mount still exist. If the proposed approach in #33203 can completely avoid this problem, this PR is not required to do anything. However, considering human intervention or other inferences, it is better to take extra step to avoid this situation.
If global device path could not be found, reconstruct can use fake information to put into the state. Based on the state, reconciler will use the available information to unmount bind mount. Unmount global mount path is not needed since it is no longer exist.

title: Idea: "merge" volumes

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
A common problem we hear today is that people want to consume a Secret or ConfigMap as a file or files in a existing directory, without hiding the other files therein.  The semantics of volumeMounts today do not allow this by default, though it can be achieved using subPath, one volumeMount per file.  A downside to this approach is that the Secret and ConfigMap file(s) are not auto-updated because bind mounts bind to the inode, not the dentry.

An idea to solve this, though it's a little tricky.  Consider the case of wanting to project one Secret file and one ConfigMap file into /etc.

1) Define Secret and ConfigMap volumes as normal
2) volumeMount them onto /vol/secret and /vol/cfgmap
2) Create a new flavor of volumeMount that merges them

```
volumeMounts:
  - name: my-secret
    mountPath: /vol/secret
  - name: my-cfgmap
    mountPath: /vol/cfgmap
  - name: my-etc
    mountPath: /etc
    merge:
      - /vol/secret
      - /vol/cfgmap
```

Kubelet would recognize that no volume named "my-etc" exists (but I think that field is required), nbut the "merge" key does exist.  It would make a temp directory and bind mount everything from the container's /etc into the temp dir, one-by-one (with a limit, maybe 1024).  Then it would iterate /vol/secret, and symlink from /etc for every file.  Repeat for cfgmap.  Finally, bind mount that onto /etc.

Net result is that /etc/exists as it did before, but it includes symlinks to volume-projected files.

The tricky part of this is that it has to have access to the container's mounted and prepared rootfs before the container starts, which I don't think is possible yet.  Filing this for future opportunities.

milestone.description: Milestone placeholder for items that didn't make it into 1.4 but should be merged before 1.5 is generally opened up

body:
This is probably not that hard to fix, but it will want an e2e case to cover it.

```
$ cat /tmp/hdls.yaml 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: headless
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  ports:
  - port: 80
  selector:
    run: headless

$ k create -f /tmp/hdls.yaml 
service "headless" created

$ k get svc headless -o yaml | grep clusterIP
  clusterIP: None

$ k get svc headless -o yaml | sed '/clusterIP/d' | k replace -f -
service "headless" replaced

$ k get svc headless -o yaml | grep clusterIP

$ sleep 10; k get svc headless -o yaml | grep clusterIP

$
```

Additionally, if I manually assign an IP it is not verified:

```
$ k get svc
NAME         CLUSTER-IP   EXTERNAL-IP     PORT(S)   AGE
headless     10.0.0.93    <none>          80/TCP    4m
hostnames    10.0.0.93    104.197.1.173   80/TCP    4d
kubernetes   10.0.0.1     <none>          443/TCP   6d
```

And kube-proxy is VERY confused.

title: AWS volume pending for detach for 30 minutes due to busy status

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

body:
During testing a AWS cluster, found AWS volume once was pending for detach about 30 minutes. According to the log, the following happened,
- controller issues a detach operation
- after detach response returns, it periodically checks the status until it reaches "detached". However, in this test, the status is "busy" all the time. 
- after reaching the timeout 30 mins, detach function returns error because the status is not "detached"
