body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**

FEATURE REQUEST

Please enable ConfigMaps to store binary files as well as character files.

**Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`):

```
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"3", GitVersion:"v1.3.6", GitCommit:"ae4550cc9c89a593bcda6678df201db1b208133b", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2016-08-26T18:13:23Z", GoVersion:"go1.6.2", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"3", GitVersion:"v1.3.6+coreos.0", GitCommit:"f6f0055b8e503cbe5fb7b6f1a2ee37d0f160c1cd", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2016-08-29T17:01:01Z", GoVersion:"go1.6.2", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
```

**Environment**:
- **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**: HP EliteOne 800 G1 AiO
- **OS** (e.g. from /etc/os-release):

```
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION="16.04.1 LTS (Xenial Xerus)"
ID=ubuntu
ID_LIKE=debian
PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 16.04.1 LTS"
VERSION_ID="16.04"
HOME_URL="http://www.ubuntu.com/"
SUPPORT_URL="http://help.ubuntu.com/"
BUG_REPORT_URL="http://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/"
UBUNTU_CODENAME=xenial
```
- **Kernel** (e.g. `uname -a`) (kubectl client):  `Linux derek-HP-EliteOne-800-G1-AiO 4.4.0-36-generic #55-Ubuntu SMP Thu Aug 11 18:01:55 UTC 2016 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux
  `
- Target environment is a three node Vagrant (VirtualBox) cluster running CoreOS 1164.1.0.

**What happened?**

After creating a ConfigMap from a directory containing a binary Java keystore file, command `kubctl describe configmap` reported a size for the binary file that was larger than the original file:

```
derek@derek-HP-EliteOne-800-G1-AiO~:$ kubectl describe configmap platinum-fix-brvm-config
Name:       platinum-fix-brvm-config
Namespace:  default
Labels:     <none>
Annotations:    <none>

Data
====
brvm-fix44.xml: 334363 bytes
keystore.jks:   2266 bytes
settings.txt:   910 bytes
derek@derek-HP-EliteOne-800-G1-AiO~:$ ls -l keystore.jks 
-rw-rw-r-- 1 derek derek 1326 Sep  9 17:52 keystore.jks
```

When run inside a container having a mounted volume created from the ConfigMap, command `ls --format=long --dereference keystore.jks` also reported a file size larger than the original: 

```
-rw-r--r--. 1 root root 2266 Sep 10 00:58 keystore.jks
```

A Java application in the container that attempted to read `keystore.jks` reported an exception claiming that the file was invalid.

**What did you expect to happen?**
- Kubernetes reports the size of the binary file in the ConfigMap as the same as the original file.
- Kubernetes container log reports the size of the binary file in the ConfigMap as the same as the original file.
- Java application successfully reads binary file `keystore.jks`.
- Result of command `file keystore.jks` should be `keystore.jks: Java KeyStore`.

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):
1. Create a ConfigMap from a directory that contains a Java keystore file (or some other binary file).
2. Run `kubectl describe configmap` and observe the file size.
3. Compare the file size in the ConfigMap to the original file size. 
4. Map the ConfigMap to a volume, mount the volume in a container, and run `ls --format=long --dereference keystore.jks` and compare the file size of the result to the original file size.

body:
This is more confusing than harmful.

I noticed while editing a pod that the YAML wrapped a string.  The below has line numbers turned on:

```
  5 apiVersion: v1
  6 kind: Pod
  7 metadata:
  8   annotations:
  9     kubernetes.io/created-by: |
 10       {"kind":"SerializedReference","apiVersion":"v1","reference":{"kind":"ReplicaSet","namespace":"default","name":"hostnames-1190964384",    "uid":"f4ff207f-6b1c-11e6-aa24-42010af00003","apiVersion":"extensions","resourceVersion":"2341030"}}
 11     kubernetes.io/limit-ranger: 'LimitRanger plugin set: cpu request for container
 12       hostnames'
 13   creationTimestamp: 2016-09-08T23:32:03Z
```

Note that line 12 is a wrap of line 11.  Apparently this is valid YAML.  Reading it as JSON shows:

```
        "annotations": {
            "kubernetes.io/created-by": "{\"kind\":\"SerializedReference\",\"apiVersion\":\"v1\",\"reference\":{\"kind\":\"ReplicaSet\",\"namespace\":\"default\",\"name\":\"hostnames-1190964384\",\"uid\":\"f4ff207f-6b1c-11e6-aa24-42010af00003\",\"apiVersion\":\"extensions\",\"resourceVersion\":\"2341030\"}}\n",
            "kubernetes.io/limit-ranger": "LimitRanger plugin set: cpu request for container hostnames"
        },
```

Rejoining the lines in the editor (kubectl edit) comes back as "Edit cancelled, no changes made."

I don't know who is deciding to wrap that, or why, but it caused me to wonder if it was broken.

title: Component configuration improvement suggestions

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: sig/cluster-lifecycle
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Cluster Lifecycle.

body:
Below are a couple of suggestions to improve the component configuration code, based on lessons we've learned in OpenShift.
## Group related options together

As mentioned [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/13146#issuecomment-153013521), we've found that it's easier to group related items together. For example, instead of having

``` yaml
kind: KubeControllerManagerConfiguration
version: v1alpha1
concurrentRSSyncs: 2
lookupCacheSizeForRS: 500
```

you could have this:

``` yaml
kind: KubeControllerManagerConfiguration
version: v1alpha1
replicaSets:
  workers: 2
  cacheSize: 500
```

This has the added advantage that similar "types" of settings can look quite similar; for example, you could have all of the various controllers that have a configurable number of workers and cache size use the consistent keys `workers` and `cacheSize`.
## Separate structs for flags, serializable config, and runtime config

Just like in Kubernetes going forward, in OpenShift, we want to minimize the number of command-line flags you have to specify to run a component. We also want to be able to serialize configuration to/from disk. And we want to be able to take the deserialized configuration, apply various transformations to it, resulting in a runtime configuration that can be used to run a component. Let's take a look at some examples to highlight the reasoning behind why we think it's necessary to have three different structs for configuration.
### Struct for flags

OpenShift has a [`MasterArgs`](https://github.com/openshift/origin/blob/de0ae2d896d072305dc9c6fc61c8abb956ae53b3/pkg/cmd/server/start/master_args.go#L31-L80) struct that holds fields into which command-line flag values are stored. This isn't meant to be an exhaustive list of every possible configuration setting; instead, its purpose is to hold "just enough" flags to be able to start up a master server. Some of the flags we support include the host & port for the master, the etcd server URL, a list of additional certificate authorities to trust, and CORS allowed origins.

You can start OpenShift without setting any of these flags, as we provide sensible defaults for them. You can also choose to customize some flags, but again the list of flags is minimal. If you want to tweak anything else, you have to invoke OpenShift and instruct it to write out a config file, which you can then edit (`openshift start --write-config=/path/to/config/dir`).
### Struct for serializable configuration

The config file generated above is the serialized representation of a second struct used for configuration (OpenShift's [`pkg/cmd/server/api/v1.MasterConfig`](https://github.com/openshift/origin/blob/de0ae2d896d072305dc9c6fc61c8abb956ae53b3/pkg/cmd/server/api/v1/types.go#L153)). This contains the full set of options neeeded to configure the component. It must be possible to populate this struct from the values specified in a config file. Once the config struct is populated, it is transformed into a struct used at runtime to run the component.
### Struct used at runtime

The struct used at runtime (e.g. [`pkg/cmd/server/origin.MasterConfig`](https://github.com/openshift/origin/blob/de0ae2d896d072305dc9c6fc61c8abb956ae53b3/pkg/cmd/server/origin/master_config.go#L92)) is not designed to be serializable. It is meant to hold information in the most appropriate format for execution. This means it has fields of types such as `admission.Interface`, `restclient.Config`, and `storage.Interface`, to name a few. These unserializable types are instantiated using the settings from the struct containing the serializable configuration details.

xref #12245

title: Fix data decode and retention mechanics

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
This is obtuse to explain so I will try my best... 

In the storage layer we decode objects that come in off the wire from etcd.  That's all objects, irrespective of what we use higher up the stack.  These are kept as raw fully unpacked api-objects in memory.  

From there we construct a series of caches, typically from the key, which is actually a mundging of the meta-data of that object.  That representation is never reflected into the object for fast access, instead we always reconstruct keys in filter-functions using the meta-data.

From there, that data is then passed through the registry and re-encoded to transfer over the wire, even though we've never used 90 of it's decoded state.  

So ... thoughts on fixing?  

Almost seems like and MVC problem. 

/cc @kubernetes/sig-scalability @smarterclayton @jeremyeder

title: etcd dependency not handled properly.

labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
`hack/update-swagger-spec.sh` calls `kube::etcd::start` by way of `hack/lib/etcd.sh`.
But kube::etcd::start() uses etcd from the path and ETCD_VERSION requires that version or later.

The dependent etcd should either be part of an image or the host machine could install the latest version on the fly to a temporary working location or verify the one on the path in an early prereq check that all dependencies on the host system are up to date.

cc @ixdy @spxtr @pwittrock @mbohlool

title: Deployment controller fixes

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
There are some issues in the deployment controller right now that need to be fixed in the short term:
- [x] Cache mutations: currently we mutate the replica set and pod caches. We should deep-copy only when we are going to mutate.
- [x] Share replica set and pod caches once we stop mutating.
- [ ] Deep-copy deployments only when we are going to mutate: currently we deep-copy deployments unconditionally.
- [x] Replica set lists: there are a lot of places in the controller where we try to list replica sets. We should list once when the deployment starts syncing and re-use those RS copies.

title: Get on a non-existent namespace should return a 404.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

body:
An example:

``` sh
$ kubectl get pods --namespace=nonexistent -o json
{
    "kind": "List",
    "apiVersion": "v1",
    "metadata": {},
    "items": []
}
```

I think it should actually return:

``` sh
$ kubectl get pods --namespace=nonexistent -o json
namespace 'nonexistent' not found.
```

body:
Forked from #3500 since the initial issue is closed...

When debugging an issue of an application, often the developer has to look into kubelet log and do some logging process. 

@coufon introduces time series and tracing to Kubelet for the node performance analysis work (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/31280). title: Ingress: Support downtimeless LoadBalancer UID changes in Google Load Balancer Controller

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

body:
Capturing a design discussion that @bprashanth and I just had, so that it doesn't get lost:
# Summary:

Currently, changing the GCE L7 Load Balancer fronting the Ingresses in a cluster involves a cluster outage for ~10 minutes, and the manual deletion and recreation of all Ingresses in the cluster.  This causes problems for Federated Ingress (where multiple clusters need to be updated to use the same GCE L7 Load Balancer, which currently causes a cluster outage).

This proposal describes how this update could be achieved with zero downtime.  I recommend that this be done before releasing Ingress to GA/stable. The implementation is pretty straightforward.  I'd be happy to volunteer to do it, unless someone else is interested.
# Detail:

Currently it's possible to change the so-called "UID" configmap entry for the Google Load Balancer Controller (GLBC).  See https://gist.github.com/bprashanth/52648b2a0b6a5b637f843e7efb2abc97 for details.

This "UID" is actually the identifier of the GCE L7 load balancer that will front all Ingresses created from that point forward. For clarity, I'll refer to it as the LB-UID henceforth.  

There is a problem though.  Each created Ingress is associated with the LB-UID that the GLBC was configured with at the time it was created.   And the GLBC always tries to ensure that there is precisely one GCE LB for the cluster, with a well-known name. So switching from one GCE LB to another involves deleting one and creating another (both with the same name).  Given that this involves a 10 minute delay, that does not work well if there are existing Ingress's, which will see a 10 minute outage.  For this reason, the GLBC does the safe thing, and refuses to delete the old GCE LB if it sees existing Ingresses in the cluster that rely on it.   So it never configures the new GCE LB (by e.g. adding all the nodes in the cluster as backends for the new GCE LB - note that nodes cannot be added as backends of multiple GCE LB's).  This means that in order to change the GCE LB UID configured in the Ingress Controller, it's necessary to first delete all Ingresses in the Cluster, reconfigure the GCE LB UID in the configmap, and then re-create all the existing ingresses.

But there is a better, no-downtime way:
1. Migrate ~half of the nodes in the cluster over to the new GCE LB (identified by the new LB-UID in the configmap)
2. flip the old external IP(s) over to the new GCE LB.
3. Wait for all traffic to drain over to the new GCE LB.  In this state, both GCE LB's are able to balance to the cluster (each via half of the nodes in the cluster).
4. Update all Ingresses to reflect the successful migration to the new GCE LB (only updating the UID annotation, as I understand).
5. Delete the old GCE-LB.

All of the above could/should be performed by the GLBC in reponse to changing it's configured LB-UID.

I just realized that I should move this to the separate repo where the GLBC lives.  Will do shortly.

cc @kubernetes/sig-network @bprashanth @thockin FYI

title: Standardize extension patterns

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: sig/architecture
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Architecture.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen
labels.description: Indicates that an issue or PR should not be auto-closed due to staleness.

body:
This occurred to me when discussing with @davidopp and has come up in multiple contexts recently. Maybe this could be split into at least 2 issues, but I'll start with 1.
1. We are developing a pattern by which we allow people to plug in their own controllers for our objects, by specifying some kind of "type" that indicates which controller has responsibility, and sometimes what policy to apply, as well. Examples:
   - [Multi-scheduler support](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/proposals/multiple-schedulers.md), currently via annotation on Pod. 
   - Ingress, currently via annotation on Ingress.
   - Deployment, discussed implementation using unsupported rollout strategies
   - HorizontalPodAutoscaling, discussed using annotations
   - StorageClass, supports multiple classes, not sure about multiple provisioners
   - Maybe NetworkPolicy applies
   - FlexVolume
   - LoadBalancer (cloud-provider-specific)
2. Sometimes we need to plumb custom parameters down to these controllers. A list of key-value pairs is not awesome. This problem is more acute for ThirdPartyResource, and we're going to have it with the Service Catalog. I suggest we adopt a schema description mechanism, such as JSONSchema. We don't need the whole REST operation side of Swagger/OpenAPI.

cc @thockin @smarterclayton @lavalamp @davidopp

title: StorageClass should not be in the extensions group

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: area/api
labels.description: Indicates an issue on api area.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

body:
The `extensions` group isn't meant to be an incubator group, its intended to hold the things already in it, resources directly related, and `thirdpartyresource`.  We've actually gone to some effort to migrate some types out: `HPA` and `Jobs` as a for instance.

Different APIs want to move at different cadences and new resources should start off in an alpha version while they sort out what they really need during their implementation phases.

We tagged an alpha of 1.4, but I think we should move these resources into their own group. I suspect they'll want new versions at a cadence to match the storage controllers, not a cadence locked to the rest of the `extensions` API.

@childsb @kubernetes/rh-cluster-infra @kubernetes/sig-api-machinery 

Assigned to @lavalamp so he'll be sure to notice and weigh in here, not as a final destination.

**Environment**:
- **Others**:

**What happened**:
I think it is independence the environment, so I did not describe them.

If I create a type of nodePort  service , kube-proxy will use net.Listen to openLocalPort in every node.
If the service have no endpoint (means pod have not started, or start failed.), the client like  curl http://xxxx:xxx will hang. It will not timeout.

I had tried it just use net.Listen to create a TCP Listener, it can be reproduce.

**What you expected to happen**:
I expected  it will timeout, if the endpoints is not ready.

I think it will infect the third-part to  access the service that the endpoint have not ready. 
The third-part client will hang.

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):
1. Create an nodePort  service without any endpoint.
2. curl http://node-ip:nodeport. The curl will always hang.
